  • Damages: England Because an EJC contains a promise not to sue elsewhere, [the innocent party] may claim [costs thrown away abroad / liability under the foreign judgment]. Per Starlight Shipping, breach is a question of law, so [summary judgment] for damages to be assessed is possible.
    • Breach lies in suing: per Starlight Shipping, whether [the claims] would succeed in [X] or fail in [the chosen forum] is irrelevant.
  • Damages: Singapore (−) Per Tradewaves (applying Sunrock Aircraft), damages "can", not "must", be awarded. [Foreign costs] should normally be sought in [the foreign action], and [the claimant] must prove the "unusual features" in Union Discount v Zoller, e.g., [foreign rules allowing costs only exceptionally] and [no foreign costs order].
  • Anti-Suit Injunction Breach of [a Singapore EJC] (arguably also of a Singapore NEJC, per Shanghai Turbo) is a contractual basis for an ASI against [respondent]'s suit in [X]. No vexation is needed, and [respondent] must show strong reasons why it should not issue (Cooperative Muratori; J6.3.1).
  • ASI: Foreign EJC (−) Where [clause X] chooses [a foreign court], Singapore generally declines to restrain [the suit in a third country] and leaves it to [the chosen court], not being an "international busybody" (Akai; J6.2.6).
  • Choice of Law Clause Not Promissory (−) Per Ace Insurance v Moose, a choice of law clause is usually declaratory, so [an ASI] against suit in [a forum applying another law] was refused. Only [very clear words] make it promissory, which would bring damages, an ASI and a recognition defence (C2).
  • Recognition Defence (±) [Debtor] resists enforcement of [X's judgment] obtained in breach of [clause X]. There is no common law authority, but per C&Y a defence is arguable: [damages for breach could cancel the judgment sum], REFJA s 5(4)(b) deems [the foreign court] to lack jurisdiction absent submission, and convergence with the statutes is desirable (Merck; J7.2.6).
    • Limits: [debtor]'s submission in [X] removes the defence, and the breach, not whether [Singapore or a foreign court] was chosen, is key. The CCAA does not prohibit recognising [a non-chosen court's judgment] under the common law or REFJA (per C&Y; J7.5).
  • Other Agreements (not examinable) A stay for breach of [an international arbitration agreement] is mandatory (s 6 IAA); for [domestic arbitration] or [mediation] it is discretionary (s 6 Arbitration Act; s 8 Mediation Act, "may").
  • Non-Suit or Settlement Agreement ["Settled; no further action in any court"] is not a jurisdiction clause but a substantive [accord and satisfaction] defence. [Proceedings in breach] may be stayed or struck out as an abuse, with [an ASI] or [damages] also possible.

1Start here: J1 in plain English

Almost every Question 1 contract contains a jurisdiction clause: a term saying which court should hear disputes. J1 is the file you open first for every contract. It does three jobs:

  1. Read the clause and work out exactly what each party promised.
  2. Check whether the Hague Convention applies (through Singapore's CCAA). If it does, it overrides the ordinary rules.
  3. Check the clause's reach: does it cover this claim and these parties, and does it validly exist?

Everything later in Question 1 depends on the answer. If someone broke the clause, the later test is strong cause (J4.3). If nobody broke it, the test is Spiliada (J4.1).

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A jurisdiction clause is like agreeing in advance where a match will be played. "We play at your home ground" is one promise. "And I won't complain that your ground is too far away" is a second. "And I won't try to play this match anywhere else" is a third. Whether someone has broken their word depends on which of these promises they actually made. J1 is about reading the agreement carefully before you accuse anyone.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Why the clause comes first: one dispute, two clauses

Alpha (Singapore) sells machines to Delta (Hong Kong). Delta refuses to pay. Alpha sues in Singapore. Delta asks the Singapore court to stop the case and send it to Hong Kong.

  • Version 1: the contract says "the courts of Hong Kong shall have exclusive jurisdiction". Alpha promised not to sue anywhere except Hong Kong, and it has sued in Singapore. Alpha is in breach, so Alpha must show strong cause to keep the case here. That is hard.
  • Version 2: the contract says "the courts of Hong Kong may hear disputes". Alpha promised nothing about Singapore. No one is in breach, so the court runs Spiliada, and Delta (if served here) must show Hong Kong is clearly more appropriate.

Same parties, same goods, same courts. The only change is one word in the clause, and it flips who carries the burden. That is why J1 is the first file you open.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Choice of court agreementA contract term picking the court(s) for disputes. Also called a jurisdiction clause.
EJCExclusive jurisdiction clause: "only the courts of X".
NEJCNon-exclusive jurisdiction clause: "the courts of X may hear disputes", other courts not ruled out.
ProrogationThe "yes, this court" part of a clause: promising to submit to the chosen court (and not to object to it).
DerogationThe "not elsewhere" part: promising not to sue in any other court.
Asymmetric clauseOne party may sue anywhere; the other may sue only in one place. Common in loan agreements.
Floating clauseThe forum is not fixed at the start: e.g. one party may later choose between two courts.
HCCCA / CCAAThe 2005 Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements, given effect in Singapore by the Choice of Court Agreements Act 2016.
Contracting StateA country that has joined the Convention.
Hartley–Dogauchi ReportThe official explanatory report on the Convention, used to interpret it.
SeparabilityThe clause is treated as a separate agreement, so attacking the main contract does not automatically kill the clause.
Good arguable case"The better of the argument": more than a prima facie case, less than a balance of probabilities.

2J1.0 Three regimes and the regime router

▤ On your pre-write: J1.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP (word for word)
J1.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP

(Three regimes: the General Division at common law (J2–J4), the CCAA (J1.2–J1.4) and the SICC (J5). The CCAA displaces both others within its scope; the SICC displaces Spiliada for cases heard there. "Not every Convention case will be an SICC case, and not every SICC case will be a Convention case" (Yeo). At common law, ask two questions: is anyone in breach, and who bears the burden?)

  1. Regime router (J1.0.2): CCAA first, then the SICC, else the common law, for [clause X] in [contract].
  2. Characterise [clause X] (J1.1): [exclusive / non-exclusive], [Singapore / foreign], [asymmetric / floating], construed under [its proper law].
  3. CCAA scope (J1.2): [actual / deemed] exclusive (s 3), not asymmetric, for [one Contracting State], concluded after [entry into force], international (s 4), civil or commercial (s 9).
  4. Singapore chosen (J1.3): [Singapore] must hear [the case] unless null and void (s 11).
  5. Singapore not chosen (J1.4): [Singapore] must stay unless [an s 12(1) exception] applies.
  6. Scope (J1.5): does [clause X] cover [the claim] and [these parties]?
  7. Existence and validity (J1.6): a good arguable case; does [the vitiating factor] reach [clause X] itself?
  8. Found jurisdiction (J3.2): [service in], where a foreign clause goes only to exercise, or [service out] under O 8 r 1(3) or r 1(1).
  9. Breach? By [claimant], in suing here, or by [defendant], in objecting to [the named Singapore court].
  10. Breach → strong cause on [the party in breach], whether [stay or set-aside], [served in or out] (J4.3).
  11. No breach → Spiliada, burden set by [service in / out] and [set-aside / stay] (J4.1; J4.2).
  12. Other effects (J1.7): [damages], [ASI], [recognition defence].
  • Links Back a Singapore [jurisdiction clause] is a gateway under para 63(3)(d)(iv) and (r) (J3.1.2), may dispense with approval under O 8 r 1(3) (J3.1.5), and is an agreement to submit, not [submission by conduct] (J2.2.3).
J1.0.1 Quick Application Template
  • CCAA: Presently, [claimant] sues [defendant] in [Singapore] on [contract], whose [clause X] gives [the courts of State] exclusive jurisdiction. The CCAA [applies, [clause X] being concluded on [date] after the HCCCA entered into force there, in an international, commercial case (J1.2) / does not apply, as [clause X] is [asymmetric / non-exclusive / within s 9]].
  • CCAA result: So [Singapore must hear the case (J1.3) / Singapore must stay unless [s 12(1) exception] applies (J1.4) / the SICC may decline only under O 2 r 3(2) (J5.3)].
  • Common law, characterise: Presently, [clause X] provides that disputes ["shall be submitted to the [exclusive / non-exclusive] jurisdiction of the courts of [Singapore / X]"]. Construed under [the proper law / Singapore law by the presumption of similarity], it is [an EJC / a NEJC] for [Singapore / X] (J1.1).
  • Scope and validity: [The claim] falls [within / outside] [clause X] because [it arises from the same incident as the contract claims], and [defendant]'s plea of [misrepresentation as to price] does not reach the clause itself (CIMB; PT Selecta) (J1.5–J1.6).
  • Breach and result: [Claimant / defendant] breaches by [suing here / objecting to Singapore], so it must show strong cause (J4.3), which it [cannot, the factors being foreseeable at contracting / can, because [unforeseeable event]]. So [stay granted / service set aside / jurisdiction exercised].
J1.0.2 Regime Router

(one line per contract, then go to the relevant part)

  • CCAA First If [clause X] is an exclusive agreement for the courts of [Contracting State] in an international, civil or commercial case, the CCAA applies (s 8) and overrides [Spiliada] and [strong cause] (per C&Y).
  • SICC Second If not, or if [Singapore] is the chosen court, ask whether [the case] is in the SICC by [a written jurisdiction agreement (J5.2) / transfer (J5.4) / joinder (J5.6)].
  • Common Law Residual Otherwise, existence is by [service in (J2) / service out (J3)], and exercise by [strong cause for an EJC or a Singapore NEJC / Spiliada for a foreign NEJC] (J4).
  • Overlap A post-2016 exclusive ["Singapore High Court"] clause includes the SICC (s 2(2)–(3) CCAA; O 2 r 2(1) SICC Rules). The CCAA decides whether [Singapore] must hear [the case]; the SICC Rules allocate it internally, subject to s 11(5) and O 2 r 4(4) (J5.4).

Singapore has three regimes for deciding whether its courts will hear a case:

RegimeWhen it appliesIts test
CCAA (Hague Convention)An exclusive clause for a Contracting State's courts, in an international civil or commercial caseChosen court must hear; others must stay (with narrow exceptions)
SICCThe case is in the SICC (by written agreement, transfer or joinder)SICC Rules, not Spiliada (J5)
Common law (General Division)Everything elseService in/out for existence; strong cause or Spiliada for exercise (J2–J4)

The CCAA displaces both other regimes within its scope. The SICC displaces Spiliada for cases heard there. As Yeo puts it, "not every Convention case will be an SICC case, and not every SICC case will be a Convention case".

🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  1. CCAA first. If the clause is exclusive for one Contracting State's courts and the case is international and commercial, the CCAA applies and overrides Spiliada and strong cause (per C&Y).
  2. SICC second. If not (or if Singapore is the chosen court), ask whether the case is in the SICC by written agreement, transfer or joinder.
  3. Common law last. Otherwise: existence by service in or out; exercise by strong cause (EJC, or a Singapore NEJC) or Spiliada (a foreign NEJC).
  4. Overlap. A post-2016 exclusive "Singapore High Court" clause includes the SICC. The CCAA decides whether Singapore must hear the case; the SICC Rules allocate it internally.
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

At common law, ask two questions: is anyone in breach, and who bears the burden? Almost every mark in the exercise stage flows from those two answers.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Routing three contracts

Alpha (Singapore) has three contracts with foreign companies. Assume each is commercial, and that Ruritania became a Contracting State in 2015.

ContractClauseRouteWhy
1. 2019 sale to Rurico (Ruritania)"The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the courts of Ruritania."CCAADeemed exclusive (s 3(2)); one Contracting State; made after entry into force; international. Singapore is not chosen, so s 12 applies (J1.4).
2. 2019 sale to Japco (Japan)"The Singapore High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction."CCAA, and the SICC can be in playExclusive for Singapore, made after 1 October 2016, international. The CCAA says Singapore must hear the case (s 11); the SICC Rules decide whether the SICC or the General Division hears it.
3. 2019 sale to Kongco (Hong Kong)"The courts of Singapore or Hong Kong may hear disputes."Common lawNon-exclusive, and it names two States, so it fails two CCAA gateways. Existence by service (J2, J3); exercise by strong cause or Spiliada (J4).

The router is one line per contract. In the exam, write that line, then go to the right file.

3J1.1 Characterising the clause

▤ On your pre-write: J1.1 CHARACTERISING THE CLAUSE (word for word)
J1.1 CHARACTERISING THE CLAUSE (write first: what [clause X] promises decides who, if anyone, is in breach)
  • Three Promises (must write) A choice of court agreement may contain (1A) a promise to submit to [the chosen court]; (1B) a promise not to object to its exercise of jurisdiction, e.g., on [FNC grounds]; and (2) a promise not to sue [anywhere else]. (1A) and (1B) are prorogation; (2) is derogation.
  • EJC v NEJC An EJC contains all three, so [claimant] suing in [a non-chosen court] breaches (2), and [defendant] objecting to [the chosen court] breaches (1B). Per Bambang Sutrisno (in Shanghai Turbo (CA)), a NEJC contains (1A) but not (2); whether it contains (1B) is construction under [its proper law].
  • How Exclusivity Is Decided Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), [clause X] is construed under [its governing law], but its effect on Singapore's jurisdiction is for [the lex fori]. Per C&Y, "exclusive" is the conclusion, not the starting point: labels get their ordinary meaning, but many clauses are [unlabelled / paired with an FNC waiver / asymmetric].
  • Wording Indicators In [clause X], ["exclusively"] → EJC; ["shall be heard by"] → mandatory, so likely exclusive under [the proper law]; ["may be referred to" / "submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of"] → NEJC.
  • SICC Clause If [clause X] names [the SICC], s 18F SCJA presumes it exclusive absent express contrary words, though whether s 18F applies where [foreign law] governs a non-CCAA clause is debated (J5.2.2).
J1.1.1 Singapore NEJC: the Contractual Approach (must write)
  • Rule Presently, [defendant] "submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Courts of Singapore" but now [seeks a stay / applies to set aside service] on [FNC grounds]. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), adopting Noble Power, Singapore takes the contractual approach (left open in Orchard Capital), not the general approach under which [a NEJC] is merely a Spiliada factor.
  • Construction Under Singapore law, "submit" means consenting to [the named court]'s jurisdiction and waiving any objection to its exercise (Yeo's "narrow waiver of objection"). Otherwise [clause X] would be "devoid of purpose" (Briggs, adopted in Shanghai Turbo (CA)), and this holds even if [Singapore] had no jurisdiction without [clause X].
  • Consequence Any challenge by [defendant], whether [setting aside service] or [a stay], even in favour of [another named court], is an attempt to escape [clause X], so [defendant] must show strong cause (J4.3).
  • Old Cases Overruled Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), High Court cases treating [a Singapore NEJC] as a mere Spiliada factor were wrongly decided. The CA went "one step further" than Bambang Sutrisno, whose clause had [an express FNC waiver].
  • Open Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), whether the same applies to [a NEJC] in [a standard form / non-negotiated contract] was left open; by analogy with Vinmar, probably yes (J4.3).
J1.1.2 Proper Law and Foreign NEJCs
  • Proper Law of the NEJC (±) Whether [clause X] contains (1B) is for [the proper law]. If [law X] is unproved, the presumption of similarity reads in the same waiver. If [Ruritanian law] is proved and implies no waiver, [clause X] contains only (1A), so [defendant]'s FNC objection is no breach and Spiliada applies (J4.1; J4.2).
  • Foreign NEJC: No Breach Either Way [Claimant] sues here though [clause X] names [the courts of X] non-exclusively. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the "wide waiver of objection" is rejected, so suing here is no breach, and [defendant]'s objection is none either, as [Singapore] is not named. Plain Spiliada applies (J4.1).
  • Weight of a Foreign NEJC Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), [clause X] shows only that [X] is an appropriate forum, not clearly more appropriate, so it carries little weight; how much depends on whether it was [closely negotiated / chosen for neutrality].
  • Drafting Around the Defaults (practice) For [a Singapore NEJC] without the waiver, add ["without prejudice to each party's right to object on FNC grounds"]; to make [a foreign NEJC] bind, add [a promise not to sue elsewhere].
  • FNC Waiver Per Bunge, where [the Singapore EJC] carries [an FNC waiver, e.g., "no Party will argue to the contrary"], grounds founded on convenience cannot amount to strong cause, so [defendant]'s reliance on [witnesses / documents abroad] fails.
J1.1.3 Floating and Multi-Forum Clauses
  • Floating Jurisdiction Clause Valid Per Shanghai Turbo (CA) and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if not too uncertain, unlike [a floating choice of law clause], which is void (C2). It needs an election mechanism, e.g., [one party's option / a prescribed event].
  • Severance Presently, [clause X] couples [a floating choice of law] with [a jurisdiction choice]. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the void law part is severable where the two are joined only by ["and"] and [the contract has a severance clause]; contrast The Iran Vojdan, where [the forum choice] was parasitic on [the law choice].
  • No Mechanism → Both Courts Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), ["Singapore/or PRC"] with no election mechanism is a NEJC to both [Singapore] and [PRC], each party submitting to whichever is seised. Letting [the claimant] elect at suit was rejected as encouraging a race to sue.
  • Several Named Fora Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the waiver applies to each named forum, so [defendant]'s objection in either [Singapore] or [X] is a breach.
J1.1.4 Clause Bank (handout exercise)
  • Foreign EJC → Strong Cause on Claimant ["exclusively to the courts of [X]"], ["exclusively to the courts of [X] or [Y]"] (two fora, all others excluded) and ["shall be heard by the courts of [X]"] (mandatory, so likely exclusive). [Claimant] suing here breaches, so [claimant] bears strong cause, whether [served in, defendant seeking a stay] or [served out] (J3.2).
  • Foreign NEJC → Spiliada ["may be heard by the courts of [X]"] or ["the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of [X]"]: no one breaches by suing here, so Spiliada, with the burden set by [service in / out] and [set-aside / stay] (J3.2; J4).
  • Singapore NEJC → Strong Cause on Defendant ["the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore"] or ["of the courts of [X] or Singapore"] (the Shanghai Turbo pattern): [defendant] objecting to [Singapore] breaches, so [defendant] bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, With Submission ["[A] may sue [B] in any court, [B] submitting to it; [B] may sue [A] only in [Y]"]. If [A] sues here, [B] agreed to submit, so [B] bears strong cause to stay; if [B] sues here, [B] breaches its [Y]-only promise and bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, Without Submission (±) If [clause X] merely lets [A] sue [B] [anywhere], without [B] submitting to that court, [A] suing here is permitted but [B] never agreed to submit, so [B]'s stay goes to Spiliada (Week 10 handout). [B] suing here still breaches [the EJC for Y] → strong cause on [B].
  • Protective Promise ["all submit to [X]; under no circumstances shall [B] be subjected to any other court"]. [A] suing [B] here breaches the second limb → strong cause on [A]; [B] suing [A] here breaches nothing → Spiliada.

This is the most important idea in J1. A jurisdiction clause can contain up to three promises.

The three promises
▤ J1.1, "must write"
  1. 1(1A) Submit: "I submit to the chosen court." (prorogation)
  2. 2(1B) Don't object: "I won't object to that court hearing the case, e.g. on forum non conveniens grounds." (prorogation)
  3. 3(2) Don't sue elsewhere: "I won't sue in any other court." (derogation)

Now match each kind of clause to the promises it contains:

Clause(1A) Submit(1B) Don't object(2) Don't sue elsewhere
EJC✓✓✓
Singapore NEJC (Singapore law)✓✓ (Shanghai Turbo)✗
NEJC generally✓Depends on construction under its proper law✗ (Bambang Sutrisno)

From the table you can see who breaches what:

  • Under an EJC, a claimant suing in a non-chosen court breaks (2); a defendant objecting to the chosen court breaks (1B).
  • Under a Singapore NEJC, a defendant objecting to Singapore breaks (1B). Suing elsewhere breaks nothing.
  • Under a foreign NEJC, suing in Singapore breaks nothing (no promise (2)), and the defendant objecting in Singapore breaks nothing either (Singapore is not the named court).
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of three separate signatures on the clause. An EJC has all three. A non-exclusive clause has the first, maybe the second, never the third. You can only accuse someone of breaking a promise they actually signed.

A memory trick for the two Latin-ish words: pro-rogation points towards the chosen court ("yes, this court"); de-rogation points away from every other court ("not there").

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The three promises in action

Clause: "The courts of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction." Alpha (Singapore) and Delta (Hong Kong) fall out.

  1. Delta sues Alpha in Hong Kong. Delta broke promise (2): it sued in a court other than the chosen one. Consequence in Singapore: Alpha can seek an ASI on the contractual basis (J6.3.1).
  2. Alpha sues Delta in Singapore, and Delta applies for a stay saying Hong Kong is more convenient. Delta broke promise (1B): it objected to the chosen court. Consequence: Delta must show strong cause (J4.3).
  3. Alpha sues Delta in Singapore and Delta simply defends. Delta has kept promise (1A). No breach by anyone.

Now change the clause to "the courts of Singapore may hear disputes" (a Singapore NEJC under Singapore law). Step 1 is no longer a breach: there is no promise (2). Step 2 is still a breach: per Shanghai Turbo, a Singapore NEJC carries promise (1B). Step 3 is unchanged.

How exclusivity is decided

Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the clause is construed under its governing law, but its effect on Singapore's jurisdiction is for the lex fori. Per C&Y, "exclusive" is the conclusion, not the starting point: labels get their ordinary meaning, but many clauses are unlabelled, paired with an FNC waiver, or asymmetric.

Words in the clauseLikely meaning
"exclusively"EJC
"shall be heard by"Mandatory, so likely exclusive under the proper law
"may be referred to" / "submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of"NEJC
Names the SICCs 18F SCJA presumes exclusive unless express words say otherwise (J5.2.2)
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
An unlabelled clause

Clause: "All disputes shall be submitted to the courts of Japan." The contract is governed by Japanese law. Is it exclusive?

  1. Which law construes it? Its governing law, Japanese law (Shanghai Turbo (CA)).
  2. Is Japanese law proved? If an expert gives evidence on how Japanese law reads "shall be submitted", follow it.
  3. If not proved, the presumption of similarity applies: the court reads it as Singapore law would. "Shall" is mandatory language, so it is likely exclusive.
  4. What follows is for Singapore law (the lex fori): if exclusive, a claimant suing in Singapore is in breach and must show strong cause.

Write it as reasoning, not a label: "exclusive" is the conclusion you reach, not the starting point.

J1.1.1 The Singapore NEJC: the contractual approach

▤ On your pre-write: J1.1.1 Singapore NEJC: the Contractual Approach (must write) (word for word)
J1.1.1 Singapore NEJC: the Contractual Approach (must write)
  • Rule Presently, [defendant] "submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Courts of Singapore" but now [seeks a stay / applies to set aside service] on [FNC grounds]. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), adopting Noble Power, Singapore takes the contractual approach (left open in Orchard Capital), not the general approach under which [a NEJC] is merely a Spiliada factor.
  • Construction Under Singapore law, "submit" means consenting to [the named court]'s jurisdiction and waiving any objection to its exercise (Yeo's "narrow waiver of objection"). Otherwise [clause X] would be "devoid of purpose" (Briggs, adopted in Shanghai Turbo (CA)), and this holds even if [Singapore] had no jurisdiction without [clause X].
  • Consequence Any challenge by [defendant], whether [setting aside service] or [a stay], even in favour of [another named court], is an attempt to escape [clause X], so [defendant] must show strong cause (J4.3).
  • Old Cases Overruled Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), High Court cases treating [a Singapore NEJC] as a mere Spiliada factor were wrongly decided. The CA went "one step further" than Bambang Sutrisno, whose clause had [an express FNC waiver].
  • Open Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), whether the same applies to [a NEJC] in [a standard form / non-negotiated contract] was left open; by analogy with Vinmar, probably yes (J4.3).
🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  • The rule. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), adopting Noble Power, Singapore takes the contractual approach to a Singapore NEJC: the clause is a promise, not just a factor in Spiliada.
  • Why. Under Singapore law "submit" means consenting to the court and waiving objections to it (Yeo's "narrow waiver of objection"). Otherwise the clause would be "devoid of purpose" (Briggs, adopted in Shanghai Turbo). This is so even if Singapore had no jurisdiction without the clause.
  • So any challenge by the defendant (setting aside service, or a stay, even in favour of another named court) is an attempt to escape the clause, and the defendant must show strong cause.
  • Old cases overruled. High Court cases treating a Singapore NEJC as a mere Spiliada factor were wrong. The CA went "one step further" than Bambang Sutrisno, whose clause had an express FNC waiver.
  • Open. Whether this applies to standard-form or non-negotiated contracts was left open; by analogy with Vinmar, probably yes.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Singapore NEJC

Clause: "Each party submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Courts of Singapore." Delta (the defendant) applies for a stay, saying Hong Kong is more convenient. Under Shanghai Turbo, Delta promised not to object to Singapore, so its stay application is itself the breach. Delta must show strong cause, and convenience factors it could foresee when contracting will rarely do.

J1.1.2 Foreign NEJCs and the proper law

▤ On your pre-write: J1.1.2 Proper Law and Foreign NEJCs (word for word)
J1.1.2 Proper Law and Foreign NEJCs
  • Proper Law of the NEJC (±) Whether [clause X] contains (1B) is for [the proper law]. If [law X] is unproved, the presumption of similarity reads in the same waiver. If [Ruritanian law] is proved and implies no waiver, [clause X] contains only (1A), so [defendant]'s FNC objection is no breach and Spiliada applies (J4.1; J4.2).
  • Foreign NEJC: No Breach Either Way [Claimant] sues here though [clause X] names [the courts of X] non-exclusively. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the "wide waiver of objection" is rejected, so suing here is no breach, and [defendant]'s objection is none either, as [Singapore] is not named. Plain Spiliada applies (J4.1).
  • Weight of a Foreign NEJC Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), [clause X] shows only that [X] is an appropriate forum, not clearly more appropriate, so it carries little weight; how much depends on whether it was [closely negotiated / chosen for neutrality].
  • Drafting Around the Defaults (practice) For [a Singapore NEJC] without the waiver, add ["without prejudice to each party's right to object on FNC grounds"]; to make [a foreign NEJC] bind, add [a promise not to sue elsewhere].
  • FNC Waiver Per Bunge, where [the Singapore EJC] carries [an FNC waiver, e.g., "no Party will argue to the contrary"], grounds founded on convenience cannot amount to strong cause, so [defendant]'s reliance on [witnesses / documents abroad] fails.
  • The proper law decides promise (1B). If the clause's proper law is unproved, the presumption of similarity reads in the same waiver as Singapore law. If proved foreign law implies no waiver, the clause contains only (1A), so an FNC objection is no breach and Spiliada applies.
  • Foreign NEJC: no breach either way. Per Shanghai Turbo, the "wide waiver of objection" is rejected. Suing here is no breach, and the defendant's objection is none either. Plain Spiliada.
  • Little weight. A foreign NEJC shows only that the foreign court is an appropriate forum, not clearly more appropriate. How much weight depends on whether it was closely negotiated or chosen for neutrality.
  • FNC waiver. Per Bunge, where a Singapore EJC carries an FNC waiver ("no Party will argue to the contrary"), grounds based on convenience cannot amount to strong cause.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
A foreign NEJC: nobody is in breach

Clause: "Disputes may be referred to the courts of Hong Kong." Alpha sues Delta in Singapore anyway, and Delta, served in Singapore, applies for a stay.

  • Did Alpha breach the clause by suing here? No. "May" gives no promise (2), so suing elsewhere is allowed.
  • Did Delta breach it by objecting? No. The named court is Hong Kong, not Singapore, so Delta made no promise about Singapore.
  • So: plain Spiliada. Delta, served in, must show Hong Kong is clearly more appropriate (J4.1).
  • What is the clause worth to Delta? Not much. It shows Hong Kong is an appropriate forum, which nobody doubted. It does not show Hong Kong is clearly more appropriate.
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A foreign NEJC is like a restaurant voucher that says "valid at Restaurant X". It tells you X will serve you. It does not stop you eating somewhere else, and it does not prove X is the best restaurant in town.

J1.1.3 Floating and multi-forum clauses

▤ On your pre-write: J1.1.3 Floating and Multi-Forum Clauses (word for word)
J1.1.3 Floating and Multi-Forum Clauses
  • Floating Jurisdiction Clause Valid Per Shanghai Turbo (CA) and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if not too uncertain, unlike [a floating choice of law clause], which is void (C2). It needs an election mechanism, e.g., [one party's option / a prescribed event].
  • Severance Presently, [clause X] couples [a floating choice of law] with [a jurisdiction choice]. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the void law part is severable where the two are joined only by ["and"] and [the contract has a severance clause]; contrast The Iran Vojdan, where [the forum choice] was parasitic on [the law choice].
  • No Mechanism → Both Courts Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), ["Singapore/or PRC"] with no election mechanism is a NEJC to both [Singapore] and [PRC], each party submitting to whichever is seised. Letting [the claimant] elect at suit was rejected as encouraging a race to sue.
  • Several Named Fora Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), the waiver applies to each named forum, so [defendant]'s objection in either [Singapore] or [X] is a breach.
SituationResult (per Shanghai Turbo (CA))
Floating jurisdiction clause with an election mechanismValid at common law if not too uncertain. Contrast a floating choice of law clause, which is void (C2).
Floating law clause joined to a jurisdiction choiceThe void law part is severable where joined only by "and" and the contract has a severance clause. Contrast The Iran Vojdan, where the forum choice was parasitic on the law choice.
"Singapore/or PRC", no election mechanismA NEJC to both; each party submits to whichever is seised. Letting the claimant elect was rejected as encouraging a race to sue.
Several named foraThe waiver applies to each named forum, so objecting in either is a breach.
⚠ TRAP
Floating jurisdiction v floating law

A floating jurisdiction clause can be valid; a floating choice of law clause is void. Do not carry one rule across to the other.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
"Singapore or PRC"

Clause: "Disputes shall be resolved by the courts of Singapore/or the PRC." There is no mechanism for either party to choose between them. Alpha sues in Singapore first. Delta applies for a stay in favour of the PRC courts.

  1. What does the clause mean? Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a NEJC to both courts: each party submits to whichever court is seised. The court refused to read it as "the claimant picks", because that would reward whoever races to court first.
  2. Is Delta in breach? Yes. The waiver of objection applies to each named forum, and Singapore is one of them. Asking for a stay objects to a named court.
  3. Result: strong cause on Delta, even though its preferred forum (the PRC) is also named in the clause.

J1.1.4 The clause bank

▤ On your pre-write: J1.1.4 Clause Bank (handout exercise) (word for word)
J1.1.4 Clause Bank (handout exercise)
  • Foreign EJC → Strong Cause on Claimant ["exclusively to the courts of [X]"], ["exclusively to the courts of [X] or [Y]"] (two fora, all others excluded) and ["shall be heard by the courts of [X]"] (mandatory, so likely exclusive). [Claimant] suing here breaches, so [claimant] bears strong cause, whether [served in, defendant seeking a stay] or [served out] (J3.2).
  • Foreign NEJC → Spiliada ["may be heard by the courts of [X]"] or ["the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of [X]"]: no one breaches by suing here, so Spiliada, with the burden set by [service in / out] and [set-aside / stay] (J3.2; J4).
  • Singapore NEJC → Strong Cause on Defendant ["the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore"] or ["of the courts of [X] or Singapore"] (the Shanghai Turbo pattern): [defendant] objecting to [Singapore] breaches, so [defendant] bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, With Submission ["[A] may sue [B] in any court, [B] submitting to it; [B] may sue [A] only in [Y]"]. If [A] sues here, [B] agreed to submit, so [B] bears strong cause to stay; if [B] sues here, [B] breaches its [Y]-only promise and bears strong cause.
  • Asymmetric, Without Submission (±) If [clause X] merely lets [A] sue [B] [anywhere], without [B] submitting to that court, [A] suing here is permitted but [B] never agreed to submit, so [B]'s stay goes to Spiliada (Week 10 handout). [B] suing here still breaches [the EJC for Y] → strong cause on [B].
  • Protective Promise ["all submit to [X]; under no circumstances shall [B] be subjected to any other court"]. [A] suing [B] here breaches the second limb → strong cause on [A]; [B] suing [A] here breaches nothing → Spiliada.
Clause bank: words → who carries which test
▤ J1.1.4 (handout exercise)
  1. 1"exclusively to the courts of [X]" or "shall be heard by the courts of [X]": foreign EJC. Claimant suing here breaches → strong cause on claimant, whether served in or out.
  2. 2"may be heard by the courts of [X]": foreign NEJC. No one breaches → Spiliada, burden set by service in/out and set-aside/stay.
  3. 3"the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore": Singapore NEJC. Defendant objecting breaches → strong cause on defendant.
  4. 4Asymmetric, with submission ("A may sue B anywhere, B submitting to it; B may sue A only in Y"): if A sues here, B must show strong cause to stay; if B sues here, B breaks its Y-only promise → strong cause on B.
  5. 5Asymmetric, without submission: A suing here is permitted, but B never agreed to submit, so B's stay goes to Spiliada (Week 10 handout).
  6. 6Protective promise ("all submit to X; under no circumstances shall B be subjected to any other court"): A suing B here breaches → strong cause on A; B suing A here breaches nothing → Spiliada.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Reading the asymmetric clause both ways

Bank sues Borrower in Singapore. Bank is allowed to sue anywhere, so no breach by Bank. If the clause also says Borrower submits to any court Bank chooses, then Borrower's stay application objects to a court it submitted to: strong cause on Borrower (item 4). If the clause has no submission by Borrower, Bank's suit is permitted but Borrower never promised not to object, so Borrower's stay goes to Spiliada (item 5).

Borrower sues Bank in Singapore. That is exactly where Borrower promised to sue, so Borrower is not in breach.

Borrower sues Bank in Indonesia. Borrower broke its "Singapore only" promise. In Singapore that is a contractual basis for an ASI (J6.3.1).

Note for the CCAA: this clause is not exclusive under the Convention (CHLOE V), so it goes to the common law, where it stays exclusive against Borrower (J1.2.1).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Characterising a clause

Presently, cl 18 provides that disputes "shall be submitted to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore". Construed under Singapore law, the proper law, it is a NEJC for Singapore containing a promise to submit and, per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a promise not to object to Singapore's exercise of jurisdiction. Delta's stay application on FNC grounds therefore breaches cl 18, so Delta must show strong cause (J4.3).

4J1.2 Does the CCAA apply?

▤ On your pre-write: J1.2 DOES THE CCAA APPLY? (s 8) (word for word)
J1.2 DOES THE CCAA APPLY? (s 8)

(Three principles: [the chosen court] must hear; [a non-chosen court] must decline; [its judgment] must be recognised (J7.5). Gateways: exclusive; one Contracting State; concluded after entry into force; international; civil or commercial. Write only those in issue.)

J1.2.1 Exclusive Choice of Court Agreement (s 3)
  • Express EJC (+) Per s 3(1), [clause X] is exclusive: concluded [in writing / by accessible electronic means], it designates [the courts of State] for disputes in connection with [contract], to the exclusion of any other court.
  • Deemed Exclusive (+) Per s 3(2), [clause X] (["the parties submit to the jurisdiction of the [State] courts"]) is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise. At common law the same unlabelled clause could go either way under [its proper law] (J1.1).
    • Rebuttal (−): [clause X] [says "non-exclusive" / allows suit "in any other competent court"], so s 3(2) is displaced and [the CCAA] does not apply.
    • Trap: per Chong (seminar), where the facts call [clause X] [non-exclusive], do not invoke s 3(2): [the CCAA] does not apply, a recurring exam error.
  • Asymmetric Clause (−) Presently, [clause X] gives [State B] exclusive jurisdiction but lets [the lender] sue [the borrower] [anywhere]. Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (VCLT art 32), such a clause is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged even on [the court's own motion], and even though [defendant] conceded the point.
    • Support: Per Etihad (EWCA) (obiter), the Convention probably excludes [asymmetric clauses] like [clause X], the Diplomatic Session having rejected a Swiss proposal to cover clauses exclusive "for some or all of the parties".
    • Counter (+): Earlier first-instance dicta (Commerzbank v Liquimar; Etihad (EWHC)) read the Convention's wording as wide enough for [clause X], but [the lender]'s reliance on them is weak after CHLOE V.
    • Consequence: At common law [clause X] stays exclusive against [the restricted party] (per C&Y), so J1.1 applies.
  • Floating Clause (±) Presently, [clause X] lets [party] choose between [Court A] and [Court B]; per C&Y, CCAA coverage is unclear. (−) Before election there is no chosen court, so arguably no s 3(1) agreement. (+) Once [notice of election] was served on [date], [clause X] crystallised into a mutually exclusive choice of [Court A], probably within the CCAA.
    • Unilateral election (±): s 3 requires agreement between the parties, but arguably [party]'s election suffices where [all parties agreed it could elect / [other party] received written notice and did not object].
  • More Than One State (−) [Clause X] designates [Singapore or England], not the courts "of one Contracting State" (s 3(1)), so it is outside the CCAA, though [possibly exclusive at common law].
  • Separability (+) Per s 5, [clause X] is independent of [contract], so its validity cannot be challenged solely because [contract] is said to be [void for misrepresentation / terminated].
J1.2.2 Contracting State and Date
  • Temporal Scope [State of chosen court] is a Contracting State, and [clause X] was concluded on [date], after the HCCCA entered into force for it (Singapore: 1 October 2016). [Check the HCCH status table.]
    • UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021; continuity across Brexit is contested, so [an English clause] concluded on [a date between them] is arguable either way.
J1.2.3 International Case (s 4)
  • International (+) Per s 4(1), [the case] is international unless the parties reside in the same Contracting State and everything else, apart from the chosen court's location, is connected only with that State. [Defendant] resides in [State], so the exception fails.
  • Company Residence Per s 6, [a company party] resides at its [statutory seat / place of incorporation / central administration / principal place of business], so [defendant] resides in [State].
  • Wholly Domestic (−) Both parties reside in [Singapore], and [contract] was negotiated and performed wholly here; only [the chosen court in State B] is foreign. So [the case] is not international and the CCAA does not apply (per C&Y).
J1.2.4 Civil or Commercial Matter (ss 9–10)
  • Civil or Commercial (+) Per C&Y, "civil or commercial" is autonomous, mainly excluding public and criminal law. [A claim for price] under [supply contract] is commercial, and insurance is not excluded merely by its subject matter (s 9(6)).
  • Excluded (−) Per s 9(1), the CCAA excludes [consumer] and [employment / collective] agreements; per s 9(2), matters such as [insolvency / carriage of goods / competition / personal injury / non-contractual property damage / rights in rem in land / IP validity]; per s 9(3), arbitration.
    • IP (±): non-contractual infringement of [patent / trade mark] (not copyright) is excluded unless it could have been brought as a breach of [contract] between the parties (s 9(2)).
    • Preliminary question (+): per s 9(5), [IP validity] raised only as a preliminary question or [defence] does not exclude the case; per s 9(7), [a State] being a party does not either.
  • Interim Measures (+) Per s 10, interim measures are outside the CCAA, so Singapore may still grant [a Mareva / an interim ASI] whatever [the chosen court] (J6.5.3).
J1.2.5 Validity, Existence and Capacity
  • Validity Presently, [party] says [clause X] is invalid for [misrepresentation / duress]. Per ss 11(1) and 12(1)(a) and the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, validity is for the law of [the chosen court's State], including its choice of law rules, a single reference point that deters forum shopping.
    • Example: if [Singapore] is chosen and [contract] is governed by [French law], Singapore's choice of law rules point to French law; even then, per s 5, [clause X] survives unless attacked directly.
  • Existence (Consent) The CCAA is silent, but per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), whether [party] consented to [clause X] is also for the law of [the chosen court], avoiding a validity and existence split.
  • Capacity If [the chosen court's law] treats capacity as validity or existence, it governs. As a non-chosen court, [Singapore] may also refuse a stay if [party] lacked capacity under Singapore law (s 12(1)(b)), also a ground to refuse recognition (s 15(1)(b); J7.5).

The CCAA has three principles: the chosen court must hear the case, a non-chosen court must decline, and the chosen court's judgment must be recognised (J7.5). But it applies only if every gateway is passed. In the exam, write only the gateways in issue.

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The CCAA is a fast lane with a strict entry gate. Once you are in, the rules are simple and strong: the chosen court must hear the case, everyone else must step aside. But to get in, the clause must pass every check at the gate. Fail one, and you are back on the ordinary road (the common law), where judges weigh things up case by case.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The gateways, one by one
  1. Exclusive? The clause does not say "exclusive", but "submit to the jurisdiction of the courts of Ruritania" with no contrary words is deemed exclusive (s 3(2)). ✓ (If the facts had called it non-exclusive, stop here: Prof Chong's point.)
  2. One Contracting State? Only Ruritania is named. ✓
  3. Date? Made in 2019, after Ruritania joined in 2015. ✓
  4. International? Alpha resides in Singapore and Rurico in Ruritania. ✓
  5. Civil or commercial, not excluded? A sale of goods. ✓ (Had it been a contract to carry the oil by sea, carriage of goods is excluded by s 9(2), and the CCAA would not apply.)

All five pass, so the CCAA applies. Ruritania, not Singapore, is chosen, so go to s 12: Singapore must stay or dismiss Alpha's action unless an exception applies (J1.4). In the exam you would write only the gateways that the facts put in doubt, here probably just gateway 1.

🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  • Express EJC. Concluded in writing (or accessible electronic means), designating the courts of one State, excluding all others (s 3(1)).
  • Deemed exclusive. "The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the [State] courts" is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise (s 3(2)). At common law, the same unlabelled clause could go either way under its proper law.
  • Asymmetric clauses are out. Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (VCLT art 32), an asymmetric clause is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged even on the court's own motion and even though the defendant conceded the point. Etihad (EWCA) (obiter) agrees: the Diplomatic Session rejected a Swiss proposal to cover clauses exclusive "for some or all of the parties". Earlier first-instance dicta (Commerzbank v Liquimar; Etihad (EWHC)) read the Convention more widely, but after CHLOE V reliance on them is weak. At common law the clause stays exclusive against the restricted party.
  • Floating clauses (±): coverage unclear. Before election, arguably no chosen court; after an election notice, arguably it crystallised into an exclusive choice.
  • More than one State: "Singapore or England" is not "of one Contracting State", so outside the CCAA.
  • Separability (s 5): the clause's validity cannot be challenged solely because the main contract is said to be void or terminated.
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Where the facts call the clause non-exclusive, do not invoke s 3(2): the CCAA does not apply. Prof Chong flagged this as a recurring exam error.

? WHY IT MATTERS
Why "international" is defined backwards

The CCAA does not list what counts as international. It describes the one case that is not: everyone and everything sits in one State, and the only foreign element is the court the parties picked. Two Singapore companies cannot turn a purely local deal into a Convention case just by writing "Hong Kong courts" into it. Anything with a real cross-border element (a foreign party, foreign performance) passes the gateway.

J1.2.5 Validity, existence and capacity

▤ On your pre-write: J1.2.5 Validity, Existence and Capacity (word for word)
J1.2.5 Validity, Existence and Capacity
  • Validity Presently, [party] says [clause X] is invalid for [misrepresentation / duress]. Per ss 11(1) and 12(1)(a) and the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, validity is for the law of [the chosen court's State], including its choice of law rules, a single reference point that deters forum shopping.
    • Example: if [Singapore] is chosen and [contract] is governed by [French law], Singapore's choice of law rules point to French law; even then, per s 5, [clause X] survives unless attacked directly.
  • Existence (Consent) The CCAA is silent, but per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), whether [party] consented to [clause X] is also for the law of [the chosen court], avoiding a validity and existence split.
  • Capacity If [the chosen court's law] treats capacity as validity or existence, it governs. As a non-chosen court, [Singapore] may also refuse a stay if [party] lacked capacity under Singapore law (s 12(1)(b)), also a ground to refuse recognition (s 15(1)(b); J7.5).

The CCAA uses one reference point to stop forum shopping: the law of the chosen court's State, including its choice of law rules (ss 11(1), 12(1)(a); Hartley–Dogauchi Report). The same law decides whether the party consented to the clause (existence), per the Report and C&Y. As a non-chosen court, Singapore may also refuse a stay if a party lacked capacity under Singapore law (s 12(1)(b)).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
One reference point in practice

A clause picks the Ruritanian courts exclusively. Rurico says the clause is void because its signatory had no authority. Rurico raises this in Singapore, and also in Ruritania.

  • In Ruritania (the chosen court), validity is tested under Ruritanian law including its choice of law rules (the Convention rule that s 11(1) gives effect to in Singapore).
  • In Singapore (not chosen), validity is also tested under Ruritanian law including its choice of law rules (s 12(1)(a)).

Both courts ask the same question under the same law, so there is no point racing to the court with the friendlier law. That is the whole purpose of the single reference point.

5J1.3 Singapore is the chosen court (s 11)

▤ On your pre-write: J1.3 SINGAPORE IS THE CHOSEN COURT (s 11) (word for word)
J1.3 SINGAPORE IS THE CHOSEN COURT (s 11)
  • Must Hear (must write) [Clause X] designates [the Singapore High Court / the SICC] and the CCAA applies (J1.2). Per s 11(1), [Singapore] must not decline unless [clause X] is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules.
  • No FNC, No Lis Pendens Per s 11(2), [Singapore] cannot decline in favour of [State B], so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies, and per C&Y no other s 11(3) ground has been prescribed. [Defendant]'s points that [witnesses / governing law] point to [State B], or that proceedings are pending there, are irrelevant.
  • Null and Void (−) [Defendant] argues [clause X] is null and void because [it was procured by fraud / [defendant]'s agent lacked authority]. That is for Singapore law including its choice of law rules (s 11(1)), and per s 5 the alleged invalidity of [contract] does not by itself affect [clause X].
  • Internal Allocation (±) Per s 11(4), Singapore's [subject-matter / value / internal allocation] rules are unaffected. But per s 11(5), on a discretionary transfer of [the case] to [another Singapore court], the court must take the parties' choice into account; otherwise, per art 8(5) HCCCA, [a foreign court] may refuse recognition against [a party] that objected in time (J5.4.2).
  • Serving Abroad: General Division (+) [Claimant] seeks approval on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021), created partly for CCAA cases, so [no nexus] and [no forum conveniens] inquiry arises (per C&Y; J3.1.1). If [contract] permits service out, no approval is needed (O 8 r 1(3); J3.1.5).
    • Open (±): whether [defendant] may still argue [the claim] is outside the CCAA, and so resist "has the jurisdiction", should be raised inter partes (J3.1.1).
  • Serving Abroad: SICC (+) No permission is needed to serve [defendant], [a party to the written jurisdiction agreement] (O 5 r 6(2)(a) SICC Rules; J5.2.4).
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If the Convention applies and the parties picked Singapore, Singapore has no choice: it must hear the case. It cannot say "another country is more convenient" or "there is already a case running abroad". The only way out is if the clause itself is null and void.

  • Must hear. Per s 11(1), Singapore must not decline unless the clause is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules.
  • No FNC, no lis pendens. Per s 11(2), Singapore cannot decline in favour of another State, so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies. Points about witnesses, governing law or pending foreign proceedings are irrelevant.
  • Null and void (−). An argument that the clause was procured by fraud or signed without authority is for Singapore law including its choice of law rules; per s 5, the alleged invalidity of the contract does not by itself affect the clause.
  • Internal allocation (±). Singapore's internal allocation rules are unaffected (s 11(4)), but on a discretionary transfer the court must take the parties' choice into account (s 11(5)); otherwise a foreign court may refuse recognition (art 8(5) HCCCA) (J5.4.2).
  • Serving abroad. In the General Division, the claimant seeks approval on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021), so no nexus or forum conveniens inquiry arises (J3.1.1). If the contract permits service out, no approval is needed (O 8 r 1(3)). In the SICC, no permission is needed to serve a party to the written jurisdiction agreement (O 5 r 6(2)(a)).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Singapore chosen in a CCAA case

Cl 20 designates the Singapore High Court exclusively and the CCAA applies (J1.2). Per s 11(1), Singapore must not decline jurisdiction unless cl 20 is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules. Per s 11(2), Delta's reliance on witnesses and pending proceedings in Japan is irrelevant, as neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
What Delta can and cannot argue under s 11

Delta (Japan) is sued in Singapore under a CCAA clause choosing Singapore. Sort its arguments:

Delta arguesDoes it work?
"All our witnesses are in Osaka."No. Forum conveniens is shut out by s 11(2).
"We already sued in Tokyo, and that case is further along."No. Pending foreign proceedings (lis pendens) are shut out too.
"The deal was a fraud, so the whole contract is void."Not by itself. Per s 5, an attack on the contract does not touch the clause.
"Our employee who signed the clause had no authority to agree to it."Possibly. That goes to whether the clause is null and void, tested under Singapore law including its choice of law rules.

Only the last line is worth Delta's time. Compare the common law, where the first two would at least be weighed.

6J1.4 Singapore is not the chosen court (s 12)

▤ On your pre-write: J1.4 SINGAPORE IS NOT THE CHOSEN COURT (s 12) (word for word)
J1.4 SINGAPORE IS NOT THE CHOSEN COURT (s 12)
  • Must Stay or Dismiss (must write) [Claimant] sued here, and [defendant] seeks a stay because [clause X] designates [the courts of State B]. Per s 12(1), "despite any other written law or rule of law", [Singapore] must stay or dismiss unless exception (a)–(e) applies; per s 12(2), a stay on other grounds remains possible.
  • Two Stages Per 6DM, the court asks (1) whether there is an exclusive agreement not designating [a Singapore court] for these proceedings, then (2) whether [an s 12(1) exception] applies.
  • Standard Per 6DM, [defendant] must show a good arguable case at stage 1, not the arbitration prima facie standard, because the CCAA has [no kompetenz-kompetenz equivalent] and [no supervisory appeal structure], and a good arguable case matches the robust common law stay analysis.
J1.4.1 Stage 1: An EJC That Does Not Designate Singapore
  • Ambiguous Clause (+) [Clause X] refers to ["the local courts" / "the courts of the Seller's country"]. Similar to 6DM, where "the local courts" in an English-law distribution agreement meant England because it renewed an earlier English-clause agreement on a related party's template, [clause X] means [State B] given [prior dealings / the template / the governing law].
  • Clause Covers Singapore or Is Outside the CCAA (−) [Claimant] answers that [clause X] [designates Singapore / is asymmetric / is non-exclusive]. Then s 12 is not engaged (CHLOE V), and [the stay] is decided at common law: [strong cause for an EJC / Spiliada for a foreign NEJC] (J4).
J1.4.2 Stage 2: The Exceptions (s 12(1)(a)–(e))
  • Starter Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), exceptions (c) and (d) apply "only in the most exceptional circumstances" and are read narrowly. If [an exception] applies, [Singapore] may exercise jurisdiction under its own law, and [defendant]'s stay falls to the common law (J4).
  • (a) Null and Void (±) [Claimant] argues [clause X] is null and void for [ground] under [State B]'s law, including its choice of law rules, not Singapore law. [Claimant] must prove [State B law] as fact; per 6DM, without evidence the argument fails.
  • (b) Incapacity (+) [Claimant] lacked capacity to conclude [clause X] under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, because of [e.g., the company's constitution] (s 12(1)(b)).
  • (c) Manifest Injustice: Rule (−) Per 6DM, adopting the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, manifest injustice covers, e.g., [no fair trial for bias or corruption in State B], [party-specific reasons precluding suit there] or [an agreement procured by fraud]. Per Brand & Herrup (in 6DM), it must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable, not speculative.
  • (c) Public Policy: Rule (−) Per 6DM, public policy means [basic norms], not [the chosen court's technical departure from a forum mandatory rule], and [clause X] is not disregarded merely because it would not bind under [Singapore domestic law].
  • (c) Fragmentation (−) Similar to 6DM, where the risk that a related individual could not be joined in England failed s 12(1)(c), [claimant]'s argument that [third party] cannot be joined in [State B] fails. The test is "very different" from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar), and [claimant] led no evidence of [State B law].
  • (c) Domestic Policy (−) Similar to Motacus (in 6DM), where England's policy of fast construction adjudication did not justify ignoring a Paris EJC, absent any evidence that enforcement could not proceed in Paris, [claimant]'s reliance on [Singapore policy on X] fails. Parliament could have made [an art 21 declaration].
  • (c) Exceptional Case (+) [Claimant] leads cogent evidence that [State B's courts are not independent / [claimant] faces arrest there / [clause X] was procured by fraud], the kind of case the Hartley–Dogauchi Report contemplates.
  • (d) Cannot Reasonably Be Performed (±) Per s 12(1)(d), this needs exceptional reasons beyond the parties' control, arguably akin to frustration. (+) [War in State B / its courts ceasing to function] means [the case] cannot be heard there. (−) Mere [delay / expense] is not enough.
  • (e) Chosen Court Declined (+) [The State B court] has [declined jurisdiction / dismissed [claimant]'s claim on jurisdictional grounds], so [Singapore] may hear [the case] under its own rules without breaching the Convention.
  • Case Management (−) Per 6DM, any risk of [inconsistent outcomes with related proceedings] can be met by a limited case-management stay of [those proceedings], especially at an early stage (J4.5).
  • Conclusion [No exception applies, so [the action] is [stayed / dismissed] under s 12(1) / exception [(x)] applies, so [defendant]'s stay is decided at common law (J4.1)].

Per s 12(1), "despite any other written law or rule of law", Singapore must stay or dismiss unless one of exceptions (a)–(e) applies. Per 6DM, the court asks two questions, and the defendant needs only a good arguable case at stage 1 (not the arbitration prima facie standard, because the CCAA has no kompetenz-kompetenz equivalent and no supervisory appeal structure).

The five exceptions in s 12(1)
▤ J1.4.2. Read (c) and (d) narrowly: "only in the most exceptional circumstances" (Hartley–Dogauchi Report)
  1. 1(a) Null and void under State B's law (including its choice of law rules). The claimant must prove that law as fact; without evidence the argument fails (6DM).
  2. 2(b) Incapacity of a party under Singapore law.
  3. 3(c) Manifest injustice or public policy. Must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable (Brand & Herrup, in 6DM): e.g. no fair trial in State B, or an agreement procured by fraud. Public policy means basic norms, not a technical departure from a forum mandatory rule.
  4. 4(d) Cannot reasonably be performed: exceptional reasons beyond the parties' control, arguably akin to frustration (war; courts not functioning). Mere delay or expense is not enough.
  5. 5(e) The chosen court has declined the case.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Fragmentation does not count

In 6DM, the claimant argued it could not join a related individual to proceedings in England. That failed s 12(1)(c). The test is "very different" from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar). So if your claimant argues "we can't join the third party in State B", it fails too, especially with no evidence of State B law. Similarly, in Motacus (in 6DM), England's policy of fast construction adjudication did not justify ignoring a Paris EJC.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The s 12 exceptions on facts

A CCAA clause picks the Ruritanian courts exclusively. Alpha sues in Singapore anyway. Run each argument through s 12(1):

Alpha's argumentExceptionLikely result
"Ruritanian courts take three years to reach trial."(d) cannot reasonably be performedFails. Delay and expense are not enough; (d) needs something like war or courts that do not function.
"We can't join Rurico's parent company in Ruritania."(c) manifest injusticeFails. That is fragmentation, which 6DM held falls far short of (c).
"The clause is void under Ruritanian law." (no expert evidence)(a) null and voidFails. Foreign law is a fact; with no evidence the argument cannot get off the ground (6DM).
"Civil war has closed the Ruritanian courts."(d)May succeed: an exceptional reason beyond the parties' control.
"The Ruritanian court has already refused to hear the case."(e) chosen court declinedSucceeds.

If an exception succeeds, the CCAA no longer forces a stay, but that is not the end: Rurico's stay application is then decided at common law (J4.1).

⚠ TRAP
Stage 1 ambiguity

In 6DM, "the local courts" in an English-law distribution agreement meant England: the agreement renewed an earlier English-clause agreement on a related party's template. Ambiguous words are read in light of prior dealings, the template and the governing law.

7J1.5 Scope of the agreement

▤ On your pre-write: J1.5 SCOPE OF THE AGREEMENT (word for word)
J1.5 SCOPE OF THE AGREEMENT (write before strong cause: if [the claim] or [the party] is outside [clause X], ordinary Spiliada applies instead (J4.1 / J4.2))
  • Governing Law Per C&Y, subject-matter and party scope are for [the proper law of clause X], not the lex fori. If [law X] is unproved, Singapore construction applies by the presumption of similarity, with [contra proferentem] as a fallback where [the governing law] recognises it.
J1.5.1 Subject-Matter Scope
  • Broad Construction (+) [Claimant] argues [the tort / statutory claim] is outside [clause X]. Per Fiona Trust, applied to jurisdiction clauses in Trisuryo and Bunge, rational businessmen are presumed to want all disputes arising out of [their relationship] decided in one forum unless [the words] clearly exclude them.
  • Reframing Rarely Escapes (+) Per The Jian He (and Rickshaw), [claimant] may frame its claim in [tort / equity], but reframing [a contractual dispute] rarely escapes a widely drafted [clause X].
  • Separate Agreement Within Scope (+) Similar to Trisuryo, where a trust claim resting on a separate oral agreement fell within the Indonesian EJC because it contradicted the deeds' warranty that the shares were free of others' rights, [claimant]'s claim under [side agreement] falls within [clause X] since it [contradicts / turns on] [a term of contract].
  • No Presumption at the Outset (−) Per COSCO (CA), the inquiry does not start from a presumption that all competing claims go to one forum; it depends on [the nature of the claims] and [clause X's express words], "forum fragmentation [being] a fact of life". Where [the claim] falls outside, fragmentation is accepted (Asiana).
  • Tests Are Tools (±) Per COSCO (CA), the causative-connection, closely-knitted and parallel-claims tests are tools, not formulae. A [tort claim] that can be recast in contract plainly falls within, and so may one met by [contractual cross-claims] from the same incident (The Angelic Grace), e.g., [an allision during cargo loading].
  • Jurisdiction Clauses Too Though COSCO (CA) concerned [an arbitration clause], scope is construed the same way for [an EJC] (Fiona Trust; per C&Y), so [defendant] may rely on it for [the tort claim].
  • Global Partners (+, persuasive) Per Global Partners (NSWCA), "in connection with" in [clause X] cannot be read down, and an EJC is construed as liberally as [an arbitration clause], securing one coherent forum for [all disputes from the relationship]. A globally operating [contract] invites multiplicity, so there is no basis for a narrow reading.
J1.5.2 Multiple Contracts and Competing Clauses
  • Extended Fiona Trust (±) [Clause X] sits in [Contract A], and [the dispute] arises under [Contract B], which has no clause. Per Allianz v Goh Andress, adopting Terre Neuve:
    • (a) Words: [clause X]'s words must be fairly capable of covering [Contract B] disputes.
    • (b) Presumption: [clause X] normally applies where [the parties] are the same and the contracts are interdependent, concluded together as one package, and/or cover [the same subject matter].
  • Nature and Ultimate Question Per Allianz, this is construction of [clause X], not incorporation into or variation of [Contract B], and the factors are guides. The question is whether [the outcome] is one the parties, as rational businesspeople, sensibly envisaged; Trisuryo is an earlier multi-contract example.
  • Competing Clauses (±) Where [Contract A] and [Contract B] contain competing clauses, there is no extended Fiona Trust presumption (Allianz). Per Bunge, adopting Oei Hong Leong, apply the clause the parties objectively intended, i.e. the one with which [the dispute] has the closest connection in its "pith and substance", presuming commercial parties do not intend [similar claims] to fall under inconsistent clauses.
    • Application: Similar to Bunge, where the Singapore EJCs in the only contracts between the two disputants governed their negative declaration claim, [clause X] governs because it is in the only contract between [claimant] and [defendant].
  • Court Clause Plus Arbitration Clause (±) Where [contract] contains both [an arbitration clause] and [a Singapore court clause], per the slides they may be reconciled as arbitration for [disputes], with the court clause conferring supervisory jurisdiction over [the arbitration].
J1.5.3 Party Scope

(argue privity first)

  • Privity First (−) [The non-party] invokes, or is sued in the teeth of, [clause X] in [the A–B contract]. Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, whether [clause X] avails claims against [third parties] is construction, and, in keeping with privity, it usually will not absent "a quite clear indication otherwise".
  • Third Party Relying: Proper Law Per C&Y, [the third party] may rely on [clause X] if [its governing law] permits. Per VKC v VJZ, CRTPA s 2(1)(b) ("purports to confer a benefit") does not apply to an EJC, as it confers [a procedural, not substantive, right] and the Act deals expressly only with [arbitration clauses] (s 9).
    • Critique (+): per Chong (seminar), the "procedural" label is wrong: if [an EJC] were merely procedural, its breach could not found [an ASI] or [damages] (J1.7).
  • Third Party Relying: Routes Left Per VKC v VJZ, [the third party] might "arguably" rely on s 2(1)(a) ([clause X] expressly provides it may enforce) or s 2(3) (identified by [name / class / description]); the equitable route (Hai Jiang 1401) was left open. So draft [an express third-party right] if protection is wanted.
  • Third Party Bound (−) Generally no, by privity, unless [the third party] takes by [assignment / subrogation / agency] or otherwise claims under [contract], taking the benefit subject to the burden (Hai Jiang 1401; J6.5.2).
  • Closely Connected Non-Parties (+, persuasive) Similar to Global Partners, where group companies named as "Indemnified Persons" who took part in the very decisions complained of were "not strangers" ("there are non parties and non parties"), so the EJC bound the claimant in its claims against them, [clause X] binds [claimant] in its claims against [the affiliates], who [implemented the contract / hold contractual indemnities].
  • Counter (−) Per Hive Marketing (NSWCA), a stay of related claims against [non-parties] is not automatic or presumptive merely because of [a risk of multiplicity]. After Asiana and COSCO (CA), Global Partners is an example of the "quite clear indication", not the default, so it fails where [the affiliates] are [strangers linked only by common ownership].
  • Bypass Manoeuvre Where [claimant] sues only [the non-party] abroad to sidestep [clause X], though [the contracting party] is the obvious defendant, the suit may be restrained as vexatious even if [clause X] does not bind [the non-party] (Clearlake, in Asiana; J6.5.2).

Even a valid clause only bites on claims and parties within its scope. If the claim or the party is outside, ordinary Spiliada applies instead. Per C&Y, scope is for the proper law of the clause; if that law is unproved, Singapore construction applies by the presumption of similarity.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scope: one clause, three claims, two defendants

A supply contract between Alpha and Delta says: "All disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Hong Kong." Alpha sues in Singapore.

  1. Claim for the unpaid price against Delta. Squarely within the words. The clause applies.
  2. Claim in tort against Delta for lies told during negotiations. Alpha calls it a tort to escape the clause. Per Fiona Trust, businesspeople are presumed to want one forum for the whole relationship, and per The Jian He, relabelling a contractual dispute as tort rarely escapes wide words like "in connection with". Likely within scope.
  3. Claim against Delta's parent company, which never signed. Per Asiana, a clause does not usually reach non-parties without "a quite clear indication". So the parent cannot rely on the Hong Kong clause by default, and that claim goes to ordinary Spiliada (J4.1).

Notice that claims 1 and 2 ask "is this dispute covered?" (subject matter), while claim 3 asks "is this person covered?" (party scope). Keep the two questions apart in your answer.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
A master agreement and its purchase orders

Alpha and Delta sign a master agreement with a Singapore EJC. Over the next year Delta sends twenty purchase orders, none of which has a jurisdiction clause. A dispute arises over order 14.

  • The parties are the same, the orders only make sense inside the master agreement, and they cover the same goods. Per Allianz, the extended Fiona Trust presumption applies: rational businesspeople would expect the master agreement's clause to cover order 14.
  • Now suppose order 14 has its own clause choosing Hong Kong. There is no presumption any more: per Bunge, ask which clause the dispute is most closely connected with in its "pith and substance". A complaint about the quality of order 14's goods probably sits with order 14's clause.
