So draft [an express third-party right] if protection is wanted.
  • Third Party Bound (−) Generally no, by privity, unless [the third party] takes by [assignment / subrogation / agency] or otherwise claims under [contract], taking the benefit subject to the burden (Hai Jiang 1401; J6.5.2).
  • Closely Connected Non-Parties (+, persuasive) Similar to Global Partners, where group companies named as "Indemnified Persons" who took part in the very decisions complained of were "not strangers" ("there are non parties and non parties"), so the EJC bound the claimant in its claims against them, [clause X] binds [claimant] in its claims against [the affiliates], who [implemented the contract / hold contractual indemnities].
  • Counter (−) Per Hive Marketing (NSWCA), a stay of related claims against [non-parties] is not automatic or presumptive merely because of [a risk of multiplicity]. After Asiana and COSCO (CA), Global Partners is an example of the "quite clear indication", not the default, so it fails where [the affiliates] are [strangers linked only by common ownership].
  • Bypass Manoeuvre Where [claimant] sues only [the non-party] abroad to sidestep [clause X], though [the contracting party] is the obvious defendant, the suit may be restrained as vexatious even if [clause X] does not bind [the non-party] (Clearlake, in Asiana; J6.5.2).
  • Privity first (−). Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, a clause usually does not cover claims against third parties absent "a quite clear indication otherwise".
  • A third party relying on the clause. Per C&Y, it may if the clause's governing law permits. Per VKC v VJZ, CRTPA s 2(1)(b) does not apply to an EJC because it confers a procedural, not substantive, right. Routes left: s 2(1)(a) (express right), s 2(3) (identified by name or class), or the equitable route (Hai Jiang 1401), left open.
  • A third party bound. Generally no, unless it takes by assignment, subrogation or agency, taking the benefit subject to the burden (Hai Jiang 1401).
  • Closely connected non-parties. In Global Partners, group companies who took part in the very decisions complained of were "not strangers". But per Hive Marketing (NSWCA), a stay against non-parties is not automatic, and after Asiana and COSCO, Global Partners is an example of the "quite clear indication", not the default.
  • Bypass manoeuvre. Suing only the non-party abroad to sidestep the clause may be restrained as vexatious (Clearlake, in Asiana) (J6.5.2).
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Prof Chong criticised VKC v VJZ's "procedural" label: if an EJC were merely procedural, breaking it could not found an ASI or damages (J1.7).

8J1.6 Existence and validity of the clause

▤ On your pre-write: J1.6 EXISTENCE, VALIDITY AND GOVERNING LAW OF THE CLAUSE (word for word)
J1.6 EXISTENCE, VALIDITY AND GOVERNING LAW OF THE CLAUSE (write where [a party] denies the clause, or attacks the contract containing it)
  • Threshold and Burden Per Vinmar, [the party relying on clause X] must show a good arguable case that it exists and applies to [the dispute], i.e. "the better of the argument": more than prima facie, less than a balance of probabilities, and not a "much better argument". The court may decide [questions of law] but will not resolve [contested facts].
  • Incorporation and Service Out Per C&Y, whether [clause X] was incorporated, e.g., by [a course of dealing], is for [the proper law]. Where [clause X] founds service out, [claimant] keeps that burden inter partes (J3.2).
  • Governing Law of the Clause Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), [clause X] may in principle have its own law, but absent [contrary provision] it follows [the main contract's proper law], an express choice for the contract implying the same for the clause. Only one party can have the better of the argument on [the governing law], and the court applies that view throughout.
  • Separability Per C&Y, separability is a matter of substantive contract law, so ask whether [the clause's governing law] recognises it. If [contract] is [voidable but unrescinded], [clause X] operates.
  • Attacking the Contract, Relying on the Clause (±) [Defendant] alleges [contract] is [voidable for misrepresentation / void for fraud] yet invokes [clause X] to stay [claimant]'s action. Per CIMB, where the parties dispute existence or validity (rather than agreeing there was no contract), [the dispute] is decided under the contract's clauses as if valid.
    • Why: otherwise a mere allegation of [fraud] would neutralise [clause X] (CIMB, adopting The Parouth and Ash v Lloyd's).
  • Infection Test Per PT Selecta and CIMB, the question is whether [the vitiating factor] also infects [clause X]. It does only where there was clearly [no concluded contract at all] or [non est factum]; [fraud / duress] in procuring the contract, or [a common mistake as to subject matter] (CIMB), does not touch consent to [clause X].
  • Application Similar to PT Selecta, where a misrepresentation plea about the payment terms (non est factum disclaimed) did not infect a clause expressly covering disputes as to "validity", [defendant]'s plea of [misrepresentation as to X] does not reach [clause X].
  • Forum Mandatory Rules (±) [Claimant] argues [clause X], sending claims to [a remote forum], is overridden by a Singapore statute (C1.7). Per the Week 9 handout (outline only, so the application is argument):
    • UCTA s 13(1) may catch [an onerous forum clause] as restricting [a right or remedy], with no s 13(2) safe harbour as there is for [arbitration].
    • CPFTA s 35(1) voids terms ousting [consumer protection] for [a consumer].
    • COGSA s 3(1) gives [the Hague-Visby Rules] the force of law for [the carriage contract].
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine Delta says, "This whole contract was a fraud, so it's void." But Delta also wants to rely on the contract's jurisdiction clause to send the case to Delta's home court. Is that allowed? Usually yes. The clause is treated as a separate agreement, and the fraud allegation is about the deal (price, quality), not about where to litigate. The clause only falls with the contract if the problem goes to consent to the clause itself.

  • Threshold. Per Vinmar, the party relying on the clause must show a good arguable case that it exists and applies: "the better of the argument". The court may decide questions of law but will not resolve contested facts.
  • Governing law of the clause. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), it can have its own law, but absent contrary provision it follows the main contract's proper law.
  • Separability. Per C&Y, a matter of substantive contract law, so ask whether the clause's governing law recognises it.
  • Attacking the contract, relying on the clause. Per CIMB, where existence or validity is disputed, the dispute is decided under the contract's clauses as if valid, otherwise a mere allegation of fraud would neutralise the clause (adopting The Parouth and Ash v Lloyd's).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
PT Selecta

A misrepresentation plea about the payment terms (non est factum disclaimed) did not infect a clause expressly covering disputes as to "validity". So if your defendant pleads misrepresentation about the price or quality of goods, that plea does not reach the clause.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Sorting the attacks on a contract

Delta wants to escape a Singapore EJC. Which attacks also bring down the clause?

Delta says…Does it reach the clause?
"Alpha lied about the machines' output, so the contract is voidable."No. The lie was about the deal, not about where to sue (CIMB; PT Selecta).
"We signed under economic pressure."No, for the same reason: duress in procuring the deal is not consent to the clause.
"We were never told this page with the clause existed and signed a document of a completely different nature."Arguably yes: that is the non est factum territory, where consent to everything, clause included, is missing.
"Negotiations never finished; there was no concluded contract at all."Yes, if clearly right: no contract, so no clause.

And remember the threshold: Alpha, relying on the clause, needs only a good arguable case that it exists and covers the dispute (Vinmar). The court will not try contested facts at this stage.

ℹ NOTE
Forum mandatory rules (argument only)

A Singapore statute may override a clause sending claims to a remote forum (C1.7). The Week 9 handout gives an outline only, so the application is argument: UCTA s 13(1) may catch an onerous forum clause (no s 13(2) safe harbour as for arbitration); CPFTA s 35(1) voids terms ousting consumer protection; COGSA s 3(1) gives the Hague-Visby Rules the force of law.

9J1.7 Other effects of the agreement

▤ On your pre-write: J1.7 OTHER EFFECTS OF THE AGREEMENT (word for word)
J1.7 OTHER EFFECTS OF THE AGREEMENT (write where [the innocent party] wants more than a stay, or [the foreign judgment] is already obtained)
  • Damages: England Because an EJC contains a promise not to sue elsewhere, [the innocent party] may claim [costs thrown away abroad / liability under the foreign judgment]. Per Starlight Shipping, breach is a question of law, so [summary judgment] for damages to be assessed is possible.
    • Breach lies in suing: per Starlight Shipping, whether [the claims] would succeed in [X] or fail in [the chosen forum] is irrelevant.
  • Damages: Singapore (−) Per Tradewaves (applying Sunrock Aircraft), damages "can", not "must", be awarded. [Foreign costs] should normally be sought in [the foreign action], and [the claimant] must prove the "unusual features" in Union Discount v Zoller, e.g., [foreign rules allowing costs only exceptionally] and [no foreign costs order].
  • Anti-Suit Injunction Breach of [a Singapore EJC] (arguably also of a Singapore NEJC, per Shanghai Turbo) is a contractual basis for an ASI against [respondent]'s suit in [X]. No vexation is needed, and [respondent] must show strong reasons why it should not issue (Cooperative Muratori; J6.3.1).
  • ASI: Foreign EJC (−) Where [clause X] chooses [a foreign court], Singapore generally declines to restrain [the suit in a third country] and leaves it to [the chosen court], not being an "international busybody" (Akai; J6.2.6).
  • Choice of Law Clause Not Promissory (−) Per Ace Insurance v Moose, a choice of law clause is usually declaratory, so [an ASI] against suit in [a forum applying another law] was refused. Only [very clear words] make it promissory, which would bring damages, an ASI and a recognition defence (C2).
  • Recognition Defence (±) [Debtor] resists enforcement of [X's judgment] obtained in breach of [clause X]. There is no common law authority, but per C&Y a defence is arguable: [damages for breach could cancel the judgment sum], REFJA s 5(4)(b) deems [the foreign court] to lack jurisdiction absent submission, and convergence with the statutes is desirable (Merck; J7.2.6).
    • Limits: [debtor]'s submission in [X] removes the defence, and the breach, not whether [Singapore or a foreign court] was chosen, is key. The CCAA does not prohibit recognising [a non-chosen court's judgment] under the common law or REFJA (per C&Y; J7.5).
  • Other Agreements (not examinable) A stay for breach of [an international arbitration agreement] is mandatory (s 6 IAA); for [domestic arbitration] or [mediation] it is discretionary (s 6 Arbitration Act; s 8 Mediation Act, "may").
  • Non-Suit or Settlement Agreement ["Settled; no further action in any court"] is not a jurisdiction clause but a substantive [accord and satisfaction] defence. [Proceedings in breach] may be stayed or struck out as an abuse, with [an ASI] or [damages] also possible.

A broken clause can do more than produce a stay:

RemedyRule
Damages (England)Per Starlight Shipping, breach is a question of law; costs thrown away abroad or liability under the foreign judgment can be claimed. Breach lies in suing, whatever the foreign claim's merits.
Damages (Singapore) (−)Per Tradewaves (applying Sunrock Aircraft), damages "can", not "must", be awarded. Foreign costs should normally be sought abroad, and the claimant must prove the "unusual features" in Union Discount v Zoller.
ASIBreach of a Singapore EJC (arguably also a Singapore NEJC, per Shanghai Turbo) is a contractual basis for an ASI: no vexation needed, and the respondent must show strong reasons (Cooperative Muratori) (J6.3.1).
ASI for a foreign EJC (−)Singapore generally declines to restrain a suit in a third country and leaves it to the chosen court, not being an "international busybody" (Akai) (J6.2.6).
Choice of law clause (−)Per Ace Insurance v Moose, usually declaratory, not promissory, so no ASI. Only very clear words make it promissory.
Recognition defence (±)No common law authority, but per C&Y arguable: damages could cancel the judgment sum; REFJA s 5(4)(b) points the same way; convergence with the statutes is desirable (Merck) (J7.2.6). Submission abroad removes it.
Non-suit or settlement agreementNot a jurisdiction clause but a substantive accord-and-satisfaction defence; proceedings in breach may be stayed or struck out as an abuse.
⚠ TRAP
Choice of court ≠ choice of law

A choice of court clause is a promise (so breach can found an ASI and damages). A choice of law clause is usually only a declaration of which law governs (Ace Insurance v Moose), so suing in a court that will apply another law is not a breach.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Everything a broken Singapore EJC can do

Delta sues Alpha in Ruritania despite a Singapore EJC. Alpha spends $200,000 defending there. What can Alpha do in Singapore?

  1. Stop it: seek an ASI on the contractual basis. Alpha need not show vexation; Delta must show strong reasons why the ASI should not issue (J6.3.1).
  2. Claim damages: the cost of defending abroad. In Singapore damages "can", not "must", be awarded (Tradewaves): Alpha should normally seek its costs in Ruritania, and must prove the "unusual features" of Union Discount v Zoller to recover them here.
  3. Resist the Ruritanian judgment if Delta wins and tries to enforce it in Singapore: arguably a recognition defence (C&Y), as long as Alpha did not submit in Ruritania (J7.2.6).

Contrast: if the contract had only said "governed by Singapore law" with no court clause, Delta suing in Ruritania would break no promise at all (Ace Insurance v Moose).

10Put it together: a worked contract

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Hypo: the Ruritanian distributor

Facts. A 2019 distribution agreement between Alpha (Singapore) and Beta (Ruritania) says: "This Agreement is governed by Singapore law. The parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore." Ruritania is not a Contracting State. Beta sues Alpha in Ruritania; Alpha sues Beta in Singapore and serves Beta in Ruritania. Beta applies to set aside service, saying Ruritania is more convenient.

  1. Regime router. Not a CCAA case: the clause is expressly non-exclusive, and Ruritania is not a Contracting State. Is the case in the SICC? No written SICC agreement on these facts, so the common law applies (J1.0.2).
  2. Characterise. A Singapore NEJC, construed under Singapore law (the express proper law). Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), it contains (1A) and (1B): Beta promised not to object to Singapore (J1.1.1).
  3. Scope and validity. The claim arises under the agreement itself; no vitiating factor is pleaded against the clause (J1.5; J1.6).
  4. Existence. Service out: a Singapore clause is a gateway, and Alpha need show only that the clause is valid, binds Beta and covers the dispute (J3.2).
  5. Breach? Beta's set-aside application on FNC grounds breaks (1B). So Beta must show strong cause (J4.3).
  6. Other effects. Beta's Ruritanian suit does not break the NEJC (no promise (2)), so an ASI would need the vexation route unless the clause is read as more (J1.7; J6).

Flip one word. Make the clause "the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore". Step 5 is unchanged (Beta still objects to Singapore, so strong cause on Beta), but step 6 changes: Beta's Ruritanian suit now breaks promise (2), so Alpha can seek an ASI on the contractual basis. And if Ruritania were a Contracting State and the clause post-dated its entry into force, step 1 changes too: the CCAA would apply, and Singapore must hear the case (s 11), with no room for Beta's forum arguments at all.

← 00: Start hereJ2: Service in and submission →
LESSON J2 · Q1 · JURISDICTION AND JUDGMENTS · ABOUT 26 MIN · 7 FLOWCHARTS · 3 ILLUSTRATIONS · 18 QUESTIONS

Existence when the defendant is in Singapore: service in and submission

⚡ BIG IDEA

The court has jurisdiction as of right over a defendant served in Singapore or who submits. For every route, name two things together: the founding provision (which part of s 16 SCJA) and the mode of service (which rule). Only a never-registered foreign company needs the Adams v Cape presence test.

PRE-WRITE J2 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR FILE
J2 Existence Of Jurisdiction: Defendant Present In Singapore (Service In And Submission)
This is your exam file, unchanged. It is long, so it starts folded: open it once to see the whole shape, then learn it piece by piece below. [Brackets] are the blanks you fill with the facts; Labels start each point; (+) helps the party relying on the rule, (−) helps the other side, (±) argue both ways. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue reference such as J4.3 to jump.

(Exercise of jurisdiction (the Spiliada stay and the overlays) is in J4, so one factor bank serves the stay, service out and strong cause. Triage any jurisdiction agreement first in J1.)

J2.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP

(Scan first. Ask (1) does the court HAVE jurisdiction over [defendant] (s 16(1) SCJA), then (2) should it EXERCISE it (J4)? If [defendant] is abroad, go to J3. Service is always required (O 6 r 4). Pair the founding provision with the mode of service: only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence.)

  1. Preliminary concepts and limits (J2.0.2: Allenger).
  2. Service in Singapore (J2.1): individuals (Maharanee); agents (O 7 r 4; Beranek); Singapore companies (s 387 CA); registered foreign companies (s 376 CA; Tao Commodity); never-registered foreign companies (Adams v Cape; Rosenberg); partnerships and LLPs (O 56); router.
  3. Submission (J2.2: Williams & Glyn's; Zoom; Shanghai Turbo; O 6 rr 7(6), 12(5)).
  4. Exercise (J4): Spiliada stay (J4.1); overlays (J4.5).
  5. Absent defendant (J3): service out; the COSCO debate (J3.0.2).
J2.0.1 Quick Application Template

Presently, [claimant] sues [defendant], a [Singapore-resident individual / company incorporated in X / foreign company registered in Singapore], for [breach of contract / tort / restitution] arising from [events] in [X]. Existence: jurisdiction is founded on [s 16(1)(a)(i) through O 7 r 2(1)(a) / ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) through s 387 or s 376 CA / s 16(1)(a)(i) through Adams v Cape presence and O 7 r 2(1)(b) or r 4 / s 16(1)(a)(ii) through O 8 r 1 via para 63(3)[(d) / (f) / (p)] / s 16(1)(b) through submission by [filing a defence on the merits]] (J2.1; J2.2; J3.1), and [the claim] is not [title to foreign land / a foreign revenue, penal or public law claim / validity of a foreign IP right / barred by act of state or immunity] (J2.0.2). Exercise: [defendant] seeks a stay under O 6 r 7(5)(b) / r 12(4)(b); there [is / is no] breach of an [EJC / NEJC] for [Y], so [strong cause (J4.3) / Spiliada (J4.1)] applies; [Y] is available and [residence / witnesses / governing law / place of the tort / related proceedings] point to [Singapore / Y]; at stage 2 [claimant] [can / cannot] show a real risk of [delay / unfair procedure / personal danger] in [Y]. Result: the court [has / lacks] jurisdiction and [will / will not] stay.

J2.0.2 Preliminary Concepts and Statutory Framework

(short opener; subject-matter limits are not examinable, so one line at most)

  • Three Sets of Rules jurisdiction may arise in the [General Division (here)], the [SICC (J5)] or under the [CCAA (J1.2–J1.4)]. Presently [there is no jurisdiction agreement / the [Singapore / X] clause is [within / outside] the CCAA] (router: J1.0.2).
  • Existence Before Exercise per C&Y, existence comes first, so [presence on a fleeting visit] founds jurisdiction and [the weak connection] goes only to a stay (J4.1). Presence and submission are as of right, but [O 7 r 4 service on an agent] and [O 8 r 1(1) service out] need permission.
  • Statutory Source: s 16 SCJA Per Art 93 Constitution and Allenger, the General Division is a creature of statute, so [defendant] must be served [in Singapore] (s 16(1)(a)(i)), served [outside Singapore] as the Rules authorise (s 16(1)(a)(ii)), or [submit] (s 16(1)(b)), or fall within other written law (ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), e.g., ss 387, 376 CA).
  • Service Founds Jurisdiction service both gives [defendant] notice and founds jurisdiction, so even [a submitting defendant] must be served (O 6 r 4), [personally / in an agreed manner under O 7 r 2(1)(d)].
  • Founding Provision + Mode of Service (must write) state [s 16(1)(a)(i) / ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) / s 16(1)(a)(ii) / s 16(1)(b)] with [O 7 r 2(1)(a) / r 2(1)(b) / r 4 / s 387 CA / s 376 CA / O 8 r 1]. Only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence for [the foreign company] (J2.1.5).
  • Why Serve In per Zoom, after service in [defendant] bears the burden on a stay, whereas on service out [claimant] bears it if [defendant] challenges existence on forum grounds (J4.0.2).
  • Subject-Matter Jurisdiction (not examinable) Per Chong (seminar), subject-matter jurisdiction is off-syllabus except for the SICC (J5.1). If [defendant] says [the claim] is non-justiciable, one line suffices: per Allenger, s 16(1) limits only in personam jurisdiction, and the court may hear any claim "unless or until prohibited either by legislation or case law", e.g., [title to foreign land / foreign penal, revenue or public law].
  • Jurisdiction vs Power jurisdiction (ss 16–17) is authority to hear [the claim]. Per Li Shengwu, s 18 and Sch 1 concern [powers and reliefs], not [subject-matter jurisdiction], e.g., a stay under [para 9] (J4.1).
  • Inherent Power to Prevent Abuse Per Emilia Shipping, it is arguable that the court's inherent power to prevent abuse, e.g., where [defendant] was [fraudulently lured here] or [property was deceptively brought here], is unaffected by s 16 (now O 3 r 2(2)).
J2.1 EXISTENCE OF JURISDICTION: SERVICE IN SINGAPORE (s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA)
J2.1.1 Natural Person Physically Present

(an individual in Singapore, however briefly)

  • Basis and Mode Per s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA, [defendant] present [at his hotel / at the trade fair] is personally served as of right under O 7 r 2(1)(a). Presence is judged at service, so it is immaterial that he [arrived that morning / left the next day].
  • Temporary Presence (+) Per Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein and Colt Industries v Sarlie, presence on [a short visit / in transit] suffices without any substantive connection, even if [the contract / accident] arose wholly in [X].
  • Fraudulently Induced Presence (−) Per Watkins v North American Land, service may be set aside for abuse of process where [claimant] lured [defendant] here by [a sham meeting], but not where he came for [business / holiday].
  • Fortuity Goes to Exercise (±) Per C&Y, [defendant]'s weak connection is irrelevant to existence but relevant to the natural forum, so [the fleeting visit] and [the foreign events] support a stay (J4.1).
  • Evaluation: Presence as the Basis (±) [Defendant] calls jurisdiction on [a short visit] arbitrary, preferring [residence / domicile / nationality]. But per Sirdar Gurdyal Singh, jurisdiction is territorial, presence is certain where [residence] is harder to prove, and FNC corrects [the fortuity].
J2.1.2 Agent of an Absent Natural Person (O 7 r 4)

([defendant] abroad; [agent] manages his affairs here)

  • O 7 r 4 Requirements With permission on a without-notice summons, [agent] may be served for [defendant] if (a) [defendant] does not reside in or is absent from Singapore; (b) at service [agent] personally controls or manages here [defendant]'s affairs specifically relating to [the action]; and (c) [agent]'s authority subsists or there is an ongoing business relationship.
  • Founding Provision and Formalities Per Beranek, O 7 r 4 rests on s 16(1)(a)(i), [defendant] being constructively present through [agent] (J3.0.2). Per C&Y, [claimant] must also post [the order and the claim] to [defendant]'s address abroad within 14 days.
  • Control or Management [Agent] must actually control [the affairs sued on], not merely [relay messages]. Rosenberg's power-to-contract test is framed for companies (J2.1.5), but per C&Y "affairs" reaches [any affairs] of an individual.
  • Exceptional (−) Per C&Y, under the old O 10 r 2 its use against [an overseas individual] was a "rare case", and the English Practice Direction required "great caution", refusing it where [claimant] could easily [serve out].
  • Liberalised (+) Per C&Y, "affairs" replaced "business or work", [O 8] has liberalised service out and [permission] is needed anyway, so O 7 r 4 now applies more readily to [defendant].
  • Service Out Available? (±) [Defendant] argues permission should be refused because [claimant] could serve out under [O 8]. Per C&Y, O 7 r 4 is not meant to make O 8 otiose, but it is unclear that permission should be withheld as a matter of course.
J2.1.3 Company Incorporated in Singapore
  • Basis and Mode Per ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) SCJA, service of [the originating claim] under s 387 CA by [leaving it at / registered post to] [company]'s registered office founds jurisdiction, so Adams v Cape need not be discussed. Per Chong (seminar), in the exam simply state this pathway; the academic argument that [presence / submission] is still needed is not covered.
J2.1.4 Registered Foreign Company (s 376 CA)

(select [company]'s current status)

  • Registrability: ss 365, 368 per s 365, [company] that [establishes a place of business / carries on business] in Singapore, or intends to, must register under s 368 first, lodging [its Singapore registered office] and [its authorised representative].
  • Carrying On Business: s 366 Per s 366(1), business includes [administering property as agent or trustee]. Per s 366(2), it excludes merely [litigating / internal meetings / a bank account / independent-contractor sales / orders accepted abroad / an isolated transaction within 31 days / holding property], so [company]'s [activity] [is / is not] business.
  • Scenario A: Registered and Trading (+) Per ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), [company] is served under s 376(a) ([its Singapore registered office]) or s 376(b) ([its authorised representative's residential or contact address]), without Adams v Cape.
  • Scenario B: Ceased Business, Not Deregistered (+) Per s 376(c), [company] that "has ceased to maintain a place of business in Singapore" is served at [its registered office in X], or under (a)–(b) if [the Singapore office / representative] remains.
  • Scenario C: Ceased and Deregistered (−) Per Tao Commodity, s 376 is unavailable after [deregistration], registration having supplied the nexus, so [claimant] must serve [company] out in [X] (J3.1).
  • Scenario C: Reply (+) But per C&Y, the plain words of s 376(c) cover [the deregistered company], ceasing business being the precursor to deregistration, and the purpose is that [companies that traded here] cannot escape [local creditors]. Tao is a Registry decision unreviewed by the CA.
  • Does s 376 Confer Jurisdiction? (±) Route 1 (C&Y, run this): s 376 itself confers jurisdiction via ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), to spare [local creditors] from [service out]. Route 2 (Tao): registration is "a statutory parallel to or substitute for" corporate presence, s 376 being only [the mode of service]. Both cover Scenarios A–B, but only Route 1 survives [deregistration].
J2.1.5 Never-Registered Foreign Company

(s 376 unavailable; s 16(1)(a)(i) is the founding provision, so Adams v Cape must be written)

  • s 376 Unavailable (must write) although Division 2 applies to [a registrable but unregistered company] (s 365), per C&Y s 376(a)–(b) fail with [no Singapore office or representative] and (c), read holistically, is not meant for [a company still trading here]. So [claimant] relies on s 16(1)(a)(i) and must prove presence.
  • Limb 1: Fixed Place Per Adams v Cape, [company] is present if it carries on business at or from a reasonably permanent fixed place, e.g., [its office at address], whether it [owns / leases / licenses] it. Per Littauer Glove, [a representative taking orders from a hotel for a few days] is not enough.
  • Limb 2: More Than a Minimal Period [company] must be there for more than a minimal period. Per Dunlop v Cudell, [a nine-day trade-fair stand] sufficed, unlike [a one-day visit].
  • Limb 3: Whose Business? where [company] acts through [a representative], it is present only if he carries on [company]'s business, not his own (Okura), shown by [premises acquired for him / fixed pay vs commission / degree of control].
  • Power to Contract (±) Per Adams v Cape, the key question is whether [the representative] can [bind company] without prior approval. Per C&Y, that power is neither exclusive nor conclusive, and [the agent] may also run [its own business] from the same place.
  • Non-Trading Company Per Adams v Cape, where [company] is [a charity / holding company], substitute [its corporate activities] for "business".
  • Mode 1: Officer (O 7 r 2(1)(b), as of right) if [company] is present, [claimant] leaves the claim with [its chairperson / president / secretary / treasurer / other officer]. Per Yeo and Beranek (J3.0.2), it is [company]'s own presence that counts, so serving [an officer on holiday] when [company] is absent is doubtful (contra COSCO; B Atmaram).
  • Mode 2: Agent (O 7 r 4, with permission) Per Rosenberg, [agent] must be obliged to bring [the claim] to [company]'s notice, [company] must carry on business at a fixed place here, and [agent] must have power to contract, otherwise [company] trades "through", not "by", him. Per C&Y, [agent] need not be [a full-time employee].
  • O 7 r 4: Link to the Action (−) Per Rosenberg, the action must relate to [the business agent manages]. Where [the cheques were drawn by the head office in X] and [agent] could do only [liaison work], service is set aside and [claimant] must serve out.
  • O 7 r 4 Narrower Than Adams v Cape Per C&Y, r 4 needs [power to contract], control of affairs specifically relating to [the action], and [permission], none of which Adams v Cape requires. So [claimant] prefers r 2(1)(b) and pleads presence alongside.
  • Unregistrable: No Place of Business (−) where [company] merely [holds a bank account / accepts orders in X] (s 366(2)) or [sells online from X] (no virtual presence: Lucasfilm, by analogy), neither s 376 nor Adams v Cape applies. [Claimant] serves out (J3.1), unless [an agent here] satisfies O 7 r 4 or [Singapore solicitors] accept service (J2.2.2).
J2.1.6 Partnerships and LLPs

(no separate personality, except the LLP)

  • Firm Name (O 56 r 1) [Claimant] may sue [the partnership / limited partnership] in its firm name if [the partners] carry on business here. Per C&Y, this gives no in personam jurisdiction, so each [partner] to be made liable must be served or submit.
  • Mode of Service (O 56 r 3(1)) serve [any partner] or [the person controlling the business at the principal place of business]; if [the firm] is dissolved, serve every partner in Singapore.
  • Sole Trader (O 56 r 9) (−) Per C&Y, r 9 does not reach [a non-resident foreign individual] trading here through [an agent], who would otherwise be worse off than [a foreign partnership], with all his Singapore assets exposed.
  • LLP Per C&Y, [the LLP] is a body corporate served [at its registered office] under LLP Act s 93 (by analogy s 387 CA), which should found jurisdiction since [s 17 SCJA] is not exhaustive.
J2.1.7 Router: Pair Status, Founding Provision and Mode
  • Individual [present here] → s 16(1)(a)(i) with O 7 r 2(1)(a); [abroad with an agent here] → O 7 r 4 (permission); otherwise [serve out] (J3.1).
  • Singapore Company [company]'s [registered office here] → ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) with s 387 by [leaving it / registered post].
  • Registered and Trading [company] on [the ACRA register] and [trading here] → ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) with s 376(a) or (b).
  • Registered, Ceased, Not Deregistered [company] still on [the register] → s 376(c) at [its registered office in X], or (a)–(b).
  • Registered, Ceased, Deregistered [company] off [the register] → s 376(c), arguing against Tao, else [serve out].
  • Registrable, Never Registered (s 365(a)) [company] with [a place of business here] → s 16(1)(a)(i) and Adams v Cape, then O 7 r 2(1)(b) on [an officer] or r 4.
  • Intends Only (s 365(b)) or Not Registrable [company] with [no presence] → [serve out] (J3.1), unless [an agent] satisfies O 7 r 4.
  • Partnership [firm name] under O 56 r 1 if [the partners carry on business here], plus jurisdiction over each [partner] sued.
J2.2 EXISTENCE OF JURISDICTION: SUBMISSION (s 16(1)(b) SCJA)
J2.2.1 Starter

[Claimant] argues [defendant] submitted by [act] under s 16(1)(b) SCJA, usually to cure [irregular service / a jurisdictional objection], though [the originating claim] must still be served (O 6 r 4). Per Allenger, submission was added to s 16 in 1993.

  • Two Levels of Jurisdiction Per Williams & Glyn's, a defendant contesting jurisdiction submits only to [the court's jurisdiction to decide jurisdiction], not to [its jurisdiction over the merits]. So [contesting service / seeking a stay pending X proceedings] while "vigorously protesting" is not submission.
  • The Test Per Zoom (adopting Williams), submission requires a step "only necessary or only useful" if [the objection] had been waived or never entertained. Per C&Y (Spamhaus), it is a clear and unequivocal step incompatible with [no jurisdiction], a question of fact on [defendant]'s conduct as a whole.
  • Scope and Effect Per C&Y, submission cures [irregular service] but cannot confer [subject-matter jurisdiction] (J2.0.2). Per Williams and Glencore, a foreign defendant may limit submission [claim by claim], unlike [a claimant].
  • Submission vs Agreement to Submit Per C&Y, [a Singapore jurisdiction clause] is a promise to submit, enforced by [service out under O 8 r 1(3) or para 63(3)(d)(iv), (r)] (J3) or [strong cause] (J4.3), not submission by conduct.
J2.2.2 Acts Amounting to Submission (+)

(select, and explain why the step is incompatible with objection)

  • Defence on the Merits / Striking Out Per C&Y (Spamhaus), filing [a merits defence] or [a striking-out application] without protest submits, and raising [an EJC in a summary judgment affidavit] is no protest.
  • Stay Sought Alone (±) Per Zoom (The Jian He; Chan Chin Cheung), [an FNC stay] sought without contesting existence ordinarily submits at common law, as [defendant] accepts jurisdiction exists. But per O 6 rr 7(6), 12(5), [a defence or affidavit] stating an exercise challenge is not submission (J2.2.4).
  • Substantive Relief in a Jurisdictional Application Per Zoom (explaining Republic of the Philippines v Maler Foundation), praying for [release of the funds] within [an immunity stay application], pursued whatever [the stay outcome], invokes rather than contests jurisdiction.
  • Participation Despite Reservations Per Shanghai Turbo (SGCA), [deep, active participation in a non-party's injunction application] went beyond [a neutral, pre-emptive procedural step], contradicting [repeated express reservations]: a reservation is "not a silver bullet".
  • Claimant and Counterclaim Per Glencore, [a foreign claimant] suing here submits to "all the incidents of litigation", including [counterclaims] and [an ASI]. Per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar (HC), filing [a counterclaim] here is likewise premised on jurisdiction.
  • Multi-Party Litigation Per Glencore, [shipowners] who [brought claims and counterclaims] in [multi-party proceedings] submitted for litigation not wholly distinct from [the litigation the ASI protected], despite later [settlement / discontinuance].
  • Instructing Local Solicitors to Accept Service Per Rothschild, [defendant] instructing [Singapore solicitors] to accept service is submission. Per Shanghai Turbo (SGCA) and COSCO (HC), it is service in Singapore under O 7 r 2(1)(d), founding [s 16(1)(a)(i)]; argue both, Yeo preferring submission (YPH lecture: COSCO "should be confined to the submission reasoning") (J3.0.2).
  • Incorporation or Registration (±) [Company] arguably submitted by [incorporation / registration] here. But per C&Y this is unnecessary since [s 387 / s 376] founds jurisdiction via ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), so run it only as [a fallback].
    • Registration (±): (−) per Tao Commodity (HC Registry), registration compelled on pain of [a fine] is not voluntary, so not submission. (+) Per Chong (seminar), [company] chose to do business here, so it arguably submitted.
J2.2.3 Acts Not Amounting to Submission (−)

(then route [claimant] back to J2.1)

  • Notice of Intention to Contest Per O 6 r 6(4), filing [a notice of intention to contest or not contest] within [14 days if served here / 21 days if served out] is not submission or a waiver of [improper service].
  • Defence or Affidavit Stating the Challenge Per O 6 rr 7(4)–(6), 12(3)–(5), [a defence / defendant's affidavit] stating that the court [has no jurisdiction / should not exercise it] is not submission, filed within [21 days if served here / 5 weeks if served out].
  • Notice of Appointment of Solicitor Per Malayan Banking v Zhang Zhencheng, [a notice of appointment of solicitor] filed to challenge jurisdiction is not submission (by parity with O 6 r 12(5)). [Claimant] cannot then serve [those solicitors], unlike in COSCO, where [defendant] agreed.
  • Case Conference Per C&Y, attending [the case conference] after signalling [a challenge] in [its defence] is not submission, the court dealing with jurisdiction first (O 9 r 7).
  • Observer; Defensive Acts Per C&Y, attending [a hearing] as an observer, caveating that [attendance is not submission] (Grains and Industrial Products), or [purely defensive participation, e.g., resisting an injunction to save one's job] (International SOS v Overton), is not submission.
  • Fall-Back Stay (Set Aside, Then Stay) Per Zoom and Williams, a stay prayed as a fall-back to [setting aside service] is not submission, even in [the same summons], the prayers being considered in sequence. Risk: arguing [the stay] first was "unnecessarily risky" in Zoom, so make clear [existence is still contested].
  • Arguing Forum Within the Challenge On service out, per Zoom, [defendant] should run forum within [the set-aside application]. Per C&Y, running [a separate stay] on the same FNC arguments is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive" and may not be tolerated under [ROC 2021 case management].
  • Stay Pending Foreign Proceedings Per Williams (as limited in Zoom), a stay pending [X's ruling on the guarantee's validity], needed to decide jurisdiction, is not submission. But this holds only if the court can stay without first assuming jurisdiction, unclear under [Sch 1 para 9 / inherent powers], Singapore lacking [an equivalent of the English statutory power].
  • Unconnected Steps Per 6DM v AE Brands Korea, [a statutory demand] issued by [defendant] outside [the suit], with a reservation, is not submission.
  • Earlier Suit; Recognition Application Per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar (HC), submission in [an earlier suit] does not carry over to [a fresh suit], and [seeking recognition of foreign receivers] is not premised on jurisdiction over [the dispute].
  • Governing Law Clause [Choosing Singapore law] for [the contract] is not submission. By analogy, per Vizcaya Partners (recognition), a choice of [law] plus [doing business here] is not even implied consent to jurisdiction.
J2.2.4 Unclear: Failed Challenges and Stays Under ROC 2021

(write where [defendant]'s challenge has failed or only a stay was sought)

  • Deemed Submission Dropped Per C&Y, ROC 2014 deemed [defendant] to submit if [its challenge failed / no order was made], regardless of voluntariness. ROC 2021 dropped this, leaving [the effect of a failed challenge] unclear.
  • Broad Reading (Defendant, argue this) O 6 rr 7(6), 12(5) treat [an existence or exercise challenge] as not submission, removing [the Zoom trap] for [a stay sought alone].
    • Support: one textbook (para 2.058) confines the rules to [filing and serving], so [arguing FNC in court] would still submit under Zoom; per Chong (seminar), that split is not obvious, the rules being "quite encompassing".
  • Narrow Reading: Failed Existence Challenge (−) Per C&Y, if [defendant] fails on existence and takes [no further step], it has not submitted, and O 9 r 8 directions should not deem [submission] against the Ideals.
  • Narrow Reading: Failed Exercise Challenge (+) Per C&Y, r 7(6) protects only [the filing], so if [the FNC stay] fails, [defendant] submits at that point, a stay accepting that jurisdiction exists. Presently [defendant]'s challenge [succeeded / failed], so [no submission / submission / academic].
  • Why It Matters Abroad (±) if [claimant] enforces in [X], X's own rules decide whether [the Singapore stay application] was submission. Per Henry v Geoprosco, [an FNC challenge] was submission, but per IGCF v Al Jomaih (PC 2025) it is a protest, not acceptance, as REFJA s 5(3)(a)(i) also provides (J7.1.2.4).

1Start here: J2 in plain English

J2 answers the first half of the jurisdiction question: does the Singapore court have power over this defendant at all? (The second half, whether it should use that power, is J4.)

The General Division is a creature of statute. Its power over a defendant comes from s 16 SCJA, which gives three routes:

RouteProvisionLesson
Defendant served in Singapores 16(1)(a)(i)J2.1 (this lesson)
Defendant served outside Singapore as the Rules allows 16(1)(a)(ii)J3
Defendant submitss 16(1)(b)J2.2 (this lesson)
Other written law (e.g. the Companies Act service rules)ss 16(2), 17(1)(c)J2.1.3–J2.1.4
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of the court as a referee who can only blow the whistle on players who are on the pitch. A player standing on the pitch (served in Singapore) is fair game, even if he only walked on a minute ago. A player who walks onto the pitch and starts playing (submits) has accepted the referee. A player in another country can only be brought in with special permission (service out, J3).

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Originating claimThe document that starts a civil case under ROC 2021.
ServiceFormally delivering the originating claim. It gives notice and founds jurisdiction, so it is always required (O 6 r 4), even for a defendant who submits.
As of rightNo court permission needed. Presence and submission are as of right.
Founding provisionThe part of s 16 SCJA that gives the court power.
Mode of serviceThe rule saying how to serve: personally (O 7 r 2(1)(a)), on a company officer (r 2(1)(b)), on an agent with permission (r 4), at a registered office (s 387 / s 376 CA).
PresenceFor a person: physically in Singapore when served. For a never-registered foreign company: carrying on business at a fixed place here (Adams v Cape).
SubmissionAccepting the court's jurisdiction by conduct, e.g. defending on the merits.
Registered foreign companyA foreign company registered in Singapore under the Companies Act (s 368), with a local office or authorised representative.

2J2.0 Preliminary concepts

▤ On your pre-write: J2.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP (word for word)
J2.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP

(Scan first. Ask (1) does the court HAVE jurisdiction over [defendant] (s 16(1) SCJA), then (2) should it EXERCISE it (J4)? If [defendant] is abroad, go to J3. Service is always required (O 6 r 4). Pair the founding provision with the mode of service: only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence.)

  1. Preliminary concepts and limits (J2.0.2: Allenger).
  2. Service in Singapore (J2.1): individuals (Maharanee); agents (O 7 r 4; Beranek); Singapore companies (s 387 CA); registered foreign companies (s 376 CA; Tao Commodity); never-registered foreign companies (Adams v Cape; Rosenberg); partnerships and LLPs (O 56); router.
  3. Submission (J2.2: Williams & Glyn's; Zoom; Shanghai Turbo; O 6 rr 7(6), 12(5)).
  4. Exercise (J4): Spiliada stay (J4.1); overlays (J4.5).
  5. Absent defendant (J3): service out; the COSCO debate (J3.0.2).
J2.0.1 Quick Application Template

Presently, [claimant] sues [defendant], a [Singapore-resident individual / company incorporated in X / foreign company registered in Singapore], for [breach of contract / tort / restitution] arising from [events] in [X]. Existence: jurisdiction is founded on [s 16(1)(a)(i) through O 7 r 2(1)(a) / ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) through s 387 or s 376 CA / s 16(1)(a)(i) through Adams v Cape presence and O 7 r 2(1)(b) or r 4 / s 16(1)(a)(ii) through O 8 r 1 via para 63(3)[(d) / (f) / (p)] / s 16(1)(b) through submission by [filing a defence on the merits]] (J2.1; J2.2; J3.1), and [the claim] is not [title to foreign land / a foreign revenue, penal or public law claim / validity of a foreign IP right / barred by act of state or immunity] (J2.0.2). Exercise: [defendant] seeks a stay under O 6 r 7(5)(b) / r 12(4)(b); there [is / is no] breach of an [EJC / NEJC] for [Y], so [strong cause (J4.3) / Spiliada (J4.1)] applies; [Y] is available and [residence / witnesses / governing law / place of the tort / related proceedings] point to [Singapore / Y]; at stage 2 [claimant] [can / cannot] show a real risk of [delay / unfair procedure / personal danger] in [Y]. Result: the court [has / lacks] jurisdiction and [will / will not] stay.

J2.0.2 Preliminary Concepts and Statutory Framework

(short opener; subject-matter limits are not examinable, so one line at most)

  • Three Sets of Rules jurisdiction may arise in the [General Division (here)], the [SICC (J5)] or under the [CCAA (J1.2–J1.4)]. Presently [there is no jurisdiction agreement / the [Singapore / X] clause is [within / outside] the CCAA] (router: J1.0.2).
  • Existence Before Exercise per C&Y, existence comes first, so [presence on a fleeting visit] founds jurisdiction and [the weak connection] goes only to a stay (J4.1). Presence and submission are as of right, but [O 7 r 4 service on an agent] and [O 8 r 1(1) service out] need permission.
  • Statutory Source: s 16 SCJA Per Art 93 Constitution and Allenger, the General Division is a creature of statute, so [defendant] must be served [in Singapore] (s 16(1)(a)(i)), served [outside Singapore] as the Rules authorise (s 16(1)(a)(ii)), or [submit] (s 16(1)(b)), or fall within other written law (ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), e.g., ss 387, 376 CA).
  • Service Founds Jurisdiction service both gives [defendant] notice and founds jurisdiction, so even [a submitting defendant] must be served (O 6 r 4), [personally / in an agreed manner under O 7 r 2(1)(d)].
  • Founding Provision + Mode of Service (must write) state [s 16(1)(a)(i) / ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) / s 16(1)(a)(ii) / s 16(1)(b)] with [O 7 r 2(1)(a) / r 2(1)(b) / r 4 / s 387 CA / s 376 CA / O 8 r 1]. Only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence for [the foreign company] (J2.1.5).
  • Why Serve In per Zoom, after service in [defendant] bears the burden on a stay, whereas on service out [claimant] bears it if [defendant] challenges existence on forum grounds (J4.0.2).
  • Subject-Matter Jurisdiction (not examinable) Per Chong (seminar), subject-matter jurisdiction is off-syllabus except for the SICC (J5.1). If [defendant] says [the claim] is non-justiciable, one line suffices: per Allenger, s 16(1) limits only in personam jurisdiction, and the court may hear any claim "unless or until prohibited either by legislation or case law", e.g., [title to foreign land / foreign penal, revenue or public law].
  • Jurisdiction vs Power jurisdiction (ss 16–17) is authority to hear [the claim]. Per Li Shengwu, s 18 and Sch 1 concern [powers and reliefs], not [subject-matter jurisdiction], e.g., a stay under [para 9] (J4.1).
  • Inherent Power to Prevent Abuse Per Emilia Shipping, it is arguable that the court's inherent power to prevent abuse, e.g., where [defendant] was [fraudulently lured here] or [property was deceptively brought here], is unaffected by s 16 (now O 3 r 2(2)).
The five building blocks
▤ J2.0.2
  1. 1Existence before exercise. Presence on a fleeting visit founds jurisdiction; the weak connection only goes to a stay (J4.1).
  2. 2Statutory source. Per Art 93 of the Constitution and Allenger, the General Division is a creature of statute, so jurisdiction must come through s 16 SCJA (or other written law).
  3. 3Service founds jurisdiction. Even a submitting defendant must be served (O 6 r 4).
  4. 4Pair the founding provision with the mode ("must write"). Only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence for a foreign company.
  5. 5Why serve in rather than out? Per Zoom, after service in the defendant bears the burden on a stay; after service out, the claimant bears it if the defendant challenges on forum grounds (J4.0.2).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Why claimants like service in

Option 1: serve Mr Wong at the conference hotel. Jurisdiction exists as of right (s 16(1)(a)(i), O 7 r 2(1)(a)). If Mr Wong wants the case moved to Hong Kong, he must apply for a stay and show Hong Kong is clearly more appropriate (Spiliada stage 1).

Option 2: wait and serve him in Hong Kong. Alpha needs the court's approval to serve out (J3). If Mr Wong challenges on forum grounds, Alpha must show Singapore is the forum conveniens.

Same dispute, same court. Option 1 puts the uphill work on the defendant; Option 2 puts it on the claimant. That is the practical reason the existence route matters, even though in both cases the court ends up with power.

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Founding provision + mode" is a door and a key. The founding provision (a part of s 16 SCJA) is the door: it is what lets the court in. The mode of service (an Order 7 rule, or the Companies Act) is the key: it is how you actually open the door. Examiners want both named in one breath, because a key without a door (or a door with no key) gets you nowhere.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
The founding-provision-plus-mode sentence

Jurisdiction over Beta Pte Ltd is founded on ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c) SCJA through service at its registered office under s 387 CA, so Adams v Cape need not be discussed.

Jurisdiction over Mr Wong is founded on s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA through personal service under O 7 r 2(1)(a) while he was present in Singapore for the conference.

🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Subject-matter jurisdiction is off-syllabus (except the SICC's). If the defendant says the claim is non-justiciable, one line is enough: per Allenger, s 16(1) limits only in personam jurisdiction, and the court may hear any claim "unless or until prohibited either by legislation or case law" (e.g. title to foreign land, foreign penal or revenue law).

ℹ NOTE
Jurisdiction v power

Jurisdiction (ss 16–17) is authority to hear the claim. Per Li Shengwu, s 18 and Sch 1 concern powers and reliefs, such as a stay under para 9. Per Emilia Shipping, it is arguable that the court's inherent power to prevent abuse (e.g. where the defendant was fraudulently lured here) is unaffected by s 16 (now O 3 r 2(2)).

3J2.1 Service in Singapore

▤ On your pre-write: J2.1.1 Natural Person Physically Present (word for word)
J2.1.1 Natural Person Physically Present

(an individual in Singapore, however briefly)

  • Basis and Mode Per s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA, [defendant] present [at his hotel / at the trade fair] is personally served as of right under O 7 r 2(1)(a). Presence is judged at service, so it is immaterial that he [arrived that morning / left the next day].
  • Temporary Presence (+) Per Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein and Colt Industries v Sarlie, presence on [a short visit / in transit] suffices without any substantive connection, even if [the contract / accident] arose wholly in [X].
  • Fraudulently Induced Presence (−) Per Watkins v North American Land, service may be set aside for abuse of process where [claimant] lured [defendant] here by [a sham meeting], but not where he came for [business / holiday].
  • Fortuity Goes to Exercise (±) Per C&Y, [defendant]'s weak connection is irrelevant to existence but relevant to the natural forum, so [the fleeting visit] and [the foreign events] support a stay (J4.1).
  • Evaluation: Presence as the Basis (±) [Defendant] calls jurisdiction on [a short visit] arbitrary, preferring [residence / domicile / nationality]. But per Sirdar Gurdyal Singh, jurisdiction is territorial, presence is certain where [residence] is harder to prove, and FNC corrects [the fortuity].

Individuals: physical presence

🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  • Basis and mode. An individual present in Singapore is personally served as of right: s 16(1)(a)(i) with O 7 r 2(1)(a). Presence is judged at the moment of service, so arriving that morning or leaving next day does not matter.
  • Temporary presence is enough (+). Per Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein and Colt Industries v Sarlie, a short visit or transit suffices, without any substantive connection.
  • Fraudulently induced presence (−). Per Watkins v North American Land, service may be set aside as an abuse where the claimant lured the defendant here with a sham meeting, but not where he came for business or a holiday.
  • Fortuity goes to exercise. Per C&Y, the weak connection is irrelevant to existence but supports a stay (J4.1).
  • Evaluation. Is presence arbitrary? Per Sirdar Gurdyal Singh, jurisdiction is territorial, presence is certain where residence is harder to prove, and forum non conveniens corrects the fortuity.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The trade fair

A German businessman attends a two-day trade fair in Singapore and is handed the originating claim at his hotel. The contract was made and performed in Germany. The court has jurisdiction (s 16(1)(a)(i), O 7 r 2(1)(a); Maharanee). Whether it should hear the case is a separate question: the German connections support a stay under Spiliada.

Change the reason he came. Suppose the claimant invented a "settlement meeting" in Singapore purely to get him here and serve him. Now the presence was fraudulently induced, and per Watkins the service may be set aside as an abuse. The line is: why was he here? A real trip (business, a holiday, a trade fair) is fine; a trap is not.

? WHY IT MATTERS
Why such a thin connection is allowed

It can feel unfair that a two-day visit gives Singapore power over a German contract. The answer is the two-stage design. Existence is kept simple and certain (was he here when served?), because presence is easy to prove and hard to argue about. Fairness is handled at the second stage, where a defendant with no real link to Singapore can ask for a stay (J4.1). Per Sirdar Gurdyal Singh, forum non conveniens corrects the fortuity.

J2.1.2 An agent of an absent individual (O 7 r 4)

▤ On your pre-write: J2.1.2 Agent of an Absent Natural Person (O 7 r 4) (word for word)
J2.1.2 Agent of an Absent Natural Person (O 7 r 4)

([defendant] abroad; [agent] manages his affairs here)

  • O 7 r 4 Requirements With permission on a without-notice summons, [agent] may be served for [defendant] if (a) [defendant] does not reside in or is absent from Singapore; (b) at service [agent] personally controls or manages here [defendant]'s affairs specifically relating to [the action]; and (c) [agent]'s authority subsists or there is an ongoing business relationship.
  • Founding Provision and Formalities Per Beranek, O 7 r 4 rests on s 16(1)(a)(i), [defendant] being constructively present through [agent] (J3.0.2). Per C&Y, [claimant] must also post [the order and the claim] to [defendant]'s address abroad within 14 days.
  • Control or Management [Agent] must actually control [the affairs sued on], not merely [relay messages]. Rosenberg's power-to-contract test is framed for companies (J2.1.5), but per C&Y "affairs" reaches [any affairs] of an individual.
  • Exceptional (−) Per C&Y, under the old O 10 r 2 its use against [an overseas individual] was a "rare case", and the English Practice Direction required "great caution", refusing it where [claimant] could easily [serve out].
  • Liberalised (+) Per C&Y, "affairs" replaced "business or work", [O 8] has liberalised service out and [permission] is needed anyway, so O 7 r 4 now applies more readily to [defendant].
  • Service Out Available? (±) [Defendant] argues permission should be refused because [claimant] could serve out under [O 8]. Per C&Y, O 7 r 4 is not meant to make O 8 otiose, but it is unclear that permission should be withheld as a matter of course.
  • Founding provision. Per Beranek, O 7 r 4 rests on s 16(1)(a)(i): the defendant is constructively present through the agent.
  • Exceptional or liberalised? (±) Under the old O 10 r 2 its use against an overseas individual was a "rare case", and the English Practice Direction required "great caution". But per C&Y, "affairs" replaced "business or work", O 8 has liberalised service out and permission is needed anyway, so r 4 now applies more readily.
  • Could the claimant serve out instead? Per C&Y, r 4 is not meant to make O 8 otiose, but it is unclear that permission should be withheld as a matter of course.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The landlord abroad

Mr Lee lives in Jakarta and owns a condominium in Singapore. A Singapore property manager, under a continuing management agreement, finds tenants, signs leases for him and handles complaints. A tenant wants to sue Mr Lee over the lease.

  • (a) Mr Lee does not reside in Singapore. ✓
  • (b) The manager personally manages Mr Lee's affairs relating to this very lease. ✓
  • (c) The management agreement is still running. ✓

So the tenant can apply for permission to serve the manager under O 7 r 4, founded on s 16(1)(a)(i): Mr Lee is treated as present through his agent (Beranek).

Contrast: if the only person in Singapore were Mr Lee's cousin, who forwards his post and passes on messages, limb (b) fails. Relaying messages is not controlling or managing his affairs, so the tenant must serve out (J3).

J2.1.3 to J2.1.4 Companies on the register

▤ On your pre-write: J2.1.3 Company Incorporated in Singapore (word for word)
J2.1.3 Company Incorporated in Singapore
  • Basis and Mode Per ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) SCJA, service of [the originating claim] under s 387 CA by [leaving it at / registered post to] [company]'s registered office founds jurisdiction, so Adams v Cape need not be discussed. Per Chong (seminar), in the exam simply state this pathway; the academic argument that [presence / submission] is still needed is not covered.
▤ On your pre-write: J2.1.4 Registered Foreign Company (s 376 CA) (word for word)
J2.1.4 Registered Foreign Company (s 376 CA)

(select [company]'s current status)

  • Registrability: ss 365, 368 per s 365, [company] that [establishes a place of business / carries on business] in Singapore, or intends to, must register under s 368 first, lodging [its Singapore registered office] and [its authorised representative].
  • Carrying On Business: s 366 Per s 366(1), business includes [administering property as agent or trustee]. Per s 366(2), it excludes merely [litigating / internal meetings / a bank account / independent-contractor sales / orders accepted abroad / an isolated transaction within 31 days / holding property], so [company]'s [activity] [is / is not] business.
  • Scenario A: Registered and Trading (+) Per ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), [company] is served under s 376(a) ([its Singapore registered office]) or s 376(b) ([its authorised representative's residential or contact address]), without Adams v Cape.
  • Scenario B: Ceased Business, Not Deregistered (+) Per s 376(c), [company] that "has ceased to maintain a place of business in Singapore" is served at [its registered office in X], or under (a)–(b) if [the Singapore office / representative] remains.
  • Scenario C: Ceased and Deregistered (−) Per Tao Commodity, s 376 is unavailable after [deregistration], registration having supplied the nexus, so [claimant] must serve [company] out in [X] (J3.1).
  • Scenario C: Reply (+) But per C&Y, the plain words of s 376(c) cover [the deregistered company], ceasing business being the precursor to deregistration, and the purpose is that [companies that traded here] cannot escape [local creditors]. Tao is a Registry decision unreviewed by the CA.
  • Does s 376 Confer Jurisdiction? (±) Route 1 (C&Y, run this): s 376 itself confers jurisdiction via ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), to spare [local creditors] from [service out]. Route 2 (Tao): registration is "a statutory parallel to or substitute for" corporate presence, s 376 being only [the mode of service]. Both cover Scenarios A–B, but only Route 1 survives [deregistration].
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A company is not a person you can hand papers to on the street. So the law uses its address on the register. A Singapore company is served at its registered office (s 387 CA). A foreign company that has registered here is served at its Singapore office or through its authorised representative (s 376 CA). The hard case is a foreign company that has stopped trading and taken itself off the register.

PointRule
Singapore companyss 16(2), 17(1)(c) SCJA through s 387 CA (leave at, or post to, the registered office). Adams v Cape need not be discussed. Per Chong (seminar), just state this pathway.
Who must registers 365: a foreign company that establishes a place of business or carries on business here (or intends to) must register under s 368.
What is "business"s 366(1) includes administering property as agent or trustee. s 366(2) excludes merely litigating, internal meetings, a bank account, independent-contractor sales, orders accepted abroad, an isolated transaction within 31 days, holding property.
Does s 376 itself confer jurisdiction? (±)Route 1 (C&Y, run this): yes, via ss 16(2), 17(1)(c), to spare local creditors from service out. Route 2 (Tao): registration is "a statutory parallel to or substitute for" presence; s 376 is only the mode. Both cover Scenarios A–B; only Route 1 survives deregistration.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three foreign companies, three scenarios
CompanyFactsScenarioWhat to write
AusCo (Australia)Registered, still runs a Singapore branch officeAServe at the registered office or on the authorised representative: s 376(a)/(b) with ss 16(2), 17(1)(c). No Adams v Cape.
UKCo (England)Registered, closed its Singapore office last year, still on the registerBs 376(c): serve at its registered office in England, or under (a)/(b) if an office or representative remains.
IndCo (India)Registered, then stopped trading and was deregisteredCArgue both: (−) Tao says s 376 is gone, so serve out; (+) C&Y says the plain words of s 376(c) still cover it, and Tao was a Registry decision.

And a fourth company that never needed to register: a Thai company whose only Singapore link is a bank account. A bank account is excluded from "carrying on business" (s 366(2)), so it never registered, and it has no place of business here either. Neither s 376 nor Adams v Cape helps: serve out (J3.1).

J2.1.5 The never-registered foreign company: Adams v Cape

▤ On your pre-write: J2.1.5 Never-Registered Foreign Company (word for word)
J2.1.5 Never-Registered Foreign Company

(s 376 unavailable; s 16(1)(a)(i) is the founding provision, so Adams v Cape must be written)

  • s 376 Unavailable (must write) although Division 2 applies to [a registrable but unregistered company] (s 365), per C&Y s 376(a)–(b) fail with [no Singapore office or representative] and (c), read holistically, is not meant for [a company still trading here]. So [claimant] relies on s 16(1)(a)(i) and must prove presence.
  • Limb 1: Fixed Place Per Adams v Cape, [company] is present if it carries on business at or from a reasonably permanent fixed place, e.g., [its office at address], whether it [owns / leases / licenses] it. Per Littauer Glove, [a representative taking orders from a hotel for a few days] is not enough.
  • Limb 2: More Than a Minimal Period [company] must be there for more than a minimal period. Per Dunlop v Cudell, [a nine-day trade-fair stand] sufficed, unlike [a one-day visit].
  • Limb 3: Whose Business? where [company] acts through [a representative], it is present only if he carries on [company]'s business, not his own (Okura), shown by [premises acquired for him / fixed pay vs commission / degree of control].
  • Power to Contract (±) Per Adams v Cape, the key question is whether [the representative] can [bind company] without prior approval. Per C&Y, that power is neither exclusive nor conclusive, and [the agent] may also run [its own business] from the same place.
  • Non-Trading Company Per Adams v Cape, where [company] is [a charity / holding company], substitute [its corporate activities] for "business".
  • Mode 1: Officer (O 7 r 2(1)(b), as of right) if [company] is present, [claimant] leaves the claim with [its chairperson / president / secretary / treasurer / other officer]. Per Yeo and Beranek (J3.0.2), it is [company]'s own presence that counts, so serving [an officer on holiday] when [company] is absent is doubtful (contra COSCO; B Atmaram).
  • Mode 2: Agent (O 7 r 4, with permission) Per Rosenberg, [agent] must be obliged to bring [the claim] to [company]'s notice, [company] must carry on business at a fixed place here, and [agent] must have power to contract, otherwise [company] trades "through", not "by", him. Per C&Y, [agent] need not be [a full-time employee].
  • O 7 r 4: Link to the Action (−) Per Rosenberg, the action must relate to [the business agent manages]. Where [the cheques were drawn by the head office in X] and [agent] could do only [liaison work], service is set aside and [claimant] must serve out.
  • O 7 r 4 Narrower Than Adams v Cape Per C&Y, r 4 needs [power to contract], control of affairs specifically relating to [the action], and [permission], none of which Adams v Cape requires. So [claimant] prefers r 2(1)(b) and pleads presence alongside.
  • Unregistrable: No Place of Business (−) where [company] merely [holds a bank account / accepts orders in X] (s 366(2)) or [sells online from X] (no virtual presence: Lucasfilm, by analogy), neither s 376 nor Adams v Cape applies. [Claimant] serves out (J3.1), unless [an agent here] satisfies O 7 r 4 or [Singapore solicitors] accept service (J2.2.2).

This is the one place where you must write Adams v Cape. Section 376 is unavailable (no Singapore office or representative, and s 376(c) is not meant for a company still trading here), so the claimant relies on s 16(1)(a)(i) and must prove the company is present.

🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  • Fixed place. Per Adams v Cape, a reasonably permanent fixed place, owned, leased or licensed. Per Littauer Glove, a representative taking orders from a hotel for a few days is not enough.
  • More than a minimal period. Per Dunlop v Cudell, a nine-day trade-fair stand sufficed, unlike a one-day visit.
  • Whose business? Per Okura, if the company acts through a representative, he must carry on the company's business, not his own: look at who acquired the premises, fixed pay v commission, degree of control.
  • Power to contract (±). Per Adams v Cape, the key question is whether the representative can bind the company without prior approval; per C&Y that power is neither exclusive nor conclusive.
  • Non-trading company. For a charity or holding company, substitute its corporate activities for "business".
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three salespeople, one test

A never-registered Italian furniture maker, Mobili SpA, has someone selling for it in Singapore. Is Mobili present?

The salespersonLimb that decides itPresent?
Paola flies in four times a year and takes orders from her hotel room for a few days each time.Limb 1: no reasonably permanent fixed place (Littauer Glove).No
Marco runs Mobili's stand at a nine-day furniture fair, signing orders on the spot.Limbs 1 and 2: a fixed stand for more than a minimal period (Dunlop v Cudell).Yes, for those nine days
Mr Lim runs his own showroom, sells ten brands including Mobili's, rents the premises himself and is paid only by commission.Limb 3: he carries on his own business, and Mobili trades through him, not by him (Okura).Probably not

For Marco's case, the claimant then serves an officer as of right (O 7 r 2(1)(b)) or applies to serve an agent (O 7 r 4). For Paola and Mr Lim, the claimant should plan to serve out (J3.1).

Mode of service once presentRule
Officer (O 7 r 2(1)(b), as of right)Leave the claim with the chairperson, president, secretary, treasurer or other officer. Per Yeo and Beranek, it is the company's own presence that counts, so serving an officer on holiday when the company is absent is doubtful (contra COSCO; B Atmaram).
Agent (O 7 r 4, with permission)Per Rosenberg: the agent must be obliged to bring the claim to the company's notice, the company must carry on business at a fixed place here, and the agent must have power to contract. The action must relate to the business the agent manages: where cheques were drawn by the head office abroad and the agent did only liaison work, service was set aside.
Which to prefer?Per C&Y, r 4 is narrower than Adams v Cape (power to contract, link to the action, permission), so plead r 2(1)(b) and presence alongside.
No place of business at allA bank account, orders accepted abroad, or online sales from abroad (no virtual presence: Lucasfilm, by analogy): neither s 376 nor Adams v Cape. Serve out (J3.1), unless an agent satisfies r 4 or Singapore solicitors accept service.

J2.1.6 to J2.1.7 Partnerships and the router

▤ On your pre-write: J2.1.6 Partnerships and LLPs (word for word)
J2.1.6 Partnerships and LLPs

(no separate personality, except the LLP)

  • Firm Name (O 56 r 1) [Claimant] may sue [the partnership / limited partnership] in its firm name if [the partners] carry on business here. Per C&Y, this gives no in personam jurisdiction, so each [partner] to be made liable must be served or submit.
  • Mode of Service (O 56 r 3(1)) serve [any partner] or [the person controlling the business at the principal place of business]; if [the firm] is dissolved, serve every partner in Singapore.
  • Sole Trader (O 56 r 9) (−) Per C&Y, r 9 does not reach [a non-resident foreign individual] trading here through [an agent], who would otherwise be worse off than [a foreign partnership], with all his Singapore assets exposed.
  • LLP Per C&Y, [the LLP] is a body corporate served [at its registered office] under LLP Act s 93 (by analogy s 387 CA), which should found jurisdiction since [s 17 SCJA] is not exhaustive.
  • Firm name (O 56 r 1): a partnership carrying on business here may be sued in its firm name, but per C&Y this gives no in personam jurisdiction, so each partner to be made liable must be served or submit.
  • Mode (O 56 r 3(1)): serve any partner, or the person controlling the business at the principal place of business.
  • Sole trader (O 56 r 9) (−): per C&Y, does not reach a non-resident foreign individual trading here through an agent.
  • LLP: a body corporate served at its registered office under LLP Act s 93 (by analogy s 387 CA).
▤ On your pre-write: J2.1.7 Router: Pair Status, Founding Provision and Mode (word for word)
J2.1.7 Router: Pair Status, Founding Provision and Mode
  • Individual [present here] → s 16(1)(a)(i) with O 7 r 2(1)(a); [abroad with an agent here] → O 7 r 4 (permission); otherwise [serve out] (J3.1).
  • Singapore Company [company]'s [registered office here] → ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) with s 387 by [leaving it / registered post].
  • Registered and Trading [company] on [the ACRA register] and [trading here] → ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) with s 376(a) or (b).
