    • O 7 r 4: per Yeo, it addresses [absent principals], supplies its own nexus ([agent]'s control of the affairs the action relates to) and needs permission, so it fits limb (ii); the Rules' in/out division need not match the SCJA's.
    • No nexus, no (ii): per Yeo, substituted service and service on [officers of foreign companies] set out no nexus, so cannot rest on (ii) and cannot reach [an absent defendant] at all.
    • Policy: per Yeo, the 1993 amendments confirmed the pre-1963 structure (territorial service as of right, extraterritorial service on connecting factors, submission); reading (i) to cover [absent defendants] "sends the wrong signal" about [Singapore]'s reach.
  • Beranek: Constructive Presence Per Beranek, the limbs divide by whether [defendant] is present, actually or constructively, when [served].
    • COSCO reached the right result for the wrong reason: [the foreign company] was constructively present through [solicitors authorised to accept service].
    • O 7 r 4 rests on limb (i): [the principal] is deemed present through [agent]. The rule asks about [agent]'s authority, not whether Singapore is appropriate; were it service out, it would sit in O 8.
    • O 7 r 2(1)(b) requires [the company itself] to be present, not merely [its officer].
  • Lecturer's Position (submit) The limbs divide by where [defendant] is. Authorising [Singapore solicitors] to accept service is submission (s 16(1)(b)), a waiver of the O 8 hoops, not "deemed presence": [the solicitors] do not carry on [defendant]'s business here (Adams v Cape).
    • O 7 r 2(1)(b) and r 4: per Chong (mid-term feedback), in line with Beranek, both arguably rest on limb (i), not (ii) (cf COSCO), so [the company] must be present and [the officer or agent] is merely the mode.
    • Rosenberg: [agent] must have power to contract, so [company] trades "by" and not merely "through" him — a strong sign [company] is present (J2.1.5). Per the slides, r 4 also reaches [a natural person] principal (J2.1.2).
    • Anomaly: per Chong (citing Toh Kian Sing), if [agent]'s control means [company] is present, how is it "absent" under O 7 r 4(a)? Unresolved; flag it in one line.
  • The Chairperson-on-Holiday Problem Presently [the dispute] is wholly foreign ([contract made and goods delivered in X]) and [the chairperson] is merely on holiday here. Per Chong (mid-term feedback), the defendant is [the company], not [the chairperson].
    • So: serving [him] under O 7 r 2(1)(b) founds jurisdiction only if [the company] is itself present (Adams v Cape; J2.1.5); Maharanee of Baroda (transient presence) is for [a natural person defendant].
    • His presence: only the practical precondition for handing [him] the papers. Without [company] presence, this is service on [an absent company], which belongs in O 8 (Week 6 slides).
    • Alternative: if [he] is here doing [the company]'s business, use O 7 r 4, meeting all of r 4(1), including control of the affairs [the action] relates to.
    • Bottom line: otherwise [claimant] could skip both Adams v Cape and O 8 by serving [the CEO] on holiday.
  • Which Route Is Most Onerous (practice) Per the slides, O 7 r 2(1)(b) is as of right, O 7 r 4 needs permission (not as of right), and O 8 r 1(1) "appropriate court" needs approval on three requirements, burden on [claimant]. So advise [claimant] to serve [defendant] in wherever it can (J2.1.6).

Before service out, ask whether the defendant can be served in Singapore after all. That sounds simple, but there is a live debate about what s 16(1)(a)(i) and (ii) actually divide.

ViewWhat divides limb (i) from limb (ii)?Consequence
COSCOWhere service occurs. A foreign company that agreed to be served through its Singapore solicitors was served in Singapore under O 7 r 2(1)(d).Easier for claimants; the judge accepted the chairman could also be served here under O 7 r 2(1)(b).
Yeo (YPH lecture)Where the defendant is. Limb (i) needs only a manner of service because the defendant's presence is the nexus; limb (ii) adds "circumstances authorised".Serving an officer on holiday cannot catch an absent company; solicitors accepting service is submission.
BeranekWhether the defendant is present, actually or constructively.COSCO right result, wrong reason (constructive presence through solicitors); O 7 r 4 rests on limb (i).
Prof Chong (submit this)Where the defendant is. Authorising solicitors is submission, not deemed presence.O 7 r 2(1)(b) and r 4 arguably rest on limb (i), so the company must be present.
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

The defendant is the company, not the chairperson. Maharanee of Baroda (transient presence) is for a natural person defendant. Otherwise a claimant could skip both Adams v Cape and O 8 just by serving the CEO on holiday. Also, always state first that the defendant cannot be served here (it is abroad, unregistered and has not instructed Singapore solicitors).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Answering the Kraft GmbH question
  1. Who is the defendant? Kraft GmbH, the company, not Herr Braun. His own presence would found jurisdiction over him (Maharanee), but he is not being sued.
  2. Is the company present? No office, staff or place of business here, so Adams v Cape fails (J2.1.5). Serving its chairman under O 7 r 2(1)(b) therefore does not catch it.
  3. O 7 r 4? Herr Braun is on holiday, not doing Kraft's business here, so the agent route fails too.
  4. So: Alpha must go through O 8, with approval, nexus and forum (J3.1).

If the opposite were allowed, a claimant could bypass every protection in O 8 just by waiting for a CEO to visit Singapore.

ℹ NOTE
Which route is most onerous?

O 7 r 2(1)(b) is as of right; O 7 r 4 needs permission; O 8 r 1(1) "appropriate court" needs approval on three requirements with the burden on the claimant. So advise the claimant to serve in wherever it can.

3J3.1 Service out: the framework

▤ On your pre-write: J3.1.1 Starter (word for word)
J3.1.1 Starter

Presently, [defendant] is in [X] and cannot be served here (J3.0.2). Per s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA, jurisdiction exists where [defendant] is served outside Singapore "in the circumstances authorised by and in the manner prescribed by" the ROC: jurisdiction with approval, not as of right.

  • Approval Per O 8 r 1(1), [the originating process] may be served out on [defendant] with approval where the court "has the jurisdiction" or "is the appropriate court".
  • Application Per O 8 r 1(2) and PD para 63(1), (4), [claimant] applies by summons without notice, with an affidavit stating why, where [defendant] is or may be found, and whether [the process]'s validity needs extending.
  • No Approval Needed Per O 8 r 1(3), none where [the contract] allows service out (J3.1.5); per O 8 r 1(4), approval for the originating process carries [later court documents] with it.
  • Route 1: "Has the Jurisdiction" Per C&Y, this presumably covers [an exclusive choice of court agreement] designating Singapore under the CCAA, where the chosen court must hear [the case] and cannot decline for forum non conveniens (CCAA s 11; J1.3). Per Chong (answer scheme), [the CCAA contract] goes on this ground.
    • Why (Yeo): read with s 16(1)(a)(ii), the limb is circular, so "has the jurisdiction" must mean jurisdiction under other written law (s 16(2) SCJA), i.e., [the General Division] as exclusively chosen court in [a Hague case].
    • Puzzle: per C&Y, if [the court] already "has" jurisdiction, it is unclear why approval is needed or on what criteria [the AR] decides.
    • Other chosen-court cases: per Yeo, where [the General Division] is chosen outside the CCAA, use "appropriate court", easily met since [defendant] must show strong cause (J3.2).
    • Agreement ≠ jurisdiction: per Yeo (citing British Wagon v Gray), [consent] alone confers no jurisdiction; an agreement to submit is not submission under s 16(1)(b) but a nexus for service out on [defendant].
    • Exercise challenge: per C&Y, outside the CCAA [defendant] may still challenge exercise (forum non conveniens, or strong cause for [a non-CCAA EJC]), the burden being on [defendant], as in a service-in case (J4).
    • SICC: per SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2), no permission is needed to serve [a party to a written jurisdiction agreement], or where [the agreement] allows service out; otherwise per O 5 r 6(1) the SICC must "have the jurisdiction" and be "appropriate" (J5).
  • Route 2: "Appropriate Court" Per PD para 63(2), restating Zoom's common law requirements, [claimant] shows (a) a good arguable case of sufficient nexus; (b) Singapore is forum conveniens; (c) a serious question to be tried against [defendant].
    • Together: per Recovery Vehicle 1, the three are assessed for consistency, not in isolation, so a finding on [the gateway] must square with [the merits].
  • Thresholds [Claimant] needs a good arguable case on [the nexus]: "the better of the argument" (Vinmar), more than a prima facie case (Bradley Lomas), but not "a much better argument" or a balance of probabilities. It needs only a serious question on [the merits] (Bradley Lomas).
  • Why Extraterritorial Jurisdiction (handout Q) Per Week 6 notes, disputes with [absent defendants] strongly connected with Singapore ([a Singapore contract / a tort here / Singapore assets]) should be triable here; otherwise [claimant] is forced abroad even where Singapore is the natural forum.
  • From Exorbitant to Appropriate Traditionally service out was "exorbitant": jurisdiction is territorial and serving [defendant] in [X] intrudes on [X]'s sovereignty, hence circumspection and the burden on [claimant] (Consistel).
    • Now: per Abela v Baadarani and Four Seasons v Brownlie (adopted by C&Y), there are no "muscular presumptions" against serving [defendant] in [X]: the decision is "a pragmatic one in the interests of efficient conduct of litigation in an appropriate forum" — "extraordinary", not "exorbitant".
    • Why (Yeo): what reaches [X] is notice of [the proceedings], not a sovereign command. Singapore courts still say "exorbitant" but mean comity-based caution; keep the caution of Société Générale v Dreyfus before hauling [a foreigner] here.
  • Why the Reform (CJC Report) Per the CJC Report, r 1(1) prescribes criteria rather than a list, so [claimant] need not scrutinise "the long list ... in the hope of fitting into one or more descriptions", and no [category that should be heard here] is accidentally omitted.
    • Cautious: per C&Y, Singapore did not adopt forum conveniens as [the sole test], but is bolder than [England], whose PD gateways remain closed.
  • Why Keep the Gateways Per Foxton J (adopted by C&Y), they supply "an objective, justifiable and ... internationally recognised nexus", which matters for comity, for recognition of [the Singapore judgment] in [X], and in the competitive dispute resolution market; the natural forum test alone "is rather more judgmental".
    • Distinct roles: per Four Seasons v Brownlie, gateways set the legal maximum of [jurisdiction]; forum conveniens only limits it and never enlarges [the court's reach].
  • One Gateway (Yeo, evaluative) Per Yeo, Singapore now has one gateway, "sufficient nexus", within the court's bounded discretion, so [a claim] outside every listed factor may still qualify. Technically [a claim] within a factor could still lack sufficient nexus, but since the reform liberalises, that is probably not intended.
    • Critique: per Yeo, it risks being "an open territory with no fence", since almost any [claim] fits (n); Singapore may answer by weighing substantive connections at the forum stage, or by a "real and substantial connection" test within [sufficient nexus].
    • Territoriality survives: per Week 6 notes, in residual form: [the factors] supply a recognised nexus, comity counsels caution, [Singapore judgments] need presence or submission abroad, and the Moçambique rule remains.
  • Is the Reform Significant? (evaluative) Partly. Per C&Y, the heads survive almost word for word, and Li Shengwu had already made (n) near open-ended. The real change is conceptual: a non-exhaustive list, no pro-[defendant] construction, appropriateness rather than [fitting a statutory box], and room to expand.
  • Round 1: Without Notice Only [claimant] is before [the AR]. Per C&Y, [claimant] bears the burden and owes full and frank disclosure of matters against it ([defendant]'s links with [X], the foreign proceedings, gateway weaknesses).
    • Non-disclosure: per Zoom and C&Y, material non-disclosure by [claimant] can found a set-aside unless [defendant] waived it.
  • Round 2: Inter Partes [Defendant] applies to set aside under O 6 r 7(5)(a) / r 12(4)(a) (5 weeks if served out); jurisdiction falls with the service. Per Zoom and Li Shengwu, the legal burden stays on [claimant] on all three requirements, though practically higher now [defendant] contests.
    • Flexibility: per C&Y (citing NML Capital and IM Skaugen), absent abuse [claimant] may rely on [a new cause of action / gateway] not in the without-notice application, and the court weighs [developments after approval].
    • Evidential burden: [defendant] must evidence its own counter-arguments, e.g., that [the contract] is governed by [X] law. Practice: per Chong (seminar), attack on all fronts, even where [one requirement] looks conclusive.
  • Nexus Per Claim Per C&Y and IM Skaugen (CA), a factor must be shown for each claim against each [defendant], so [contract and tort] claims need one each. One factor per claim suffices, the factors being disjunctive (Li Shengwu, citing Tassell v Hallen).
    • No aggregation: per IM Skaugen (CA), [distinct claims] cannot be pooled, and an assignment does not merge [the assigned claims] into one aggregate claim.
    • Exception: per C&Y, (a) turns on [defendant], not the claim. Approval may be granted on terms or for part of [the claim].
  • Interpreting the Factors Per C&Y: read [the factors] more liberally now they sit in a PD; no need to resolve doubts in [defendant]'s favour; old O 11 case law still helps; English (PD 6B) and NSW cases help with care.
    • Choice of law: per C&Y, Singapore choice of law rules decide whether [a "contract" exists] or [a claim is "founded on a tort"] (C2; C3).
  • Defendant's Options When Served Out (handout) Presently, [defendant] has been served in [X] and must choose:
    • Ignore: risks [a default judgment], though it may be unenforceable in [X], where its assets are, if [X] requires presence or submission.
    • Set aside (existence): no nexus, no serious question, Singapore not forum conveniens, or non-disclosure; burden on [claimant]; usually [defendant]'s best first move (J4.2).
    • Stay (exercise): forum non conveniens or [a foreign EJC / arbitration clause]; burden on [defendant] (J4.1).
    • Defend on the merits (submission), or go on the offensive: sue in [X] or seek an ASI against [claimant] (J6).
    • What decides it: where the burden lies, the strength of [the nexus], where [defendant]'s assets are, costs, and the submission risk.
  • Recognition Implication (evaluative) Per Week 6 slides, O 8 jurisdiction is not internationally recognised at common law, which looks only to presence in, or submission to, [the adjudicating forum] (J7). So [the Singapore judgment] may be unenforceable in [X] or wherever [defendant]'s assets lie; weigh this before preferring Singapore.

Two grounds for approval

GroundWhenNotes
"Has the jurisdiction" (Route 1)Presumably an exclusive Singapore clause under the CCAA (s 11): the chosen court must hear the case (C&Y; Chong's answer scheme puts the CCAA contract here)Per Yeo, the limb would be circular otherwise, so it means jurisdiction under other written law (s 16(2) SCJA). Per C&Y, it is a puzzle why approval is needed at all. Outside the CCAA, use "appropriate court" (easily met, since the defendant must show strong cause).
"Appropriate court" (Route 2)Everything elsePD para 63(2), restating Zoom: (a) good arguable case of nexus; (b) forum conveniens; (c) serious question. Per Recovery Vehicle 1, assessed together for consistency.
🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  • Thresholds. Good arguable case on the nexus ("the better of the argument", Vinmar; more than prima facie, Bradley Lomas). Only a serious question on the merits.
  • Round 1 (without notice). Only the claimant is before the registrar. It bears the burden and owes full and frank disclosure of points against it; material non-disclosure can found a set-aside (Zoom).
  • Round 2 (inter partes). The defendant applies to set aside (O 6 r 7(5)(a) / r 12(4)(a); 5 weeks if served out). Per Zoom and Li Shengwu, the legal burden stays on the claimant on all three requirements. Absent abuse, the claimant may rely on a new cause of action or factor (NML Capital; IM Skaugen).
  • Nexus per claim. A factor for each claim against each defendant (IM Skaugen (CA)); one factor per claim is enough (Li Shengwu). Distinct claims cannot be pooled, and an assignment does not merge them.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Full and frank disclosure

In Round 1, Alpha's affidavit says nothing about the fact that Beta had already sued Alpha in Bangkok over the same contract. That fact plainly matters to forum conveniens. In Round 2, Beta raises it. Material non-disclosure can itself found a set-aside (Zoom), quite apart from whether Singapore really is the right forum.

The lesson for a claimant: put the bad points in your own affidavit. For a defendant: always check what the claimant told the registrar, because an omission is a free extra ground of attack.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
One factor per claim

Alpha sues Beta (Thailand) on two claims: (1) breach of a contract negotiated and concluded at Alpha's Singapore office, and (2) negligent misstatement for a report Beta's engineers wrote in Bangkok, on which Alpha relied in Singapore.

  • Claim 1: para 63(3)(d)(i), made here.
  • Claim 2: needs its own factor. (f)(i) fails (the act was in Bangkok); try (f)(ii), damage here, if Alpha's loss was suffered in Singapore and is not "merely trivial".

Alpha cannot borrow the contract's factor for the tort claim: claims are not pooled (IM Skaugen (CA)). If claim 2 has no factor, approval to serve it out fails, even though claim 1 goes ahead.

🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Attack on all fronts, even where one requirement looks conclusive. And when you name a factor, name the sub-limb: "para 63(3)(d)(i)", not just "(d)".

Why service out at all? (the evaluation points)

From "exorbitant" to "appropriate"
▤ J3.1.1, evaluative points
  1. 1Traditionally exorbitant. Jurisdiction is territorial and serving abroad intrudes on another State's sovereignty, hence circumspection and the burden on the claimant (Consistel).
  2. 2Now pragmatic. Per Abela v Baadarani and Four Seasons v Brownlie (adopted by C&Y), no "muscular presumptions" against service out: "extraordinary", not "exorbitant". Per Yeo, what reaches the foreign State is notice, not a sovereign command.
  3. 3Why the reform. Per the CJC Report, criteria replace a closed list, so claimants need not hunt "the long list ... in the hope of fitting into one or more descriptions".
  4. 4Why keep the factors. Per Foxton J (adopted by C&Y), they give "an objective, justifiable and ... internationally recognised nexus"; per Four Seasons, gateways set the maximum and forum conveniens only limits it.
  5. 5One gateway? Per Yeo, Singapore now has one gateway, "sufficient nexus", which risks "an open territory with no fence". Per C&Y, the heads survive almost word for word; the real change is conceptual.
  6. 6Recognition risk. Per the Week 6 slides, O 8 jurisdiction is not recognised at common law abroad, which looks only to presence or submission (J7), so the Singapore judgment may be unenforceable where the assets are.
The defendant's options when served out
▤ J3.1.1 (handout)
  1. 1Ignore: risks a default judgment, though it may be unenforceable in the defendant's home State.
  2. 2Set aside (existence): usually the best first move, since the burden stays on the claimant (J4.2).
  3. 3Stay (exercise): forum non conveniens or a foreign clause; burden on the defendant (J4.1).
  4. 4Defend on the merits (submission), or go on the offensive: sue at home or seek an ASI (J6).

4J3.1.2 Requirement (a): picking the para 63(3) factor

▤ On your pre-write: J3.1.2 Requirement (a): Good Arguable Case of Nexus (the para 63(3) Factors) (word for word)
J3.1.2 Requirement (a): Good Arguable Case of Nexus (the para 63(3) Factors)

(select the factor(s); plead several in the alternative, then the non-exhaustive fallback; mark each as merits-engaging or neutral for J3.1.4)

  • (a) Domicile, Residence, Business or Property: Nature [Claimant] seeks relief against [defendant], who is [domiciled / ordinarily resident / carrying on business / has property] in Singapore. Per Elan Impex, [claimant] must show a good arguable case basis to seek relief from [defendant].
    • Catch-all: the connection is with [defendant], not [the claim], so [contract, tort and restitution] claims can all be lumped under (a).
    • Neutral: (a) says nothing about [the merits], so requirement (c) must be proved separately against [defendant] (J3.1.4).
  • (a) Domicile Per C&Y, Singapore law decides domicile. Per Peters Roger, [defendant]'s domicile of origin ([father's if legitimate and born in his lifetime / mother's otherwise]) persists until a domicile of choice is acquired by voluntary residence plus an intention to remain and make a home in [country].
    • Citizens: the Women's Charter s 3(5) presumption that [Singapore citizens] are domiciled here may guide [the court], though arguably it is confined to family matters (C&Y).
    • Company: per Gasque v IRC, [company] is domiciled in [its place of incorporation].
  • (a) Ordinary Residence Per Levene v IRC, residence "with some degree of continuity and apart from accidental or temporary absences", voluntarily adopted with settled purpose (Tjong Very Sumito); here [defendant]'s [years in Singapore / employment here] [suffice / do not].
    • Companies: per C&Y, no uniform meaning; the tax test (central management and control) is inapt for [amenability], and it is strongly arguable that Adams v Cape presence of [company] establishes ordinary residence.
  • (a) Carrying on Business Per C&Y, it applies to [individuals] as well as [companies], with no fixed-place or minimal-period requirement on the wording, so it appears enough that [defendant] is carrying on business here when permission is sought.
  • (a) Property Per Lehman Brothers, [the property, e.g., shares / a bank account] need not relate to [the claim]; per Bunge it need not be substantial (a share in a Singapore subsidiary sufficed). But: per C&Y, insubstantial [property] weakens the forum analysis under (b).
  • (b) Injunction [Claimant] seeks an injunction ordering [defendant] to do or refrain from [X] in Singapore. Per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar v Chilton, it must be part of the substantive relief with a reasonable prospect of grant.
    • Not enough: an interlocutory [Mareva] (Karaha Bodas), or a mandatory injunction compelling [defendant] to perform [the agreement] abroad (C&Y).
    • ASI: per its wording, (b) covers only conduct "in Singapore", and per C&Y interlocutory injunctions are excluded, so it does not obviously carry [an ASI against the X proceedings]. Per Chong (answer scheme), seek [the ASI] as ancillary relief in [the substantive action] served out, so amenability comes from that service (J6).
  • (c) Necessary or Proper Party: The Anomaly [Foreign defendant] (D2) is a necessary or proper party to the claim against [anchor defendant] (D1), duly served. Per AK Investment, this head is anomalous: it rests on no territorial connection between [the claim] and Singapore (The Brabo).
    • Caution: per AK Investment, [D2] must not be brought in "as a matter of course" (The Golden Mariner) merely because the alternative is [two suits].
  • (c) The Anchor Claim Per AK Investment, that D1 is sued only to bring in [D2] is not fatal (The Brabo; Derby v Larsson), but the claim against [D1] must not be "bound to fail" (otherwise D1's presence is a device). A point of law going to [jurisdiction] is normally decided now.
    • Duly served: per C&Y, if [D1] has not been duly served when the application is made, it is dismissed, and approval wrongly given is set aside unless [claimant] obtains retroactive leave; irregular service of [D1] may be curable.
    • Collapse: per Elan Impex, if the action against [D1] is struck out, [D2] ceases to be a necessary or proper party.
  • (c) Is D2 a Proper Party? Per AK Investment (adopting Massey v Heynes), ask whether, had [D1] and [D2] both been here, both would have been proper parties: the claims must involve "one investigation", be "closely bound up" or share a "common thread" ([the same transaction / conspiracy]).
    • Merits: per AK Investment, a serious issue against [D2] is the summary judgment test (Seaconsar); per J H Rayner, [D2] with a good defence ([limitation / no privity]) cannot be a proper party.
    • Limits: per C&Y, [an additional trustee] who is not a joint trustee of the same trust is not necessary; England bars chaining (serving [D3] off [D2] served under the same head). (c) is neutral, so run J3.1.4.
    • Application: per Chong (AY23-24 feedback), [D2]'s pre-contractual misrepresentation and [D1]'s post-contractual breach of [the supply contract] share no common question of law or fact, so [D2] is not a proper party (unless [D1] is sued vicariously).
  • (d) Contract: Two Requirements Per C&Y, [claimant]'s claim must [enforce / rescind / annul / recover damages in respect of] a contract, and [the contract] must be (i) made in Singapore or through an essential step here; (ii) made through [an agent] here for a principal abroad; (iii) governed by Singapore law; or (iv) contain a Singapore jurisdiction term.
  • (d) Existence and Denial of the Contract Per Tecnomar, [claimant] needs only a good arguable case that [the contract] exists, so [defendant]'s denial of [formation / authority] is not fatal.
    • Which law: per C&Y, formation is tested by [the contract]'s proper law under Singapore PIL, not Singapore domestic law, so a contract valid under [X] law counts though it lacks consideration.
    • Claim denying the contract: per C&Y, once unclear, but now largely academic: the list is non-exhaustive and may be read generously, so [a claim that the contract is void] qualifies if one of [limbs (i)–(iv)] is shown.
  • (d) "A Contract": Parties Per C&Y, unsettled whether [the contract] must be between [claimant] and [defendant]. Against: Chen v BHNV held (d) "plainly inapplicable" against [a non-party defendant].
    • For: per C&Y, [an assignee / subrogated insurer / third party entitled to enforce under the proper law] steps into the original party's shoes and may rely on (d) against [defendant].
  • (d)(i) Made in Singapore Per C&Y, it is open whether domestic law or choice of law rules locate formation. Assuming domestic law, per Transniko, a contract by [telephone / instantaneous communication] is made where [offeror] receives acceptance, and one accepted by conduct where [the conduct] occurred.
    • Counterparts: per C&Y, a contract signed in counterpart by [claimant] and [defendant] may be made in two places.
    • Essential step: includes negotiations culminating in [the contract]. Per DJS Solutions, a contract negotiated over [WhatsApp] by [claimant]'s director, who was based here and ran [claimant]'s business from Singapore, was made here although he travelled.
  • (d)(ii) Through an Agent Here Per National Mortgage, [agent] needs only authority to negotiate, not to contract. Per DJS Solutions, [the relief] must relate to the contract made by or through [defendant]'s agent, not merely one [agent] introduced.
  • (d)(iii) Governed by Singapore Law Per Shanghai Turbo and Recovery Vehicle 1, apply Singapore choice of law rules ([express / implied / objective proper law]: C2) to [the contract].
    • Not decisive: per Amin Rasheed, [the policy] was impliedly governed by English law, yet leave to serve out was refused because [Kuwait] was the appropriate forum (J4.2).
  • (d)(iv) Jurisdiction Term Per Vizcaya Partners (adopted by C&Y), an agreement to submit to [Singapore] is not inferred from a Singapore governing law clause; [claimant] needs [cl X] itself to give the Singapore court jurisdiction. Where [the clause] exists, see (r) and J3.2.
  • (d) Neutral Factor Each limb is a connecting factor that says nothing about [breach], so requirement (c) must be proved separately (J3.1.4). Hence [claimant] who says no contract was formed may still use (d), needing only a good arguable case of [the Singapore connection].
  • (e) Breach in Singapore [Defendant] [failed to deliver / pay here], or broke [the contract] in [X] in a way that made performance in Singapore impossible. Per C&Y, this turns on place of breach and place of performance, the latter fixed by [an express term] or the proper law.
    • Alternative places (−): per C&Y (citing Recovery Vehicle 1), where [the obligation] could be performed in [Singapore or X], non-performance is not a breach "in Singapore".
    • Repudiation: per Mutzenbecher, the place of breach is arguably where [defendant]'s repudiatory act, e.g., [the wrongful sale], occurred.
  • (e) Multiple or Continuing Breaches Where [goods] were due here but [defendant] wrongfully [sold them in X], there is both a failure to perform here and a repudiatory act abroad. Per C&Y (citing Briggs), [claimant] may rely on the Singapore breach, but relief is limited to [losses flowing from it].
    • Continuing breach: per C&Y, the forum finding may colour where [the breach] is located, so a Singapore [natural forum] tends to locate it here.
    • Merits-engaging: whether there is a breach at all is decided by [the contract]'s proper law (C2), so a good arguable case of breach under [that law] subsumes requirement (c) (J3.1.4).
  • (f) Tort: Characterisation Per C&Y (citing IM Skaugen (HC), unchallenged on appeal), "tort" is tested by Singapore's choice of law rules: double actionability with the flexible exception (Rickshaw), for local and foreign torts alike. So [claimant] may use (f) though [the claim] fails under Singapore law, if the exception applies [law X] (C3).
    • Equitable claims: per Recovery Vehicle 1 (HC), [dishonest assistance / knowing receipt / breach of directors' duties] were described as torts; such claims may need (f) because (o) covers only restitution and claims against [trustees or fiduciaries] (C&Y).
  • (f) Double Actionability at the Gateway: Unresolved Per IM Skaugen (HC), there is no good arguable case in tort unless [the claim] is actionable under both laws, for both limbs of (f). Per Nippon Catalyst, the rule is irrelevant to service out, being directed at fairness, not at locating [the forum].
    • Shen Sophie: IM Skaugen's broad approach should be followed, but the view was expressed mainly for the natural forum stage, and the court "say[s] no more" about [the gateway stage], so [the split] stands.
    • For (submit): per Shen Sophie, it weeds out [claims bound to fail at trial], and the court must locate [the tort] anyway, the place of the tort being prima facie the natural forum (JIO).
    • Against: per Shen Sophie, nothing in (f) requires locating [the lex loci delicti], and it forces expert evidence of [X] law early. Per Yeo, weeding out [weak claims] is the serious-question filter's job, so keep choice of law for [the trial].
    • Safe course: plead actionability under Singapore law and [law X] (C3), and flag the controversy for [the examiner].
  • (f)(i) Act or Omission Here [The tort], wherever committed, is constituted at least in part by [an act / omission] in Singapore.
    • Internet: per Chen v BHNV, [the posting / sending] occurs where [defendant] was based at the time.
    • Omission: per IM Skaugen (HC), it occurs where [the person who failed to act] was, not where the effect of [the failure] was felt.
    • Misrepresentation abroad: per Chong (AY23-24 feedback), where [the misrepresentation] was made in [X], use (f)(ii), not (f)(i), with (n) in the alternative for [claimant].
  • (f)(ii) Damage Here: Threshold [Claimant]'s claim is founded on, or seeks damages for, damage suffered in Singapore. Per IM Skaugen (CA), not all [the damage] need be here, but it must not be "merely trivial"; contrast Nippon Catalyst (followed in Vibrant Group), requiring it to be "significant".
    • Damage, not its effects: per IM Skaugen (CA), distinguish the financial act of incurring [the loss] from its end result felt here by [claimant], which does not suffice.
    • Not enough: per Nippon Catalyst, that [claimant] is a Singapore entity with a Singapore account into which [defendant] failed to pay; per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar v Chilton, [legal fees] incurred here on the service-out application itself.
  • (f)(ii) Damage Here: Scope of Recovery Per C&Y, a claim founded on damage (damage as a constituent element) lets [claimant] recover all its losses, including those in [X]; a claim for damages only recovers [the Singapore damage].
    • Effects felt here: per C&Y, whether [effects merely felt in Singapore] can found a nexus under the non-exhaustive list "remains to be seen"; if so, [claimant] recovers only Singapore damage.
    • Merits-engaging: a good arguable case of [a tortious act / damage] here subsumes requirement (c) for [claimant] (J3.1.4).
  • (f) Statutory Localisation Per Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025 s 101, a Part 10–12 tort is treated as committed in Singapore if any element [was initiated in or from Singapore / was perceived here / caused harm here], which carries [the online claim] into (f).
    • Defamation: per Week 4 materials, each [publication] is a separate tort, and few [foreign-publication claims] clear the nexus and forum hurdles (C3).
  • (g)–(h) Immovables in Singapore (g) [possession / title] of [immovable property] here, but not unpaid rent (Agnew v Usher); (h) e.g., enforcing [trustee]'s duty to account for sale proceeds of local land held on trust, though already sold (Stype Investments), or [an assignee]'s repairing covenant (Tassell v Hallen).
  • (i) Debts and Movables (i) [a debt secured on immovables], or rights in [movables] here, including beneficial ownership of shares in [a Singapore company] (Goodwill Enterprise).
  • (i) Cryptoassets Per Cheong Jun Yoong v Three Arrows, there being no settled rule, there is a good arguable case that [the cryptoassets] are located where the person controlling [the private key] resides (residence, not domicile, best showing control).
    • Status: the Appellate Division did not decide the point, since [factor (p)] was independently made out and [claimant] needed only one factor.
  • (j) Trusts [Claimant] seeks to execute the trusts of [a written instrument] that ought to be executed according to Singapore law, against [defendant] as trustee. Per C&Y, [the trust property] need not be in Singapore, so [an absconding trustee] cannot escape by removing assets.
    • Governing law: absent an express choice, the law with the closest and most real connection governs [the trust] (Trisuryo Garuda); a modern deed may let it change where [a successor trustee] operates elsewhere (Ivanishvili v Credit Suisse).
  • (k)–(l) Estates and Administration (k) administration of the estate of [deceased], who died domiciled in Singapore; (l) an administration action within O 32 ROC concerning [the estate / trust].
  • (m) Enforcement of Judgment or Award [Claimant] sues on [the foreign judgment / award] against [judgment debtor] abroad. Per C&Y, "judgment" means a foreign judgment enforceable by common law action, in executable form (Karaha Bodas).
    • Outside (m): per C&Y, local judgments and judgments registrable under [REFJA / RECJA], notice of registration being servable on [the debtor] abroad without permission (J7).
    • No pre-judgment Mareva: per Karaha Bodas (following Mercedes-Benz v Leiduck), (m) cannot found a Mareva over [defendant]'s local assets in anticipation of [a judgment] not yet obtained.
    • Forum: per Licea v Curacao Drydock, forum conveniens is irrelevant to [an enforcement action], which is not a fresh suit against [the debtor].
    • Assets: per Demirel, [assets in Singapore] are not required, but [claimant] must show a real prospect of a legitimate benefit; per C&Y, filter by forum conveniens or legitimate benefit, not both (J7).
  • (n) Claims under Written Law [Claimant]'s claim is made under [s X of the Act]. Per Li Shengwu, "any other written law" bears its plain meaning: no genus unites the CDSA and TSOFA beyond serious crimes, so ejusdem generis is rejected, and "any" means any Singapore statute.
    • Applied: per Li Shengwu, [the AG's committal claim] fell within (n) as a claim under s 7(1) SCJA, not [a tangential statutory reference].
  • (n) The Over-Expansion Objection Per Li Shengwu (obiter, as read by C&Y), [claimant] could in principle rely on s 18(1) with para 14 of the First Schedule (power to grant "all reliefs and remedies at law and in equity") for almost any [civil claim].
    • Answer: the risk is "more illusory than real": [claimant] still needs a good arguable case that the facts justify those powers, and Singapore must still be forum conveniens, so a claim lacking [a Singapore connection] will in all likelihood be set aside.
    • But: per Li Shengwu, s 18 and the First Schedule confer powers and reliefs on [the court], not subject-matter jurisdiction — "the critical difference" from s 7 relied on by [the AG].
  • (o) Restitution or Fiduciary Per Chen v BHNV, two conjunctive requirements: [the claim] is restitutionary or against [defendant] as trustee or fiduciary, and [defendant]'s liability arises out of [an act, e.g., receipt of the funds] done in Singapore.
    • Scope: per C&Y, a quantum meruit qualifies only if [it rests on unjust enrichment], not contract (Rabiah Bee); equitable compensation, an account of profits and [a constructive trust] are covered.
  • (p) Cause of Action Arose in Singapore Per Kishinchand (applied in Vibrant Group), ask where in substance [the cause of action] arose; per IM Skaugen (CA), a fact-centric review of all material facts; per Li Shengwu, where "the essential factual material" arose. Per C&Y, the difference is negligible, and not all [the facts] need arise here.
    • Application: per Kishinchand, [the beneficiary]'s location on acquiring [the interest] and [the trustee]'s location at vesting were insignificant; where [claimant] gave instructions and the trust's purpose (operating [an overseas account] for a Singapore business) located it here.
    • Not a cause of action: per Li Shengwu, [a committal application] is quasi-criminal, not founded on a civil "cause of action", so [the AG] could not use (p).
  • (q) Contribution or Indemnity Per Ang Ming Chuang, a claim for [contribution / indemnity] in respect of a liability enforceable by proceedings in Singapore against [defendant]; per C&Y, if [the claim] derives from a Singapore statute, (s) is also available.
  • (r) Submission or Agreement to Submit The claim concerns "matters in which [defendant] has submitted or agreed to submit". Per C&Y, submission by a step in [the Singapore proceedings] founds jurisdiction anyway, so (r) is mainly used for agreement, where [the contract] neither provides a local method of service nor allows service out (else O 8 r 1(3)).
    • Agreement ≠ submission: per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a Singapore [EJC / NEJC] is an agreement to submit, satisfying (r) and (d)(iv); submission itself is [defendant]'s conduct in the proceedings under s 16(1)(b) (J2.2).
    • (r) or (d)(iv)? Per C&Y, (r) does not limit the kinds of claim; [the agreement] does, its scope construed under its proper law. So (r) carries [a tort / restitution claim] within the clause (J1.5), whereas (d) needs a claim in respect of [the contract].
    • Neutral: prove (c) separately (J3.1.4); the forum limb falls away in practice, since [defendant]'s objection to [Singapore] is itself a breach (J3.2).
  • (s) Construction or Enforcement of Written Law Per Li Shengwu and C&Y, confined to Singapore written law. [A claim] enforces a statute only where (i) the statute gives a right to bring [the claim], or (ii) it is brought for contravention of [a statutory rule] with prescribed consequences.
    • Power-conferring provisions: per Li Shengwu, it is "incongruous" to speak of enforcing them, so [claimant]'s claim under [the Act] qualifies but [a committal application] does not, its purpose being to protect the administration of justice.
  • (t)–(u) Committal and Pre-Action Disclosure Per PD para 63(3)(t), a committal order under O 23; per (u), production of [documents / information] to identify possible parties, trace [property] before proceedings, or in the interests of justice.
    • Effect: the Li Shengwu problem (no "cause of action" under (p), no "enforcement" under (s)) now has its own factor, so [claimant] cites (t) first and (n) in the alternative for [the committal].
  • Fallback: Non-Exhaustive List (must write) In any event, per the CJC Report and C&Y, para 63(3) is non-exhaustive, so approval may be given though [the claim] falls outside a restrictive reading, provided sufficient nexus is shown, here because [defendant has substantial assets here / the transaction was structured through Singapore].
    • Query (evaluative): per AK Investment, not every listed factor shows a nexus at all (gateway (c); also (a) property unrelated to [the claim]); weak links are filtered through forum (J3.1.3). Conversely, per Yeo, [a claim] within a listed factor probably has [sufficient nexus].
    • Restraint: per C&Y, how far courts will go remains to be seen; keeping the old heads may signal self-restraint, so [claimant] argues [the closest listed factor] first.
  • Pattern: Negative Declaration that No Contract Exists Presently, [claimant] seeks a declaration that no contract was concluded with [defendant], which is suing on it in [X].
    • Usable (1): (d)(i), as [the negotiations were conducted and concluded here], needing only a good arguable case of the connection; (d)(iii), if the putative proper law of [the alleged contract] is Singapore law (Lew v Nargolwala; C2).
    • Usable (2): (p), arguably, reading "cause of action" generously, [the formation events] having occurred here; (n), through para 14 of the First Schedule (Li Shengwu) for [the declaration].
    • Not usable: (e) ([claimant] alleges no breach; [the breach claim] is [defendant]'s, in [X]); (c) (no anchor defendant); (b) (an ASI against [the X proceedings] is separate: J6); (s) (no Singapore statute).
    • Then: none of these engages the merits of [the declaration], so state the serious question separately (J3.1.4), and [the case] is won or lost on forum (J4.2).
    • Clause in a related contract: where [a concluded contract between the parties] has a Singapore EJC wide enough to catch [the dealings], [defendant]'s forum objection is a breach requiring strong cause (Bunge; J3.2).
    • Infection: but [claimant] who says no contract was concluded must meet the infection point before relying on [that contract's clause] (J1.6).

This is where most marks sit. Match the claim to the factor, plead several in the alternative, then add the non-exhaustive fallback.

FactorKey rules (all from the pre-write)Merits?
(a) Defendant's linkDomicile (Singapore law; Peters Roger; a company in its place of incorporation, Gasque); ordinary residence (Levene; Tjong Very Sumito); carrying on business (individuals too, no fixed place needed); property (need not relate to the claim, Lehman Brothers; need not be substantial, Bunge). Catch-all: links to the defendant, not the claim.Neutral
(b) InjunctionOrdering conduct in Singapore, part of the substantive relief (Lakshmi v Chilton). Not a Mareva (Karaha Bodas). Not obviously an ASI: per Chong, seek the ASI as ancillary relief in the substantive action served out (J6).–
(c) Necessary or proper partyAnomalous: no territorial link (AK Investment; The Brabo). Anchor claim against D1 must not be "bound to fail"; D1 must be duly served. Proper party if the claims involve "one investigation" / a "common thread" (Massey v Heynes).Neutral
(d) Contract(i) made here or an essential step here (Transniko; DJS Solutions); (ii) through an agent here (authority to negotiate is enough, National Mortgage); (iii) Singapore law by Singapore choice of law rules; (iv) a Singapore jurisdiction term (not inferred from a governing law clause, Vizcaya). Good arguable case of existence only (Tecnomar).Neutral
(e) Breach herePlace of breach and place of performance. If performable in Singapore or abroad, non-performance is not a breach "in Singapore" (Recovery Vehicle 1).Engages merits
(f) Tort(i) act or omission here; (ii) damage here, not "merely trivial" (IM Skaugen (CA)) v "significant" (Nippon Catalyst). "Tort" is tested by Singapore choice of law (double actionability, C3).Engages merits
(g)–(i) PropertyImmovables here; debts and movables here, including shares in a Singapore company; cryptoassets arguably where the private-key controller resides (Cheong Jun Yoong v Three Arrows, not decided on appeal).–
(j) TrustsTrusts of a written instrument that ought to be executed according to Singapore law; trust property need not be here.–
(m) JudgmentsA foreign judgment enforceable by common law action. No pre-judgment Mareva (Karaha Bodas). Forum conveniens irrelevant (Licea).–
(n) Written law"Any" Singapore statute (Li Shengwu). Over-expansion risk "more illusory than real".–
(o) RestitutionRestitutionary or fiduciary claim and liability from an act done here (Chen v BHNV).–
(p) Cause of action hereWhere in substance it arose (Kishinchand; IM Skaugen (CA); Li Shengwu).Engages merits
(r) Submission or agreementMainly for agreement to submit: a Singapore EJC or NEJC satisfies (r) and (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). (r) can carry tort claims within the clause; (d) needs a contract claim.Neutral
(s)–(u)Enforcing Singapore written law; committal (t); pre-action disclosure (u).–

FactsBest factorWhy
A Thai company that owns a Singapore condominium is sued for unpaid invoices that have nothing to do with the condo(a), property hereThe property need not relate to the claim (Lehman Brothers) and need not be substantial (Bunge).

Plead every factor that fits, then the non-exhaustive fallback. A marker cannot give credit for a factor you did not name.

Three factors to know in depth

(c) Necessary or proper party

(f) Tort: act here or damage here

  • (f)(i) act or omission here: internet posting occurs where the defendant was based (Chen v BHNV); an omission occurs where the person who failed to act was (IM Skaugen (HC)). Per Chong, a misrepresentation made abroad uses (f)(ii), with (n) in the alternative.
  • (f)(ii) damage here: not all damage need be here, but it must not be "merely trivial" (IM Skaugen (CA)), contrast "significant" (Nippon Catalyst). Distinguish incurring the loss from its effects felt here. A Singapore account into which the defendant failed to pay is not enough (Nippon Catalyst).
  • Scope of recovery. A claim founded on damage recovers all losses; a claim for damages recovers only the Singapore damage (C&Y).
  • Double actionability at the gateway: unresolved. IM Skaugen (HC) requires actionability under both laws; Nippon Catalyst says the rule is irrelevant to service out. Safe course: plead actionability under both laws and flag the split.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Damage here, or just felt here?

A Tokyo company promised to pay Alpha into Alpha's Singapore bank account and did not. Alpha says it suffered damage in Singapore. Per Nippon Catalyst, a Singapore account into which the defendant failed to pay is not enough: Alpha only feels the effect of a loss here.

Contrast a Singapore client who, relying on a negligent report emailed from London, pays out money from its Singapore office and later finds the investment worthless. Here there is a stronger argument that loss was incurred in Singapore, so (f)(ii) is arguable, provided the damage here is not "merely trivial" (IM Skaugen (CA)). Argue both sides; the line is between incurring the loss and merely feeling its effects.

(d) Contract and the negative declaration pattern

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
A claimant who says "there is no contract"

Alpha seeks a declaration that no contract was concluded with Beta, which is suing on it in Ruritania. Usable: (d)(i), if the negotiations were concluded here; (d)(iii), if the putative proper law is Singapore law (Lew v Nargolwala); arguably (p); (n) through para 14 of the First Schedule. Not usable: (e) (Alpha alleges no breach), (c) (no anchor defendant), (b) (an ASI is separate), (s) (no statute). None engages the merits, so state the serious question separately, and the case is won or lost on forum.

5J3.1.3 Requirement (b): forum conveniens

▤ On your pre-write: J3.1.3 Requirement (b): Singapore is Forum Conveniens (word for word)
J3.1.3 Requirement (b): Singapore is Forum Conveniens

(full factor bank in J4.2, so that one bank serves the stay, service out and strong cause)

  • Standard Presently, [claimant] must show Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (Spiliada; AK Investment); being merely as appropriate as [X] is not enough (Sudarga).
    • Flag: per Oro Negro, Singapore need only be "on balance" the more appropriate forum, "whether by a hair or by a mile" (Siemens); cite both and argue [the facts] in the alternative for [claimant].
  • Burden Per Zoom, the Spiliada test is the same as on a stay; only the burden differs. It stays on [claimant] without notice and on [defendant]'s set-aside; only a stay after [valid service] puts stage 1 on [defendant].
    • Run: J4.2 with the stage 1 factors (J4.1.2), [the SICC factor] (J4.4) and stage 2 (J4.1.3), weighed for [the facts].
  • If Stage 1 Fails: Second Bite? Unsettled. Per Konamaneni and Allenger, failure is "the end of the matter", since otherwise [the court] would confer jurisdiction where none was established. Per Spiliada itself, Yeo and Shen Sophie, [claimant] may still show substantial injustice in [X].
    • Open: Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA) left it open (Chong); per C&Y, stage 2 should apply to [claimant], O 8 having expanded [jurisdiction] (J4.2).
  • Service In v Out: Why It Matters Per Week 6 notes, whether Spiliada arises after service in or out changes the burden ([claimant] v [defendant]), the stage 2 debate, and the weight given to [jurisdiction founded as of right].
  • Jurisdiction Agreement Where [a party] is in breach of [the jurisdiction agreement], strong cause on [that party] replaces this inquiry (J3.2; J4.3).

The Spiliada test is the same as on a stay; only the burden differs (Zoom). Here the claimant must show Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (Spiliada; AK Investment); being merely as appropriate is not enough (Sudarga). But per Oro Negro, "on balance" suffices, "whether by a hair or by a mile" (Siemens): cite both. The full factor bank is in J4.2.

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

On a stay, Spiliada has two halves: the defendant shows another court is clearly better (stage 1), then the claimant can still say "but I would suffer injustice there" (stage 2). On service out, the claimant carries the forum burden from the start. The open question is whether a claimant who loses stage 1 still gets its stage 2 argument. One side says no: if Singapore is not the right forum, the court should never reach abroad at all. The other side says yes: a claimant facing real injustice abroad should not be shut out just because more connecting factors point elsewhere. Write both, and note the CA has left it open.

6J3.1.4 Requirement (c): serious question to be tried

▤ On your pre-write: J3.1.4 Requirement (c): Serious Question to be Tried (word for word)
J3.1.4 Requirement (c): Serious Question to be Tried
  • When It Is Subsumed (+) Per Bradley Lomas (adopted in Li Shengwu and C&Y; also IM Skaugen (CA)), where [the gateway] itself engages the merits, a good arguable case on it clears the lower merits bar, so (c) need not be shown separately by [claimant].
    • Examples: (e) [a breach committed here]; (f) [a tortious act, omission or damage here]; (p) [the cause of action arising here].
  • When It Must Be Proved Separately (−) Per Bradley Lomas and C&Y, where [the gateway] is a neutral connecting factor, (c) is a distinct hurdle: (a) and (r) expressly, and on the same logic (d) and (c) (J3.1.2); for [a negative declaration], (n) and (p) too.
    • Standard: per Seaconsar (cited in AK Investment), a substantial question of fact or law that [claimant] bona fide wishes to try, i.e., not frivolous or vexatious; here [prima facie evidence of breach / documented loss] suffices.
    • Time bar: per Recovery Vehicle 1, [a time-barred claim] cannot meet the merits requirement, so check [the applicable limitation period] (FLPA; C1).
  • Questions of Fact and Law Per Bradley Lomas, on fact the court looks primarily at [claimant]'s case and does not try disputes on affidavit, though [defendant] may show the evidence is incomplete or plainly wrong.
    • Law: per Bradley Lomas, the court may go fully into [the issue] and refuse approval if [claimant]'s case is bound to fail.
    • But: per AK Investment, it will not decide a controversial question of law in [a developing area] on hypothetical facts, unless the point goes to [the existence of jurisdiction].
  • Purpose Per American Cyanamid and Seaconsar (Week 6 handout), it screens out [a frivolous or vexatious claim] against [a foreign defendant]; it is a merits filter, and the court does not decide [difficult questions of law] at this stage.

On fact, the court looks primarily at the claimant's case and does not try disputes on affidavit. On law, it may go fully into the issue and refuse approval if the claim is bound to fail (Bradley Lomas), but it will not decide a controversial point in a developing area on hypothetical facts (AK Investment).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
When the serious question bites

Alpha serves Beta out under para 63(3)(d)(iii) (the contract is governed by Singapore law). That factor says nothing about whether Beta broke the contract, so Alpha must show a serious question separately. If Beta shows the claim is clearly time-barred, Alpha fails requirement (c), however strong the nexus.

Had Alpha instead relied on (e) (breach here), proving a good arguable case that Beta breached the contract in Singapore would already clear the lower merits bar, so (c) is subsumed.

7J3.1.5 No approval needed: O 8 r 1(3)

▤ On your pre-write: J3.1.5 Service Out Without the Court's Approval (O 8 r 1(3)) (word for word)
J3.1.5 Service Out Without the Court's Approval (O 8 r 1(3))

(write where [the contract] says anything about service of process)

  • Rule Per O 8 r 1(3), approval "is not required if service out of Singapore is allowed under a contract between the parties", so [claimant] may serve [defendant] in [X] without the three requirements.
    • Basis: per C&Y, party autonomy; an incremental step from the old O 10 r 3 (contractual local method of service, even on [an overseas defendant], for [claims under that contract]).
    • Scope: per C&Y, it presumably applies where [the parties] submitted to Singapore by contract and the contract permits service out; a bare [Singapore clause] with no service provision must go through r 1(1) (J3.2).
    • SICC contrast: it mirrors SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2) (J5.2.4), but not exactly: r 1(3) asks for [a contract allowing service], not [a choice of court agreement].
  • NW Corp: Read Widely Per NW Corp, [a clause] choosing [English law], referring disputes to the Singapore courts and providing for "service of process by registered mail" fell within r 1(3), so posting [the originating process] to [defendant] in Hong Kong needed no approval.
    • Reasons: the rule says "out of", not "outside", Singapore, so no place of [service] need be named; a contract "allows" service out if it agrees to service of Singapore process on [a foreign defendant] not ordinarily here.
    • Purpose: per NW Corp, r 1(3) spares [claimant] a redundant approval where [defendant] has consented to jurisdiction being founded by service, consistent with the Ideals of expedition and efficiency.
    • Context: the clause named the Singapore courts in the same breath, and [the contract] recorded [defendant]'s Hong Kong place of business, so "service of process" could only mean service of Singapore process abroad.
  • What "Allowed" Means (Yeo, evaluative) Per Yeo, three readings: [the contract] allows (i) [an agreed method] that can work in or out of Singapore; (ii) a method expressly or impliedly usable for service out; or (iii) service out without prior approval.
    • Choice: (i) clashes with O 8 r 2(1)(a), which contemplates service out "in the manner agreed" after approval, so [a bare agreed method] is not enough; (ii) is most persuasive, since [defendant] cannot claim surprise; (iii) fits party autonomy and differs little from (ii).
    • Rationale: per Yeo, an agreement allowing service out is an implied agreement to submit, so [defendant]'s submission may be qualified, e.g., by [a reservation of objections].
  • GD v SICC (Yeo) Per Yeo, agreeing to [SICC jurisdiction] alone allows service out without approval (SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2)(a)), but agreeing only to [General Division jurisdiction] does not, even in a Hague case; Yeo argues the latter should also suffice.
  • Consequence for the Defendant Per NW Corp, service under r 1(3) founds jurisdiction without approval, so [defendant] cannot dispute its existence, only its exercise on natural forum grounds, where the burden is [defendant]'s own (J4.1).
    • Clause naming Singapore: where [the contract] also names the Singapore courts, [defendant]'s forum challenge is itself a breach, so it must show strong cause (J3.2; J4.3).
  • Related Routes Where [the agreed mode] is service in Singapore, it is service in under O 7 r 2(1)(d) (COSCO; J3.0.2). Per C&Y, r 2(1)(d) is looser than old O 10 r 3: [the action] need not relate to the contract containing the agreed method, and the agreement need not be [a contract] (no consideration).
    • Solicitors: where [defendant] instructs Singapore solicitors to accept service, it is treated as service in (C&Y), better analysed as submission (Yeo; J2.2.2). Per C&Y, the practical difference between [service in by agreement] and [r 1(3)] is now small.

Approval "is not required if service out of Singapore is allowed under a contract between the parties".

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
NW Corp

A clause chose English law, referred disputes to the Singapore courts and provided for "service of process by registered mail". The claimant posted the originating process to the defendant in Hong Kong without approval. Valid: the rule says "out of", not "outside", Singapore, so no place need be named; a contract "allows" service out if it agrees to service of Singapore process on a foreign defendant. Consequence: the defendant cannot dispute existence, only exercise, where the burden is its own; and if the contract names the Singapore courts, its forum challenge is itself a breach (strong cause).

  • Scope. Presumably where the parties submitted by contract and the contract permits service out; a bare Singapore clause with no service provision goes through r 1(1) (C&Y).
  • What "allowed" means (Yeo): three readings; reading (ii), a method expressly or impliedly usable for service out, is most persuasive.
  • GD v SICC. Agreeing to SICC jurisdiction alone allows service out without approval (SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2)(a)); agreeing only to General Division jurisdiction does not, even in a Hague case (Yeo argues it should).
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

O 8 r 1(3) is a pre-agreed delivery address. If the parties already agreed in their contract how court papers may be sent abroad ("by registered mail to the address below"), the court does not need to give permission again: the defendant gave it in advance. The price for the defendant is that it can no longer argue the court lacks power; it can only argue the court should not use it.

8J3.1.6 Mode: the hierarchy of service

▤ On your pre-write: J3.1.6 Mode of Service: the Hierarchy of Service (word for word)
J3.1.6 Mode of Service: the Hierarchy of Service

(write whenever [claimant] has served, or wants to serve, [defendant] by substituted service or on solicitors)

  • Two Sequential Steps (must write) Per Beranek, ask first about the right to serve [defendant], then about the mode of serving [the originating process].
    • Right: [defendant] present here → as of right (s 16(1)(a)(i)); [defendant] absent → only through O 8, by approval (r 1(1)) or agreement (r 1(3)).
    • Mode: personal service on [defendant] (O 6 r 4, per C&Y), or, if impracticable, substituted service (O 7 r 7, per Yeo) or dispensation with personal service (O 7 r 1(2), per Xu Xiangrong) on [the facts].
  • Consistel: The Hierarchy Per Consistel, where [defendant] left Singapore before [the originating process] was issued, [claimant] must first seek permission to serve out; substituted service arises only if personal service is impracticable — "a hierarchy of service which must be adhered to".
    • Reasons: personal service is not impracticable merely because [defendant] is abroad; comity requires circumspection over [an absent defendant]; otherwise [claimant] would bypass the court's scrutiny of forum conveniens, making the service-out rules otiose.
    • Not retrospective: that substituted service in fact brought [the claim] to [defendant]'s notice does not validate it after the event.
  • Consistel's Exceptions (±) Per Consistel, substituted service without first serving out is allowed where [defendant] (i) left Singapore to evade [service] (Re Urquhart), or (ii) moves constantly between countries, so personal service is futile (Ng Swee Hong).
    • Applied: neither applied in Consistel: [the defendants] had long lived in [the UAE], made enquiries when told of the attempted service, and were not peripatetic.
    • Status: Beranek doubted the exceptions, but it is an AR decision and Consistel is High Court, so per Chong (seminar), [claimant] and [defendant] should both follow Consistel.
  • Substituted Service Out Per Janesh s/o Rajkumar ("CHEFPIERRE"), the court may order substituted service out of jurisdiction on [an unknown defendant] ([by email / NFT airdrop / social media]), using its inherent power though no rule expressly provides for it (Yeo).
    • So: Janesh goes to the mode, not the right; [claimant] still needs approval under O 8 r 1(1) to serve [defendant], and Consistel is untouched.
  • The Shortcut Cases (−) Three cases let [claimant] reach [an absent defendant] by service in Singapore:
    • COSCO: service on [defendant]'s Singapore solicitors, who confirmed authority to accept [service], is service in under O 7 r 2(1)(d) and s 16(1)(a)(i) — better explained as submission (Yeo) or constructive presence (Beranek) (J3.0.2).
    • Xu Xiangrong v Fu Xianwei: no approval to serve out is needed before personal service on [a foreign defendant] is dispensed with, where ordinary service is then effected here ([by email to his Singapore solicitors]), following Madison Pacific (approval is needed only if [the document] is served out).
    • Xu caveat: where [defendant] is abroad and has not submitted, the court should still consider forum "for good order", with circumspection given comity towards [X].
    • Malayan Banking v Zhang Zhencheng: a notice of appointment of [solicitor] filed to challenge jurisdiction is not submission (by parity with O 6 r 12(5)), so [claimant] cannot then serve [that solicitor].
    • Malayan Banking caveat: the alternative prayer to dispense with personal service on [defendant], raised only on appeal, was rejected, but [a fresh application] is not barred.
  • Evaluation Per Chong (seminar), Consistel's hierarchy (followed in Beranek) is the correct framework, and COSCO and Malayan Banking are wrong. They and Xu Xiangrong each let [claimant] reach [an absent defendant] while skipping step 1, the scrutiny of nexus and forum (J3.0.2).
    • Application: presently, [claimant] [did / did not] obtain approval before [the substituted service / dispensation], so service [is / is not] liable to be set aside.
  • Full and Frank Disclosure Per C&Y, because the application is without notice, [claimant] must disclose matters against approval ([defendant]'s connections with [X], the foreign proceedings, gateway weaknesses). Material non-disclosure can found [a setting aside] (Zoom).
  • Not retrospective. That substituted service in fact reached the defendant does not validate it.
  • Janesh ("CHEFPIERRE"): substituted service out by email or NFT airdrop on an unknown defendant goes to the mode, not the right; approval under O 8 r 1(1) is still needed.
  • The shortcut cases (−): COSCO (service on solicitors here), Xu Xiangrong (dispensing with personal service without approval to serve out), Malayan Banking (a notice of appointment is not submission, so its solicitor cannot be served).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Three hard-to-serve defendants
DefendantWhat to do
Mr Tan left Singapore for Kuala Lumpur last month and lives openly there.Step 1: approval under O 8. Step 2: serve him personally in Kuala Lumpur. Substituted service only if personal service proves impracticable.
Mr Ng left Singapore the night before the claim was issued, precisely to avoid being served.A Consistel exception: a defendant who fled to evade service (Re Urquhart). The court may allow substituted service.
An unknown hacker who stole cryptoassets, known only by a wallet address.Approval under O 8 r 1(1) is still needed (the right to serve out); email or an NFT airdrop is only the mode (Janesh).

The pattern: never use a convenient mode to skip the right to serve out.

🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Consistel's hierarchy (followed in Beranek) is the correct framework; COSCO and Malayan Banking are wrong. They and Xu Xiangrong each let the claimant reach an absent defendant while skipping step 1, the scrutiny of nexus and forum. Beranek doubted Consistel's exceptions, but Beranek is an AR decision and Consistel is High Court: both sides should follow Consistel.

9J3.2 When a jurisdiction agreement is in play

▤ On your pre-write: J3.2 FOUNDING JURISDICTION UNDER A JURISDICTION AGREEMENT WHERE [DEFENDANT] IS ABROAD (word for word)
J3.2 FOUNDING JURISDICTION UNDER A JURISDICTION AGREEMENT WHERE [DEFENDANT] IS ABROAD (where [defendant] is served in Singapore as of right, a foreign clause goes only to exercise: J4.0.2)
  • Route Per Week 9 slides and C&Y, if [the contract] allows service out, serve [defendant] without approval (O 8 r 1(3); J3.1.5); strictly this needs only an agreement to service out, not [a choice of court agreement], though the two usually come together.
    • Which ground: otherwise seek approval under O 8 r 1(1): "has the jurisdiction" is arguably reserved for [CCAA cases] (J1.3); at common law use "appropriate court" and the three PD para 63(2) requirements against [defendant] (J3.1.1).
    • SICC: for [an SICC clause], including a post-2016 "Singapore High Court" clause, no permission is needed (SICC Rules O 5 r 6(2)(a)), and exercise is tested under O 2 r 3 (Chong, answer scheme; J5) for [the claim].
  • Singapore EJC or NEJC: In Principle v In Practice (must write) Per Week 9 slides, [claimant] relies on [the Singapore clause] against [defendant]:
    • In principle, [claimant] must still make out all three requirements against [defendant], even inter partes.
    • Nexus: [the clause] itself, under para 63(3)(r) ([defendant] "agreed to submit") or (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA); J3.1.2).
    • In practice, [claimant] need only show a good arguable case that [the clause] is valid, binds [defendant] and covers [the dispute] (J1.5–J1.6), plus a serious question, shown separately because (d)(iv) and (r) are neutral (J3.1.4).
    • Forum: need not be proved. If [defendant] contests it, that breaches its promise, so per Shanghai Turbo (CA) [defendant] bears strong cause (J4.3), whether it challenges existence or exercise; if [defendant] never raises it, [claimant] need prove nothing.
  • Singapore Clause With No Promise Under Its Proper Law First construe [the clause] under its proper law (J1.1). Per Chong (answer scheme), where [cl 15], read under [Ruritanian law], contains no promise, [defendant] breaches nothing by objecting, so the test is plain forum conveniens, burden on [claimant].
    • Then: [the Singapore clause] is only a factor; weigh [the governing law] against the possibility of transfer to the SICC (J4.4), and raise the Konamaneni stage 2 issue if stage 1 points to [X] (J3.1.3).
  • Non-Party Defendant Per Chong (AY23-24 feedback), [the clause] cannot be used to saddle [a non-party, e.g., the director] with a burden, and facts far less exceptional than Global Partners v Babcock & Brown do not bring [him] within its party scope (J1.5).
    • So: [claimant] must show Singapore is forum conveniens, and [the SICC] has no primary jurisdiction over [him], only transfer under SICC Rules O 2 r 4(1)(c) (J5).
  • Inter Partes Attacks: Burden by Limb [Defendant] may attack any or all limbs, and the burden on [claimant] or [defendant] depends on which:
    • Nexus ("there is no agreement" / "it is void" / "it does not cover [this dispute]"): the burden stays on [claimant], the agreement being the basis of extraordinary jurisdiction.
    • Serious question: on [claimant], as for any claim against [defendant].
    • Forum ("Singapore is not forum conveniens") or stay instead: [defendant] is in breach of [the EJC / NEJC], so strong cause, burden on [defendant]; the burden is always on the party seeking release from its promise (Week 9 slides; Shanghai Turbo (CA)).
  • Foreign EJC: Strong Cause on Claimant Throughout [Claimant] sues here despite [the EJC for X], so it is in breach. Without notice: it needs a nexus through another factor ([defendant]'s residence or property here / a breach or tort here), a serious question, and strong cause in place of forum conveniens.
    • Inter partes: per C&Y and Week 9 slides, the burden on every limb stays on [claimant], and the same holds if [defendant] seeks a stay instead of a set-aside.
    • Note the reversal when served in: [defendant] applies for the stay, yet [claimant] must show strong cause (J4.3).
  • Foreign NEJC: Plain Spiliada [Claimant] is not in breach of [the foreign NEJC] (Shanghai Turbo; J1.1), so the forum limb is ordinary Spiliada, the clause carrying little weight.
    • Burden: on a set-aside (existence), [claimant] must show Singapore is clearly forum conveniens (J4.2); on a stay (exercise), [defendant] bears stage 1 (J4.1).
  • Strategy (must write) Advise [claimant] and [defendant] as follows:
    • Advising [claimant]: serve in wherever possible. Served in, [defendant] is usually confined to a stay and bears stage 1; served out, [claimant] must clear all three limbs (Zoom; C&Y).
    • Advising [defendant] served out: challenge existence (set aside), not exercise; unless [defendant] is itself in breach, the burden then stays on [claimant] throughout.
    • Fall-back stay: per Zoom, not submission, but running it on the same material is "wholly unnecessary and likely counter-productive"; per Zoom, it takes on a burden [defendant] could have left with [claimant] (J4.2).

This section shows how a clause changes the service-out analysis. The trick is that the burden can flip depending on who is in breach.

Defendant attacks…Burden on
Nexus ("no agreement", "void", "does not cover this")Claimant: the agreement is the basis of extraordinary jurisdiction
Serious questionClaimant
Forum or seeks a stay (Singapore clause)Defendant: it is in breach, so strong cause; the burden is always on the party seeking release from its promise
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Same Thai defendant, three clauses

Alpha serves Beta in Thailand. Beta applies to set aside, arguing Thailand is the better forum.

ClauseNexusForum argument
"Exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts"The clause itself: para 63(3)(r) and (d)(iv). Alpha shows it is valid, binds Beta and covers the dispute.Beta objecting is a breach, so Beta must show strong cause.
"Exclusive jurisdiction of the Thai courts"Alpha needs another factor, since the clause points away from Singapore.Alpha is in breach by suing here, so Alpha must show strong cause throughout.
"The Thai courts may hear disputes"Another factor.No breach: on a set-aside, Alpha must show Singapore is the forum conveniens.
⚠ TRAP
A Singapore clause with no promise

First construe the clause under its proper law (J1.1). Per Chong's answer scheme, if cl 15, read under Ruritanian law, contains no promise, the defendant breaches nothing by objecting, so the test is plain forum conveniens with the burden on the claimant. The Singapore clause is then just a factor. And a clause cannot saddle a non-party (e.g. a director) with a burden (Chong, AY23-24 feedback).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Strategy advice

Alpha should serve Beta in Singapore wherever possible: served in, Beta is usually confined to a stay and bears stage 1, whereas served out, Alpha must clear all three requirements (Zoom; C&Y). Conversely, Beta, if served out, should challenge existence by applying to set aside rather than seek a stay, since unless Beta is itself in breach of a clause the burden then stays on Alpha throughout.

10Put it together: a worked service-out application

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Hypo: the Thai buyer

Facts. Alpha (Singapore) agreed by WhatsApp from its Singapore office to sell machines to Beta (Thailand), delivery FOB Singapore. The contract chooses Singapore law but has no jurisdiction or service clause. Beta refuses to take delivery in Singapore and says the machines were misdescribed by Alpha's agent. Beta has no presence in Singapore. Alpha wants to sue in Singapore.

  1. Threshold. Beta is in Thailand, unregistered, and has not instructed Singapore solicitors: it cannot be served here, so s 16(1)(a)(ii) with O 8 (J3.0.2).
  2. Route. No clause allows service out, and no CCAA clause, so approval on the "appropriate court" ground (J3.1.1).
  3. (a) Nexus. Para 63(3)(d)(i) (made here: the WhatsApp negotiations and acceptance from Alpha's Singapore office, DJS Solutions), (d)(iii) (Singapore law), and (e) (failure to take delivery here). Plead (p) in the alternative, then the non-exhaustive fallback (J3.1.2).
  4. (b) Forum. Alpha must show Singapore is clearly more appropriate (or "on balance", Oro Negro): Singapore law, delivery here, Alpha's witnesses here, against Beta's Thai witnesses on misdescription (J4.2).
  5. (c) Serious question. Subsumed by (e), which engages the merits; (d) alone would need it shown separately (J3.1.4).
  6. Mode. Personal service on Beta in Thailand first (J3.1.6).
  7. Beta's response. Beta should apply to set aside, keeping the burden on Alpha (J3.2).

What if the contract had said "Disputes shall be heard by the Singapore courts; service may be effected by courier to Beta's Bangkok office"? Then Alpha needs no approval at all (O 8 r 1(3), NW Corp): it simply couriers the claim. Beta can no longer dispute existence, and if it argues Thailand is more convenient, it is breaking its promise not to object, so Beta must show strong cause (J4.3).
