LESSON J5 · Q1 · JURISDICTION AND JUDGMENTS · ABOUT 21 MIN · 7 FLOWCHARTS · 2 ILLUSTRATIONS · 11 QUESTIONS

The SICC: written agreements, transfer and joinder

⚡ BIG IDEA

The SICC is a division of the High Court for international commercial cases. A case gets there in three ways: a written jurisdiction agreement (primary jurisdiction), transfer from the General Division ("more appropriate"), or joinder. Once there under a written agreement, Spiliada and strong cause disappear: the SICC declines only if hearing the case is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of process.

PRE-WRITE J5 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR FILE
J5 The Singapore International Commercial Court (Sicc)
This is your exam file, unchanged. It is long, so it starts folded: open it once to see the whole shape, then learn it piece by piece below. [Brackets] are the blanks you fill with the facts; Labels start each point; (+) helps the party relying on the rule, (−) helps the other side, (±) argue both ways. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue reference such as J4.3 to jump.

(Run right after the General Division analysis for each contract: Chong's sample-final framework puts "Gen Div" and "SICC" side by side. CCAA applicability and regime overlap: J1.0.2. The SICC factor in the General Division's Spiliada: J4.4. Legend: (+) helps [party wanting the SICC]; (−) helps [party resisting it]; (±) argue both ways.)

J5.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP
  1. Nature and subject matter (J5.1): a division of the General Division (s 18A SCJA); [the claim] must be international and commercial (s 18D; O 2 r 1(3)), presumed under [a written jurisdiction agreement] (O 2 r 1(8)).
  2. Route 1, written jurisdiction agreement (J5.2): O 2 r 1(1), (7); s 18F exclusivity [forum mandatory rule or not]; O 2 r 2 reading of ["Singapore High Court"] clauses [procedural or substantive]; service out as of right (O 5 r 6(2)).
  3. Exercise (J5.3): O 2 r 3(2)–(3) only: no Spiliada, no strong cause; [defendant] must show [no international and commercial character / abuse of process]; then transfer, stay or dismissal (O 2 r 3(5)–(6)).
  4. Route 2, transfer GD → SICC (J5.4): [the case] moves only if the SICC is "more appropriate" (O 2 r 4(1)(c)); [HCCCA] cases need every party's consent, possibly deemed (O 2 r 4(4), (7)) or by variation (O 2 r 5(1)); no relitigating jurisdiction (O 2 r 4(8)).
  5. SICC → GD (J5.5): O 2 r 4(5), [all parties] consenting; O 2 r 5(2) for [an HCCCA SICC-only clause].
  6. Route 3, joinder (J5.6): s 18D(3); O 10 rr 5–7; service on [third party C] abroad with permission (O 5 r 6(1)), no FNC; [C]'s stay under O 2 r 3(2).
J5.0.1 Quick Application Template

Presently, [claimant] sues [defendant] in the SICC on [contract], whose [clause X] names [the SICC / the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Subject matter: [the claim] is international as [defendant]'s place of business is in [State], and commercial as it arises from [a supply relationship]; the General Division could hear it and no prerogative relief is sought (s 18D(1); O 2 r 1(1)) (J5.1). Route: [primary jurisdiction under [clause X] (J5.2), so transfer need not be discussed / transfer from the General Division under O 2 r 4(1) (J5.4) / joinder under s 18D(3) (J5.6)]. Service: [as of right under O 5 r 6(2)(a) / with permission under O 5 r 6(1)]. Exercise: no Spiliada; the SICC declines only under O 2 r 3(2), for [lack of international and commercial character / abuse of process] (J5.3). Result: the SICC [has / lacks] jurisdiction and [will / will not] hear [the claim].

J5.1 THE SICC: NATURE AND SUBJECT-MATTER JURISDICTION
  • Nature (write one line) Per s 18A SCJA, the SICC (launched 5 January 2015) is a division of the General Division, so a national court: [its judgment] is a Singapore High Court judgment, enforceable in [State] as such (including under the HCCCA); appeals lie to the Court of Appeal; and jurisdiction over [defendant] still rests on s 16 SCJA.
  • Court, Not Tribunal Unlike [an arbitral tribunal], the SICC can coerce [third party C] into the proceedings (J5.6). Per Parliament, though arbitration-influenced, it is "a new way of thinking about international dispute resolution".
  • Special Features (use where relevant) Presently, [the dispute] turns on [foreign law / foreign evidence rules]. The SICC has international judges, may disapply Singapore evidence rules, including on privilege (s 18K SCJA), and may decide foreign law on submissions instead of proof (s 18L).
  • Confidentiality and Counsel Where [the parties] want [confidentiality / their own foreign counsel], the SICC may allow it (O 16 r 9; s 18M), more readily in "offshore" cases with no substantial connection to Singapore.
  • Standalone Rules Where the SICC Rules are silent on [issue], the SICC may do what is necessary, applying the ROC with modifications or looking to [foreign law / international practice] (O 1 r 11(3)). Per C&Y, the standalone SICC Rules 2021 (from 1 April 2022) stress its independence and international character, including procedural flexibility responsive to international commerce (O 1 r 3).
  • Subject Matter (s 18D) Presently, [claimant]'s [claim] falls within [category]. The SICC hears (1) international and commercial actions the General Division could hear in its original civil jurisdiction (s 18D(1)); (2) IAA proceedings on international commercial arbitration (s 18D(2)); (3) pre-action applications for documents, injunctions or search orders, and committal; and (4) international and commercial corporate insolvency, restructuring and dissolution.
  • IAA Proceedings (±) Where [the application] concerns [an international commercial arbitration], permission is needed to serve out (O 5 r 6), and the SICC may decline under O 2 r 3(2) (C&Y). Per C&Y, "international" follows IAA s 5(2), "commercial" the Model Law art 1(1) note, and [investment / State] arbitrations may be included.
J5.1.1 International and Commercial (O 2 r 1(3))
  • International (+) Per O 2 r 1(3)(a), [the action] is international if [one party's place of business / where a substantial part of the obligations is to be performed / the subject matter's closest connection] is outside Singapore, or all parties named on filing expressly agreed it relates to more than one State. Presently, [defendant]'s place of business is [State].
  • Place of Business Per O 2 r 1(4)–(6), [party]'s place of business is where it carries on business; if [several], the one most closely connected to [the written jurisdiction agreement]; if none, its habitual residence. It is fixed when [the agreement] was concluded (or, on transfer, when [the case] began or as the General Division decides).
  • Commercial (+) Per O 2 r 1(3)(b), [the action] is commercial if its subject matter arises from a commercial relationship, contractual or not, or it is an in personam IP dispute, or all parties expressly agreed so. The parties themselves need not be in a commercial relationship (O 2 r 1(5)). Presently, [claim] arises from [a [distribution / construction / loan] relationship].
  • Presumption (+) Per O 2 r 1(8), as each party submitted under [clause X], [the action] is presumed international and commercial, subject to the SICC's review under O 2 r 3 (C&Y). Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [the facts] are objectively international and commercial, say so briefly and move on.
  • Rebuttal (−) [Defendant] rebuts the presumption: [both parties trade only in Singapore / all obligations were performed here / the dispute is [a residential tenancy / an individual's guarantee]]. Even where the parties agreed [the case] into scope (O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii), (b)(iii)), per C&Y the SICC may decline it as contrary to its character (O 2 r 3(2)) (J5.3).
J5.2 ROUTE 1: WRITTEN JURISDICTION AGREEMENT
J5.2.1 Starter and Conditions (O 2 r 1(1))
  • Starter (must write) Presently, [claimant] filed in the SICC relying on [clause X]. Per O 2 r 1(1) and s 18D(1), the SICC has jurisdiction if, when first filed, (a) [the action] is international and commercial (J5.1.1) and one the General Division could hear; (b) each named party submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement; and (c) no prerogative relief is sought.
  • In Personam Basis Per the slides, jurisdiction over [defendant] is founded by service under s 16(1)(a) SCJA (J5.2.4). [Clause X] is a promise; s 16(1)(b) submission is a separate basis, needing conduct such as [filing a defence on the merits] (J2.2).
  • Written Jurisdiction Agreement (+) Per O 2 r 1(7), [clause X] is a written jurisdiction agreement: [the parties]' agreement to submit to the [exclusive / non-exclusive] jurisdiction of the SICC, [in writing / in an accessible form usable for later reference]. Per C&Y, both EJCs and NEJCs qualify.
  • Primary Jurisdiction Ends the Inquiry Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), if [clause X] gives the SICC primary jurisdiction over [the claim against defendant], transfer need not be discussed; transfer matters only for [a party or claim outside clause X] (J5.4).
J5.2.2 Exclusive or Not? (s 18F SCJA)
  • Presumption of Exclusivity (+) Per s 18F(1), absent express contrary words in [clause X] (s 18F(2)), [the parties] are taken to have agreed (a) to submit exclusively to the SICC; (b) to carry out [its judgment] without undue delay; and (c) to waive recourse to [foreign courts] against the judgment or its enforcement, so far as validly waivable.
  • When Does s 18F Apply? (route by facts) Per C&Y, route [clause X] by [its governing law]:
    • CCAA case: s 3(2) CCAA deems [clause X] exclusive whether [Singapore / foreign] law governs it, so s 18F need not be argued.
    • Singapore law governs [clause X]: s 18F applies, so [clause X] is exclusive absent [express non-exclusive wording].
    • Non-CCAA case, [foreign law] governing: debated. s 18F governs [clause X] only if it is a forum mandatory rule, as [the party wanting exclusivity] argues and [the party resisting] denies (C1.7). C&Y take no side, noting that Yip and Chong differ.
  • s 18F Is a Forum Mandatory Rule (+) Per Chong (Chong & Yip 2019 article), s 18F applies to [clause X] whatever its governing law: (i) the presumption against extraterritoriality is rebutted for a court set up to hear [international disputes]; (ii) s 18F(1)(a) is inspired by art 3(b) HCCCA (now s 3(2) CCAA); (iii) it keeps [non-CCAA SICC clauses] consistent with [CCAA SICC clauses].
  • s 18F Is Not Mandatory (−) Per Yip (same article), s 18F applies only where Singapore law governs [clause X] (in a CCAA case, s 3(2) CCAA deems exclusivity: C&Y). Party autonomy is an important undergirding value of the SICC (C&Y), and a presumption rebuttable by contrary words is not [an overriding mandatory rule]. So [clause X] is construed under [foreign law], under which it is [non-exclusive].
    • Reply (+): per C&Y, the SICC balances [party autonomy] against [expedience], as O 2 r 2(1) shows.
    • Why it matters: little for exercise, as O 2 r 3 treats [EJCs and NEJCs] alike (J5.3). It matters for breach: per C&Y, suing in [foreign court] breaches only an exclusive SICC clause, founding [an ASI / damages] (J6.3.1.3; J1.7).
J5.2.3 Clauses Naming the High Court or General Division (O 2 r 2)
  • Post-2016 High Court Clause Includes the SICC (+) Presently, [clause X], concluded on [date] (on or after 1 October 2016), names [the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2)–(3) CCAA, it includes the SICC unless [a contrary intention] appears, so [claimant] may file directly in the SICC.
    • Critique (−): Per C&Y, O 2 r 2(1) seems to bar evidence that [the parties] [never contemplated the SICC], contrary to Singapore's contextual interpretation and to party autonomy.
    • Reply (+): Per C&Y, the lost autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability of [the SICC judgment] in [State] and fits the SICC's international template; per Hartley–Dogauchi, "the courts of France" lets French law allocate internally.
    • Specific Reference Needed? (−): Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), arguably [clause X] needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it, so [defendant] resists [primary jurisdiction].
  • Pre-2016 Clause (−) Per O 2 r 2(2), [clause X], concluded on [date] before 1 October 2016, "does not of itself" submit to the SICC. Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), there is no primary jurisdiction, so [claimant] sues in the General Division and seeks [a transfer] (J5.4).
  • SICC-Only Clause (−) Per O 2 r 2(3), [clause X], naming [the SICC] alone, is not "of itself" submission to the General Division, so [claimant] suing there cannot rely on it alone (C&Y).
  • Foreign Law Governs [Clause X]: O 2 r 2(1) Procedural or Substantive? (±) Per the slides, this is open where [foreign law] governs [clause X]:
    • (+) Party wanting the SICC: O 2 r 2(1) is a forum rule on internal allocation and on the scope of submission to a Singapore court, so the lex fori applies though [contract] is governed by [foreign law].
    • (−) Party resisting the SICC: construing [clause X] is substance for its proper law, [foreign law], as party autonomy requires; under it, ["the High Court of Singapore"] excludes the SICC.
    • If Singapore law governs: per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), the question does not arise: O 2 r 2(1) applies to [clause X], and absent [express contrary words] s 18F makes it exclusive (C&Y).
J5.2.4 Serving [Defendant] Out of Singapore (O 5 r 6)
  • No Permission Needed (+) Presently, per O 5 r 6(2), [defendant] in [State] may be served out without permission, being [a party to the written jurisdiction agreement (r 6(2)(a)) / bound by [contract] allowing service out (r 6(2)(b))], whether or not [clause X] mentions service. Per O 5 r 6(5), the SICC may still review jurisdiction under O 2 r 3.
  • Permission Needed (±) Otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), permission is granted if the SICC "has the jurisdiction to hear the action and it is appropriate for the case to be heard in the Court". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, so [defendant]'s [Spiliada factors] are irrelevant; appropriateness turns on [the SICC's international and commercial character] (J5.3).
J5.2.5 Challenging the Existence of Jurisdiction

(Apply within 14 days after serving the Defendant's Statement (O 2 r 7). A [defendant] disputing service may apply to set it aside (O 2 r 6).)

  • Attack the Clause (−) [Defendant] argues [clause X] is [void / never agreed] for [mistake / misrepresentation / duress / lack of authority]. Reply (+): per s 5 CCAA (CCAA cases) and the common law (J1.6), [clause X] is separable, so an attack on [contract] alone does not touch it.
  • Attack the Nature of the Dispute (−) Per O 2 r 1(8), [defendant] rebuts the presumption by showing [the action] is not [international / commercial] (J5.1.1).
  • Consequence of a Successful Challenge Per O 2 r 3(5), if the SICC lacks jurisdiction over [the claim], it must transfer [the case] to the General Division if that court has jurisdiction and [all parties] consent; otherwise it may dismiss, stay or make any order.
  • Deemed Consent to Transfer Per O 2 r 3(6), [a "High Court" / "General Division" clause] counts as each party's consent to the General Division hearing [the case], justifiably given the clause's express scope (C&Y).
  • Finality Per O 2 r 3(7), a decision that the SICC has and will exercise jurisdiction over [the claim], or a transfer of [the case] to the General Division, is final unless [permission to appeal] is granted.
J5.3 EXERCISE OF JURISDICTION IN THE SICC (O 2 r 3)
  • The Test (must write) Presently, [defendant] asks the SICC to decline because [the dispute centres on [State] / [State B] law governs]. Per O 2 r 3(2), the SICC may decline only if exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process, on its own motion or [on application] (O 2 r 3(4)).
  • Foreign Connections Irrelevant (+) Per O 2 r 3(3), as there is [a written jurisdiction agreement], the SICC must not decline "solely on the ground that the action … is connected to a jurisdiction other than Singapore". Per C&Y and Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), there is no Spiliada balancing, Australian test or strong cause, so [defendant]'s links to [State] count for nothing.
  • Same Test for EJCs and NEJCs (+) Per C&Y, the old O 110 r 8 "appropriateness" wording left room to treat an NEJC differently; the 2021 Rules close that gap, as the SICC Committee intended. So although [clause X] is non-exclusive, [defendant] cannot rely on [State B] being more appropriate.
  • Justification (if asked to evaluate) Per the SICC User Guide (Note 1), connections are ignored because [the parties] agreed in writing to "an international court"; per C&Y this is circular, the SICC not being a true international court. C&Y prefer party autonomy: [commercial parties] may choose [a neutral, specialist forum] and must accept the consequences.
  • Contrary to International and Commercial Character (−) Presently, [the dispute] is in substance [a local dispute between Singapore residents / a consumer-type claim], brought in only by [the parties' agreement] under O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii) or (b)(iii). Per C&Y, hearing it may be contrary to the SICC's international and commercial character.
  • Objectively International and Commercial (+) Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), as [the action] is objectively international and commercial, with [defendant] in [State], there is little ground for the SICC to decline.
  • Abuse of Process (−) Presently, [claimant] filed in the SICC only to [delay [State B] proceedings already well advanced / relitigate [issue] decided in [State B]]. Per O 2 r 3(2), that abuses the SICC's process (cf tactical "wait and see" conduct, J6.3.1.3).
  • Consequence Per O 2 r 3(5)–(6), if the SICC declines, it must transfer [the case] to the General Division where that court has jurisdiction and [all parties] consent (deemed for [a "High Court" clause]); otherwise it may dismiss or stay (J5.2.5).
J5.4 ROUTE 2: TRANSFER FROM THE GENERAL DIVISION TO THE SICC (s 18J(2) SCJA; O 2 r 4)

(Per C&Y, the main source of SICC cases so far. Apply within 28 days, with evidence of the transfer conditions and any consent (O 2 r 7). Per the slides, existence was founded under General Division rules: [service in (J2) / service out under O 8 (J3)].)

J5.4.1 Non-CCAA Case (O 2 r 4(1))
  • Requirements (must write) Presently, [party] seeks transfer of [claimant]'s General Division action, or the court acts on its own motion after hearing [the parties] (O 2 r 4(3)). Per O 2 r 4(1), it may transfer if (a) [the action] is international and commercial when the order is made; (b) no prerogative relief is sought; and (c) the SICC is more appropriate.
  • Only Route Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme; AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [clause X] [predates 1 October 2016 / does not cover [the claim against C]], the SICC has no primary jurisdiction, so [claimant] reaches it only by transfer under the O 2 r 4(1)(c) "more appropriate" test.
  • More Appropriate (+) Per C&Y, relevant factors (the Rules give none) are the international elements and their relevance; the SICC's capability to handle them; [the parties]' level of consent; and connections to Singapore. Presently, [the dispute] turns on [foreign law, decidable on submissions (s 18L) / technical [construction / shipping] issues].
    • International Judge: Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), [an International Judge from [State]] with expertise in [foreign law] favours the SICC (J4.4).
    • Weak Singapore Link: Per C&Y, a case poorly connected to Singapore is arguably more suited to the SICC, given its international character, so [the dispute]'s [few Singapore links] help [claimant].
    • Consent: Per C&Y, as the General Division may transfer without every party's consent, it should lean towards transfer where [all / most] parties consent, as [defendant] does here.
    • Overlap with Spiliada: Per C&Y, where [defendant] seeks a stay at the jurisdictional stage, most factors other than consent are weighed at Spiliada stage 1, where [the SICC factor] alone cannot displace [State] (IM Skaugen; J4.4).
  • Not More Appropriate (−) [The dispute] is [a straightforward Singapore-law debt claim / largely domestic], and [a General Division judge] can resolve it expeditiously (cf C&Y on SICC → General Division transfers), so no SICC feature makes transfer more appropriate.
J5.4.2 CCAA Case With a "High Court" or "General Division" EJC (O 2 rr 4(4), 4(7), 5(1))
  • Every Party's Consent (must write) Presently, the CCAA applies and [clause X] names [the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Per O 2 r 4(4), transfer also needs every party's consent. Per C&Y, this exceeds s 11(5) CCAA ("take into account") to protect HCCCA recognition: art 8(5) lets [a foreign court] refuse recognition against [a party] that objected in time.
  • Deemed Consent (+) Per O 2 r 4(7), where [clause X] names the receiving court, each party is treated as consenting. With O 2 r 2(1) (a post-2016 "High Court" clause includes the SICC), consent is doubly deemed (C&Y), so [defendant] is treated as consenting although it [objects].
    • Counter (−): Per C&Y, it is unclear whether deemed consent meets the CCAA threshold. [Defendant] objected in time, so [the SICC judgment] risks refusal under art 8(5) in [State], where its assets are; arguably the General Division should insist on actual consent.
    • Discretion Only: Per s 15(4)(b) CCAA (the art 8(5) equivalent), the risk arises only where [the transfer] was discretionary, not mandated by [internal allocation rules].
  • SICC Expressly Excluded (±) Presently, [clause X] names [the High Court] "excluding the SICC". Per O 2 r 5(1), transfer may be conditional on every party varying [clause X] to name the SICC. Per C&Y, the rule is strictly unnecessary (no transfer without consent anyway) but nudges [the parties] to vary, securing clean HCCCA enforcement.
  • Handout Question Can a "High Court" EJC case started in [the General Division] be transferred without breaching the HCCCA? Yes, per O 2 r 4(4) and (7), if [every party] consents, actually or by deemed consent, subject to the art 8(5) risk where [a party] objected in time.
J5.4.3 After Transfer: No Relitigation of Jurisdiction
  • Existence (−) Per O 2 r 4(8)(b)(i), the SICC "must not reconsider whether it has jurisdiction unless there has been a material change in circumstances such that the court may cease to have jurisdiction". Presently, [defendant] [can / cannot] reopen it, as there [is / is no] such change, e.g., [a new party / no valid service on [defendant]].
  • Exercise (−) Per the slides, O 2 r 3(2) [and arguably (3)] applies in principle, but [the General Division] will usually have decided [the stay] already. Arguably [defendant]'s consent to the transfer also waives objection.
J5.5 TRANSFER FROM THE SICC TO THE GENERAL DIVISION (O 2 rr 4(5), 5(2))
  • Requirements (+) Presently, [the parties] sued in the SICC under [clause X] but now find [the claims are not truly international / no SICC feature is needed]. Outside O 2 r 3(5), per O 2 r 4(5) a party may apply with all parties' consent if the General Division has jurisdiction (it does: s 18A) and is more appropriate (C&Y).
  • More Appropriate: Low Threshold (+) Per C&Y, as all parties consent, the threshold is low; relevant are whether [the international elements] are germane to [the dispute] and whether [a Singapore judge] can resolve it expeditiously.
  • Not More Appropriate (−) Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [the action] is objectively international and commercial, as with [defendant] in [State], it is hard to see why the General Division is more appropriate.
  • CCAA SICC-Only Clause (±) Per O 2 r 5(2), where the CCAA applies and [clause X] names only the SICC, transfer may be conditional on every party varying [clause X] to name the General Division (C&Y). Deemed consent applies where [the clause] names the receiving court (O 2 r 4(7)).
J5.6 ROUTE 3: JOINDER OF ADDITIONAL PARTIES (s 18D(3) SCJA; O 10)
  • Starter (must write) Presently, [party] seeks to join [third party C] to [SICC action]. Per s 18D(3)–(4), once the SICC has jurisdiction over an international and commercial action, it may hear claims by or against additional parties (joinder, counterclaims, third- and subsequent-party proceedings) if the action as a whole stays international and commercial; [C]'s claims need not be (C&Y).
  • Key Advantage (+) Per C&Y (citing the SICC Committee Report), this coercive joinder is a key advantage over arbitration: [C], though [a non-signatory], can be bound in [one proceeding].
  • Requirements (+) Per O 10 r 5(1), [C] may be joined if the O 10 joinder requirements are met and the claims by or against [C] seek no prerogative relief and are appropriate for the SICC, which considers its international and commercial character (O 10 r 5(3)).
  • Connected Issues (+) Per O 10 r 6(1), joining [C] is appropriate "so that the Court can resolve all the matters in dispute in the proceedings or any issues that are connected to those matters". Presently, [C]'s role as [guarantor / co-contractor / alleged conspirator] is bound up with [the main dispute].
  • No Common Questions (−) Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), joinder fails where [the claim against C] shares no common question of law or fact with [the claim against defendant], e.g., [a pre-contractual tort] against [a post-contractual breach].
  • No Written Agreement Needed (+) Per O 10 r 5(2), [C] need not have submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement, unless [C] is [a State or sovereign], which must have (C&Y).
  • Permission (±) Per O 10 r 7(1), SICC permission is generally required, on application by [an existing party] or [C] itself (O 10 r 7(3)), but not where [C] submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement and the originating application is not yet served (O 10 r 7(2)(a)).
  • Service on [C] in Singapore Per O 5 r 2, [C] in [Singapore] is personally served, founding jurisdiction under s 16 SCJA (apply J2.1 to [C's status]).
  • Service on [C] Abroad (±) Per O 5 r 6(2), [C] in [State] is served without permission if party to a written jurisdiction agreement or [an agreement allowing service out]; otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), with permission if the SICC "has the jurisdiction" and "it is appropriate". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, unlike the General Division's test (J3.1).
  • C Resists Joinder (−) Presently, [C] seeks a stay under O 2 r 3(2). Per the slides, O 2 r 3(3) (the foreign-connections bar) protects only parties to [a written jurisdiction agreement]. The User Guide ignores connections because the parties agreed in writing; [C] did not, so the SICC may weigh [C]'s links with [State].
  • Burden Arguably [the party seeking joinder] bears it, as it must show the claims against [C] are "appropriate" for the SICC (O 10 r 5(1)(b)(ii)).
J5.7 LINKS TO OTHER FILES
  • ASIs Per C&Y, [an SICC written jurisdiction agreement] supplies sufficient interest unless [the claim] is not international and commercial or abuses process (J6.2.1). Breach of an exclusive SICC clause may need no strong reasons test, or a modified one; for an NEJC, the SICC should refrain if [foreign proceedings] came first (J6.3.1.3).
  • ASI Sought From the SICC Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), if [the SICC] has primary jurisdiction under [clause X], the O 2 r 3(2) test arguably governs [the ASI application]. For HCCCA cases see J6.5.3; s 10 CCAA leaves interim measures outside the Act.
  • Spiliada in the General Division Per Rappo, a possible SICC transfer is relevant if [claimant] articulates [the SICC feature] suited to [the dispute]; per IM Skaugen, it cannot alone displace [the natural forum] (J4.4).
  • Damages for Breach Per C&Y, suing in [foreign court] in breach of [an exclusive SICC / CCAA clause] breaches [contract] (J1.7).
  • Recognition [The chosen court]'s judgment is recognised under CCAA Part 3 (J7.5). For [an SICC judgment] abroad, art 8(5) non-recognition after a contested transfer is why the transfer rules insist on consent (J5.4.2).

1Start here: J5 in plain English

Prof Chong's answer framework runs the SICC side by side with the General Division for each contract. After you have worked out whether the General Division has and will exercise jurisdiction, ask: could this case be in the SICC instead, and on what route?

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The SICC is a special international courtroom inside the Singapore High Court building. It has judges from around the world, can hear foreign law argued by lawyers instead of proved by experts, and is built for cross-border business disputes. You can get a case into that room three ways: you booked it in advance (a written agreement), the ordinary courtroom sends it across (transfer), or you are pulled in because you are part of a case already there (joinder).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Why the room matters: one argument, two courtrooms

Alpha (Singapore) sues Beta (Vietnam). Beta argues: "Everything happened in Vietnam, so Vietnam is the better forum."

General Division, no clauseSICC, under a written SICC agreement
TestSpiliada (J4.1)O 2 r 3(2): contrary to the SICC's character, or abuse of process
Beta's Vietnam argumentThe heart of stage 1: it may well win a stayIrrelevant: the SICC must not decline "solely" because the action is connected to Vietnam (O 2 r 3(3))
Likely resultStay possibleThe SICC hears the case

Same parties, same facts, same argument. In the SICC under a written agreement, the argument that might win in the General Division simply does not count.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
SICCSingapore International Commercial Court, a division of the General Division (s 18A SCJA), launched 5 January 2015. A national court, not a tribunal.
Primary jurisdictionThe SICC hears the case because the parties signed a written jurisdiction agreement for it.
Written jurisdiction agreementAn agreement in writing (or accessible electronic form) to submit to the SICC, exclusively or not (O 2 r 1(7)).
International and commercialThe SICC's subject-matter limit (s 18D; O 2 r 1(3)).
TransferMoving a case from the General Division to the SICC (O 2 r 4) or back.
JoinderAdding a third party to an SICC case (s 18D(3); O 10).
s 18F SCJAPresumes an SICC clause is exclusive unless it expressly says otherwise.
O 2 r 2A post-2016 "Singapore High Court" clause includes the SICC.
O 2 r 3The SICC's only exercise test: contrary to its character, or an abuse of process.

2J5.1 What the SICC is and what it hears

▤ On your pre-write: J5.1 THE SICC: NATURE AND SUBJECT-MATTER JURISDICTION (word for word)
J5.1 THE SICC: NATURE AND SUBJECT-MATTER JURISDICTION
  • Nature (write one line) Per s 18A SCJA, the SICC (launched 5 January 2015) is a division of the General Division, so a national court: [its judgment] is a Singapore High Court judgment, enforceable in [State] as such (including under the HCCCA); appeals lie to the Court of Appeal; and jurisdiction over [defendant] still rests on s 16 SCJA.
  • Court, Not Tribunal Unlike [an arbitral tribunal], the SICC can coerce [third party C] into the proceedings (J5.6). Per Parliament, though arbitration-influenced, it is "a new way of thinking about international dispute resolution".
  • Special Features (use where relevant) Presently, [the dispute] turns on [foreign law / foreign evidence rules]. The SICC has international judges, may disapply Singapore evidence rules, including on privilege (s 18K SCJA), and may decide foreign law on submissions instead of proof (s 18L).
  • Confidentiality and Counsel Where [the parties] want [confidentiality / their own foreign counsel], the SICC may allow it (O 16 r 9; s 18M), more readily in "offshore" cases with no substantial connection to Singapore.
  • Standalone Rules Where the SICC Rules are silent on [issue], the SICC may do what is necessary, applying the ROC with modifications or looking to [foreign law / international practice] (O 1 r 11(3)). Per C&Y, the standalone SICC Rules 2021 (from 1 April 2022) stress its independence and international character, including procedural flexibility responsive to international commerce (O 1 r 3).
  • Subject Matter (s 18D) Presently, [claimant]'s [claim] falls within [category]. The SICC hears (1) international and commercial actions the General Division could hear in its original civil jurisdiction (s 18D(1)); (2) IAA proceedings on international commercial arbitration (s 18D(2)); (3) pre-action applications for documents, injunctions or search orders, and committal; and (4) international and commercial corporate insolvency, restructuring and dissolution.
  • IAA Proceedings (±) Where [the application] concerns [an international commercial arbitration], permission is needed to serve out (O 5 r 6), and the SICC may decline under O 2 r 3(2) (C&Y). Per C&Y, "international" follows IAA s 5(2), "commercial" the Model Law art 1(1) note, and [investment / State] arbitrations may be included.
J5.1.1 International and Commercial (O 2 r 1(3))
  • International (+) Per O 2 r 1(3)(a), [the action] is international if [one party's place of business / where a substantial part of the obligations is to be performed / the subject matter's closest connection] is outside Singapore, or all parties named on filing expressly agreed it relates to more than one State. Presently, [defendant]'s place of business is [State].
  • Place of Business Per O 2 r 1(4)–(6), [party]'s place of business is where it carries on business; if [several], the one most closely connected to [the written jurisdiction agreement]; if none, its habitual residence. It is fixed when [the agreement] was concluded (or, on transfer, when [the case] began or as the General Division decides).
  • Commercial (+) Per O 2 r 1(3)(b), [the action] is commercial if its subject matter arises from a commercial relationship, contractual or not, or it is an in personam IP dispute, or all parties expressly agreed so. The parties themselves need not be in a commercial relationship (O 2 r 1(5)). Presently, [claim] arises from [a [distribution / construction / loan] relationship].
  • Presumption (+) Per O 2 r 1(8), as each party submitted under [clause X], [the action] is presumed international and commercial, subject to the SICC's review under O 2 r 3 (C&Y). Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [the facts] are objectively international and commercial, say so briefly and move on.
  • Rebuttal (−) [Defendant] rebuts the presumption: [both parties trade only in Singapore / all obligations were performed here / the dispute is [a residential tenancy / an individual's guarantee]]. Even where the parties agreed [the case] into scope (O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii), (b)(iii)), per C&Y the SICC may decline it as contrary to its character (O 2 r 3(2)) (J5.3).
🔍 THE PRE-WRITE, IN EVERYDAY WORDS
  • A national court (write one line). Its judgment is a Singapore High Court judgment, enforceable abroad as such (including under the HCCCA); appeals go to the Court of Appeal; jurisdiction over the defendant still rests on s 16 SCJA.
  • A court, not a tribunal. Unlike arbitration, it can coerce a third party into the proceedings (J5.6).
  • Special features (use where relevant): international judges; may disapply Singapore evidence rules, including privilege (s 18K); may decide foreign law on submissions instead of proof (s 18L); confidentiality and foreign counsel (O 16 r 9; s 18M), more readily in "offshore" cases.
  • What it hears (s 18D): international and commercial actions the General Division could hear; IAA proceedings on international commercial arbitration; pre-action applications; international commercial insolvency.

J5.1.1 International and commercial

▤ On your pre-write: J5.1.1 International and Commercial (O 2 r 1(3)) (word for word)
J5.1.1 International and Commercial (O 2 r 1(3))
  • International (+) Per O 2 r 1(3)(a), [the action] is international if [one party's place of business / where a substantial part of the obligations is to be performed / the subject matter's closest connection] is outside Singapore, or all parties named on filing expressly agreed it relates to more than one State. Presently, [defendant]'s place of business is [State].
  • Place of Business Per O 2 r 1(4)–(6), [party]'s place of business is where it carries on business; if [several], the one most closely connected to [the written jurisdiction agreement]; if none, its habitual residence. It is fixed when [the agreement] was concluded (or, on transfer, when [the case] began or as the General Division decides).
  • Commercial (+) Per O 2 r 1(3)(b), [the action] is commercial if its subject matter arises from a commercial relationship, contractual or not, or it is an in personam IP dispute, or all parties expressly agreed so. The parties themselves need not be in a commercial relationship (O 2 r 1(5)). Presently, [claim] arises from [a [distribution / construction / loan] relationship].
  • Presumption (+) Per O 2 r 1(8), as each party submitted under [clause X], [the action] is presumed international and commercial, subject to the SICC's review under O 2 r 3 (C&Y). Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [the facts] are objectively international and commercial, say so briefly and move on.
  • Rebuttal (−) [Defendant] rebuts the presumption: [both parties trade only in Singapore / all obligations were performed here / the dispute is [a residential tenancy / an individual's guarantee]]. Even where the parties agreed [the case] into scope (O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii), (b)(iii)), per C&Y the SICC may decline it as contrary to its character (O 2 r 3(2)) (J5.3).
  • Place of business is where it carries on business; if several, the one most closely connected to the agreement; if none, habitual residence. Fixed when the agreement was concluded (O 2 r 1(4)–(6)).
  • The parties need not be in a commercial relationship themselves (O 2 r 1(5)).
  • Rebuttal (−): both parties trade only in Singapore, everything was performed here, or the dispute is a residential tenancy or an individual's guarantee. Even where the parties agreed it into scope, the SICC may decline it as contrary to its character (O 2 r 3(2)).
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Where the facts are objectively international and commercial, say so briefly and move on (AY23-24 mid-term feedback). Do not spend marks proving the obvious.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Four actions: international and commercial?
ActionInternational?Commercial?Verdict
Singapore seller v Vietnamese buyer over a supply contractYes: a party's place of business is abroadYes: a commercial relationshipIn. One line in the exam.
Two Singapore companies, but most of the building work was to be done in IndonesiaYes: a substantial part of the obligations performed abroadYesIn.
Two Singapore companies, everything done here, but the contract says "the parties agree this dispute is international"Yes, by express agreement (O 2 r 1(3)(a))YesIn on paper, but the SICC may decline it as contrary to its international and commercial character (O 2 r 3(2)).
A Singapore landlord v a local tenant over a flatNoNo: a residential tenancyOut. General Division only.

3J5.2 Route 1: a written jurisdiction agreement

▤ On your pre-write: J5.2.1 Starter and Conditions (O 2 r 1(1)) (word for word)
J5.2.1 Starter and Conditions (O 2 r 1(1))
  • Starter (must write) Presently, [claimant] filed in the SICC relying on [clause X]. Per O 2 r 1(1) and s 18D(1), the SICC has jurisdiction if, when first filed, (a) [the action] is international and commercial (J5.1.1) and one the General Division could hear; (b) each named party submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement; and (c) no prerogative relief is sought.
  • In Personam Basis Per the slides, jurisdiction over [defendant] is founded by service under s 16(1)(a) SCJA (J5.2.4). [Clause X] is a promise; s 16(1)(b) submission is a separate basis, needing conduct such as [filing a defence on the merits] (J2.2).
  • Written Jurisdiction Agreement (+) Per O 2 r 1(7), [clause X] is a written jurisdiction agreement: [the parties]' agreement to submit to the [exclusive / non-exclusive] jurisdiction of the SICC, [in writing / in an accessible form usable for later reference]. Per C&Y, both EJCs and NEJCs qualify.
  • Primary Jurisdiction Ends the Inquiry Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), if [clause X] gives the SICC primary jurisdiction over [the claim against defendant], transfer need not be discussed; transfer matters only for [a party or claim outside clause X] (J5.4).
O 2 r 1(1): primary jurisdiction ("must write")
▤ J5.2.1. Tested when the action is first filed.
  1. 1The action is international and commercial and one the General Division could hear.
  2. 2Each named party submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement (EJC or NEJC both qualify, per C&Y).
  3. 3No prerogative relief is sought.
  • In personam basis. Jurisdiction over the defendant is still founded by service under s 16(1)(a) SCJA. The clause is a promise; submission under s 16(1)(b) is a separate basis needing conduct (J2.2).
  • Primary jurisdiction ends the inquiry. Per Chong (AY23-24 feedback), if the clause gives the SICC primary jurisdiction over the claim, transfer need not be discussed. Transfer matters only for a party or claim outside the clause.

J5.2.2 Is the SICC clause exclusive? (s 18F)

▤ On your pre-write: J5.2.2 Exclusive or Not? (s 18F SCJA) (word for word)
J5.2.2 Exclusive or Not? (s 18F SCJA)
  • Presumption of Exclusivity (+) Per s 18F(1), absent express contrary words in [clause X] (s 18F(2)), [the parties] are taken to have agreed (a) to submit exclusively to the SICC; (b) to carry out [its judgment] without undue delay; and (c) to waive recourse to [foreign courts] against the judgment or its enforcement, so far as validly waivable.
  • When Does s 18F Apply? (route by facts) Per C&Y, route [clause X] by [its governing law]:
    • CCAA case: s 3(2) CCAA deems [clause X] exclusive whether [Singapore / foreign] law governs it, so s 18F need not be argued.
    • Singapore law governs [clause X]: s 18F applies, so [clause X] is exclusive absent [express non-exclusive wording].
    • Non-CCAA case, [foreign law] governing: debated. s 18F governs [clause X] only if it is a forum mandatory rule, as [the party wanting exclusivity] argues and [the party resisting] denies (C1.7). C&Y take no side, noting that Yip and Chong differ.
  • s 18F Is a Forum Mandatory Rule (+) Per Chong (Chong & Yip 2019 article), s 18F applies to [clause X] whatever its governing law: (i) the presumption against extraterritoriality is rebutted for a court set up to hear [international disputes]; (ii) s 18F(1)(a) is inspired by art 3(b) HCCCA (now s 3(2) CCAA); (iii) it keeps [non-CCAA SICC clauses] consistent with [CCAA SICC clauses].
  • s 18F Is Not Mandatory (−) Per Yip (same article), s 18F applies only where Singapore law governs [clause X] (in a CCAA case, s 3(2) CCAA deems exclusivity: C&Y). Party autonomy is an important undergirding value of the SICC (C&Y), and a presumption rebuttable by contrary words is not [an overriding mandatory rule]. So [clause X] is construed under [foreign law], under which it is [non-exclusive].
    • Reply (+): per C&Y, the SICC balances [party autonomy] against [expedience], as O 2 r 2(1) shows.
    • Why it matters: little for exercise, as O 2 r 3 treats [EJCs and NEJCs] alike (J5.3). It matters for breach: per C&Y, suing in [foreign court] breaches only an exclusive SICC clause, founding [an ASI / damages] (J6.3.1.3; J1.7).

Section 18F(1) says that, absent express contrary words, the parties are taken to have agreed (a) to submit exclusively to the SICC, (b) to carry out its judgment without undue delay, and (c) to waive recourse to foreign courts against it, so far as validly waivable. But does s 18F apply when foreign law governs the clause?

? WHY IT MATTERS

For exercise, exclusivity matters little: O 2 r 3 treats EJCs and NEJCs alike (J5.3). It matters for breach: suing abroad breaks only an exclusive SICC clause, which can found an ASI or damages (J6.3.1.3; J1.7).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Where s 18F makes the difference

Clause: "The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore International Commercial Court." It does not say "exclusive" or "non-exclusive". Beta sues Alpha in Hanoi. Alpha wants an ASI.

  • If Singapore law governs the clause: s 18F applies, so the clause is exclusive. Beta's Hanoi suit is a breach, giving Alpha the contractual basis for an ASI.
  • If Vietnamese law governs the clause: argue whether s 18F still applies as a forum mandatory rule. Chong says yes (so breach again); Yip says no (so Vietnamese law decides whether the clause is exclusive, and if it is not, Beta's suit breaks nothing and Alpha must show vexation or oppression instead, J6.3.2).
  • If it is a CCAA case: s 3(2) CCAA deems "submit to the jurisdiction of the courts of [State]" exclusive anyway, so the debate disappears.

J5.2.3 "Singapore High Court" clauses (O 2 r 2)

▤ On your pre-write: J5.2.3 Clauses Naming the High Court or General Division (O 2 r 2) (word for word)
J5.2.3 Clauses Naming the High Court or General Division (O 2 r 2)
  • Post-2016 High Court Clause Includes the SICC (+) Presently, [clause X], concluded on [date] (on or after 1 October 2016), names [the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2)–(3) CCAA, it includes the SICC unless [a contrary intention] appears, so [claimant] may file directly in the SICC.
    • Critique (−): Per C&Y, O 2 r 2(1) seems to bar evidence that [the parties] [never contemplated the SICC], contrary to Singapore's contextual interpretation and to party autonomy.
    • Reply (+): Per C&Y, the lost autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability of [the SICC judgment] in [State] and fits the SICC's international template; per Hartley–Dogauchi, "the courts of France" lets French law allocate internally.
    • Specific Reference Needed? (−): Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), arguably [clause X] needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it, so [defendant] resists [primary jurisdiction].
  • Pre-2016 Clause (−) Per O 2 r 2(2), [clause X], concluded on [date] before 1 October 2016, "does not of itself" submit to the SICC. Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), there is no primary jurisdiction, so [claimant] sues in the General Division and seeks [a transfer] (J5.4).
  • SICC-Only Clause (−) Per O 2 r 2(3), [clause X], naming [the SICC] alone, is not "of itself" submission to the General Division, so [claimant] suing there cannot rely on it alone (C&Y).
  • Foreign Law Governs [Clause X]: O 2 r 2(1) Procedural or Substantive? (±) Per the slides, this is open where [foreign law] governs [clause X]:
    • (+) Party wanting the SICC: O 2 r 2(1) is a forum rule on internal allocation and on the scope of submission to a Singapore court, so the lex fori applies though [contract] is governed by [foreign law].
    • (−) Party resisting the SICC: construing [clause X] is substance for its proper law, [foreign law], as party autonomy requires; under it, ["the High Court of Singapore"] excludes the SICC.
    • If Singapore law governs: per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), the question does not arise: O 2 r 2(1) applies to [clause X], and absent [express contrary words] s 18F makes it exclusive (C&Y).
IssueThe arguments
Critique of O 2 r 2(1) (−)Per C&Y, it seems to bar evidence that the parties never contemplated the SICC, contrary to contextual interpretation and party autonomy. Reply (+): the lost autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability and fits the international template (Hartley–Dogauchi: "the courts of France" lets French law allocate internally).
SICC-only clauseNot "of itself" submission to the General Division (O 2 r 2(3)).
Foreign law governs the clause (±)(+) O 2 r 2(1) is a forum rule on internal allocation, so the lex fori applies. (−) Construction is substance for the clause's proper law, under which "the High Court of Singapore" may exclude the SICC. If Singapore law governs, the question does not arise (Chong).
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Before October 2016, nobody signing a "Singapore High Court" clause was thinking about the SICC in the way the rules now treat it, so the rules do not drag those older clauses into the SICC. For clauses made from October 2016 onwards, the rules say "High Court" is a building with several rooms, and the SICC is one of them: naming the building gets you into any room, unless you said otherwise.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Two "Singapore High Court" clauses, two dates
  • Clause signed March 2015: "the Singapore High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction". Before 1 October 2016, so it does not "of itself" submit to the SICC (O 2 r 2(2)). Alpha sues in the General Division and, if it wants the SICC, seeks a transfer (J5.4).
  • Clause signed March 2018: the same words. On or after 1 October 2016, so it includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears (O 2 r 2(1)). Alpha may file directly in the SICC, though Chong's answer scheme notes an argument that a more specific SICC reference is needed for primary jurisdiction.

J5.2.4 to J5.2.5 Service and challenges

▤ On your pre-write: J5.2.4 Serving [Defendant] Out of Singapore (O 5 r 6) (word for word)
J5.2.4 Serving [Defendant] Out of Singapore (O 5 r 6)
  • No Permission Needed (+) Presently, per O 5 r 6(2), [defendant] in [State] may be served out without permission, being [a party to the written jurisdiction agreement (r 6(2)(a)) / bound by [contract] allowing service out (r 6(2)(b))], whether or not [clause X] mentions service. Per O 5 r 6(5), the SICC may still review jurisdiction under O 2 r 3.
  • Permission Needed (±) Otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), permission is granted if the SICC "has the jurisdiction to hear the action and it is appropriate for the case to be heard in the Court". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, so [defendant]'s [Spiliada factors] are irrelevant; appropriateness turns on [the SICC's international and commercial character] (J5.3).
  • No permission needed (O 5 r 6(2)) to serve abroad a party to the written jurisdiction agreement (r 6(2)(a)) or one bound by a contract allowing service out (r 6(2)(b)), whether or not the clause mentions service.
  • Permission otherwise (O 5 r 6(1)): the SICC must "have the jurisdiction" and it must be "appropriate". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, so Spiliada factors are irrelevant.
▤ On your pre-write: J5.2.5 Challenging the Existence of Jurisdiction (word for word)
J5.2.5 Challenging the Existence of Jurisdiction

(Apply within 14 days after serving the Defendant's Statement (O 2 r 7). A [defendant] disputing service may apply to set it aside (O 2 r 6).)

  • Attack the Clause (−) [Defendant] argues [clause X] is [void / never agreed] for [mistake / misrepresentation / duress / lack of authority]. Reply (+): per s 5 CCAA (CCAA cases) and the common law (J1.6), [clause X] is separable, so an attack on [contract] alone does not touch it.
  • Attack the Nature of the Dispute (−) Per O 2 r 1(8), [defendant] rebuts the presumption by showing [the action] is not [international / commercial] (J5.1.1).
  • Consequence of a Successful Challenge Per O 2 r 3(5), if the SICC lacks jurisdiction over [the claim], it must transfer [the case] to the General Division if that court has jurisdiction and [all parties] consent; otherwise it may dismiss, stay or make any order.
  • Deemed Consent to Transfer Per O 2 r 3(6), [a "High Court" / "General Division" clause] counts as each party's consent to the General Division hearing [the case], justifiably given the clause's express scope (C&Y).
  • Finality Per O 2 r 3(7), a decision that the SICC has and will exercise jurisdiction over [the claim], or a transfer of [the case] to the General Division, is final unless [permission to appeal] is granted.
  • Attacking the clause (−): void for mistake, misrepresentation, duress. Reply (+): separability (s 5 CCAA; common law, J1.6).
  • Attacking the nature of the dispute: rebut the O 2 r 1(8) presumption.
  • If the challenge succeeds (O 2 r 3(5)): the SICC must transfer to the General Division if it has jurisdiction and all parties consent (a "High Court" clause counts as consent: O 2 r 3(6)); otherwise dismiss or stay.

4J5.3 Exercise in the SICC: O 2 r 3

▤ On your pre-write: J5.3 EXERCISE OF JURISDICTION IN THE SICC (O 2 r 3) (word for word)
J5.3 EXERCISE OF JURISDICTION IN THE SICC (O 2 r 3)
  • The Test (must write) Presently, [defendant] asks the SICC to decline because [the dispute centres on [State] / [State B] law governs]. Per O 2 r 3(2), the SICC may decline only if exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process, on its own motion or [on application] (O 2 r 3(4)).
  • Foreign Connections Irrelevant (+) Per O 2 r 3(3), as there is [a written jurisdiction agreement], the SICC must not decline "solely on the ground that the action … is connected to a jurisdiction other than Singapore". Per C&Y and Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), there is no Spiliada balancing, Australian test or strong cause, so [defendant]'s links to [State] count for nothing.
  • Same Test for EJCs and NEJCs (+) Per C&Y, the old O 110 r 8 "appropriateness" wording left room to treat an NEJC differently; the 2021 Rules close that gap, as the SICC Committee intended. So although [clause X] is non-exclusive, [defendant] cannot rely on [State B] being more appropriate.
  • Justification (if asked to evaluate) Per the SICC User Guide (Note 1), connections are ignored because [the parties] agreed in writing to "an international court"; per C&Y this is circular, the SICC not being a true international court. C&Y prefer party autonomy: [commercial parties] may choose [a neutral, specialist forum] and must accept the consequences.
  • Contrary to International and Commercial Character (−) Presently, [the dispute] is in substance [a local dispute between Singapore residents / a consumer-type claim], brought in only by [the parties' agreement] under O 2 r 1(3)(a)(ii) or (b)(iii). Per C&Y, hearing it may be contrary to the SICC's international and commercial character.
  • Objectively International and Commercial (+) Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), as [the action] is objectively international and commercial, with [defendant] in [State], there is little ground for the SICC to decline.
  • Abuse of Process (−) Presently, [claimant] filed in the SICC only to [delay [State B] proceedings already well advanced / relitigate [issue] decided in [State B]]. Per O 2 r 3(2), that abuses the SICC's process (cf tactical "wait and see" conduct, J6.3.1.3).
  • Consequence Per O 2 r 3(5)–(6), if the SICC declines, it must transfer [the case] to the General Division where that court has jurisdiction and [all parties] consent (deemed for [a "High Court" clause]); otherwise it may dismiss or stay (J5.2.5).

This is the big difference from the General Division. With a written jurisdiction agreement, no Spiliada, no Australian test, no strong cause.

  • Same test for EJCs and NEJCs (+). The old O 110 r 8 "appropriateness" wording left room to treat a NEJC differently; the 2021 Rules close that gap (C&Y).
  • Why ignore connections? Per the SICC User Guide (Note 1), the parties agreed in writing to "an international court"; per C&Y that is circular, as the SICC is not a true international court. C&Y prefer party autonomy: commercial parties may choose a neutral specialist forum and must live with it.
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Picking the SICC is like two companies from different countries agreeing to meet in a neutral city. Nobody expects the meeting place to be close to either of them; that is the point. So it would make no sense for one side to say later, "but the meeting place has nothing to do with us." The only good reasons to call off the meeting are that it was never the kind of meeting the venue hosts (contrary to its character), or that one side is using it to play games (abuse).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Abuse of process in the SICC

Beta sued Alpha in Hanoi two years ago, and trial there is almost finished. Alpha, losing, now files in the SICC under their written SICC agreement, asking for the same relief. Beta asks the SICC to decline. The Vietnamese connections are irrelevant (O 2 r 3(3)), but an action filed only to delay well-advanced foreign proceedings, or to relitigate, can be an abuse of process, so the SICC may decline (O 2 r 3(2)).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exercise in the SICC

Beta asks the SICC to decline because the dispute centres on Vietnam and Vietnamese law governs. Per O 2 r 3(3), as there is a written jurisdiction agreement, the SICC must not decline solely because the action is connected to Vietnam; there is no Spiliada balancing or strong cause (C&Y; Chong). The action is objectively international and commercial, Beta being in Vietnam, and there is no suggestion of abuse, so the SICC will hear it (O 2 r 3(2)).

5J5.4 Route 2: transfer from the General Division

▤ On your pre-write: J5.4 ROUTE 2: TRANSFER FROM THE GENERAL DIVISION TO THE SICC (s 18J(2) SCJA; O 2 r 4) (word for word)
J5.4 ROUTE 2: TRANSFER FROM THE GENERAL DIVISION TO THE SICC (s 18J(2) SCJA; O 2 r 4)

(Per C&Y, the main source of SICC cases so far. Apply within 28 days, with evidence of the transfer conditions and any consent (O 2 r 7). Per the slides, existence was founded under General Division rules: [service in (J2) / service out under O 8 (J3)].)

J5.4.1 Non-CCAA Case (O 2 r 4(1))
  • Requirements (must write) Presently, [party] seeks transfer of [claimant]'s General Division action, or the court acts on its own motion after hearing [the parties] (O 2 r 4(3)). Per O 2 r 4(1), it may transfer if (a) [the action] is international and commercial when the order is made; (b) no prerogative relief is sought; and (c) the SICC is more appropriate.
  • Only Route Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme; AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [clause X] [predates 1 October 2016 / does not cover [the claim against C]], the SICC has no primary jurisdiction, so [claimant] reaches it only by transfer under the O 2 r 4(1)(c) "more appropriate" test.
  • More Appropriate (+) Per C&Y, relevant factors (the Rules give none) are the international elements and their relevance; the SICC's capability to handle them; [the parties]' level of consent; and connections to Singapore. Presently, [the dispute] turns on [foreign law, decidable on submissions (s 18L) / technical [construction / shipping] issues].
    • International Judge: Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), [an International Judge from [State]] with expertise in [foreign law] favours the SICC (J4.4).
    • Weak Singapore Link: Per C&Y, a case poorly connected to Singapore is arguably more suited to the SICC, given its international character, so [the dispute]'s [few Singapore links] help [claimant].
    • Consent: Per C&Y, as the General Division may transfer without every party's consent, it should lean towards transfer where [all / most] parties consent, as [defendant] does here.
    • Overlap with Spiliada: Per C&Y, where [defendant] seeks a stay at the jurisdictional stage, most factors other than consent are weighed at Spiliada stage 1, where [the SICC factor] alone cannot displace [State] (IM Skaugen; J4.4).
  • Not More Appropriate (−) [The dispute] is [a straightforward Singapore-law debt claim / largely domestic], and [a General Division judge] can resolve it expeditiously (cf C&Y on SICC → General Division transfers), so no SICC feature makes transfer more appropriate.
J5.4.2 CCAA Case With a "High Court" or "General Division" EJC (O 2 rr 4(4), 4(7), 5(1))
  • Every Party's Consent (must write) Presently, the CCAA applies and [clause X] names [the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Per O 2 r 4(4), transfer also needs every party's consent. Per C&Y, this exceeds s 11(5) CCAA ("take into account") to protect HCCCA recognition: art 8(5) lets [a foreign court] refuse recognition against [a party] that objected in time.
  • Deemed Consent (+) Per O 2 r 4(7), where [clause X] names the receiving court, each party is treated as consenting. With O 2 r 2(1) (a post-2016 "High Court" clause includes the SICC), consent is doubly deemed (C&Y), so [defendant] is treated as consenting although it [objects].
    • Counter (−): Per C&Y, it is unclear whether deemed consent meets the CCAA threshold. [Defendant] objected in time, so [the SICC judgment] risks refusal under art 8(5) in [State], where its assets are; arguably the General Division should insist on actual consent.
    • Discretion Only: Per s 15(4)(b) CCAA (the art 8(5) equivalent), the risk arises only where [the transfer] was discretionary, not mandated by [internal allocation rules].
  • SICC Expressly Excluded (±) Presently, [clause X] names [the High Court] "excluding the SICC". Per O 2 r 5(1), transfer may be conditional on every party varying [clause X] to name the SICC. Per C&Y, the rule is strictly unnecessary (no transfer without consent anyway) but nudges [the parties] to vary, securing clean HCCCA enforcement.
  • Handout Question Can a "High Court" EJC case started in [the General Division] be transferred without breaching the HCCCA? Yes, per O 2 r 4(4) and (7), if [every party] consents, actually or by deemed consent, subject to the art 8(5) risk where [a party] objected in time.
J5.4.3 After Transfer: No Relitigation of Jurisdiction
  • Existence (−) Per O 2 r 4(8)(b)(i), the SICC "must not reconsider whether it has jurisdiction unless there has been a material change in circumstances such that the court may cease to have jurisdiction". Presently, [defendant] [can / cannot] reopen it, as there [is / is no] such change, e.g., [a new party / no valid service on [defendant]].
  • Exercise (−) Per the slides, O 2 r 3(2) [and arguably (3)] applies in principle, but [the General Division] will usually have decided [the stay] already. Arguably [defendant]'s consent to the transfer also waives objection.

Per C&Y, transfer is the main source of SICC cases so far. Existence was founded under the General Division's rules (service in or out).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Arguing a transfer

Alpha sued Beta in the General Division under a 2014 "Singapore High Court" clause. The contract is governed by Vietnamese law, and the dispute turns on the meaning of technical shipbuilding specifications. Alpha applies to transfer to the SICC.

  1. (a) International and commercial when the order is made: Beta is in Vietnam, a shipbuilding contract. ✓
  2. (b) No prerogative relief. ✓
  3. (c) More appropriate? (+) Vietnamese law can be decided on submissions in the SICC (s 18L) instead of by competing experts; technical construction issues; an International Judge with expertise in Vietnamese law could sit (Chong). (−) Beta does not consent; Singapore links are thin, which cuts both ways.

On balance the SICC looks more appropriate, so transfer is likely. Had this been a simple Singapore-law debt claim against a local company, a General Division judge could deal with it expeditiously, and transfer would be refused.

⚠ TRAP
Overlap with Spiliada

Where the defendant seeks a stay at the jurisdiction stage, most of these factors (other than consent) are weighed at Spiliada stage 1, where the SICC factor alone cannot displace the natural forum (IM Skaugen; J4.4).

🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Where the clause predates 1 October 2016, or does not cover the claim against a third party C, the SICC has no primary jurisdiction, so the claimant reaches it only by transfer under the O 2 r 4(1)(c) "more appropriate" test (sample-final answer scheme; AY23-24 feedback).

  • SICC Expressly Excluded (±) Presently, [clause X] names [the High Court] "excluding the SICC". Per O 2 r 5(1), transfer may be conditional on every party varying [clause X] to name the SICC. Per C&Y, the rule is strictly unnecessary (no transfer without consent anyway) but nudges [the parties] to vary, securing clean HCCCA enforcement.
  • Handout Question Can a "High Court" EJC case started in [the General Division] be transferred without breaching the HCCCA? Yes, per O 2 r 4(4) and (7), if [every party] consents, actually or by deemed consent, subject to the art 8(5) risk where [a party] objected in time.
  • Every party's consent (O 2 r 4(4)) goes beyond s 11(5) CCAA ("take into account"), to protect HCCCA recognition.
  • "Excluding the SICC" clauses: transfer may be conditional on every party varying the clause (O 2 r 5(1)).
  • Handout question. Can a "High Court" EJC case started in the General Division be transferred without breaching the HCCCA? Yes, if every party consents, actually or by deemed consent, subject to the art 8(5) risk where a party objected in time.
▤ On your pre-write: J5.4.3 After Transfer: No Relitigation of Jurisdiction (word for word)
J5.4.3 After Transfer: No Relitigation of Jurisdiction
  • Existence (−) Per O 2 r 4(8)(b)(i), the SICC "must not reconsider whether it has jurisdiction unless there has been a material change in circumstances such that the court may cease to have jurisdiction". Presently, [defendant] [can / cannot] reopen it, as there [is / is no] such change, e.g., [a new party / no valid service on [defendant]].
  • Exercise (−) Per the slides, O 2 r 3(2) [and arguably (3)] applies in principle, but [the General Division] will usually have decided [the stay] already. Arguably [defendant]'s consent to the transfer also waives objection.
  • After transfer, the SICC "must not reconsider whether it has jurisdiction unless there has been a material change in circumstances" (O 2 r 4(8)(b)(i)).
▤ On your pre-write: J5.5 TRANSFER FROM THE SICC TO THE GENERAL DIVISION (O 2 rr 4(5), 5(2)) (word for word)
J5.5 TRANSFER FROM THE SICC TO THE GENERAL DIVISION (O 2 rr 4(5), 5(2))
  • Requirements (+) Presently, [the parties] sued in the SICC under [clause X] but now find [the claims are not truly international / no SICC feature is needed]. Outside O 2 r 3(5), per O 2 r 4(5) a party may apply with all parties' consent if the General Division has jurisdiction (it does: s 18A) and is more appropriate (C&Y).
  • More Appropriate: Low Threshold (+) Per C&Y, as all parties consent, the threshold is low; relevant are whether [the international elements] are germane to [the dispute] and whether [a Singapore judge] can resolve it expeditiously.
  • Not More Appropriate (−) Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [the action] is objectively international and commercial, as with [defendant] in [State], it is hard to see why the General Division is more appropriate.
  • CCAA SICC-Only Clause (±) Per O 2 r 5(2), where the CCAA applies and [clause X] names only the SICC, transfer may be conditional on every party varying [clause X] to name the General Division (C&Y). Deemed consent applies where [the clause] names the receiving court (O 2 r 4(7)).
  • SICC → General Division (O 2 r 4(5)): all parties consent and the General Division is more appropriate. Low threshold given consent. But where the action is objectively international and commercial, it is hard to see why the General Division is more appropriate (Chong).

6J5.6 Route 3: joinder

▤ On your pre-write: J5.6 ROUTE 3: JOINDER OF ADDITIONAL PARTIES (s 18D(3) SCJA; O 10) (word for word)
J5.6 ROUTE 3: JOINDER OF ADDITIONAL PARTIES (s 18D(3) SCJA; O 10)
  • Starter (must write) Presently, [party] seeks to join [third party C] to [SICC action]. Per s 18D(3)–(4), once the SICC has jurisdiction over an international and commercial action, it may hear claims by or against additional parties (joinder, counterclaims, third- and subsequent-party proceedings) if the action as a whole stays international and commercial; [C]'s claims need not be (C&Y).
  • Key Advantage (+) Per C&Y (citing the SICC Committee Report), this coercive joinder is a key advantage over arbitration: [C], though [a non-signatory], can be bound in [one proceeding].
  • Requirements (+) Per O 10 r 5(1), [C] may be joined if the O 10 joinder requirements are met and the claims by or against [C] seek no prerogative relief and are appropriate for the SICC, which considers its international and commercial character (O 10 r 5(3)).
  • Connected Issues (+) Per O 10 r 6(1), joining [C] is appropriate "so that the Court can resolve all the matters in dispute in the proceedings or any issues that are connected to those matters". Presently, [C]'s role as [guarantor / co-contractor / alleged conspirator] is bound up with [the main dispute].
  • No Common Questions (−) Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), joinder fails where [the claim against C] shares no common question of law or fact with [the claim against defendant], e.g., [a pre-contractual tort] against [a post-contractual breach].
  • No Written Agreement Needed (+) Per O 10 r 5(2), [C] need not have submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement, unless [C] is [a State or sovereign], which must have (C&Y).
  • Permission (±) Per O 10 r 7(1), SICC permission is generally required, on application by [an existing party] or [C] itself (O 10 r 7(3)), but not where [C] submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement and the originating application is not yet served (O 10 r 7(2)(a)).
  • Service on [C] in Singapore Per O 5 r 2, [C] in [Singapore] is personally served, founding jurisdiction under s 16 SCJA (apply J2.1 to [C's status]).
  • Service on [C] Abroad (±) Per O 5 r 6(2), [C] in [State] is served without permission if party to a written jurisdiction agreement or [an agreement allowing service out]; otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), with permission if the SICC "has the jurisdiction" and "it is appropriate". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, unlike the General Division's test (J3.1).
  • C Resists Joinder (−) Presently, [C] seeks a stay under O 2 r 3(2). Per the slides, O 2 r 3(3) (the foreign-connections bar) protects only parties to [a written jurisdiction agreement]. The User Guide ignores connections because the parties agreed in writing; [C] did not, so the SICC may weigh [C]'s links with [State].
  • Burden Arguably [the party seeking joinder] bears it, as it must show the claims against [C] are "appropriate" for the SICC (O 10 r 5(1)(b)(ii)).

Coercive joinder is a key advantage over arbitration: a non-signatory can be bound in one proceeding (C&Y, citing the SICC Committee Report).

  • No written agreement needed for C (O 10 r 5(2)), unless C is a State or sovereign.
  • Permission generally required (O 10 r 7(1)), but not where C submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement and the originating application is not yet served.
  • Burden arguably on the party seeking joinder.
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Joinder fails where the claim against C shares no common question of law or fact with the claim against the defendant, e.g. a pre-contractual tort against a post-contractual breach (AY23-24 feedback).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Two versions of C
  • Version 1: C made the defective components that Beta supplied to Alpha. Whether the components were defective is a common question in both claims. The action as a whole stays international and commercial. Joinder is possible (s 18D(3); O 10), and C needs no written agreement (O 10 r 5(2)). If C resists under O 2 r 3(2), the SICC can weigh C's Vietnamese links, because the r 3(3) bar protects only parties to a written agreement.
  • Version 2: Alpha's claim against C is for misrepresentations C made before the contract, while the claim against Beta is for a breach long after it. No common question of law or fact, so joinder fails (Chong).

This is the SICC's edge over arbitration: an arbitral tribunal could not force C in at all.

ℹ NOTE
J5.7 Links to other files

An SICC written agreement supplies sufficient interest for an ASI (J6.2.1); if the SICC has primary jurisdiction, O 2 r 3(2) arguably governs an ASI application in the SICC (Chong). The SICC factor in the General Division's Spiliada is J4.4. Recognition of the chosen court's judgment: J7.5.

7Put it together: the SICC column for one contract

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Hypo: three claims, three routes

Contract A (2020): "the Singapore International Commercial Court shall have jurisdiction", Singapore law, Alpha (Singapore) v Beta (Vietnam). → Route 1. International (Beta in Vietnam) and commercial; written agreement; s 18F makes it exclusive (Singapore law governs). Serve Beta in Vietnam as of right (O 5 r 6(2)(a)). Beta's "Vietnam is more convenient" fails: O 2 r 3(3).

Contract B (2014): "the Singapore High Court". → Pre-2016, so no primary jurisdiction (O 2 r 2(2)). Sue in the General Division; seek transfer under O 2 r 4(1), arguing Vietnamese law can be decided on submissions (s 18L).

Claim C: Beta's director, Mr Chen, is sued for a pre-contractual misrepresentation. → He is not party to the clause. Joinder under O 10 fails if the claims share no common question; otherwise, if he resists under O 2 r 3(2), the SICC may weigh his Vietnamese connections, since the r 3(3) bar protects only parties to the agreement.

LESSON J6 · Q1 · JURISDICTION AND JUDGMENTS · ABOUT 24 MIN · 7 FLOWCHARTS · 3 ILLUSTRATIONS · 16 QUESTIONS

Anti-suit injunctions: stopping a party suing abroad

⚡ BIG IDEA

An ASI is an order against a person, not a foreign court, telling it to stop suing abroad. Name your basis first, because the elements differ. Contractual: amenability, breach of the clause, no strong reasons. Vexation: amenability, sufficient interest (usually natural forum), vexation, no undue injustice. Abuse of process: amenability and Singapore's self-evident interest in protecting its own process.

PRE-WRITE J6 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR FILE
J6 Anti-Suit Injunctions
This is your exam file, unchanged. It is long, so it starts folded: open it once to see the whole shape, then learn it piece by piece below. [Brackets] are the blanks you fill with the facts; Labels start each point; (+) helps the party relying on the rule, (−) helps the other side, (±) argue both ways. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue reference such as J4.3 to jump.

(An ASI is an equitable in personam order against [respondent], not [foreign court], restraining it from [commencing / continuing] [foreign proceedings]; breach is contempt. It indirectly interferes with [foreign court], so comity runs through every step (SNIA; C&Y). Judgment already given abroad: AEI (J7.6). Legend: (+) helps [applicant]; (−) helps [respondent]; (±) argue both ways.)

J6.0 SKELETON / ROADMAP
  1. Preliminary points (J6.0.2): is it an ASI (Oro Negro); power [s 4(10) CLA / s 18(2) SCJA / s 12A IAA / s 4(10A) CLA]; [interim / permanent] (Grover v SetClear); [General Division / SICC] (BCS v Baker); a foreign refusal to stay is no bar (Lakshmi); apply promptly (Sun Travels).
  2. Pick the basis (J6.0.1): the Kirkham factors are no box-ticking statute, and [applicant] must name its [contractual / vexation / abuse of process] basis, as the elements differ (Cooperative Muratori; slide 20):
    • [Contractual]: amenability + breach of [clause X] + no strong reasons; natural forum and injustice drop out (Cooperative Muratori).
    • [Vexation]: amenability + sufficient interest, usually [Singapore as natural forum] + vexation + no undue injustice to [respondent] (Kirkham).
    • [Abuse of process]: amenability + self-evident interest; [respondent]'s [foreign advantage] is no answer (BCS v Baker).
  3. Amenability (J6.1): [respondent] [submitted / was validly served]; always required (Cooperative Muratori; C&Y); cf Akai.
  4. Sufficient interest (J6.2): [Singapore EJC / NEJC / SICC clause] (J6.2.1); [Singapore's process] (J6.2.2); alternative fora (J6.2.3); single forum (J6.2.4); dual fora (J6.2.5); [foreign EJC] (J6.2.6); [foreign-seated arbitration] (J6.2.7).
  5. Legitimate interest, any one suffices (J6.3; Sun Travels; BCS v Baker): breach of [clause X], then strong reasons, then delay (J6.3.1); vexation, clearest cases only (J6.3.2); abuse of [Singapore's process] (J6.3.3); [Singapore public policy] (J6.3.4).
  6. No undue injustice to [respondent] (J6.4): vexation only; [undertakings] neutralise; a cynically created advantage counts for little; conclusion (J6.4.1).
  7. Special situations (J6.5): anti-anti-suit (J6.5.1); [third parties], slide 19's four scenarios (J6.5.2); [HCCCA] (J6.5.3); anti-enforcement injunctions (pointer J6.5.4; full in J7.6).
J6.0.1 Quick Application Template
  • Starter: Presently, [applicant] seeks an [interim / permanent] ASI from the [General Division / SICC] restraining [respondent] from [continuing [claim] in [foreign court]]. Per SNIA and Lakshmi, as it indirectly interferes with [foreign court], it issues only where the ends of justice require, with caution. [Applicant] bears the burden (Kirkham; C&Y) and must name its basis (Cooperative Muratori).
  • [Contractual ASI]: [Respondent] is amenable (J6.1); suing in [foreign court] breaches [clause X], construed under [proper law] (J6.3.1); and [respondent] shows no strong reasons, its [delay / third-party / fragmentation] point failing (J6.3.1.4) (Cooperative Muratori). Natural forum does not arise.
  • [Vexation ASI]: [Respondent] is amenable (J6.1); Singapore has interest as [the clearly more appropriate forum / protector of [insolvency / Singapore-centred dealings]] (J6.2.3–J6.2.4); [foreign proceedings] are vexatious for [bad faith / relitigation / a lost contribution claim] (J6.3.2); and [respondent] loses [no legitimate advantage / one neutralised by [undertaking]] (J6.4).
  • [Abuse of Process ASI]: [Respondent] is amenable (J6.1); Singapore's interest in protecting [Suit X judgment] is self-evident (J6.2.2); and [foreign claim] [relitigates / collaterally attacks] [Suit X] (J6.3.3). [Respondent]'s [foreign advantage] is no answer (BCS v Baker).
  • Result: The ASI [is / is not] granted [on [applicant]'s undertaking to [X] / only until [preconditions in clause X] are met] [, though delay let [foreign proceedings] reach [stage]] (J6.3.1.5; J6.4.1).
J6.0.2 Preliminary Points

(Use only the points the facts raise.)

  • Is It an ASI? Per Oro Negro, an ASI restrains [respondent] from commencing or continuing [proceedings in [foreign court]]. Presently, the order only stops [respondent] [purporting to act for [applicant]]. Similar to Oro Negro, it is not an ASI though it practically ends [foreign proceedings], so this framework does not apply (C&Y).
    • [Statutory Moratorium]: Per C&Y, ss 64–65 IRDA let the court restrain [local / foreign] proceedings against [company] proposing [a scheme / compromise]: in effect a statutory ASI, outside this general framework.
  • Source of Power Per C&Y, the [General Division] may grant injunctions "just or convenient" under s 4(10) CLA, and has the s 18(2) SCJA First Schedule powers (para 14; the handout also lists para 5). Presently, [applicant] seeks a [permanent] ASI, whose source is unsettled:
    • (−) Per Swift-Fortune (CA, arguably obiter as a Mareva case) and Hilton (HC, Ang J, bound by it), s 4(10) is [interlocutory] only, and [permanent] power lies in s 18(2) with para 14 SCJA.
    • (+) Per R1 International (HC), and Chan, Tan and Poon on a plain reading (per C&Y), s 4(10) also gives [permanent] power. The CA in Sun Travels merely noted Ang J's view, so it turns on whether "by an interlocutory order" governs [injunctions] or only [receivers] (C&Y).
  • Arbitration Per R1 International and C&Y, an [interim] ASI in aid of [Singapore / foreign]-seated arbitration issues under s 12A(2) with s 12 IAA, whatever [the seat] (s 12A(1)). A [permanent] ASI for [a foreign seat] is not found in s 12A (J6.2.7).
