▤ On your pre-write: J7.0.3 Common Law Procedure: Serving the Originating Claim (word for word)
J7.0.3 Common Law Procedure: Serving the Originating Claim

(common law route only; for CCAA orders see J7.5.2)

Presently, [creditor] enforces [the X judgment] by a fresh action in the General Division, so [debtor] must be served with [the originating claim]; service founds in personam jurisdiction.

  • Service In [Debtor] is in Singapore, so [creditor] serves as of right under [s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA with O 7 r 2(1)(a) (individual) / ss 16(2), 17(1)(c) SCJA with s 387 or s 376 CA (company) / s 16(1)(a)(i) with Adams v Cape presence (unregistered foreign company)] (J2.1).
  • Service Out: Framework [Debtor] is in [Y], so per s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA and O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021, [creditor] must show Singapore "is the appropriate court". Per para 63(2) SCPD 2021, that needs (a) a good arguable case of nexus; (b) forum conveniens; and (c) a serious question on [the merits].
  • Nexus (+) Per para 63(3)(m) SCPD 2021, [the action] enforces [the X judgment], one enforceable at common law in executable form (C&Y). [Creditor] needs a good arguable case, more than a prima facie case (Bradley Lomas; J3.1).
  • Merits Subsumed (±) Per Li Shengwu (J3.1.4), a serious question need not be shown separately where the factor engages the merits. Arguably (m) does, the merits being whether [the X judgment] is enforceable; otherwise [creditor] shows a serious question on [the J7.1 requirements].
  • Assets in Singapore? (±) (−) [Debtor] has no [assets] here. (+) Per Demirel (Eng), assets are not required, but [creditor] must show a real prospect of a legitimate benefit, e.g., [future assets / examining [debtor] / a judgment about to go stale].
  • Forum Conveniens: Required? (±) (+) Per Licea v Curacao, FNC does not arise as enforcement is not a fresh suit on [the merits], consistent with Art 13(2) Hague Judgments Convention. (−) [Debtor]: England (Demirel) and Canada (Chevron v Yaiguaje) keep an FC or FNC filter, so per C&Y Licea may be revisited.
  • Why FC Is Ill-Fitting (+) Per C&Y, (i) FC picks one forum for [the merits], whereas enforcement may be pursued in [Singapore and Y]; (ii) the court facilitates an obligation [the X court] already fixed rather than adjudicating; (iii) requiring both FC and a legitimate benefit is overkill for [creditor], who already holds a judgment.
  • Filter Against Abuse (±) (−) Per C&Y, some filter is sensible, as [creditor] may sue not to reach assets but to [harass [debtor] / launder [the X judgment] through a Singapore judgment]. (+) That concern is absent: [creditor] targets [debtor]'s [assets / bank accounts] in Singapore.
  • Alternatively, FC Satisfied (+) (if time) Even if FC is required, [creditor] satisfies it under Spiliada (J4.1), [debtor]'s [assets in Singapore] pointing to Singapore as [the place of enforcement].

3J7.1 Common law requirements

▤ On your pre-write: J7.1.0 Starter (word for word)
J7.1.0 Starter

Per C&Y (cf Ong Han Nam), [creditor] must show that [the X judgment] is (a) on the merits; (b) given by a court with international jurisdiction over [debtor]; (c) final and conclusive; and (d) a fresh money judgment for a definite sum that is not a tax, fine or penalty. The same apply to recognition, save (d).

(a) On the merits

▤ On your pre-write: J7.1.1 Judgment on the Merits (word for word)
J7.1.1 Judgment on the Merits

Per The Sennar (No 2), [the X judgment] is on the merits as [the X court] [found the facts / stated the law / applied it to [liability / quantum]], not merely [a point of procedure].

  • Default Judgment (+) Per C&Y, [the default judgment] is on the merits although [debtor] did not appear and [the X court] may not have considered [the evidence]; non-participation goes only to fraud (J7.2.2) or natural justice (J7.2.3).
  • Interlocutory Judgment (±) Per C&Y, [the X ruling on [issue]] counts if it finally decides that issue and is not on a "procedural" issue. Per The Sennar (No 2), a ruling that [the claim is barred by [a Y jurisdiction clause]] is substantive, but one on [service / security for costs] is not.
  • Limitation Ruling (+) Per s 5 FLPA, [the X court]'s dismissal of [the claim] as time-barred under [X / Y / Singapore] law is deemed on the merits, so it can be [enforced / pleaded as res judicata against [party]].
  • Judgment on a Judgment (−) [The X judgment] merely declares [the Y judgment] enforceable in [X]. Per Sang Cheol Woo (not following Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead (HK)), it is unenforceable at common law, and per REFJA s 3(4)(c) not registrable. [Creditor] must enforce [the Y judgment] directly.
  • Why Not (−) Per C&Y, [the X judgment] (i) never examined [the issues], so is not on the merits; (ii) decides only its territorial effect in [X] (Merck: no estoppel, J7.3.2.4); and (iii) would launder [the Y judgment], Singapore testing [the X court] instead of [the Y court].
  • Contrary View (+) [Creditor] relies on Desert Palace (HC), which saw no difficulty in enforcing [a judgment on a judgment]; per C&Y it did not grapple with the theory, so [the X judgment] remains [unenforceable].
  • Default judgments are on the merits; non-participation goes only to fraud or natural justice.
  • Interlocutory rulings count if they finally decide the issue and are not "procedural" (The Sennar (No 2): a ruling that the claim is barred by a jurisdiction clause is substantive).
  • Limitation rulings are deemed on the merits (s 5 FLPA).
  • A judgment on a judgment (one that merely declares another court's judgment enforceable) is not enforceable (Sang Cheol Woo, not following Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead): it never examined the issues, and would launder the original judgment. Enforce the original directly.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The laundering problem

Beta wins a judgment against Alpha in Country A. Alpha was never present in A and never submitted, so that judgment would fail requirement (b) in Singapore. Beta then goes to Country B, whose court simply declares the A judgment enforceable there, and brings B's order to Singapore.

If Singapore enforced B's order, the defect in the A judgment would disappear: the judgment would be "laundered" through B. That is why a judgment on a judgment is not enforceable (Sang Cheol Woo). Beta must bring the original A judgment and meet the requirements for it.

(b) International jurisdiction: presence or submission

▤ On your pre-write: J7.1.2 International Jurisdiction of [the X court] (word for word)
J7.1.2 International Jurisdiction of [the X court]

[Creditor] must prove that [debtor] was present in [X] (J7.1.2.1–J7.1.2.3) or submitted to [the X court] (J7.1.2.4–J7.1.2.5).

  • Singapore's Rules (−) Per C&Y, the test is Singapore's conflict rules, narrower than Singapore's own bases, with no mirror image. So [the X court]'s [service-out jurisdiction] does not count, and its own finding on [jurisdiction] creates no estoppel (J7.3.2.3).
  • Four Grounds Per Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom (SGCA), [debtor] must have been [present in [X]] or have [claimed or counterclaimed / voluntarily appeared / agreed in advance to submit]. Residence is not listed (J7.1.2.2).
  • Closed Categories (−) Per Schibsby v Westenholz, the grounds are closed. [Creditor] cannot rely on [X]'s real and substantial connection with [the claim], a Canadian ground (Beals v Saldanha) Singapore has not adopted.
⚠ TRAP
Singapore's rules, not the foreign court's

International jurisdiction is tested by Singapore's conflict rules, which are narrower than Singapore's own jurisdiction rules (no mirror image). So the foreign court's service-out jurisdiction does not count, and its own finding on jurisdiction creates no estoppel. Per India v Deutsche Telekom, there are four grounds: presence; claiming or counterclaiming; voluntary appearance; prior agreement to submit. The categories are closed (Schibsby v Westenholz): no "real and substantial connection" ground (Beals v Saldanha, a Canadian ground Singapore has not adopted).

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"No mirror image" means Singapore is stricter with foreign courts than with itself. Singapore lets its own courts reach defendants abroad by service out (J3). But when a foreign court does the same thing to a Singapore defendant, Singapore will not count that judgment unless the defendant was present in that country or submitted to its court. A foreign court's long-arm reach is its own business; it does not bind Singapore.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Did Ruritania have international jurisdiction over Alpha?
FactsResult
The debtor is Mr Lim, an individual trader, served while on a week's holiday in RuritaniaPresent (voluntary physical presence, even temporary, is enough, Adams v Cape)
Alpha had no office in Ruritania; its rep took orders from a hotel for a few daysNot present (Littauer Glove)
The Ruritanian court gave permission to serve Alpha in Singapore under its own long-arm rulesDoes not count: the foreign court's service-out jurisdiction is not a ground
Alpha filed a full defence on the merits in RuritaniaSubmission
Alpha appeared only to argue an EJC for Singapore, lost, and took no further partNot submission (Nimbus)
The contract said "the parties submit to the courts of Ruritania"Submission by agreement (United Malayan Banking)
The contract chose Ruritanian law, and Alpha did business thereNot submission, on these facts alone (Vizcaya)
Submission by conduct: the key debates
▤ J7.1.2.4
  1. 1Submits (+): suing in X (including related counterclaims), or a merits defence (Malaysia Marine).
  2. 2Does not submit (−): objecting to jurisdiction under a clause, losing, then taking no part (Nimbus).
  3. 3Setting aside on FNC grounds: Henry v Geoprosco said submission. But per IGCF (PC), Henry's existence/exercise line is "unrealistic and irrational"; REFJA s 5(3)(a)(i)(C) reverses it; per C&Y, a failed set-aside on any ground is a protest.
  4. 4Stay application: (+) on Henry's logic, submission; (−) per IGCF, a protest unless more was sought.
  5. 5Whose law? Singapore law, with the foreign procedure as context (Giant Light Metal).
  6. 6Inchoate submission: consent extends to a closely connected claim where fair (Giant Light Metal: the same claim refiled after settlement talks failed; Murthy v Sivajothi: related fraud cross-claims).
  7. 7Not submission: unilateral inclusion as a creditor in a composition plan (Humpuss); choosing X law plus doing business in X (Vizcaya).

(c) Final and conclusive; (d) definite sum

▤ On your pre-write: J7.1.3 Final and Conclusive (word for word)
J7.1.3 Final and Conclusive

Per Sang Cheol Woo, [the X judgment] is final and conclusive if (a) [the X court] cannot vary, reopen or set it aside, though [the X appellate court] may hear an appeal; and (b) [the X court] regards it as res judicata. Per Humpuss and Carl Zeiss, this is tested by [X] law, proved by [expert evidence].

  • Default Judgment (+) Per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry, [the default judgment] is final if given final effect until set aside, although [debtor] may still apply to [the X court] to set it aside.
  • Interlocutory Judgment (±) Per Lakshmi, [the X interlocutory ruling on [issue]] is final if it finally decides [the parties]' rights on that issue, but not if [provisional / decided on a good arguable case and reopenable at trial] (First Laser).
  • Appeal Pending (±) (+) Per C&Y, a pending appeal to [the X appellate court] does not as such defeat finality, though Singapore may [stay enforcement]. (−) But as in Sang Cheol Woo (a provisionally enforceable Seoul High Court judgment was not res judicata under Korean law until the Supreme Court ruled), check [X] law.
  • Limitation Knock-On (+) Per Sang Cheol Woo, the six-year period then runs from when [the X judgment] became final under [X] law, i.e., [the final appellate decision on [date]], consistent with REFJA s 4(1)(b) (J7.2.8).
▤ On your pre-write: J7.1.4 Fresh Money Judgment for a Definite Sum (word for word)
J7.1.4 Fresh Money Judgment for a Definite Sum
  • Definite Sum (+) Per C&Y, [the sum] must be fixed or arithmetically ascertainable, and [a costs order] is enforceable if final and definite, even where [the merits judgment] has no money order.
  • Fresh Obligation (±) Per Poh Soon Kiat, whether [the X judgment] imposes a fresh obligation to pay [sum] depends on [X] law. As in Poh Soon Kiat ("shall remain liable" in a later Californian fraudulent-transfer judgment was surplusage), where [the later X order] restates liability under [the earlier judgment], [creditor] must sue on [the earlier judgment].
  • Non-Money Judgment (−) Per C&Y, [an order for specific performance / an injunction] is not enforceable at common law, a relic of indebitatus assumpsit. [Creditor] must register under REFJA or the CCAA (J7.4.1; J7.5.1), or sue afresh and plead [the X judgment] as res judicata (J7.3.1).
  • Reform (±) Per C&Y, following Merck's call for convergence, the common law should enforce [non-money relief] as REFJA, the CCAA and Canada (Pro-Swing v Elta) do; the indirect route via [res judicata] already reaches [the same result], less efficiently.
  • Money Order Among Other Orders (+) Per Giant Light Metal, a definite-sum order made among [other orders] founds an action in debt. As in Giant Light Metal (refund due once the buyer made the generator sets available for collection), [creditor] has [made [the goods] available], so [the refund] is payable.
  • Severance of Mixed Orders (±) (−) Per Giant Light Metal (obiter), severance is confined to [penal or revenue] elements. (+) Per C&Y, [the money order] should be severable whenever it is not interdependent with [the non-money order].
  • Tax, Fine or Penalty (−) [The X judgment] for [tax / a fine / a penalty] payable to [the X State] is not enforceable (J7.2.5).
RequirementKey rules
Final and conclusiveThe foreign court cannot vary or reopen it, and treats it as res judicata (Sang Cheol Woo), tested by foreign law proved by expert evidence (Humpuss; Carl Zeiss). A default judgment is final until set aside. A pending appeal does not as such defeat finality, but check foreign law (in Sang Cheol Woo, a provisionally enforceable Seoul High Court judgment was not res judicata until the Supreme Court ruled).
Definite sumFixed or arithmetically ascertainable; a final costs order counts. A later order that merely restates liability is surplusage: sue on the earlier judgment (Poh Soon Kiat). A definite-sum order among other orders founds a debt action (Giant Light Metal).
Non-money ordersNot enforceable at common law (a relic of indebitatus assumpsit); per C&Y, reform is due, following Merck's call for convergence.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Two orders that fail (c) or (d)
  • Not yet final. A court of first instance gives judgment, and under that country's law the judgment is only provisionally enforceable and not yet res judicata until the highest court rules. In Sang Cheol Woo, a Seoul High Court judgment was in exactly that position, so it was not final and conclusive until the Supreme Court ruled. The lesson: a pending appeal does not automatically defeat finality; prove what the foreign law says.
  • Not money. A foreign court orders Alpha to hand over shipping documents. That is not a definite sum, so it cannot be enforced by a common law debt action. Beta must sue afresh in Singapore and plead the foreign judgment as res judicata (J7.3.1), or use the CCAA if it applies.
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Reciprocity: one line is enough. Merck left it open and later cases have not discussed it, so the judgment is not barred on that ground.

4J7.2 Common law defences

▤ On your pre-write: J7.2.0 Starter (word for word)
J7.2.0 Starter

Presently, although [the X judgment] satisfies J7.1, [debtor] resists enforcement on the ground of [fraud / natural justice / public policy / penal law / breach of [clause] / an inconsistent judgment / limitation].

The burden is on the debtor (Eleven v Boxsentry). And Singapore never reviews the merits: an error of fact or law by the foreign court is irrelevant (Godard v Gray), save possibly a patent error of Singapore law (open after Merck).

Fraud

▤ On your pre-write: J7.2.2 Fraud (word for word)
J7.2.2 Fraud

Per Hong Pian Tee, the test depends on the type of fraud. Per Ee Hoong Liang, extrinsic fraud is fraud [debtor] had no opportunity to examine and challenge, going to [the X court]'s jurisdiction; intrinsic fraud is fraud it could challenge, going to the merits, e.g., [false statements at trial] (Ong Han Nam).

  • Extrinsic Fraud (−) Presently, [witnesses were bribed / [debtor] was never served / [creditor] induced [debtor] to let judgment go by default]. Per Hong Pian Tee, Abouloff applies: no new evidence is needed, and [debtor] may raise the fraud though [it was rejected in [X] / it is raised here for the first time].
  • Intrinsic Fraud (+) Presently, [perjury / forged documents] at [the X trial] go to the merits. Per Hong Pian Tee, [debtor] needs fresh evidence that reasonable diligence would not have uncovered and that would likely have changed the result; presently [new evidence] [was / was not] discoverable.
  • Materiality (+) Per Ong Han Nam, for either type the fraud must have produced [the X judgment]; a catalogue of [creditor]'s [non-disclosures] is not enough unless it was the effective cause of [the X findings].
  • Characterisation (+) As in Ee Hoong Liang (non-disclosure of settlement payouts going to quantum was intrinsic), [creditor]'s [concealment of [fact]] goes to [the merits / quantum], so [debtor] must meet the diligence test.
  • Default and Summary Judgments (+) Per Eleven v Boxsentry, the intrinsic test applies to [a default judgment] though [debtor] took no part. Per Ee Hoong Liang, [a summary judgment] that [debtor] knew of is not akin to a default judgment.
  • Domestic Cases Irrelevant (+) Per Ee Hoong Liang, [debtor] cannot invoke Takhar or Façade v Mero (no diligence requirement), which concern [domestic judgments]; comity applies, and Singapore is not an appellate tribunal over [the X court].
  • Critique (±) (−) Per C&Y, Hong Pian Tee takes the side of the fraudster against his negligent opponent (Briggs), and [the extrinsic/intrinsic line] is hard to draw (Beals). (+) But the SGCA has reaffirmed it (Ong Han Nam), so [debtor]'s [lack of diligence] is fatal.
  • Exam Focus Per Chong (seminar), classify [the fraud] as extrinsic or intrinsic; [the elements of deceit] need not be proved.
  • Fraud by the Court (±) (−) Per C&Y, extrinsic fraud includes fraud by [the X court], e.g., [a bribed judge], overlapping with natural justice, so Abouloff applies. (+) Per the slides, whether Abouloff or Hong Pian Tee governs is open; arguably, if [an appeal] was available in [X], [debtor] could challenge it (Ee Hoong Liang).
    • Chong's view (−): per Chong (seminar), treat it as extrinsic for policy reasons, as [debtor] can hardly raise [the corruption] before [that court].
  • Threshold and Bars (+) Per Owens Bank v Bracco, [debtor] needs plausible evidence of a prima facie case. Per C&Y, fraud cannot be raised where [pleading it is abusive] or [a second X judgment] has rejected it (House of Spring Gardens v Waite), which in Singapore matters mainly for [extrinsic fraud].
  • Default judgments: the intrinsic test still applies though the debtor took no part (Eleven v Boxsentry); a summary judgment the debtor knew of is not like a default judgment (Ee Hoong Liang).
  • Domestic fraud cases (Takhar; Façade v Mero) are irrelevant: comity applies (Ee Hoong Liang).
  • Critique: Hong Pian Tee sides with the fraudster against a negligent opponent (Briggs), but the SGCA has reaffirmed it.
🎓 WHAT PROF CHONG SAID

Classify the fraud as extrinsic or intrinsic; you need not prove the elements of deceit. For fraud by the court (a bribed judge), treat it as extrinsic for policy reasons: the debtor can hardly raise the corruption before that court.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Classify the fraud
Alpha's complaint about Beta's foreign judgmentTypeWhat Alpha must show
Beta paid Alpha's lawyer to let the case go by defaultExtrinsic: Alpha never had a chance to challenge itFraud that produced the judgment; no new evidence needed (Abouloff)
Beta's witness lied at trial about the delivery dateIntrinsic: Alpha could have cross-examinedFresh evidence, not discoverable with reasonable diligence, likely to change the result
Beta relied on a forged invoice, which Alpha could have checked against its own records but did notIntrinsicFails: lack of diligence is fatal (Ong Han Nam)
The foreign judge was bribedTreat as extrinsic (Chong)Alpha could hardly complain to that judge

Why the difference? Intrinsic fraud is something the foreign court already had the chance to deal with. Letting the debtor reargue it in Singapore would mean reviewing the merits, which Singapore never does.

Natural justice, public policy, penal laws

▤ On your pre-write: J7.2.3 Natural Justice (word for word)
J7.2.3 Natural Justice

Per Jacobson v Frachon (C&Y), [the X court] must have given [debtor] notice and then an opportunity to present its case. Presently, [debtor] [was never served / received [the claim] only [after judgment]], so [the X judgment] [is / is not] recognised.

  • Default After Proper Service (+) Per Sang Cheol Woo and C&Y, [debtor], [personally served], chose not to appear in [X]; letting [the default judgment] go by is no breach.
  • Later Participation No Cure (−) As in Paulus Tannos (PKPU summons not served in time; later participation under protest irrelevant), [debtor]'s later participation in [the X process] does not cure lack of notice of [the proceedings] before [the order].
  • Whose View (±) (−) Per Paulus Tannos, Singapore alone decides, unbound by [the X court]'s view that [service] was proper. (+) But where [debtor]'s [appeal on notice] is pending in [X], ruling is premature, as [the X appellate court] may correct it.
  • Substantial Justice (±) (−) Per Adams v Cape, natural justice extends to substantial justice, e.g., [damages set at counsel's average award without assessing each claim]. (+) Per Paulus Tannos and Sang Cheol Woo, it is unclear Singapore adopts this, and [debtor] should first seek correction in [X].
  • Mere Irregularity or Merits (+) Per Sang Cheol Woo, breach of [debtor]'s reasonable expectation that [X procedural rule] would apply is no defence; complaints about [Korea's deemed confession rule / the damages assessment] were merits challenges [already reviewed by the X appellate court].
  • Natural justice: notice, then an opportunity to present the case (Jacobson v Frachon). A debtor personally served who chose not to appear has no complaint (Sang Cheol Woo). Later participation does not cure lack of notice (Paulus Tannos). Singapore decides for itself, but should wait if an appeal on notice is pending abroad.
▤ On your pre-write: J7.2.4 Public Policy (word for word)
J7.2.4 Public Policy

Per Burswood, a higher standard than domestic public policy applies. Per Poh Soon Kiat (applied in Sang Cheol Woo), enforcement must (a) offend a fundamental principle of justice or deep-rooted tradition of Singapore; (b) offend the general community; (c) offend fundamental morality, decency or liberty; or (d) go against a rule protecting the public interest. Presently, enforcing [the X judgment] [does / does not] offend [limb] because [reason].

  • Hierarchy (±) Per Poh Soon Kiat, statutory policy outranks common law "higher" international policy, which outranks domestic policy. Per C&Y and Chong (seminar), a statute is not automatically international policy; only one of an equally high, extraterritorial kind counts, a matter of interpretation (JIO Minerals); presently [statute] [is / is not] of that kind.
  • Judgment, Not Cause of Action (+) Per Merck and C&Y, at common law the effect of enforcing [the X judgment] must offend, not [the cause of action], unlike RECJA s 3(2)(f). So [the X judgment] on [a claim unknown to Singapore law] is not refused for that alone.
  • Egregious Cause (−) Per C&Y, [a cause of action] as egregious as [a contract under extreme physical duress / a drug-trafficking contract (ED&F Man v Haryanto)] infects [the X judgment]. Per Israel Discount Bank, a judgment on [a guarantee procured by undue influence] may be refused.
  • Critique of Israel Discount (+) Per C&Y, Israel Discount Bank wrongly looks to [the cause of action] absent egregiousness, and [undue influence] is arguably only domestic policy, so [the X judgment] should be enforced.
  • Breach of a Singapore ASI (−) Per Nimbus and C&Y, [the X judgment] obtained in breach of [a Singapore ASI against [creditor]] is contrary to public policy (J6). Breach of [a foreign ASI] is arguably not, by itself (analysis).
  • Gambling: Statutory Policy (−) Per Venetian Macau (HC 2026, REFJA), adopting Poh Soon Kiat, gambling save as regulated is contrary to Singapore policy. As s 5(2) CLA is statutory, it prevails over [higher international policy], so enforcing [the X judgment] on [a casino debt] is contrary to public policy.
  • Gambling: Common Law Route (−) Per Poh Soon Kiat (obiter), a judgment not registrable under RECJA for its gambling cause is likewise unenforceable at common law, implying s 5(2) CLA infects [the X judgment]. Per Venetian Macau, s 5(2) draws no distinction between [direct claims] and [actions on foreign judgments]; convergence (Merck) points the same way.
  • Gambling: Creditor's Reply (±) (+) [Creditor] relies on Burswood (s 5(2) only domestic policy), which the HC followed in Star v Yong Khong Yoong. (−) Per Venetian Macau, Burswood turned on the repealed RECJA's cause-of-action test and binds only there, so [the X judgment] is unenforceable.
  • Recharacterisation (±) (−) Per Poh Soon Kiat (left open), [the action on the X judgment] may be recharacterised as a direct claim for [the gambling debt], caught by s 5(2) CLA. (+) [Creditor]: it sues on [the judgment debt], and common law policy targets the judgment, not [the wager] (Merck).
  • Statutory Interest (+) As in Sang Cheol Woo (Korea's statutory 20% judgment interest, payable to the private creditor to deter delay, offended no public policy), [the X award of [interest / costs]] is enforceable.
  • Different Foreign Policy (+) Per Yap Chai Ling, that [X]'s public policy on [issue] differs from Singapore's does not mean Singapore's is breached.
  • No Estoppel; No New Facts (±) (−) Per Yukos and India v Deutsche Telekom, [the X court]'s ruling on [X]'s public policy creates no estoppel on Singapore's (J7.3.2.3). (+) But per Wu Shun Foods, [debtor] cannot raise [a fact] going to Singapore policy that it should have raised in [X].
IssueRule
The judgment, not the cause of actionAt common law, the effect of enforcing the judgment must offend (Merck), unless the cause is egregious (extreme duress; drug trafficking, ED&F Man v Haryanto). Israel Discount Bank (undue influence) is criticised by C&Y.
GamblingPer Venetian Macau (HC 2026, REFJA), adopting Poh Soon Kiat: s 5(2) CLA is statutory, so it prevails; a casino-debt judgment is contrary to public policy. Burswood turned on the repealed RECJA's cause-of-action test. Per Chong, Venetian Macau is authoritative for the common law too.
Not contraryKorea's 20% statutory judgment interest payable to a private creditor (Sang Cheol Woo); a foreign policy that merely differs (Yap Chai Ling).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Two judgments, two answers
  • A Macau casino's judgment against a Singapore gambler for unpaid gaming debts. A Singapore statute (s 5(2) CLA) expresses the policy against enforcing gambling debts, and it is the kind of policy that reaches across borders, so enforcement is contrary to public policy (Venetian Macau). The gambler wins.
  • A Korean judgment that adds 20% statutory interest a year, payable to the private creditor. High, but it is a private creditor's recovery, not a penalty, and a policy that merely differs from Singapore's is not enough. Enforced (Sang Cheol Woo).

The difference is not how harsh the foreign rule feels. It is whether enforcing this judgment would offend a Singapore policy of the highest, international kind.

▤ On your pre-write: J7.2.5 Foreign Penal, Revenue and Other Public Laws; Punitive Damages (word for word)
J7.2.5 Foreign Penal, Revenue and Other Public Laws; Punitive Damages

Per Maler Foundation, [the X judgment] is not recognised if it directly or indirectly enforces [X]'s penal, revenue or other public law. Characterisation is for the lex fori; per Huntington v Attrill, "penal" means a suit in favour of the State for penalties. Presently, [the X proceedings] were [brought by [State agency] / for forfeiture to the State / for unpaid [tax]].

  • Label Not Conclusive (−) Per Maler Foundation, a place in [X]'s criminal code, or a civil form, is not conclusive. As in Maler Foundation (State-pursued civil forfeiture of officials' presumptively ill-gotten property, in the State's favour, was penal), [the forfeiture / disgorgement order] is penal.
  • Non-Money and In Rem (−) Per Maler Foundation and C&Y, the exclusion applies equally to [a judgment in rem / a forfeiture order over [property]].
  • Private Creditor (+) Per Raulin v Fischer (Eng), a sum recoverable by [creditor], a private litigant, in its own interest is enforceable. As in Sang Cheol Woo (statutory interest to a private creditor was not penal, penal meaning payable to the State), [the X award] is not penal.
  • Punitive Damages to a Private Party (±) (+) Per C&Y, refusing [the X punitive award] would be anomalous when Singapore awards punitive damages in tort (ACB v Thomson Medical). (−) But the point is uncertain, Licea leaving open [US RICO treble damages]; s 4(5) REFJA and s 16 CCAA limit [non-compensatory damages], and courts may take their cue from them.
  • Public Component (−) Per Schnabel v Lui (NSW), punitive damages punishing [non-compliance with the X court's orders] are penal though paid to [creditor]. (+) Contrast Benefit Strategies (SA): punitive damages for [brazen fraud] have no public element.
  • Severance (+) Per Licea, where [the X judgment] awards [compensatory sum] and [punitive sum], [creditor] enforces the unobjectionable part if clearly identifiable and separable; compare s 4(5) REFJA (J7.4.1) and ss 16, 19 CCAA (J7.5.4).
  • Penal, revenue and public laws (Maler Foundation): not recognised if they enforce the foreign State's penal, revenue or public law. Labels are not conclusive: State-pursued civil forfeiture was penal (Maler).
  • Private creditor (+): a sum recoverable by a private litigant in its own interest is enforceable (Raulin v Fischer; Sang Cheol Woo).
  • Punitive damages to a private party (±): refusing them would be anomalous given ACB v Thomson Medical (C&Y), but Licea left treble damages open. Sever the clearly separable compensatory part (Licea).

5J7.3 Recognition: the judgment as res judicata

▤ On your pre-write: J7.3.0 Starter (word for word)
J7.3.0 Starter

Presently, [the X judgment] may be res judicata in [the Singapore action] because it raises [cause of action estoppel (J7.3.1) / issue estoppel (J7.3.2) / abuse under Henderson v Henderson (J7.3.3)].

  • Representation Not to Rely (−) Per Showlag v Mansour (C&Y), [party] who represented that it would not rely on [the X judgment] may be met by an estoppel by representation (a cross-estoppel), barring its plea of [res judicata].

Recognition uses the judgment as a shield (the matter is decided) or to bind on an issue. It needs requirements (a)–(c) and no defence, but no money requirement.

J7.3.1 Cause of action estoppel

▤ On your pre-write: J7.3.1 Cause of Action Estoppel (word for word)
J7.3.1 Cause of Action Estoppel

Per Arnold, it arises where the cause of action in [the Singapore action] is identical to that in [the X proceedings], between the same parties or privies, on the same subject matter; per C&Y it is an absolute bar absent [fraud / collusion].

  • No Merger (+) Per Ocean Tankers (SGCA, preliminary view), [the original claim] does not merge into [the X judgment], unlike a Singapore judgment, so [the X loser] could re-sue on it here; whether [registration under REFJA or the CCAA] merges it is "arguable".
  • Shield (+) [The unsuccessful X claimant] re-sues [defendant] in Singapore on [the same cause], so [defendant] pleads [the X judgment] as res judicata, e.g., [a German declaration of non-liability under [contract]] against [a Singapore breach claim] (slides).
  • Sword for Non-Money Judgments (+) Per C&Y, [the X winner], holding [an X order for specific performance / an injunction] outside REFJA and the CCAA, sues afresh on [the same cause] and pleads [the X judgment]; if recognisable, it binds without [the merits] being reopened.

The same cause of action, the same parties, the same subject matter: an absolute bar absent fraud or collusion (Arnold). Per Ocean Tankers (preliminary view), the original claim does not merge into a foreign judgment, unlike a Singapore one. A non-money winner can sue afresh and plead the foreign judgment (the indirect route to enforcing a non-money order).

J7.3.2 Issue estoppel

▤ On your pre-write: J7.3.2.1 Requirements (word for word)
J7.3.2.1 Requirements

Per Merck (adopting The Sennar (No 2)), [party] must show (a) a foreign judgment capable of recognition; (b) identical parties or privies; and (c) the same issue. Presently, [the X judgment] meets J7.1.1–J7.1.3 and no defence applies; [A] and [B] were parties to both; and [the issue: governing law / breach / validity of [clause]] arises in both.

  • Necessary, Not Collateral (±) Per Merck (citing Carl Zeiss), [the X finding on [issue]] must have been necessary to [the X court]'s decision, not collateral; presently it [was / was not] essential to [the result].
  • Finality Per Issue (±) Per Merck, the decision on [the specific issue] must be final under [X] law; for [a civil law judgment], only [the dispositif] may bind, not [the reasoning].
  • Identity of Issue (−) Per Gonzalo Gil White (SGCA), [the party relying] bears the burden, with special caution for foreign rulings. Ask (1) were [the issues] framed the same way; and (2) if so, did they arise under different laws? If so, no identity.
  • Identity: Application (−) As in Gonzalo Gil White (Mexican concurso rulings under Mexican law shared no identity with a Singapore-law claim), [the X ruling under [X law]] does not decide [the Singapore-law issue]; look at identity of [issues], not [consequences].
  • Outer Limits (−) Per Merck, no estoppel where (i) [the issue] is one Singapore decides for itself (J7.3.2.3); (ii) [the X judgment] is territorially limited to [X]; (iii) [party], a foreign defendant, had bona fide reasons, e.g., [cost / triviality / unfamiliar procedure] (Carl Zeiss), not to contest [the issue] fully; or (iv) Singapore's substantive public policy forestalls it.
  • Why Caution for Defendants (−) Per C&Y, [the X claimant] chose [X], whereas [defendant] was brought there, may rationally have limited its defence, and may not have expected [the issue] to bind it worldwide.
  • Pure Law (−) Per Merck, no estoppel arises on [a pure question of law] that does not directly affect [the parties]' rights.
Issues Singapore decides for itself (no estoppel)
▤ J7.3.2.3
  1. 1International jurisdiction (whether the debtor submitted): otherwise Singapore would "sub-contract" the question (Desert Sun).
  2. 2Forum non conveniens: a foreign natural-forum ruling does not bind a Singapore ASI application (Lakshmi).
  3. 3Singapore public policy (India v Deutsche Telekom).
  4. 4Whether the HCCCA applies: each Contracting State decides for itself (Chong's answer scheme).
IssueCan it found an estoppel?
Governing lawYes (Merck; Per Chong (seminar): not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it itself), but only if decided at final trial, not on a stay on a good arguable case (First Laser). Different foreign choice of law rules are immaterial (First Laser), but if the issue arose under different laws there is no identity (Gonzalo Gil White; per Chong, read narrowly).
An exemption clause void under UCTA as an overriding ruleNo: Merck's public policy limit blocks it.
Procedural or interlocutory rulingsDebated: Merck (no) v Lakshmi (yes); narrow approach in Desert Sun; broad in The Sennar (No 2).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Does the earlier ruling bind?
  1. A Hong Kong court, after a full trial, held that English law governs Alpha and Beta's contract. Later, in Singapore, Beta argues Singapore law governs. Estoppel likely: governing law can found an issue estoppel when decided at final trial (Merck).
  2. The same finding, but made on a stay application on a good arguable case. No estoppel: it was not decided finally (First Laser).
  3. A Mexican court ruled on Beta's rights under Mexican law. In Singapore, Alpha's claim arises under Singapore law. No estoppel: the issue arose under a different law, so it is not the same issue (Gonzalo Gil White, read narrowly per Chong).
  4. The foreign court found that Alpha submitted to its jurisdiction. No estoppel: international jurisdiction is something Singapore always decides for itself (Desert Sun).

J7.3.3 Rule in Henderson v Henderson

Presently, [party] raises [issue / claim] in Singapore that could and should have been raised in [the X proceedings], so [other party] pleads abuse. Per Humpuss, the court weighs all the circumstances, including whether [the Singapore action] collaterally attacks [the X judgment], [fresh evidence], and bona fide reasons, e.g., [reason], for not raising it in [X].

  • Not Every Point (+) Per Humpuss, [the X litigation] need not have covered every point for [party]'s raising of [point] here to be abusive.

  • One-Line Router Per ss 3, 4(7)(a), [a judgment of a gazetted X court] may be registered and then has local force; per s 7(1), [creditor] cannot then sue on it at common law (J7.0.2).
J7.4.1 Analogues: What Is Enforced
  • Non-Money Relief (±) Per s 4(4), [an injunction / specific performance order] is registrable if "just and convenient", unlike at [common law] (J7.1.4).
  • Excess Damages (±) Per s 4(5), only [the compensatory part] of [treble / punitive damages] is registered; compare Licea at [common law] (J7.2.5).
  • Excluded (−) Per ss 2(1), 3(4), [taxes, fines and penalties] and [a judgment on a judgment] fall outside REFJA, as at common law (J7.1.1; J7.2.5).
J7.4.3 Analogues: Jurisdiction and Defences
  • Residence, Not Presence (−) Per s 5(3)(a)(iv), [debtor] must have been [resident / a company with its principal place of business] in [X]; mere presence does not suffice, unlike at common law (J7.1.2).
  • Protest Is Not Submission (+) Per s 5(3)(a)(i), appearing only to [contest jurisdiction / invite the X court not to exercise it / protect seized property] is not submission, matching IGCF against Henry v Geoprosco (J7.1.2.4).
  • Breach of Agreement (−) Per s 5(4)(b), [the X court] is not deemed to have jurisdiction where [the X proceedings] breached [the clause] and [debtor] did not submit: the analogue for the common law defence (J7.2.6).
  • Fraud and Public Policy (±) Per s 5(1)(a)(iv)–(v), registration is set aside for [fraud] or where enforcing [the X judgment] offends public policy. Per Chong (seminar), as REFJA words public policy like the common law, Venetian Macau is authoritative for [the common law] too (J7.2.2; J7.2.4).
ℹ NOTE
REFJA, for comparison only

Not examinable as a regime. Use it only as an analogue for the common law under Merck's convergence aim: it registers non-money relief (s 4(4)); registers only the compensatory part of excess damages (s 4(5)); needs residence, not mere presence (s 5(3)(a)(iv)); treats a protest appearance as no submission (s 5(3)(a)(i)); and denies jurisdiction where the foreign suit breached a clause (s 5(4)(b)).

J7.5 The CCAA

▤ On your pre-write: J7.5.0 Starter (word for word)
J7.5.0 Starter

Presently, [the X judgment] comes from [the chosen court] in [X], a Contracting State, so [creditor] applies under the CCAA rather than suing afresh. Per s 13(4), the court must recognise or enforce it unless a ground in ss 14–16 applies, the list being exhaustive.

The CCAA applies where the judgment comes from the chosen court (or its transferee) of a Contracting State under an exclusive clause. The court must recognise or enforce it unless a ground in ss 14–16 applies, the list being exhaustive (s 13(4)).

PointRule
What counts as a "judgment"A final decision on the merits, consent or default judgment, costs, and non-money judgments (s 2(1)); interim relief is excluded (s 10; Motacus). Judicial settlements are enforced like judgments (s 20).
ProcedureApply under s 13(1) and O 37 without a fresh action; serve the order abroad without permission (O 37 r 6(4)). No limitation period, but if no longer enforceable in the State of origin, Singapore cannot enforce it (s 13(2)).
Narrower than the common lawExhaustive grounds, "manifestly", procedural fraud only, binding findings; so an intrinsic fraud plea fares worse than at common law (C&Y).
A non-chosen court's judgmentOutside the CCAA, which does not bar its enforcement under REFJA or common law; argue the common law breach defence (J7.2.6).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
CCAA recognition in practice

A 2020 clause chose the Ruritanian courts exclusively, and Ruritania is a Contracting State. The Ruritanian court orders Alpha to pay US$1m and to deliver up certain moulds. Beta applies in Singapore under s 13(1) and O 37.

  • Both parts can be recognised and enforced: the CCAA covers non-money judgments too (s 2(1)), unlike the common law.
  • Alpha says the Ruritanian judge got the facts wrong. Irrelevant: no review of the merits.
  • Alpha says Beta's witness lied at trial. That is intrinsic fraud, and the CCAA allows only procedural fraud (s 14), so Alpha does worse here than it would at common law.
  • Alpha says it never received notice of the Ruritanian claim in time to defend. That is a mandatory ground for refusal (s 14).

7J7.6 Anti-enforcement injunctions

▤ On your pre-write: J7.6 ANTI-ENFORCEMENT INJUNCTIONS (AEI) (word for word)
J7.6 ANTI-ENFORCEMENT INJUNCTIONS (AEI)

(The single home for AEIs; J6.5.4 points here. Use where [debtor] wants Singapore to restrain [creditor] from relying on or enforcing [the X judgment] in [X / Y / worldwide]. Run the J6 ASI requirements first, then this overlay. Per C&Y, breach of an AEI is contempt.)

J7.6.0 Starter

Presently, [debtor] seeks an AEI restraining [creditor] from [relying on / enforcing] [the X judgment] in [X / Y / worldwide]. Per Sun Travels and C&Y, beyond the usual ASI requirements (J6), [debtor] must show exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability.

  • Why Caution (−) Per Sun Travels, an AEI implies [debtor] delayed in not seeking an ASI earlier, wastes [the X court]'s time and costs, stops [other courts] deciding recognition themselves, and interferes with execution in [X]; it is akin to nullifying [the X judgment].
  • Breach or Vexation Not Enough (−) Per Sun Travels, neither [creditor]'s breach of [the EJC / arbitration clause] nor [vexatious conduct] suffices alone, and party autonomy is no separate basis (Arkhangelsky creates no "agreement" category).
  • Fraud (+) Per Sun Travels, [creditor]'s fraud in obtaining [the X judgment], e.g., [perjury / forged evidence], is an exceptional circumstance, as in Ellerman Lines v Read (reliance on a Turkish judgment procured by [the salvor]'s perjury was restrained).
  • No Knowledge (+) Per Sun Travels (citing Ecobank), [debtor] did not know [the X judgment] was being sought until [it was delivered], e.g., [obtained secretly or too quickly], so its delay is not unconscionable.
  • Delay (±) Per Sun Travels, mere passage of time is not enough; delay counts against [debtor] only when coupled with [knowledge] and/or [prejudice to [creditor] or third parties such as the X court]. Simply limiting [the relief] to reflect the delay, as the judge did, is not the answer.
  • Applicant's Silence (−) Per Sun Travels, both sides' conduct matters: if [debtor] knew of [the fraud] before [the X judgment] but stayed silent, the equities may tilt against it.
  • No Closed List (±) Per Sun Travels, a new category needs the equities to favour relief: either a response to [creditor]'s [unconscionable conduct], or [debtor] has not lost equity through [unconscionable delay]. As in Sun Travels (Hilton delayed until after the Maldivian judgment), [debtor]'s [delay] [defeats / does not defeat] the AEI.
  • Alternatives (+) Per Sun Travels, AEIs "should generally be refused", so [debtor] should instead [resist recognition in Singapore (J7.2) / claim damages for breach of [clause] (J1.7) / resist enforcement in [Y]].

An AEI stops the creditor relying on or enforcing the foreign judgment. Run the J6 ASI requirements first, then add the Sun Travels overlay: exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability. AEIs "should generally be refused".

? WHY IT MATTERS

Why so cautious? An AEI implies the debtor delayed in not seeking an ASI earlier, wastes the foreign court's time, stops other courts deciding recognition themselves, and is akin to nullifying the foreign judgment (Sun Travels). Mere passage of time is not enough to refuse; delay counts against the debtor only with knowledge and/or prejudice. And if the debtor knew of the fraud but stayed silent, the equities may tilt against it. The alternatives: resist recognition here, claim damages for breach of the clause, or resist enforcement abroad.

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An ASI stops a race before it is run. An AEI tries to cancel the result after the race is over, and in every country at once. That is a much bigger step: the foreign court has already done all the work, and other countries never get to decide for themselves whether to recognise the result. So the debtor must explain why it did not ask for an ASI earlier, and show something exceptional, such as a fixed race (fraud) or a race it never knew was being run.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
AEI or not?
Debtor's positionAEI?
Beta sued in breach of a Singapore EJC. Alpha knew from the start but did nothing until Beta won.No. Breach alone is not enough, and Alpha's delay with knowledge counts against it.
Beta won by bribing the key witness, which Alpha discovered only after judgment.Possibly yes: fraud in obtaining the judgment (Ellerman Lines v Read).
Beta served the claim at an address it knew Alpha had left; Alpha first heard of the case when the judgment arrived.Possibly yes: Alpha did not know until judgment, so its delay is not unconscionable (Ecobank).

8Put it together: a worked judgment

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Hypo: the Ruritanian default judgment

Beta obtained a default judgment for US$2m in Ruritania against Alpha, a Singapore company. Ruritania is not a Contracting State or gazetted. Alpha had a sales office in Ruritania for three years. The contract had a Singapore EJC. Alpha says it was served at the wrong address and knew nothing until judgment.

  1. Enforce or recognise? Beta wants money: enforcement.
  2. Regime: not CCAA (Ruritania was not the chosen court), not REFJA: common law (J7.0.2).
  3. Requirements: a default judgment is on the merits; Alpha was present in Ruritania (a fixed office for three years, Adams v Cape); final under Ruritanian law (proved by expert); a definite sum (J7.1).
  4. Defences: (i) natural justice: no notice of the proceedings (Jacobson v Frachon; Paulus Tannos); (ii) arguably extrinsic fraud if Beta deliberately used a wrong address (Abouloff applies); (iii) breach of the Singapore EJC: promissory, Alpha did not submit, so the defence is arguable though undecided (J7.2.6).
  5. AEI? If Beta tries to enforce in a third country, Alpha could seek an AEI: no knowledge until judgment is an exceptional circumstance (Sun Travels, citing Ecobank) (J7.6).
