✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Why the answer is Australia

For negligence, the key element is the careless act. Reliance is only one route to a duty of care, and loss can be felt anywhere the claimant happens to be. So the tort is located where the audit was done, Australia, even though the claimant relied and suffered loss in Singapore (Vibrant Group).

Now change the tort pleaded. If the claimant sued for a misrepresentation directed at it, the key elements are receipt and reliance, so the tort would be located where it received and relied on the statement, Singapore, unless that place was fortuitous (JIO). Same facts, different tort, different place. That is why the pleaded tort decides the location.

C3.3.3 to C3.3.4 Applying limb 2, and the statutory rules

▤ On your pre-write: C3.3.3 Applying Limb 2 (word for word)
C3.3.3 Applying Limb 2

Limb 2 is satisfied if [law X] gives [some civil remedy] for [the conduct].

  • Limb 2 Fails Where [law X] [bars the head / provides a defence] or imposes no liability between [these parties] (Lord Wilberforce, Boys v Chaplin), so [defendant] escapes unless [law X] is displaced (C3.6.3).
  • Time Bar [law X]'s [shorter period] bars [the claim] via s 3(2) FLPA, as Georgian law did in Ivanishvili (C3.9.2).

Limb 2 is met if the foreign law gives some civil remedy. It fails if the foreign law bars the head, provides a defence, or imposes no liability between these parties. A shorter foreign time bar applies via FLPA s 3(2) (as Georgian law did in Ivanishvili).

▤ On your pre-write: C3.3.4 Statutory Deeming: Online Harms and Haze (word for word)
C3.3.4 Statutory Deeming: Online Harms and Haze

(claims under OSRAA or THPA)

  • OSRAA s 101: Tort Deemed in Singapore Per s 101 OSRAA 2025, a [Part 10 / 11 / 12] tort is treated as in Singapore if any element was (a) initiated in or from Singapore, (b) perceived here, or (c) caused [damage] here, so [the post viewed here] makes it a local tort.
    • Effect (Yeo): s 101 replaces the substance test with a statutory connecting factor, so both limbs point to [Singapore law], giving [the OSRAA torts] the character of overriding mandatory rules.
    • Jurisdiction (Yeo): it secures [nexus] and a factual presumption that Singapore is [forum conveniens], leaving FNC to sieve out [opportunistic foreign claims].
    • Exception: [defendant] may argue for [law X] where Singapore is so fortuitous that [serious injustice] results, but only exceptionally, given Parliament's intent to protect [Singapore residents] (Yeo).
    • No s 101 connection (rare): the substance test applies, [the tort] is likely abroad, and [claimant] recovers only the common denominator of [the OSRAA] and [law X] (Yeo).
    • Unilateral reading: s 101 may be a unilateral rule with no exception, but Yeo prefers [the multilateral reading] as [the wording] only redefines the connecting factor.
    • Critique (Yeo): if [law X] protects [the victim] better, s 101 still imposes [the lower OSRAA standard].
  • OSRAA s 102: No Contracting Out Per s 102, [exclusion / jurisdiction / arbitration terms] inconsistent with Parts 11 or 12 ([Administrators / Platforms]) are void unless fair and reasonable, Part 10 ([Communicators]) not being covered (C3.8.2).
    • Choice of law clause: [a foreign COL clause] cannot exclude [OSRAA liability], party autonomy being unrecognised in tort (Yeo; C3.6.5).
  • THPA s 6(4): Limb 2 Abrogated Per s 6(4) THPA 2014, [conduct in or outside Singapore] causing haze is actionable "whether or not" actionable abroad, so [defendant] cannot rely on [law X] for [burning in X].
    • Standing: per s 6(3), [a person] suffering [personal injury / property damage / economic loss] in Singapore sues, still proving [the statutory tort] under Singapore law.
    • Nature: an express statutory displacement of limb 2 for [haze claims], not a use of [the flexible exception].
StatuteEffect
OSRAA s 101A Part 10–12 tort is treated as committed in Singapore if any element was initiated in or from Singapore, perceived here, or caused damage here. Per Yeo: a statutory connecting factor replacing the substance test, giving these torts the character of overriding mandatory rules; FNC sieves out opportunistic foreign claims. Exception only where Singapore is so fortuitous that serious injustice results.
OSRAA s 102Exclusion, jurisdiction or arbitration terms inconsistent with Parts 11 or 12 are void unless fair and reasonable (not Part 10). A foreign choice of law clause cannot exclude OSRAA liability.
THPA s 6(4)Haze-causing conduct in or outside Singapore is actionable "whether or not" actionable abroad: an express statutory displacement of limb 2. Claimant must suffer injury, damage or loss in Singapore (s 6(3)).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
How the statutes cut the analysis short
  • Doxxing from abroad. A user in Malaysia posts a Singapore resident's home address and phone number, and the post is seen in Singapore. If this is a Part 10–12 OSRAA harm, s 101 treats the tort as committed in Singapore (it was perceived and caused damage here). No substance test is needed, and a foreign choice of law or exclusion clause cannot remove the liability where s 102 applies.
  • Haze. Fires on a plantation abroad send haze over Singapore, and a Singapore business loses income. Under THPA s 6(4) the conduct is actionable "whether or not" it is actionable where the fires were lit. Limb 2 simply drops out, provided the loss was suffered in Singapore (s 6(3)).
  • Ordinary defamation is not an OSRAA Part 10–12 harm, so it stays under double actionability (C3.7).

5C3.4 Local torts

▤ On your pre-write: C3.4 LOCAL TORTS (TORT COMMITTED IN SINGAPORE) (word for word)
C3.4 LOCAL TORTS (TORT COMMITTED IN SINGAPORE)
  • Double Actionability Applies to Local Torts Per Rickshaw, rejecting Metall's English-law-only rule as "unduly parochial" and contrary to comity, [conversion / negligence] in Singapore still runs both limbs, both pointing to [Singapore law].
    • Point of difference: the exception may apply [foreign law] where [the Singapore locus] is purely fortuitous, no stricter test applying, though "a liberal approach must be eschewed" (Rickshaw).
    • Why England differs: per Yeo (cited in Rickshaw), before Red Sea [the lex fori] could not be displaced, so [a lex fori rule for local torts] made sense.
  • Displacing Singapore Law (−) [Defendant] argues Singapore is fortuitous as [both parties reside in X], as in Briggs' Changi transit-lounge brawl between [Australians flying home], so [Australian law] applies.
  • Rickshaw Facts (+) the CA kept [Singapore law] as most [connecting factors] were here and the German-contract defence was "vague and unclear", so [claimant] argues [the defence is unparticularised].
    • Further reasons: no evidence was adduced on [deceit], and the German clause was conceded non-exclusive (C3.6.5), so [the clause] did not reach [the torts].
  • Briggs' Critique the torts arose from [an employment relationship] under [a German-law clause] and were pleaded in tort to avoid [German law], so the exception should have applied [the contract's proper law] (C3.6.5).
    • C&Y: fortuity should be one ground only, a test on the significance of [connections, including the contract] giving more room, as English courts applying [the contract's law] show (Trafigura).

The fight happened in Singapore, so on double actionability both limbs point to Singapore law. But the two Australians had no connection to Singapore beyond a few hours in a transit lounge. This is the textbook case for saying the Singapore locus is purely fortuitous, so the exception may apply Australian law instead. Contrast an ordinary local tort, where the parties live or do business here: Singapore law simply applies.

In Rickshaw, the CA kept Singapore law: most connecting factors were here, no evidence was adduced on deceit under German law, and the German clause was conceded non-exclusive. Briggs's critique: the torts arose from an employment relationship under a German-law clause and were pleaded in tort to avoid German law, so the exception should have applied the contract's law. C&Y: fortuity should be one ground only; a test on the significance of connections, including the contract, gives more room (Trafigura).

6C3.5 Foreign law not pleaded or not proved

▤ On your pre-write: C3.5 PROOF OF FOREIGN LAW AND THE PRESUMPTION OF SIMILARITY (word for word)
C3.5 PROOF OF FOREIGN LAW AND THE PRESUMPTION OF SIMILARITY (cross-refer C1.6)
  • Foreign Law Not Pleaded Per EFT Holdings (applying Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong), pleading [law X] is voluntary, so if [defendant] does not plead it, no conflicts issue arises and [Singapore law] applies without [the presumption].
    • C&Y framing: the same result is put as a presumption that [law X] equals [Singapore law].
  • Pleaded but Not Proved unproved [law X] is presumed similar where fair (Brownlie; C1.6.3), though [the party bearing the burden] may simply fail (EFT).
  • Limits of the Presumption [the party resisting it] argues it fails for [law X] because:
    • FNC: the court may accept that [civil law X] probably differs without [proof] (Rickshaw, citing PT Jaya Putra; JIO).
    • Intrusive relief abroad: no [injunction] against [conduct in X] on a bare presumption (OMG Holdings), explained by [the relief sought] (EFT).
    • Damages: for [damages / an account], the presumption presumably applies (C&Y), so [claimant] limits [the relief].
  • Cf Brownlie (UK) the default rule governs [unpleaded law] and the presumption [pleaded but unproved law], supporting the EFT split (C1.6.3).
SituationResult
Defendant does not plead foreign lawPleading is voluntary, so no conflicts issue arises and Singapore law applies (EFT Holdings, applying Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong). C&Y frame the same result as a presumption.
Pleaded but not provedPresumed similar where fair (Brownlie); otherwise the party bearing the burden may simply fail (EFT).
LimitsAt the FNC stage, the court may accept that a civil law system probably differs without proof (Rickshaw; JIO). No injunction against conduct abroad on a bare presumption (OMG Holdings); damages presumably fine.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Who has to bring up the foreign law?

Alpha sues Beta in Singapore for negligence in an accident in Ruritania.

  • Beta says nothing about Ruritanian law. Limb 2 exists for the defendant's benefit, so if Beta does not plead it, no conflicts issue arises: the court applies Singapore law, and Alpha only has to make out the Singapore tort (EFT Holdings).
  • Beta pleads that Ruritanian law gives no liability, but proves nothing. The court may presume Ruritanian law is similar to Singapore law where that is fair. If it is not fair, Beta, who carries the burden on limb 2, may simply fail to make out its defence.
  • Beta pleads and proves Ruritanian law with an expert. Now limb 2 is live, and the claim succeeds only for what Ruritanian law also allows.

So in practice the defendant decides whether limb 2 is ever tested.

C3.6.1 Starter

Per Rickshaw, the exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea) may displace [the lex fori], [the lex loci delicti] or both for the law with the most significant relationship to [the issue] and the parties, so [party] argues [country X] is fortuitous because [factors].

  • Threshold Per Rickshaw, courts "must not be quick" to apply it unless [the displaced law] is purely fortuitous and applying it causes [injustice], on "clear and satisfying grounds" (Lord Wilberforce), lest it become [a proper law of the tort].
  • Strictly Applied per Rickshaw, it is "imperative" that [the exception] be strictly applied, favouring certainty over flexibility, so [party] needs [clear fortuity], not [a more favourable law].
  • Fortuity and Injustice: Conjunctive? unclear, but per C&Y applying [a fortuitous law] is itself [the injustice], so fortuity is the real test.
    • Stricter: than Red Sea and Ang Ming Chuang (weighing contacts) and Lord Wilberforce's interest analysis, so [claimant] leads with [fortuity].
    • Critique (C&Y): fortuity is too restrictive and should be one way of showing [an insignificant connection], so [party] argues [the weak connection] suffices.

  • Burden on the Invoking Party [the invoking party] must prove [the connecting factors] and [the foreign law] (Red Sea), a "vague and unclear" defence failing (Rickshaw).

The exception may displace the lex fori, the lex loci delicti, or both, for the law with the most significant relationship. But per Rickshaw, courts "must not be quick" to use it: only where the displaced law is purely fortuitous, on "clear and satisfying grounds", and it must be strictly applied, favouring certainty over flexibility.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The two classic cases, side by side
Boys v ChaplinRed Sea
FactsTwo British servicemen stationed in Malta; a road accident in Malta. English law allowed general damages for pain and suffering; Maltese law allowed only special damages.A building in Saudi Arabia was defective. The insurer, sued in Hong Kong, counterclaimed directly against the supplier of the faulty materials. Hong Kong law required the insurer to pay first (subrogation); Saudi law allowed a direct claim.

Why?Malta had no real interest in applying its damages rule to two British servicemenHong Kong's only link was incorporation; all or virtually all factors pointed to Saudi Arabia

In Singapore, Rickshaw adds a strict filter: the displaced law must be purely fortuitous. C&Y doubt whether Malta was truly fortuitous in Boys, since the soldiers were stationed there, not passing through.

★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In contract, the parties can pick the law. In tort, Singapore has never clearly said they can. So when a contract says "all disputes between us are governed by English law" and one party sues in tort, there are two ways to try to get English law: (1) say parties may choose the law for torts too (open, but "just a small step away" per C&Y), or (2) squeeze it through the flexible exception, which Rickshaw makes hard because the other laws must be purely fortuitous. Write both routes and say the point is undecided (Ong Ghee Soon).

ℹ NOTE
C3.6.6 Public policy is not a ground for the exception

In Kuwait Airways, the majority excised an Iraqi confiscatory resolution via the exception, but Lord Scott said the exception is for applying the most connected law, not disapplying parts of it; Lord Steyn used public policy instead. After Rickshaw, Iraq was not fortuitous, so use public policy (C1.8).

    • Practice: few such claims reach Singapore, given [the O 8 r 1 / PD para 63 nexus] and [little reputational damage here] (C&Y).
    • OSRAA: s 101 reaches only [Part 10 to 12 harms, e.g., harassment or doxxing] (Yeo), so [common law defamation] stays under double actionability (C3.3.4).
  • Reform Carve-Out the SAL LRC 2003 would keep double actionability for personal defamation, the lex fori limb filtering [foreign law] incompatible with [Singapore's free speech values], and move [business defamation] to [the lex loci delicti] (C3.10).
  • Gutnick: the publisher's server-law rule (New Jersey) was rejected; Kirby J's global publication rule was left to legislatures. The UK now has a single publication rule (Defamation Act 2013 s 8).
  • Policy choice (Mills): the law of upload favours free speech ("race to the top"), download favours reputation ("race to the bottom").
  • Reform: the SAL LRC 2003 would keep double actionability for personal defamation.

Each place where the post is downloaded and read is a separate publication, so a separate tort (Gutnick). The Singapore publication is a local tort: both limbs point to Singapore law. The Malaysian and Indonesian publications each need double actionability with that country's law, and since the place of publication is prima facie the natural forum for each, a stay of those parts is likely. A claimant who wants a simple case here usually sues only on the Singapore publication.

IP and passing off

▤ On your pre-write: C3.7.2 Intellectual Property and Passing Off (word for word)
C3.7.2 Intellectual Property and Passing Off
  • Territoriality per C&Y, statutory [copyright / patent / trade mark] rights are territorial: conduct abroad cannot infringe [a Singapore right], nor conduct here [a Utopian right].
  • Validity Separate [validity] follows the law of [the place of creation], and [the Singapore court] may lack jurisdiction where infringement turns on [foreign validity] (C&Y).
  • Scenarios (forum Singapore; no conventions) run [the right's origin] against [the place of infringement]:
    • (i) Singapore right infringed abroad: fails both limbs, and [the lex fori] is not fortuitous for [a Singapore right].
    • (ii) Utopian right infringed here: fails both limbs, [Singapore as locus] not being fortuitous for [the infringing acts].
    • (iii) Foreign right infringed there: [a Malaysian copyright infringed in Malaysia] may succeed via the exception displacing [a fortuitous lex fori], if [Singapore has jurisdiction] (cf Pearce v Ove Arup).
  • Passing Off a common law tort, so [territoriality] is no bar, but per OMG Holdings [an injunction] against passing off in [Malaysia] needs [Malaysian law] proved (C3.5).

Statutory IP rights are territorial (C&Y). Forum Singapore, no conventions:

ScenarioResult
(i) Singapore right infringed abroadFails both limbs; the lex fori is not fortuitous for a Singapore right
(ii) Utopian right infringed in SingaporeFails both limbs; Singapore as locus is not fortuitous for the infringing acts
(iii) Malaysian copyright infringed in MalaysiaMay succeed via the exception displacing a fortuitous lex fori, if Singapore has jurisdiction (cf Pearce v Ove Arup)
Passing offA common law tort, so territoriality is no bar; but an injunction against passing off in Malaysia needs Malaysian law proved (OMG Holdings)
★ IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A Singapore trade mark is like a Singapore driving licence: it gives rights in Singapore only. Copying the mark in Malaysia does not infringe it, just as driving in Malaysia is not governed by your Singapore licence. That is why scenario (i) fails: under Singapore law, there is no Singapore-right infringement when the acts happen abroad. Passing off is different because it protects goodwill, a common law right not tied to a registration, so territoriality does not block it in the same way.

9C3.8 When contract meets tort

▤ On your pre-write: C3.8.1 Contract Relied on to Negate the Tort (word for word)
C3.8.1 Contract Relied on to Negate the Tort

(the contract answers an element, e.g., [a licence / a right to remain])

  • Two Questions Per C&Y (North), (i) the effect of [the contract] on tort liability is a tort question for double actionability, and (ii) its validity a contract question for [its proper law, law Y].
  • Galaxias [the trespass] was an English tort, so English law held [a contractual right to remain] negates trespass, but Greek law (the proper law) showed [the crew] were lawfully discharged, so [the claim] succeeded.
  • In Singapore [a local tort] itself runs double actionability, and for a tort in [X] with [a law Y contract], (i) follows the lex fori and [law X] and (ii) [law Y] (North).
Two questions whenever a contract is raised against a tort claim
▤ C3.8, per C&Y (North)
  1. 1Effect of the contract on tort liability (does it negate an element, or is the clause admissible as a defence?): a tort question, for double actionability.
  2. 2Validity of the contract or clause: a contract question, for its proper law.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Galaxias

The crew's trespass claim was an English tort, so English law held that a contractual right to remain would negate trespass. But Greek law, the contract's proper law, showed the crew had been lawfully discharged: no right to remain. So the claim succeeded.

Notice the two questions working together. The tort law asked: "would a contractual right to stay on board be a defence to trespass?" (yes). The contract's law answered: "did the crew still have that right?" (no). Neither law alone gave the answer.

▤ On your pre-write: C3.8.2 Contractual Exemption or Limitation Clause as a Defence to Tort (word for word)
C3.8.2 Contractual Exemption or Limitation Clause as a Defence to Tort
  • The Problem cl [X], valid under [law Y], excludes [negligence] liability that Singapore law [bars / subjects to reasonableness] ([s 2(1) / s 2(2) UCTA]).
    • Sayers: [an English worker] injured on [a Nigerian rig] was limited by [his Dutch employer]'s cl 8 compensation scheme, void under s 1(3) Law Reform (Personal Injuries) Act 1948 but valid in Dutch law.
  • Majority (Salmon and Stamp LJJ): Contractual Characterisation only the proper law of the contract mattered, and it being Dutch, "this action is dead" (Salmon LJ), so if [law Y] validates cl [X], [the claim] fails.
    • Critique (C&Y): treating [the issue] as wholly contractual is simplistic, ignoring [question (i)], so [claimant] argues [Singapore's policy] on admissibility.
  • Lord Denning: Proper Law of the Issue "we cannot apply two systems of law", so he applied the law closest to [the issues], Dutch ("Nigeria is out"), cl 8 "turn[ing] the scale" against [English law].
    • Critique (C&Y): he never asked what effect [the clause] has on [tort liability] (North).
    • Do not mix up the judgments: Salmon LJ found [the contract] Dutch, whereas Lord Denning found it English and reached Dutch via [the tort].
    • Application: [law Y] is closest to [the issue] as [the relationship is centred there].
  • Preferred Approach (Kahn-Freund; North; cf Brodin v A/R Seljan) (1) admissibility is a tort question for double actionability, and (2) validity a contract question for [its proper law], so cl [X], valid under [law Y], succeeds only if admissible under both [Singapore law] and [the lex loci delicti].
    • Incidental question: [the forum's] COL rules (simple, but [forum shopping]) or [the tort law's] (Harris: coherent, avoiding "the law of no one state") pick [the contract's law].
    • Which to choose: per C&Y, it may track Singapore's views on [renvoi] and [party autonomy] in tort.
    • Pre-existing contract: the exception may apply [law Y] to both questions (C3.6.5), though Rickshaw declined for [the employment contract].
    • OSRAA overlay: s 102 voids [the clause] as an admissibility rule (Yeo), or as [procedural / mandatory] even on [the Sayers view] (C3.3.4).
  • Non-Party Reliance [a co-employee] cannot invoke cl [X] unless [the proper law] allows it (Ong Ghee Soon).
⚠ TRAP
Do not mix up the Sayers judgments

Salmon LJ found the contract Dutch. Lord Denning found it English and reached Dutch law through the tort. C&Y criticise the majority as simplistic (it ignores the effect question) and Lord Denning for never asking what effect the clause has on tort liability.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The preferred approach on the Sayers facts, if sued in Singapore
  1. Validity (a contract question): is the clause valid under its proper law? Dutch law says yes.
  2. Admissibility (a tort question, double actionability): may a contract clause be raised as a defence to this negligence claim under Singapore law (limb 1) and under the law of the place of the tort (limb 2)? Both must allow it.
  3. Result: the clause defeats the claim only if it passes both steps. If either tort law refuses to let a clause of this kind exclude negligence liability for personal injury, the claim survives, even though the clause is valid in Dutch law.

The two-question split keeps contract questions with the contract's law and tort questions with the tort rule. That is why C&Y (following North) prefer it.

10C3.9 to C3.11 Overlays, evaluation and other obligations

▤ On your pre-write: C3.9.1 Damages (word for word)
C3.9.1 Damages

(cross-refer C1.4)

  • Traditional Per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads ([pain and suffering]) are substantive, so [the head] must exist under both laws, but quantum is procedural, so [Singapore law] assesses it.
  • Remoteness and Mitigation substantive (C&Y), so double actionability governs whether [the loss] is too remote or [the failure to mitigate] bars it.
  • Goh Suan Hee Critique Per Goh Suan Hee (obiter), the split is "wholly artificial" (cf Pfeiffer v Rogerson; Art 15(c) Rome II), so if quantum is substantive [claimant] recovers only [the lower figure, e.g., the cap under law X].
    • Status: open; [the lex loci delicti]'s rules of law on assessment would apply but [pure fact questions] stay with [the forum], and [the award gap] was a neutral FNC factor (C1.4; J4).
▤ On your pre-write: C3.9.2 Limitation (word for word)
C3.9.2 Limitation

(cross-refer C1.5.3)

  • Lex Loci Delicti's Period Per s 3(1) and s 3(2) FLPA 2012, [law X]'s domestic limitation period alone applies, renvoi being excluded (ss 3(5), 6(2)), so [the claim] [is / is not] barred, subject to s 4(2) undue hardship (C1.5.4).
    • No double hurdle: unlike s 1(2) UK FLPA 1984 (Metall), and where both limbs are [Singapore law] or [law X] is unpleaded, the Limitation Act applies.
  • Tactical Consequence per s 3(2) FLPA, locating the tort in [Singapore] avoids [law X]'s [shorter period] (C3.3).
  • After the Exception per C&Y, [the single lex causae]'s period applies: [law X]'s if the lex fori goes (Red Sea), the Limitation Act if [the lex loci delicti] goes (Boys), and [law Z]'s for a third law.
OverlayRule
DamagesHeads substantive (must exist under both laws); quantum traditionally procedural (Boys; Harding v Wealands). Goh Suan Hee (obiter): "wholly artificial"; open. Remoteness and mitigation substantive.
Limitation (FLPA s 3(2))The lex loci delicti's domestic period alone, subject to s 4(2) undue hardship. No double hurdle (unlike UK s 1(2), Metall). Locating the tort in Singapore avoids a shorter foreign period.
After the exceptionThe single lex causae's period: the foreign law's if the lex fori goes (Red Sea); the Limitation Act if the lex loci delicti goes (Boys); the third law's if both go.
Renvoi (one sentence)Never applied in tort (Credit Suisse Life v Ivanishvili, PC); formally open in Singapore; Neilson (HCA) unpersuasive.
▤ On your pre-write: C3.10 EVALUATION AND ALTERNATIVES (word for word)
C3.10 EVALUATION AND ALTERNATIVES (deploy where the question invites a view on retention or reform)
  • Critique of Double Actionability the lex fori limb is "parochial" (Red Sea, quoting the Law Commission; C&Y), born of [tort's criminal-law roots] with no [forum-connection requirement], so [claimant] fails only because [Singapore law] bars [the head].
  • SAL LRC's Five Reasons the lex fori limb is (1) out of step with [globalisation], (2) inconsistent with [other common law systems], (3) obsolete as [a default avoiding proof], (4) unnecessary given FNC and public policy, and (5) a blunt instrument for [forum interests].
  • Judicial Signals IM Skaugen ("an anachronism"); Ang Ming Chuang (would have departed [but for precedent]); Xiamen Xinjingdi ("may one day need to be reconsidered"); Lew v Nargolwala ([the lex fori] inappropriate even as [a contract fallback]).
  • Defence of the Rule limb (a) shields [Singapore defendants] from [foreign liability unknown here], limb (b) protects [defendants] and comity (EFT; Metall), and the exception gives [flexibility] (Rickshaw).
  • Reform for Parliament per Rickshaw, reform is for Parliament, with a "wise and judicious" use of the exception meanwhile, though C&Y note [the LRC proposal]'s inaction and Lew's logic for [judicial reform].
  • Departures from English Common Law Singapore applies the rule to local torts (C3.4), tests fortuity (C3.6), applies only [the lex loci delicti's period] (C3.9.2), and keeps [the common law], England having legislated (PIL(MP)A 1995; Rome II).
  • Australia Zhang v Renault (and Pfeiffer interstate) apply [the lex loci delicti] with no exception, renvoi filling [the gap] (Neilson), so [law X] alone would govern.
  • Canada Tolofson v Jensen applies [the lex loci delicti], with some flexibility for [international, not interprovincial, torts] (C&Y), so [law X] governs unless [displaced].
  • England and New Zealand statute (PIL(MP)A 1995; NZ 2017) applies [the lex loci delicti] with a flexible exception (s 12, Trafigura), the UK keeping double actionability for [defamation] and Rome II governing [most later torts].
  • Rome II Art 4(1) applies the law where [the damage] occurs (lex loci damni), whatever [the place of the event], sparing [the substance test], with party autonomy (Art 14) and no renvoi (Art 24).
    • Locus critique: the substance test depends on [the elements as alleged] under [the lex fori] (handout question), favouring lex loci damni.
  • US Interest Analysis Babcock v Jackson weighs [the states' interests], but per C&Y it is politically sensitive and queries whether PIL should serve [foreign state interests] at all.
  • Proper Law of the Tort (Morris) the law of [the most significant relationship], weighing [place of conduct and injury, residence, pre-existing relationship], was rejected in Boys and Red Sea for [uncertainty], the exception already importing it.
    • Online critique (Yeo): a physical locus is increasingly out of touch, though s 101 OSRAA may entrench [the place-of-tort factor] against [judicial development].
  • Singapore Reform Proposal the SAL LRC (2003) proposed [the lex loci delicti] with a "significantly more substantially connected" exception, excluding [personal defamation], never enacted.
  • C&Y Reform Package (1) abolish [the lex fori limb], and (2) give effect to [tort COL clauses] via the exception, so submit [retain / reform].
Evaluation: should double actionability survive?
▤ C3.10
  1. 1Against: the lex fori limb is "parochial" (Red Sea); the SAL LRC's five reasons (globalisation, inconsistency, obsolete, unnecessary given FNC and public policy, blunt); judicial signals (IM Skaugen: "an anachronism"; Ang Ming Chuang; Xiamen Xinjingdi).
  2. 2For: limb (a) shields Singapore defendants from liability unknown here; limb (b) protects defendants and comity; the exception gives flexibility.
  3. 3Reform is for Parliament (Rickshaw). The SAL LRC (2003) proposed the lex loci delicti with a "significantly more substantially connected" exception; never enacted. C&Y: abolish the lex fori limb and give effect to tort choice of law clauses.
  4. 4Elsewhere: Australia and Canada apply the lex loci delicti (Zhang v Renault; Tolofson); England and NZ by statute with an exception; Rome II Art 4(1) the place of damage; US interest analysis (Babcock v Jackson).
▤ On your pre-write: C3.11 OTHER OBLIGATIONS (OUTLINE ONLY) (word for word)
C3.11 OTHER OBLIGATIONS (OUTLINE ONLY)
  • Equitable Obligations Per Rickshaw, [the fiduciary / confidence claim] founded on [the contract] follows [its proper law] (C1.1.5; Rappo), a separate equitable category being left open.
    • Directors' duties: the law of [the place of incorporation] (Focus Energy), which [party autonomy] cannot vary (Base Metal Trading).
    • Breach of confidence without a relationship: unclear: [tort] (Yeo), [unjust enrichment] or [the proper law of the obligation] (Innovia Films).
    • Knowing receipt: the place of [enrichment / receipt] (Thahir v Pertamina; El Ajou), though [its fault element] leans to tort.
    • Dishonest assistance: a tort, so double actionability (Grupo Torras), problematic if [law X] alone governs and has [no accessory liability].
  • Unjust Enrichment per Dicey Rule 230 (adopted), the proper law of [the obligation]: (a) [the contract]'s (putative) proper law, (b) [the lex situs] for land (doubted), else (c) [the place of enrichment].
    • CIMB v Dresdner: [an intended but void contract] goes to (a) unless [the vitiating factor] infects [the COL clause]; [no meeting of minds] goes to (c).
    • Place of enrichment: prefer [immediate over ultimate] enrichment if balanced (HSBC v UOB), and [bribes in Singapore accounts] made [Singapore law] apply (Thahir v Pertamina).
    • Illegality: per Esben Finance (provisional), the [Foster / Ralli] comity principle extends to [unjust enrichment claims], subject to [stultification].
  • Trusts [express trusts] follow [the settlor's chosen law] or closest connection (Trisuryo: [a Singapore SPV] implied Singapore law); for [resulting / constructive trusts], C&Y prefer [the lex situs] to [the event's law] (Rappo).
  • Slide Questions [promissory estoppel] on [contractual non-performance] follows the contract's proper law, and [undue influence] is material validity for [the proper law], unless it infects [the COL clause] (CIMB).

11Put it together: three worked pathways

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pathway A: cross-border misrepresentation (C3.12)

D in Hong Kong emails C in Singapore a false statement; C relies on it here and invests. (1) Limb 1: deceit or negligent misstatement if all done here (C3.2). (2) Locus: received and relied on in Singapore, not fortuitous, so a local tort (C3.3.2): both limbs point to Singapore law. (3) D must plead Hong Kong law if it wants to argue otherwise (C3.5). (4) The Misrepresentation Act applies only if a related contract is Singapore-law (C3.7).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pathway B: online defamation

A post is read in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia: three torts (Gutnick). The Singapore one is local. The other two need double actionability with Malaysian and Indonesian law, and a stay is likely. OSRAA s 101 only reaches a parallel OSRAA tort (harassment, doxxing).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pathway C: contract clause as a defence

An employer's Dutch-law contract caps injury compensation; the employee is hurt on a rig in Nigeria. Run the Sayers majority (proper law only), then Lord Denning (law closest to the issue), then the preferred approach: admissibility under Singapore law and the lex loci delicti, validity under Dutch law (C3.8.2).

START HERE · ABOUT 21 MIN · 28 QUESTIONS

How the sheet works, and how an answer uses it

⚡ BIG IDEA

The exam hands you a statement to attack or defend. Each archetype is a ready-made route through one family of statements; your job is to spot the family, then fill the route with the question's own words.

1What the exam asks of you

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a friend says something bold, like "everyone's opinion about right and wrong is equally good". Your job is not to shout yes or no. It is to find the part that is true, show exactly where it goes too far, and say why, using the thinkers from class as your witnesses. The sheet is a box of pre-built arguments for the kinds of bold statements the examiner likes to make.

LAW301 essay questions almost always look the same. You get a short, confident statement in quotation marks, then an instruction such as "Critically evaluate and comment on this statement by reference to the theories of Rawls, Finnis, Hart, and Devlin covered in this course, and any relevant illustrations". Liu's own sample (Sample Question 1, worth 50% of the paper) reads:

"Legislators governing a pluralist society should treat all moral opinions as equally valid. This can be achieved by refraining from passing any law restricting liberty unless it is objectively necessary to protect others from a wrongdoer's conduct. Only then can legislators avoid imposing on citizens a fixed conception of the good life."

Three things are true of nearly every statement like this:

  1. It has a kernel of truth. Here: a pluralist state should not force one way of life on everyone.
  2. It overreaches through one or two loaded words. Here: "equally valid", "objectively", "wrongdoer", "only then".
  3. It belongs to a family. This one belongs to the pluralism family (archetype 6), with help from the scepticism family (archetype 4) and the enforcement-of-morals family (archetype 7).

A strong answer does three matching things: it grants the kernel, pins the overreach on the loaded word, and explains the difference with a principle from the course. The sheet is organised so that each of these steps is already half-written for you.

? WHY IT MATTERS
Why "archetype"?

An archetype is a recurring kind of exam statement. Liu's questions change their facts and wording, but they keep returning to the same eleven arguments: what law is (2), the rule of law (3), whether morality is objective (4), Finnis (5), pluralism (6), enforcing morals (7), unjust laws (8), judges (9), lawyers (10), the Constitution (11), and who decides (12). Learn the eleven routes and almost any statement becomes familiar.

2The sheet at a glance

The printed sheet has sixteen sections. You do not read it front to back in the exam; you jump to the part you need. Here is the map:

SectionWhat it holdsWhen you use it
1 EngineThe map, menus of openings and closings, organising distinctions, a self-critique bank, a "signature ledger"Planning every answer
2–12 ArchetypesOne family of statement each, in course orderThe body of your answer
13 Across topicsComparisons (13.1) and current controversies (13.2)"Compare" questions, or a fresh example
14 Theorist bankA card per thinker: claim, test, strength, critique, verdictWhen a question names a theorist
15 FrameworksStep-by-step tests (Fuller's checklist, Finnis's permissibility test, Rawls's legitimacy test …)Problem questions and applying a theory
16 Singapore bankArticles, cases, Hansard quotes, statutesIllustrations

There is also a prep page (section 0), not printed, which holds the five-minute routine, the trigger table that maps question words to blocks, and the 1,500-word frame. This site uses the trigger table at the top of every lesson.

How the numbering works
▤ The sheet's decimal numbering (new numbering, 4 Nov)
  1. 1A whole number is a section: 7 is the enforcement-of-morals archetype.
  2. 2A decimal is a block inside it: 7.3 is "Devlin's jury box, rightly read".
  3. 3Distinctions in the engine carry brackets: 1.3(4) is "aim v mechanism".
  4. 4Theorist cards are 14.n (14.13 is Hart's Law, Liberty and Morality); frameworks are 15.n; Singapore material is 16.n.

Blocks cross-refer constantly: "(8.3)" inside block 11.5 means "see block 8.3 for the detail". On this site every such number is a blue link.

3How to read an archetype block

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Each block is like a recipe card for one kind of statement. The title says what dish it is. The small italic words are the "smells" that tell you this recipe is needed. The three numbered lines are the recipe itself: first admit what's right, then bring in a thinker, then say "so…". The tags underneath are optional extras: the best case for the other side, a warning, an extra ingredient.

Every archetype section (2–12) is built the same way:

  • Position: one sentence stating your overall stance for the whole family. Use it once, rewritten in the question's own words.
  • Intro: a model opening paragraph with gaps.
  • Blocks (such as 7.1, 7.2 …): one per sub-family of statement.
  • Conclusion: a model closing paragraph with gaps.

Each block has the same anatomy. Open block 7.11 below and compare it with the labels that follow.

▤ On your sheet: 7.11 Polls are not a mandate (word for word)
7.11 Polls are not a mandate poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
  1. A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise: in 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to [the conduct], following the majority is oppression; if not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns (Pragmatism 302).
  3. So [majority support] is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
  • STEELMAN Majority rule treats citizens as equals (Indranee, 2007: 16.3; 12.3).
  • CONCEDE Consensus gauges, not grounds: in Liu's map of the 2007 replies, majority opinion "can be an indication of objective morality"†; yet majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch" (JO 331–32).
Anatomy of a block
▤ Using 7.11 "Polls are not a mandate"
  1. 1Number and title: "7.11 Polls are not a mandate" names the move.
  2. 2Trigger words (the grey italic after the dot): poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide. If a question uses words like these, this block is a candidate.
  3. 3Line 1, the kernel or first step: a poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise (Hri Kumar's 2007 point).
  4. 4Line 2, the theorist or authority: TSH's dilemma: if there is a right, following the majority is oppression; if not, the moral question returns.
  5. 5Line 3, the "So" line: the verdict, written so it can become a topic sentence: majority support is evidence, never a reason that settles the matter.
  6. 6Tags: STEELMAN gives the best case for the statement; CONCEDE gives the honest weakness in your own side.

The square brackets

Words in square brackets, such as "[majority support]" or "[the statement]", are slots. You replace them with the question's own words. This is what stops an answer reading like a pasted template: the move is pre-built, but every sentence speaks the question's language.

The tags

TagWhat it meansHow to use it
STEELMANThe best case for the statementOne short paragraph early on, so the examiner sees you took it seriously
FORMaterial supporting your lineEvidence for your thesis
AGAINSTMaterial against the statement (or a reply)Your attack
TRAPA common mistakeRead before you write; never make it
CONCEDEA weakness in your own sideOne sentence of self-critique, usually in the last body section
QUALIFYA nuance that narrows a claimStops you overclaiming
JUDGE, LAWYER, LEGISLATOR, OFFICIAL, CITIZENWhat the point means for that actorUse when the question names that actor

The symbols

  • † means the point comes from Liu's slides or the public record rather than a reading.
  • (Liu, W10) means Liu said it in the Week 10 lecture; S13 and S14 are sessions 13 and 14.
  • Page references such as "(PS 618)" or "(Devlin 15)" mean you may quote the words in quotation marks. The prep page's rule: quote only lines the sheet gives with a page; otherwise paraphrase.
ℹ NOTE
Where the example statements come from

In every lesson, a statement tagged with a question number (such as Q61) is quoted from your practice bank, "LTP Practice Exam Questions (Merged)". A statement without a number is a short paraphrase built from the block's trigger words, so you can see the kind of wording that calls for the block.

⚠ TRAP
Don't paste the block

The prep page's rules say: use the Position line once, in the question's terms, and "never paste a default paragraph". The numbered lines are a skeleton. In the exam, each becomes two or three sentences fitted to the facts in front of you.

4Theorist cards and frameworks

Two other kinds of block appear outside the archetypes.

Theorist cards (section 14)

Each card answers the same questions about one thinker, so that you can compare them quickly. Here is the card for Hart's Law, Liberty and Morality:

▤ On your sheet: 14.13 Hart: Law, Liberty and Morality (word for word)
14.13 Hart: Law, Liberty and Morality LLM 13–52 · use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, 7.9
  • PURPOSE May the criminal law enforce morality as such, beyond preventing harm to others?
  • CLAIM Coercion is prima facie objectionable and needs a countervailing good; paternalism and public decency can supply one, but bare moral condemnation cannot.
  • TEST → 15.7. (1) A question of critical morality about enforcing positive morality (LLM 20). (2) Two costs: punishing offenders and coercing those who never offend (21). (3) Paternalism where consent is defective (33). (4) Decency: punish the public act (41).
  • STRENGTH Bigamy, if punished to protect religious feelings from a public act, is punished "neither as irreligious nor as immoral but as a nuisance" (LLM 41); whether to punish turns on contestable estimates of offence against freedom lost (43).
  • CRITIQUE TSH: "a critique could be made" that paternalism is "in the ultimate analysis, based on morals" (Pragmatism 288) → reply: Hart grants that applying his grounds takes moral judgement (LLM 20); he denies only punishing immorality as such (Liu, W9).
  • VERDICT Hart wins the case against punishing private immorality as such, though moral judgment still decides where his paternalism and decency bite.
LabelMeans
PURPOSEThe question this thinker is answering
CLAIMTheir answer in one sentence
TESTHow to apply it (often pointing to a framework in 15)
STRENGTHThe best thing about it
CRITIQUE → replyThe main objection, and how the thinker (or you) answers
CONCEDEWhat you should honestly give up
SAYA short quotable phrase
TRAPA common misreading
VERDICTYour one-line overall judgement

Frameworks (section 15)

A framework is a step-by-step test with a key question and a verdict rule. Use one when the question gives facts and asks what a theorist would say (problem questions), or when you want to show a theory applied rather than described.

▤ On your sheet: 15.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient) (word for word)
15.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient) key question: what justifies this coercion, besides immorality as such? · use: 7.9
  • Coercion is "prima facie objectionable" (LLM 20). (1) Harm to others? Distress at "the bare knowledge" of others' conduct does not count (46–47). (2) Paternalism, if consent is defective: punishing drug supply "except under medical prescription" (32–33).
  • (3) Public decency: offence "serious and likely", weighed against the freedom lost (42–43). (4) Moralism alone: never. Verdict rule (mine, on Liu's map: all law rests on force, criminal law most directly, W9): the more coercive the measure (punish, regulate, promote), the stronger the reason needed; Hart's own question is punishment only.

Section 1 is printed first because you use it for every answer. Here it is in full, followed by what each part is for.

1.2 Menus
Hook: source This is almost verbatim [George, as TSH reports him / Thunder's summary of the amoral view / Devlin's case for enforcement]; the question is whether its author's own qualification survives.
Hook: word Everything turns on "[without exception / necessarily / simply / always / rightfully]", and that word commits the statement to more than it can defend.
Hook: ally turns The statement's natural ally is [Hart / Devlin / Pepper / Rawls], yet he rejects its conclusion.
Hook: case [Riggs / the 2007 retain-but-don't-enforce compromise / Ordinance 11 / the Jaffa Cakes case†] tests the statement at once.
Hook: concession The statement is right that [kernel]. It does not follow that [overreach], because [principle].
Hook: self-application (once per script) The statement is itself [a philosophy / a moral verdict], so it cannot be true in the sense it claims.
Thesis: numbered (default) I make [two / three] claims: (1) [limb 1]; (2) [limb 2]; (3) [limb 3].
Thesis: distinction The statement is right about [A] and wrong about [B]; the difference is [1.3 principle].
Thesis: who and what [The majority / the Constitution / the role] settles who decides, not what is right.
Thesis: conditional If "[word]" means [X], the statement holds but is trivial; if it means [Y], it is false, and [Y] is the reading it needs.
Thesis: two hats As an MP I would [vote against / amend]; as a judge I would [enforce it / read it down]; the answers differ because the roles ask different questions.
Steelman (120–150 words) The best case for the statement is [X], which [Singapore example] supports. It shows [kernel], but not [overreach].
Close: verdict and principle (default) The statement is therefore [verdict], because [governing principle].
Close: back to the hook Read again, "[the opening word or case]" shows [what the essay established].
Close: actor (only if the question names one) For [the judge / the MP / the lawyer], this means [one concrete consequence].
  • Roadmap: none, or one sentence: I take the [two limbs] in turn, using the difference between [A] and [B].
  • Memorable lines, one per script: A constitutional democracy can move moral questions between institutions, but cannot remove them. · Law is a floor, not a ceiling. · Easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory. · Thunder: "To simply point to the role is to give up explaining it."
  • Reformulation ("a defensible version would read …"): once per script, where one sentence repairs the statement.

1.4 Self-critique bank
  • CONCEDE TSH's catch: where, for realists, consensus has gone "dreadfully wrong" while a local legislature tries to do right, the formula is "problematic and not merely ineffective" (JO 332; 8.5). Concede: consensus gauges, not grounds.
  • CONCEDE Radbruch and Alexy: Alexy grants that candour is "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall"; answer with his replies (8.3).
  • CONCEDE Finnis: his list of goods is contested; accessible is not accepted; incommensurable goods leave much open; Liu: self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing, and the means/side-effect line is "artificial" (5.3, 5.7). Disagreement is not falsity, but it limits coercion.
  • CONCEDE Dworkin: fit is often not unique, so whose political morality decides? (9.5)
  • CONCEDE Thunder: virtue under-determines cases: "There will inevitably be substantial disagreement on particular cases" (10.5).
  • CONCEDE Rawls: public reason may still end in a vote; Hart: where paternalism stops is itself "based on morals" (TSH, Pragmatism 288), though he never punishes immorality as such (7.1); Pepper: "extreme" is never defined, so his lawyer weighs morality throughout (10.1).

  • 4, 6 ☐ durian (4.1 only) · ☐ "no Switzerland of ambivalence" (4.5) · ☐ planets (4.7; alt: stick bent in water) · ☐ the whip, "an option" (6.8; alt: trustee, not stenographer) · ☐ TSH's hunter, slave-owner reply (6.5; alt: Finnis's public stand)

1.1 The map

A table from course topic to lead archetype, cards and tests. If a question is about the rule of law, the map sends you to archetype 3, card 14.6 (Fuller) and framework 15.1.

1.2 The menus

Ready-made hooks (first sentences), theses, a steelman frame and closes. Pick one of each, never the same twice in a script. The default thesis is numbered ("I make three claims …"); the default close is "verdict and principle".

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
A hook from the menu, filled in

Menu: Hook: word. "Everything turns on '[without exception / necessarily / simply / always / rightfully]', and that word commits the statement to more than it can defend."

Filled for Sample Question 1: Everything turns on "equally valid", and that phrase commits the statement to more than it can defend: a legislator who treats every moral opinion as equally valid has already taken a moral side.

1.3 Organising distinctions

The most powerful tool on the sheet. Each distinction splits a statement into a part that is right and a part that is wrong. "Who decides v what is right" (1.3(1)) answers almost any majority-will statement: a vote settles who may make law, not what the law should say. Choose one per answer and let it shape the body.

1.4 Self-critique bank

Honest weaknesses of the positions you are likely to defend (TSH's "catch", Finnis's contested list of goods, Dworkin's non-unique fit). One or two sentences inside your last body section.

1.5 Signature ledger

Memorable examples (the "grudge informer", the "effluent" case, Jaffa Cakes) with a home block and an alternate, so you never reuse the same example in two answers.

6From question to answer in five minutes

The prep page gives a five-minute routine. In short:

  1. Scan. Circle every word that appears in the trigger table and note its move in the margin.
  2. Source. If the statement paraphrases a theorist (for example, George as TSH reports him, or Thunder's "just focus on the law"), name that theorist in your first two sentences.
  3. Actors. Underline the actor the question names (judge, MP, official, lawyer, citizen). This is the actor lock: end each body paragraph on that actor.
  4. Route. Choose one lead section and one organising distinction.
  5. Build. Hook, distinction, thesis → steelman → body sections → self-critique in the last → close.
The 1,500-word frame
▤ Prep page 0.3
  1. 1Opening 120–150 words: hook, distinction, thesis, at most one roadmap sentence.
  2. 2Steelman 120–150 words: the best case for the statement.
  3. 3Three body sections of 280–320 words (or four of 220–240), self-critique inside the last.
  4. 4Conclusion 100–130 words: verdict and principle, no recap of theorists.

Each body paragraph (about 300 words) follows a pattern: the claim in the quote's words → one theorist developed in 2–3 sentences → the strongest objection → your reply → one illustration → a "so" line.

7Worked example: Sample Question 1

Let us run the routine on Liu's sample statement.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Step 1: scan the words
  • "equally valid" → trigger table: aim v mechanism → 6.10, 4.7.
  • "objectively" → same row (6.10): the word "objectively" presupposes moral realism.
  • "protect others from a wrongdoer's conduct" → harm principle → 7.1; "wrongdoer" presupposes a wrong.
  • "Only then" → the statement claims its mechanism is the only means to its aim (Liu's chain reading in 6.10).
  • "legislators" → actor lock: the MP.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Step 2: route

Lead section 6 (pluralism), using block 6.10, with Hart (7.2, 7.9) and Devlin (7.3) for the harm part. Distinction 1.3(4) aim v mechanism: the aim (don't impose a fixed conception of the good life) is defensible; the mechanism (treat all opinions as equally valid, legislate only on harm) is neither neutral nor necessary.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Step 3: opening and thesis

Everything turns on "equally valid", and that phrase commits the statement to more than it can defend. The statement's aim, that legislators should not impose a fixed conception of the good life, is sound; Rawls and Finnis both share it. But I make three claims: (1) treating all opinions as equally valid is itself a moral position, which defeats itself; (2) the harm mechanism is not the only way to the aim, since Hart allows paternalism where consent is defective; and (3) it is not neutral, since Rawls himself files Mill's liberalism among comprehensive doctrines. The aim survives only by dropping the mechanism.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Step 4: body plan
  1. Rawls (6.1, 6.11): legitimacy needs reasons all reasonable citizens could accept, but "reasonable" is not "equally valid": unreasonable doctrines are excluded. Rawls's neutrality is of justification, not outcome.
  2. Finnis (5.5, 6.2): a range of reasonable opinions, not all; the common good is a framework, not a life-plan, so the aim survives without equal validity.
  3. Hart v Devlin (7.2, 7.3): Hart's paternalism (defective consent) shows harm-to-others is not the only ground; Devlin shows any society takes a moral stand. Self-critique: Rawls's public reason may still end in a vote (1.4).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Step 5: close (verdict and principle)

The statement is therefore partly right: its aim is the liberal's and the natural lawyer's alike. But its mechanism fails, because equal respect for persons does not require equal validity for opinions.

You will meet this question again in Lesson 6, where block 6.10 is taught in full.

Lesson 2: What law is →
LESSON 2 · ARCHETYPE 2 · ABOUT 43 MIN · 35 QUESTIONS

LP v NLT, and why theory matters

⚡ BIG IDEA

Saying what counts as "law" is already an evaluation, so the choice between legal positivism and natural law is live, and hard cases such as Riggs v Palmer turn on a theory of what law's grounds are.

ARCHETYPE 2 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
2 LP v NLT, and why theory matters
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position Naming [law] is an evaluation, so LP v NLT is a live choice, and hard cases such as Riggs turn on a theory of law's grounds.
Intro [The statement] treats identifying law as neutral and theory as optional. LP's two theses, law as social fact and no necessary link with morality (W1b slides 5–6†), are coherent; but LP must still evaluate whose recognition counts, and in Riggs judges agreed the law bound them yet split over what it required. So [the statement] is [wrong / partly right]: theory decides hard cases, and Riggs shows judges splitting over which materials count as law.
2.1 Descriptive? neutral, objective, merely describes, cross-purposes
  1. LP and NLT are not at [cross-purposes]: both ask what law is (TSH CJ 84 n 28).
  2. Treating [official recognition] as conclusive is a choice: once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, its injustice is "treated as irrelevant" (TSH CJ 106).
  3. So LP is not simply [neutral and objective], and preferring it for a pluralist state is a value choice.
  • STEELMAN Lawyers "look up the books", and must know the law before reforming it (Harris 16); LP arose in states without a shared moral base (Liu, W1).
  • FOR Liu's slides†: LP finds law in what courts uphold, so its premise becomes its conclusion; equating what people regard as law with law "involves an evaluation, and is not merely descriptive" (W1b slide 15).
  • TRAP "No necessary connection" allows contingent ones, incorporation and critique (W1b slide 7†): Riggs' maxim, a legal rule with moral content, troubles no positivist (Liu, W1).
  • AGAINST Finnis doubts law is describable from a "rubbish heap" of facts without evaluative criteria (TSH CJ 106 n 124).
2.2 Internal "ought" mere commands, habit, Hart concedes moral evaluation
  1. Law is more than [commands obeyed from habit]: Hart's rules carry an internal "ought", a critical reflective attitude.
  2. But that "ought" need not be moral: Hart allows acceptance out of fear, self-interest or habit (Harris 119).
  3. So Hart escapes [mere habit] without conceding moral evaluation.
  • Dworkin: if officials obeying Hitler "only out of fear" accepted the rule, Hart's difference from Austin "becomes elusive"; else, it seems, there was "no law in Nazi Germany" (LE ch 1).
2.3 Elitist? only the devout, religious faith, any judge strikes down
  1. NLT does not rest on [moral truths only the devout can see]: natural law, unlike divine law, can be apprehended by reason (TSH CJ 87).
  2. So NLT does not [license any judge to strike down]: the RF voids only intolerably unjust statutes (8.2–8.3); for Finnis unjust law is no nullity to disregard (Harris 18).
  • QUALIFY Strong NLT (every rule must embody morality) would have judges second-guess tax law; weak NLT strips legal status only at extreme divergence, a law to execute all redheads (Liu, W1). Grotius made natural law secular (Harris 11); Aquinas's four kinds: eternal, divine, natural, human (W1b slide 13†).
  • CONCEDE TSH admits "no easy answer" on who pronounces natural law (CJ 99): concede judges' doubtful authority below the threshold (12.1).
2.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers? all but name
  1. Fuller and Dworkin are NLT's allies, not [natural lawyers in all but name]: neither lets injustice as such defeat validity.
  2. Fuller's is a thin "procedural natural law"†: legality demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be" (MOL 47).
  3. So [all but name] overstates: Dworkin's judge must "interpret the legal history he finds" (AMP), leaving intolerable injustice open.
  • CONCEDE Dworkin finds even weak NLT "unpersuasive" as an account of usage (LE ch 1): concede it; defend NLT as a theory of grounds.
2.5 Judges disagree? only about obeying, plain words, no law to apply
  1. [Judges only disagree about obeying] mistakes theoretical disagreement for defiance: in Riggs all accepted the law's authority but split over what it required.
  2. In McLoughlin, too, the Lords agreed on the result but split over whether courts may let policy limit liability (2.8; 9.2).
  3. So [no law to apply] assumes the plain-fact view; which arguments count as law is the point in dispute.
  • Dworkin: LP's pretence defence shows judges as "well-meaning liars", its borderline defence as "simpletons"; these were "pivotal" cases (LE ch 1).
  • QUALIFY Liu thinks Dworkin unfair to LP: it need not turn every disagreement into an empirical one, and soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests (Harris 121) (Liu, W1).
  • Terms (LE ch 1): empirical disagreement disputes whether agreed grounds of law are met, theoretical the grounds themselves; the plain-fact view and semantic theories hide the latter.
  • LAWYER Run both policy arguments (9.2).
2.6 Theory useless? luxury, optional, irrelevant, no client needed, good dictionary, Jaffa Cakes
  1. Fish grants [the statement] a kernel: Rawls cited in court is likely to be regarded "at best as window dressing and at worst as showing off".
  2. Yet marshalling rules "takes place within an enterprise that is purposive"; without "some strong intuition of the general project", rehearsing them is "an empty gesture" (Fish).
  3. So [theory is a luxury] confuses citing theory with using it: easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9); hard cases, on rival ones.
  • Jaffa Cakes† (United Biscuits (UK) Ltd (No 2), LON/91/160): the VAT tribunal used core attributes, class commonalities, thought experiments and social context: indirectly, a "philosophy of cakeness and biscuitness". Held cake (stale cakes harden, biscuits soften): both sides agreed the factors but weighed them differently, the shape of most jurisprudential disputes (Liu, W1). TSH: purpose may settle "vehicles"; contested words like "law" engage LP v NLT (CJ 90).
  • Leff†: "[Y]ou can't know that a thing is not being done well until you know what it is that is being done"; excellence presupposes theory.
  • AGAINST [Theory cannot help anyone decide] fails: disagreement is not absence of fact (4.7). Constitution: 11.7.
2.7 Singapore pragmatism prevailing philosophy, pragmatic, no blank slate
  1. [Singapore's prevailing philosophy] is often called pragmatism: keeping s 377A in 2007, the Government called its approach "a pragmatic one that maintains Singapore's social cohesion" (Pragmatism 302).
  2. Yet pragmatism is a theory: in any "postmodern pragmatic" society, the view that law is whatever a court says "glosses over" guiding principles (TSH CJ 89).
  3. So [philosophy is unnecessary here] fails: "The purpose of theory is to guide practice" (TSH CJ 89).
  • AGAINST "[I]n law, as in life, we simply cannot shun the question" of right and wrong (Pragmatism 304).
2.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin
  1. Riggs turned on whether a clear statute has unstated exceptions; McLoughlin, on whether policy may distinguish precedent.
  2. Each answer presupposes a theory of [law].
CardRiggs v PalmerMcLoughlin v O'Brian
FactsElmer, 16, poisoned his grandfather lest he revoke the will; literally, the statute of wills let him inherit.Not at the scene, she saw her injured family, begrimed, in hospital hours later; a daughter died.
Held5–2: Elmer took nothing.5–0, reversing the CA: her shock was recoverable.
MajorityEarl: intention, and maxims with "their foundation in universal law" (511); this "takes from him no property" (514).On reasons, Wilberforce, Edmund-Davies, Russell: policy may limit liability, but not here.
DissentGray: it "does not lie within the domain of conscience" (515); courts cannot "add to the respondent's penalties" (519).None; on reasons, Scarman: line-drawing policy "not justiciable" (431); Bridge: stopping at decided cases is "an unwarranted abdication" (441).

  • Liu's two readings of Riggs (he picks neither): (a) both sides argued about law, the majority's including common-law principle, so Dworkin overstates; (b) the dispute was whether law is "always subject to universal fundamental principles of morality" (W1b slide 2†), as Earl's "universal law" (511) suggests. Neither kept to the statute's four corners (W1).
  • McLoughlin below: trial, unforeseeable; CA, foreseeable but confined to the scene by policy. Wilberforce's "three elements": class (close ties), proximity in time and space ("aftermath"), means: sight or hearing, not report (422–23).
Conclusion [The statement] is [wrong / partly right]. LP rightly ties law to sources, and Dworkin is unfair to paint it as blind to theoretical disagreement. But naming law is an evaluation, and rival theories split Riggs and the Lords' reasons in McLoughlin: theory is not optional. A weak NLT earns its keep only at extreme injustice (8); Riggs needed no such extreme, only a choice of theory about law's grounds.

1Start here: archetype 2 in plain English

Archetype 2 is about one question: what makes something count as "law"? The statements in this family usually claim one of two things. Either working out what the law is is easy and neutral ("just look it up"), or legal theory is a pointless extra. Your answer, every time, is the same at heart: choosing a test for what counts as law is already a judgement, so theory is doing real work, especially in hard cases.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Legal positivism (LP)Law is whatever the proper sources say: statutes, cases, what officials recognise. Whether it is good or bad is a separate question.
Natural law theory (NLT)Law answers to a higher moral standard that reason can work out, so a truly monstrous rule fails as law.
Strong v weak NLTStrong: every rule must be moral to be law. Weak: a rule stops being law only when it is extremely unjust. You only ever defend weak.
Separation thesisLP's claim that law and morality are not necessarily linked. They often overlap; they don't have to.
Internal point of viewTreating a rule as a standard you ought to follow, not just as a habit or a threat (Hart).
Plain-fact viewDworkin's name for "law is simply what was enacted; look it up".
Empirical v theoretical disagreementEmpirical: we agree what counts as law but dispute whether it was met. Theoretical: we dispute what counts as law in the first place.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says naming law "is an evaluation". Put simply: deciding what counts as law means deciding what matters, so the fight between positivism and natural law is a real one, and in a hard case like Riggs the result depends on which view the judge takes.

The Intro says: the statement thinks spotting law is neutral and theory is optional. Positivism makes sense, but it still has to choose whose recognition counts, and in Riggs every judge accepted the law bound them yet they split over what it said. The Conclusion says: positivism is right that law comes from sources, but picking those sources is a choice, and that choice split the judges. Natural law only bites at extreme injustice; Riggs didn't need that, only a theory of what law is.

The eight blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
2.1"Positivism just describes; natural law preaches."Both answer the same question, what law is. Picking "what officials recognise" as the test is already a choice.
2.2"Hart's 'ought' admits law needs morality."Hart's "ought" means treating a rule as a standard, which you can do for selfish reasons. It isn't a moral ought.
2.3"Natural law is for believers and lets any judge strike down laws."Natural law is worked out by reason, not faith, and only extreme injustice is in question.
2.4"Fuller and Dworkin are secret natural lawyers."They are allies, but neither says an unjust law stops being law.
2.5"Judges only ever disagree about whether to obey."In Riggs and McLoughlin they all wanted to follow the law; they disagreed about what it was.
2.6"Theory is a luxury; a dictionary will do."Even the Jaffa Cakes tribunal needed a theory of what a cake is. You use theory even when you don't name it.
2.7"Singapore is pragmatic, so it needs no theory."Pragmatism is itself a theory.
2.8(Case cards)Riggs and McLoughlin are your proof for every block above.
ℹ NOTE
How to use this table

Come back to it after each block. If you can say the right-hand column in your own words for every row, you understand the archetype.

2The big picture: what is law?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two referees argue about a football match. One says, "A goal is whatever the rulebook says is a goal." The other says, "A goal is what the rulebook says, but the rulebook exists to make a fair game, so if a rule would reward cheating, it isn't really doing its job." Both care about rules. They disagree about what makes something count. Legal positivism is the first referee; natural law theory is the second.

Archetype 2 is the foundation of the course. Its statements ask: what is law, and does it matter which answer we give? Two families of theory compete.

Legal positivism (LP)

Liu's slides give LP two theses (W1b slides 5–6†):

  1. Social fact (sources) thesis. Whether something is law depends on social facts: what was enacted, by whom, and whether officials recognise it.
  2. Separation thesis. There is no necessary connection between law and morality. A law can be valid and wicked.

The word "necessary" is the key. Positivists accept that law and morality are often connected (most laws ban murder; many statutes use moral words like "reasonable"). They deny only that a rule must be moral to be law.

Two positivists matter here:

  • Austin: law is the command of a sovereign, habitually obeyed, backed by a sanction. Candid ("the existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another") but crude.
  • Hart: law is a union of primary rules (duties: don't steal) and secondary rules (rules about rules: recognition, change, adjudication). Officials accept the rules from an internal point of view: they treat them as standards they ought to follow, not merely as habits or threats.

Natural law theory (NLT)

NLT says law is answerable to a higher standard knowable by reason. Aquinas called an unjust law "a corruption of law". Liu distinguishes:

  • Strong NLT: every rule must embody morality to be law. That would have judges second-guessing tax law.
  • Weak NLT: a rule loses legal status only at extreme divergence from morality, such as a law to execute all redheads (Liu, W1).

Most modern NLT, and every version you should defend, is weak. Finnis, for instance, says an unjust law is not a nullity to disregard; it merely lacks its usual moral power to bind (Harris 18).

Dworkin: law as interpretation

Dworkin attacks the positivists' plain-fact view: the idea that law is just a matter of looking up what was enacted. He notes two kinds of disagreement:

KindWhat is disputedExample
EmpiricalWhether agreed grounds of law are met (was the statute passed?)Did Parliament enact s 5?
TheoreticalWhat the grounds of law areDoes a statute carry unstated moral exceptions? (Riggs)

If judges disagree theoretically, then the plain-fact view cannot be the whole truth: judges are arguing about what law is, not just looking it up.

The cast for archetype 2
▤ Theorist bank 14.1–14.5; Liu W1
  1. 1Austin (14.3): law = sovereign's command, backed by sanction.
  2. 2Hart (14.4): rules accepted from the internal point of view; rule of recognition.
  3. 3Aquinas and NLT (14.2): unjust law is a corruption of law.
  4. 4Dworkin (14.5): law is interpretive; theoretical disagreement.
  5. 5Fish (14.1): practice happens inside a purposive enterprise; theory is not a luxury.
  6. 6TSH (CJ): pragmatism is itself a theory; LP and NLT both ask what law is.
