32.1 Descriptive?

▤ On your sheet: 2.1 Descriptive? (word for word)
2.1 Descriptive? neutral, objective, merely describes, cross-purposes
  1. LP and NLT are not at [cross-purposes]: both ask what law is (TSH CJ 84 n 28).
  2. Treating [official recognition] as conclusive is a choice: once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, its injustice is "treated as irrelevant" (TSH CJ 106).
  3. So LP is not simply [neutral and objective], and preferring it for a pluralist state is a value choice.
  • STEELMAN Lawyers "look up the books", and must know the law before reforming it (Harris 16); LP arose in states without a shared moral base (Liu, W1).
  • FOR Liu's slides†: LP finds law in what courts uphold, so its premise becomes its conclusion; equating what people regard as law with law "involves an evaluation, and is not merely descriptive" (W1b slide 15).
  • TRAP "No necessary connection" allows contingent ones, incorporation and critique (W1b slide 7†): Riggs' maxim, a legal rule with moral content, troubles no positivist (Liu, W1).
  • AGAINST Finnis doubts law is describable from a "rubbish heap" of facts without evaluative criteria (TSH CJ 106 n 124).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A positivist says, "I'm just describing law, like a map-maker describes a coastline." But a map-maker has to decide where the coast is at high tide or low tide. Deciding whose recognition makes something "law" is that kind of choice. So the "neutral description" already contains a judgement.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Positivists are neutral scientists who just describe law. Natural lawyers are preachers telling us what law should be. They're talking past each other."

  1. They're not talking past each other. Both are answering the same question, what is law? They just give different answers.
  2. Positivism's test is a choice. It says law is what officials recognise. That means if the top court upholds a horribly unjust rule, positivism treats the injustice as irrelevant to whether it is law. Deciding that injustice doesn't count is a decision about what matters.
  3. So positivism isn't purely neutral. You can still prefer it, for example in a society where people disagree about morals, but that preference is itself a value judgement.

The extras: the STEELMAN gives positivism its due (lawyers really do look things up). The TRAP reminds you positivists never say law has nothing to do with morality, only that the two don't have to be linked.

Remember: choosing a test for law is already a judgement.

The statement this answers. "Positivism simply describes law neutrally and objectively; natural law preaches. The two are at cross-purposes." (Practice Q4 has this shape.)

The move in three steps.

  1. They are not at cross-purposes. TSH: LP and NLT both ask the same question, what law is (CJ 84 n 28). NLT is not a theory of what law ought to be; it is a rival theory of what law is.
  2. Choosing official recognition as the test is a choice. Once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, LP treats its injustice as "irrelevant" to its legal status (TSH CJ 106). That is a decision about what matters.
  3. So LP is not simply neutral and objective, and preferring it for a pluralist state is a value choice.

The supporting material.

  • STEELMAN. Lawyers really do "look up the books", and you must know what the law is before you can reform it (Harris 16). LP grew up in states without a shared moral base (Liu, W1). That is a good reason to prefer it, but it is a value reason.
  • FOR. Liu's slide: equating what people regard as law with law "involves an evaluation, and is not merely descriptive" (W1b slide 15†).
  • AGAINST. Finnis doubts law can be described from a "rubbish heap" of facts without evaluative criteria for what is important.
⚠ TRAP
"No necessary connection" is not "no connection"

LP allows contingent links between law and morality. A legal rule with moral content (like Riggs's maxim that no one may profit from his own wrong) troubles no positivist: it is law because it was posited in the common law, not because it is moral (Liu, W1). Never write "positivists say law has nothing to do with morality".

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready sentences

LP and NLT are not at cross-purposes: both ask what law is (TSH CJ 84 n 28). Treating official recognition as conclusive is itself a choice, since once the highest court upholds a manifestly unjust rule, its injustice is "treated as irrelevant" (TSH CJ 106). So positivism is not simply neutral, and preferring it for a pluralist state is a value choice, not a fact.

42.2 Internal "ought"

▤ On your sheet: 2.2 Internal "ought" (word for word)
2.2 Internal "ought" mere commands, habit, Hart concedes moral evaluation
  1. Law is more than [commands obeyed from habit]: Hart's rules carry an internal "ought", a critical reflective attitude.
  2. But that "ought" need not be moral: Hart allows acceptance out of fear, self-interest or habit (Harris 119).
  3. So Hart escapes [mere habit] without conceding moral evaluation.
  • Dworkin: if officials obeying Hitler "only out of fear" accepted the rule, Hart's difference from Austin "becomes elusive"; else, it seems, there was "no law in Nazi Germany" (LE ch 1).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two drivers stop at a red light at 3 a.m. with no one around. One stops only because a camera might fine her. The other stops because "that's the rule and I should follow it". Hart says law only makes sense if some people (especially officials) take the second attitude. But that "should" need not be a moral should: you can accept a rule because it's convenient or habitual.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Hart says people follow law because they think they ought to. 'Ought' is a moral word, so Hart has secretly admitted law needs morality."

  1. Hart does say law is more than habit. People (especially officials) treat legal rules as standards: "you should stop at the red light, and I can criticise you if you don't."
  2. But that "should" isn't necessarily moral. You can accept a rule as a standard out of fear, self-interest or plain habit.
  3. So Hart gets past Austin's "law is just habit and threats" without bringing morality in.

The extra: Dworkin pushes back. If obeying out of fear counts as accepting a rule, Hart looks no different from Austin; if it doesn't count, Nazi Germany seems to have had no law. Your reply: even someone who obeys from fear treats the rules as standards, which a habit does not.

Remember: "ought" here means "this is the standard", not "this is morally right".

The statement. "In explaining law through the internal point of view and the language of 'ought', Hart concedes that law cannot be understood without moral evaluation." (Practice Q6.)

The move.

  1. Law is more than commands obeyed from habit: Hart's rules carry an internal "ought", a "critical reflective attitude" (Harris 118).
  2. But that "ought" need not be moral: Hart allows acceptance out of fear, self-interest or habit (Harris 119).
  3. So Hart escapes "mere habit" (Austin's problem) without conceding moral evaluation.

Dworkin's pressure point. If Nazi officials obeyed Hitler "only out of fear" and that counts as acceptance, Hart's difference from Austin "becomes elusive"; if it does not count, then it seems there was "no law in Nazi Germany" (LE ch 1). Your reply (card 14.4): acceptance even from fear still treats the rules as standards, which a mere habit does not.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Spot the difference
  • Habit (Austin): "People usually stop at red lights."
  • Internal point of view (Hart): "Drivers ought to stop at red lights, and a driver who doesn't is open to criticism."
  • Moral evaluation (what the statement wrongly attributes to Hart): "Stopping at red lights is morally right."

Hart needs the second, not the third.

52.3 Elitist?

▤ On your sheet: 2.3 Elitist? (word for word)
2.3 Elitist? only the devout, religious faith, any judge strikes down
  1. NLT does not rest on [moral truths only the devout can see]: natural law, unlike divine law, can be apprehended by reason (TSH CJ 87).
  2. So NLT does not [license any judge to strike down]: the RF voids only intolerably unjust statutes (8.2–8.3); for Finnis unjust law is no nullity to disregard (Harris 18).
  • QUALIFY Strong NLT (every rule must embody morality) would have judges second-guess tax law; weak NLT strips legal status only at extreme divergence, a law to execute all redheads (Liu, W1). Grotius made natural law secular (Harris 11); Aquinas's four kinds: eternal, divine, natural, human (W1b slide 13†).
  • CONCEDE TSH admits "no easy answer" on who pronounces natural law (CJ 99): concede judges' doubtful authority below the threshold (12.1).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Some people think natural law means "the priests decide what's right and judges must obey them". But natural law, as the course teaches it, is about what reason can work out, which anyone can do. And modern natural lawyers don't let any judge tear up any law they dislike; only truly monstrous laws are in question.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Natural law only works if you share a religious faith, and it lets any judge throw out a law he dislikes."

  1. Not faith, reason. Natural law is something anyone can work out by thinking. It is different from divine law, which is revealed in scripture.
  2. Not any law, only the extreme. The Radbruch formula (Lesson 8) voids only intolerably unjust laws, and Finnis says even an unjust law isn't something you can just ignore.

The extras: QUALIFY with strong v weak natural law. Strong would let judges second-guess tax law; weak strips legal status only from something like a law to execute all redheads. CONCEDE that nobody has an easy answer to who gets to say what natural law requires.

Remember: reasoned, not revealed; extreme, not merely unfair.

The statement. "Natural law theory rests on moral truths only the devout can see, and licenses any judge to strike down whatever offends his faith."

The move.

  1. NLT does not rest on truths only the devout can see: natural law, unlike divine law, can be apprehended by reason (TSH CJ 87). Grotius even made natural law secular (Harris 11).
  2. NLT does not license any judge to strike down laws: the Radbruch formula voids only intolerably unjust statutes (8.2–8.3), and for Finnis unjust law is no nullity to disregard (Harris 18).

Qualify with strong v weak. Strong NLT would have judges second-guess tax law; weak NLT strips legal status only at extreme divergence (the redheads law). Aquinas's four kinds of law help here: eternal, divine, natural, human (W1b slide 13†). Divine law is revealed; natural law is reasoned.

Concede. TSH admits there is "no easy answer" on who pronounces natural law (CJ 99). Concede that judges' authority below the threshold is doubtful (archetype 12).

62.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers?

▤ On your sheet: 2.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers? (word for word)
2.4 Fuller, Dworkin natural lawyers? all but name
  1. Fuller and Dworkin are NLT's allies, not [natural lawyers in all but name]: neither lets injustice as such defeat validity.
  2. Fuller's is a thin "procedural natural law"†: legality demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be" (MOL 47).
  3. So [all but name] overstates: Dworkin's judge must "interpret the legal history he finds" (AMP), leaving intolerable injustice open.
  • CONCEDE Dworkin finds even weak NLT "unpersuasive" as an account of usage (LE ch 1): concede it; defend NLT as a theory of grounds.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Fuller and Dworkin both say law isn't just "whatever's written down". That makes them sound like natural lawyers. But neither says "a very unjust law stops being law". They are cousins of natural law, not members of the family.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Fuller and Dworkin both say law isn't just what's written down, so they're really natural lawyers."

  1. They're on natural law's side, but not in its family. The test for a natural lawyer is: can injustice, on its own, stop a rule being law? Neither Fuller nor Dworkin says yes.
  2. Fuller cares about the form of law: rules must be clear, public, not retroactive and so on. A rule can pass all his tests and still be wicked.
  3. Dworkin's judge has to work with the legal history he is given. If that history is wicked, Dworkin offers no escape route, so extreme injustice is left unanswered.

The extra: CONCEDE that Dworkin thinks even weak natural law is a poor account of how people use the word "law". Agree, and say natural law is a theory of what grounds law, not of word usage.

Remember: allies, not members.

The statement. "Fuller and Dworkin are natural lawyers in all but name." (Practice Q7.)

The move.

  1. They are NLT's allies, not natural lawyers: neither lets injustice as such defeat validity.
  2. Fuller offers a thin "procedural natural law"†: his eight requirements of legality (generality, promulgation, prospectivity and so on) demand rules "however fair or unfair they may be" (MOL 47). A clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked (Lesson 3).
  3. Dworkin makes law interpretive, but his judge must "interpret the legal history he finds" (AMP), so integrity offers no exit from a wicked legal history. Intolerable injustice is left open.

Concede. Dworkin finds even weak NLT "unpersuasive" as an account of how we use the word "law" (LE ch 1). Concede that; defend NLT as a theory of grounds, not of word usage.

72.5 Judges disagree?

▤ On your sheet: 2.5 Judges disagree? (word for word)
2.5 Judges disagree? only about obeying, plain words, no law to apply
  1. [Judges only disagree about obeying] mistakes theoretical disagreement for defiance: in Riggs all accepted the law's authority but split over what it required.
  2. In McLoughlin, too, the Lords agreed on the result but split over whether courts may let policy limit liability (2.8; 9.2).
  3. So [no law to apply] assumes the plain-fact view; which arguments count as law is the point in dispute.
  • Dworkin: LP's pretence defence shows judges as "well-meaning liars", its borderline defence as "simpletons"; these were "pivotal" cases (LE ch 1).
  • QUALIFY Liu thinks Dworkin unfair to LP: it need not turn every disagreement into an empirical one, and soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests (Harris 121) (Liu, W1).
  • Terms (LE ch 1): empirical disagreement disputes whether agreed grounds of law are met, theoretical the grounds themselves; the plain-fact view and semantic theories hide the latter.
  • LAWYER Run both policy arguments (9.2).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two judges disagree about a will. A cynic says, "They both know what the law says; one just doesn't want to obey it." Dworkin says no: they both want to obey the law, but they disagree about what the law is, because they disagree about what makes something law in the first place.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "When judges disagree, they all know what the law says; some just won't obey it. And when the old cases run out, there's no law left, so the judge should just weigh social goals."

  1. That mistakes one kind of disagreement for another. In Riggs, every judge accepted that the law bound them. They split over what the law required: does the wills statute have an unwritten "no murderers" exception?
  2. Same in McLoughlin. All five Lords agreed the mother won, but disagreed about why, and about whether courts may use policy to limit liability.
  3. So "no law left" only follows if law is just the written rules (the plain-fact view), and that is exactly what the judges were arguing about.

The extra: Dworkin says positivism's two escape routes make judges look like "well-meaning liars" or "simpletons". QUALIFY with Liu: that's unfair, because soft positivism can let moral tests into law.

Remember: judges argue about what the law is, not just whether to obey it.

The statement. "When judges divide, they are never disagreeing about what the law is, only about whether to obey it … once the precedents run out, the judge has no law to apply." (Practice Q2.)

The move.

  1. "Judges only disagree about obeying" mistakes theoretical disagreement for defiance. In Riggs, all the judges accepted the law's authority but split over what it required.
  2. In McLoughlin, too, the Lords agreed on the result but split over whether courts may let policy limit liability (2.8; 9.2).
  3. So "no law to apply" assumes the plain-fact view; which arguments count as law is the very point in dispute.

Dworkin's jibe. LP has two defences against theoretical disagreement, and both make judges look bad: the pretence defence (judges pretend to find law they are really making) shows them as "well-meaning liars"; the borderline defence (they are just arguing about the edge of a word) shows them as "simpletons". These were "pivotal" cases (LE ch 1).

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Liu thinks Dworkin is unfair to LP. LP need not turn every disagreement into an empirical one; soft positivism lets the rule of recognition adopt moral tests (Harris 121) (Liu, W1). Use this as your QUALIFY: Dworkin is right that theory is in play, but wrong that positivism is blind to it.

⚠ TRAP
Know the two Dworkin terms cold

Empirical: disputes whether agreed grounds of law are met. Theoretical: disputes the grounds themselves. The plain-fact view and "semantic theories" hide the second kind (LE ch 1).

82.6 Theory useless?

▤ On your sheet: 2.6 Theory useless? (word for word)
2.6 Theory useless? luxury, optional, irrelevant, no client needed, good dictionary, Jaffa Cakes
  1. Fish grants [the statement] a kernel: Rawls cited in court is likely to be regarded "at best as window dressing and at worst as showing off".
  2. Yet marshalling rules "takes place within an enterprise that is purposive"; without "some strong intuition of the general project", rehearsing them is "an empty gesture" (Fish).
  3. So [theory is a luxury] confuses citing theory with using it: easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9); hard cases, on rival ones.
  • Jaffa Cakes† (United Biscuits (UK) Ltd (No 2), LON/91/160): the VAT tribunal used core attributes, class commonalities, thought experiments and social context: indirectly, a "philosophy of cakeness and biscuitness". Held cake (stale cakes harden, biscuits soften): both sides agreed the factors but weighed them differently, the shape of most jurisprudential disputes (Liu, W1). TSH: purpose may settle "vehicles"; contested words like "law" engage LP v NLT (CJ 90).
  • Leff†: "[Y]ou can't know that a thing is not being done well until you know what it is that is being done"; excellence presupposes theory.
  • AGAINST [Theory cannot help anyone decide] fails: disagreement is not absence of fact (4.7). Constitution: 11.7.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Someone says, "You don't need to know what a cake is to decide if a Jaffa Cake is a cake; just look it up." But the tribunal that actually decided it had to work out what makes something a cake: what it's made of, how it goes stale, how people eat it. That is theory, done quietly.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Legal theory is a luxury for academics. A practical lawyer only needs the statute, the cases and a dictionary."

  1. Grant the kernel. Fish agrees that quoting philosophers in court would look like showing off. Practitioners rarely cite theory.
  2. But they use it all the time. Applying rules only makes sense if you have some sense of what the whole enterprise is for. Without that, reciting rules is "an empty gesture".
  3. So "theory is a luxury" confuses naming theory with using it. Easy cases rest on a theory everyone shares; hard cases on rival theories.

The example: in the Jaffa Cakes case the tribunal didn't open a dictionary. It asked what makes a cake a cake (stale cakes go hard, biscuits go soft) and weighed the factors. Both sides agreed on the factors but weighed them differently, which is what most theory disputes look like.

Remember: you can use theory without ever saying its name.

The statement. "Jurisprudence is an academic luxury … To decide whether Jaffa Cakes were cakes or biscuits for VAT purposes, the tribunal needed only the legislation, the case law and a good dictionary." (Practice Q1.)

The move (Fish on both sides).

  1. Fish grants a kernel: Rawls cited in court is likely to be regarded "at best as window dressing and at worst as showing off". Explicit theory rarely appears in practice.
  2. Yet marshalling rules "takes place within an enterprise that is purposive"; without "some strong intuition of the general project", rehearsing rules is "an empty gesture" (Fish).
  3. So "theory is a luxury" confuses citing theory with using it: easy cases rest on a shared theory (9.9); hard cases, on rival ones.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The Jaffa Cakes case (United Biscuits (UK) Ltd (No 2))†

The VAT tribunal did not reach for a dictionary. It used core attributes, commonalities with the class, thought experiments and social context: indirectly, a "philosophy of cakeness and biscuitness". It held the Jaffa Cake a cake, partly because stale cakes harden while biscuits soften. Both sides agreed on the relevant factors but weighed them differently: the shape, Liu says, of most jurisprudential disputes (W1).

TSH adds: purpose may settle easy words like "vehicles"; contested words like "law" engage LP v NLT (CJ 90).

Also usable.

  • Leff†: "you can't know that a thing is not being done well until you know what it is that is being done"; excellence presupposes theory.
  • AGAINST "theory cannot help anyone decide": disagreement is not the absence of a fact (4.7).

92.7 Singapore pragmatism

▤ On your sheet: 2.7 Singapore pragmatism (word for word)
2.7 Singapore pragmatism prevailing philosophy, pragmatic, no blank slate
  1. [Singapore's prevailing philosophy] is often called pragmatism: keeping s 377A in 2007, the Government called its approach "a pragmatic one that maintains Singapore's social cohesion" (Pragmatism 302).
  2. Yet pragmatism is a theory: in any "postmodern pragmatic" society, the view that law is whatever a court says "glosses over" guiding principles (TSH CJ 89).
  3. So [philosophy is unnecessary here] fails: "The purpose of theory is to guide practice" (TSH CJ 89).
  • AGAINST "[I]n law, as in life, we simply cannot shun the question" of right and wrong (Pragmatism 304).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Calling yourself "practical, not philosophical" is like saying "I don't have an accent". Everyone speaks with some accent; you just don't notice your own. Pragmatism is a philosophy too.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Singapore is a practical country. We do what works, so legal philosophy is unnecessary here."

  1. Admit the label fits. When the Government kept s 377A in 2007, it called its approach "a pragmatic one".
  2. But pragmatism is a philosophy too. Saying "law is whatever the court decides" hides the principles that guide the decision; it doesn't remove them.
  3. So "philosophy is unnecessary" fails. As TSH puts it, theory's job is to guide practice.

Remember: "we're just practical" is itself a position, like having an accent you can't hear.

The statement. "Singapore's prevailing philosophy is pragmatism: we have no use for legal theory here."

The move.

  1. Singapore's approach is often called pragmatism: keeping s 377A in 2007, the Government called its approach "a pragmatic one that maintains Singapore's social cohesion" (Pragmatism 302).
  2. Yet pragmatism is a theory: in any "postmodern pragmatic" society, the view that law is whatever a court says "glosses over" guiding principles (TSH CJ 89).
  3. So "philosophy is unnecessary here" fails: "The purpose of theory is to guide practice" (TSH CJ 89).

AGAINST. "In law, as in life, we simply cannot shun the question" of right and wrong (Pragmatism 304).

102.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin

▤ On your sheet: 2.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin (word for word)
2.8 Case cards: Riggs and McLoughlin
  1. Riggs turned on whether a clear statute has unstated exceptions; McLoughlin, on whether policy may distinguish precedent.
  2. Each answer presupposes a theory of [law].

Neither kept to the statute's four corners (W1).

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Riggs: a teenager poisons his grandfather to get the inheritance sooner. The law about wills, read literally, says he inherits. Should a court read in an unwritten exception? McLoughlin: a mother rushes to hospital and sees her family horribly injured. Earlier cases only covered people at the scene of the accident. Can she sue for the shock? Both cases ask: what counts as the law when the written rules don't clearly answer?

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

What these cards are for: they are your evidence. Almost every block in archetype 2 points back to them.

  1. Riggs asks: does a clear statute have exceptions it doesn't spell out? (Can a murderer inherit under a will law that says nothing about murderers?) The majority said no inheritance; the dissent said stick to the words.
  2. McLoughlin asks: when earlier cases only covered people at the scene, can policy reasons stop the court going further? All five Lords let the mother recover, but gave different reasons.
  3. The point of both: whichever answer a judge gives depends on a theory of what law is. That is why theory isn't optional.

How to read the table: the LP, Dworkin and ALR rows show how each theory would explain the same case. You don't need all of them; pick the row that answers the statement in front of you.

Remember: Riggs = unwritten exceptions; McLoughlin = same result, different reasons.

These two cases are your evidence for the whole archetype. Learn the table well.

Riggs v Palmer

  • Facts. Elmer, 16, poisoned his grandfather lest he revoke the will. Read literally, the statute of wills let him inherit.
  • Held. 5–2: Elmer took nothing.
  • Majority (Earl). Statutes are read by their makers' intention and by maxims with "their foundation in universal law" (511); denying the inheritance "takes from him no property" (514).
  • Dissent (Gray). The question "does not lie within the domain of conscience" (515); courts cannot "add to the respondent's penalties" (519).

Three readings. LP: Gray's posited text; or Earl's maxim is itself posited common law with moral content, which LP accepts (Liu, W1); else a gap for discretion. Dworkin: two morally grounded theories: Gray's guards "an important principle of justice" (fixed penalties); Earl's, coherence. ALR: rules "picked from the mass available" fit results reached on other grounds (Harris 100).

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Liu gives two readings of Riggs and picks neither: (a) both sides argued about law, the majority's including common-law principle, so Dworkin overstates; (b) the dispute was whether law is "always subject to universal fundamental principles of morality" (W1b slide 2†), as Earl's "universal law" suggests. Either way, neither side kept to the statute's four corners (W1).

McLoughlin v O'Brian

  • Facts. Not at the scene, the mother saw her injured family, begrimed, in hospital hours later; a daughter died.
  • Held. 5–0, reversing the Court of Appeal: her shock was recoverable.
  • Reasons split. Wilberforce, Edmund-Davies and Russell: policy may limit liability, but not here. Scarman: line-drawing policy is "not justiciable" (431). Bridge: stopping at decided cases would be "an unwarranted abdication" (441).
  • Below. Trial judge: unforeseeable. Court of Appeal: foreseeable but confined to the scene by policy.
  • Wilberforce's three elements (422–23): class of claimant (close ties), proximity in time and space (the "aftermath"), and means (sight or hearing, not report).

11Putting it together: Practice Q2

"When judges divide, they are never disagreeing about what the law is, only about whether to obey it. In Riggs v Palmer, the majority simply ignored the plain words of the statute of wills to deny a murderer his inheritance, and in doing so usurped the legislature. Novel cases such as McLoughlin v O'Brien are different: once the precedents run out, the judge has no law to apply and should openly weigh the community's social and economic goals, including the risk of opening the floodgates."
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "never disagreeing about what the law is" → 2.5 (theoretical disagreement).
  • "simply ignored the plain words" → the word "simply" (Hook: word); 2.8 Riggs.
  • "usurped" → usurpation (12.2) for one sentence.
  • "precedents run out", "floodgates" → 9.2 (principle v policy).
  • Lead: archetype 2. Distinction: 1.3(8) principle v policy, or theoretical v empirical disagreement.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

Everything turns on "simply". The statement assumes that the plain words of a statute simply are the law, so that a court reading in an exception defies it. That is the plain-fact view, and it is the very point the judges in Riggs disputed. I make three claims: (1) judicial splits are often theoretical disagreements about law's grounds, not quarrels about obedience; (2) the Riggs majority did not usurp the legislature but read the statute by its makers' intention and the common law's maxims; and (3) when precedent runs out, the judge still has law to apply: principle, not open policy-weighing.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Dworkin's theoretical disagreement (2.5): Riggs judges all accepted the law's authority; they split on what it required. Steelman with Liu: soft positivism can absorb moral tests, so Dworkin is unfair to LP.
  2. Riggs (2.8): Earl's intention and maxims v Gray's fixed penalties; both morally grounded (Dworkin). The majority's maxim is itself posited common law (Liu), so "ignored" overstates.
  3. McLoughlin and floodgates (9.2): all five allowed recovery, but Scarman held line-drawing policy not justiciable while Bridge called stopping "an unwarranted abdication". The statement's own advice (weigh social goals openly) is Scarman's target, so it usurps more than the Riggs majority did. Self-critique: fit is often not unique (1.4).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore wrong in its premise and its advice. Judges divide over what law is, not only whether to obey it, and the Riggs majority read the law rather than defied it. When precedent runs out, a court still argues from principle; it is weighing social goals openly, not reading in a maxim, that hands the legislature's work to judges.

LESSON 3 · ARCHETYPE 3 · ABOUT 41 MIN · 37 QUESTIONS

Rule of law and Fuller

⚡ BIG IDEA

The rule of law is a real but thin morality. It binds rulers and comes in degrees, but it cannot guarantee that the laws it governs are just.

ARCHETYPE 3 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
3 Rule of law and Fuller
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The rule of law] is a real but thin morality: it binds rulers and comes in degrees, but cannot guarantee [just laws].
Intro [The statement] treats legality as [mere efficiency / a guarantee of justice]. For Fuller, total failure of one requirement leaves something "not properly called a legal system at all" (MOL 39); otherwise legality is "always a matter of degree" (PFL 646). I [agree only in part]: legality restrains rulers and exposes their aims to criticism, but cannot make bad laws just.
3.1 Ranking rank them; not all equally important
  1. Fuller lets priority vary by branch of law and kind of rule (MOL 93), so I rank [prospectivity in crime] first.
  2. Fuller finds the retrospective criminal statute "universally condemned" (MOL 59); non-enforcement of [s 377A] strained congruence but left the system standing, so congruence for one rule ranks last.
  3. Yet breaches "tend to become cumulative": unclarity "may beget the necessity for retroactive laws" (MOL 92), so low rank never licenses neglect.
  • Requirements "may be in opposition" (Liu's slide†): curative retroactivity (MOL 93).
3.2 Unenforced law sham; mockery; enforce fully or repeal; moral signpost
  1. ["A sham"] overstates: open non-enforcement strains congruence, yet one rule, unlike a system, survives rare enforcement.
  2. TSH: the 2007 "overt announcement" "violated Fuller's requirement", but "showcased the competing value" of a symbolic message (Pragmatism 299).
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: law can exempt the trivial openly, as s 95† does for slight harm.
  • STEELMAN Perera: non-enforcement "places too much power in the hands of the Government and the AGC" (Hansard, 28 Nov 2022).
  • Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022)†: the AG's 2018 assurance bound him until clear notice (7.7). Liu: before it, non-enforcement was official action, not a rule (pure divergence), and as discretion it hit generality; after it, officials' statements can silently change the law (W2).
  • CONCEDE TSH is harsher (breach, not strain): concede the breach, defending only the trade-off.
3.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral) neither inner nor moral; a tyrant could follow it; guarantees justice; one rule fails
  1. [A tyrant could follow it] is half right: legality is moral but thin; at minimum it demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be" (MOL 47).
  2. It is moral because reciprocity grounds the duty (MOL 39–40), it treats people as responsible agents†, and it binds even a self-seeking monarch (PFL 644–45).
  3. So [legality guarantees justice] fails: wicked aims can run through clear, public rules; intolerable injustice needs the RF (8.3).
  • STEELMAN Liu's slide†: "The label seems misapplied"; the concern "is really with efficacy".
  • AGAINST Inner and outer morality decay together "almost inevitably" (PFL 645).
  • Single rule: secret or retroactive, it grounds no moral duty (MOL 39); unclear, it is "less a law" (MOL 63 n 21); validity is for the RF (8).
  • CONCEDE A regime can meet all eight and still be wicked (Liu's slide†): concede that, not that legality is morally empty.
3.4 Discretion rule of men; unfettered discretion; enforced only against critics
  1. ["Every grant of discretion is a small surrender"] overstates: only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men.
  2. Fuller condemns a 1934 Nazi statute "undermined as it is by uncontrolled administrative discretion" (PFL 654); [enforcement only against critics] approaches it.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits legality if bounded by law and reviewable.
  • JUDGE Review legality, not merits: Art 35(8)† discretion is subject to Art 12 (Ramalingam†). Liu: discretion erodes generality by degree: principled restraint is fine; protecting allies and punishing foes is not (W2).
3.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions purest expression of the rule of law; like cases alike
  1. Mandatory sentences look like ["the purest expression of the rule of law"], but they buy certainty, not justice.
  2. Fuller: Hart's "justice in the administration of the law" treats like cases alike "by whatever elevated or perverted standards the word 'like' may be defined" (PFL 646).
  3. So [leaving nothing to judges] is just only if the line tracks real differences in harm or fault.
3.6 Rules v standards same standard for those who cannot meet it; learner driver; clear rules
  1. Holding [a learner driver] to the ordinary standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma (MOL 72); by analogy with strict civil liability, a "surcharge" on risky activity (MOL 75) can justify it, never in crime (MOL 77).
  2. Fuller's antinomy: aloof justice is "bound at times to be harsh", intimate justice cannot be "evenhanded", so law tempers the reasonable man (MOL 72).
  3. So [clear rules are always better] overstates: "good faith" standards can clarify; specious clarity can harm more than honest vagueness (MOL 64).
  • Nettleship v Weston†: a learner owes the ordinary driver's standard; Cook v Cook† lowered it where the passenger knew (later overruled: Imbree v McNeilly, 2008†).
3.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis duty springs from authority; goodwill; crisis; simply majority will
  1. [The duty springs from authority] is the command view, which "confuses fidelity to law with deference for established authority" (MOL 63).
  2. Reciprocity grounds the duty: once government finally and completely ruptures it, "nothing is left on which to ground the citizen's duty" (MOL 40).
  3. So [goodwill] cannot suffice: "No single concentration of intelligence, insight, and good will" can secure law's enterprise (MOL 91).
  • Voter: where officials disregard rules, "at some point obedience becomes futile", like "casting a vote that will never be counted" (MOL 39).
  • AGAINST [Majority will, accurately expressed]: tracking a shifting majority breaks constancy, like Rex's daily amendments (MOL 37).
  • QUALIFY Crisis: "grim necessity" may hide a weapons appropriation; Fuller sees "no emergency" justifying a secret law "creating a new crime" (MOL 92).
3.8 Judge-made law never fully prospective; announced after the dispute; retrospective overruling
  1. Adjudication is partly retrospective, so ["can never fully satisfy"] holds in form, though a new rule may only confirm "views already widely held" (MOL 92).
  2. In civil cases retrospective overruling is [a price worth paying]: prospective rulings remove a private litigant's incentive to challenge bad precedent (MOL 56–57).
  3. Crime differs: a retrospective overruling would leave men "branded as criminals" for relying on a judicial interpretation (MOL 58).
  • Abdul Nasir† (CA 1997): life imprisonment means natural life, prospectively only (8.6); it engages constancy, not "branded as criminals".
3.9 Thin v thick; Marx ruling-class slogan; instrument of power; whims of officials
  1. ["A slogan" for class power] overstates: legal form binds rulers too, since "law cannot be built on law" (PFL 645).
  2. Liu's slide† answers the Marxist: law "has its own character", applying legal criteria "with reference to standards of universality and equity" (crits: 9.3).
  3. So thin legality beats ["the whims of its officials"]: published rules give notice and invite criticism (MOL 51).
  • STEELMAN Liu: law drags "the monster out into the light": a regime that nails its colours to the mast can be criticised, organised against and fled, while arbitrary power shows no pattern. Against: rules legitimise and spread evil ("it's the law") (W2).
Conclusion [The statement] is [right only in part]. Legality binds rulers, respects subjects as agents, exposes aims to criticism and comes in degrees, so ["not a legal system at all"] needs total failure. But it is thin and cannot guarantee just laws; intolerable injustice is the Radbruch formula's work.

1Start here: archetype 3 in plain English

Archetype 3 is about the rule of law: the idea that a country should be governed through proper rules rather than the whims of whoever is in charge. The course's guide is Lon Fuller, who lists eight things rules need to be (general, public, forward-looking, clear, consistent, possible to obey, stable, and actually applied). The statements in this family push one of two extremes: either "the rule of law is just efficient management that a tyrant could use", or "if you follow the rule of law, you get justice". Your answer sits in the middle: the rule of law is a real moral good, but a thin one. It ties the rulers' hands and treats people as adults, but it can't make a bad law good.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Legality / the rule of lawGoverning through rules that people can know and follow, and that officials actually stick to.
DesiderataFuller's word for his eight requirements. "Desideratum" just means "something wanted".
Inner morality of lawFuller's name for the eight requirements: the morality built into the form of law, whatever the law's content.
Thin v thickThin: the rule of law is about form (clear, public rules). Thick: it also demands just content. The sheet treats it as thin.
ReciprocityA two-way deal: government gives you knowable rules and judges you by them; you obey.
CongruenceOfficials do what the rules say. Non-enforcement of a rule is a congruence problem.
Prospective / retrospectiveProspective: applies to the future. Retrospective: punishes or changes the rules for acts already done.
Matter of degreeLegality isn't all-or-nothing. A system can be more or less legal; only total failure of a requirement means "no legal system at all".

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says the rule of law "is a real but thin morality". Put simply: following Fuller's eight requirements really is good (it restrains rulers and comes in degrees), but it can't guarantee that the laws themselves are fair.

The Intro says: the statement treats legality as either mere efficiency or a guarantee of justice. For Fuller, only total failure of a requirement destroys a legal system; anything less is a question of degree. You agree only in part: legality restrains rulers and exposes their aims, but cannot make bad laws just. The Conclusion repeats this and hands extreme injustice over to the Radbruch formula (Lesson 8).

The nine blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
3.1"Rank Fuller's eight requirements."It depends on the area of law. In crime, no retroactive punishment comes first; one unenforced rule comes last. But one failure tends to cause others.
3.2"An unenforced law is a sham: enforce it or repeal it."It's a real cost, but one rule can survive. Sometimes a law sends a symbolic message, and law can openly exempt trivial cases.
3.3"Fuller's morality isn't moral; a tyrant could follow it."Half right: legality is thin, so a tyrant could. But it is still moral: it binds rulers and treats people as responsible adults.
3.4"Every bit of discretion undermines the rule of law."Only uncontrolled discretion does. Discretion that is limited by law and reviewable by courts is fine.
3.5"Mandatory sentences are the purest rule of law."They give certainty, not justice. Treating cases "alike" is only fair if the line is drawn in the right place.
3.6"Hold everyone to the same standard; clear rules always win."Fuller says law balances evenness against fairness to individuals. Clear rules aren't always better.
3.7"We obey because the state has authority."No: we obey because of a two-way deal. If government breaks its side completely, the duty to obey goes.
3.8"Judge-made law is always retroactive."True in form, and usually acceptable in civil cases. In crime it would be unfair to punish people who relied on the courts.
3.9"The rule of law is a mask for the powerful."Once the powerful use law, it binds them too, and published rules let people see, criticise and resist.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Legality is good, comes in degrees, and binds rulers; it is not the same as justice.

2The big picture: Fuller's inner morality of law

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a king who wants to rule by law but gets everything wrong. He decides each case on a whim. He keeps his rulebook secret. He punishes people for things that were allowed yesterday. He writes rules nobody can understand, rules that contradict each other, rules nobody could obey, and changes them daily. And his officials ignore the rules anyway. His subjects can't follow anything. Fuller says that isn't a bad legal system; it isn't a legal system at all.

Lon Fuller's The Morality of Law (MOL) begins with the story of King Rex, who fails to make law in eight different ways. Each failure matches one of Fuller's eight requirements of legality (his "desiderata"), which together make up law's inner morality:

Fuller's eight desiderata
▤ MOL 39; framework 15.1
  1. 1General: there must be rules at all, not case-by-case rulings.
  2. 2Promulgated: the rules must be published (available, not necessarily known by all).
  3. 3Prospective: rules govern the future, not the past.
  4. 4Clear: people can understand them.
  5. 5Consistent: they don't contradict each other.
  6. 6Possible: they don't demand the impossible.
  7. 7Constant: they don't change too often.
  8. 8Congruent: officials actually act on the rules as announced.

Three ideas organise the archetype:

  1. Degree. Total failure of any one requirement yields something "not properly called a legal system at all" (MOL 39). Short of that, legality is "always a matter of degree" (PFL 646).
  2. Reciprocity. Government says, "Here are the rules; follow them, and we will judge you by them." Citizens' duty to obey rests on government keeping its side (MOL 39–40).
  3. Thinness. Legality is about form. A clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked. So the rule of law is moral, but thin: it does not guarantee just content.
⚠ TRAP
Liu's three clarifications (W2)

(1) Generality means having rules at all, not that rules must be broad: palm-tree justice, bills of attainder and unfettered discretion fail it. (2) Promulgation needs access, not universal knowledge. (3) Prospectivity bars only abuse: some retroactive laws are fine.

33.1 Ranking

▤ On your sheet: 3.1 Ranking (word for word)
3.1 Ranking rank them; not all equally important
  1. Fuller lets priority vary by branch of law and kind of rule (MOL 93), so I rank [prospectivity in crime] first.
  2. Fuller finds the retrospective criminal statute "universally condemned" (MOL 59); non-enforcement of [s 377A] strained congruence but left the system standing, so congruence for one rule ranks last.
  3. Yet breaches "tend to become cumulative": unclarity "may beget the necessity for retroactive laws" (MOL 92), so low rank never licenses neglect.
  • Requirements "may be in opposition" (Liu's slide†): curative retroactivity (MOL 93).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If you had to give up one of the eight, which would hurt least? Fuller says it depends on the area of law. Punishing people for yesterday's lawful act is the worst sin in criminal law. One rule that the police quietly don't enforce is bad but survivable. But beware: one failure tends to cause another.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The question, in everyday words: "Fuller says his eight requirements aren't equally important. Which matters most and which least? Use a Singapore example."

  1. Fuller says the ranking changes with the area of law. So pick an area. In criminal law, the top requirement is prospectivity: never punish people for something that was legal when they did it.
  2. Why that order. Fuller says retroactive criminal laws are "universally condemned". At the bottom: congruence for a single rule. Singapore not enforcing s 377A was a gap between rule and practice, but the legal system as a whole kept working.
  3. But a warning. Failures spread. An unclear law can later need a retroactive law to fix it. So "least important" never means "safe to ignore".

The extra: the requirements can pull against each other. A retroactive law can sometimes cure an earlier legality failure.

Remember: rank by area of law, then warn that breaches pile up.

The question. "Fuller says his eight requirements are not all equally important. Rank them and justify your ranking, using a Singapore illustration." (Practice Q27.)

The move.

  1. Fuller lets priority vary by branch of law and kind of rule (MOL 93), so rank prospectivity in criminal law first.
  2. Fuller finds the retrospective criminal statute "universally condemned" (MOL 59). Non-enforcement of s 377A strained congruence but left the system standing, so congruence for one rule ranks last.
  3. Yet breaches "tend to become cumulative": unclarity "may beget the necessity for retroactive laws" (MOL 92), so a low rank never licenses neglect.

Also. Requirements "may be in opposition" (Liu's slide†): a curative retroactive statute can fix an earlier legality failure (MOL 93).

43.2 Unenforced law

▤ On your sheet: 3.2 Unenforced law (word for word)
3.2 Unenforced law sham; mockery; enforce fully or repeal; moral signpost
  1. ["A sham"] overstates: open non-enforcement strains congruence, yet one rule, unlike a system, survives rare enforcement.
  2. TSH: the 2007 "overt announcement" "violated Fuller's requirement", but "showcased the competing value" of a symbolic message (Pragmatism 299).
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: law can exempt the trivial openly, as s 95† does for slight harm.
  • STEELMAN Perera: non-enforcement "places too much power in the hands of the Government and the AGC" (Hansard, 28 Nov 2022).
  • Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022)†: the AG's 2018 assurance bound him until clear notice (7.7). Liu: before it, non-enforcement was official action, not a rule (pure divergence), and as discretion it hit generality; after it, officials' statements can silently change the law (W2).
  • CONCEDE TSH is harsher (breach, not strain): concede the breach, defending only the trade-off.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A sign says "No ball games" but the park warden openly says he'll never enforce it. Is the sign a sham? Not entirely: it still says something about what the park wants. But the gap between what the rule says and what officials do is a real cost: Fuller calls it a failure of congruence.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "If the state openly says it won't enforce a law, that law is fake. Either enforce it properly or get rid of it. Criminal law isn't for sending moral messages."

  1. "Fake" goes too far. Openly not enforcing a rule is a real strain on congruence (rule and practice don't match). But one rule can survive that; a whole system couldn't.
  2. TSH's view. The 2007 announcement on s 377A did break Fuller's requirement, but it showed a competing value at work: the law's symbolic message.
  3. So "enforce or repeal" is too black and white. Law can openly let trivial cases off, as s 95 of the Penal Code does for slight harm.

The extras: the STEELMAN (Perera, Hansard): non-enforcement gives too much power to the Government and prosecutors. CONCEDE that TSH calls it a breach, not just a strain; you defend only the trade-off.

Remember: strained, not a sham; the question is whether the trade-off is worth it.

The statement. "A law that the state openly declines to enforce is a sham … it must either be enforced fully or be repealed, because the criminal law is not a moral signpost." (Practice Q14.)

The move.

  1. "A sham" overstates: open non-enforcement strains congruence, yet one rule, unlike a system, survives rare enforcement.
  2. TSH: the 2007 "overt announcement" "violated Fuller's requirement", but "showcased the competing value" of a symbolic message (Pragmatism 299).
  3. So "enforce fully or repeal" is too stark: law can exempt the trivial openly, as s 95 of the Penal Code† does for slight harm.

STEELMAN. Perera (Hansard, 28 Nov 2022): non-enforcement "places too much power in the hands of the Government and the AGC".

Singapore detail. In Tan Seng Kee (CA 2022)† the Attorney-General's 2018 assurance bound him until clear notice. Liu: before the assurance, non-enforcement was official action, not a rule (pure divergence), and as discretion it hit generality; after it, officials' statements can silently change the law (W2).

CONCEDE. TSH is harsher than "strain": she calls it a breach. Concede the breach; defend only the trade-off.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The "imagining the President's death" offence

Practice Q14 compares s 377A to the old Penal Code s 121A (before 2019)†, which punished "imagining" the President's death, hurt or restraint with death or life imprisonment. Liu used it as an example of congruence and discretion problems (W2 slide 11). A law that is never and could never be properly enforced is the clearest congruence failure; s 377A's announced non-enforcement is a milder, open one.

53.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral)

▤ On your sheet: 3.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral) (word for word)
3.3 Tyrant (and what makes legality moral) neither inner nor moral; a tyrant could follow it; guarantees justice; one rule fails
  1. [A tyrant could follow it] is half right: legality is moral but thin; at minimum it demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be" (MOL 47).
  2. It is moral because reciprocity grounds the duty (MOL 39–40), it treats people as responsible agents†, and it binds even a self-seeking monarch (PFL 644–45).
  3. So [legality guarantees justice] fails: wicked aims can run through clear, public rules; intolerable injustice needs the RF (8.3).
  • STEELMAN Liu's slide†: "The label seems misapplied"; the concern "is really with efficacy".
  • AGAINST Inner and outer morality decay together "almost inevitably" (PFL 645).
  • Single rule: secret or retroactive, it grounds no moral duty (MOL 39); unclear, it is "less a law" (MOL 63 n 21); validity is for the RF (8).
  • CONCEDE A regime can meet all eight and still be wicked (Liu's slide†): concede that, not that legality is morally empty.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Could a cruel dictator follow all eight rules? Probably yes: publish clear, general, forward-looking laws that are evil. So legality isn't the same as justice. But following the eight rules still does something good: it lets people know where they stand and plan their lives, and it treats them as adults who can choose to obey.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Fuller's 'morality of law' is really just a recipe for running a country efficiently. A dictator could follow it as easily as a democrat."

  1. Half right. Legality is thin: it asks for clear, public, general rules whatever they say, fair or unfair. So yes, a dictator could in principle publish clear wicked laws.
  2. But it's still moral, for three reasons. It rests on a two-way deal (reciprocity). It treats people as responsible adults who can plan and choose. And it binds even a selfish ruler to his own rules.
  3. So "legality guarantees justice" is wrong too. Evil aims can run through clear rules. For truly monstrous laws you need a different tool, the Radbruch formula (Lesson 8).

The extras: STEELMAN (Liu): maybe the right word is "efficacy", not "morality". AGAINST (Fuller): in practice, good form and good content tend to fall apart together, because evil regimes need secrecy and retroactivity. CONCEDE that a regime can meet all eight and still be wicked, but never concede that legality is morally empty.

Remember: thin but not empty.

The statement. "Fuller's 'inner morality of law' is neither inner nor moral. It is a recipe for efficient governance that a tyrant could follow as faithfully as a democrat." (Practice Q20.)

The move.

  1. "A tyrant could follow it" is half right: legality is moral but thin; at minimum it demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be" (MOL 47).
  2. It is moral because (a) reciprocity grounds the duty to obey (MOL 39–40); (b) it treats people as responsible agents†; and (c) it binds even a self-seeking monarch (PFL 644–45).
  3. So "legality guarantees justice" fails: wicked aims can run through clear, public rules; intolerable injustice needs the Radbruch formula (8.3).

The two sides.

  • STEELMAN (Liu's slide†): "The label seems misapplied"; the concern "is really with efficacy".
  • AGAINST (Fuller): inner and outer morality decay together "almost inevitably" (PFL 645). Evil regimes find legality inconvenient: they need secrecy and retroactivity.
  • Single rule: a secret or retroactive rule grounds no moral duty (MOL 39); an unclear one is "less a law" (MOL 63 n 21). Validity, though, is the Radbruch formula's question (8).
⚠ TRAP
Concede the right thing

Concede: a regime can meet all eight and still be wicked (Liu's slide†). Don't concede: that legality is morally empty.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready sentences

The statement is half right. Legality is thin: it demands rules "however fair or unfair they may be" (MOL 47), so a tyrant could, in principle, publish clear and general rules for wicked ends. But it is not morally empty. It treats subjects as responsible agents who can plan and choose; it grounds their duty to obey in reciprocity (MOL 39–40); and, as Fuller argues, inner and outer morality tend to decay together (PFL 645). Legality cannot guarantee just laws; that is the Radbruch formula's work.

63.4 Discretion

▤ On your sheet: 3.4 Discretion (word for word)
3.4 Discretion rule of men; unfettered discretion; enforced only against critics
  1. ["Every grant of discretion is a small surrender"] overstates: only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men.
  2. Fuller condemns a 1934 Nazi statute "undermined as it is by uncontrolled administrative discretion" (PFL 654); [enforcement only against critics] approaches it.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits legality if bounded by law and reviewable.
  • JUDGE Review legality, not merits: Art 35(8)† discretion is subject to Art 12 (Ramalingam†). Liu: discretion erodes generality by degree: principled restraint is fine; protecting allies and punishing foes is not (W2).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A referee who can give a penalty "whenever she likes" isn't refereeing by the rules. A referee who must give penalties for fouls but can judge what counts as a foul is still refereeing by rules. Discretion inside rules is fine. Discretion with no limits is rule by people, not law.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Every time the law lets an official decide for themselves, the rule of law loses a bit. Singapore gives officials lots of discretion, so it isn't really committed to legality."

  1. That goes too far. Discretion is only a problem when it's uncontrolled: then it really is rule by people, not law.
  2. Fuller's example is a 1934 Nazi law ruined by uncontrolled discretion. Using the law only against critics comes close to that.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits the rule of law as long as it is limited by law and can be checked by the courts.

The extras: JUDGE: courts review whether discretion was used lawfully, not whether it was wise. The Attorney-General's power to prosecute (Art 35(8)) is still subject to equal protection in Art 12 (Ramalingam). Liu: it's a matter of degree. Principled restraint is fine; protecting friends and punishing enemies isn't.

Remember: bounded and reviewable discretion is fine; unbounded is not.

The statement. "Every grant of discretion is a small surrender of the rule of law to the rule of men. Singapore's wide grants of executive and prosecutorial discretion therefore sit uneasily with its professed commitment to legality." (Practice Q18.)

The move.

  1. "Every grant … is a small surrender" overstates: only uncontrolled discretion turns law into rule by men.
  2. Fuller condemns a 1934 Nazi statute "undermined as it is by uncontrolled administrative discretion" (PFL 654); enforcement only against critics approaches it.
  3. So Singapore's discretion fits legality if bounded by law and reviewable.

JUDGE. Review legality, not merits: the Attorney-General's prosecutorial discretion under Art 35(8)† is subject to Art 12 (Ramalingam†). Liu: discretion erodes generality by degree: principled restraint is fine; protecting allies and punishing foes is not (W2).

73.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions

▤ On your sheet: 3.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions (word for word)
3.5 Mandatory sentences, presumptions purest expression of the rule of law; like cases alike
  1. Mandatory sentences look like ["the purest expression of the rule of law"], but they buy certainty, not justice.
  2. Fuller: Hart's "justice in the administration of the law" treats like cases alike "by whatever elevated or perverted standards the word 'like' may be defined" (PFL 646).
  3. So [leaving nothing to judges] is just only if the line tracks real differences in harm or fault.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A rule says: "Anyone caught with more than a set amount of a drug gets one fixed sentence." It's predictable and applies equally. But "equal" only means fair if the rule draws its line in the right place. If two very different offenders fall on the same side of the line, treating them "alike" is not justice.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Fixed sentences and legal presumptions are the rule of law at its best: everyone is treated the same, and judges' personal views don't come in."

  1. They look like the rule of law at its best, but what they deliver is certainty, not justice.
  2. Fuller's point: treating "like cases alike" works with any standard, good or terrible. It depends entirely on what you count as "alike".
  3. So taking judges out of it is only fair if the rule's line matches real differences in harm or blame. If very different offenders land on the same side of the line, "equal" treatment is unfair.

Link: Lesson 7 (7.8) adds that whether to punish and how much to punish are separate questions, so a harsh fixed penalty needs its own justification.

Remember: consistent is not the same as just.

The statement. "Mandatory sentences and statutory presumptions are the purest expression of the rule of law: they treat like cases alike and leave nothing to the personal views of judges." (Practice Q19.)

The move.

  1. Mandatory sentences look like "the purest expression of the rule of law", but they buy certainty, not justice.
  2. Fuller: Hart's "justice in the administration of the law" treats like cases alike "by whatever elevated or perverted standards the word 'like' may be defined" (PFL 646). Consistency can serve any standard.
  3. So leaving nothing to judges is just only if the line tracks real differences in harm or fault.

Pair with 7.8: whether to punish and how severely are "distinct and independent questions" (Hart LLM 36), so a harsh mandatory penalty needs its own justification.

83.6 Rules v standards

▤ On your sheet: 3.6 Rules v standards (word for word)
3.6 Rules v standards same standard for those who cannot meet it; learner driver; clear rules
  1. Holding [a learner driver] to the ordinary standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma (MOL 72); by analogy with strict civil liability, a "surcharge" on risky activity (MOL 75) can justify it, never in crime (MOL 77).
  2. Fuller's antinomy: aloof justice is "bound at times to be harsh", intimate justice cannot be "evenhanded", so law tempers the reasonable man (MOL 72).
  3. So [clear rules are always better] overstates: "good faith" standards can clarify; specious clarity can harm more than honest vagueness (MOL 64).
  • Nettleship v Weston†: a learner owes the ordinary driver's standard; Cook v Cook† lowered it where the passenger knew (later overruled: Imbree v McNeilly, 2008†).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Should a learner driver be judged by the standard of an ordinary competent driver, even though they can't meet it? A clear rule ("everyone drives to the same standard") is easy to apply but can be harsh. A flexible standard ("what's reasonable for you") is kinder but less even. Fuller says law has to live with that tension.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "A fair system holds everyone to the same standard, even people who can't meet it" and "clear rules always beat flexible standards".

  1. The learner-driver problem. Holding a learner to the normal driver's standard is Fuller's "reasonable man" dilemma. In civil law it can be justified, like an extra charge on doing something risky. In criminal law, never.
  2. Fuller's tension. Justice that treats everyone identically is sometimes harsh; justice tailored to each person can't be even-handed. So law softens the "reasonable man" standard at the edges.
  3. So "clear rules are always better" goes too far. A standard like "good faith" can be clear enough, and a rule that only looks clear can do more harm than one that is honestly vague.

The cases: Nettleship held a learner to the normal standard; Australia's Cook v Cook lowered it, then Imbree (2008) reversed that. Courts swinging back and forth is the tension in action.

Remember: evenness and individual fairness pull against each other.

The statements. "A fair legal system holds everyone to the same standard, even those who cannot meet it." (Q23) "Clear rules are always better than flexible standards." (Q24)

The move.

  1. Holding a learner driver to the ordinary standard is Fuller's reasonable-man dilemma (MOL 72). By analogy with strict civil liability, a "surcharge" on risky activity (MOL 75) can justify it; never in crime (MOL 77).
  2. Fuller's antinomy: aloof justice is "bound at times to be harsh"; intimate justice cannot be "evenhanded"; so law tempers the reasonable man (MOL 72).
  3. So "clear rules are always better" overstates: "good faith" standards can clarify, and specious clarity can harm more than honest vagueness (MOL 64).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The learner-driver cases†
  • Nettleship v Weston: a learner owes the ordinary driver's standard.
  • Cook v Cook (Australia): lowered it where the passenger knew the driver was a learner; later overruled by Imbree v McNeilly (2008).

The swing back shows the antinomy in action: courts chose evenhandedness over intimacy.

93.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis

▤ On your sheet: 3.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis (word for word)
3.7 Authority, reciprocity, crisis duty springs from authority; goodwill; crisis; simply majority will
  1. [The duty springs from authority] is the command view, which "confuses fidelity to law with deference for established authority" (MOL 63).
  2. Reciprocity grounds the duty: once government finally and completely ruptures it, "nothing is left on which to ground the citizen's duty" (MOL 40).
  3. So [goodwill] cannot suffice: "No single concentration of intelligence, insight, and good will" can secure law's enterprise (MOL 91).
  • Voter: where officials disregard rules, "at some point obedience becomes futile", like "casting a vote that will never be counted" (MOL 39).
  • AGAINST [Majority will, accurately expressed]: tracking a shifting majority breaks constancy, like Rex's daily amendments (MOL 37).
  • QUALIFY Crisis: "grim necessity" may hide a weapons appropriation; Fuller sees "no emergency" justifying a secret law "creating a new crime" (MOL 92).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Why obey the law? "Because the government says so" is the command view. Fuller says it's more like a deal: the government gives you clear, stable rules and judges you by them; you follow them. If the government tears up its side completely, there's nothing left to ground your duty.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Even when COVID rules changed constantly, people had to obey, because the state has authority" and "governments follow the law only because they want to".

  1. "Because the state says so" is the command view. Fuller says it mixes up being loyal to law with bowing to whoever holds power.
  2. The real basis is a two-way deal. Government gives you knowable rules and judges you by them; you follow them. If government breaks its side completely, nothing is left to support your duty.
  3. So goodwill isn't enough. No single person, however wise and well-meaning, can keep the legal system working alone.

Fuller's pictures: obeying rules that officials ignore is like voting in an election where your vote is never counted. Following a shifting majority every day breaks stability, like King Rex's daily rule changes. QUALIFY for crisis: emergencies can justify fast changes, but never a secret law creating a new crime. COVID rules changed fast but were published and forward-looking.

Remember: the duty to obey rests on reciprocity, not raw authority.

The statements. "During COVID-19, the rules changed constantly … yet citizens were right to obey them. The duty to obey springs from the authority of the state." (Q15) "Any government ultimately follows the law because it wants to." (Q21)

The move.

  1. "The duty springs from authority" is the command view, which "confuses fidelity to law with deference for established authority" (MOL 63).
  2. Reciprocity grounds the duty: once government finally and completely ruptures it, "nothing is left on which to ground the citizen's duty" (MOL 40).
  3. So goodwill cannot suffice: "No single concentration of intelligence, insight, and good will" can secure law's enterprise (MOL 91).

Fuller's images.

  • The voter: where officials disregard rules, "at some point obedience becomes futile", like "casting a vote that will never be counted" (MOL 39).
  • Majority will: tracking a shifting majority breaks constancy, like Rex's daily amendments (MOL 37).
  • Crisis (QUALIFY): "grim necessity" may hide a weapons appropriation; Fuller sees "no emergency" justifying a secret law "creating a new crime" (MOL 92). COVID rules that changed fast but were published and prospective strain constancy; a secret new crime would be another matter.

103.8 Judge-made law

▤ On your sheet: 3.8 Judge-made law (word for word)
3.8 Judge-made law never fully prospective; announced after the dispute; retrospective overruling
  1. Adjudication is partly retrospective, so ["can never fully satisfy"] holds in form, though a new rule may only confirm "views already widely held" (MOL 92).
  2. In civil cases retrospective overruling is [a price worth paying]: prospective rulings remove a private litigant's incentive to challenge bad precedent (MOL 56–57).
  3. Crime differs: a retrospective overruling would leave men "branded as criminals" for relying on a judicial interpretation (MOL 58).
  • Abdul Nasir† (CA 1997): life imprisonment means natural life, prospectively only (8.6); it engages constancy, not "branded as criminals".
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When a judge decides a new point, the rule is announced after the events happened, so it is a bit retroactive. Usually that's fine because the judge is often just confirming what people already expected. But in criminal law, punishing someone for relying on what the courts had said was lawful would be unfair.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Judges only announce the law after a dispute has happened, so the common law can never be fully public in advance or forward-looking."

  1. True in form. A judge's ruling applies to events that already happened. But often the ruling only confirms what people already expected.
  2. In civil cases that's a price worth paying. If rulings only applied to the future, the person who brought the case would gain nothing, so nobody would bother challenging bad precedents.
  3. Criminal cases are different. Changing the law backwards would turn people into criminals for relying on what the courts had said.

The example: in Abdul Nasir, the Court of Appeal said "life imprisonment" means the rest of your life, not 20 years, but applied that only to future cases. That protects stability; it doesn't make anyone a criminal after the fact.

Remember: retroactive in form; acceptable in civil cases; not in crime.

The statement. "The common law can never fully satisfy Fuller's requirements of promulgation and prospectivity, because judges announce the law only after a dispute has arisen." (Practice Q22.)

The move.

  1. Adjudication is partly retrospective, so "can never fully satisfy" holds in form, though a new rule may only confirm "views already widely held" (MOL 92).
  2. In civil cases retrospective overruling is a price worth paying: purely prospective rulings remove a private litigant's incentive to challenge bad precedent (MOL 56–57).
  3. Crime differs: a retrospective overruling would leave men "branded as criminals" for relying on a judicial interpretation (MOL 58).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Abdul Nasir (CA 1997)†

The Court of Appeal held that life imprisonment means natural life (not 20 years), but applied the new reading prospectively only. That engages constancy (a stable law people can plan around), not "branded as criminals", because no one was made a criminal by it.

113.9 Thin v thick; Marx

▤ On your sheet: 3.9 Thin v thick; Marx (word for word)
3.9 Thin v thick; Marx ruling-class slogan; instrument of power; whims of officials
  1. ["A slogan" for class power] overstates: legal form binds rulers too, since "law cannot be built on law" (PFL 645).
  2. Liu's slide† answers the Marxist: law "has its own character", applying legal criteria "with reference to standards of universality and equity" (crits: 9.3).
  3. So thin legality beats ["the whims of its officials"]: published rules give notice and invite criticism (MOL 51).
  • STEELMAN Liu: law drags "the monster out into the light": a regime that nails its colours to the mast can be criticised, organised against and fled, while arbitrary power shows no pattern. Against: rules legitimise and spread evil ("it's the law") (W2).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A Marxist says "the rule of law" is just a fancy costume for the powerful. Fuller replies that once the powerful dress in law, the costume constrains them too: they have to follow their own published rules, which tells everyone what they're doing and lets people criticise, resist or leave.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "The rule of law is just a nice slogan that the ruling class uses to stay in power" and "persecuting a minority by published, general laws is no better than doing it on officials' whims".

  1. "Just a slogan" goes too far. Once rulers use legal form, it binds them too. You can't build law out of law alone; someone has to commit to following the rules first.
  2. Liu's answer to the Marxist: law has a character of its own. It applies standards of universality and equity, which can be turned against the powerful.
  3. So thin legality beats officials' whims. Published rules warn people what's coming and open the rulers up to criticism.

The extra: Liu's image is that law drags "the monster out into the light". A regime that writes down its aims can be criticised, organised against, or escaped; arbitrary power shows no pattern. The other side: calling something "the law" can make evil look respectable.

Remember: published wickedness is still wickedness, but it is easier to see and resist.

The statements. "Law is the instrument of the ruling class, dressed in the language of universality and equity." (Q17) "A regime that strips a minority … through carefully drafted, published and general statutes is no better than one that does so through the whims of its officials." (Q12)

The move.

  1. "A slogan for class power" overstates: legal form binds rulers too, since "law cannot be built on law" (PFL 645): some commitment to legality must come first.
  2. Liu's slide† answers the Marxist: law "has its own character", applying legal criteria "with reference to standards of universality and equity" (the crits return in 9.3).
  3. So thin legality beats "the whims of its officials": published rules give notice and invite criticism (MOL 51).
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Liu's image: law drags "the monster out into the light". A regime that nails its colours to the mast can be criticised, organised against and fled, while arbitrary power shows no pattern. Against: rules can legitimise and spread evil ("it's the law") (W2). Use both sides.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready sentences

The victims may suffer the same, but they are not equally placed. Published, general, prospective rules tell them what is coming, invite criticism (MOL 51) and bind the rulers who made them, since "law cannot be built on law" (PFL 645). Legality drags the monster into the light (Liu, W2). It cannot make the statutes just; that requires a substantive standard such as the Radbruch formula.

12Putting it together: Practice Q12

"A regime that strips a minority of its homes and livelihoods through carefully drafted, published and general statutes is no better than one that does so through the whims of its officials; the victims suffer exactly the same. Law has only ever been the instrument of whichever class holds power, and 'the rule of law' is a slogan that dresses that power up as something respectable. A society is truly ruled by law rather than by men only when its laws are substantively just."

Instruction: Fuller, Hart, Marxism.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "no better than … whims" → 3.9 (thin v thick).
  • "instrument of whichever class" and "slogan" → 3.9 (Marx).
  • "only when its laws are substantively just" → 3.3 (legality ≠ justice), 1.3(13) form v content.
  • Hook: word: "only". Thesis: distinction: the statement is right about content (legality cannot make law just) and wrong about form (legality is not worthless).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement runs together two claims: that legality is worthless, and that only just laws are truly law. The first is wrong and the second confuses form with content. I make three claims: (1) published, general rules leave victims better placed than whims, because they give notice and bind rulers; (2) the rule of law is no mere class slogan, since its form constrains those who use it; but (3) the statement is right that legality cannot guarantee just laws, so a regime may be ruled by law and still be wicked.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Fuller's thin morality (3.3, 3.9): reciprocity, agency, "law cannot be built on law"; monster into the light.
  2. The efficacy objection and the Marxist (3.3, 3.9): Liu's slide†: perhaps it is efficacy, not morality; Marx: legitimation. Reply: Fuller's decay-together thesis (PFL 645); law's own character (universality, equity).
  3. "Only when substantively just" (3.3, 8): the definitional move is the Radbruch formula's, not Fuller's; concede that a regime can meet all eight and still be wicked.

The statement is therefore right only in part. Legality binds rulers, respects subjects as agents and exposes their aims to criticism, so carefully drafted statutes are not the same as whims. But legality is thin: it cannot make bad laws just, and naming intolerable injustice "not law" is the Radbruch formula's task, not Fuller's.
