LESSON 4 · ARCHETYPE 4 · ABOUT 34 MIN · 32 QUESTIONS

Moral objectivity and scepticism

⚡ BIG IDEA

The sceptic's case is inconclusive, and the sceptic's own demands (tolerate! don't judge!) presuppose moral truth. Fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not for tolerance as dogma or silence.

ARCHETYPE 4 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
4 Moral objectivity and scepticism
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position The sceptic's case is inconclusive and its demands presuppose moral truth, so [the sceptic's conclusion] fails: fallibility calls for deliberation and provisional judgement, not [tolerance as dogma / silence].
Intro That morality is [just opinion / a social construct] is offered as a reason for [tolerance / neutrality / keeping it out of law]. That conclusion is itself a moral demand the sceptic cannot ground. I argue that [the statement] [fails / is overstated]: disagreement and unprovability do not show there is no moral truth, and realism demands deliberation, not imposition.
4.1 Map just opinion; eye of the beholder; durian; nobody has proved; varies by culture
  1. [The statement] runs together relativism (cultures differ), scepticism (no standard, or none we can know) and non-cognitivism (mere sentiment).
  2. On Hume's non-cognitivism a moral claim is like [disliking durian], neither true nor false; realists hold it can be true or false.
  3. So [nobody has proved it] bites only if proof means deduction, a test natural science fails too (Harris 13).
  • Liu's replies†: "shades of grey" is "not even an argument"; "merely opinions" assumes "the very point being contended".
  • TRAP "Subjective" is not "controversial" (heliocentrism); moral realism is unrelated to legal realism (Harris 98; Liu, W3).
  • STEELMAN Hume seems no extreme relativist: reason as "slave of the passions" may mean shared emotions supply premises; rules of justice are "artificial" but "not arbitrary" (Harris 13–14).
4.2 Self-refutation all moral opinions are equally valid; who are you to judge; intolerant; social construct
  1. The sceptic's [we must tolerate / no one may judge] is itself an objective moral demand of the kind the statement denies.
  2. A [social construct] that binds outsiders abandons subjectivism; if that binding rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist (TSH).
  3. So [the statement] defeats itself; true subjectivism, taken to its end, leaves its adherents no reply to genocide but force.
  • CONCEDE Self-refutation binds only the sceptic who makes demands, and settles no content: further debate is "a squabble within the family of moral realists" (Think 35). Concede: realism must still argue for each norm.
  • TRAP TSH's domain is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist (Liu, W3); the sceptic who says none are bound is consistent but argues for nothing ("True skepticism", W3 slide 8†).
4.3 Appeals nobody can agree; we have been wrong before; it is safer; imposing values
  1. That [nobody can agree] shows that someone is wrong, not that there is nothing to be right about (4.7).
  2. TSH explains disagreement: the mores of the times pervert reason, weakness yields to passion, and self-interest hardened by habit dulls conscience.
  3. So [we have been wrong before] counsels slowness, not abstention: calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer.
  • STEELMAN Humility: coerce only on what is widely shared. Yet that is a realist's case: genuine realism "entails a commitment to deliberation" (Think 33).
  • Imposition: "moral realists are not the only ones who can be bigoted and intolerant" (Think 33).
  • CONCEDE The realist's weak point is access: consensus can err, and in 2007 both camps were "persons who think they are right, and absolutely so" (Pragmatism 304). Concede: realism settles no case alone; it demands reasons.
4.4 Is–ought Hume showed; no ought from is; biology tells us nothing; studies show; natural; so legislators should
  1. Hume's gap holds: [the biological facts] alone cannot settle whether a practice should be legal.
  2. Finnis draws no ought from facts: the basic goods are self-evident, and facts such as [embryology] show only how they apply.
  3. So [it tells us nothing] overstates: once an ought-premise is agreed, facts fix the stakes.
  • Hume's two arguments†: (1) wrongness lies "not in the act but in our sentiments", as reason knows only relations of ideas and matters of fact ("Statement X"); (2) no "ought" from an "is".
  • AGAINST Replies: (1)† "Is Statement X self-refuting?" Being neither, by its own test it is neither true nor false. (2) The gap is only logical: agreed ought-premises (eg "the dignity of man") plus facts yield oughts (Harris 13).
4.5 Hidden judgment consensual and harms no one else; not wrong; victimless; the state should stay neutral
  1. Calling [X] not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict, not a neutral fact.
  2. The hidden premise is autonomy's primacy, which rests on equal worth; unlimited, it leaves everyone "equally worthless"; limited, it is a moral law (TSH).
  3. So [the law should stay neutral] fails: where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices; there is no "Switzerland of ambivalence" (Thio, 2007).
  • Finnis's charge: appealing only to "what people subjectively prefer", then grounding that in the value of self-governance, is "outright self-contradiction" (Abortion 90–91).
4.6 Whatever is enacted? law is whatever people say is law; whatever Parliament enacts; separation is safer
  1. If [law is whatever is enacted], nothing stands above the lawgiver: Liu asks whether that makes man "the ultimate lawgiver"† over his fellows.
  2. Saying [citizens are safer] if law may have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power.
  3. So natural law stays a touchstone for criticising [what is enacted], without denying that merely unjust enactments are law.
  • Alexy: only the "strong" connection thesis risks uncritical legitimation; the weak one (RF) keeps law open to critique (47–49). Hart's case for separation: 8.2.
Conclusion [The statement] therefore [fails / is overstated]: scepticism cannot deliver the [tolerance / safety / neutrality] it promises, since that promise is itself a moral norm, and its reasons are "inconclusive" (Think 32), though that proves no moral fact. The realist's weak point is access, not existence: consensus can err, and in 2007 both camps claimed moral truth. So I hold moral judgements provisionally, demanding more of them the more coercive the law.
4.7 Objectivity anchor
Paragraph Demanding [tolerance / deference] because [morality is just opinion / personal / a social construct] defeats itself: it binds others, which abandons subjectivism; if that demand rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist. Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets; the unproven is not the false. Refusing to act on a moral judgement may amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out is itself a moral choice. Realism demands deliberation and provisional judgement, not imposition (TSH, Think 27–34).
  • Use: 4.1–4.3, 4.5 (just opinion; nobody can agree; it is safer); 11.7 (personal morality; private conscience); 6.10 (equally valid); 7.5 (neutral); 10.4 (no one can say objectively).

1Start here: archetype 4 in plain English

Archetype 4 is about one question: is there such a thing as a moral truth, or is morality just opinion? The statements here almost always do two things at once. First they say morality is opinion, taste or culture. Then they draw a conclusion for law: "so the law must stay neutral", "so nobody may judge", "so we must tolerate everything". Your answer has a simple shape: the conclusion is itself a moral rule, so the sceptic can't have it both ways. Then you concede honestly that being a realist doesn't tell you which moral answers are right; it only tells you to argue for them carefully.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Moral realismSome moral claims are actually true or false, whatever anyone thinks ("torturing for fun is wrong" is true).
RelativismMorality varies by culture, and no culture's view is truer than another's.
ScepticismThere is no moral truth, or there may be one but we can't know it.
Non-cognitivismMoral claims are expressions of feeling, like "yuck" or "yay": neither true nor false (Hume).
SubjectivismMorality is whatever each person feels or believes. The sheet uses it as the general label for "it's just opinion".
Self-refutationAn argument that undercuts itself, like saying "never say never".
Is–ought gapHume's point that facts alone ("is") can't tell you what you should do ("ought") without a moral premise.
Provisional judgementHolding a moral view firmly enough to act on, but open to being shown wrong.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says the sceptic's case "is inconclusive" and "its demands presuppose moral truth". Put simply: the sceptic hasn't proved there's no moral truth, and the moment the sceptic says "so you must tolerate", they are relying on a moral truth. Being fallible means think carefully and hold views provisionally; it doesn't mean "tolerate everything" or "say nothing".

The Intro says: the statement uses "morality is just opinion" as a reason for tolerance or neutrality, but that conclusion is a moral demand the sceptic can't support. The Conclusion says: scepticism can't deliver what it promises, though this doesn't prove moral facts exist either. The realist's real weakness is knowing the right answer, not whether there is one. So hold moral views provisionally, and demand more of them the more coercive the law.

The seven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
4.1"Morality is just opinion; nobody's proved anything."Separate the three kinds of sceptic. "Unproved" only bites if proof means maths-style proof, which science fails too.
4.2"All views are equally valid, so you must tolerate.""You must tolerate" is a moral rule. The sceptic either drops it or becomes a realist.
4.3"Nobody agrees, and we've been wrong before."Disagreement means someone's wrong, not that nobody's right. Past mistakes call for care, not silence.
4.4"You can't get an ought from an is."True: facts need a moral premise. Add one, and facts matter a lot.
4.5"It's consensual and harms no one, so it's not wrong; stay neutral."That is a moral view (that autonomy comes first). There's no neutral ground.
4.6"Law is whatever Parliament enacts; that's safer.""Safer" is a moral claim. Natural law stays a yardstick for criticising what's enacted.
4.7(Ready-made paragraph)A four-step paragraph you can drop into any question about "just opinion".
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

"You must tolerate" is a moral rule, so a sceptic who demands it has already left scepticism behind.

2The big picture: is morality just opinion?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Some people say "right and wrong are just opinions, like liking or hating durian". If that were true, then "you must respect other people's opinions" would also be just an opinion, which nobody else would have to accept. The sceptic wants everyone to be tolerant, but tolerance is a moral rule. That's the trap the sceptic falls into.

This archetype handles statements that say morality is subjective, relative or mere feeling, and then draw a conclusion for law: "so the law should be neutral", "so no judge may impose values", "so tolerate everything". Your job is to separate three different sceptical claims, show that the sceptic's conclusion defeats itself, and then concede honestly what the realist cannot prove.

Three kinds of sceptic (4.1)

PositionClaimExample sentence
RelativismMorality varies by culture; no culture's view is truer"Every culture draws the line in a different place."
ScepticismThere is no moral standard, or none we can know"Nobody has ever proved which side is correct."
Non-cognitivism (Hume)Moral claims express feelings; they are neither true nor false"A moral view is like a taste for durian."

Against all three stands moral realism: some moral claims are true or false independently of what anyone believes.

The cast

  • David Hume: two famous arguments. (1) Wrongness lies "not in the act but in our sentiments", since reason knows only relations of ideas and matters of fact (Liu calls this "Statement X"†). (2) No "ought" can be derived from an "is".
  • Tan Seow Hon (TSH), "The Problems with Moral Subjectivism" (Think 2017): subjectivists cannot hold anyone to a standard without becoming realists, so their moral dialogue is "gravely limited" (card 14.7).
  • Finnis: the basic goods are self-evident; he draws no ought from facts (Lesson 5).
  • Alexy: only a strong law–morality connection risks uncritical legitimation; the weak one keeps law open to critique (Lesson 8).
⚠ TRAP
Two words that trip students
  1. "Subjective" is not "controversial". Heliocentrism was once controversial; it was never subjective.
  2. Moral realism has nothing to do with legal realism (the American school about judges, Lesson 9) (Harris 98; Liu, W3).

34.1 Map

▤ On your sheet: 4.1 Map (word for word)
4.1 Map just opinion; eye of the beholder; durian; nobody has proved; varies by culture
  1. [The statement] runs together relativism (cultures differ), scepticism (no standard, or none we can know) and non-cognitivism (mere sentiment).
  2. On Hume's non-cognitivism a moral claim is like [disliking durian], neither true nor false; realists hold it can be true or false.
  3. So [nobody has proved it] bites only if proof means deduction, a test natural science fails too (Harris 13).
  • Liu's replies†: "shades of grey" is "not even an argument"; "merely opinions" assumes "the very point being contended".
  • TRAP "Subjective" is not "controversial" (heliocentrism); moral realism is unrelated to legal realism (Harris 98; Liu, W3).
  • STEELMAN Hume seems no extreme relativist: reason as "slave of the passions" may mean shared emotions supply premises; rules of justice are "artificial" but "not arbitrary" (Harris 13–14).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Nobody has proved it" sounds strong. But we can't "prove" most things the way we prove maths: not even in science. If "proof" means a watertight deduction, then science fails the test too. So the sceptic must mean something weaker, and then the argument loses its punch.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Morality is just opinion. Cultures disagree, nobody has ever proved who's right, and a moral view is like liking or hating durian."

  1. The statement mixes up three different ideas. Cultures differ (relativism). There's no moral standard, or none we can know (scepticism). Moral claims are just feelings (non-cognitivism). Pull them apart before answering.
  2. The durian idea is Hume's. If moral claims are like tastes, they are neither true nor false. A realist says they can be true or false.
  3. So "nobody has proved it" only works if "proof" means a watertight logical deduction. By that test, natural science can't prove its theories either.

The extras: Liu's quick replies: "it's all shades of grey" isn't an argument, and "they're merely opinions" assumes the very point being argued about. TRAP: "subjective" doesn't mean "controversial" (the Earth going round the Sun was once controversial, never subjective). STEELMAN: be fair to Hume; he wasn't an extreme relativist and thought rules of justice "artificial" but "not arbitrary".

Remember: split the three sceptics, then ask what "proof" means.

The statement. "Morality is just opinion. Every culture draws the line between right and wrong in a different place, and after thousands of years nobody has proved which side is correct … a moral view can no more be true or false than a taste for durian." (Practice Q28.)

The move.

  1. The statement runs together relativism (cultures differ), scepticism (no standard, or none we can know) and non-cognitivism (mere sentiment). Split them.
  2. On Hume's non-cognitivism a moral claim is like disliking durian, neither true nor false; realists hold it can be true or false.
  3. So "nobody has proved it" bites only if proof means deduction, a test natural science fails too (Harris 13).

Liu's quick replies†: "shades of grey" is "not even an argument" (grey is still a shade between black and white); "merely opinions" assumes "the very point being contended".

STEELMAN (fair to Hume). Hume seems no extreme relativist: reason as "slave of the passions" may mean shared emotions supply moral premises; rules of justice are "artificial" but "not arbitrary" (Harris 13–14).

44.2 Self-refutation

▤ On your sheet: 4.2 Self-refutation (word for word)
4.2 Self-refutation all moral opinions are equally valid; who are you to judge; intolerant; social construct
  1. The sceptic's [we must tolerate / no one may judge] is itself an objective moral demand of the kind the statement denies.
  2. A [social construct] that binds outsiders abandons subjectivism; if that binding rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist (TSH).
  3. So [the statement] defeats itself; true subjectivism, taken to its end, leaves its adherents no reply to genocide but force.
  • CONCEDE Self-refutation binds only the sceptic who makes demands, and settles no content: further debate is "a squabble within the family of moral realists" (Think 35). Concede: realism must still argue for each norm.
  • TRAP TSH's domain is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist (Liu, W3); the sceptic who says none are bound is consistent but argues for nothing ("True skepticism", W3 slide 8†).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A sceptic says, "There are no moral rules, so you MUST tolerate everyone." But "you must tolerate" is a moral rule. Either the sceptic drops the demand (and then has nothing to say to a bully) or keeps it (and is no longer a sceptic).

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "All moral views are equally valid. Who are you to judge? Anyone who insists otherwise is intolerant."

  1. "You must tolerate" and "no one may judge" are moral rules. They are exactly the kind of objective moral demand the statement says don't exist.
  2. The same goes for "it's a social construct". If a society's morality binds outsiders too, it's no longer just one group's opinion. And if the reason is that every person has equal worth, the sceptic is now a moral realist.
  3. So the statement defeats itself. A truly consistent subjectivist has no answer to genocide except force: there's nothing left to argue with.

The extras: TRAP: TSH's argument is about moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist. A sceptic who makes no demands at all is consistent, but argues for nothing. CONCEDE: this argument doesn't tell you which moral views are right; that's still "a squabble within the family of moral realists".

Remember: a sceptic who demands tolerance is a realist in disguise.

The statements. "All moral opinions are equally valid." "Who are you to judge?" "Condemn as intolerant any legislator who insists otherwise." "Morality is a social construct."

The move.

  1. The sceptic's "we must tolerate" or "no one may judge" is itself an objective moral demand of the kind the statement denies.
  2. A social construct that binds outsiders abandons subjectivism; if that binding rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist (TSH, Think 27–28: a relativist who binds outsiders invokes a "meta-cultural standard").
  3. So the statement defeats itself; true subjectivism, taken to its end, leaves its adherents no reply to genocide but force (TSH's genocide hypothetical: "Moral dialogue in fact breaks down", Think 30).
⚠ TRAP
Know exactly what TSH proves

TSH's domain is moral persuasion, not proof that moral facts exist (Liu, W3). The sceptic who says no one is bound by anything is consistent, but argues for nothing ("True skepticism", W3 slide 8†). Self-refutation catches only the sceptic who makes demands.

CONCEDE. Self-refutation settles no content: further debate is "a squabble within the family of moral realists" (Think 35). Concede that realism must still argue for each norm.

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Exam-ready sentences

Demanding tolerance because morality is just opinion defeats itself: the demand binds others, which subjectivism cannot do. If it rests on the equal worth of persons, the sceptic is, in TSH's terms, "just another moral realist". That shows only that a sceptic who argues must turn realist; it does not settle which norms are true, a "squabble within the family of moral realists" (Think 35).

54.3 Appeals

▤ On your sheet: 4.3 Appeals (word for word)
4.3 Appeals nobody can agree; we have been wrong before; it is safer; imposing values
  1. That [nobody can agree] shows that someone is wrong, not that there is nothing to be right about (4.7).
  2. TSH explains disagreement: the mores of the times pervert reason, weakness yields to passion, and self-interest hardened by habit dulls conscience.
  3. So [we have been wrong before] counsels slowness, not abstention: calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer.
  • STEELMAN Humility: coerce only on what is widely shared. Yet that is a realist's case: genuine realism "entails a commitment to deliberation" (Think 33).
  • Imposition: "moral realists are not the only ones who can be bigoted and intolerant" (Think 33).
  • CONCEDE The realist's weak point is access: consensus can err, and in 2007 both camps were "persons who think they are right, and absolutely so" (Pragmatism 304). Concede: realism settles no case alone; it demands reasons.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"People have always disagreed, so there's no right answer." But people disagreed about whether the Earth goes round the Sun. Disagreement shows that someone is wrong, not that nobody can be right. And "we were wrong before about slavery" only makes sense if there's a right answer we were wrong about.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Nobody can agree. We've been wrong before. It's safer not to judge. Imposing values is intolerant."

  1. Disagreement shows someone is wrong, not that there's nothing to be right about. People disagreed about the solar system too.
  2. TSH explains why people disagree: the attitudes of the times distort reasoning, weakness gives in to passion, and self-interest (hardened by habit) dulls conscience.
  3. So "we've been wrong before" means go slowly, not stay silent. Calling slavery a mistake only makes sense if there was a right answer.

The extras: STEELMAN: humility says only use law to force what's widely shared. But that's a realist's argument too: real realism means deliberating. On "imposing", realists aren't the only ones who can be intolerant. CONCEDE: the realist's weak spot is knowing the answer; in 2007 both sides on s 377A were certain they were right.

Remember: disagreement calls for care, not for giving up.

  2. TSH explains disagreement: the mores of the times pervert reason, weakness yields to passion, and self-interest hardened by habit dulls conscience.
  3. So "we have been wrong before" counsels slowness, not abstention: calling slavery an error presupposes a right answer.

64.4 Is–ought

▤ On your sheet: 4.4 Is–ought (word for word)
4.4 Is–ought Hume showed; no ought from is; biology tells us nothing; studies show; natural; so legislators should
  1. Hume's gap holds: [the biological facts] alone cannot settle whether a practice should be legal.
  2. Finnis draws no ought from facts: the basic goods are self-evident, and facts such as [embryology] show only how they apply.
  3. So [it tells us nothing] overstates: once an ought-premise is agreed, facts fix the stakes.
  • Hume's two arguments†: (1) wrongness lies "not in the act but in our sentiments", as reason knows only relations of ideas and matters of fact ("Statement X"); (2) no "ought" from an "is".
  • AGAINST Replies: (1)† "Is Statement X self-refuting?" Being neither, by its own test it is neither true nor false. (2) The gap is only logical: agreed ought-premises (eg "the dignity of man") plus facts yield oughts (Harris 13).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"The embryo has human DNA, so abortion is wrong." Hume says you're missing a step: facts alone can't tell you what you should do. You need a moral premise too, like "it's wrong to kill a human being". Add that, and the facts suddenly matter a lot.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Hume proved you can't get an 'ought' from an 'is'. Biology tells us nothing about what the law should be. (Or: studies show X, so legislators should do Y.)"

  1. Hume is right about the gap. Facts about embryos or biology, on their own, can't decide whether something should be legal.
  2. Finnis doesn't try to jump the gap. He says the basic goods (life, knowledge and so on) are self-evident; the facts only show how those goods apply.
  3. So "biology tells us nothing" goes too far. Once you agree on a moral premise, the facts decide a lot.

Worked through: fact: the embryo is a living human organism. Missing moral premise: it's wrong to intentionally kill an innocent human being. Conclusion: abortion should be restricted. Hume's gap just means the middle step must be argued for. The dispute shrinks to that one premise.

The extra: Hume's other argument ("wrongness is in our feelings, since reason only knows ideas and facts") can be turned on itself: that claim is neither an idea-relation nor a fact, so by its own test it's neither true nor false.

Remember: facts plus an agreed moral premise give you an ought.

The statements. "Hume showed you cannot get an ought from an is." "Biology tells us nothing about what the law should be." "Studies show X, so legislators should Y."

The move.

  1. Hume's gap holds: the biological facts alone cannot settle whether a practice should be legal.
  2. Finnis draws no ought from facts: the basic goods are self-evident, and facts such as embryology show only how they apply.
  3. So "it tells us nothing" overstates: once an ought-premise is agreed, facts fix the stakes.

Hume's two arguments† and the replies:

HumeReply
(1) Wrongness lies in our sentiments, since reason knows only relations of ideas and matters of fact ("Statement X")"Is Statement X self-refuting?"†: it is itself neither a relation of ideas nor a matter of fact, so by its own test it is neither true nor false
(2) No "ought" from an "is"The gap is only logical: agreed ought-premises (e.g. "the dignity of man") plus facts yield oughts (Harris 13)
Framework 15.2: is–ought repair
▤ Liu's method (W3); Harris 12–14
  1. 1List the premises a neutral listener must accept; mark the moral ones, hidden ones too.
  2. 2Split the facts (is) from the conclusion (ought): no ought follows from is alone.
  3. 3Supply the missing major premise; once agreed, the parties "can go on to deduce ought-conclusions" (Harris 13).
  4. 4Test that premise: self-evident on reflection (Finnis), or mere preference? Argue about the premise, not the inference.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Repairing an argument

"Robert George shows the embryo is a living human organism. Therefore abortion should be banned." (cf. Practice Q59)

  • Fact (is): the embryo is a living human organism.
  • Missing premise (ought): it is wrong intentionally to kill an innocent human being.
  • Conclusion: abortion should be restricted.

Hume's gap only shows the missing premise must be argued for. Once it is supplied (or agreed), the biology matters enormously. The dispute shrinks to the bedrock premise.

74.5 Hidden judgment

▤ On your sheet: 4.5 Hidden judgment (word for word)
4.5 Hidden judgment consensual and harms no one else; not wrong; victimless; the state should stay neutral
  1. Calling [X] not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict, not a neutral fact.
  2. The hidden premise is autonomy's primacy, which rests on equal worth; unlimited, it leaves everyone "equally worthless"; limited, it is a moral law (TSH).
  3. So [the law should stay neutral] fails: where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices; there is no "Switzerland of ambivalence" (Thio, 2007).
  • Finnis's charge: appealing only to "what people subjectively prefer", then grounding that in the value of self-governance, is "outright self-contradiction" (Abortion 90–91).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"It's not wrong because it's between consenting adults and hurts no one." That sounds neutral, but it assumes something big: that what consenting adults choose matters most. That's a moral view (and a good one, maybe!), but it's not "no view at all".

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "X isn't wrong, because the adults involved agree to it and nobody else gets hurt. So the state should stay neutral."

  1. "It's not wrong because it's consensual and harmless" is a moral verdict. It isn't a neutral fact; it's a view about what makes things wrong.
  2. The hidden premise is that personal choice comes first, and that rests on everyone having equal worth. Taken without limits, it leaves everyone "equally worthless"; with limits, it's a moral law.
  3. So "the law should stay neutral" fails. Deciding where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices. As Thio put it in 2007, there's no "Switzerland of ambivalence".

The extra: Finnis's charge: appealing only to what people prefer, and then justifying that by the value of self-governance, contradicts itself.

Remember: "harmless and consensual" is a moral argument, not a way of avoiding one.

The statement. "Act X is not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else; the state should stay neutral." (Practice Q75.)

The move.

  1. Calling X not wrong because it is consensual and harms no one else is a moral verdict, not a neutral fact.
  2. The hidden premise is autonomy's primacy, which rests on equal worth. Unlimited, it leaves everyone "equally worthless"; limited, it is a moral law (TSH).
  3. So "the law should stay neutral" fails: where harm stops and whose consent counts are moral choices; there is no "Switzerland of ambivalence" (Thio, 2007).

Finnis's charge. Appealing only to "what people subjectively prefer", then grounding that in the value of self-governance, is "outright self-contradiction" (Abortion 90–91).

84.6 Whatever is enacted?

▤ On your sheet: 4.6 Whatever is enacted? (word for word)
4.6 Whatever is enacted? law is whatever people say is law; whatever Parliament enacts; separation is safer
  1. If [law is whatever is enacted], nothing stands above the lawgiver: Liu asks whether that makes man "the ultimate lawgiver"† over his fellows.
  2. Saying [citizens are safer] if law may have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power.
  3. So natural law stays a touchstone for criticising [what is enacted], without denying that merely unjust enactments are law.
  • Alexy: only the "strong" connection thesis risks uncritical legitimation; the weak one (RF) keeps law open to critique (47–49). Hart's case for separation: 8.2.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If "law is whatever Parliament says", then nothing is above Parliament. Some people say that's safer for citizens. But "it's safer" is a moral claim about what's good for people. You can't escape morality by saying the law has no moral limits.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Law is whatever Parliament enacts. Keeping law and morality separate is safer for citizens."

  1. If law is whatever's enacted, nothing stands above the lawmaker. Liu asks whether that makes humans "the ultimate lawgiver" over each other.
  2. "Safer for citizens" is itself a moral claim about safety, freedom and power.
  3. So natural law stays useful as a yardstick for criticising what's enacted, without saying that every unjust law stops being law.

The extra: Alexy: only the strong version (every unjust law is no law) risks blessing whatever the state does. The weak version (the Radbruch formula, Lesson 8) keeps law open to criticism.

Remember: natural law is a yardstick, not a delete button.

The statements. "Law is whatever people say is law." "Law is whatever Parliament enacts." "Separating law from morality is safer for citizens."

The move.

  1. If law is whatever is enacted, nothing stands above the lawgiver: Liu asks whether that makes man "the ultimate lawgiver"† over his fellows.
  2. Saying citizens are safer if law may have any content is itself a moral claim about safety, liberty and power.
  3. So natural law stays a touchstone for criticising what is enacted, without denying that merely unjust enactments are law.

Alexy: only the strong connection thesis (every unjust law is not law) risks uncritical legitimation; the weak one (the Radbruch formula) keeps law open to critique (47–49). Hart's case for separation: 8.2.

94.7 Objectivity anchor

▤ On your sheet: 4.7 Objectivity anchor (word for word)
4.7 Objectivity anchor
Paragraph Demanding [tolerance / deference] because [morality is just opinion / personal / a social construct] defeats itself: it binds others, which abandons subjectivism; if that demand rests on equal moral worth, the sceptic is a moral realist. Disagreement no more disproves moral facts than disputes over the number of planets; the unproven is not the false. Refusing to act on a moral judgement may amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out is itself a moral choice. Realism demands deliberation and provisional judgement, not imposition (TSH, Think 27–34).
  • Use: 4.1–4.3, 4.5 (just opinion; nobody can agree; it is safer); 11.7 (personal morality; private conscience); 6.10 (equally valid); 7.5 (neutral); 10.4 (no one can say objectively).
🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

What this block is: not an argument against one statement but a ready-made paragraph you can drop into any answer where someone says "morality is just opinion".

  1. Self-refutation: demanding tolerance because morality is opinion binds other people, which subjectivism can't do.
  2. Disagreement isn't proof of no answer: people once disagreed about how many planets there are. Unproved is not the same as false.
  3. Not judging is a choice: refusing to act on a moral view can amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out of law is itself a moral decision.
  4. Realism means care: believing in moral truth demands discussion and provisional judgement, not forcing views on others.

Remember: four beats: self-refuting, disagreement ≠ no fact, neutrality is a choice, realism means deliberation.

This block is a ready-made paragraph you can adapt in any archetype where scepticism appears. Learn its four moves:

  1. Self-refutation: demanding tolerance because morality is opinion binds others, which abandons subjectivism.
  2. Disagreement ≠ no fact: disputes no more disprove moral facts than disputes over the number of planets; the unproven is not the false. (Alternate signature: a stick looks bent in water, yet is straight.)
  3. Refusing to judge is a choice: refusing to act on a moral judgment may amount to acting on its opposite, so keeping morality out of law is itself a moral choice.
  4. Realism → deliberation: realism demands deliberation and provisional judgment, not imposition (TSH, Think 27–34).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Where else the anchor works
  • 4.1–4.3, 4.5: "just opinion"; "nobody can agree"; "it is safer".
  • 11.7: "personal morality", "private conscience" (the Constitution question).
  • 6.10: "equally valid" (Sample Question 1).
  • 7.5: "neutral".
  • 10.4: "no one can say objectively what a virtuous lawyer would do".

10Putting it together: Practice Q28

"Morality is just opinion. Every culture draws the line between right and wrong in a different place, and after thousands of years nobody has proved which side is correct; even so-called universal human rights are merely one tradition's preferences. Since nothing in ethics is black and white, a moral view can no more be true or false than a taste for durian. A multicultural society should therefore accept that no conduct is objectively wrong, and condemn as intolerant any legislator or judge who uses the law to insist otherwise."

Instruction: Hume, Finnis, Alexy; and what the analysis suggests about moral scepticism in law-reform arguments.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "just opinion", "every culture", "nobody has proved", "durian" → 4.1 map.
  • "nothing in ethics is black and white" → Liu: "shades of grey" is not an argument.
  • "condemn as intolerant" → 4.2 self-refutation.
  • "legislator or judge" → actors; Alexy on judges (4.6, 8.3).
  • Lead 4; distinction: existence v access (the realist's weak point is access, not existence).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement asks a multicultural society to "condemn as intolerant" anyone who insists some conduct is objectively wrong. That demand is itself an objective moral claim, so the statement defeats itself. I make three claims: (1) it runs together relativism, scepticism and Hume's non-cognitivism, and none shows there is no moral truth; (2) its conclusion, tolerance as a duty binding legislators and judges, presupposes the very objectivity it denies; but (3) the sceptic is right that our access to moral truth is fallible, which calls for deliberation and provisional judgement in law reform, not for silence.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Hume and the map (4.1, 4.4): durian; "nobody has proved" assumes deductive proof; Hume steelmanned (shared passions; "artificial" not "arbitrary"); Statement X self-refuting.
  2. Self-refutation and Finnis (4.2, 4.4): "condemn as intolerant" binds others; TSH: equal worth makes the relativist a realist; Finnis's goods are self-evident, not inferred from culture or fact.
  3. Alexy, judges and law reform (4.6, 8.3): the weak connection thesis keeps law open to critique; consensus on rights answers the relativist in rights-steeped states. Self-critique: consensus can err; in 2007 both camps claimed certainty (4.3 CONCEDE).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close (answering the extra question)

Moral scepticism is therefore a poor tool for law reform. It cannot deliver the tolerance it promises, since that promise is a moral norm, and its reasons are "inconclusive" (Think 32). Reformers do better to argue openly for the moral premise their proposal needs, holding it provisionally and demanding more of it the more coercive the law.

LESSON 5 · ARCHETYPE 5 · ABOUT 38 MIN · 35 QUESTIONS

Finnis for law-makers

⚡ BIG IDEA

Finnis gives legislators real limits (never intend to destroy a basic good) and a framework common good, then leaves much to prudence. He guides law-makers without dictating to them.

ARCHETYPE 5 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
5 Finnis for law-makers
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position Finnis gives legislators real limits on [the issue] and leaves much to prudence.
Intro The statement assumes that a theory of the good must either [dictate how citizens live / offer no guidance]. Finnis shows a third path. Seven basic goods and nine requirements of practical reasonableness yield a few absolute limits, such as never intending to kill the innocent, and a common good that is a framework, not a life-plan. Within those limits legislators choose prudently, and reasonable people may differ.
5.1 Goods and priorities basic goods; obviously good; just taste; rank the goods; golfer
  1. Finnis's seven basic goods are self-evident, not inferred: anyone reflecting on why he acts can grasp [knowledge] as good "in itself" (NLNR 85–86).
  2. The goods are "all equally fundamental, though you can prioritise"†: "there is no objective hierarchy amongst them" (NLNR 92).
  3. So life-plans, not the state, rank the goods, and [the state must do the ranking] does not follow.
  • Golfer: passing a drowning stranger is "indifference to the good of others whom one could easily help" (NLNR V.4).
  • Seven goods (W4 slide 3†): life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness, "religion" ("agnostic or negative" answers count, NLNR 89). Pre-moral: morality comes with the nine requirements (V.1). Liu's test: strip out every use to the other goods; is something left (W4)?
  • QUALIFY Liu (W4): gossip is low-grade knowledge (NLNR 84–85); suicide shows life's deprivation, not rejection; lacking a good does not unmake it; pleasure is an aspect, not the point (96–97).
5.2 The nine requirements as structure plan of life; detachment; commitment; efficiency; transpose to a legislature
  1. Nine requirements of practical reasonableness structure the pursuit of goods, and most transpose to [a legislature], though a state has no single life-plan (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, each "fundamental, underived, irreducible" (V.1), though to Liu they read as prudent advice: neglecting (4) or (5) looks unwise rather than immoral (W5).
  • (1) Coherent plan of life; (2) no arbitrary preference among values, (3) or persons (Golden Rule); (4) detachment: no fanatical policy; (5) commitment: keep faith; (6) efficiency within reason (5.4); (7) respect every basic value in every act (5.3); (8) common good (5.5); (9) conscience.
5.3 Absolutes and double effect shoot one hostage; scientist; a foreseen death is just as dead
  1. The seventh requirement yields absolutes, such as never taking life "directly as a means" (Harris 15), so [shooting one hostage to free ten] is barred.
  2. Acts are individuated primarily by intention: damaging a good as means or end differs from damaging it as a side effect, but plans cannot be characterised "ad lib" (NLNR V.7).
  3. So [a foreseen death is just as dead] misses the point: side effects are judged too, by fairness and commitments, not by a sum.
  • Scientist†: intending only knowledge, he takes a living person's heart; even as a side effect, the death is "impermissible because unfair".
  • Pregnancy cases† (applied): chemotherapy or removing a cancerous womb treats the mother, death a side effect; direct termination intends it; pre-eclampsia is hard (my reading).
  • QUALIFY Liu: the line is "honestly pretty artificial": out of step with intuitions (odd for the self-evident), a poor guide facing an attacker, and a heavy limit on autonomy, since consent cures nothing (W5).
  • TRAP Double effect is Aquinas's; for Finnis the casuists' doctrines "are not themselves the principles of practical reasonableness" (V.7). Intention, not foresight: a certain death can be a side effect (W4 slide 9†).
5.4 Against utilitarianism greatest happiness; whatever makes them happy; maximise preferences; healthcare savings
  1. Finnis calls [the greatest happiness] "intrinsically incoherent and senseless" outside "limited technical contexts": goods are incommensurable, so act- and rule-utilitarianism are "not so much false as senseless" (NLNR 154; V.6).
  2. So maximising [satisfied preferences] is reasonable only inside the other requirements, as efficiency, and never as the measure of right.
  • "Over a wide range of preferences and wants" maximising is reasonable, but sadists' preferences are discounted and "certain intentional killings, frauds" excluded (NLNR V.6).
  • Nozick's experience machine (NLNR 95): against pleasure as the point of it all, a sensible person "would not choose to plug into the experience machine at all": "one wants to do certain things". QUALIFY Liu: the class split about 14–10, so intuition is a fragile proof; Finnis needs only that turning goods into units of pleasure loses something (W4).
  • STEELMAN Efficiency is "a real requirement" (V.6), so [healthcare savings] matter; but life is a basic good, not a cost to net off.
5.5 From person to state transpose to the state; common good; minimal framework; online falsehoods; closer to liberalism
  1. Finnis's common good is "a set of conditions" enabling members "to attain for themselves reasonable objectives" (NLNR 155).
  2. A state is no ship bound for one port: "Committing oneself to a life-plan is not at all like setting oneself to bake a cake" (NLNR 155).
  3. Yet it is "definite enough to exclude a considerable number of types of political arrangement, laws, etc." (155), so [almost no guidance] understates Finnis.
  • LEGISLATOR Liu's working summary†: law is a framework; facilitate the goods; never intend to damage them; may prohibit acts that do; then prudence (hate speech, fake news), weighing chilling effects "in particular places"†.
  • CONCEDE Finnis is less liberal than he looks: we must "favour the basic forms of good and ... discourage their contraries" (NLNR V.4). Concede non-neutrality; the state still keeps only peace and justice (Abortion 77).
5.6 Human nature: urges or ends? human nature; follow nature; urges; live in the moment
  1. "Following nature" can mean obeying urges or pursuing ends; the Stoics saw man as having "natural essences or ends", known by "the reflective intellect" (Harris 7).
  2. Finnis infers nothing from urges: many, like "the urge to gratuitous cruelty", answer to no good, and there is "no inference from fact to value" (NLNR 91, 85).
  3. So [law should give people what they want] mistakes urges for goods: it is "unreasonable to live merely from moment to moment, following immediate cravings" (NLNR V.2).
  • Seligman and Tierney: minds built for prospection fit the life-plan judged from one's death, but cannot ground it. Liu: the plan sets policies (greens at every meal), not a deathbed test for each lunch (W4); Finnis borrows Rawls's "rational plan of life" (V.2).
  • CONCEDE Harris: reflecting on inclinations, "are not assumptions of fact about human nature inevitably going to form part of the content of the reflection?" (Harris 15). Concede the mixture: Harris still calls it "reasoning" (16).
5.7 Finnis tested critically evaluate; self-evident; who decides; is gambling play?
  1. Finnis's weak points are method and the seventh requirement: self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing, and the means/side-effect line is "artificial" (Liu, W4–5); and accessible is not accepted (is [casino gambling] play?).
  2. He replies that there is "no magic in the number seven" (NLNR 92), and that dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", not "perfectly reasonable" (Abortion 84).
  3. So concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what [the state] may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
Conclusion Finnis therefore gives legislators real limits: never intend to destroy a basic good, never treat one as worthless, and secure conditions in which each citizen pursues his own plan. Beyond that, [the issue] calls for prudence; and since his self-evidence rests on contested intuitions and his means/side-effect line is, for Liu, artificial, disagreement about the goods counsels restraint in coercion. The statement is [overstated]: Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them.

1Start here: archetype 5 in plain English

Archetype 5 asks: what can John Finnis's natural law tell a law-maker? Finnis says some things are good for every human being (life, knowledge, friendship and so on), and that there are rules for pursuing them reasonably. The statements in this family usually push one of two extremes. Either Finnis's theory is a blueprint that tells the state how everyone must live, or it is so vague it gives no guidance at all. Your answer takes the middle path: Finnis sets a few firm limits (never deliberately destroy a basic good), and leaves the rest to sensible judgement, where reasonable people can differ.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Basic goodsSeven things worth having for their own sake: life, knowledge, play, beauty, friendship, practical reasonableness, and "religion" (thinking about life's ultimate meaning).
Self-evidentYou see it's good just by thinking about why you do things. It isn't worked out from facts about nature.
IncommensurableCan't be measured on one scale. You can't say how many units of friendship equal one unit of knowledge.
Pre-moralThe goods on their own don't tell you what's right. Morality only comes in with the nine requirements.
Practical reasonablenessUsing good sense in your choices. It is both one of the goods and the name for Finnis's nine requirements.
The nine requirementsFinnis's rules for choosing well: have a plan, don't play favourites, don't be fanatical, keep commitments, be efficient within reason, never act directly against a good, serve the common good, follow your conscience.
Double effect / side effectThe difference between aiming at a harm and accepting it as a foreseen side effect of aiming at something else.
Common goodFor Finnis, not one shared life-plan but the conditions that let everyone pursue their own goals reasonably.
PrudencePractical judgement about the best way to act in particular circumstances.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says Finnis gives legislators "real limits" and "leaves much to prudence". Put simply: Finnis rules some laws out completely, but for most questions he tells legislators to use good judgement, and he accepts that sensible people will reach different answers.

The Intro says: the statement assumes a theory of the good must either dictate how people live or say nothing useful. Finnis offers a third path: seven goods and nine requirements give a few absolute limits (such as never intending to kill an innocent person), and a common good that is a framework, not a life-plan. The Conclusion says: Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them. And because his "self-evident" goods rest on contested intuitions, disagreement about them counsels caution before using the law to force them.

The seven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
5.1"Finnis's goods are just his taste; someone must rank them."They're self-evident on reflection, and none ranks above another. Each person ranks them in their own life-plan, not the state.
5.2"The nine requirements are for individuals, not legislatures."Most of them carry over to a legislature, though a state has no single life-plan.
5.3"Just count the lives: shoot one hostage to save ten."Never deliberately destroy a basic good. Aiming at a death differs from accepting it as a side effect.
5.4"Aim at the greatest happiness."Goods can't be added up on one scale, so "maximise the total" makes no sense outside narrow technical problems.
5.5"Finnis's common good is a plan for everyone (or no guidance at all)."It's a framework of conditions, not one destination. But it still rules out many laws.
5.6"Follow nature; give people what they want."Following urges isn't following nature. A craving for cruelty answers to no good.
5.7"Critically evaluate Finnis."His weak spots are self-evidence and the side-effect line. Reasonable disagreement limits what the state may force.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Finnis gives a few hard limits plus a framework; inside it, prudence and reasonable disagreement.

2The big picture: Finnis's new natural law

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of a good life as a garden with seven kinds of plant: health, learning, play, beauty, friendship, wisdom in choosing, and a sense of meaning. You can't grow them all equally; you choose. But nine gardening rules tell you how to choose well (plan, don't play favourites, don't obsess, keep promises, don't waste, never deliberately trample a plant, help the neighbourhood garden, follow your conscience). A government is like the council that keeps the shared paths and water running so everyone can garden. It doesn't tell you what to plant.

John Finnis's Natural Law and Natural Rights (NLNR) rebuilds natural law without deriving "ought" from facts about nature. Three layers:

Layer 1: the seven basic goods

The seven basic goods
▤ NLNR 85–97; W4 slide 3†
  1. 1Life (health, survival, procreation).
  2. 2Knowledge (for its own sake).
  3. 3Play (activity enjoyed for itself).
  4. 4Aesthetic experience (beauty).
  5. 5Sociability (friendship).
  6. 6Practical reasonableness (bringing intelligence to one's choices).
  7. 7"Religion" (concern with the ultimate order of things; "agnostic or negative" answers count, NLNR 89).

They are self-evident: grasped by anyone who reflects on why they act, not inferred from facts ("there is no inference from fact to value", NLNR 85). They are pre-moral: on their own they don't yet say what is right. And they are incommensurable: "there is no objective hierarchy amongst them" (NLNR 92).

Layer 2: the nine requirements of practical reasonableness

These turn goods into morality. All nine bind together, each "fundamental, underived, irreducible" (V.1):

#RequirementIn a sentence
1Coherent plan of lifeDon't live moment to moment
2No arbitrary preference among valuesDon't dismiss any basic good as worthless
3No arbitrary preference among personsThe Golden Rule
4DetachmentNo fanatical commitment to one project
5CommitmentKeep faith with your commitments
6Efficiency, within reasonConsequences matter, but only within limits
7Respect every basic value in every actNever choose directly against a basic good
8The common goodFavour and foster the common good of your communities
9Follow your conscienceAct on your own reasonable judgement

Layer 3: the common good and the state

The common good is "a set of conditions" enabling members "to attain for themselves reasonable objectives" (NLNR 155). The state's role is "not ... to make people integrally good but only to maintain peace and justice" (Abortion 77), on principles "accessible to all people whatever their religious beliefs" (78).

35.1 Goods and priorities

▤ On your sheet: 5.1 Goods and priorities (word for word)
5.1 Goods and priorities basic goods; obviously good; just taste; rank the goods; golfer
  1. Finnis's seven basic goods are self-evident, not inferred: anyone reflecting on why he acts can grasp [knowledge] as good "in itself" (NLNR 85–86).
  2. The goods are "all equally fundamental, though you can prioritise"†: "there is no objective hierarchy amongst them" (NLNR 92).
  3. So life-plans, not the state, rank the goods, and [the state must do the ranking] does not follow.
  • Golfer: passing a drowning stranger is "indifference to the good of others whom one could easily help" (NLNR V.4).
  • Seven goods (W4 slide 3†): life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness, "religion" ("agnostic or negative" answers count, NLNR 89). Pre-moral: morality comes with the nine requirements (V.1). Liu's test: strip out every use to the other goods; is something left (W4)?
