★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Is knowledge more important than friendship? Finnis says there's no fixed ranking: each is basic. A scholar might put knowledge first, a parent family first. That's fine. Ranking happens in each person's life-plan, not by the state.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Finnis's basic goods are just his personal taste. And someone has to decide which goods matter most."

  1. Not taste: self-evident. Ask yourself why you're doing something, and keep asking. You end up at things like knowledge or friendship, which you see are good in themselves. They're not worked out from facts.
  2. No fixed ranking. Finnis says all seven goods are "equally fundamental", though each person can put some first. There's "no objective hierarchy".
  3. So the ranking is done in each person's life-plan, not by the state. "The state must rank them" doesn't follow.

The extras: the golfer who walks past a drowning stranger to make his tee time shows the limit: you can prioritise your goods, but not by treating someone else's life as nothing. Liu's test for a basic good: take away everything it's useful for; is anything left that's worth having?

Remember: self-evident, unranked, ranked by each person's plan.

The statements. "Finnis's 'basic goods' are just his taste." "The goods must be ranked." "Obviously some goods matter more."

The move.

  1. The seven goods are self-evident, not inferred: anyone reflecting on why they act can grasp knowledge as good "in itself" (NLNR 85–86).
  2. The goods are "all equally fundamental, though you can prioritise"†: "there is no objective hierarchy amongst them" (NLNR 92).
  3. So life-plans, not the state, rank the goods, and "the state must do the ranking" does not follow.

Liu's test (W4): strip out every use a candidate good has for the other goods; is something left? If so, it may be basic. Liu's further points: gossip is low-grade knowledge (NLNR 84–85); suicide shows life's deprivation, not its rejection; lacking a good does not unmake it; pleasure is an aspect, not the point (96–97).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The golfer (NLNR V.4)

A golfer passes a drowning stranger to keep a tee time. Finnis calls this "indifference to the good of others whom one could easily help". It breaches requirement (3) (no arbitrary preference among persons): you can prioritise your goods, but not by treating others' lives as nothing.

45.2 The nine requirements as structure

▤ On your sheet: 5.2 The nine requirements as structure (word for word)
5.2 The nine requirements as structure plan of life; detachment; commitment; efficiency; transpose to a legislature
  1. Nine requirements of practical reasonableness structure the pursuit of goods, and most transpose to [a legislature], though a state has no single life-plan (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, each "fundamental, underived, irreducible" (V.1), though to Liu they read as prudent advice: neglecting (4) or (5) looks unwise rather than immoral (W5).
  • (1) Coherent plan of life; (2) no arbitrary preference among values, (3) or persons (Golden Rule); (4) detachment: no fanatical policy; (5) commitment: keep faith; (6) efficiency within reason (5.4); (7) respect every basic value in every act (5.3); (8) common good (5.5); (9) conscience.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The nine requirements are like the rules of a good kitchen: plan your menu, don't waste, don't ruin any ingredient on purpose, cook for others fairly. A government kitchen can follow most of the same rules, though it doesn't cook one meal for everyone.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The question, in everyday words: "Finnis's nine requirements are written for one person living their life. Can a parliament use them?"

  1. Mostly yes. The requirements organise how goods are pursued, and most carry over to a legislature: make coherent policy, don't treat citizens unequally without reason, don't pursue one goal fanatically, be efficient, never authorise acts aimed at destroying a basic good, serve the common good. The one that doesn't fit neatly is the single life-plan, since a country has millions of plans (5.5).
  2. All nine count together, and Finnis says none comes from another. Liu's doubt: some, like not being fanatical (4) or keeping commitments (5), sound more like sensible advice than morality. Neglecting them seems unwise, not wicked.

Remember: the nine requirements are a structure a legislature can borrow, minus the single life-plan.

The question. "Most of Finnis's requirements are framed for an individual. Can they guide a legislature?" (Practice Q52.)

The move.

  1. Nine requirements structure the pursuit of goods, and most transpose to a legislature, though a state has no single life-plan (5.5).
  2. All nine bind together, each "fundamental, underived, irreducible" (V.1). To Liu, though, some read as prudent advice: neglecting detachment (4) or commitment (5) looks unwise rather than immoral (W5).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Transposing to a legislature
  • (1) Plan: coherent legislative programmes, not knee-jerk laws.
  • (3) No arbitrary preference among persons: bars arbitrary distinctions between citizens (15.4).
  • (4) Detachment: no fanatical policy (one goal pursued at any cost).
  • (6) Efficiency: cost–benefit within limits.
  • (7) Respect every basic value: never authorise acts that intend to destroy a basic good.
  • (8) Common good: facilitate conditions for all.

55.3 Absolutes and double effect

▤ On your sheet: 5.3 Absolutes and double effect (word for word)
5.3 Absolutes and double effect shoot one hostage; scientist; a foreseen death is just as dead
  1. The seventh requirement yields absolutes, such as never taking life "directly as a means" (Harris 15), so [shooting one hostage to free ten] is barred.
  2. Acts are individuated primarily by intention: damaging a good as means or end differs from damaging it as a side effect, but plans cannot be characterised "ad lib" (NLNR V.7).
  3. So [a foreseen death is just as dead] misses the point: side effects are judged too, by fairness and commitments, not by a sum.
  • Scientist†: intending only knowledge, he takes a living person's heart; even as a side effect, the death is "impermissible because unfair".
  • Pregnancy cases† (applied): chemotherapy or removing a cancerous womb treats the mother, death a side effect; direct termination intends it; pre-eclampsia is hard (my reading).
  • QUALIFY Liu: the line is "honestly pretty artificial": out of step with intuitions (odd for the self-evident), a poor guide facing an attacker, and a heavy limit on autonomy, since consent cures nothing (W5).
  • TRAP Double effect is Aquinas's; for Finnis the casuists' doctrines "are not themselves the principles of practical reasonableness" (V.7). Intention, not foresight: a certain death can be a side effect (W4 slide 9†).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Two doctors. One gives a patient a strong painkiller to ease pain, knowing it may shorten life. The other gives an overdose in order to end life. Both patients die. Finnis says the acts are different: the first doctor aims at relieving pain and accepts the death as a side effect; the second aims at death. The seventh requirement forbids aiming at the destruction of a basic good, but it judges side effects differently.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Morality is about results. If shooting one hostage frees ten, shoot. If one person's heart could save thousands, take it."

  1. Requirement 7 sets absolute limits. Never take a life directly as a means to something else. So shooting one hostage to free ten is ruled out.
  2. What you intend defines the act. Damaging a good on purpose (as your aim or your method) is different from damaging it as a side effect. But you can't just redescribe your plan however suits you.
  3. So "a foreseen death is just as dead" misses the point. Side effects are still judged, by fairness and by your commitments, but not by adding up totals.

The extras: the scientist who takes a living person's heart for research does wrong even if he says the death is a side effect: it's unfair (would he accept it if he were the victim?). QUALIFY (Liu): the aim/side-effect line feels "pretty artificial" and doesn't help much when facing an attacker. TRAP: double effect is Aquinas's doctrine, not Finnis's principle, and a certain death can still be a side effect.

Remember: requirement 6 weighs consequences; requirement 7 can veto.

The statement. "Morality is about outcomes, and a decent person simply counts the lives at stake. If a gunman will release ten hostages once you shoot one of them, you should shoot; and a scientist who could save thousands by removing one person's heart should do so." (Practice Q38.)

The move.

  1. The seventh requirement yields absolutes, such as never taking life "directly as a means" (Harris 15), so shooting one hostage to free ten is barred.
  2. Acts are individuated primarily by intention: damaging a good as means or end differs from damaging it as a side effect, but plans cannot be characterised "ad lib" (NLNR V.7).
  3. So "a foreseen death is just as dead" misses the point: side effects are judged too, by fairness and commitments, not by a sum.

The scientist†: intending only knowledge, he takes a living person's heart; even if the death were a side effect, it is "impermissible because unfair" (the Golden Rule check).

Framework 15.3: is this act permissible?
▤ NLNR V.7; Harris 15
  1. 1Which basic good is pursued?
  2. 2Is a basic good damaged as end or means? Then wrong: "Do not choose directly against a basic value."
  3. 3Side effects must pass the golden rule: "would I ... have thought the act reasonable had I been the person harmed?" Intended damage: never. Side effects: only if fair.
Liu's rulings
▤ 15.3; W5
  1. 1Barred: shooting the hostage (even a volunteer); pushing the man off the footbridge; self-injury for insurance; the death penalty ("even if it's Hitler"); euthanasia; suicide.
  2. 2Permitted or arguable: switching the trolley; triage; a lung-damaging mining job; shooting to disarm with death foreseen.
  3. 3Requirement (6) weighs; requirement (7) vetoes.
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Liu thinks the means/side-effect line is "honestly pretty artificial": out of step with intuitions (odd for something meant to be self-evident), a poor guide when facing an attacker, and a heavy limit on autonomy, since consent cures nothing (W5).

⚠ TRAP
Two traps
  1. Double effect is Aquinas's doctrine; for Finnis the casuists' doctrines "are not themselves the principles of practical reasonableness" (V.7).
  2. Intention, not foresight: a death can be certain and still a side effect (W4 slide 9†).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Pregnancy cases† (applied; the sheet marks this "my reading")

Chemotherapy, or removing a cancerous womb, treats the mother; the unborn child's death is a side effect. A direct termination intends the death. Pre-eclampsia is hard.

65.4 Against utilitarianism

▤ On your sheet: 5.4 Against utilitarianism (word for word)
5.4 Against utilitarianism greatest happiness; whatever makes them happy; maximise preferences; healthcare savings
  1. Finnis calls [the greatest happiness] "intrinsically incoherent and senseless" outside "limited technical contexts": goods are incommensurable, so act- and rule-utilitarianism are "not so much false as senseless" (NLNR 154; V.6).
  2. So maximising [satisfied preferences] is reasonable only inside the other requirements, as efficiency, and never as the measure of right.
  • "Over a wide range of preferences and wants" maximising is reasonable, but sadists' preferences are discounted and "certain intentional killings, frauds" excluded (NLNR V.6).
  • Nozick's experience machine (NLNR 95): against pleasure as the point of it all, a sensible person "would not choose to plug into the experience machine at all": "one wants to do certain things". QUALIFY Liu: the class split about 14–10, so intuition is a fragile proof; Finnis needs only that turning goods into units of pleasure loses something (W4).
  • STEELMAN Efficiency is "a real requirement" (V.6), so [healthcare savings] matter; but life is a basic good, not a cost to net off.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Utilitarianism says: add up all the happiness, pick the biggest total. Finnis says you can't add apples, music and friendship into one number. There's no common unit. So "maximise the total good" isn't just wrong, it's meaningless, except for small technical problems.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Laws should aim at the greatest happiness of the greatest number. A good system gives people whatever makes them happy. Smokers save the health system money."

  1. Finnis says that's not just wrong but meaningless. The goods can't be measured in one unit, so you can't add them up and find the "biggest total". Outside narrow technical problems, maximising makes no sense.
  2. So satisfying preferences is fine inside the other requirements, as part of being efficient (requirement 6). It can never be the test of what's right.

The extras: maximising is fine across a wide range of ordinary wants, but sadists' preferences don't count and some acts (intentional killing, fraud) are off the table. The experience machine: most people wouldn't plug into a machine that fakes perfect experiences, because we want to do things, not just feel them. Liu notes his class split 14–10 on this, so it's a weak proof. On smokers: efficiency matters, but life is a basic good, not a cost to subtract.

Remember: efficiency yes, as one requirement; maximising the total, no.

The statements. "Lawmakers should aim at the greatest happiness of the greatest number." (Q30) "A good legal system gives people whatever makes them happy." (Q37) "Smokers save the healthcare system money." (Q35)

The move.

  1. Finnis calls the greatest happiness "intrinsically incoherent and senseless" outside "limited technical contexts": the goods are incommensurable, so act- and rule-utilitarianism are "not so much false as senseless" (NLNR 154; V.6).
  2. So maximising satisfied preferences is reasonable only inside the other requirements, as efficiency (requirement 6), and never as the measure of right.

Detail. "Over a wide range of preferences and wants" maximising is reasonable, but sadists' preferences are discounted and "certain intentional killings, frauds" excluded (NLNR V.6).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The experience machine (NLNR 95)

Nozick imagines a machine that gives you any experience you want while you float in a tank. Against pleasure as the point of it all, Finnis says a sensible person "would not choose to plug into the experience machine at all": "one wants to do certain things".

QUALIFY (Liu, W4): the class split about 14–10, so intuition is a fragile proof. Finnis needs only that turning goods into units of pleasure loses something.

STEELMAN. Efficiency is "a real requirement" (V.6), so healthcare savings matter; but life is a basic good, not a cost to net off (the smokers argument, Q35).

75.5 From person to state

▤ On your sheet: 5.5 From person to state (word for word)
5.5 From person to state transpose to the state; common good; minimal framework; online falsehoods; closer to liberalism
  1. Finnis's common good is "a set of conditions" enabling members "to attain for themselves reasonable objectives" (NLNR 155).
  2. A state is no ship bound for one port: "Committing oneself to a life-plan is not at all like setting oneself to bake a cake" (NLNR 155).
  3. Yet it is "definite enough to exclude a considerable number of types of political arrangement, laws, etc." (155), so [almost no guidance] understates Finnis.
  • LEGISLATOR Liu's working summary†: law is a framework; facilitate the goods; never intend to damage them; may prohibit acts that do; then prudence (hate speech, fake news), weighing chilling effects "in particular places"†.
  • CONCEDE Finnis is less liberal than he looks: we must "favour the basic forms of good and ... discourage their contraries" (NLNR V.4). Concede non-neutrality; the state still keeps only peace and justice (Abortion 77).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A family can agree on one holiday destination. A country can't: millions of people want different lives. So Finnis's state doesn't pick a destination. It builds the roads, keeps them safe and fair, and bans driving people off cliffs. That still rules out a lot of bad laws.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Finnis's common good means the state plans everyone's life" or "it's so vague it gives almost no guidance" or "it's really just liberalism".

  1. The common good is a set of conditions, not a destination. It means the conditions that let people reach their own reasonable goals.
  2. A state isn't a ship heading to one port. Finnis says committing to a life-plan is nothing like baking a cake to a recipe.
  3. But it isn't empty either. It's definite enough to rule out many kinds of laws and political systems. So "almost no guidance" undersells Finnis.

The extras: LEGISLATOR: Liu's summary: law is a framework; help people pursue the goods; never aim to damage them; you may ban acts that do; then use good judgement (on hate speech or fake news, think about chilling effects in the particular place). CONCEDE: Finnis is less liberal than he looks: the state should favour the goods and discourage their opposites. It is not neutral, but its job is still only peace and justice.

Remember: framework, not blueprint, but a framework with teeth.

The statements. "Finnis's common good transposes to the state as a plan for everyone's life." "It gives almost no guidance." "It is closer to liberalism than Finnis admits." (Q47, Q53)

The move.

  1. Finnis's common good is "a set of conditions" enabling members "to attain for themselves reasonable objectives" (NLNR 155).
  2. A state is no ship bound for one port: "Committing oneself to a life-plan is not at all like setting oneself to bake a cake" (NLNR 155).
  3. Yet it is "definite enough to exclude a considerable number of types of political arrangement, laws, etc." (155), so "almost no guidance" understates Finnis.
Liu's working summary for legislators
▤ W4 slides 11–12†; 15.4
  1. 1Law is a framework.
  2. 2Facilitate the goods.
  3. 3Never intend to damage them.
  4. 4May prohibit acts that do.
  5. 5Then prudence: e.g. hate speech, fake news, weighing chilling effects "in particular places".
Framework 15.4: may the state legislate this?
▤ Abortion 77–84; Liu W5
  1. 1Two uses: judge laws directly (authorising an act against a good is wrong) and judge facilitation; coordination counts (driving on one side of the road).
  2. 2Aim: "peace and justice", not making people "integrally good".
  3. 3Means: never intend damage to a good; may prohibit acts that intend it.
  4. 4Reasons "accessible to all people whatever their religious beliefs".
  5. 5Prudence: non-enforcement can be reasonable, to avoid "a war that one cannot win" (84).

CONCEDE. Finnis is less liberal than he looks: we must "favour the basic forms of good and ... discourage their contraries" (NLNR V.4). Concede non-neutrality; the state still keeps only peace and justice (Abortion 77).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Applying it: online falsehoods (POFMA)

Knowledge is a basic good, and falsehoods corrupt it, so the state may act against deliberate falsehood. But the means are a matter of prudence: a broad law may chill true speech and so damage the very good it protects. Finnis gives a limit (never intend to damage knowledge) and a direction (protect the conditions for knowledge), then leaves the fine-tuning to prudence: guidance, not dictation.

85.6 Human nature: urges or ends?

▤ On your sheet: 5.6 Human nature: urges or ends? (word for word)
5.6 Human nature: urges or ends? human nature; follow nature; urges; live in the moment
  1. "Following nature" can mean obeying urges or pursuing ends; the Stoics saw man as having "natural essences or ends", known by "the reflective intellect" (Harris 7).
  2. Finnis infers nothing from urges: many, like "the urge to gratuitous cruelty", answer to no good, and there is "no inference from fact to value" (NLNR 91, 85).
  3. So [law should give people what they want] mistakes urges for goods: it is "unreasonable to live merely from moment to moment, following immediate cravings" (NLNR V.2).
  • Seligman and Tierney: minds built for prospection fit the life-plan judged from one's death, but cannot ground it. Liu: the plan sets policies (greens at every meal), not a deathbed test for each lunch (W4); Finnis borrows Rawls's "rational plan of life" (V.2).
  • CONCEDE Harris: reflecting on inclinations, "are not assumptions of fact about human nature inevitably going to form part of the content of the reflection?" (Harris 15). Concede the mixture: Harris still calls it "reasoning" (16).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Follow your nature" could mean "do what you crave right now" or "become what you're capable of being". Finnis means the second. A craving to be cruel is natural in one sense, but it doesn't point to anything good.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Follow human nature. Law should give people what they naturally want. Live in the moment."

  1. "Follow nature" can mean two things: obey your urges, or pursue what humans are capable of. The older natural lawyers meant the second, worked out by thinking.
  2. Finnis takes nothing from urges. Some urges, like gratuitous cruelty, point at no good at all, and you can't get values from facts anyway.
  3. So "give people what they want" mistakes cravings for goods. Finnis says it is unreasonable to live moment to moment, following whatever you crave.

The extras: Seligman and Tierney's research says our minds are built to plan ahead. That fits Finnis's life-plan but can't prove it. Liu: a life-plan sets general policies ("vegetables at every meal"), not a deathbed test for every lunch. CONCEDE (Harris): when you reflect on what you're drawn to, facts about human nature probably creep in. Admit the mix; it's still reasoning.

Remember: urges aren't goods.

The statements. "Follow nature." "Law should give people what their nature wants." "We should live in the moment." (Q37, Q45)

The move.

  1. "Following nature" can mean obeying urges or pursuing ends; the Stoics saw man as having "natural essences or ends", known by "the reflective intellect" (Harris 7).
  2. Finnis infers nothing from urges: many, like "the urge to gratuitous cruelty", answer to no good, and there is "no inference from fact to value" (NLNR 91, 85).
  3. So "law should give people what they want" mistakes urges for goods: it is "unreasonable to live merely from moment to moment, following immediate cravings" (NLNR V.2).

Seligman and Tierney (card 14.9; summary only, so paraphrase): our minds are built for prospection, pulled by ends rather than pushed by the past. That fits Finnis's planner (requirement 1) but cannot ground it: it is an illustration, never a proof. Liu: the life-plan sets policies (greens at every meal), not a deathbed test for each lunch (W4); Finnis borrows Rawls's "rational plan of life" (V.2).

CONCEDE (Harris). Reflecting on inclinations, "are not assumptions of fact about human nature inevitably going to form part of the content of the reflection?" (Harris 15). Concede the mixture; Harris still calls it "reasoning" (16).

95.7 Finnis tested

▤ On your sheet: 5.7 Finnis tested (word for word)
5.7 Finnis tested critically evaluate; self-evident; who decides; is gambling play?
  1. Finnis's weak points are method and the seventh requirement: self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing, and the means/side-effect line is "artificial" (Liu, W4–5); and accessible is not accepted (is [casino gambling] play?).
  2. He replies that there is "no magic in the number seven" (NLNR 92), and that dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", not "perfectly reasonable" (Abortion 84).
  3. So concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what [the state] may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Finnis says the goods are obvious. But are they? Is casino gambling "play"? Is it obvious to everyone? If reasonable people disagree, maybe the state should be careful about forcing Finnis's answer on them, even if Finnis is right.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The question, in everyday words: "Critically evaluate Finnis. Is casino gambling 'play'? Is pornography 'aesthetic experience'?"

  1. His weak spots: (a) "self-evident" goods rest on intuitions that may come from upbringing; (b) the aim/side-effect line is, for Liu, "artificial"; (c) a good being accessible to everyone doesn't mean everyone accepts it. Is casino gambling play?
  2. His replies: there's "no magic in the number seven" (the list could change), and people who disagree may simply be mistaken without being blameworthy, not "perfectly reasonable".
  3. So concede to Rawls: even if Finnis is right about what's good, reasonable disagreement limits what the state may force on people.

The example: gambling can be enjoyed for itself (play), but compulsive gambling damages family life and friendships. Finnis's theory doesn't settle it mechanically, which argues for regulating rather than banning.

Remember: Finnis may be right about the good and still have to respect disagreement when it comes to coercion.

The statement. "Critically evaluate Finnis's theory." (Q51: is casino gambling play? Is pornography aesthetic experience?)

The move.

  1. Finnis's weak points are method and the seventh requirement: self-evidence rests on intuitions shaped by upbringing, and the means/side-effect line is "artificial" (Liu, W4–5). And accessible is not accepted: is casino gambling play?
  2. He replies that there is "no magic in the number seven" (NLNR 92), and that dissent may be "inculpably erroneous", not "perfectly reasonable" (Abortion 84).
  3. So concede to Rawls that reasonable disagreement limits what the state may coerce, even where Finnis is right about the good.
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Is casino gambling play?

For: it is an activity people may enjoy for itself. Against: compulsive gambling serves no good and damages others (family life, sociability). Finnis's framework doesn't answer this mechanically: the good is accessible, but whether a particular activity realises it is disputed. That is the "accessible ≠ accepted" gap (1.3(12)), and it counsels restraint in coercion (regulate rather than ban; cf. the casino levy in Q44).

10Putting it together: Practice Q47

"Finnis tells legislators clearly what they must never do but offers them almost no guidance on what they should do."

Instruction: Finnis's theory and at least one illustration such as POFMA or casino gambling.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "never" → absolutes (5.3, 15.3).
  • "almost no guidance" → 5.5 (common good "definite enough to exclude"), 15.4.
  • Hook: concession: the statement is right that the absolutes are clearest; it does not follow that the rest is empty.
  • Distinction: 1.3(12) accessible v accepted, for the self-critique.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement is right that Finnis's clearest teaching is negative: never choose directly against a basic good. It does not follow that he offers almost no guidance, because his common good is a framework "definite enough to exclude a considerable number of types of political arrangement, laws, etc." (NLNR 155). I make three claims: (1) the seventh requirement gives absolute limits; (2) the common good and Liu's working summary give positive direction (facilitate the goods, prohibit acts that intend their destruction); and (3) prudence fills the rest, which is a strength, though contested goods limit how far the state may coerce.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. What never (5.3, 15.3): hostage, scientist; intention, not foresight; Liu's "artificial" critique.
  2. What should (5.5, 15.4): conditions, not a cake; facilitate goods; accessible reasons; POFMA example: knowledge as a good, chilling effects as prudence.
  3. Prudence and its limit (5.7): casino gambling: is it play? accessible ≠ accepted; concede to Rawls that disagreement limits coercion.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

Finnis therefore gives legislators real limits and a real direction: never intend to destroy a basic good, never treat one as worthless, and secure conditions in which each citizen pursues his own plan. Beyond that he leaves room for prudence, which is guidance of the right kind for a pluralist state. The statement is overstated: Finnis guides law-makers without dictating to them.

Archetype 5 on one card

LESSON 6 · ARCHETYPE 6 · ABOUT 47 MIN · 40 QUESTIONS

Pluralist legislation: Rawls v Finnis

⚡ BIG IDEA

No law on a contested issue is neutral. Its reasons must be accessible to every citizen (Rawls's discipline), sound on the merits (Finnis and TSH) and prudently fitted to circumstances.

ARCHETYPE 6 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
6 Pluralist legislation: Rawls v Finnis
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position No law on [the issue] is neutral; its reasons must be accessible to every citizen, sound on the merits and fitted to circumstances.
Intro The statement asks [Parliament] to [take no side / rest only on grounds every citizen shares]. Rawls rightly requires reasons each citizen could accept, but his neutrality is of justification, not outcome: [permitting X] still takes a moral side. I argue that [accessible is not accepted / process rests on substance]: a law's reasons must be open to all, sound and prudently fitted to circumstances.
6.1 Rawls grounds every citizen can share; majority; civility
  1. Rawls asks more than [a majority], less than unanimity: power is legitimate only under constitutional essentials all citizens "may reasonably be expected to endorse" (PL 137).
  2. Public reason binds judges "more strictly", officials, candidates and citizens voting as if legislators (PRR 133–36), on essentials and basic justice "so far as possible" (PL 137–38), never churches or media (PRR 134).
  3. So [civility, not justifications] inverts Rawls: civility is a moral duty to justify, though when officials and citizens follow public reason, the majority's enactment is "legitimate law" (PRR 135–37).
  • AGAINST Finnis's dilemma (W5b slide 3†): read predictively, the test gives "a particularly gross form of veto" (Abortion 79); read normatively, it judges merits, as calling rationalist believers "mistaken" does (80).
  • QUALIFY TSH: Rawls "surely does not mean to equate public reason with majority views", so must show pro-choice votes not unreasonable (Religion 528); Finnis: "sheer power of numbers" (14.10).
  • Basis: Rawls's deepest divide: one reasonable good (Plato to Aquinas, "the dominant tradition", PL 134–35) v reasonable pluralism; power is "the power of free and equal citizens as a collective body" (136).
6.2 Not neutral takes no side; neutral fact
  1. That [the state takes no side] is a moral position: even Rawls concedes that "our actions nevertheless imply" a view on salvation (PL 153).
  2. Even its filter is moral: "unreasonable" means refusing fair terms, not being false, and who counts as reasonable is the dispute (6.11).
  3. So [neutrality] is unattainable: even MOE's "secular" sexuality curriculum "reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family" (Masagos, 2022).
  • AGAINST Finnis on method: the thin theory is "arbitrary", a "radical emaciation of human good" (NLNR V.3); what the Original Position rejects is not thereby unjust (V.4).
  • TRAP A doctrine holding "outside the church there is no salvation" may be true; it is unreasonable because it "proposes to use the public's political power" to enforce it (PL 138). Tolerance need not be a tenet, only not hostile to reciprocity (Liu, W6).
  • AGAINST Slide 9†: liberal neutrality favours doctrines already "institutionally and socially reinforced"; Rawls: "itself a moral conception" (PL 147).
6.3 OC v modus vivendi what the faiths share; overlap of convictions; modus vivendi
  1. [Legislating what the faiths share] is Devlin's shared morality, not Rawls's OC: a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice.
  2. Each affirms it on its own moral grounds, so it holds "regardless of shifts in the distribution of political power", as a modus vivendi cannot (PL 148).
  3. So OC is no [modus vivendi in philosophical dress], though "reasonable" decides who belongs.
  • QUALIFY Finnis: pro-choice writers share no view of the unborn, so there is no "overlapping consensus" except in the result (Abortion 91).
  • OC is on principles, not reasons: the Golden Rule, held as divine teaching or as reciprocity (Liu, W5); secular doctrines join too (Kant, Mill: PL 145). Tolerance works outside the overlap: I may be right, yet legislating it would be unfair (Liu, W6).
6.4 Sorting reasons whose morality is admissible; four MPs
  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than [whose morality is admissible]: Rawls sorts reasons by kind, Chua by motive, Finnis and TSH by merit.
  2. Rawls treats secular comprehensive arguments "the same way" as religious ones (PRR 148), but admits Catholic common-good views "expressed in terms of political values" (142).
  3. So the lines blur: in TSH's Catch-22, religious reasons would fail Rawls's test while Chua dismissed medical ones as a facade, a test "more far-reaching than Rawls's" (Religion 532).
  • CONCEDE Rawls: merit-sorting rests on disputed premises; TSH replies that process too rests "on substantive values" (Religion 538). Concede: merit settles truth, not coercion (5.7).
  • Liu (W6): a bad reason is not a non-public one, nor a motive the justification; a Kantian's "all lying is wrong" is barred too. Public reason moves with the background culture (PRR 142–43).
6.5 Abortion nobody can say when life begins; stand aside; free not to have one; slavery; compromise
  1. [A permissive law is neutral] fails: Chua said learned men "have not been able to agree", then declared an early conception "is not a human being" (Religion 529–30).
  2. If [nobody can say when life begins], TSH's hunter (after Brown), unsure what moves behind a bush, should not fire (Religion 530).
  3. So [Parliament] cannot stand aside: permission "settles the metaphysical question" (Religion 529); argue for limits from accessible consequences (537–38).
  • Rawls (PL) called a doctrine denying the first-trimester "qualified right" "to that extent unreasonable"; later he said Catholics "need not exercise" it, by then accepting arguments against the right, framed in political values, as public reason: for Finnis, a slave-owner's reply, "mere impudence or thoughtlessness" (Abortion 89; TSH, Religion 527–28).
  • AGAINST TSH: Macedo's "fairly close call" middle is no neutral midpoint but stems from non-cognitivism: a pro-life middle (ban plus aid, easier adoption, penalties on providers not women) "would be rejected by pro-choicers", as she reports Wolfe and George (Religion 534–36).
  • AGAINST Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls: children reared for paedophiles and killed painlessly in their sleep plainly fail it, so he asks "why Rawls draws the boundary of justice, fairness and reciprocity at birth" (Abortion 86), and why "the child a week before birth" faces "the uttermost coercion" (87).
  • CONCEDE TSH: consensus on human worth "does not currently extend to the details of who is entitled to be treated as human" (Religion 538); argue for circumspection, not victory.
  • TRAP Finnis's article is no argument that abortion is wrong (Liu, W6): it tests Rawls's promise of fair terms without settling deep questions. Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is no person, else it would be owed fair terms.
  • Slide 7†: is the unborn a clump of cells? If not, must the woman "house" it (Thomson's violinist)? Either branch settles a moral question; Finnis: Thomson lends such views a "reasonable" status they lack (Abortion 88).
6.6 Finnis for law-makers never v should; rank the goods
  • See 5.
6.7 Religion religious arguments; faith condemns it; exemption
  1. Public reason bars no argument for being religious: the Good Samaritan may be cited if public reasons follow "in due course" (PRR 144, 146).
  2. Finnis's basic good of religion, open to "agnostic or negative" answers (NLNR 89), supports [religious freedom]; Rawls protects it because denying basic liberties "normally" breaks reciprocity (PRR 138).
  3. So [ban it because a faith condemns it] fails, though TSH warns that a "national interest" test may leave religion "little practical impact" (Religion 513).
  • TSH: political values render religious perspectives "nugatory" wherever an issue counts as metaphysical (Religion 515); whether it is political is itself contested (polygamy, 538), as Liu's slide asks: "Is this begging the question?" (W5a slide 7†).
6.8 Whip party discipline; conscience; one clear voice
  1. A whipped House "may not be representative of the majority opinion" (TSH, CJ 96), so [one clear voice] need not show what justice requires.
  2. For TSH, lifting the whip "on certain occasions" is "an option", with each member encouraged to see his role "in deciphering higher law"; another is judicial (CJ 96–97).
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason; treating [s 377A] as "policy", not conscience (Shanmugam, 2022), is itself a moral judgment.
  • Precedent: abortion free votes in 1969 and 1974, "arguably an endorsement" of considering religious perspectives (TSH, Religion 506–07).
6.9 Close make people better
  1. Moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation, but [the law's task is to make people better] overreaches.
6.10 Aim and mechanism equally valid; objectively necessary; wrongdoer; only then; fixed conception of the good life
  1. The statement's aim, not imposing [a fixed conception of the good life], and its harm-to-others mechanism come apart.
  2. The mechanism is neither necessary, since Hart's paternalism answers defective consent, not immorality (7.2), nor neutral: Rawls files Mill's liberalism among comprehensive doctrines (PL 145).
  3. So [the statement] keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism: Finnis supplies substance, Rawls discipline, Hart a presumption against coercion.
  • "Objectively" presupposes realism; "wrongdoer", a wrong; "others", who counts (6.5); "equally valid" defeats itself (4.7).
  • Liu's model (W9): read the sentences as a chain: (2) is the means to (1), and "only then" makes it the only means. Finnis: a range of valid opinions, not one; protecting others is a ground, not the only one. Rawls: "equally valid" a priori, not for unreasonable doctrines; critics: toleration is itself imposed.
6.11 Freestanding yet overriding freestanding; overriding; contradictory
  1. "Freestanding" means derived from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free: the conception is "political (but of course moral)" (PL 140–41).
  2. On essentials and basic justice, political values normally override because they are "very great values", governing "the basic framework of social life" (PL 138–40); reasonable doctrines can support them, and the cooperative virtues are "political capital" (157).
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable, but for dissenters the label "reasonable" does the overriding, and TSH asks what standard grounds it (Religion 516).
  • STEELMAN Masagos echoes Rawls: decisions apply "secular, universal values and not individual religious beliefs" (2022); even Finnis: 14.10.
Conclusion The statement is therefore [wrong / overstated / partly right]. Rawls rightly demands coercion justifiable to every citizen, and his "unreasonable" condemns refusing fair terms, not error; but neutrality cannot deliver it: any law on [the issue] takes a moral side, as Finnis's abortion test case shows. Pluralism asks equal respect for persons, not equal validity for opinions: reasons must be accessible, sound and prudently fitted to circumstances.

1Start here: archetype 6 in plain English

Archetype 6 asks: how should a country make laws when its people hold very different religious and moral views? Rawls says: on basic questions, give reasons every reasonable citizen could accept, not reasons that only make sense inside your own religion or philosophy. Finnis and TSH push back: some reasons are simply better than others, and "taking no side" is itself a side. The statements in this family usually claim that the state can, and should, be neutral. Your answer: no law on a contested issue is neutral. What you can ask is that its reasons are open to everyone, actually good, and sensibly fitted to the situation.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Pluralism / reasonable pluralismA society where free, sensible people end up with different religions and moral views. Rawls thinks this is normal, not a mistake.
Comprehensive doctrineA full worldview covering how to live: a religion, or a philosophy like Kant's or Mill's.
Political conception of justiceA narrower set of shared political values (freedom, equality, fairness) that people of many worldviews can sign up to.
Public reasonArguing for laws on basic questions using those shared political values, so others could reasonably accept your reasons.
ReciprocityOffering reasons you honestly think others could accept, not just understand.
Overlapping consensus (OC)Each worldview supports the same political principles for its own reasons, so the agreement is stable.
Modus vivendiA truce between rivals that lasts only while neither side is strong enough to win.
Reasonable / unreasonableFor Rawls, "unreasonable" means refusing fair terms (wanting state power to impose your worldview), not being false.
Accessible v acceptedA reason can be open to everyone to assess (accessible) without everyone agreeing with it (accepted).

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says no law on the issue "is neutral" and its reasons must be "accessible", "sound" and "fitted to circumstances". Put simply: whatever Parliament does, including doing nothing, takes a moral side. So instead of pretending to be neutral, give reasons anyone can examine, make sure they are good reasons, and apply them sensibly to the facts.

The Intro says: the statement asks Parliament to take no side, or to use only grounds every citizen shares. Rawls is right that reasons should be ones others could accept, but his neutrality is about how a law is justified, not about its result: permitting something still takes a moral side. The Conclusion says: equal respect for persons is not the same as treating every opinion as equally valid.

The blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
6.1"Laws must rest on grounds every citizen shares."Rawls asks more than a majority but less than unanimity: reasons all could reasonably accept. Finnis: that's either a veto or a hidden judgement on merits.
6.2"The state should take no side."Taking no side is a side. Even Rawls admits his view has moral implications.
6.3"OC is just a truce in fancy dress."No: in an OC each side agrees for its own reasons, so it survives shifts in power. A truce doesn't.
6.4"Rawls and Finnis only disagree about whose morality counts."They sort reasons differently: Rawls by kind, some politicians by motive, Finnis and TSH by merit.
6.5"On abortion the state should stand aside."Permitting abortion already answers the hard question. If you're unsure what's behind the bush, don't shoot.
6.7"Religious arguments have no place in law-making."They're allowed if public reasons follow. Religious freedom is protected by both Rawls and Finnis.
6.8"Whipped votes can't discern justice."True that a whipped vote may not reflect opinion; but a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason.
6.9(Short closing blocks; 6.6 points to Lesson 5)Moral truth limits law, but "make people better" goes too far.
6.10Sample Question 1: "treat all opinions as equally valid; ban only harm to others."The aim (don't impose one way of life) is fine; the mechanism is neither necessary nor neutral.
6.11"Rawls's view is freestanding yet overriding: a contradiction."Freestanding means "not built from one worldview", not "value-free". The real issue is who counts as "reasonable".
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Neutral in justification is not neutral in result: every law on a contested issue takes a side, so its reasons must be open, sound and fitted to the facts.

2The big picture: making law for people who disagree

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Five flatmates of different religions share a kitchen. They need house rules. One option: "the majority's religion decides". Rawls says that's unfair: rules about the basics should be justified by reasons everyone could accept as fair, even if they believe different things. Finnis replies: fine, but some reasons are simply better than others, and pretending to take no side is itself taking a side.

This archetype covers statements about how a pluralist society (one with many religions and moral views) should legislate. It is the home of Liu's Sample Question 1. The two main theorists disagree about method, not about whether law needs moral justification.

Rawls: political liberalism

IdeaPlain meaning
Reasonable pluralismFree people reasonably end up with different religious and moral doctrines
Liberal principle of legitimacyPower is legitimate only under constitutional essentials all citizens "may reasonably be expected to endorse" (PL 137)
Public reasonOn essentials and basic justice, justify coercion by political values others could reasonably accept
ReciprocityOffer reasons others "might also reasonably accept", not merely understand
Overlapping consensus (OC)Each reasonable doctrine endorses the political conception for its own reasons
Modus vivendiA truce based on the balance of power: it collapses when power shifts
The provisoReligious or comprehensive reasons may be offered if public reasons follow "in due course"
Reasonable ≠ true"Unreasonable" means refusing fair terms (e.g. seeking to use state power to impose one's doctrine), not being false

Finnis and TSH: the critics

  • Finnis (Abortion, Natural Law, and Public Reason): public reason either gives "a particularly gross form of veto" or secretly judges the merits; it leaves the gravest questions to "sheer power of numbers"; why draw the boundary of reciprocity at birth?
  • TSH (Religion in the Abortion Discourse in Singapore): judge arguments by accessibility and merit, not religious motive; bracketing a metaphysical question already answers it; the "delineation of a political sphere is artificial".

36.1 Rawls

▤ On your sheet: 6.1 Rawls (word for word)
6.1 Rawls grounds every citizen can share; majority; civility
  1. Rawls asks more than [a majority], less than unanimity: power is legitimate only under constitutional essentials all citizens "may reasonably be expected to endorse" (PL 137).
  2. Public reason binds judges "more strictly", officials, candidates and citizens voting as if legislators (PRR 133–36), on essentials and basic justice "so far as possible" (PL 137–38), never churches or media (PRR 134).
  3. So [civility, not justifications] inverts Rawls: civility is a moral duty to justify, though when officials and citizens follow public reason, the majority's enactment is "legitimate law" (PRR 135–37).
  • AGAINST Finnis's dilemma (W5b slide 3†): read predictively, the test gives "a particularly gross form of veto" (Abortion 79); read normatively, it judges merits, as calling rationalist believers "mistaken" does (80).
  • QUALIFY TSH: Rawls "surely does not mean to equate public reason with majority views", so must show pro-choice votes not unreasonable (Religion 528); Finnis: "sheer power of numbers" (14.10).
  • Basis: Rawls's deepest divide: one reasonable good (Plato to Aquinas, "the dominant tradition", PL 134–35) v reasonable pluralism; power is "the power of free and equal citizens as a collective body" (136).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Rawls is not saying "do whatever the majority wants", and he is not saying "only pass laws everyone agrees with". He's in between: on basic questions, give reasons that any reasonable person could accept as fair. If you do that and still lose a vote, the result is legitimate.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Laws must rest only on grounds every citizen can share" and "democracy is just majority rule plus being polite".

  1. Rawls sits between majority rule and unanimity. Power is legitimate only when it follows basic constitutional principles that all citizens could reasonably be expected to accept.
  2. Who has to follow public reason? Judges most strictly; then officials, candidates, and citizens when they vote (as if they were legislators). It applies to basic questions, "so far as possible". It never binds churches or the media.
  3. So "civility, not justification" gets Rawls backwards. For Rawls, civility is the duty to justify. If people do that and the majority still passes a law, it is legitimate.

The extras: AGAINST (Finnis's dilemma): if "could reasonably accept" means "will actually accept", any stubborn group gets a veto; if it means "should accept", Rawls is secretly judging the merits after all. QUALIFY (TSH): Rawls can't just equate public reason with majority views.

Remember: more than a majority, less than unanimity, and Finnis's veto-or-merits dilemma.

The statement. "Laws must rest only on grounds that every citizen can share." (Q36) "Democracy is majority rule plus civility." (Q41)

The move.

  1. Rawls asks more than a majority, less than unanimity: power is legitimate only under constitutional essentials all citizens "may reasonably be expected to endorse" (PL 137).
  2. Public reason binds judges "more strictly", then officials, candidates and citizens voting as if legislators (PRR 133–36), on essentials and basic justice "so far as possible" (PL 137–38); never churches or media (PRR 134).
  3. So "civility, not justifications" inverts Rawls: civility is a moral duty to justify, though when officials and citizens follow public reason, the majority's enactment is "legitimate law" (PRR 135–37).

AGAINST: Finnis's dilemma (W5b slide 3†):

Reading of "may reasonably be expected to endorse"Problem
Predictive (will people actually endorse it?)"a particularly gross form of veto" (Abortion 79): any stubborn group blocks law
Normative (should reasonable people endorse it?)Then it judges the merits, as calling rationalist believers "mistaken" does (80)

QUALIFY. TSH: Rawls "surely does not mean to equate public reason with majority views", so he must show pro-choice votes are not unreasonable (Religion 528). Rawls's deepest divide: one reasonable good (Plato to Aquinas, "the dominant tradition", PL 134–35) v reasonable pluralism. Power is "the power of free and equal citizens as a collective body" (136).

46.2 Not neutral

▤ On your sheet: 6.2 Not neutral (word for word)
6.2 Not neutral takes no side; neutral fact
  1. That [the state takes no side] is a moral position: even Rawls concedes that "our actions nevertheless imply" a view on salvation (PL 153).
  2. Even its filter is moral: "unreasonable" means refusing fair terms, not being false, and who counts as reasonable is the dispute (6.11).
  3. So [neutrality] is unattainable: even MOE's "secular" sexuality curriculum "reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family" (Masagos, 2022).
  • AGAINST Finnis on method: the thin theory is "arbitrary", a "radical emaciation of human good" (NLNR V.3); what the Original Position rejects is not thereby unjust (V.4).
  • TRAP A doctrine holding "outside the church there is no salvation" may be true; it is unreasonable because it "proposes to use the public's political power" to enforce it (PL 138). Tolerance need not be a tenet, only not hostile to reciprocity (Liu, W6).
  • AGAINST Slide 9†: liberal neutrality favours doctrines already "institutionally and socially reinforced"; Rawls: "itself a moral conception" (PL 147).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A referee who "takes no side" still has to decide whether a goal counts. Choosing "no side" is a decision with effects. Even Rawls admits his political liberalism takes a view on some deep questions.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "The state should take no side on how anyone should live."

  1. "Taking no side" is a moral position. Even Rawls admits that what we do politically implies a view on deep questions like salvation.
  2. Even Rawls's filter is moral. He sets aside "unreasonable" views, meaning views that refuse fair terms, not views that are false. But who counts as reasonable is exactly what's in dispute.
  3. So true neutrality can't be achieved. Even Singapore's "secular" sexuality curriculum, a minister said in 2022, reflects the national stance on the family.

The extras: AGAINST: Finnis calls Rawls's thin list of goods "arbitrary", and liberal neutrality tends to favour views that are already dominant. TRAP: for Rawls, a religion saying "no salvation outside the church" might be true; it's only unreasonable if it wants state power to enforce it.

Remember: "no side" is a side.

The statement. "The state should take no side on how anyone should live." (Q42)

The move.

  1. That "the state takes no side" is a moral position: even Rawls concedes that "our actions nevertheless imply" a view on salvation (PL 153).
  2. Even its filter is moral: "unreasonable" means refusing fair terms, not being false, and who counts as reasonable is the dispute (6.11).
  3. So neutrality is unattainable: even MOE's "secular" sexuality curriculum "reflects the national posture on the heterosexual family" (Masagos, 2022).

More.

  • AGAINST (Finnis on method): the thin theory is "arbitrary", a "radical emaciation of human good" (NLNR V.3); what the Original Position rejects is not thereby unjust (V.4).
  • AGAINST (slide 9†): liberal neutrality favours doctrines already "institutionally and socially reinforced"; Rawls himself: it is "itself a moral conception" (PL 147).
⚠ TRAP
Unreasonable ≠ false

A doctrine holding "outside the church there is no salvation" may be true; it is unreasonable only because it "proposes to use the public's political power" to enforce it (PL 138). And tolerance need not be one of a doctrine's tenets; the doctrine just must not be hostile to reciprocity (Liu, W6).

56.3 OC v modus vivendi

▤ On your sheet: 6.3 OC v modus vivendi (word for word)
6.3 OC v modus vivendi what the faiths share; overlap of convictions; modus vivendi
  1. [Legislating what the faiths share] is Devlin's shared morality, not Rawls's OC: a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice.
  2. Each affirms it on its own moral grounds, so it holds "regardless of shifts in the distribution of political power", as a modus vivendi cannot (PL 148).
  3. So OC is no [modus vivendi in philosophical dress], though "reasonable" decides who belongs.
  • QUALIFY Finnis: pro-choice writers share no view of the unborn, so there is no "overlapping consensus" except in the result (Abortion 91).
  • OC is on principles, not reasons: the Golden Rule, held as divine teaching or as reciprocity (Liu, W5); secular doctrines join too (Kant, Mill: PL 145). Tolerance works outside the overlap: I may be right, yet legislating it would be unfair (Liu, W6).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A modus vivendi is two rivals agreeing to a ceasefire because neither can win right now: if one gets stronger, the deal is off. An overlapping consensus is different: each side, for its own deep reasons, believes the deal is right, so it lasts even if power changes.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Rawls's overlapping consensus is really just a truce dressed up in philosophy" or "Parliament should legislate whatever the religions agree on".

  1. "Legislate what the faiths share" isn't Rawls's idea. That's closer to Devlin's shared morality (Lesson 7). Rawls's OC is agreement on a political idea of justice, not on shared moral rules.
  2. Each worldview supports it for its own reasons. A Christian might back the Golden Rule as God's teaching; a secular person as fairness. Because each side believes in it, it holds even if the balance of power changes. A truce wouldn't.
  3. So OC is not a truce in disguise, though the word "reasonable" decides who gets to be part of it.

The extras: QUALIFY (Finnis): on abortion, pro-choice writers share no view about the unborn; they only agree on the result. Liu: tolerance can work outside the overlap too: "I might be right, but forcing it on others by law would be unfair."

Remember: a truce lasts while power is balanced; an OC lasts because each side believes in it.

The statements. "Rawls's overlapping consensus is nothing more than a modus vivendi in philosophical dress." (Q48) "Legislate what the faiths share." (Q40)

The move.

  1. "Legislating what the faiths share" is Devlin's shared morality, not Rawls's OC: OC is a consensus of reasonable doctrines on a political conception of justice.
  2. Each affirms it on its own moral grounds, so it holds "regardless of shifts in the distribution of political power", as a modus vivendi cannot (PL 148).
  3. So OC is no modus vivendi in philosophical dress, though "reasonable" decides who belongs.

More.

  • QUALIFY (Finnis): pro-choice writers share no view of the unborn, so there is no "overlapping consensus" except in the result (Abortion 91).
  • OC is on principles, not reasons: the Golden Rule, held as divine teaching or as reciprocity (Liu, W5); secular doctrines join too (Kant, Mill: PL 145). Tolerance works outside the overlap: I may be right, yet legislating it would be unfair (Liu, W6).

66.4 Sorting reasons

▤ On your sheet: 6.4 Sorting reasons (word for word)
6.4 Sorting reasons whose morality is admissible; four MPs
  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than [whose morality is admissible]: Rawls sorts reasons by kind, Chua by motive, Finnis and TSH by merit.
  2. Rawls treats secular comprehensive arguments "the same way" as religious ones (PRR 148), but admits Catholic common-good views "expressed in terms of political values" (142).
  3. So the lines blur: in TSH's Catch-22, religious reasons would fail Rawls's test while Chua dismissed medical ones as a facade, a test "more far-reaching than Rawls's" (Religion 532).
  • CONCEDE Rawls: merit-sorting rests on disputed premises; TSH replies that process too rests "on substantive values" (Religion 538). Concede: merit settles truth, not coercion (5.7).
  • Liu (W6): a bad reason is not a non-public one, nor a motive the justification; a Kantian's "all lying is wrong" is barred too. Public reason moves with the background culture (PRR 142–43).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Four MPs oppose a bill. One says "my faith forbids it". One says "it will hurt vulnerable people". One says "it's against human dignity". One quotes a study. Which reasons count? Rawls sorts by kind (political or comprehensive). Some politicians sort by motive (are you secretly religious?). Finnis and TSH sort by merit (is the argument good?).

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Rawls and Finnis agree law needs moral justification; they only disagree about whose morality is allowed" (or a question setting out four MPs' reasons).

  1. They disagree about more than that. They sort reasons in different ways. Rawls sorts by kind (political value or full worldview?). Some politicians, like Chua, sort by motive (is this person secretly religious?). Finnis and TSH sort by merit (is it a good argument?).
  2. Rawls treats secular worldviews the same as religious ones. A Kantian's "all lying is wrong" is barred like a religious argument. But he accepts Catholic arguments if they're put in political terms.
  3. So the lines blur. TSH's Catch-22: religious reasons would fail Rawls's test, while Chua brushed aside medical reasons as a cover. That motive test goes further than Rawls ever did.

The extras: CONCEDE (Rawls's side): judging by merit relies on disputed premises. TSH replies that Rawls's process relies on values too. Concede that merit settles what's true, not what may be forced on people. Liu: a bad reason isn't automatically a non-public one, and a motive isn't the justification.

Remember: kind (Rawls), motive (Chua), merit (Finnis and TSH).

The statements. "Rawls and Finnis agree that law must be morally justified; they disagree only about whose morality is admissible." (Q49) "Four MPs speak …" (Q58)

The move.

  1. Rawls and Finnis differ on more than whose morality is admissible: Rawls sorts reasons by kind, Chua by motive, Finnis and TSH by merit.
  2. Rawls treats secular comprehensive arguments "the same way" as religious ones (PRR 148), but admits Catholic common-good views "expressed in terms of political values" (142).
  3. So the lines blur: in TSH's Catch-22, religious reasons would fail Rawls's test while Chua dismissed medical ones as a façade, a test "more far-reaching than Rawls's" (Religion 532).

CONCEDE (Rawls): merit-sorting rests on disputed premises; TSH replies that process too rests "on substantive values" (Religion 538). Concede: merit settles truth, not coercion (5.7).

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

A bad reason is not a non-public one, nor is a motive the justification. A Kantian's "all lying is wrong" is barred too (it is comprehensive). Public reason moves with the background culture (PRR 142–43) (Liu, W6).

76.5 Abortion

▤ On your sheet: 6.5 Abortion (word for word)
6.5 Abortion nobody can say when life begins; stand aside; free not to have one; slavery; compromise
  1. [A permissive law is neutral] fails: Chua said learned men "have not been able to agree", then declared an early conception "is not a human being" (Religion 529–30).
  2. If [nobody can say when life begins], TSH's hunter (after Brown), unsure what moves behind a bush, should not fire (Religion 530).
  3. So [Parliament] cannot stand aside: permission "settles the metaphysical question" (Religion 529); argue for limits from accessible consequences (537–38).
  • Rawls (PL) called a doctrine denying the first-trimester "qualified right" "to that extent unreasonable"; later he said Catholics "need not exercise" it, by then accepting arguments against the right, framed in political values, as public reason: for Finnis, a slave-owner's reply, "mere impudence or thoughtlessness" (Abortion 89; TSH, Religion 527–28).
  • AGAINST TSH: Macedo's "fairly close call" middle is no neutral midpoint but stems from non-cognitivism: a pro-life middle (ban plus aid, easier adoption, penalties on providers not women) "would be rejected by pro-choicers", as she reports Wolfe and George (Religion 534–36).
  • AGAINST Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls: children reared for paedophiles and killed painlessly in their sleep plainly fail it, so he asks "why Rawls draws the boundary of justice, fairness and reciprocity at birth" (Abortion 86), and why "the child a week before birth" faces "the uttermost coercion" (87).
  • CONCEDE TSH: consensus on human worth "does not currently extend to the details of who is entitled to be treated as human" (Religion 538); argue for circumspection, not victory.
  • TRAP Finnis's article is no argument that abortion is wrong (Liu, W6): it tests Rawls's promise of fair terms without settling deep questions. Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is no person, else it would be owed fair terms.
  • Slide 7†: is the unborn a clump of cells? If not, must the woman "house" it (Thomson's violinist)? Either branch settles a moral question; Finnis: Thomson lends such views a "reasonable" status they lack (Abortion 88).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Someone says: "Nobody knows when life begins, so the law should stay out and let each woman decide." TSH replies with a hunter: if you don't know whether the thing moving behind the bush is a deer or a person, you don't shoot. And a law that lets everyone decide has already decided something: that the unborn may be ended.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "On abortion the state should step back. Nobody can say when life begins, so letting each woman decide imposes nothing on anyone."

  1. A permissive law isn't neutral. In Parliament, Chua said experts couldn't agree, and then declared that an early embryo "is not a human being". That's taking a side.
  2. TSH's hunter: if you aren't sure whether what's moving behind a bush is a deer or a person, you don't fire. Uncertainty argues for caution, not permission.
  3. So Parliament can't stand aside. Allowing abortion "settles the metaphysical question". Argue for limits using reasons everyone can assess, such as consequences.

The extras: Rawls first called denying a first-trimester right "unreasonable", then backed off; Finnis calls that like a slave-owner's reply. Finnis also asks why Rawls's fairness starts at birth: what about the child a week before? CONCEDE (TSH): agreement on human worth doesn't yet extend to who counts as human, so argue for caution, not victory. TRAP: Finnis's article doesn't prove abortion is wrong; it tests Rawls's promise of fair terms.

Remember: permitting is deciding.

The statement. "On abortion, the state's only proper course is to stand aside. Since nobody can say when human life begins, a law leaving the decision to each pregnant woman imposes no view on anyone." (Q43)

The move.

  1. "A permissive law is neutral" fails: Chua said learned men "have not been able to agree", then declared an early conception "is not a human being" (Religion 529–30).
  2. If nobody can say when life begins, TSH's hunter (after Brown), unsure what moves behind a bush, should not fire (Religion 530).
  3. So Parliament cannot stand aside: permission "settles the metaphysical question" (Religion 529); argue for limits from accessible consequences (537–38).

The supporting lines.

  • Rawls's retreat: Rawls (in PL) called a doctrine denying a first-trimester "qualified right" "to that extent unreasonable"; later he said Catholics "need not exercise" it, by then accepting arguments against the right, framed in political values, as public reason. For Finnis, that is like a slave-owner's reply: "mere impudence or thoughtlessness" (Abortion 89; TSH, Religion 527–28).
  • AGAINST (TSH on compromise): Macedo's "fairly close call" middle is no neutral midpoint but stems from non-cognitivism; a pro-life middle (ban plus aid, easier adoption, penalties on providers not women) "would be rejected by pro-choicers" (Religion 534–36).
  • AGAINST (Finnis turns reciprocity on Rawls): children reared for paedophiles and killed painlessly in their sleep plainly fail reciprocity, so why does Rawls draw the boundary of justice "at birth" (Abortion 86), leaving "the child a week before birth" to "the uttermost coercion" (87)?
  • CONCEDE (TSH): consensus on human worth "does not currently extend to the details of who is entitled to be treated as human" (Religion 538); argue for circumspection, not victory.

Finnis's article is not an anti-abortion argument

Liu (W6): Finnis's article tests Rawls's promise of fair terms without settling deep questions. Rawls and Reiman assume the unborn is no person, else it would be owed fair terms. Don't write "Finnis proves abortion is wrong".
