86.6 Finnis for law-makers, and 6.9 Close

▤ On your sheet: 6.6 Finnis for law-makers (word for word)
6.6 Finnis for law-makers never v should; rank the goods
  • See 5.
▤ On your sheet: 6.9 Close (word for word)
6.9 Close make people better
  1. Moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation, but [the law's task is to make people better] overreaches.
🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

These two short blocks, in everyday words:

  • 6.6 is a signpost: questions about what Finnis tells law-makers ("never v should", ranking the goods) are answered in Lesson 5.
  • 6.9 answers "the law's job is to make people good". Moral truth does set limits on law, but that goes too far: even Finnis says the state's job is only to keep peace and justice, not to make people good through and through.

Remember: law has moral limits, not a mission to perfect people.

These two short blocks point elsewhere. 6.6 sends you to archetype 5 (Finnis's "never v should", ranking the goods): see Lesson 5. 6.9 answers "the law's task is to make people better": moral truth, not neutrality, limits legislation, but "make people better" overreaches. Finnis himself says the state's role is "not ... to make people integrally good but only to maintain peace and justice" (Abortion 77).

96.7 Religion

▤ On your sheet: 6.7 Religion (word for word)
6.7 Religion religious arguments; faith condemns it; exemption
  1. Public reason bars no argument for being religious: the Good Samaritan may be cited if public reasons follow "in due course" (PRR 144, 146).
  2. Finnis's basic good of religion, open to "agnostic or negative" answers (NLNR 89), supports [religious freedom]; Rawls protects it because denying basic liberties "normally" breaks reciprocity (PRR 138).
  3. So [ban it because a faith condemns it] fails, though TSH warns that a "national interest" test may leave religion "little practical impact" (Religion 513).
  • TSH: political values render religious perspectives "nugatory" wherever an issue counts as metaphysical (Religion 515); whether it is political is itself contested (polygamy, 538), as Liu's slide asks: "Is this begging the question?" (W5a slide 7†).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Can a religious person argue for a law using their faith? Rawls: yes, as long as you also give reasons others could accept. Finnis: religion (the search for meaning) is itself one of the basic goods, so the state should protect it. Both protect religious freedom, but neither says "ban it because my faith condemns it".

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Religious arguments have no place in making laws" or "ban X because the faith condemns it".

  1. Public reason doesn't ban an argument just for being religious. You may cite the Good Samaritan, as long as you also give public reasons "in due course".
  2. Both theorists protect religious freedom. For Finnis, "religion" (searching for life's meaning, including agnostic answers) is a basic good. For Rawls, denying basic liberties normally breaks reciprocity.
  3. So "ban it because a faith condemns it" fails. But TSH warns that if laws must pass a "national interest" test, religion may end up having little real effect.

The extra: TSH's sharper point: once an issue is labelled "metaphysical", religious views get set aside. But whether something is political or metaphysical is itself disputed (polygamy). Liu's slide asks, "Is this begging the question?"

Remember: religious reasons are allowed, with public reasons to follow; "my faith condemns it" alone is not enough.

The statements. "Religious arguments have no place in law-making." "Ban X because the faith condemns it." "Can a state that treats religion as a basic good be fair to non-believers?" (Q41, Q50)

The move.

  1. Public reason bars no argument for being religious: the Good Samaritan may be cited if public reasons follow "in due course" (PRR 144, 146).
  2. Finnis's basic good of religion, open to "agnostic or negative" answers (NLNR 89), supports religious freedom; Rawls protects it because denying basic liberties "normally" breaks reciprocity (PRR 138).
  3. So "ban it because a faith condemns it" fails, though TSH warns that a "national interest" test may leave religion "little practical impact" (Religion 513).

TSH's sharper point: political values render religious perspectives "nugatory" wherever an issue counts as metaphysical (Religion 515). Whether an issue is political is itself contested (polygamy, 538), as Liu's slide asks: "Is this begging the question?" (W5a slide 7†).

106.8 Whip

▤ On your sheet: 6.8 Whip (word for word)
6.8 Whip party discipline; conscience; one clear voice
  1. A whipped House "may not be representative of the majority opinion" (TSH, CJ 96), so [one clear voice] need not show what justice requires.
  2. For TSH, lifting the whip "on certain occasions" is "an option", with each member encouraged to see his role "in deciphering higher law"; another is judicial (CJ 96–97).
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason; treating [s 377A] as "policy", not conscience (Shanmugam, 2022), is itself a moral judgment.
  • Precedent: abortion free votes in 1969 and 1974, "arguably an endorsement" of considering religious perspectives (TSH, Religion 506–07).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When a party "whips" its MPs, they must vote the party line. Does a whipped vote tell us what the people think is just? Not necessarily: it tells us what the party leadership decided. Lifting the whip lets MPs vote their conscience, but conscience is not the same as public reason either.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "MPs who vote on moral questions the way their party tells them, rather than by conscience, can't claim to be working out what justice requires."

  1. Partly true. A whipped vote may not reflect what most people (or most MPs) actually think, so "one clear voice" doesn't prove what justice requires.
  2. TSH's option: lift the whip on certain occasions, so each MP can see their role as working out "higher law". Courts are another option.
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, which isn't necessarily the same as public reason. And calling s 377A a matter of "policy" rather than conscience, as Shanmugam did in 2022, is itself a moral judgement.

The extra: Singapore allowed free votes on abortion in 1969 and 1974, which TSH says was arguably an endorsement of considering religious views.

Remember: whip = party line; free vote = conscience; neither is automatically public reason.

The statement. "Legislators who vote on moral questions according to party discipline rather than conscience cannot claim to be discerning what justice requires." (Q46)

The move.

  1. A whipped House "may not be representative of the majority opinion" (TSH, CJ 96), so "one clear voice" need not show what justice requires.
  2. For TSH, lifting the whip "on certain occasions" is "an option", with each member encouraged to see his role "in deciphering higher law"; another option is judicial (CJ 96–97).
  3. So a free vote serves conscience, not necessarily public reason; treating s 377A as "policy", not conscience (Shanmugam, 2022), is itself a moral judgment.

Precedent: abortion free votes in 1969 and 1974 were "arguably an endorsement" of considering religious perspectives (TSH, Religion 506–07).

116.10 Aim and mechanism

▤ On your sheet: 6.10 Aim and mechanism (word for word)
6.10 Aim and mechanism equally valid; objectively necessary; wrongdoer; only then; fixed conception of the good life
  1. The statement's aim, not imposing [a fixed conception of the good life], and its harm-to-others mechanism come apart.
  2. The mechanism is neither necessary, since Hart's paternalism answers defective consent, not immorality (7.2), nor neutral: Rawls files Mill's liberalism among comprehensive doctrines (PL 145).
  3. So [the statement] keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism: Finnis supplies substance, Rawls discipline, Hart a presumption against coercion.
  • "Objectively" presupposes realism; "wrongdoer", a wrong; "others", who counts (6.5); "equally valid" defeats itself (4.7).
  • Liu's model (W9): read the sentences as a chain: (2) is the means to (1), and "only then" makes it the only means. Finnis: a range of valid opinions, not one; protecting others is a ground, not the only one. Rawls: "equally valid" a priori, not for unreasonable doctrines; critics: toleration is itself imposed.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Your aim: get to the airport. Your mechanism: "only take the number 7 bus". The aim is fine; the mechanism is neither the only way nor even a reliable one. Sample Question 1 is like that: its aim (don't force one way of life on everyone) is good, but its mechanism (treat all opinions as equally valid; only legislate against harm to others) doesn't work.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement (Sample Question 1), in everyday words: "In a diverse society, lawmakers should treat all moral views as equally valid. To do that, only restrict freedom when it's truly needed to protect others from a wrongdoer. That's the only way to avoid forcing one idea of the good life on everyone."

  1. Split the aim from the method. The aim is: don't impose one idea of the good life. The method is: only ban harm to others. They come apart.
  2. The method is neither needed nor neutral. Not needed: Hart allows some laws protecting people from themselves when their consent is defective (Lesson 7). Not neutral: Rawls himself counts Mill's harm principle as one full worldview among others.
  3. So you can keep the aim only by dropping the method. Finnis gives the substance, Rawls the discipline of reasons, Hart a starting presumption against coercion.

Word by word: "objectively" assumes moral truth exists; "wrongdoer" assumes something is wrong; "others" raises who counts (the unborn?); "equally valid" defeats itself (4.7). Liu's tip: read the sentences as a chain, where "only then" claims the method is the only way.

Remember: good aim, broken mechanism.

The statement (Sample Question 1). "Legislators governing a pluralist society should treat all moral opinions as equally valid. This can be achieved by refraining from passing any law restricting liberty unless it is objectively necessary to protect others from a wrongdoer's conduct. Only then can legislators avoid imposing on citizens a fixed conception of the good life."

The move.

  1. The statement's aim (not imposing a fixed conception of the good life) and its harm-to-others mechanism come apart.
  2. The mechanism is neither necessary, since Hart's paternalism answers defective consent, not immorality (7.2), nor neutral: Rawls files Mill's liberalism among comprehensive doctrines (PL 145).
  3. So the statement keeps its aim only by dropping its mechanism: Finnis supplies substance, Rawls discipline, Hart a presumption against coercion.

Word by word. "Objectively" presupposes realism; "wrongdoer" presupposes a wrong; "others" raises who counts (6.5); "equally valid" defeats itself (4.7).

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Liu's model (W9): read the three sentences as a chain. Sentence (2) is the means to (1), and "only then" makes it the only means. Finnis: a range of valid opinions, not one; protecting others is a ground, not the only one. Rawls: "equally valid" a priori, but not for unreasonable doctrines; critics: toleration is itself imposed.

126.11 Freestanding yet overriding

▤ On your sheet: 6.11 Freestanding yet overriding (word for word)
6.11 Freestanding yet overriding freestanding; overriding; contradictory
  1. "Freestanding" means derived from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free: the conception is "political (but of course moral)" (PL 140–41).
  2. On essentials and basic justice, political values normally override because they are "very great values", governing "the basic framework of social life" (PL 138–40); reasonable doctrines can support them, and the cooperative virtues are "political capital" (157).
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable, but for dissenters the label "reasonable" does the overriding, and TSH asks what standard grounds it (Religion 516).
  • STEELMAN Masagos echoes Rawls: decisions apply "secular, universal values and not individual religious beliefs" (2022); even Finnis: 14.10.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Rawls says his political values are "freestanding" (they don't depend on any religion or philosophy) yet they "override" religious views on basic questions. Isn't that contradictory? Not quite: freestanding means "not built from one doctrine", not "value-free". And reasonable people can accept that fair terms come first. The rub is who gets labelled "reasonable".

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Rawls says his political values stand on their own, yet he also says they beat everyone's religious and moral views. That's a contradiction."

  1. "Freestanding" doesn't mean "value-free". It means not built from any one worldview. Rawls says it is political, "but of course moral".
  2. Why they normally win: on basic questions, political values are "very great values" that shape the framework of social life. Reasonable worldviews can support them, and the habits of cooperation they build are "political capital".
  3. So there's no contradiction for people who count as "reasonable". But for those who disagree, the label "reasonable" is doing the overriding, and TSH asks what standard justifies the label.

The extra: STEELMAN: Singapore's minister echoed Rawls in 2022: decisions apply "secular, universal values", not individual religious beliefs.

Remember: freestanding ≠ value-free; the fight is over the word "reasonable".

The statement. "Rawls's political conception is both freestanding and overriding, which is contradictory."

The move.

  1. "Freestanding" means derived from no comprehensive doctrine, not value-free: the conception is "political (but of course moral)" (PL 140–41).
  2. On essentials and basic justice, political values normally override because they are "very great values", governing "the basic framework of social life" (PL 138–40); reasonable doctrines can support them, and the cooperative virtues are "political capital" (157).
  3. So there is no contradiction for the reasonable, but for dissenters the label "reasonable" does the overriding, and TSH asks what standard grounds it (Religion 516).

STEELMAN. Masagos echoes Rawls: decisions apply "secular, universal values and not individual religious beliefs" (2022). Even Finnis grants the reciprocity ideal "seems broadly reasonable" (card 14.10).

13Putting it together: Sample Question 1 in full

You planned this in Lesson 1. Here it is with the archetype's material in place.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Paragraph 1: Rawls (6.1, 6.2, 6.11), about 300 words

Claim: the statement's aim echoes Rawls, but "equally valid" is not Rawls's view. Rawls asks for reasons all reasonable citizens could accept (PL 137) and excludes unreasonable doctrines; "unreasonable" condemns refusing fair terms, not error (PL 138). His neutrality is of justification, not of outcome, and he concedes our actions "nevertheless imply" a view (PL 153). Objection: the label "reasonable" does the overriding (TSH, Religion 516). Reply: Rawls's standard is moral though political. Illustration: Masagos (2022), secular universal values. So: Rawls supports the aim but not "equal validity".

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Paragraph 2: Finnis (5.5, 6.2), about 300 words

Claim: a pluralist state can avoid a fixed conception of the good life without treating opinions as equally valid. Finnis's common good is "a set of conditions" (NLNR 155), not a cake; the state keeps "peace and justice" (Abortion 77). Objection: Finnis is non-neutral; he would "favour the basic forms of good". Reply: concede non-neutrality; no law is neutral (6.2). Illustration: POFMA protecting knowledge with prudence. So: the aim survives on substantive grounds.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Paragraph 3: Hart and Devlin, with self-critique (7.2, 7.3, 1.4), about 300 words

Claim: the mechanism is neither necessary nor sufficient. Hart allows paternalism where consent is defective (LLM 32–33), so harm to others is not the only ground; Devlin shows every society takes a moral stand, though majority dislike is "not nearly enough" (Devlin 17). Self-critique: Rawlsian public reason may still end in a vote (1.4). So: replace "only harm to others" with a presumption against coercion that rises with the coercion used (7.9).

✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore partly right. Its aim, that a pluralist state should not impose one way of life, is shared by Rawls and Finnis alike. But its mechanism fails: treating all opinions as equally valid defeats itself, and legislating only against harm to others is neither neutral nor the only route to the aim. Pluralism asks equal respect for persons, not equal validity for opinions.

LESSON 7 · ARCHETYPE 7 · ABOUT 50 MIN · 44 QUESTIONS

Enforcement of morals

⚡ BIG IDEA

Every answer to "should law enforce morality?", repeal included, takes a moral stand. The real question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.

ARCHETYPE 7 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
7 Enforcement of morals
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position Every answer to [whether law should enforce morality], repeal included, takes a moral stand; the question is which reasons justify which degree of coercion.
Intro [The statement] treats [harm / autonomy / majority feeling] as a neutral test of when law may coerce. None is neutral: what counts as harm, and whose feelings count, are moral questions. I argue that [the statement] is [right / wrong / only partly right]: the issue is which reasons justify how much coercion.
7.1 Harm as plain fact Wolfenden got it right; only harm to others; plain matter of fact; a sham
  1. [Harm is a plain matter of fact] fails: what counts as harm, and who counts as an other, are moral questions.
  2. Hart's real question is whether the bare fact that positive morality condemns [X] is any reason to punish it.
  3. So [the quarrel is a sham] fails: both sides moralise, but they hold "divergent critical principles" (Hart), not merely rival moral codes.
  • STEELMAN Mill: "over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign"†; Hart: liberty may be "a value in itself" (LLM 21).
  • AGAINST Liu: what "concerns others? Everything?"† Wolfenden itself guards decency and the vulnerable; Devlin: its own bans on "corruption" presuppose a public morality (Devlin 9).
  • TRAP Not positivism: Hart and Devlin agreed the laws were law and argued what law should be; Hart's thought is modular, so a positivist could back Devlin (Liu, W7, W9).
7.2 Paternalism, offence line protect adults from themselves; sale and consumption; offensive; public decency
  1. [Never protect adults from themselves] is Mill's anti-paternalism, at lengths Hart says "may now appear to us fantastic".
  2. Hart's paternalism protects defective consent, not virtue: it supports [restricting sale], not obviously jailing the user it protects.
  3. So [the line is easy to draw] fails: paternalism and offence both turn on whose choices and feelings count.
  • FOR Hart: punishing drug supply "even to adults, except under medical prescription" is explicable as protecting buyers; "transitory desires", clouded judgement and subtle pressure weaken consent (LLM 32–33).
  • AGAINST TSH: morals pick targets (apotemnophilia v dangerous sports: Pragmatism 288). Hart's offence ground covers public indecency, not distress at "the bare knowledge" of private acts (LLM 46–47); teetotallers: 12.6.
7.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read majority disgust; revulsion; act swiftly; behind closed doors; Clapham omnibus; right-minded man
  1. [Majority disgust is reason enough] borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin refuses to count heads and wants slowness and, "more tentatively", privacy: not a majority to [act swiftly / ignore closed doors].
  3. So [majority feeling is the voice of the community] fails: disgust is only "a good indication", and Devlin also demands "a deliberate judgement that the practice is injurious to society".
  • Devlin 15: for the law-maker, majority opinion is "surely not enough"; the standard "does not depend on the counting of heads": what twelve at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on (Pollock's "practical morality").
  • Devlin 17: "not nearly enough" that "a majority dislike a practice"; disgust counts only if "deeply felt and not manufactured"; those "swayed simply by disgust" would be "wrong".
  • STEELMAN Devlin: "No society can do without intolerance, indignation, and disgust" (17).
  • AGAINST No expected unanimity on contested issues; Hart: critical morality must test that judgement (his racist society, LLM 18–19).
  • Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, not its conclusion: he gave no "opinion one way or the other" (2) and "eventually" backed decriminalisation (Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022; Liu, W9), though in 1959 repeal's difficulty was "strongly militating against" change (18).
7.4 Disintegration chain reaction; inevitably; end of society; slippery slope
  1. [Repeal begins the end of society] is trivial if a society just is its present morality, and unproven as a prediction.
  2. Hart: nothing shows that private deviation threatens society "like treason"; there is "much evidence against it".
  3. So [inevitably] overstates: only the principled slope bites, and Art 156 now shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge.
Reading (Liu's four†)Verdict
Society is its moralitytrivial; Hart: "absurd"; change is like "a peaceful constitutional change" (LLM 51–52)
Empirical collapseHart: seemingly no permissive drift in Europe (LLM 52)
Interpersonal bonds (George)the loss "may not be regrettable" to those rejecting a shared life (Pragmatism 289)
Principled slope (Pragmatism 304)Lawrence to Obergefell; Masterpiece Cakeshop, Bull v Hall†; contrast Art 156
  • STEELMAN Devlin: immorality, like subversion, is "capable in their nature of threatening the existence of society" (13–14 n). Reply: that gives law jurisdiction, not a reason to punish [X].
  • QUALIFY Whose morality? s 377A's origin looked like "happenstance" (Shanmugam, 2022; it dates only from 1938: Pragmatism 293); but keeping it in 2007 was a choice.
  • QUALIFY Liu (W9): recast as mere change, it cannot justify harsh sanctions; Devlin fears fragmentation and presupposes a consensus that pluralist Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may lack or keep only by coercion. Most jurists, Liu thinks, side with Hart.
7.5 Repeal neutral? takes no side; neutral; stands aside; leaves each citizen free
  1. [Repeal takes no side] fails: withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis: every society "takes a public stand" on abortion; Shanmugam called repeal "the right thing to do", itself a verdict.
  3. So [repeal is neutral] holds only weakly: withdrawal is not endorsement, but its reasons are never neutral.
  • FOR Shanmugam (2022): crime "generally" needs "a public order or public interest issue" (16.3); private consensual adult acts raise no "law-and-order concerns" (also Faishal).
7.6 2007 majority opinion; what prevailed; the 2007 compromise; live and let live
  1. In 2007 [majority feeling] prevailed, with Devlin's slowness and privacy: s 377A was kept but not proactively enforced.
  2. Proponents met [no harm / religious only] with other grounds and spill-over, largely avoiding Devlin's treason and disintegration theses (Pragmatism 297: perhaps two speeches came closer).
  3. So [majority feeling decides] describes the 2007 result, not its reasons: debate had moved "from arguments of toleration and privacy to arguments about rights" (Pragmatism 301), and its motive, deference to the majority or protecting what was right, was a "point of equivocation" (300–01); by 2022 tolerance had shifted.
  • AGAINST Spill-over to marriage and adoption: in TSH's words, "tangible harm in the form of public consequences" (Pragmatism 298). Thio: harm can be "both physical and intangible"; per TSH, she explained that homosexuality could be viewed as contrary to biological design (300–01).
7.7 Consistency, non-enforcement arbitrary; inconsistent; sham; enforce fully or repeal; unenforced; moral signpost
  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement alone makes [s 377A] arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin concedes "There is no logic to be found in this": each crime is weighed on its own, so legal adultery proves nothing.
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: announced non-enforcement breached Fuller's congruence yet still sent "a symbolic message" (Pragmatism 299).
  • AGAINST Unenforced law gives police and prosecutors "formidable discriminatory powers" (Hart LLM 27); "a sword hanging over" gay men (Shanmugam).
  • QUALIFY TSH: policing varies with the offence; a 2007 MP: some laws, eg nudity visible to the public eye, are hard to police (Pragmatism 300).
7.8 Wrong before; order v good we were wrong before; slavery; keep order, not make people good; how severely
  1. [We were wrong before] defeats itself: calling a past law an error presupposes a right answer.
  2. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery; that warrants Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons, not abstention.
  3. So [keep order, not make people good] fits Devlin's legal "minimum"; Stephen punishes vice as such; Finnis aims at the common good.
  • Hart: whether to punish and how severely are "distinct and independent questions" (LLM 36), so a harsh penalty needs its own case.
7.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote enforce morality; regulate private behaviour; their own lives; promote; defend marriage
  1. [Enforcing morality] can mean punishing, regulating or promoting, and the justification needed rises with the coercion used.
  2. Hart: coercion is "prima facie objectionable": it punishes offenders, constrains everyone else, and in sexual matters may cause "misery of a quite special degree".
  3. So [legislators should not enforce morality] fails as stated, since all law promotes some morality, but it holds for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone.
  • CONCEDE Promotion coerces too (curricula, media rules, adoption); Rawls: appeals to monogamy "as such" reflect comprehensive doctrines (PRR 147), though he leaves the question open (n 38). Concede: promotion needs public reasons (6.1); Liu reads the 2022 package as arguably Rawlsian (13.2).
7.10 Sin, crime and religion religious grounds; sin; a faith condemns it; without exception
  1. In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, "sin and crime are separate categories".
  2. Even Devlin concedes law "can no longer rely on doctrines in which citizens are entitled to disbelieve", so [a faith-based ban] needs a secular reason.
  3. So a ban [without exception] fails twice: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and it would catch sacramental or temple use.
7.11 Polls are not a mandate poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
  1. A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise: in 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to [the conduct], following the majority is oppression; if not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns (Pragmatism 302).
  3. So [majority support] is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
  • STEELMAN Majority rule treats citizens as equals (Indranee, 2007: 16.3; 12.3).
  • CONCEDE Consensus gauges, not grounds: in Liu's map of the 2007 replies, majority opinion "can be an indication of objective morality"†; yet majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch" (JO 331–32).
Conclusion The statement is therefore [right / wrong / only partly right]. No answer, repeal included, is neutral, and Hart v Devlin is a moral quarrel, not a positivist one. Harm, defective consent or public offence may justify punishment; majority feeling is evidence, never the reason, and Devlin's disintegration thesis suits a society in deep agreement, not a pluralist one; promotion needs public reasons. Singapore's 2022 package fits: a Wolfenden-like presumption (public order or public interest) for crime, Art 156 for marriage.

1Start here: archetype 7 in plain English

Archetype 7 asks: should the law punish things just because most people think they are immoral? The famous version is the debate over s 377A, the law against sex between men, which Singapore kept in 2007 (without enforcing it) and repealed in 2022. On one side are Mill and Hart: only stop people harming others. On the other is Devlin: a society may protect its shared morality, as it protects itself from treason. The statements in this family usually claim that one test (harm, personal choice, or majority feeling) is a neutral, obvious answer. Your answer: every position here, including repeal, is a moral position. The useful question is which reasons justify how much force.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Harm principleMill's rule: the state may only coerce someone to stop them harming others.
PaternalismUsing law to protect people from themselves (e.g. drug laws).
Legal moralismUsing law to enforce morality as such, even with no harm to anyone.
Positive v critical moralityPositive: what a society actually believes. Critical: the principles we use to judge those beliefs.
Wolfenden ReportA 1957 English report saying private consensual homosexual acts between adults should not be crimes: private morality is "not the law's business".
Devlin's jury boxDevlin's test for shared morality: what a reasonable person, after discussion, would feel strongly enough to condemn. Not a head count.
Disintegration thesisDevlin's claim that a society can fall apart if its shared morality is not protected.
Coercion gradientPunishing, regulating and promoting are different levels of force; the stronger the force, the stronger the reason needed.
Art 156The constitutional provision added in 2022 that shields laws on man–woman marriage from challenge under fundamental liberties.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says every answer, "repeal included, takes a moral stand". Put simply: keeping a ban, repealing it, or staying out are all moral choices. So don't ask "should law touch morality at all?" Ask "is this reason strong enough to justify this much force?"

The Intro says: the statement treats harm, autonomy or majority feeling as a neutral test. None is: what counts as harm, and whose feelings count, are moral questions. The Conclusion says: harm, defective consent or public offence may justify punishment; majority feeling is evidence, never the reason by itself; Devlin's thesis fits a society in deep agreement, not a diverse one. Singapore's 2022 package fits this: crime needs a public-order or public-interest reason, and Art 156 protects marriage law.

The eleven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
7.1"Harm is a plain fact, so Wolfenden needed no moral judgement."What counts as harm, and who counts as "others", are moral questions.
7.2"Never protect adults from themselves; but punish offence."Hart allows protecting people whose consent is weak. Both lines turn on whose choices and feelings count.
7.3"Majority disgust is reason enough."Devlin himself said head-counting and disgust alone aren't enough; he wanted slowness and deliberate judgement.
7.4"Repeal will inevitably lead to the collapse of society."Unproven. Only the "principled slope" has bite, and Art 156 now guards against it.
7.5"Repeal takes no side."Repeal rests on a moral judgement too. Not endorsing isn't the same as being neutral.
7.6"In 2007, majority opinion rightly won."That describes the result, not the reasons. The debate had moved to rights and harms.
7.7"Enforcing some morals but not others is arbitrary."Inconsistency alone doesn't make a law a sham; each offence is weighed on its own.
7.8"We were wrong before, so don't enforce morality."Saying we were wrong assumes there's a right answer. Be slow, not silent.
7.9"Legislators should not enforce morality."All law promotes some morality. What matters is how much force: punishing private conduct for immorality alone is the hard case.
7.10"A faith condemns it, so ban it."Sin and crime are different. A ban needs a reason that works for everyone.
7.11"85% support the ban; let the people decide."A poll is evidence, not a mandate. If there's a right at stake, following the majority could be oppression.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Every answer is a moral stand; match the strength of the reason to the amount of force.

2The big picture: Hart v Devlin

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Should the law punish things that are "immoral" even if nobody else is hurt? One side (Mill, Hart) says: only stop people harming others; leave private life alone. The other side (Devlin) says: a society is held together by shared values, and it may protect them like it protects itself from treason. This lesson teaches you to see that both sides are making moral arguments, and that the useful question is how much force each reason can justify.

The players

WhoPosition in one line
MillHarm principle: power may be used against someone only to prevent harm to others; "over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign"†
Wolfenden CommitteePrivate consensual homosexual acts between adults should not be crimes: private morality is "not the law's business"; the criminal law guards public order and decency and protects the vulnerable
DevlinSociety may protect its shared morality by law, against conduct beyond the limits of tolerance; found via the reasonable man in the jury box
StephenThe extreme thesis: law may punish "the grosser forms of vice" as such
HartCoercion is "prima facie objectionable"; paternalism (defective consent) and public decency can justify it, bare immorality cannot
TSH (Pragmatism)The moral question cannot be shunned; maps six functions of criminal law; analyses the 2007 s 377A debate

Key distinctions

  • Positive morality (what a society actually believes) v critical morality (principles used to judge it). Hart's question is one of critical morality: is the bare fact that positive morality condemns X any reason to punish X?
  • Harm v paternalism v moralism: preventing harm to others; protecting people from themselves; enforcing morality as such.
  • Punish v regulate v promote (1.3(5)): the coercion gradient (7.9).

The Singapore story

YearWhat happened
1938s 377A enacted (its origin looked like "happenstance": Shanmugam, 2022; Pragmatism 293)
2007Parliament kept s 377A but the Government said it would not proactively enforce it (the "retain but don't enforce" compromise)
2022Parliament repealed s 377A (in force 3 Jan 2023) and added Art 156, shielding man–woman marriage laws from Part 4 challenge
⚠ TRAP
Hart v Devlin is not positivism v natural law

Hart and Devlin agreed the laws were law; they argued about what law should be. Hart's thought is modular, so a positivist could back Devlin (Liu, W7, W9). Never write "Hart the positivist therefore opposed enforcing morals".

harsh or mandatory penaltywhether to punish ≠ how much7.8, 3.5

37.1 Harm as plain fact

▤ On your sheet: 7.1 Harm as plain fact (word for word)
7.1 Harm as plain fact Wolfenden got it right; only harm to others; plain matter of fact; a sham
  1. [Harm is a plain matter of fact] fails: what counts as harm, and who counts as an other, are moral questions.
  2. Hart's real question is whether the bare fact that positive morality condemns [X] is any reason to punish it.
  3. So [the quarrel is a sham] fails: both sides moralise, but they hold "divergent critical principles" (Hart), not merely rival moral codes.
  • STEELMAN Mill: "over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign"†; Hart: liberty may be "a value in itself" (LLM 21).
  • AGAINST Liu: what "concerns others? Everything?"† Wolfenden itself guards decency and the vulnerable; Devlin: its own bans on "corruption" presuppose a public morality (Devlin 9).
  • TRAP Not positivism: Hart and Devlin agreed the laws were law and argued what law should be; Hart's thought is modular, so a positivist could back Devlin (Liu, W7, W9).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Only harm to others counts, and harm is just a fact." But is offence harm? Is a broken family harm? Is damage to "society" harm? Deciding what counts as harm, and who counts as "another person", means making moral choices.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Wolfenden got it exactly right: the law should only stop harm to others, and harm is just a fact, no moral judgement needed" or "the liberal v conservative fight is fake, because both sides talk about harm".

  1. Harm isn't a plain fact. Deciding what counts as harm, and who counts as an "other", needs moral judgement.
  2. Hart's real question is narrower: is the bare fact that most people condemn something any reason, on its own, to punish it?
  3. So the quarrel isn't fake. Both sides make moral arguments, but they rely on genuinely different principles for judging society's morality.

The extras: STEELMAN: Mill: "over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign"; Hart: liberty may be valuable in itself. AGAINST: Liu asks what doesn't concern others. Wolfenden itself protected public decency and the vulnerable. TRAP: this isn't positivism v natural law; Hart and Devlin agreed the laws were law and argued about what law should be.

Remember: "harm" already contains a moral judgement.

The statement. "The Wolfenden Committee got it exactly right … since harm is a plain matter of fact, it calls for no moral judgment at all." (Q61) "The liberal–conservative quarrel is a sham: both sides point to harm." (Q66)

The move.

  1. "Harm is a plain matter of fact" fails: what counts as harm, and who counts as an other, are moral questions.
  2. Hart's real question is whether the bare fact that positive morality condemns X is any reason to punish it.
  3. So "the quarrel is a sham" fails: both sides moralise, but they hold "divergent critical principles" (Hart), not merely rival moral codes.

The support.

  • STEELMAN: Mill: "over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign"†; Hart: liberty may be "a value in itself" (LLM 21).
  • AGAINST: Liu: what "concerns others? Everything?"† Wolfenden itself guards decency and the vulnerable; Devlin: its own bans on "corruption" presuppose a public morality (Devlin 9).
  • TSH: "harm" and "self-regarding" are indeterminate, and if only legal interests count, "there appears to be circularity" (Pragmatism 287; card 14.12).

47.2 Paternalism, offence line

▤ On your sheet: 7.2 Paternalism, offence line (word for word)
7.2 Paternalism, offence line protect adults from themselves; sale and consumption; offensive; public decency
  1. [Never protect adults from themselves] is Mill's anti-paternalism, at lengths Hart says "may now appear to us fantastic".
  2. Hart's paternalism protects defective consent, not virtue: it supports [restricting sale], not obviously jailing the user it protects.
  3. So [the line is easy to draw] fails: paternalism and offence both turn on whose choices and feelings count.
  • FOR Hart: punishing drug supply "even to adults, except under medical prescription" is explicable as protecting buyers; "transitory desires", clouded judgement and subtle pressure weaken consent (LLM 32–33).
  • AGAINST TSH: morals pick targets (apotemnophilia v dangerous sports: Pragmatism 288). Hart's offence ground covers public indecency, not distress at "the bare knowledge" of private acts (LLM 46–47); teetotallers: 12.6.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Mill said never protect adults from themselves. Hart said that's too strong: sometimes people's choices aren't really free (addiction, pressure, being young). So the law may restrict selling dangerous drugs to protect buyers. But that's different from jailing the users for being immoral. And "offence" only counts for things done in public, not for being upset that something happens behind closed doors.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "A liberal state must never use criminal law to protect adults from themselves, but it may punish what offends public decency."

  1. "Never protect adults from themselves" is Mill's view, held so strictly that Hart says it may now seem "fantastic".
  2. Hart allows some paternalism, but to protect weak or clouded consent, not to make people virtuous. That supports restricting the sale of drugs, not obviously jailing the user the law is meant to protect.
  3. So the line isn't easy to draw. Both paternalism and offence depend on whose choices and whose feelings count.

The extras: FOR: Hart explains drug-supply laws as protecting buyers, whose consent can be weakened by passing cravings, poor judgement or pressure. AGAINST: TSH: morals decide which risky choices we target (the law targets wanting a healthy limb amputated, yet allows dangerous sports). Hart's offence ground covers indecency in public, not distress at merely knowing something happens in private.

Remember: protect weak consent, not virtue; offence means public, not private.

The statement. "A liberal state must never use the criminal law to protect adults from themselves … The state may, however, punish conduct that offends public decency." (Q64)

The move.

  1. "Never protect adults from themselves" is Mill's anti-paternalism, at lengths Hart says "may now appear to us fantastic".
  2. Hart's paternalism protects defective consent, not virtue: it supports restricting sale, not obviously jailing the user it protects.
  3. So "the line is easy to draw" fails: paternalism and offence both turn on whose choices and feelings count.

FOR (Hart): punishing drug supply "even to adults, except under medical prescription" is explicable as protecting buyers; "transitory desires", clouded judgement and subtle pressure weaken consent (LLM 32–33).

AGAINST (TSH): morals pick the targets: why ban apotemnophilia (wanting a healthy limb amputated) but allow dangerous sports? (Pragmatism 288). Hart's offence ground covers public indecency, not distress at "the bare knowledge" of private acts (LLM 46–47). Teetotallers: see 12.6.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Sale v consumption

A bill bans "the sale and consumption of alcohol". Split it:

This split is the move students most often miss (12.6).

  • Sale: Hart's paternalism can support licensing or restricting supply to protect buyers whose consent may be clouded.
  • Consumption: jailing the drinker punishes the very person paternalism claims to protect; harder to justify.

57.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read

▤ On your sheet: 7.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read (word for word)
7.3 Devlin's jury box, rightly read majority disgust; revulsion; act swiftly; behind closed doors; Clapham omnibus; right-minded man
  1. [Majority disgust is reason enough] borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin refuses to count heads and wants slowness and, "more tentatively", privacy: not a majority to [act swiftly / ignore closed doors].
  3. So [majority feeling is the voice of the community] fails: disgust is only "a good indication", and Devlin also demands "a deliberate judgement that the practice is injurious to society".
  • Devlin 15: for the law-maker, majority opinion is "surely not enough"; the standard "does not depend on the counting of heads": what twelve at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on (Pollock's "practical morality").
  • Devlin 17: "not nearly enough" that "a majority dislike a practice"; disgust counts only if "deeply felt and not manufactured"; those "swayed simply by disgust" would be "wrong".
  • STEELMAN Devlin: "No society can do without intolerance, indignation, and disgust" (17).
  • AGAINST No expected unanimity on contested issues; Hart: critical morality must test that judgement (his racist society, LLM 18–19).
  • Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, not its conclusion: he gave no "opinion one way or the other" (2) and "eventually" backed decriminalisation (Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022; Liu, W9), though in 1959 repeal's difficulty was "strongly militating against" change (18).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

People often think Devlin said "if most people find it disgusting, ban it". He didn't. He said: imagine twelve ordinary people who discuss it calmly; would they all agree it's intolerable? Even then, go slowly and respect privacy. Disgust is a clue, not a verdict.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "When ordinary people feel disgust at a practice, that proves it threatens society, so Parliament should act swiftly, even behind closed doors."

  1. This borrows Devlin's starting point but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin didn't count heads. He wanted law-makers to go slowly and, "more tentatively", to respect privacy. He did not want a majority to act fast or ignore what happens behind closed doors.
  3. So majority feeling isn't automatically the voice of society. Devlin said disgust is only "a good indication"; he also required a deliberate judgement that the practice harms society.

What Devlin actually said: majority opinion is "surely not enough". His test is what twelve random people would agree on unanimously after discussion. Disgust counts only if "deeply felt and not manufactured". STEELMAN: no society can do without some intolerance and disgust. AGAINST: on contested issues there's no expected unanimity, and Hart says critical morality must test that judgement (a racist society's disgust proves nothing).

Remember: Devlin is slower and more careful than the people who quote him.

The statement. "Every society is entitled to defend its way of life. When ordinary citizens feel disgust at a practice, that feeling is the surest evidence that it threatens the shared values …" (Q62)

The move.

  1. "Majority disgust is reason enough" borrows Devlin's premise but drops his safeguards.
  2. Devlin refuses to count heads and wants slowness and, "more tentatively", privacy: not a majority to act swiftly or ignore closed doors.
  3. So "majority feeling is the voice of the community" fails: disgust is only "a good indication", and Devlin also demands "a deliberate judgement that the practice is injurious to society".

Devlin's own words.

  • Devlin 15: for the law-maker, majority opinion is "surely not enough"; the standard "does not depend on the counting of heads": what twelve at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on (Pollock's "practical morality").
  • Devlin 17: "not nearly enough" that "a majority dislike a practice"; disgust counts only if "deeply felt and not manufactured"; those "swayed simply by disgust" would be "wrong".
  • STEELMAN: "No society can do without intolerance, indignation, and disgust" (17).
  • AGAINST: no expected unanimity on contested issues; Hart: critical morality must test that judgment (his racist society, LLM 18–19).
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Devlin attacked Wolfenden's approach, not its conclusion: he gave no "opinion one way or the other" (2) and "eventually" backed decriminalisation (Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022; Liu, W9), though in 1959 repeal's difficulty was "strongly militating against" change (18).

Framework 15.6: Devlin's interrogatories
▤ Devlin 7–19
  1. 1May society judge morals? May law enforce that judgment? Always, or on what principles?
  2. 2Not "the counting of heads": what would twelve at random "after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on?
  3. 3Elastic principles: "maximum individual freedom that is consistent with the integrity of society"; "a real feeling of reprobation".
  4. 4A vice "so abominable that its mere presence is an offence" may be eradicated; one tolerable if confined calls for a balance.
  5. 5Verdict rule: a majority's dislike is "not nearly enough". Law sets "the minimum and not ... the maximum".
⚠ TRAP
Devlin is a cultural relativist (Liu, W7)

Monogamy binds because it is "built into the house in which we live" (9); honest belief, "right or wrong", makes immorality "a question of fact" (22). Privacy is only "to be taken into account" (18–19). So Devlin enforces a society's actual morality, not objective truth (card 14.15).

67.4 Disintegration

▤ On your sheet: 7.4 Disintegration (word for word)
7.4 Disintegration chain reaction; inevitably; end of society; slippery slope
  1. [Repeal begins the end of society] is trivial if a society just is its present morality, and unproven as a prediction.
  2. Hart: nothing shows that private deviation threatens society "like treason"; there is "much evidence against it".
  3. So [inevitably] overstates: only the principled slope bites, and Art 156 now shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge.
Reading (Liu's four†)Verdict
Society is its moralitytrivial; Hart: "absurd"; change is like "a peaceful constitutional change" (LLM 51–52)
Empirical collapseHart: seemingly no permissive drift in Europe (LLM 52)
Interpersonal bonds (George)the loss "may not be regrettable" to those rejecting a shared life (Pragmatism 289)
Principled slope (Pragmatism 304)Lawrence to Obergefell; Masterpiece Cakeshop, Bull v Hall†; contrast Art 156
  • STEELMAN Devlin: immorality, like subversion, is "capable in their nature of threatening the existence of society" (13–14 n). Reply: that gives law jurisdiction, not a reason to punish [X].
  • QUALIFY Whose morality? s 377A's origin looked like "happenstance" (Shanmugam, 2022; it dates only from 1938: Pragmatism 293); but keeping it in 2007 was a choice.
  • QUALIFY Liu (W9): recast as mere change, it cannot justify harsh sanctions; Devlin fears fragmentation and presupposes a consensus that pluralist Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may lack or keep only by coercion. Most jurists, Liu thinks, side with Hart.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Devlin said: shared morality holds society together, so losing it could make society fall apart. But what does "fall apart" mean? If it just means "society changes", that's not a disaster. If it means "chaos follows", where's the evidence? The strongest version is a slippery slope of principle: once you accept one argument, the next step follows logically.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Decriminalising homosexual sex will inevitably set off a chain reaction: same-sex marriage, then claims against religious businesses. It's the beginning of the end of society."

  1. "The end of society" is either trivial or unproven. If a society just is its current morality, any change "ends" it (trivially true). As a prediction about collapse, it has no evidence.
  2. Hart: nothing shows that private conduct threatens society like treason, and there is much evidence against it.
  3. So "inevitably" goes too far. The only version with bite is the principled slope (one legal argument leading to the next), and Art 156 now shields marriage law from that.

Liu's four readings: (1) society = its morality: trivial; change is like a peaceful constitutional change. (2) Society will collapse: no sign of that in Europe. (3) Bonds between people weaken: may not matter to those who reject that shared life. (4) Principled slope: the US went from Lawrence to Obergefell; Singapore added Art 156. QUALIFY: s 377A dates only from 1938, so "our morality" is partly accident; and Liu says Devlin assumes a consensus that a diverse society like Singapore may lack.

Remember: only the principled slope bites.

The statement. "Decriminalising homosexual conduct inevitably sets off a chain reaction … same-sex marriage and discrimination claims against religious businesses must follow." (Q63)

The move.

  1. "Repeal begins the end of society" is trivial if a society just is its present morality, and unproven as a prediction.
  2. Hart: nothing shows that private deviation threatens society "like treason"; there is "much evidence against it".
  3. So "inevitably" overstates: only the principled slope bites, and Art 156 now shields marriage laws from fundamental-liberties challenge.
Liu's four readings of disintegration
▤ 7.4 table; Pragmatism 289, 304; LLM 51–52
  1. 1Society is its morality → trivial; Hart: "absurd"; change is like "a peaceful constitutional change".
  2. 2Empirical collapse → Hart: seemingly no permissive drift in Europe.
  3. 3Interpersonal bonds (George) → the loss "may not be regrettable" to those rejecting a shared life.
  4. 4Principled slope (TSH) → Lawrence to Obergefell; Masterpiece Cakeshop, Bull v Hall†; contrast Art 156.

More.

  • STEELMAN: Devlin: immorality, like subversion, is "capable in their nature of threatening the existence of society" (13–14 n). Reply: that gives law jurisdiction, not a reason to punish X.
  • QUALIFY: whose morality? s 377A's origin looked like "happenstance" (Shanmugam, 2022; it dates only from 1938: Pragmatism 293); but keeping it in 2007 was a choice.
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Recast as mere change, disintegration cannot justify harsh sanctions. Devlin fears fragmentation and presupposes a consensus that pluralist Singapore, unlike 1950s England, may lack or keep only by coercion. Most jurists, Liu thinks, side with Hart (W9).

77.5 Repeal neutral?

▤ On your sheet: 7.5 Repeal neutral? (word for word)
7.5 Repeal neutral? takes no side; neutral; stands aside; leaves each citizen free
  1. [Repeal takes no side] fails: withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis: every society "takes a public stand" on abortion; Shanmugam called repeal "the right thing to do", itself a verdict.
  3. So [repeal is neutral] holds only weakly: withdrawal is not endorsement, but its reasons are never neutral.
  • FOR Shanmugam (2022): crime "generally" needs "a public order or public interest issue" (16.3); private consensual adult acts raise no "law-and-order concerns" (also Faishal).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Repealing the law takes no side: it just leaves people free." But deciding that something shouldn't be a crime is a decision about right and wrong in public life. Even the Minister who repealed s 377A called it "the right thing to do": that's a moral verdict.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Repealing the law takes no side; it just leaves everyone free. The state simply stands aside."

  1. Repeal isn't neutral. Withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis: every society "takes a public stand". And the Minister himself called repeal "the right thing to do", which is a moral verdict.
  3. So repeal is neutral only in a weak sense. Not punishing something isn't the same as approving it, but the reasons for repeal are never neutral.

The extra: FOR: Shanmugam (2022): crime generally needs a public order or public interest issue, and private consensual acts between adults raise no law-and-order concerns.

Remember: not punishing ≠ endorsing, but it's still a moral choice.

The statements. "Repeal takes no side; it leaves each citizen free." "The state stands aside."

The move.

  1. "Repeal takes no side" fails: withdrawing the criminal law rests on a moral judgement about what the state may punish.
  2. Finnis: every society "takes a public stand" on abortion; Shanmugam called repeal "the right thing to do", itself a verdict.
  3. So "repeal is neutral" holds only weakly: withdrawal is not endorsement, but its reasons are never neutral.

FOR: Shanmugam (2022): crime "generally" needs "a public order or public interest issue" (16.3); private consensual adult acts raise no "law-and-order concerns". Singapore's position is "broadly similar" to Wolfenden's.

87.6 2007

▤ On your sheet: 7.6 2007 (word for word)
7.6 2007 majority opinion; what prevailed; the 2007 compromise; live and let live
  1. In 2007 [majority feeling] prevailed, with Devlin's slowness and privacy: s 377A was kept but not proactively enforced.
  2. Proponents met [no harm / religious only] with other grounds and spill-over, largely avoiding Devlin's treason and disintegration theses (Pragmatism 297: perhaps two speeches came closer).
  3. So [majority feeling decides] describes the 2007 result, not its reasons: debate had moved "from arguments of toleration and privacy to arguments about rights" (Pragmatism 301), and its motive, deference to the majority or protecting what was right, was a "point of equivocation" (300–01); by 2022 tolerance had shifted.
  • AGAINST Spill-over to marriage and adoption: in TSH's words, "tangible harm in the form of public consequences" (Pragmatism 298). Thio: harm can be "both physical and intangible"; per TSH, she explained that homosexuality could be viewed as contrary to biological design (300–01).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In 2007 Singapore kept s 377A but promised not to actively enforce it. Was that just "the majority wins"? TSH shows it was more complicated: the people who wanted to keep it gave other reasons (spill-over to marriage and adoption), and the debate had shifted to rights.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "In 2007, majority opinion won, and rightly so. Live and let live."

  1. In 2007 majority feeling did shape the result, with Devlin-style caution: s 377A was kept but not actively enforced.
  2. But the arguments used weren't Devlin's. Supporters of the law answered "it harms no one" with other grounds, such as knock-on effects on marriage and adoption, rather than Devlin's treason or collapse claims.
  3. So "majority feeling decides" describes the 2007 outcome, not its reasons. TSH notes the debate had moved from toleration and privacy to arguments about rights, and it was unclear whether the motive was deference to the majority or protecting what was right. By 2022, attitudes had shifted.

The extra: AGAINST: the knock-on worry was, in TSH's words, "tangible harm in the form of public consequences". Thio argued harm can be physical or intangible.

Remember: the 2007 result followed the majority; the 2007 reasons were about harm and rights.

The statement. "In 2007 majority opinion prevailed, and rightly so: live and let live."

The move.

  1. In 2007 majority feeling prevailed, with Devlin's slowness and privacy: s 377A was kept but not proactively enforced.
  2. Proponents met "no harm" or "religious only" objections with other grounds and spill-over, largely avoiding Devlin's treason and disintegration theses (Pragmatism 297: perhaps two speeches came closer).
  3. So "majority feeling decides" describes the 2007 result, not its reasons: debate had moved "from arguments of toleration and privacy to arguments about rights" (Pragmatism 301), and its motive, deference to the majority or protecting what was right, was a "point of equivocation" (300–01); by 2022 tolerance had shifted.

AGAINST: spill-over to marriage and adoption, in TSH's words "tangible harm in the form of public consequences" (Pragmatism 298). Thio: harm can be "both physical and intangible"; per TSH, she explained that homosexuality could be viewed as contrary to biological design (300–01).

97.7 Consistency, non-enforcement

▤ On your sheet: 7.7 Consistency, non-enforcement (word for word)
7.7 Consistency, non-enforcement arbitrary; inconsistent; sham; enforce fully or repeal; unenforced; moral signpost
  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement alone makes [s 377A] arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin concedes "There is no logic to be found in this": each crime is weighed on its own, so legal adultery proves nothing.
  3. So [enforce fully or repeal] is too stark: announced non-enforcement breached Fuller's congruence yet still sent "a symbolic message" (Pragmatism 299).
  • AGAINST Unenforced law gives police and prosecutors "formidable discriminatory powers" (Hart LLM 27); "a sword hanging over" gay men (Shanmugam).
  • QUALIFY TSH: policing varies with the offence; a 2007 MP: some laws, eg nudity visible to the public eye, are hard to police (Pragmatism 300).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Adultery isn't a crime, so making gay sex a crime is inconsistent!" Devlin admits there's no neat logic: each kind of conduct is judged on its own. And a law that isn't enforced isn't automatically a sham: it can still send a message, though it gives officials worrying power.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "A legislature that enforces some moral rules (s 377A) but not others (adultery) is arbitrary. And a law that isn't enforced is a sham: enforce it or repeal it."

  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement, on its own, makes the law arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin admits "there is no logic to be found in this": each offence is weighed on its own merits, so the fact that adultery is legal proves nothing about s 377A.
  3. So "enforce or repeal" is too stark. Announcing non-enforcement broke Fuller's congruence requirement (Lesson 3), but the law still sent "a symbolic message".

The extras: AGAINST: an unenforced law gives police and prosecutors "formidable discriminatory powers" (Hart); Shanmugam called it "a sword hanging over" gay men. QUALIFY: how much policing a law gets naturally varies; some laws are hard to police anyway.

Remember: inconsistent isn't automatically arbitrary; unenforced isn't automatically a sham.

The statement. "A legislature that enforces some moral norms but not others is acting arbitrarily." (Q70)

The move.

  1. Neither inconsistency nor non-enforcement alone makes s 377A arbitrary or a sham.
  2. Devlin concedes "There is no logic to be found in this": each crime is weighed on its own, so legal adultery proves nothing.
  3. So "enforce fully or repeal" is too stark: announced non-enforcement breached Fuller's congruence yet still sent "a symbolic message" (Pragmatism 299).

AGAINST: unenforced law gives police and prosecutors "formidable discriminatory powers" (Hart LLM 27); "a sword hanging over" gay men (Shanmugam). QUALIFY: TSH: policing varies with the offence; a 2007 MP noted some laws (e.g. nudity visible to the public eye) are hard to police (Pragmatism 300).

107.8 Wrong before; order v good

▤ On your sheet: 7.8 Wrong before; order v good (word for word)
7.8 Wrong before; order v good we were wrong before; slavery; keep order, not make people good; how severely
  1. [We were wrong before] defeats itself: calling a past law an error presupposes a right answer.
  2. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery; that warrants Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons, not abstention.
  3. So [keep order, not make people good] fits Devlin's legal "minimum"; Stephen punishes vice as such; Finnis aims at the common good.
  • Hart: whether to punish and how severely are "distinct and independent questions" (LLM 36), so a harsh penalty needs its own case.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"We were wrong about slavery, so don't use law to enforce morals." But to say we were wrong about slavery, there must be a right answer. That lesson teaches care and humility, not giving up. And "the law should just keep order" is a view some theorists hold (Devlin's minimum), while others go further.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "We've been wrong about morality before (slavery), so we shouldn't use law to enforce it now" and "the law is there to keep order, not to make people good".

  1. "We were wrong before" defeats itself. Calling a past law a mistake assumes there was a right answer.
  2. Siew's point in 2007: disgust was once used to defend slavery. That's a reason for Devlin's caution and Hart's demand for reasons, not for giving up moral judgement.
  3. "Keep order, not make people good" matches Devlin's legal "minimum". Stephen goes further and punishes vice as such; Finnis aims at the common good.

The extra: Hart: whether to punish and how severely are separate questions, so a harsh penalty needs its own justification.

Remember: past errors call for care, not silence.

The statements. "We have been wrong about morality before, so we should not use law to enforce it now." (Q34) "The law exists to keep order, not to make people good." (Q71)

The move.

  1. "We were wrong before" defeats itself: calling a past law an error presupposes a right answer.
  2. As Siew argued in 2007, disgust once defended slavery; that warrants Devlin's slowness and Hart's demand for reasons, not abstention.
  3. So "keep order, not make people good" fits Devlin's legal "minimum"; Stephen punishes vice as such; Finnis aims at the common good.

Hart: whether to punish and how severely are "distinct and independent questions" (LLM 36), so a harsh penalty needs its own case. (Card 14.14: Hart still lets wickedness be "a partial determinant" of severity.)

117.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote

▤ On your sheet: 7.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote (word for word)
7.9 Coercion gradient: punish, regulate, promote enforce morality; regulate private behaviour; their own lives; promote; defend marriage
  1. [Enforcing morality] can mean punishing, regulating or promoting, and the justification needed rises with the coercion used.
  2. Hart: coercion is "prima facie objectionable": it punishes offenders, constrains everyone else, and in sexual matters may cause "misery of a quite special degree".
  3. So [legislators should not enforce morality] fails as stated, since all law promotes some morality, but it holds for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone.
  • CONCEDE Promotion coerces too (curricula, media rules, adoption); Rawls: appeals to monogamy "as such" reflect comprehensive doctrines (PRR 147), though he leaves the question open (n 38). Concede: promotion needs public reasons (6.1); Liu reads the 2022 package as arguably Rawlsian (13.2).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Enforcing morality" can mean three very different things: jailing people (punish), licensing or restricting (regulate), or encouraging through schools and ads (promote). The more force involved, the stronger the reason you need. Almost all law promotes some morality; the hard question is punishment.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Legislators shouldn't enforce morality. Let people run their own lives." Or: "The state should defend marriage."

  1. "Enforcing morality" can mean three things: punishing, regulating, or promoting. The more force used, the stronger the reason needed.
  2. Hart: coercion is objectionable unless justified. It punishes offenders, restricts everyone else, and in sexual matters can cause special misery.
  3. So "never enforce morality" is wrong as stated, because all law promotes some morality. But it is right about punishing private consensual conduct purely for being immoral.

The extra: CONCEDE: promoting a view also involves some pressure (school curricula, media rules, adoption rules). Rawls says appeals to monogamy "as such" come from full worldviews. So promotion needs public reasons too; Liu reads the 2022 package as arguably Rawlsian.

Remember: punish, regulate, promote: rising force, rising justification.

The statements. "Legislators should not enforce morality." "The state should let people regulate their own lives." "The state should defend marriage." (Q36, Q68)

The move.

  1. "Enforcing morality" can mean punishing, regulating or promoting, and the justification needed rises with the coercion used.
  2. Hart: coercion is "prima facie objectionable": it punishes offenders, constrains everyone else, and in sexual matters may cause "misery of a quite special degree".
  3. So "legislators should not enforce morality" fails as stated, since all law promotes some morality, but it holds for punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone.

CONCEDE: promotion coerces too (curricula, media rules, adoption); Rawls: appeals to monogamy "as such" reflect comprehensive doctrines (PRR 147), though he leaves the question open (n 38). Concede: promotion needs public reasons (6.1); Liu reads the 2022 package as arguably Rawlsian (13.2).

Framework 15.7: Hart, may the criminal law prohibit it?
▤ LLM 20–47; W9
  1. 1Coercion is "prima facie objectionable": what countervailing good justifies it?
  2. 2Harm to others? (Distress at "the bare knowledge" of others' conduct does not count.)
  3. 3Paternalism, if consent is defective (drug supply "except under medical prescription").
  4. 4Public decency: offence "serious and likely", weighed against freedom lost.
  5. 5Moralism alone: never.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
The 2022 package on the gradient

TSH calls it a deliberate split: criminal law withdrawn, marriage promoted (14.17).

  • Punish: withdrawn (s 377A repealed). Hart's lines survive: non-consensual acts, acts with young persons and public indecency stay crimes (Shanmugam, 2022).
  • Promote: Art 156 lets law "define, regulate, protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote" man–woman marriage.

127.10 Sin, crime and religion

▤ On your sheet: 7.10 Sin, crime and religion (word for word)
7.10 Sin, crime and religion religious grounds; sin; a faith condemns it; without exception
  1. In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, "sin and crime are separate categories".
  2. Even Devlin concedes law "can no longer rely on doctrines in which citizens are entitled to disbelieve", so [a faith-based ban] needs a secular reason.
  3. So a ban [without exception] fails twice: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and it would catch sacramental or temple use.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A sin is wrong in the eyes of a faith. A crime is something the state punishes. In a country of many faiths, you can't make something a crime just because one faith calls it a sin; you need a reason that works for everyone. Even Devlin agreed.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "This conduct goes against religious teaching, so make it a crime. Ban it without exception."

  1. Sin and crime are different. As Pritam Singh said in Parliament in 2022, in a secular society "sin and crime are separate categories".
  2. Even Devlin agreed law "can no longer rely on doctrines in which citizens are entitled to disbelieve". So a ban based on faith needs a secular reason too.
  3. So a ban "without exception" fails twice: one faith can't alone justify forcing others, and a blanket ban would also catch religious uses, such as sacramental or temple use.

Remember: a sin becomes a crime only with a reason everyone can assess.

The statements. "This conduct offends religious teaching, so it should be a crime." "Ban it without exception."

The move.

  1. In any secular society, as Pritam Singh said in 2022, "sin and crime are separate categories".
  2. Even Devlin concedes law "can no longer rely on doctrines in which citizens are entitled to disbelieve", so a faith-based ban needs a secular reason.
  3. So a ban "without exception" fails twice: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others, and it would catch sacramental or temple use.

137.11 Polls are not a mandate

▤ On your sheet: 7.11 Polls are not a mandate (word for word)
7.11 Polls are not a mandate poll; 85% at least somewhat support; most citizens; let the people decide
  1. A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise: in 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to [the conduct], following the majority is oppression; if not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns (Pragmatism 302).
  3. So [majority support] is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.
  • STEELMAN Majority rule treats citizens as equals (Indranee, 2007: 16.3; 12.3).
  • CONCEDE Consensus gauges, not grounds: in Liu's map of the 2007 replies, majority opinion "can be an indication of objective morality"†; yet majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch" (JO 331–32).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A poll says 70% "frown on" something. That doesn't mean 70% want people jailed for it. And even if they did, if people have a right to do it, the majority overruling them is oppression. Polls are evidence of what people think, not proof of what's right.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "85% of citizens at least somewhat support the ban. Let the people decide."

  1. Disapproval isn't a mandate to criminalise. In 2007, Hri Kumar pointed out that the 70% in a survey who "frowned on" the conduct were never asked whether it should be a crime.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if people have a right to the conduct, following the majority is oppression; if they don't, following the majority is democracy. Either way, you're back to the moral question.
  3. So majority support is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles the matter.

The extras: STEELMAN: majority rule treats citizens as equals (Indranee, 2007). CONCEDE: majority opinion can be a sign of what's morally right, but majorities were wrong about slavery.

Remember: a poll measures opinion; it doesn't settle rights.

The statement. "85% of citizens at least somewhat support the ban; let the people decide."

The move.

  1. A poll of disapproval is no mandate to criminalise: in 2007, Hri Kumar noted, the 70% who "frowned on" it were never asked about criminalising.
  2. TSH's dilemma: if there is a right to the conduct, following the majority is oppression; if not, it is democracy, so the moral question returns (Pragmatism 302).
  3. So majority support is evidence to weigh, never a reason that settles what the law should be.

STEELMAN: majority rule treats citizens as equals (Indranee, 2007: "we would go with the majority view, unless there is a reason to protect the minority position"). CONCEDE: consensus gauges, not grounds: in Liu's map of the 2007 replies, majority opinion "can be an indication of objective morality"†; yet majorities erred on slavery, and TSH admits a "catch" (JO 331–32).

14Putting it together: Practice Q61

"The Wolfenden Committee got it exactly right. The only legitimate purpose of the criminal law is to stop people harming others, and what consenting adults do in private is none of the state's business. This simple principle is all a legislator needs: since harm is a plain matter of fact, it calls for no moral judgment at all. Adopting it would finally end the quarrels over 'public morality' that have dogged the criminal law for centuries."

Instruction: Mill, Hart, Devlin.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "exactly right", "only legitimate purpose" → Hook: word ("only"); 7.1 and 7.2 (Hart's paternalism shows harm is not the only ground).
  • "plain matter of fact … no moral judgment" → 7.1 line 1.
  • "finally end the quarrels" → 7.1 line 3 ("sham" family).
  • Hook: ally turns: the statement's natural ally is Hart, yet he rejects its claim that harm is the only ground.
  • Distinction: 1.3(5) punish v regulate v promote.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement's natural ally is Hart, yet Hart rejects it twice over. He allows the criminal law to protect people whose consent is defective, so harm to others is not its only legitimate purpose; and he insists that applying his principles takes moral judgment. I make three claims: (1) harm is not a plain fact, since what counts as harm and who counts as "others" are moral questions; (2) the harm principle is not all a legislator needs, since paternalism and public decency can justify regulation; but (3) the statement is right where it matters most: punishing private consensual conduct for immorality alone is unjustified.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Mill and Wolfenden, steelmanned and tested (7.1): "over his own body and mind…"; Wolfenden's own decency and vulnerability grounds; Devlin: "corruption" presupposes public morality; TSH: circularity.
  2. Hart's grounds (7.2, 7.9): drug supply paternalism; offence v bare knowledge; the coercion gradient; Singapore 2022: Hart's lines survive repeal.
  3. Devlin rightly read, and the quarrel (7.3, 7.4): no head-counting, slowness, privacy; disintegration fails except as principled slope; self-critique: Hart's paternalism "in the ultimate analysis, based on morals" (TSH, Pragmatism 288).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore right about its conclusion and wrong about its reasons. Wolfenden's line, private consensual adult conduct is not the criminal law's business, survives, and Singapore's 2022 repeal adopted something "broadly similar". But the line is drawn by moral argument, not read off the facts, and it will not end the quarrels, because those quarrels are about which reasons justify how much coercion.
