LESSON 8 · ARCHETYPE 8 · ABOUT 50 MIN · 39 QUESTIONS

Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity

⚡ BIG IDEA

An unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust (Radbruch, Alexy), and whether something is law never settles whether the judge or citizen should obey it (Hart).

ARCHETYPE 8 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
8 Unjust laws, Radbruch and retroactivity
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [An unjust law] stays law unless intolerably unjust, but validity never settles whether [the judge or citizen] should obey.
Intro [The statement] runs two questions together: is [the statute] law, and must anyone obey it? I [agree only in part]: unjust law stays law unless intolerably unjust (Radbruch, Alexy), and validity never settles obedience (Hart).
8.1 Grudge informer Nazi statute; denounced her husband; could never shelter
  1. Whether [the Nazi statute] was "law" decides who bears the cost of past injustice.
  2. Hart left two honest options: let her go, or punish under "a frankly retrospective law" (PS 619); the latter, Fuller replies, voids Nazi laws as applied to informers "for purposes of that statute at least" (PFL 649).
  3. So [she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute] can hold even if it was law: on Alexy's reading, Bamberg voided no statute (59–60).
  • 1944: she denounced her husband's anti-Hitler remarks; sentenced to death, he was sent to the front; 1949: convicted under the 1871 Code (PS 618–19).
  • Fuller defends the courts: if all Nazi statutes were law, informers were "guiltless"; the issue seems to be who does "the dirty work" (PFL 649); courts, "living participants" in an emergency, could not wait, risking self-help (655).
  • QUALIFY Alexy: Bamberg convicted her on "a controversial criminal law construction" he leaves open (59, n 112).
  • Liu: any open form will do (no defence to invoke the named Nazi laws), though she reported under what was procedurally law (W10); Alexy's "evident" reply fits: the formula defeats a defence, creating no liability (61).
8.2 Hart's best case law is law; no law at all; speak plainly; simply refuse; considers unfair
  1. Hart answers [judges raised on "law is law" will never resist]: validity leaves open "the final moral question" of obedience (PS 618).
  2. Speaking plainly, [the decree] is "law but too evil to be obeyed", a condemnation "everyone can understand" (PS 620).
  3. So [he should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair] states the strong connection thesis, which "no serious non-positivist defends" (Alexy 52).
  • STEELMAN Hart's best point is honesty: denying evil law the name breeds romantic optimism that all values fit one system, and "insincerity" about a dilemma (PS 620).
  • Fuller: Radbruch saw the dilemma; LP gives fidelity to law no "coherent meaning", and Hart's dilemma, as Fuller states it, "makes no sense" (PFL 655–56).
  • AGAINST That LP disarmed German lawyers is "an extraordinary naïveté" (PS 617): elsewhere "law is law" went with "the most enlightened liberal attitudes" (618).
  • QUALIFY Radbruch (1946) wrote to arm judges against the next tyranny; Hart (1958): useless during the regime, unneeded after (Liu, W11). Hart and Fuller talk across purposes: a wicked regime meeting all eight desiderata leaves the formula question open (PFL 656; Liu, W10).
8.3 Alexy's replies how the word is used; any neutral standpoint; eye of the beholder; reaching back; determined tyranny
  1. Alexy grants [that is simply how the word is used] to observers, but a judge applying Ordinance 11, a citizenship decree, joins a procedure claiming correctness (41–42).
  2. So [the decree is law] holds only for observers: a judge refusing it on legal grounds must call it "prima-facie law but in the end not law at all" (42).
Objection (use two; Liu: language weakest, effectiveness speculative both ways)Alexy's reply
ClarityAdequacy before simplicity; at the extreme, the ethical problem is also legal (43–45)
EffectivenessLargely conceded (49); if lawyers share a consensus, resistance gains legal grounds; risk effect (12.5)

Democracy, dispensabilityCore area only, else no judicial review (56); nulla poena may be unamendable (art 79(3), 57); Singapore: 11.7
  • CONCEDE Hart's candour objection is "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall" (Alexy 60–61): exempt past actors via nulla poena, or, better, the injustice was so "evident" that the legal position is "simply determined" (61).
  • Ordinance 11 (Reich Citizenship Law) deprived people of citizenship (W10 slide 9†) on racist criteria; the Federal Constitutional Court (1968) found its injustice "intolerable" and "evident" (Alexy 52): such destruction "has nothing in common with law and justice" (48). Not the informer statutes (1934, 1938), which Liu once confused (W10).
8.4 Does the label matter? a quarrel about words; his conscience belongs to his private life; lawbreaker
  1. The label is a definitional quarrel, neither side less honest (Hart judges effect, Alexy concept: Liu, W11), but no mere [quarrel about words]: it decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute.
  2. Even Hart, though the wife's fate might be the same either way, holds candour "not just one among many minor virtues" (PS 620).
  3. So [his conscience belongs to his private life] restates pre-war Radbruch, the view Hart says he recanted (PS 616–17).
ActorLaw (LP, Hart)Not law (Radbruch, Alexy)
Judgeapplies it, or refuses on moral grounds: confusion at "its height" (PFL 655)refuses on legal grounds (Alexy 49)
Legislatorbound only by the master rule (Week 13†)legislates to a higher standard (CJ 85)

8.5 A stable democracy unelected veto; substitutes his own morality; for Parliament to repeal; must never invalidate
  1. In a stable democracy the formula is a narrow check, not [an unelected veto]: legislation stands unless intolerably unjust (TSH JO 329).
  2. For TSH, judges must show intolerable injustice by broad historical consensus: racial genocide and slavery qualify; abortion limits did not in 1973, nor, for now, opposite-sex marriage laws (JO 330–31).
  3. So [judges must never invalidate a law on grounds of justice] holds for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's to repeal (JO 331), not for genocide.
  • AGAINST TSH: since constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on "equal moral worth", Arts 9 and 12 "may legitimately import a higher law (including Radbruch's formula)" (JO 333–34); consensus generally checks "idiosyncratic personal ideologies" (332).
  • CONCEDE TSH's "catch" (JO 331): "decades on", the formula could impose a worldwide same-sex marriage trend; where consensus has, for realists, "gone dreadfully wrong" while a local legislature tries to do right, it is "problematic and not merely ineffective" (332).
  • CONCEDE Amid judicial oligarchies, consensus may "reflect the views of select groups of judges". Concede both; I accept her reply: "an autocrat, a few oligarchs, or even a brute majority" would do no better (JO 333).
  • QUALIFY Liu: drawing on common morality, the formula is a transitional safeguard, "primarily a tool of resistance", idle once morality has fully shifted (W11; cf Alexy 55).
8.6 Retroactivity retrospective laws are always unjust; life imprisonment; overnight
  1. [Retrospective laws are always unjust] confuses a cost with a verdict: a curative statute may be "essential to advance the cause of legality" (MOL 53).
  2. The core is the new crime, "commanding a man today to do something yesterday" (MOL 59), which even Hart grants may be "odious" (PS 619).
  3. So [the statement] nearly holds for new crimes, but a longer term is "less so" (MOL 93), and civil overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).
  • Keep apart: "branded as criminals" concerns overruling a reading that conduct was not criminal (MOL 57–58); Abdul Nasir† (3.8) engages constancy (MOL 79–80).
  • Liu's test: retroactivity is abuse when it undermines guidance (bad faith, frequency, after-the-fact punishment); leniency (MDA re-sentencing) is not, though fairness to prisoners is external morality; the common law is retroactive by default (W2).
8.7 Obey or disobey? obligation to obey; has done nothing wrong; will they be punished; fidelity means deference; highest court
  1. [The statement] merges three questions: a legal duty to obey, and moral duties to obey or disobey.
  2. Fidelity is not deference: Rex's subjects stayed "faithful to him as king", not to his law, "for he never made any" (MOL 41).
  3. So [the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong] holds legally for Hart, for Radbruch only below the threshold; morally it stays open.

  • Pages: PS 617–20; MOL 39–41; Alexy 47–48; Harris 9, 18; NLNR V.7.
  • CITIZEN Punished? While the regime lasts, yes, either way: he "must reckon with the usual consequences" (Hoerster, in Alexy 46).
  • JUDGE Highest court says "law": for observers and LP it is; for participants its ruling "lays claim to correctness" (Alexy 58–59), so at extreme injustice a later court or lawyer may call it legally wrong; below that, it is law (47–48). Lower courts: 15.10.
  • STEELMAN Why obey at all? Liu's pigeon feeder (W10): deterrence makes her comply but is no moral reason, and "others will copy" justifies punishing her, not her obeying. Fair play does: she gains from institutions others uphold, and fairness between citizens (Rawls) asks her to keep laws she rejects. Assume the duty; the topic is its exceptions. Every reason to obey is moral; legality only says the rule is law, so a positivist has the same reasons (W10).
8.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb† racist statute; discriminates by race or faith; not even an attempt at justice
  1. Radbruch's second limb asks not how unjust [the statute] is but whether it attempts justice: where equality "is deliberately betrayed", it "lacks completely the very nature of law"†.
  2. So [the judge must apply it] fails for a statute aimed at one race; morally, too, no role excuses applying "a facially racist law" (Thunder 328).
  • Radbruch's tiers (W10 slide 2†): positive law prevails "even when its content is unjust"; at an "intolerable level" it is "flawed law" that "must yield to justice"; betrayed equality, no law at all. Liu: tier 2 is no nullity, but the outcome is the same (W10).
  • CONCEDE "Equality" is contested (Westen, as LMS (CA) noted, JO 317): confine the limb to deliberate, facial betrayal, tested as in 8.5; unjust outcomes: 1.3(10).
Conclusion [The statement] is [overstated]. Validity never settles what [the actor] should do. A law surviving the formula is shown not intolerably unjust, never just: that question stays with Parliament and conscience. Deviating can be unjust too: the judge's morality may be wrong (Hoerster's "Nazi morality" judge, Alexy 53), and Radbruch himself warned of "frightful dangers" (PFL 656).

1Start here: archetype 8 in plain English

Archetype 8 asks: is a very unjust law still a law, and do you have to obey it? The story behind it is Nazi Germany. After the war, German courts had to decide what to do with people who had acted under Nazi laws. Hart says: call it law, but say plainly that it is too evil to obey. Radbruch (and later Alexy) says: at the extreme, it isn't law at all. The statements in this family usually mix two questions together: is it law? and must I obey? Your answer pulls them apart: an unjust law stays law unless it is intolerably unjust, and even a valid law doesn't settle whether you should obey it.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
ValidityWhether a rule counts as law in a system. It's a separate question from whether to obey.
Radbruch formula (RF)Unjust law still counts as law, unless its injustice reaches an "intolerable" level, or it deliberately betrays equality. Then it is not law.
Strong v weak connection thesisStrong: every unjust law is not law. Weak (Radbruch, Alexy): only extremely unjust law is not law. Nobody serious defends the strong one.
Grudge informerA wife who, in 1944, reported her husband's anti-Hitler remarks to get rid of him. After the war, was she protected by the Nazi law she acted under?
Retroactive (retrospective) lawA law that reaches back to change the legal position of acts already done.
Nulla poena sine legeLatin for "no punishment without a law": you can't be punished for something that wasn't a crime when you did it.
Participant v observerAn observer describes a legal system from outside; a participant (like a judge) has to decide and claims to decide correctly. Alexy thinks this changes the answer.
Fidelity to lawBeing faithful to law itself, not just obeying whoever is in power.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says an unjust law "stays law unless intolerably unjust, but validity never settles whether [the judge or citizen] should obey". Put simply: most unjust laws are still laws; only the truly monstrous ones lose that status. And whether something is law is a different question from whether you should obey it.

The Intro says: the statement runs together "is this law?" and "must anyone obey it?". You agree only in part: unjust law stays law unless intolerably unjust (Radbruch, Alexy), and being law never settles obedience (Hart). The Conclusion adds a warning: surviving the formula only shows a law isn't intolerably unjust, never that it is just. And judges ignoring law can be unjust too: a judge's own morality might be wrong.

The eight blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
8.1"The grudge informer could never shelter behind a Nazi statute."Whether it was "law" decides who bears the cost. Hart gives two honest options: let her go, or punish her under an openly retroactive law.
8.2"Judges raised on 'law is law' never resist; a judge should refuse whatever he finds unfair."Hart: validity doesn't settle obedience. Say it's "law but too evil to be obeyed". Refusing anything you find unfair goes far too far.
8.3"Calling it 'law' is just how the word is used."True for observers. But a judge applying a monstrous decree has to call it "not law at all".
8.4"It's only a quarrel about words."The label decides who may lawfully refuse and who can hide behind the statute. That matters.
8.5"In a democracy, judges must never strike down laws for injustice."True for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's job. Not for genocide or slavery.
8.6"Retroactive laws are always unjust."Creating new crimes after the fact is nearly always unjust. But some retroactive laws repair earlier failures.
8.7"You're obliged to obey; if you obey, you've done nothing wrong."Split three questions: legal duty to obey, moral duty to obey, moral duty to disobey.
8.8"A judge must apply even a racist statute."Radbruch's second test: a law that deliberately betrays equality isn't even trying to be just, so it's no law.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

"Is it law?" and "should I obey?" are two different questions; only extreme injustice changes the first.

2The big picture: is a wicked law still law?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

During the Nazi era, a woman reported her husband to the authorities for criticising Hitler, hoping to get rid of him. Under Nazi statutes, what she did was lawful. After the war, should a court punish her? If the Nazi statutes were "law", she seems to have done nothing illegal. If they were so evil they were "not law", she has no legal shield. This lesson is about that choice, and why it matters who makes it and how honestly.

Two questions are always in play, and the statements in this archetype love to run them together:

  1. Is it law? (validity)
  2. Should anyone obey it? (obligation)

The three positions

TheoristIs a wicked statute law?What follows
Hart (1958, PS)Yes, but it may be "too evil to be obeyed"Separate law as it is from law as it ought to be. If you want to punish, pass a frankly retrospective statute
Fuller (1958, PFL)Nazi law so failed legality ("the party in the streets", secret and retroactive laws) that it is doubtful how much of a legal system survivedFidelity to law needs law's inner morality
Radbruch, AlexyNot law, if intolerably unjust (the Radbruch formula)Judges and lawyers deny it legal character

The Radbruch formula (RF) in three tiers (W10 slide 2†)

Radbruch's tiers
▤ W10 slide 2†; Alexy 40–41
  1. 1Positive law prevails "even when its content is unjust".
  2. 2At an "intolerable level" of injustice it is "flawed law" that "must yield to justice".
  3. 3Where equality "is deliberately betrayed", it "lacks completely the very nature of law".

Liu: tier 2 is no nullity, but the outcome is the same (W10). "Not law" at tier 2 is Alexy's reading (40).

Alexy's key idea: observer v participant

An observer (a historian, a sociologist) reports what was treated as law. A participant (a judge deciding a case, a lawyer arguing one) asks what the correct legal answer is. Alexy grants that, for observers, Ordinance 11 was "law". But a judge applying it joins a procedure that "lays claim to correctness", and extreme injustice fails that claim. So for the participant, it is "prima-facie law but in the end not law at all" (42).

38.1 Grudge informer

▤ On your sheet: 8.1 Grudge informer (word for word)
8.1 Grudge informer Nazi statute; denounced her husband; could never shelter
  1. Whether [the Nazi statute] was "law" decides who bears the cost of past injustice.
  2. Hart left two honest options: let her go, or punish under "a frankly retrospective law" (PS 619); the latter, Fuller replies, voids Nazi laws as applied to informers "for purposes of that statute at least" (PFL 649).
  3. So [she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute] can hold even if it was law: on Alexy's reading, Bamberg voided no statute (59–60).
  • 1944: she denounced her husband's anti-Hitler remarks; sentenced to death, he was sent to the front; 1949: convicted under the 1871 Code (PS 618–19).
  • Fuller defends the courts: if all Nazi statutes were law, informers were "guiltless"; the issue seems to be who does "the dirty work" (PFL 649); courts, "living participants" in an emergency, could not wait, risking self-help (655).
  • QUALIFY Alexy: Bamberg convicted her on "a controversial criminal law construction" he leaves open (59, n 112).
  • Liu: any open form will do (no defence to invoke the named Nazi laws), though she reported under what was procedurally law (W10); Alexy's "evident" reply fits: the formula defeats a defence, creating no liability (61).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The grudge informer case is the test everyone uses. Hart says: either let her go, or openly pass a new law that punishes her retroactively, admitting it's a hard choice. Fuller says the post-war courts were right to treat the Nazi statutes as not law for her. Alexy adds a twist: the court that convicted her didn't actually void any statute.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "The grudge informer could never hide behind a Nazi statute, because evil laws aren't law."

  1. The real issue is who pays for past injustice. Whether the Nazi statute counts as "law" decides whether she gets off or bears the cost.
  2. Hart's two honest options: let her go, or punish her under a law that openly admits it is retroactive. Fuller replies that the second option is really just declaring the Nazi laws void for informers anyway.
  3. So you can agree she shouldn't shelter behind the statute even if it was law. On Alexy's reading, the post-war court didn't actually void any statute.

The facts: in 1944 she reported her husband's anti-Hitler remarks; he was sentenced to death but sent to the front instead. In 1949 she was convicted under the old 1871 Criminal Code. Fuller defends the courts: they were in the middle of an emergency and couldn't wait. Liu: any honest approach works; she can't use the Nazi laws as a defence.

Remember: the label decides who bears the cost.

The statement. "The Nazi experience proves that those who insist 'law is law' were simply wrong … the wife who denounced her husband could never shelter behind a Nazi statute." (Q16)

The facts. 1944: she denounced her husband's anti-Hitler remarks; he was sentenced to death and then sent to the front. 1949: she was convicted under the 1871 Criminal Code (PS 618–19).

The move.

  1. Whether the Nazi statute was "law" decides who bears the cost of past injustice.
  2. Hart left two honest options: let her go, or punish under "a frankly retrospective law" (PS 619). Fuller replies that the courts' approach voids Nazi laws as applied to informers "for purposes of that statute at least" (PFL 649).
  3. So "she could never shelter behind a Nazi statute" can hold even if it was law: on Alexy's reading, the Bamberg court voided no statute (59–60).

More.

  • Fuller defends the courts: if all Nazi statutes were law, informers were "guiltless"; the issue seems to be who does "the dirty work" (PFL 649); courts, "living participants" in an emergency, could not wait, risking self-help (655).
  • QUALIFY (Alexy): Bamberg convicted her on "a controversial criminal law construction" he leaves open (59, n 112).
  • Liu: any open form will do (no defence to invoke the named Nazi laws), though she reported under what was procedurally law (W10). Alexy's "evident" reply fits: the formula defeats a defence, creating no liability (61).
⚠ TRAP
Hart got the facts wrong

Bamberg voided no 1934 statute, as Hart supposed; Hart later conceded the error (Alexy 59–60; card 14.18 TRAP).

48.2 Hart's best case

▤ On your sheet: 8.2 Hart's best case (word for word)
8.2 Hart's best case law is law; no law at all; speak plainly; simply refuse; considers unfair
  1. Hart answers [judges raised on "law is law" will never resist]: validity leaves open "the final moral question" of obedience (PS 618).
  2. Speaking plainly, [the decree] is "law but too evil to be obeyed", a condemnation "everyone can understand" (PS 620).
  3. So [he should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair] states the strong connection thesis, which "no serious non-positivist defends" (Alexy 52).
  • STEELMAN Hart's best point is honesty: denying evil law the name breeds romantic optimism that all values fit one system, and "insincerity" about a dilemma (PS 620).
  • Fuller: Radbruch saw the dilemma; LP gives fidelity to law no "coherent meaning", and Hart's dilemma, as Fuller states it, "makes no sense" (PFL 655–56).
  • AGAINST That LP disarmed German lawyers is "an extraordinary naïveté" (PS 617): elsewhere "law is law" went with "the most enlightened liberal attitudes" (618).
  • QUALIFY Radbruch (1946) wrote to arm judges against the next tyranny; Hart (1958): useless during the regime, unneeded after (Liu, W11). Hart and Fuller talk across purposes: a wicked regime meeting all eight desiderata leaves the formula question open (PFL 656; Liu, W10).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Hart's big point is honesty. Say "this is the law, but it is too evil to obey." Everyone understands that. Saying "it isn't really law" can hide the hard choice and make people think law and morality always fit together nicely.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "German judges trained in 'law is law' could never resist the Nazis" and "a judge should simply refuse to apply whatever he thinks unfair".

  1. Hart: saying something is valid law leaves open "the final moral question" of whether to obey it. So positivism doesn't make judges obey everything.
  2. Speak plainly: the decree is "law but too evil to be obeyed". Everyone can understand that.
  3. So "refuse whatever he considers unfair" is the strong version (every unjust law isn't law), which Alexy says "no serious non-positivist defends".

The extras: STEELMAN: Hart's best point is honesty: pretending evil laws aren't law hides a real dilemma. AGAINST: blaming positivism for Nazi judges is "an extraordinary naïveté"; elsewhere "law is law" went with very liberal attitudes. QUALIFY (Liu): Radbruch wanted to arm judges against the next tyranny; Hart says the formula is useless during a regime and unneeded after it.

Remember: "law, but too evil to obey" (Hart) v "not law at all" (Radbruch), and neither says "refuse whatever's unfair".

The statements. "An unjust statute is no law at all, and a judge asked to apply an enactment he considers unfair should simply refuse." (Q77) "Judges raised on 'law is law' will never resist."

The move.

  1. Hart answers "judges raised on 'law is law' will never resist": validity leaves open "the final moral question" of obedience (PS 618).
  2. Speaking plainly, the decree is "law but too evil to be obeyed", a condemnation "everyone can understand" (PS 620).
  3. So "he should simply refuse whatever he considers unfair" states the strong connection thesis, which "no serious non-positivist defends" (Alexy 52).

More.

  • STEELMAN: Hart's best point is honesty: denying evil law the name breeds romantic optimism that all values fit one system, and "insincerity" about a dilemma (PS 620).
  • Fuller: Radbruch saw the dilemma; LP gives fidelity to law no "coherent meaning", and Hart's dilemma, as Fuller states it, "makes no sense" (PFL 655–56).
  • AGAINST: that LP disarmed German lawyers is "an extraordinary naïveté" (PS 617): elsewhere "law is law" went with "the most enlightened liberal attitudes" (618).
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Radbruch (1946) wrote to arm judges against the next tyranny; Hart (1958) replied that the formula is useless during the regime and unneeded after (Liu, W11). And Hart and Fuller talk across purposes: a wicked regime meeting all eight desiderata leaves the formula question open (PFL 656; Liu, W10).

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Opponents of Radbruch give several objections: it's confusing, it doesn't work, it's uncertain, morality is relative, and it undermines democracy. Alexy answers each. You only need two in an exam, and Liu thinks the language objection is the weakest and the effectiveness one is guesswork either way.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Calling a wicked decree 'law' is just how the word is used. There's no neutral standpoint, and justice is in the eye of the beholder. Reaching back to undo it is unfair."

  1. Alexy accepts the "word use" point, for observers. But a judge applying Ordinance 11 (the Nazi decree that stripped people of citizenship on racist grounds) is a participant, taking part in a process that claims to get things right.
  2. So "the decree is law" holds only from the outside. A judge who refuses it on legal grounds must call it "prima facie law but in the end not law at all".

The table of objections: pick two. Clarity: at the extreme, the moral problem is also a legal one. Effectiveness: largely conceded. Certainty: the more extreme the injustice, the more obvious it is. Relativism: in rights-respecting states, shared rights should stop a judge with "Nazi morality". Democracy: only the core of extreme cases. CONCEDE: Hart's honesty objection is "the strongest argument" against Alexy, "but not its downfall", because the injustice was so evident that the legal position was already settled.

Remember: observers can call it law; a judge deciding the case can't.

The statement. "Seen from any neutral standpoint, a decree stripping a whole class of people of their citizenship, issued through the proper channels and enforced by the state's officials, is law; that is simply how the word is used." (Q79)

The move.

  1. Alexy grants "that is simply how the word is used" to observers, but a judge applying Ordinance 11, a citizenship decree, joins a procedure claiming correctness (41–42).
  2. So "the decree is law" holds only for observers: a judge refusing it on legal grounds must call it "prima-facie law but in the end not law at all" (42).
The objections and Alexy's replies (use two)
▤ Alexy 43–62; Liu: language weakest, effectiveness speculative both ways
  1. 1Clarity: adequacy before simplicity; at the extreme, the ethical problem is also legal (43–45).
  2. 2Effectiveness: largely conceded (49); but if lawyers share a consensus, resistance gains legal grounds; and the risk effect (12.5): officials know they may later be prosecuted.
  3. 3Certainty: "the more extreme the injustice, the more certain the knowledge of it"; only an absolutist objects (52–53).
  4. 4Relativism: in rights-steeped states, rights consensus should thwart Hoerster's "Nazi morality" judge (53–55); the minimum core is unargued here (55, 62).
  5. 5Democracy, dispensability: core area only, else no judicial review (56); nulla poena may be unamendable (art 79(3), 57); Singapore: 11.7.

CONCEDE: Hart's candour objection is "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall" (Alexy 60–61). Answer: exempt past actors via nulla poena, or, better, the injustice was so "evident" that the legal position is "simply determined" (61).

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Ordinance 11

The Reich Citizenship Law's Ordinance 11 deprived people of citizenship (W10 slide 9†) on racist criteria. The Federal Constitutional Court (1968) found its injustice "intolerable" and "evident" (Alexy 52): such destruction "has nothing in common with law and justice" (48). Don't confuse it with the informer statutes (1934, 1938), as Liu once did (W10).

Framework 15.8: should a judge deny it legal character?
▤ Alexy 40–61
  1. 1Take the participant's view (say, a judge), not the observer's.
  2. 2Weak thesis: legal character is lost only at an "intolerable degree" of injustice.
  3. 3Concede: definitions "cannot, as such, change reality" (48–49); candour is the strongest objection.
  4. 4Verdict rule: deny legal character only where the injustice was evident when done: no covert retroactivity.

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Who cares whether we call it 'law' or 'not law'? What matters is what people do." But the label changes things: whether a judge can refuse on legal grounds, whether a citizen can hide behind the statute, whether a lawyer can call it lawless in court.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Whether we call it 'law' is just a quarrel about words. A judge's conscience belongs to his private life."

  1. It is a definitional quarrel, but not a trivial one. Neither side is less honest (Hart cares about effects, Alexy about the concept). The label decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute.
  2. Even Hart says candour (being honest about what you're doing) is "not just one among many minor virtues".
  3. So "his conscience belongs to his private life" is exactly the pre-war Radbruch view, which Hart says Radbruch later gave up.

How to read the table: it shows what each actor (judge, legislator, lawyer, citizen) does if the decree is law (Hart) or not law (Radbruch, Alexy). Under Hart, a judge refuses on moral grounds; under Alexy, on legal grounds. A citizen who refuses is a lawbreaker under Hart. Under Alexy, a citizen who obeys can't hide behind the decree if its injustice was "evident". AGAINST: Fuller says words here strongly affect attitudes, and Nazi law failed even his eight requirements.

Remember: the label decides who can lawfully refuse.

The statement. "Whether a wicked statute deserves the name 'law' is a quarrel about words … A judge has sworn to apply whatever has been validly enacted, and his conscience belongs to his private life." (Q78)

The move.

  1. The label is a definitional quarrel, neither side less honest (Hart judges effect, Alexy concept: Liu, W11), but no mere quarrel about words: it decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute.
  2. Even Hart, though the wife's fate might be the same either way, holds candour "not just one among many minor virtues" (PS 620).
  3. So "his conscience belongs to his private life" restates pre-war Radbruch, the view Hart says he recanted (PS 616–17).
What the label changes, actor by actor
▤ 8.4 table
  1. 1Judge: if law, applies it or refuses on moral grounds (confusion at "its height", PFL 655); if not law, refuses on legal grounds (Alexy 49).
  2. 2Legislator: if law, bound only by the master rule; if not, legislates to a higher standard (CJ 85).
  3. 3Lawyer: if law, may refuse, but "what he refuses to obey is still the law"; if not, should denounce it as having "no legal character".
  4. 4Citizen: if law, the refuser is a lawbreaker and the obeyer lawful (morally open); if not, the refuser is still punished while the regime lasts, and the obeyer is unsheltered if the injustice was "evident".

AGAINST (Fuller): words here have "a powerful effect on human attitudes" (PFL 649), and Nazi law failed legality itself: the Roehm statute, "the party in the streets" (650–52).

78.5 A stable democracy

▤ On your sheet: 8.5 A stable democracy (word for word)
8.5 A stable democracy unelected veto; substitutes his own morality; for Parliament to repeal; must never invalidate
  1. In a stable democracy the formula is a narrow check, not [an unelected veto]: legislation stands unless intolerably unjust (TSH JO 329).
  2. For TSH, judges must show intolerable injustice by broad historical consensus: racial genocide and slavery qualify; abortion limits did not in 1973, nor, for now, opposite-sex marriage laws (JO 330–31).
  3. So [judges must never invalidate a law on grounds of justice] holds for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's to repeal (JO 331), not for genocide.
  • AGAINST TSH: since constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on "equal moral worth", Arts 9 and 12 "may legitimately import a higher law (including Radbruch's formula)" (JO 333–34); consensus generally checks "idiosyncratic personal ideologies" (332).
  • CONCEDE TSH's "catch" (JO 331): "decades on", the formula could impose a worldwide same-sex marriage trend; where consensus has, for realists, "gone dreadfully wrong" while a local legislature tries to do right, it is "problematic and not merely ineffective" (332).
  • CONCEDE Amid judicial oligarchies, consensus may "reflect the views of select groups of judges". Concede both; I accept her reply: "an autocrat, a few oligarchs, or even a brute majority" would do no better (JO 333).
  • QUALIFY Liu: drawing on common morality, the formula is a transitional safeguard, "primarily a tool of resistance", idle once morality has fully shifted (W11; cf Alexy 55).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In Nazi Germany, the formula made sense. But in a normal democracy like Singapore, should judges ever strike down laws for being unjust? TSH says: almost never. Only when the injustice is so extreme that people everywhere, for a long time, agree it's monstrous (genocide, slavery). Otherwise it's Parliament's job.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "In a stable democracy, the Radbruch formula is an unelected veto. A judge would be substituting his own morality. Unjust laws are for Parliament to repeal, so judges must never strike down a law on grounds of justice."

  1. In a stable democracy the formula is a narrow check, not a veto. Laws stand unless intolerably unjust.
  2. TSH's test: judges must show intolerable injustice by a broad historical consensus. Genocide and slavery qualify; abortion limits did not in 1973, and opposite-sex marriage laws don't for now.
  3. So "never strike down for injustice" is right for ordinary injustice, which is Parliament's job to fix. It's wrong for genocide.

The extras: AGAINST (TSH): since the Constitution rests on equal moral worth, Arts 9 and 12 may bring in a higher law, including the formula. CONCEDE (TSH's "catch"): decades on, a global consensus could push something like same-sex marriage onto a local legislature; and consensus might reflect a few judges. Her reply: an autocrat, a few elites or a brute majority would do no better. QUALIFY (Liu): the formula is mainly a tool of resistance during transitions.

Remember: ordinary injustice goes to Parliament; only the intolerable goes to judges.

AGAINST: TSH: since constitutional supremacy rests most soundly on "equal moral worth", Arts 9 and 12 "may legitimately import a higher law (including Radbruch's formula)" (JO 333–34); consensus generally checks "idiosyncratic personal ideologies" (332).

88.6 Retroactivity

▤ On your sheet: 8.6 Retroactivity (word for word)
8.6 Retroactivity retrospective laws are always unjust; life imprisonment; overnight
  1. [Retrospective laws are always unjust] confuses a cost with a verdict: a curative statute may be "essential to advance the cause of legality" (MOL 53).
  2. The core is the new crime, "commanding a man today to do something yesterday" (MOL 59), which even Hart grants may be "odious" (PS 619).
  3. So [the statement] nearly holds for new crimes, but a longer term is "less so" (MOL 93), and civil overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).
  • Keep apart: "branded as criminals" concerns overruling a reading that conduct was not criminal (MOL 57–58); Abdul Nasir† (3.8) engages constancy (MOL 79–80).
  • Liu's test: retroactivity is abuse when it undermines guidance (bad faith, frequency, after-the-fact punishment); leniency (MDA re-sentencing) is not, though fairness to prisoners is external morality; the common law is retroactive by default (W2).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Retroactive laws are always unjust." Mostly true for making new crimes ("you did something legal yesterday; today it's a crime and you're punished"). But a law that retroactively fixes a technical mistake, or reduces sentences, can actually help people.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Retroactive laws are always unjust. Changing what 'life imprisonment' means overnight is a clear example."

  1. "Always unjust" confuses a cost with a verdict. Retroactivity is a cost, but a law that reaches back to fix an earlier legality failure may be needed (Fuller).
  2. The core wrong is creating a new crime after the fact: "commanding a man today to do something yesterday". Even Hart agrees that may be "odious".
  3. So the statement nearly holds for new crimes. A longer sentence is "less so", and changes in civil law through court rulings are a price worth paying (3.8).

The extras: keep the cases apart: being "branded as criminals" is about overruling a ruling that said conduct was lawful; Abdul Nasir (life means life, applied only to the future) is about stability. Liu's test: retroactivity is abuse when it undermines the law's ability to guide (bad faith, frequent changes, punishing after the fact). Making a sentence more lenient is not abuse.

Remember: new crimes after the fact: almost always wrong; other retroactivity: depends.

The statements. "Retrospective laws are always unjust." (Q25) "A theory that wicked laws are 'not law' is a solution in search of a problem: a new parliament can simply pass statutes reaching back in time." (Q81)

The move.

  1. "Retrospective laws are always unjust" confuses a cost with a verdict: a curative statute may be "essential to advance the cause of legality" (MOL 53).
  2. The core is the new crime, "commanding a man today to do something yesterday" (MOL 59), which even Hart grants may be "odious" (PS 619).
  3. So the statement nearly holds for new crimes, but a longer term is "less so" (MOL 93), and civil overruling is a price worth paying (3.8).

Keep apart: "branded as criminals" concerns overruling a reading that conduct was not criminal (MOL 57–58); Abdul Nasir† (3.8) engages constancy (MOL 79–80).

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Liu's test: retroactivity is abuse when it undermines guidance (bad faith, frequency, after-the-fact punishment). Leniency (e.g. re-sentencing under the Misuse of Drugs Act) is not, though fairness to prisoners is external morality. The common law is retroactive by default (W2).

98.7 Obey or disobey?

▤ On your sheet: 8.7 Obey or disobey? (word for word)
8.7 Obey or disobey? obligation to obey; has done nothing wrong; will they be punished; fidelity means deference; highest court
  1. [The statement] merges three questions: a legal duty to obey, and moral duties to obey or disobey.
  2. Fidelity is not deference: Rex's subjects stayed "faithful to him as king", not to his law, "for he never made any" (MOL 41).
  3. So [the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong] holds legally for Hart, for Radbruch only below the threshold; morally it stays open.
TheoristLegal dutyMoral duty to obeyMoral duty to disobey

Fullerby degree; none on total failurefrom reciprocity; none once "finally and completely" ruptured"no simple principle" short of rupture, as under Hitler

  • CITIZEN Punished? While the regime lasts, yes, either way: he "must reckon with the usual consequences" (Hoerster, in Alexy 46).
  • JUDGE Highest court says "law": for observers and LP it is; for participants its ruling "lays claim to correctness" (Alexy 58–59), so at extreme injustice a later court or lawyer may call it legally wrong; below that, it is law (47–48). Lower courts: 15.10.
  • STEELMAN Why obey at all? Liu's pigeon feeder (W10): deterrence makes her comply but is no moral reason, and "others will copy" justifies punishing her, not her obeying. Fair play does: she gains from institutions others uphold, and fairness between citizens (Rawls) asks her to keep laws she rejects. Assume the duty; the topic is its exceptions. Every reason to obey is moral; legality only says the rule is law, so a positivist has the same reasons (W10).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three separate questions hide in "must I obey?": (1) does the law legally require it? (2) do I have a moral duty to obey? (3) do I have a moral duty to disobey? Different theorists answer them differently. The table below is the cheat-code.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Citizens are obliged to obey the law. Someone who obeys has done nothing wrong; fidelity to law means deferring to the highest court."

  1. Split three questions: Is there a legal duty to obey? A moral duty to obey? A moral duty to disobey?
  2. Fidelity isn't deference. Fuller's King Rex: his subjects stayed loyal to him as king, not to his law, "for he never made any".
  3. So "the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong" is legally true for Hart, and for Radbruch only below the "intolerable" line. Morally, it's still an open question.

How to read the table: each row is a theorist; each column is one of the three questions. For example, Hart: legal duty yes; moral duty not settled by validity; moral duty to disobey past a certain level of wickedness. Aquinas: an unjust law is "a corruption of law" (no legal duty), though you might obey to avoid scandal or danger.

The extras: CITIZEN: while the regime lasts, you'll be punished either way. JUDGE: if the highest court says "law", observers accept it, but at extreme injustice a later court may call it legally wrong. STEELMAN (Liu's pigeon feeder): fear of punishment isn't a moral reason to obey, but fair play is: she benefits from rules others keep.

Remember: legal duty, moral duty to obey, moral duty to disobey: three separate questions.

The statement. "The citizen who defies an unjust statute may be admirable, but he is a lawbreaker; the citizen who obeys it has done nothing wrong … Fidelity to law means exactly this: deference to what the lawmaker has commanded." (Q78)

The move.

  1. The statement merges three questions: a legal duty to obey, and moral duties to obey or disobey.
  2. Fidelity is not deference: Rex's subjects stayed "faithful to him as king", not to his law, "for he never made any" (MOL 41).
  3. So "the citizen who obeys has done nothing wrong" holds legally for Hart, for Radbruch only below the threshold; morally it stays open.
The obligation grid
▤ PS 617–20; MOL 39–41; Alexy 47–48; Harris 9, 18; NLNR V.7
  1. 1Hart: legal duty yes; moral duty to obey not settled by validity; duty to disobey past "a certain degree of iniquity".
  2. 2Fuller: legal duty by degree, none on total failure; moral duty from reciprocity, none once "finally and completely" ruptured; "no simple principle" short of rupture.
  3. 3Radbruch, Alexy: no legal duty past intolerable injustice or betrayed equality; below that, law open to moral critique; judges and lawyers deny legal character.
  4. 4Aquinas: none: "a corruption of law"; no moral duty, except perhaps to avoid "scandal or some particular danger".
  5. 5Finnis: not a nullity; moral duty not prima facie, but can arise lest a system on the whole just weaken; never choose "directly against a basic value".

CITIZEN: punished? While the regime lasts, yes, either way: he "must reckon with the usual consequences" (Hoerster, in Alexy 46).

JUDGE: the highest court says "law": for observers and LP it is; for participants its ruling "lays claim to correctness" (Alexy 58–59), so at extreme injustice a later court or lawyer may call it legally wrong; below that, it is law. Lower courts: Kennedy's five courses (15.10).

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Why obey at all? Liu's pigeon feeder (W10). A woman feeds pigeons against a by-law. Deterrence makes her comply but is no moral reason; "others will copy" justifies punishing her, not her obeying. Fair play does give a reason: she gains from institutions others uphold, and fairness between citizens (Rawls) asks her to keep laws she rejects. Assume the duty; the topic is its exceptions. Every reason to obey is moral; legality only says the rule is law, so a positivist has the same reasons.

108.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb

▤ On your sheet: 8.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb† (word for word)
8.8 Radbruch's betrayal-of-equality limb† racist statute; discriminates by race or faith; not even an attempt at justice
  1. Radbruch's second limb asks not how unjust [the statute] is but whether it attempts justice: where equality "is deliberately betrayed", it "lacks completely the very nature of law"†.
  2. So [the judge must apply it] fails for a statute aimed at one race; morally, too, no role excuses applying "a facially racist law" (Thunder 328).
  • Radbruch's tiers (W10 slide 2†): positive law prevails "even when its content is unjust"; at an "intolerable level" it is "flawed law" that "must yield to justice"; betrayed equality, no law at all. Liu: tier 2 is no nullity, but the outcome is the same (W10).
  • CONCEDE "Equality" is contested (Westen, as LMS (CA) noted, JO 317): confine the limb to deliberate, facial betrayal, tested as in 8.5; unjust outcomes: 1.3(10).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Radbruch's last tier isn't about how much injustice. It asks: is this law even trying to be just? A law aimed at one race, on purpose, isn't trying. It betrays equality, so it isn't law at all.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "A judge must apply a racist statute, because it's the law."

  1. Radbruch's second test isn't about how unjust the law is, but whether it even tries to be just. Where equality is "deliberately betrayed", the statute "lacks completely the very nature of law".
  2. So "the judge must apply it" fails for a law aimed at one race. Morally too, Thunder says no role excuses applying "a facially racist law".

Radbruch's three tiers: (1) ordinary unjust law still wins; (2) at an "intolerable" level it is "flawed law" that "must yield to justice"; (3) where equality is deliberately betrayed, it's no law at all. Liu: tier 2 isn't strictly void, but the outcome is the same. CONCEDE: "equality" is contested, so limit this test to deliberate betrayal written on the face of the law.

Remember: a law that doesn't even try to treat people as equals isn't law.

The statements. "A statute that discriminates by race or faith must still be applied." "The judge must apply it."

The move.

  1. Radbruch's second limb asks not how unjust the statute is but whether it attempts justice: where equality "is deliberately betrayed", it "lacks completely the very nature of law"†.
  2. So "the judge must apply it" fails for a statute aimed at one race; morally, too, no role excuses applying "a facially racist law" (Thunder 328).

CONCEDE: "equality" is contested (Westen, as LMS (CA) noted, JO 317). Confine the limb to deliberate, facial betrayal, tested as in 8.5. Unjust outcomes of just rules are different: 1.3(10) and 10.11.

11Putting it together: Practice Q78

"Whether a wicked statute deserves the name 'law' is a quarrel about words; what matters is how people ought to act. A judge has sworn to apply whatever has been validly enacted, and his conscience belongs to his private life, not to his courtroom. The citizen who defies an unjust statute may be admirable, but he is a lawbreaker; the citizen who obeys it has done nothing wrong, for he has simply kept faith with the law. Fidelity to law means exactly this: deference to what the lawmaker has commanded."

Instruction: Fuller, Hart, Radbruch.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "quarrel about words" → 8.4.
  • "conscience belongs to his private life" → 8.4 line 3 (pre-war Radbruch).
  • "lawbreaker", "done nothing wrong" → 8.7 (obligation grid).
  • "Fidelity … means … deference" → 8.7 line 2; 3.7.
  • Actors: judge and citizen: one section each. Distinction: 1.3(6) validity v obligation.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement runs two questions together: whether a wicked statute is law, and what anyone should do about it. It is right that the second matters most, and wrong that the first is idle. I make three claims: (1) the label is no mere quarrel about words, because it decides who may lawfully refuse and who may shelter behind the statute; (2) a judge's oath binds him to law, but at intolerable injustice, on Radbruch's formula, there is no law to apply; and (3) fidelity to law is not deference, so the obedient citizen's legality settles nothing about his moral position.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. The label (8.4, 8.2): Hart's honesty v Alexy's participant; Liu: effect v concept; the actor table; Fuller: words shape attitudes.
  2. The judge (8.2, 8.3, 8.5): "law but too evil to be obeyed" v "prima-facie law but in the end not law"; conscience in private life is pre-war Radbruch, which he recanted; in a stable democracy only BHC-level injustice.
  3. The citizen and fidelity (8.7): obligation grid; Rex's subjects; Hoerster: the citizen must reckon with consequences; pigeon feeder. Self-critique: Alexy grants candour is the strongest objection.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Validity never settles what the judge or citizen should do, and fidelity to law is fidelity to an enterprise that respects its subjects, not deference to whoever commands. A law that survives the Radbruch formula is shown to be not intolerably unjust, never to be just: that question stays with Parliament and conscience.

LESSON 9 · ARCHETYPE 9 · ABOUT 45 MIN · 40 QUESTIONS

Adjudication: Dworkin, ALR, CLS

⚡ BIG IDEA

Judges justify by fit and political morality. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and in the open cases political morality, not personal preference, closes them.

ARCHETYPE 9 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
9 Adjudication: Dworkin, ALR, CLS
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The statement] overstates: judges justify by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, not all.
Intro [The statement] treats adjudication as [politics in robes]. Realists rightly show that canons and ratios leave some cases open, and crits that principles meet counterprinciples. But a judge cannot predict his own ruling; he must justify it, by the reading that best fits and justifies the law (Dworkin). So rules leave some cases open, not all, and political morality, not preference, closes them.
9.1 ALR decide first, prediction, canons, ratios read narrowly or widely
  1. Realism rightly says [canons and ratios] leave hard cases open, but a judge must justify, not predict.
  2. Practitioners may predict, "but judges themselves cannot. They must purport to justify" (Harris 102); "alas, I must find for the defendant" predicts nothing on its face (108).
  3. So [law is prediction] holds at most for counsel; Llewellyn called realism "a method nothing more" (Harris 103).
  • FOR Cheng San GRC (GE 1997)†: candidates stood inside polling stations; s 82(1)(d) bars waiting "outside", (e) loitering "within a radius of 200 metres" (pre-2023). Literal: outside only; purposive: the mischief, and "at or near". The AG advised no offence. Precise canons, uncertain outcome (Liu, W11).
  • QUALIFY Liu: ALR oversimplifies: a judge can write any decision, but reputation, reversal, time and credibility (Denning) make a flimsy one costly. Kennedy's correction: law, a "medium", constrains like bricks, relative to one's project; moving it costs "work and the credibility risk" (526, 559).
  • QUALIFY Weak and strong readings: on Harris's minimal reading, "'rules' are not all that matter" (100); in extreme form, all reasoning is "mere surface talk" (102).
9.2 Dworkin v ALR precedent runs out, judges legislate, floodgates, social goals
  1. Saying [the judge legislates once precedent runs out] mistakes a theoretical disagreement about law's grounds for a gap.
  2. In McLoughlin all five Lords allowed the appeal, yet split: Scarman held line-drawing policy "not justiciable" (431); Edmund-Davies called that "as novel as it is startling" (427).
  3. So leaving [floodgates] to Parliament is Scarman's contested view, which I defend as a choice, not as the case's lesson.
  • AGAINST Floodgates: policy or principle (Week 1b slide 3†)? As court congestion and insurance cost, policy, beyond "the limits of the forensic process" (Scarman 431); as liability out of proportion to fault, principle.
  • QUALIFY Bridge weighed the policy grounds offered, found them "wholly insufficient", and called stopping at decided cases "an unwarranted abdication" (441).
9.3 CLS v Dworkin neutral framework, exceptions prove the rule, drawn up by an elite, tear it down
  1. Unger rightly denies [contract law is a neutral framework]: each principle meets a counterprinciple that the dominant view files as an anomaly (Unger 74–75).
  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant contract theory rules far less than it claims (Unger 58).
  3. Yet [tear it down] overreaches: condemning hidden interests needs a non-subjective standard, which Finnis's basic goods supply (5.1).
  • FOR Doctrine legitimates hierarchy "even when it is deployed by someone who thinks he is forwarding progressive causes" (Harris 109): hidden interests (Week 1b slide 17†); crits generally distance themselves from Marxist instrumentalism (110).
  • STEELMAN The crit's best point is conservatism: fit crowns the past's dominant principle and files fairness (duress, undue influence: Week 11 slide 14†) as exceptions; the fixes become "arbitrarily selective" (Unger 74).
  • AGAINST Harris: the liberal must show reformed legalism yields more "incremental justice" than "deconstruction for its own sake" (113).
  • QUALIFY ALR v CLS (Liu, W1): same description, law is politics; split on "what next?": ALR keeps the system, given good judges; CLS would remake it, exposing class interests.
9.4 Precedent and theory like cases alike, stare decisis, authority for argument
  1. Precedent cannot replace theory: [treating like cases alike] needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral.
  2. Was a mother reaching hospital two hours later like one at the scene? Only a principle, foreseeability or physical risk, can say.
  3. So [precedent, not justice, makes law fair] fails: stare decisis itself is contested, strict or relaxed, and needs justification.
  • AGAINST Relaxed precedent yields when "sufficiently wrong" (Law's Empire); interpretation "must contain a doctrine of mistake" (AMP).
9.5 Right answer single right answer, whatever coheres, never refuse an unjust statute
  1. [A single right answer] is possible in principle: interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be best.
  2. But fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation", and then "substantive political theory" decides (AMP).
  3. So [he need never refuse an unjust statute] fails: Dworkin gives no threshold; the Radbruch formula, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus, does (15.13).
  • CONCEDE Dworkin: a judge's best reading rests on "beliefs other judges need not share" (AMP). Concede no demonstrable answer; insist the choice is political, not personal (9.8).
  • QUALIFY Liu: where the practice itself includes the formula, a Dworkinian judge can fit and still refuse extreme injustice (W11); fit is a matter of degree (Denning; the German nullity courts). TSH's catch: 8.5.
9.6 Judge-variance study outcomes vary by judge, change the bench
  1. A realist reads [the variance findings] as fact scepticism confirmed; they indict judges who fail to justify, not Dworkin's normative theory.
  • Rule v fact scepticism (W11 slide 8†): Llewellyn's "paper rules" (Harris 99); Frank's "upper courtitis": the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies (100). Liu: appeal only moves the discretion up a level (W11).
9.7 Synthesis answers the realists, victory to the crits
  1. Dworkin's judge answers [the realists]: he must justify by fit and value, and cannot predict his own ruling.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly; Harris reads Unger's jibe at "a pre-established harmony" as aimed at Dworkin (113).
  3. So victory to the crits follows only if value is subjective; Liu's third option, natural law, would say which principle should win (Riggs?: Week 11 slide 15†).
  • QUALIFY Liu: Dworkin is text-first: the judge brings his political theory but owes his duty to that law, close to Fuller's fidelity; the crits are goal-first, moulding the text to the transformative aim. The work can overlap; the starting point differs (W11).
9.8 "Necessarily" implicated? necessarily, always, every case, common law and statutes, constitutional democracy
  1. [Theories of law] are always implicated: a judge who claims simply to apply the statute has taken a side on what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always presupposed (legality; reasons to defer to clear words) but is an operative ground only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So [necessarily implicated] holds for theory and for morality as presupposition, not for morality as the ground of every decision.
  • Morality enters: for Hart, at most where rules run out (PS 615); for Fuller, in fidelity, viewed with the judge's "responsibility for making law what it ought to be" (PFL 647); for Dworkin, in every proposition of law (15.9).
  • FOR Riggs: two morally grounded theories of a statute: Earl's "intention of the makers" (509) against Gray's "What power or warrant have the courts to add to the respondent's penalties" (519).
  • STEELMAN Hart: rules have a "core of central meaning" where morality sits idle (PS 615); LMS refused to judge a law's object without legal standards (TSH JO 318). Reply: restraint is itself a theory of judging.
9.9 Why judges converge shared backgrounds, converge, what apart from rules
  1. Judges converge less because of [shared backgrounds] than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer who "soaked himself in the 'folkways'" of an appellate court could predict outcomes "eight times out of ten" (100).
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory; [the tenth case] is where that theory is argued, not predicted.
  • FOR ALR's "underlying ethical pluralism" (Week 1b slide 16†); Kennedy: shared rule-application is "not in fact objectivity" (562), though he sometimes "can't budge" a rule (560–61).
  • AGAINST Dworkin: hard cases are "perhaps just" those where fit yields no unique reading (AMP).
9.10 Chain novelist, author and critic chain novel, author, critic, one coherent story
  1. The artist interprets as he creates, the critic creates as he interprets; yet "there is a difference between interpreting while creating and creating while interpreting" (AMP).
  2. Each chain novelist after the first has "the dual responsibilities of interpreting and creating"; after the second, "no single author" has intentions that decide (AMP).
  3. So the judge, "a partner in a complex chain enterprise", has a duty "to interpret the legal history he finds, not to invent a better history" (AMP).
  • QUALIFY Fit has "no algorithm"; value is political, not aesthetic (Dworkin's "political hypothesis", AMP).
  • AGAINST Kennedy's judge works the field toward "how-I-want-to-come-out" (518; 13.1).
Conclusion [The statement] is [overstated]. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and the cost of a flimsy ruling keeps most judges close to them; there, judges must justify by fit and political morality, starting from the text, not the goal: neither prediction nor preference. Theory is always implicated and morality always presupposed, but morality decides only where fit runs out or injustice becomes intolerable.

1Start here: archetype 9 in plain English

Archetype 9 asks: when judges decide cases, are they applying law or just doing politics? Three camps answer. The American Legal Realists (ALR) say judges decide first and find reasons afterwards, so law is really a prediction of what judges will do. Critical Legal Studies (CLS) goes further: legal rules are full of contradictions that hide whose interests win. Dworkin replies that judges must justify their decisions, by the reading that best fits the existing law and makes it morally best. The statements in this family usually say "it's all politics in robes". Your answer: that overstates. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and in the open cases judges still have to justify, using principle, not personal preference.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
American Legal Realism (ALR)The view that law is what judges actually do, and judges are moved by more than rules. "Law is a prediction."
Critical Legal Studies (CLS) / critsThe view that law is politics: every principle comes with an opposite principle, and the "exceptions" hide whose interests are protected. Unger is the key name.
Canons and ratiosCanons: rules for reading statutes (literal, purposive…). Ratio: the reason a case was decided, which can be read narrowly or widely.
Fit and justificationDworkin's two tests: does a reading fit the past law, and does it show the law in its best moral light?
Principle v policyPrinciple: arguments about people's rights. Policy: arguments about society's goals (cost, floodgates). Dworkin says judges should decide on principle.
FloodgatesThe worry that allowing one claim will open the way to a flood of similar claims.
Stare decisisFollowing precedent: deciding like cases alike.
Rule v fact scepticismRule sceptics doubt rules decide cases. Fact sceptics say the real uncertainty is how the facts are found at trial.
Chain novelDworkin's picture of the judge as one writer in a chain, adding a chapter that has to fit the story so far.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says judges "justify by fit and political morality, and rules leave some cases open, not all". Put simply: the realists and crits are right that rules don't settle every case. But judges can't just predict or pick; they have to give the reading that best fits and justifies the law. In the open cases, it's political morality (principle), not personal taste, that decides.

The Intro says: the statement treats judging as "politics in robes". Realists show canons and ratios leave some cases open; crits show principles meet counterprinciples. But a judge can't predict their own ruling; they must justify it. The Conclusion adds that the cost of a weak judgment (being overturned, losing credibility) keeps most judges close to the rules, and that judges start from the text, not from the goal.

The ten blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
9.1"Judges decide first; law is just prediction."Lawyers may predict, but judges must justify. A judge can't predict their own ruling.
9.2"When precedent runs out, judges legislate."That's a disagreement about what counts as law, not a gap. McLoughlin: same result, different reasons.
9.3"Contract law is a neutral framework" or "tear it down".Unger rightly shows it isn't neutral. But tearing it down needs a standard to judge by.
9.4"Precedent, not justice, makes law fair."Deciding which cases are "alike" needs a moral principle.
9.5"There's always one right answer, so never refuse an unjust statute."One best reading is possible in principle, but Dworkin gives no threshold for extreme injustice.
9.6"Results vary by judge, so law is just the judge."That shows some judges fail to justify properly, not that Dworkin's theory is wrong.
9.7"Dworkin beats the realists only by handing victory to the crits."Only if values are subjective. Natural law could say which principle should win.
9.8"Theory and morality are necessarily in every decision."Theory, yes. Morality is always in the background, but only decides hard cases.
9.9"Judges agree only because of shared backgrounds."They agree because they share a practice of justification.
9.10"The judge writes the next chapter of one coherent story."Yes, but the judge must interpret the history they find, not invent a better one.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Rules leave some cases open, not all; in the open ones, judges must justify by principle, not preference.

2The big picture: what do judges do?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Three people watch a judge. The realist says: "She decides what she wants, then dresses it up with legal reasons; if you want to know the law, predict what she'll do." The critical legal scholar says: "The legal reasons can always point both ways, and they quietly favour the powerful." Dworkin says: "She can't just predict herself. She has to find the reading of the law that best fits what's already there and makes the most moral sense of it, like the next author in a novel written by many hands."

SchoolCore claimKey names
American Legal Realism (ALR)Law is a prediction of what officials will do; rules leave leeways; fact-finding steers outcomesLlewellyn ("paper rules"), Frank ("upper courtitis")
DworkinLaw is interpretive: the best reading fits the legal record and shows it in its best moral lightLaw's Empire, A Matter of Principle
Critical Legal Studies (CLS)Doctrine is contradictory (principle v counterprinciple) and legitimates hierarchyUnger, Kennedy

Three distinctions you need

  • Rule scepticism v fact scepticism (W11 slide 8†): rule sceptics (Llewellyn) say the rules don't decide; fact sceptics (Frank) say whoever finds the facts decides whether a rule applies.
  • Principle v policy (1.3(8)): arguments about rights (for courts) v arguments about collective goals (for legislatures).
  • Presupposed v operative (1.3(2)): morality is always presupposed in judging (legality, reasons to defer), but it is an operative ground only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

ALR v CLS (W1): same description, "law is politics"; they split on what next? ALR keeps the system, given good judges; CLS would remake it, exposing class interests. And Dworkin is text-first (the judge brings political theory but owes his duty to that law, close to Fuller's fidelity) while the crits are goal-first (moulding the text to the transformative aim) (W11).

39.1 ALR

▤ On your sheet: 9.1 ALR (word for word)
9.1 ALR decide first, prediction, canons, ratios read narrowly or widely
  1. Realism rightly says [canons and ratios] leave hard cases open, but a judge must justify, not predict.
  2. Practitioners may predict, "but judges themselves cannot. They must purport to justify" (Harris 102); "alas, I must find for the defendant" predicts nothing on its face (108).
  3. So [law is prediction] holds at most for counsel; Llewellyn called realism "a method nothing more" (Harris 103).
  • FOR Cheng San GRC (GE 1997)†: candidates stood inside polling stations; s 82(1)(d) bars waiting "outside", (e) loitering "within a radius of 200 metres" (pre-2023). Literal: outside only; purposive: the mischief, and "at or near". The AG advised no offence. Precise canons, uncertain outcome (Liu, W11).
  • QUALIFY Liu: ALR oversimplifies: a judge can write any decision, but reputation, reversal, time and credibility (Denning) make a flimsy one costly. Kennedy's correction: law, a "medium", constrains like bricks, relative to one's project; moving it costs "work and the credibility risk" (526, 559).
  • QUALIFY Weak and strong readings: on Harris's minimal reading, "'rules' are not all that matter" (100); in extreme form, all reasoning is "mere surface talk" (102).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A realist says, "Law is just a prediction of what the judge will do." That's useful for a lawyer advising a client. But the judge can't use it: she can't sit there predicting her own decision. She has to decide, and give reasons. So realism describes the lawyer's view, not the judge's.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Anyone who watches the courts knows judges decide first and find reasons afterwards. So the only honest definition of law is a prediction of what judges will do."

  1. Realism is right that canons and ratios can leave hard cases open. But a judge has to justify a decision, not predict it.
  2. Lawyers can predict; judges can't. As Harris puts it, judges "must purport to justify". A judge who says "alas, I must find for the defendant" isn't making a prediction.
  3. So "law is prediction" works at most for lawyers advising clients. Even Llewellyn called realism "a method, nothing more".

The example: at the 1997 Cheng San election, candidates stood inside polling stations. The law banned waiting "outside" and loitering "within a radius of 200 metres". Literally, inside wasn't covered; on a purposive reading, it was. The rules of interpretation were precise, but the outcome wasn't.

The extras: QUALIFY (Liu): realism oversimplifies. A judge can write any decision, but reputation, being overturned and credibility make a weak one costly. Kennedy: law is a "medium", like bricks, that constrains you depending on what you're trying to build.

Remember: lawyers predict; judges justify.

The statement. "Anyone who watches the courts knows that judges decide first and find reasons afterwards … The only honest definition of law is therefore a prediction of what judges will actually do." (Q85)

The move.

  1. Realism rightly says canons and ratios leave hard cases open, but a judge must justify, not predict.
  2. Practitioners may predict, "but judges themselves cannot. They must purport to justify" (Harris 102); "alas, I must find for the defendant" predicts nothing on its face (108).
  3. So "law is prediction" holds at most for counsel; Llewellyn called realism "a method nothing more" (Harris 103).
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Cheng San GRC (General Election 1997)†

Candidates stood inside polling stations. Section 82(1)(d) of the elections law barred waiting "outside", and (e) barred loitering "within a radius of 200 metres" (pre-2023).

The Attorney-General advised there was no offence. Precise canons, uncertain outcome (Liu, W11). This is the realist's best illustration; your reply is that a judge would still have to justify a choice between the readings.

  • Literal reading: (d) speaks of "outside", so being inside is not caught.
  • Purposive reading: look at the mischief (influencing voters near the station), and "at or near".

QUALIFY (Liu): ALR oversimplifies. A judge can write any decision, but reputation, reversal, time and credibility (Denning) make a flimsy one costly. Kennedy's correction: law is a "medium" that constrains like bricks, relative to one's project; moving it costs "work and the credibility risk" (526, 559).

QUALIFY (weak and strong readings): on Harris's minimal reading, "'rules' are not all that matter" (100); in extreme form, all reasoning is "mere surface talk" (102). The weak reading is true; the strong one is not.

49.2 Dworkin v ALR

▤ On your sheet: 9.2 Dworkin v ALR (word for word)
9.2 Dworkin v ALR precedent runs out, judges legislate, floodgates, social goals
  1. Saying [the judge legislates once precedent runs out] mistakes a theoretical disagreement about law's grounds for a gap.
  2. In McLoughlin all five Lords allowed the appeal, yet split: Scarman held line-drawing policy "not justiciable" (431); Edmund-Davies called that "as novel as it is startling" (427).
  3. So leaving [floodgates] to Parliament is Scarman's contested view, which I defend as a choice, not as the case's lesson.
  • AGAINST Floodgates: policy or principle (Week 1b slide 3†)? As court congestion and insurance cost, policy, beyond "the limits of the forensic process" (Scarman 431); as liability out of proportion to fault, principle.
  • QUALIFY Bridge weighed the policy grounds offered, found them "wholly insufficient", and called stopping at decided cases "an unwarranted abdication" (441).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"When precedent runs out, the judge just makes law up." Dworkin says no: there's still law there, in the principles behind the precedents. The judges in McLoughlin all agreed the mother should win, but argued about whether courts can use policy (like "too many lawsuits!") to limit who can sue. That's an argument about what law is, not a gap.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "When the old cases run out, the judge has no choice but to make new law. Whether a mother who sees her injured family in hospital can sue isn't answered by any rule."

  1. That mistakes a disagreement about what counts as law for a gap in the law. (This is Dworkin's "theoretical disagreement" from Lesson 2.)
  2. In McLoughlin, all five Lords let the mother sue, but disagreed why. Scarman said deciding where to draw the line on policy grounds wasn't for courts; Edmund-Davies called that "as novel as it is startling".
  3. So "leave floodgates to Parliament" is Scarman's contested view. You can defend it, but as a choice, not as the lesson of the case.

The extras: AGAINST: is "floodgates" policy or principle? If it's about court congestion and insurance costs, it's policy (beyond what courts can assess). If it's about liability out of proportion to fault, it's principle. QUALIFY: Bridge did weigh the policy reasons, found them "wholly insufficient", and said stopping at decided cases would be "an unwarranted abdication".

Remember: no rule ≠ no law; the judges were arguing about what the law was.

59.3 CLS v Dworkin

▤ On your sheet: 9.3 CLS v Dworkin (word for word)
9.3 CLS v Dworkin neutral framework, exceptions prove the rule, drawn up by an elite, tear it down
  1. Unger rightly denies [contract law is a neutral framework]: each principle meets a counterprinciple that the dominant view files as an anomaly (Unger 74–75).
  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant contract theory rules far less than it claims (Unger 58).
  3. Yet [tear it down] overreaches: condemning hidden interests needs a non-subjective standard, which Finnis's basic goods supply (5.1).
  • FOR Doctrine legitimates hierarchy "even when it is deployed by someone who thinks he is forwarding progressive causes" (Harris 109): hidden interests (Week 1b slide 17†); crits generally distance themselves from Marxist instrumentalism (110).
  • STEELMAN The crit's best point is conservatism: fit crowns the past's dominant principle and files fairness (duress, undue influence: Week 11 slide 14†) as exceptions; the fixes become "arbitrarily selective" (Unger 74).
  • AGAINST Harris: the liberal must show reformed legalism yields more "incremental justice" than "deconstruction for its own sake" (113).
  • QUALIFY ALR v CLS (Liu, W1): same description, law is politics; split on "what next?": ALR keeps the system, given good judges; CLS would remake it, exposing class interests.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Contract law says "people are free to make any deal". But it also has rules that protect people from unfair deals (duress, undue influence). The crits say: these aren't small exceptions, they're a whole rival principle (fairness, community) that the law pretends is minor. Fine, but if you want to tear the system down, you need some standard to say what's better.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Contract law is a neutral framework that just gives effect to free choices between equals" or "private law is a set of deals drawn up by an elite: tear it down".

  1. Unger is right that it isn't neutral. Every principle (freedom of contract) meets a counterprinciple (fairness), and the dominant view files the counterprinciple away as an "exception".
  2. With all those exceptions, the main contract theory controls far less of the law than it claims.
  3. But "tear it down" goes too far. To condemn hidden interests, you need a standard that isn't just opinion, and Finnis's basic goods (Lesson 5) can supply one.

The extras: STEELMAN: the crits' best point is that "fit" (Dworkin) tends to crown the past's dominant principle and treat fairness rules (duress, undue influence) as oddities. AGAINST (Harris): the crits must show that tearing down produces more justice than reform. QUALIFY (Liu): realists and crits agree law is politics, but split on what to do next. Realists keep the system (given good judges); crits would rebuild it.

Remember: not neutral, but not worth demolishing without a standard.

  2. With its exclusions, exceptions and repressions, the dominant contract theory rules far less than it claims (Unger 58).
  3. Yet "tear it down" overreaches: condemning hidden interests needs a non-subjective standard, which Finnis's basic goods supply (5.1).
