69.4 Precedent and theory

▤ On your sheet: 9.4 Precedent and theory (word for word)
9.4 Precedent and theory like cases alike, stare decisis, authority for argument
  1. Precedent cannot replace theory: [treating like cases alike] needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral.
  2. Was a mother reaching hospital two hours later like one at the scene? Only a principle, foreseeability or physical risk, can say.
  3. So [precedent, not justice, makes law fair] fails: stare decisis itself is contested, strict or relaxed, and needs justification.
  • AGAINST Relaxed precedent yields when "sufficiently wrong" (Law's Empire); interpretation "must contain a doctrine of mistake" (AMP).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Treat like cases alike" sounds simple. But is a mother arriving at the hospital two hours later "like" a mother at the crash scene? You can't answer without a principle saying which differences matter. That principle is moral.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Precedent guarantees like cases are treated alike; that, not justice, makes the common law fair" or "following precedent replaces argument with authority".

  1. Precedent can't replace theory. "Treat like cases alike" needs a test for which differences matter, and that test is a moral one.
  2. Example: was a mother who arrived at the hospital two hours later "like" one at the accident scene? Only a principle (foreseeability, or physical risk) can tell you.
  3. So "precedent, not justice, makes law fair" fails. Even how strictly to follow precedent is disputed and needs justifying.

The extra: Dworkin: precedent gives way when "sufficiently wrong"; any interpretation must include "a doctrine of mistake".

Remember: "alike" is a moral judgement.

The move.

  1. Precedent cannot replace theory: treating like cases alike needs a test of which differences matter, and that test is moral.
  2. Was a mother reaching hospital two hours later like one at the scene? Only a principle, foreseeability or physical risk, can say.
  3. So "precedent, not justice, makes law fair" fails: stare decisis itself is contested, strict or relaxed, and needs justification.

AGAINST: relaxed precedent yields when "sufficiently wrong" (Law's Empire); interpretation "must contain a doctrine of mistake" (AMP).

79.5 Right answer

▤ On your sheet: 9.5 Right answer (word for word)
9.5 Right answer single right answer, whatever coheres, never refuse an unjust statute
  1. [A single right answer] is possible in principle: interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be best.
  2. But fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation", and then "substantive political theory" decides (AMP).
  3. So [he need never refuse an unjust statute] fails: Dworkin gives no threshold; the Radbruch formula, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus, does (15.13).
  • CONCEDE Dworkin: a judge's best reading rests on "beliefs other judges need not share" (AMP). Concede no demonstrable answer; insist the choice is political, not personal (9.8).
  • QUALIFY Liu: where the practice itself includes the formula, a Dworkinian judge can fit and still refuse extreme injustice (W11); fit is a matter of degree (Denning; the German nullity courts). TSH's catch: 8.5.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Dworkin thinks hard cases have one best answer, the way a good critic thinks one reading of a poem is best. But even he admits the "fit" test often leaves several readings standing, and then the judge's political morality decides. And his theory doesn't say when a law is so evil a judge should refuse it.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "The ideal judge reads the law as one coherent story. Because there's always a single right answer, he need never refuse an unjust statute."

  1. One best answer is possible in principle. Interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be the best.
  2. But Dworkin admits fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation"; then the judge's political theory decides.
  3. So "he need never refuse an unjust statute" fails. Dworkin gives no point at which injustice becomes too much; the Radbruch formula does (Lesson 8).

The extras: CONCEDE: Dworkin says a judge's best reading rests on beliefs other judges needn't share, so there's no provable right answer. But the choice is still political (about principle), not personal. QUALIFY (Liu): if a legal system already includes the Radbruch formula, a Dworkinian judge can fit the law and refuse extreme injustice.

Remember: one best answer in principle, but no built-in limit for extreme injustice.

The statement. "The ideal judge reads the whole of the law as one coherent story … Because the law always holds a single right answer, he need never refuse an unjust statute." (Q84)

The move.

  1. A single right answer is possible in principle: interpretation neither finds law ready-made nor invents it, so one reading can be best.
  2. But fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation", and then "substantive political theory" decides (AMP).
  3. So "he need never refuse an unjust statute" fails: Dworkin gives no threshold; the Radbruch formula, gauged by TSH's broad historical consensus, does (15.13).

CONCEDE: Dworkin: a judge's best reading rests on "beliefs other judges need not share" (AMP). Concede there is no demonstrable answer; insist the choice is political, not personal (9.8).

89.6 Judge-variance study

▤ On your sheet: 9.6 Judge-variance study (word for word)
9.6 Judge-variance study outcomes vary by judge, change the bench
  1. A realist reads [the variance findings] as fact scepticism confirmed; they indict judges who fail to justify, not Dworkin's normative theory.
  • Rule v fact scepticism (W11 slide 8†): Llewellyn's "paper rules" (Harris 99); Frank's "upper courtitis": the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies (100). Liu: appeal only moves the discretion up a level (W11).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A study finds that the result depends on which judge you get. The realist says "Told you so: law is just the judge." But it might just show some judges aren't doing their job well. Dworkin's theory says how judges should decide; it doesn't claim they all do.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The question, in everyday words: "A study finds that similar cases come out differently depending on the judge. What would a realist say?"

  1. A realist would say: "Proof! It's the facts and the judge, not the rules." That's fact scepticism.
  2. Your reply: the study criticises judges who fail to justify properly. It doesn't refute Dworkin, whose theory is about how judges should decide, not how they all do.

The extras: rule scepticism (Llewellyn's "paper rules" don't decide cases) v fact scepticism (Frank: the trial court's fact-finding decides whether a rule even applies). Liu: appeals only move the discretion up a level.

Remember: "judges differ" is a fact about judges, not a refutation of a theory about how they should judge.

The question. "Suppose a study found that outcomes of materially similar cases varied significantly by judge. What would a realist conclude?" (Q90)

The move. A realist reads the variance findings as fact scepticism confirmed; they indict judges who fail to justify, not Dworkin's normative theory.

More: rule v fact scepticism (W11 slide 8†): Llewellyn's "paper rules" (Harris 99); Frank's "upper courtitis": the fact-finder decides whether a rule applies (100). Liu: appeal only moves the discretion up a level (W11).

99.7 Synthesis

▤ On your sheet: 9.7 Synthesis (word for word)
9.7 Synthesis answers the realists, victory to the crits
  1. Dworkin's judge answers [the realists]: he must justify by fit and value, and cannot predict his own ruling.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly; Harris reads Unger's jibe at "a pre-established harmony" as aimed at Dworkin (113).
  3. So victory to the crits follows only if value is subjective; Liu's third option, natural law, would say which principle should win (Riggs?: Week 11 slide 15†).
  • QUALIFY Liu: Dworkin is text-first: the judge brings his political theory but owes his duty to that law, close to Fuller's fidelity; the crits are goal-first, moulding the text to the transformative aim. The work can overlap; the starting point differs (W11).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Dworkin beats the realists by saying judges must justify, not predict. But to justify, he uses "fit", which might just crown whatever the law already says, and his "value" step might just be the judge's politics. If moral values are subjective, the crits win. If there's an objective answer (natural law), they don't.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Dworkin's judge can answer the realists, but only by handing victory to the crits."

  1. Dworkin does answer the realists: his judge must justify by fit and value, and can't just predict.
  2. But the crits have a point: "fit" may crown freedom of contract and treat fairness as an oddity. Harris reads Unger's jibe about "a pre-established harmony" as aimed at Dworkin.
  3. So the crits only win if values are subjective. Liu's third option is natural law, which could say which principle should win.

The extra: QUALIFY (Liu): Dworkin starts from the text; the judge brings a political theory but owes duty to the law, close to Fuller's fidelity. The crits start from the goal and shape the text to it. Their work can overlap, but their starting points differ.

Remember: crits win only if values are just opinion.

The statement. "Dworkin's judge can answer the American Legal Realists, but only by handing victory to the Critical Legal Scholars." (Q88)

The move.

  1. Dworkin's judge answers the realists: he must justify by fit and value, and cannot predict his own ruling.
  2. But fit may crown freedom of contract and file fairness as an anomaly; Harris reads Unger's jibe at "a pre-established harmony" as aimed at Dworkin (113).
  3. So victory to the crits follows only if value is subjective; Liu's third option, natural law, would say which principle should win (Riggs?: Week 11 slide 15†).

109.8 "Necessarily" implicated?

▤ On your sheet: 9.8 "Necessarily" implicated? (word for word)
9.8 "Necessarily" implicated? necessarily, always, every case, common law and statutes, constitutional democracy
  1. [Theories of law] are always implicated: a judge who claims simply to apply the statute has taken a side on what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always presupposed (legality; reasons to defer to clear words) but is an operative ground only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So [necessarily implicated] holds for theory and for morality as presupposition, not for morality as the ground of every decision.
  • Morality enters: for Hart, at most where rules run out (PS 615); for Fuller, in fidelity, viewed with the judge's "responsibility for making law what it ought to be" (PFL 647); for Dworkin, in every proposition of law (15.9).
  • FOR Riggs: two morally grounded theories of a statute: Earl's "intention of the makers" (509) against Gray's "What power or warrant have the courts to add to the respondent's penalties" (519).
  • STEELMAN Hart: rules have a "core of central meaning" where morality sits idle (PS 615); LMS refused to judge a law's object without legal standards (TSH JO 318). Reply: restraint is itself a theory of judging.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Theory and morality are necessarily involved in every judicial decision." Half true. Every judge relies on some theory of what law is (even "I just apply the statute" is a theory). And morality is always in the background (why should we follow clear words?). But morality isn't the reason for deciding most everyday cases; it only steps in for hard cases and monstrous laws.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Theories of law and morality are necessarily involved in every judicial decision."

  1. Theories of law are always involved. A judge who says "I'm just applying the statute" has already taken a view about what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always in the background (the value of legality, reasons for respecting clear words), but it only decides cases in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So "necessarily" is right for theory and for morality in the background, but not for morality as the reason for every decision.

The extras: for Hart, morality enters at most where rules run out; for Fuller, through fidelity to law; for Dworkin, in every proposition of law. FOR: Riggs shows two moral theories of one statute. STEELMAN (Hart): rules have a "core of central meaning" where morality isn't needed. Reply: holding back is itself a theory of judging.

Remember: theory always; morality in the background always; morality deciding only sometimes.

The statement. "Theories of law and morality are necessarily implicated in every judicial decision, whether on the common law or statutes, in a constitutional democracy."

The move.

  1. Theories of law are always implicated: a judge who claims simply to apply the statute has taken a side on what counts as law.
  2. Morality is always presupposed (legality; reasons to defer to clear words) but is an operative ground only in hard cases and at intolerable injustice.
  3. So "necessarily implicated" holds for theory and for morality as presupposition, not for morality as the ground of every decision.

Where morality enters, for each theorist: Hart: at most where rules run out (PS 615). Fuller: in fidelity, viewed with the judge's "responsibility for making law what it ought to be" (PFL 647). Dworkin: in every proposition of law (15.9).

FOR: Riggs: two morally grounded theories of a statute: Earl's "intention of the makers" (509) against Gray's "What power or warrant have the courts to add to the respondent's penalties" (519).

STEELMAN: Hart: rules have a "core of central meaning" where morality sits idle (PS 615); LMS refused to judge a law's object without legal standards (TSH JO 318). Reply: restraint is itself a theory of judging.

119.9 Why judges converge

▤ On your sheet: 9.9 Why judges converge (word for word)
9.9 Why judges converge shared backgrounds, converge, what apart from rules
  1. Judges converge less because of [shared backgrounds] than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer who "soaked himself in the 'folkways'" of an appellate court could predict outcomes "eight times out of ten" (100).
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory; [the tenth case] is where that theory is argued, not predicted.
  • FOR ALR's "underlying ethical pluralism" (Week 1b slide 16†); Kennedy: shared rule-application is "not in fact objectivity" (562), though he sometimes "can't budge" a rule (560–61).
  • AGAINST Dworkin: hard cases are "perhaps just" those where fit yields no unique reading (AMP).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Most of the time, judges agree. Why? Not just because they went to the same schools. It's because they've learned the same way of giving legal reasons. Easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory without noticing. Hard cases are where that shared theory runs out and gets argued.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Judges agree only because they share the same backgrounds. What else, apart from rules, could explain it?"

  1. They agree less because of backgrounds than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Llewellyn found a lawyer who soaked himself in a court's "folkways" could predict results eight times out of ten.
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory. The tenth case is where that theory gets argued about, not predicted.

The extras: FOR: Kennedy: shared application of rules is "not in fact objectivity", though sometimes he "can't budge" a rule. AGAINST: Dworkin: hard cases may simply be the ones where fit gives no unique answer.

Remember: shared practice of justifying, not just shared backgrounds.

The statement. "Judges converge only because of shared backgrounds; what apart from rules explains agreement?"

The move.

  1. Judges converge less because of shared backgrounds than because they share a practice of justification.
  2. Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer who "soaked himself in the 'folkways'" of an appellate court could predict outcomes "eight times out of ten" (100).
  3. So easy cases are easy because lawyers share a theory; the tenth case is where that theory is argued, not predicted.

FOR: ALR's "underlying ethical pluralism" (Week 1b slide 16†); Kennedy: shared rule-application is "not in fact objectivity" (562), though he sometimes "can't budge" a rule (560–61). AGAINST: Dworkin: hard cases are "perhaps just" those where fit yields no unique reading (AMP).

129.10 Chain novelist, author and critic

▤ On your sheet: 9.10 Chain novelist, author and critic (word for word)
9.10 Chain novelist, author and critic chain novel, author, critic, one coherent story
  1. The artist interprets as he creates, the critic creates as he interprets; yet "there is a difference between interpreting while creating and creating while interpreting" (AMP).
  2. Each chain novelist after the first has "the dual responsibilities of interpreting and creating"; after the second, "no single author" has intentions that decide (AMP).
  3. So the judge, "a partner in a complex chain enterprise", has a duty "to interpret the legal history he finds, not to invent a better history" (AMP).
  • QUALIFY Fit has "no algorithm"; value is political, not aesthetic (Dworkin's "political hypothesis", AMP).
  • AGAINST Kennedy's judge works the field toward "how-I-want-to-come-out" (518; 13.1).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine a novel written chapter by chapter by different authors. You're writing chapter 10. You can't ignore chapters 1–9 (fit), but you also want the story to be as good as possible (value). That's Dworkin's judge: interpret what's there, then write the next chapter well, without rewriting the earlier ones.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "The ideal judge reads the law as one coherent story written by many hands, and writes the next chapter."

  1. Dworkin's picture: an artist interprets as he creates; a critic creates as he interprets. But those aren't the same thing.
  2. In a chain novel, every writer after the first must both interpret and create. After the second, no single author's intentions settle what the story means.
  3. So the judge is "a partner in a complex chain enterprise", with a duty "to interpret the legal history he finds, not to invent a better history".

The extras: QUALIFY: there's "no algorithm" for fit, and the value side is political, not artistic. AGAINST: Kennedy's judge works the materials towards "how-I-want-to-come-out".

Remember: write the next chapter, but it has to fit the book.

The statement. "The ideal judge reads the whole of the law as one coherent story, written by many hands, and writes the next chapter …" (Q84)

The move.

  1. The artist interprets as he creates, the critic creates as he interprets; yet "there is a difference between interpreting while creating and creating while interpreting" (AMP).
  2. Each chain novelist after the first has "the dual responsibilities of interpreting and creating"; after the second, "no single author" has intentions that decide (AMP).
  3. So the judge, "a partner in a complex chain enterprise", has a duty "to interpret the legal history he finds, not to invent a better history" (AMP).

QUALIFY: fit has "no algorithm"; value is political, not aesthetic (Dworkin's "political hypothesis", AMP). AGAINST: Kennedy's judge works the field toward "how-I-want-to-come-out" (518; 13.1).

Kennedy v the chain novel
▤ 13.1
  1. 1Shared: both put the judge inside inherited materials: fit and value constrain Dworkin's; work and credibility risk, Kennedy's (559).
  2. 2Split: Kennedy starts from "how-I-want-to-come-out" (518), Dworkin from the text (Liu, W11). Kennedy answers "always a right answer" with felt indeterminacy and "free ethical or political choice" (562), disclaiming a verdict (561).

13Putting it together: Practice Q85

"Anyone who watches the courts knows that judges decide first and find reasons afterwards. Whether a Prime Minister found inside a polling station has broken the rule against loitering within 200 metres of it turns not on the statute but on which canon of interpretation the judge happens to prefer, and the statutory instruction to favour the Act's purpose merely adds one more option. Precedents fare no better: they can be read narrowly, read widely or dismissed as archaic at will. The only honest definition of law is therefore a prediction of what judges will actually do."

Instruction: ALR, Dworkin, Hart; plus implications for how lawyers argue and judges justify.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "decide first" → 9.1 (a judge cannot predict himself).
  • polling station, canons → 9.1 Cheng San GRC.
  • "read narrowly, read widely … at will" → 9.1 QUALIFY (weak and strong readings), 9.4.
  • "only honest definition … prediction" → 9.1 line 3.
  • Hook: case (Cheng San). Distinction: 1.3(7) observer v participant fits too: prediction is the observer's stance.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

Cheng San GRC is the realist's best case: precise canons, literal and purposive, pointed different ways, and the Attorney-General advised no offence. But it shows less than the statement claims. I make three claims: (1) canons and ratios leave some cases open, as the weak realist reading holds, but not all; (2) prediction is a lawyer's stance, while a judge cannot predict his own ruling and must justify it, by fit and political morality; and (3) "at will" ignores the costs of a flimsy ruling, so judges are constrained even where the rules run out.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. The realist kernel (9.1, 9.6): Cheng San; rule v fact scepticism; weak reading true.
  2. Justify, not predict (9.1, 9.2, 15.9): Harris 102; Dworkin's fit and value; Hart's core of central meaning for easy cases; McLoughlin's divided reasons.
  3. Constraint and the crits (9.1 QUALIFY, 9.3, 9.10): Liu's costs; Kennedy's medium; self-critique: fit often not unique (1.4). Implications: lawyers argue fit and value, not just odds; judges state the political morality openly.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Rules leave some cases open, not all, and the cost of a flimsy ruling keeps most judges close to them. Where they run out, judges must justify by fit and political morality, starting from the text, not the goal: neither prediction nor preference.

LESSON 10 · ARCHETYPE 10 · ABOUT 48 MIN · 41 QUESTIONS

Lawyering: Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy

⚡ BIG IDEA

The lawyer's role is moral. Law sets a floor, and prudence, moral dialogue and rare objection decide the hard cases above it. Pepper and Thunder differ more in mindset than in outcome.

ARCHETYPE 10 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
10 Lawyering: Pepper, Thunder, Kennedy
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The statement] fails: the lawyer's role is moral; law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide hard cases above it.
Intro [The statement] assumes the lawyer's role can be sealed off from morality, the view Thunder caricatures as "just focus on the law" (316). Yet even Pepper defends that role morally, by appeal to autonomy and equality. I [reject / qualify] it: the role is moral, bounded by law, and its hard cases call for prudence, dialogue and, rarely, refusal.
10.1 Floor turn away a client, distaste, abuses his position, hidden bodies
  1. [Turning a client away abuses his position] overstates Pepper: choice of client is "troubling if it leads to foreclosure of a person's access to the law" (634).

  • AGAINST Inequality: the rich buy more law, so a filter could level it → replies: access to justice; distribution is not content; filters may hurt the poor more (Pepper 619–20; Liu, S13).

Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels: Pepper defends the role morally and keeps objection, which needs a lawyer weighing morality throughout; Thunder accepts role morality and that no legal system is perfect. 1Start here: archetype 10 in plain English

Archetype 10 asks: can a good person be a lawyer, and should a lawyer's own morals affect what they do for a client? Pepper says the lawyer should help with anything lawful: the law already marks the limits, and a lawyer who screens clients by their own morals becomes a gatekeeper over access to law. Thunder says the lawyer stays a moral person at work: the job exists to serve justice, so a good lawyer has to bring their judgement with them. The statements in this family usually try to seal the lawyer's role off from morality ("just do your job", "if no rule forbids it, you may do it"). Your answer: the lawyer's role is itself moral. The law sets the floor, and above it, prudence, conversation with the client and (rarely) refusal decide the hard cases.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Standard conception / amoral roleThe lawyer helps the client with anything lawful and doesn't judge the client's aims. Pepper defends it as morally justified, not morally empty.
Client autonomyThe client's right to make their own lawful choices, which the lawyer should respect.
Access to lawPeople need lawyers to use the law; if lawyers turned clients away on moral grounds, access would depend on lawyers' tastes.
Moral dialogueThe lawyer raising moral concerns with the client, as a conversation, without deciding for them.
Conscientious objectionThe lawyer refusing to help on grounds of conscience. Pepper says this should be rare.
Natural-teleological viewThunder's view that law exists for purposes naturally good for humans, like justice. "Teleological" means "about purpose".
Role moralityThe special duties that come with a role (a police officer, a lawyer). Thunder accepts these exist, but not as a sealed-off world.
Neo-Kantian moralityA style of moral thinking Thunder blames for the amoral view: it treats rules as the whole of morality and makes role-based reasons look suspicious.
PrudencePractical wisdom: knowing how to apply good values to a real situation.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says the lawyer's role "is moral; law sets a floor, and prudence, dialogue and rare objection decide hard cases above it". Put simply: you can't separate lawyering from morality, because even Pepper's "just help the client" is a moral argument. The law sets the minimum. Above that, use good judgement, talk to your client, and only occasionally refuse.

The Intro says: the statement assumes the role can be sealed off from morality, which Thunder caricatures as "just focus on the law". But even Pepper defends that role on moral grounds (autonomy and equality). The Conclusion says: Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels. They differ more in mindset than in outcomes, and the tighter the conduct rules, the smaller the gap. The real question is how often conscience may override the role: rarely, openly, after dialogue.

The eleven blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
10.1"A lawyer who turns away a client on moral grounds abuses his position."That overstates Pepper. And spotting his "extreme cases" needs the lawyer to weigh morality all the time.
10.2"Tell clients how the law is actually enforced."Accurate advice is fine, but if law is only what officials do, "don't encourage lawbreaking" becomes empty.
10.3"Is moral dialogue a real answer?"Partly: it's useful but costly, and some clients won't engage. For Thunder it's normal practice.
10.4"Lawyers are like soldiers; private morals make them judges and liars."Pointing to the role doesn't explain it. A lawyer stays accountable as a person.
10.5"If no rule forbids it, a lawyer may do it."The rules are a floor, not the whole picture. They exist for a purpose.
10.6"Defending a guilty client is wrong."No: a fair trial is the role working. Refusal fits only an unjust system or a monstrous law.
10.7"Juniors following lawful orders bear no responsibility."Lawful isn't the same as blameless. Raise it first; refuse only where others would be seriously harmed.
10.8"Leave your conscience at the door; theory isn't relevant."That describes how lawyers are trained, not why it's right. It's an unexamined theory itself.
10.9"In transactional work the lawyer must supply moral scrutiny."Partly true: with no judge or opposing counsel, the realist danger is greatest.
10.10"Just do your job; you're a hired gun."Thunder traces that view to realism plus a rule-based morality. But a diagnosis isn't a refutation.
10.11(Liu's scenarios)Ask in order: is the system just? Is this rule intolerable? Is only this outcome unjust?
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

The lawyer's role is moral: law is the floor; above it, prudence, dialogue and rare, open objection.

2The big picture: can a good person be a lawyer?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A client asks a lawyer for help doing something legal but nasty (say, evicting a tenant on a technicality). One view (Pepper): the lawyer should help: the law already says what's forbidden, and it's not the lawyer's place to judge clients. Another view (Thunder): the lawyer is still a person with a conscience; the job exists to serve justice, so a good lawyer stays a good person. This lesson shows the two are closer than they look.

Pepper: the amoral ethical role

Stephen Pepper defends the "standard conception" of the lawyer as morally justified, not morally empty:

  1. Law is "a public good available to all"; autonomy is "a moral good" (616).
  2. People need lawyers to access law; if lawyers screened clients by their own morals, we would have "rule by an oligarchy of lawyers" (617).
  3. Equality: screening would "compound inequality upon inequality" (620). If conduct is bad enough, "it would seem that it ought to be made explicitly unlawful" (618).
  4. So the lawyer helps with anything lawful; the limit is the law, not the lawyer's morality (626).
  5. Safety valves: moral dialogue with the client, choice of client, and conscientious objection, "rarely exercised" (633).

Thunder: the good person as lawyer

David Thunder argues that a lawyer's role is justified only by its contribution to justice and human flourishing:

  1. Natural-teleological view: law is "intended ultimately (though not always immediately)" for ends "naturally good for man" (314).
  2. The lawyer's function is "to further justice, public order, and the rule of law" (323).
  3. The lawyer stays accountable "as a human being" (330); roles are not a "pocket universe" (Liu).
  4. Diagnosis: the amoral view draws its appeal from "the unwitting collaboration of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality" (314).
  5. Virtues: courage against "pressure to conform", moderation, prudence.

Kennedy (for judges)

Kennedy's five courses (15.10) belong to judges, not junior lawyers (10.7 JUDGE). In this archetype he appears for training and outlook: "Will law school warp my mind?" (554).

⚠ TRAP
Pepper ≠ legal positivism

LP only identifies what the law is; a moral decision about what to do remains (Hart v Radbruch). So an LP may side with Pepper or Thunder. Pepper is hard to square with NLT, for which finding the law already involves morality (Liu, S13).

  2. Pepper's best case is a dilemma: conduct "sufficiently 'bad'" should, it seems, be "made explicitly unlawful"; if not, why impose "the happenstance" of one lawyer's conscience (618)?

Pepper's best argument: if something is bad enough, make it illegal. Otherwise, why should the client's access to the law depend on the luck of which lawyer they hire? But Pepper also says lawyers can object in "extreme cases". To spot an extreme case, the lawyer has to be thinking morally all the time. So his "amoral" lawyer isn't so amoral.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The extras: AGAINST: words like "abuses" and "denies" are moral premises. QUALIFY: Pepper leaves four areas for the lawyer's own choices: whether to practise, which clients, dialogue, and objection. TRAP: Pepper isn't the same as legal positivism; a positivist could side with either Pepper or Thunder. On inequality: the rich can buy more law, but filtering clients may hurt the poor more.

Remember: even "don't judge your client" is a moral position.

Remember: realism about enforcement can quietly empty "the law" of meaning.

Remember: rules are the minimum, not the goal.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Mei, a junior associate (Q103)

Mei's partner tells her to plead a limitation defence that will defeat a debt the company privately admits it owes to a small family business. Pleading the time bar is lawful, yet the win may be unjust: dialogue first (raise it with the partner and, through the partner, the client). 1210.10 Thunder's diagnosis and the natural-teleological view

▤ On your sheet: 10.10 Thunder's diagnosis and the natural-teleological view (word for word)
10.10 Thunder's diagnosis and the natural-teleological view why we hold such views, purpose of law, hired gun, just do your job
  1. Thunder traces the amoral view's appeal "in large part" to "the unwitting collaboration of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality" (314).
  2. Neo-Kantianism tends to make role-based reasons "morally suspect" (319), prudence, "the bread and butter of the legal profession", amoral, and right conduct separate from the good life (320).
  3. Realism gives the view "a congenial philosophical home" (321); against both, law is "intended ultimately (though not always immediately)" for ends "naturally good for man" (314).
  • STEELMAN Pepper: access to law makes the lawyer "a good person" (634).
  • CONCEDE A diagnosis is no refutation, and Thunder is "less concerned to counter Pepper's argument blow by blow" (315); Liu doubts the neo-Kantian half and adds a likelier source, the intuition that a lawyer should not substitute his judgment for the client's, which Thunder shares (S13). Concede; 10.1 must answer it.
  • QUALIFY Same act, different reasons (Liu, S13): a Thunder lawyer may disclose a live victim as part of the role, or because duties "as a human being" trump it; a Pepper lawyer may too, but only as extreme-case objection. The gap is mindset, not necessarily outcome, and the positive law sets how wide it is.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Thunder asks: why do so many people believe lawyers should be "hired guns"? Two hidden influences: (1) a philosophy that says morality is only about following universal rules (so the craft of good judgement looks amoral), and (2) legal realism (law is just what officials do). Against both, Thunder says law exists for real human goods like justice.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Just do your job. The lawyer is a hired gun, and the purpose of the law is whatever the client wants."

  1. Thunder's diagnosis: the amoral view is appealing largely because of two things working together: legal realism and neo-Kantian morality.
  2. What neo-Kantianism does: it makes reasons that come from a role look morally suspect, treats prudence (the lawyer's everyday skill) as amoral, and separates right action from living a good life.
  3. What realism adds: a comfortable philosophical home for the amoral view. Against both, Thunder says law is ultimately meant for ends that are naturally good for people.

The extras: STEELMAN (Pepper): giving people access to law makes the lawyer "a good person". CONCEDE: a diagnosis isn't a refutation, and Liu doubts the neo-Kantian part; a likelier source is the intuition that lawyers shouldn't substitute their judgement for the client's, which Thunder shares. QUALIFY: the same act (revealing where a live victim is) can come from different reasons in each camp; the gap is mindset more than outcome.

Remember: Thunder explains why people hold the amoral view; you still need 10.1 to answer it.

The statement. "Just focus on doing your job: the lawyer is a hired gun, and the purpose of law is the client's."

The move.

  1. Thunder traces the amoral view's appeal "in large part" to "the unwitting collaboration of legal realism and neo-Kantian morality" (314).
  2. Neo-Kantianism tends to make role-based reasons "morally suspect" (319), prudence ("the bread and butter of the legal profession") amoral, and right conduct separate from the good life (320).
  3. Realism gives the view "a congenial philosophical home" (321); against both, law is "intended ultimately (though not always immediately)" for ends "naturally good for man" (314).

STEELMAN: Pepper: access to law makes the lawyer "a good person" (634).

CONCEDE: a diagnosis is no refutation, and Thunder is "less concerned to counter Pepper's argument blow by blow" (315). Liu doubts the neo-Kantian half and adds a likelier source: the intuition that a lawyer should not substitute his judgment for the client's, which Thunder shares (S13). Concede; 10.1 must answer it.

🎓 WHAT LIU SAID

Same act, different reasons (S13). A Thunder lawyer may disclose a live victim as part of the role, or because duties "as a human being" trump it; a Pepper lawyer may too, but only as extreme-case objection. The gap is mindset, not necessarily outcome (1.3(18)), and the positive law sets how wide it is.

⚠ TRAP
"Just focus on the law" is the target

Thunder's "just focus on the law" (316) voices the amoral view he rejects, as does the practice question's "Just focus on doing your job" (14.24 TRAP). Name it as Thunder's caricature in your hook.

1310.11 Liu's three scenarios

▤ On your sheet: 10.11 Liu's three scenarios† (word for word)
10.11 Liu's three scenarios† racist statute, coerced evidence, hide behind the system, institutional wrong
  1. Ask in order†: is the system by and large just; if so, is this rule intolerably unjust; if not, is this outcome unjust?
  2. Calling an unjust result the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's, only moves the question†: is the institution justified by truth-finding, by dignity, or by replacement costs?
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good rather than excused; Pepper names both as adversary-system defences (622 n 36).
  • Pepper limits client autonomy "by the law, not by the lawyer's morality" (626). If the RF denies a racist statute legal character, even his lawyer may refuse (15.12).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

When something feels unjust, ask where the injustice is. Is the whole legal system rotten? Is this particular law monstrous? Or is the law fine but this one result unfair (like a guilty person going free because evidence was obtained by force)? The right response is different for each.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

What this block does: it gives you a checklist for when a lawyer feels the result is unjust.

  1. Ask in order: is the system by and large just? If so, is this rule intolerably unjust? If not, is only this outcome unjust?
  2. Saying "it's the institution's fault, not mine" just moves the question: is the institution justified by finding the truth, by respecting dignity, or just by the cost of replacing it?
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part genuinely good, rather than merely excused. Pepper names both as defences of the adversarial system.

The verdicts: only this outcome unjust (e.g. a coerced confession is excluded): defend fully. The rule is intolerable: refuse, or argue the Radbruch formula. The whole system is unjust: the role gives no shelter. Even Pepper's lawyer may refuse a racist statute if the formula says it isn't law.

Remember: system, then rule, then outcome.

The move.

  1. Ask in order†: is the system by and large just; if so, is this rule intolerably unjust; if not, is this outcome unjust?
  2. Calling an unjust result the institution's wrong, not the lawyer's, only moves the question†: is the institution justified by truth-finding, by dignity, or by replacement costs?
  3. Only truth and dignity make the lawyer's part good rather than merely excused; Pepper names both as adversary-system defences (622 n 36).

Pepper limits client autonomy "by the law, not by the lawyer's morality" (626). If the Radbruch formula denies a racist statute legal character, even his lawyer may refuse (15.12).

  2. 2If so, is this rule intolerably unjust?

14Putting it together: Practice Q95

"A lawyer who turns away a client, or refuses to help him do something lawful, because he finds it distasteful abuses his position. The law already marks out what society will not tolerate; above that floor the client's conscience, not the lawyer's, must govern, for the client can neither work the legal machinery alone nor check the advice he is given. Even when a murder suspect reveals where he hid the bodies of his two victims and one turns out to be still alive, the lawyer must keep that confidence. A lawyer who imposes his own morals denies his client equal access to justice."

Instruction: Pepper and Thunder.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "turns away a client", "abuses" → 10.1 (first-class citizenship; the verbs are moral premises).
  • "law already marks out … floor" → 10.5 (floor, not ceiling).
  • hidden bodies, live victim → 10.1 (Hidden bodies, Q95 only).
  • "denies equal access" → 10.1 AGAINST (inequality).
  • Hook: source: the statement is almost Pepper's own case; test it against his own qualification (rare objection). Distinction: 1.3(3) floor v ceiling.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

This is almost verbatim Pepper's case for the lawyer's amoral role, and the question is whether Pepper's own qualification survives it. It does not survive the hidden-bodies example. I make three claims: (1) Pepper is right that screening clients by a lawyer's taste threatens access to law; (2) but the law is a floor, not a ceiling, and Pepper himself keeps conscientious objection open for extreme cases such as a live victim; and (3) spotting those cases requires a lawyer who weighs morality throughout, so Thunder's good person as lawyer differs from Pepper's more in mindset than in outcome.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Pepper steelmanned (10.1, 15.11): autonomy, equality, oligarchy of lawyers; the dilemma (make it unlawful, or why one lawyer's happenstance?).
  2. The floor and the live victim (10.1, 10.5): "abuses" and "denies" are moral premises; objection "rarely exercised" but may reveal "the live victim"; Liu: weighing morality all the time.
  3. Thunder and the gap (10.4, 10.10): role not a pocket universe; "to simply point to the role is to give up explaining it"; same act, different reasons. Self-critique: virtue under-determines cases (1.4).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Pepper and Thunder are closer than their labels: Pepper defends the role morally and keeps objection, which needs a lawyer weighing morality throughout; Thunder accepts role morality and that no legal system is perfect. The live question is how often conscience may override the role: rarely and openly, after dialogue, and certainly where a confidence would leave a living victim to die.

LESSON 11 · ARCHETYPE 11 · ABOUT 48 MIN · 39 QUESTIONS

Constitution and judicial role

⚡ BIG IDEA

A supreme written Constitution relocates the natural law v positivism debate rather than settling it. Courts should presume validity, yet void intolerable injustice.

ARCHETYPE 11 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
11 Constitution and judicial role
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The statement] is [overstated]: the Constitution relocates, not settles, the NLT v LP debate; courts should presume validity save at intolerable injustice.
Intro [The statement] assumes a supreme, written Constitution settles what law is. It does not: Art 4 is a master rule only because it is accepted, and Part 4's "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal" are contested moral terms. I [qualify] it: courts should presume validity, yet void intolerable injustice.
11.1 Supremacy Art 4; supreme law; settled it; check the text
  1. Art 4 makes [the written Constitution] supreme, but a master rule exists only because it is accepted: "We may not infer it from the written text alone" (TSH CJ 89).
  2. So [the Constitution sets the criteria of validity] only formally: Part 4's moral terms force a choice of school (11.2, 11.3).
  • AGAINST LP "does not shed light upon such morally loaded concepts" (TSH CJ 90): should the state define "'person', 'life' and 'liberty' when it is not the giver of life?" (CJ 102).
  • QUALIFY Teo Soh Lung (HC) rejected basic features (CJ 92 n 52), left open in YVK (2015) (JO 316 n 67); TSH relies on equal moral worth: even a genocide amendment falls to the RF (JO 333–34).
  • TRAP Never argue that the Constitution includes morality, so NLT wins: that makes you "an LP who is very happy that morality is now part of the positive law" (a student's line Liu endorsed, S14). TSH's own thesis: "constitutionalism is an affirmation of a higher law" (CJ 102).
  • CONCEDE Liu: in practice the master-rule point "doesn't necessarily lead to much"; what matters is how theory shapes judges' duty to law (S14).
11.2 Art 9(1) "law" validly passed; fair trial only; invent rights; caning; international norms
  1. Reading "law" as [whatever is validly passed] begs the question: what breaches Art 9 would not be in force (TSH CJ 103).
  2. On my application of TSH's test, [caning for third-time littering] survives the other readings and falls under the RF only if broad historical consensus condemns it; arguably none does.
  3. So stopping at [fair-trial rules] is a choice of theory, not text; the RF adds only a floor against intolerable injustice.
  • FOR YVK (2015): courts cannot create a right absent from the Constitution "out of whole cloth" as natural law, so none against caning (no ruling on natural law's view of it; George: 12.1).
  • AGAINST TSH: the CA targeted US substantive due process, "the antithesis of natural law theory" (JO 329). LMS: no privacy right; Art 9 covers unlawful deprivation of life and detention (JO 311); YVK (2015)† adds unlawful use of force.
  • STEELMAN Richer readings risk making "each judge a law unto himself" (CJ 103); TSH: letting manifest injustice stand "defeats the very purpose of certainty" (CJ 105).
ReadingAuthority
validly passedJabar dictum; YVK (2010)†: not about constitutionality; Nguyen read it to include constitutional validity (CJ 103 n 110)
natural justiceOng Ah Chuan left substantive fairness open (CJ 104); YVK (2015)†: procedural; TEH (HC): Art 12 imports none (JO 317)
not absurd or arbitraryYVK (2010)† suggested it; TSH: TEH's plea failed on evidence, not principle (JO 311)
international lawNguyen: statute beats custom (CJ 105); YVK (2010)†: read consistently where possible; no inhuman-punishment bar adopted
11.3 Art 12 intelligible line; legitimate object; unelected legislators; left-handed drivers
  1. For LMS (CA), [an intelligible line rationally related to the object] usually suffices, since courts are not "mini-legislatures" (JO 318).
  2. On [a double fee for left-handed drivers], the CA asks if the line rationally serves its aim; the HC would also void an "inherently bad" aim (JO 316).
  3. So [judges who probe the object become legislators] overstates: the RF voids only intolerable injustice, a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness (JO 325).
  • FOR LMS (CA): a threshold test; no free-standing legitimacy review, only a "limited element of illegitimacy"; Wednesbury rejected; use Art 12(2) (JO 317–18).
  • QUALIFY Not cleanly LP v NLT: "extreme illogicality and/or incoherence" fails a limb, and a women-driving ban "might" fail limb two (JO 318); TSH calls the test "a manifestation of the workings of natural law" (JO 317).
  • AGAINST TSH: "Equality is empty of content without a higher moral law", since the question is which differences are "morally significant", so moral arguments are not "extra-legal" under Art 12(1) (JO 325); without it, laws treating everyone "equally badly" pass (W13 slide 18†).
11.4 Four walls within its own four walls; foreign values; universal morality
  1. [Reading the Constitution primarily "within its own four walls"], as Colin Chan did (TSH CJ 82; LP, per Liu's slide†), need not exclude universal standards.
  2. Reading Haw Tua Tau charitably, TSH finds that fairness "was universal, though its specific manifestation varied according to local conditions" (CJ 82).
  3. So [universal morality] need not mean foreign values, if confined to manifest injustice (11.5).
  • CONCEDE Higher law cuts both ways: a "true-blue Thomist" may get judges with "quite a different view of dignity" (Lawrence; TSH CJ 93). Concede: no wide review, only a narrow trigger.
  • QUALIFY Liu (S14): TSH's LP is too narrow: LP mandates little but allows more. Where the text points to a moral concept, an LP judge may follow it outward, as commercial reasonableness imports trade practice; a purposive LP may read the Constitution as guarding individuals. TSH: then "Reference to natural law" is "mandatory" (CJ 101); can he stop at popular morality?
11.5 Who decides (courts) for Parliament, not the courts; ballot box; unelected judges; activism
  1. I accept that [contested rights are for Parliament], but only until "the threshold of injustice in Radbruch's formula is met" (TSH JO 329).
  2. So [judges must never invalidate a law for injustice] goes too far: rubber-stamping is a vice too (12.2), and intolerable injustice must fall.
  • STEELMAN Rajeevan (HC 1998), per TSH: the legislature "rightfully determines the rights of the individual" absent specific guarantees (CJ 94).
  • Threshold (BHC: 15.13): met for genocide and slavery; not for Roe, Obergefell or Women's Charter s 12 (JO 330–31); catch: 11.7.
  • QUALIFY LMS left Hart v Devlin to the Legislature (JO 321; 16); TSH: only "if no constitutional right was at stake" (JO 324).
  • LEGISLATOR Where "objective morality is not clear", a deliberative democracy "can take a stand through its legislature" (JO 329): 12.3.
  • Close: Liu's last slide†: "Who decides? … We are back where we started. But, wiser."
11.6 Art 156 repeal; marriage; leave it to Parliament; courts are binary
  1. In 2022 [change through Parliament] came: s 377A went, and Art 156, intended as "a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism" (TSH, Marriage), shielded man-woman marriage laws from Part 4.
  2. So [leaving it to Parliament] moved the question rather than removed it: a two-thirds majority (Art 5(2)) put those laws beyond Part 4 (11.7).
  • FOR Shanmugam: courts "can only make binary decisions" (Hansard, 29 Nov 2022).
  • QUALIFY TSH: repeal was for risk, not unconstitutionality, so differentiating laws are "not incoherent in principle" (Marriage). After UKM, s 377A "failed to do the work", which "might explain the change of tactic" (Marriage).
11.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary? neither philosophy nor personal morality; always sufficient; I just apply the law; my morals are private; without exception
  1. [The statement] is itself a legal philosophy, too moralised for the positivist and too amoral for the natural lawyer.
  2. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion: "Law is not morality; do not let it supplant morality" (PS 618).
  3. So [compliance always gives sufficient moral guidance] fails: law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open terms need theory.
  • Dilemma: Hart's penumbral judge may have to reach beyond the law; Dworkin's finds the answer in community morality that is also law (Harris 122): theory either way.
  • LAWYER Law is a floor: it "is concerned with the minimum and not with the maximum" (Devlin 19); Pepper's own premise implies the same (10.1).
  • Art 5(2): a "special two-thirds majority" amends most provisions (TSH, Marriage), with no express core like Basic Law art 79(3) (Alexy 56–57; implied limits: 11.1); so treating compliance as moral guidance hands judgment to whoever holds two-thirds.
  • STEELMAN Personal morality is subjective, so keep it out; most cases are routine: "to be occupied with the penumbra is one thing, to be preoccupied with it another" (PS 615).
  • AGAINST A natural-law judge refusing manifest injustice "expresses his fidelity to law" and is "not merely acting according to his conscience" (TSH CJ 85); subjectivism defeats itself: 4.7.
  • Without exception: try an as-applied Art 15 challenge, though Art 15(4), read literally, lacks ICCPR art 18(3)'s "necessary" test (TSH CJ 107 n 132): 12.6.
  • CONCEDE TSH's catch (8.5): consensus gauges, not grounds.
11.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers what makes it legitimate; consent; unamendable; basic features; separation of powers; gatekeeper
  1. [The people's acceptance] cannot found legitimacy: the framers' will "begs the question of why it should continue to bind us", and treating non-revolt "as acquiescence is artificial" (TSH CJ 91).
  2. "Only by understanding our co-equal dignity under natural law is our consent meaningful" (CJ 91); NLT answers from within, while LP must borrow another moral or political theory (Liu, S14).
  3. So [NLT defeats the separation of powers] fails: on the weak thesis morality overrides only at the Radbruch threshold, and TSH agrees "representative legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms" (JO 329).
  • QUALIFY Liu's two further answers: reason converges, so properly applied all three branches reach one result; and NLT v LP asks what law is, separation of powers how power is organised, so a democrat or a dictator could hold either (S14).
  • AGAINST Gatekeeper: an LP judge defers, leaving the legislature as moral gatekeeper; an NLT judge tests law against higher law, so the conflict is real (Radbruch). German courts applied the formula to a fallen regime's laws (Liu, W11); whether Singapore judges hold it is "debatable", and they prefer a constitutional basis; against a sitting legislature it is untested (S14).
  • Basic features: Kesavananda (India) held some unamendable, those suggested including "the separation of powers" and the "secular character" (TSH CJ 91–92); rejected here (11.1). Liu: easier for NLT, as a good constitution has a telos some amendments destroy; TSH: argue from natural law, not by "second-guessing the intention of the constitution-framers" (92).
Conclusion [The statement] is [overstated]: Art 4 and Part 4 relocate, not settle, the NLT v LP debate, so judges choose a theory whenever they read "law" or "equal". The Constitution narrows the practical gap between NLT and LP judges and makes Radbruch's formula rarely needed, but leaves open the extreme case, our attitude to law, and who decides by what standard (Liu, S14). Judges should presume validity but void intolerable injustice; no clause relieves anyone of conscience.

1Start here: archetype 11 in plain English

Archetype 11 asks: now that Singapore has a supreme, written Constitution, is the old fight between positivism and natural law over? The statements in this family usually say yes: "the text settles it; judges just check the Constitution." Your answer: no. The Constitution moves the debate to a new place; it doesn't end it. Article 4 is supreme only because people accept it, and words like "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal" in Part 4 are moral words that need a theory to interpret. So courts should normally presume laws are valid, but still strike down intolerable injustice.

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
Art 4 (supremacy)The Constitution is the highest law; any law inconsistent with it is void.
Part 4 (fundamental liberties)The rights part of the Constitution, including Art 9 (life and liberty "save in accordance with law") and Art 12 (equality).
Master ruleHart's idea (the rule of recognition): the top rule that says what counts as law. It exists because officials accept it, not because it is written down.
"In accordance with law" (Art 9)The key phrase: does "law" mean anything Parliament validly passed, or must it also meet basic standards of fairness?
Reasonable classification test (Art 12)The court asks whether a law's line between groups is intelligible and rationally linked to its purpose. Lim Meng Suang (LMS) used this to uphold s 377A.
Four wallsReading the Constitution only from its own text, without importing outside moral ideas (Colin Chan).
Broad historical consensus (BHC)TSH's test for when injustice is "intolerable": widely agreed across history and nations, as with genocide and slavery.
Basic features doctrineIndia's idea that some parts of a constitution can't be amended at all. Singapore's courts have rejected it.
Art 156Added in 2022: laws based on man–woman marriage can't be challenged under Part 4.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says the Constitution "relocates, not settles, the NLT v LP debate; courts should presume validity save at intolerable injustice". Put simply: having a written Constitution changes where the argument happens (now it's about how to read "law" and "equal"), but judges still need a theory. They should usually respect Parliament's laws, and only refuse ones that are intolerably unjust.

The Intro says: the statement assumes a written Constitution settles what law is. It doesn't: Art 4 works because it's accepted, and Part 4's key words are contested moral terms. The Conclusion adds: the Constitution narrows the practical gap between natural-law and positivist judges, and makes the Radbruch formula rarely needed. But it leaves open the extreme case, and who decides by what standard. No clause relieves anyone of conscience.

The eight blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
11.1"Art 4 settled the debate; judges just check the text."A master rule exists because it's accepted, not because it's written. And Part 4's moral words force a choice of theory.
11.2"'Law' in Art 9 just means whatever Parliament validly passes."That reading goes in a circle, since an Art 9 breach would not be valid law anyway. Choosing the narrow reading is a choice of theory, not something the text forces.
11.3"Equality only asks for an intelligible, rational line."That's the usual test, but courts probing a law's aim aren't becoming legislators.
11.4"Read the Constitution within its own four walls; no foreign values."Universal standards don't have to mean foreign values, if they're limited to manifest injustice.
11.5"Rights are for Parliament, not courts."Yes, until the Radbruch threshold is met. Rubber-stamping intolerable injustice is a vice too.
11.6"Leave marriage to Parliament; courts are blunt."That's what happened in 2022 with Art 156, but it moved the question rather than removing it.
11.7"With a Constitution, judges need no philosophy or personal morality."That claim is a philosophy. Law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open words need theory.
11.8"The Constitution is legitimate because people consent; NLT ruins separation of powers."Consent alone can't ground legitimacy. Weak natural law only overrides at the extreme, so separation of powers survives.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

The Constitution relocates the debate; it doesn't settle it, because its key words need a theory.

2The big picture: does a written Constitution end the debate?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Someone says: "Singapore has a written Constitution that's the supreme law. So we don't need philosophy: just check the text." But the text uses words like "law", "life", "liberty" and "equal". What do those words mean? To answer, a judge has to choose a theory. And why is the Constitution supreme in the first place? Because people accept it, which is a fact the text can't create by itself.

This archetype is about Singapore's Constitution and how far judges may go in reading moral ideas into it. You need four Articles, a handful of cases and two of TSH's articles.

The Articles you need
▤ 16.1; TSH CJ, JO, Marriage
  1. 1Art 4 (with Art 162): the Constitution is supreme; later inconsistent law is void; earlier law is read to conform.
  2. 2Art 5(2): two-thirds of elected MPs amend most provisions, with no express unamendable core like Germany's Basic Law art 79(3).
  3. 3Art 9(1): "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty save in accordance with law".
  4. 4Art 12: "All persons are equal before the law and entitled to the equal protection of the law".
  5. 5Art 156 (2022): law may "define, regulate, protect, safeguard, support, foster and promote" marriage; Part 4 cannot void laws based on the man–woman definition.
The cases you need
▤ 16.2
  1. 1Ong Ah Chuan (PC): Art 9 "law" includes fundamental rules of natural justice.
  2. 2Jabar (CA 1995): dictum: law validly passed binds, whether or not "fair, just and reasonable".
  3. 3Colin Chan (HC 1994): Constitution read "within its own four walls".
  4. 4LMS (Lim Meng Suang, CA 2014): s 377A passes Art 12; courts are not "mini-legislatures".
  5. 5YVK (Yong Vui Kong, CA 2010, 2015): 2010 hinted at a test of absurd or arbitrary laws; 2015: no right made "out of whole cloth" as natural law (no anti-caning right).
  6. 6Teo Soh Lung (HC): basic-features doctrine rejected. Rajeevan (HC 1998): the legislature "rightfully determines the rights of the individual".

TSH's two articles

  • Constitutional Jurisprudence (CJ): the LP–NLT debate "can never be settled" by "any declaration of supremacy" (89); contested terms force a choice of school; "constitutionalism is an affirmation of a higher law" (102).
  • Between Judicial Oligarchy and Parliamentary Supremacy (JO, 2016): courts should presume legislation constitutional unless Radbruch's threshold is met, shown by broad historical consensus (BHC) (15.13).

311.1 Supremacy

▤ On your sheet: 11.1 Supremacy (word for word)
11.1 Supremacy Art 4; supreme law; settled it; check the text
  1. Art 4 makes [the written Constitution] supreme, but a master rule exists only because it is accepted: "We may not infer it from the written text alone" (TSH CJ 89).
  2. So [the Constitution sets the criteria of validity] only formally: Part 4's moral terms force a choice of school (11.2, 11.3).
  • AGAINST LP "does not shed light upon such morally loaded concepts" (TSH CJ 90): should the state define "'person', 'life' and 'liberty' when it is not the giver of life?" (CJ 102).
  • QUALIFY Teo Soh Lung (HC) rejected basic features (CJ 92 n 52), left open in YVK (2015) (JO 316 n 67); TSH relies on equal moral worth: even a genocide amendment falls to the RF (JO 333–34).
  • TRAP Never argue that the Constitution includes morality, so NLT wins: that makes you "an LP who is very happy that morality is now part of the positive law" (a student's line Liu endorsed, S14). TSH's own thesis: "constitutionalism is an affirmation of a higher law" (CJ 102).
  • CONCEDE Liu: in practice the master-rule point "doesn't necessarily lead to much"; what matters is how theory shapes judges' duty to law (S14).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A rulebook can say "I am the top rulebook", but that sentence only works if people treat the book as the top rulebook. Hart called that acceptance the "rule of recognition". So Art 4 is supreme because officials accept it, not just because it says so. And once you're inside it, the big moral words still need interpreting.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "The old quarrel about whether law must be moral is over in Singapore. Art 4 makes the Constitution supreme and voids inconsistent laws, so judges don't need any higher law; they just check the text."

  1. Art 4 makes the Constitution supreme, but a master rule exists only because it's accepted. As TSH puts it, "we may not infer it from the written text alone".
  2. So the Constitution sets the test for valid law only on paper. Part 4's moral words ("life", "liberty", "equal") still force a judge to pick a theory.

The extras: AGAINST: positivism doesn't explain morally loaded words, and TSH asks whether the state should define "life" when it isn't the giver of life. QUALIFY: Singapore's High Court rejected the idea of unamendable basic features, but TSH says even a genocide amendment would fall to the Radbruch formula. TRAP: don't argue "the Constitution includes morality, so natural law wins"; that just makes you a positivist who likes moral content. CONCEDE (Liu): in practice the master-rule point may not lead to much; what matters is how theory shapes a judge's duty to the law.

Remember: written supremacy rests on acceptance, and its words need interpreting.

The trap Liu endorsed (S14)

Art 9(1): nobody loses life or liberty "save in accordance with law". If "law" just means "whatever Parliament validly passed", the protection is empty: any statute satisfies it. So courts have tried richer readings: fair procedure, no absurd or arbitrary laws, international standards. Each reading is a theory choice.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Art 9(1) says no one loses life or liberty 'save in accordance with law', and 'law' can only mean a law validly passed by Parliament. Anything richer invites judges to invent rights."

  1. That reading goes in a circle. Whether a law was "validly passed" depends on whether it fits the Constitution, Art 9 included, since a law breaching Art 9 would not be in force. So it can't tell you what Art 9 requires.
  2. Applying TSH's test to a hypothetical caning for third-time littering: it survives the other readings, and only falls under the Radbruch formula if broad historical consensus condemns it. Arguably none does.
  3. So stopping at fair-trial rules is a choice of theory, not something the text requires. The Radbruch formula adds only a floor against intolerable injustice.

AGAINST (TSH): that case was aimed at US-style substantive due process, which is "the antithesis of natural law theory". STEELMAN: richer readings risk making "each judge a law unto himself".

Remember: "law" in Art 9 needs a theory; the narrow reading is one too.

511.3 Art 12

▤ On your sheet: 11.3 Art 12 (word for word)
11.3 Art 12 intelligible line; legitimate object; unelected legislators; left-handed drivers
  1. For LMS (CA), [an intelligible line rationally related to the object] usually suffices, since courts are not "mini-legislatures" (JO 318).
  2. On [a double fee for left-handed drivers], the CA asks if the line rationally serves its aim; the HC would also void an "inherently bad" aim (JO 316).
  3. So [judges who probe the object become legislators] overstates: the RF voids only intolerable injustice, a narrower ground than Wednesbury unreasonableness (JO 325).
  • FOR LMS (CA): a threshold test; no free-standing legitimacy review, only a "limited element of illegitimacy"; Wednesbury rejected; use Art 12(2) (JO 317–18).
  • QUALIFY Not cleanly LP v NLT: "extreme illogicality and/or incoherence" fails a limb, and a women-driving ban "might" fail limb two (JO 318); TSH calls the test "a manifestation of the workings of natural law" (JO 317).
  • AGAINST TSH: "Equality is empty of content without a higher moral law", since the question is which differences are "morally significant", so moral arguments are not "extra-legal" under Art 12(1) (JO 325); without it, laws treating everyone "equally badly" pass (W13 slide 18†).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Equality doesn't mean everyone is treated identically; laws classify people all the time (adults v children, drivers v pedestrians). Courts ask whether the line drawn is sensible and linked to the law's purpose. The harder question: what if the purpose itself is bad? The Court of Appeal mostly won't ask that; TSH says equality is empty without a moral standard.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Equal protection only asks whether a law draws an intelligible line rationally linked to its purpose" or a hypothetical: "a law doubles the licence fee for left-handed taxi drivers".

  1. For Lim Meng Suang (Court of Appeal), that test usually suffices, because courts are not "mini-legislatures".
  2. On left-handed drivers, the Court of Appeal would ask whether the line rationally serves the aim. The High Court would also strike down an "inherently bad" aim.
  3. So "judges who look at a law's aim become legislators" goes too far. The Radbruch formula voids only intolerable injustice, a narrower ground than ordinary unreasonableness.

The extras: QUALIFY: it isn't neatly positivist v natural law: even LMS said extreme illogicality fails, and a ban on women driving "might" fail. TSH calls the test a sign of natural law at work. AGAINST (TSH): "Equality is empty of content without a higher moral law", because the question is which differences are morally significant. Otherwise a law treating everyone "equally badly" passes.

Remember: deciding which differences matter is a moral question.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Left-handed taxi drivers (Q109)

The minister says the double fee improves road safety.

  • CA approach (LMS): is there an intelligible differentia (left- v right-handed)? Is it rationally connected to road safety? If there is no evidence left-handers are less safe, the link fails.
  • HC approach: would also ask whether the aim is "inherently bad".
  • TSH: which differences are morally significant? Handedness is not, absent evidence.
  • RF: irrelevant; a fee is not intolerable injustice.

611.4 Four walls

▤ On your sheet: 11.4 Four walls (word for word)
11.4 Four walls within its own four walls; foreign values; universal morality
  1. [Reading the Constitution primarily "within its own four walls"], as Colin Chan did (TSH CJ 82; LP, per Liu's slide†), need not exclude universal standards.
  2. Reading Haw Tua Tau charitably, TSH finds that fairness "was universal, though its specific manifestation varied according to local conditions" (CJ 82).

Where the text points to a moral concept, an LP judge may follow it outward, as commercial reasonableness imports trade practice; a purposive LP may read the Constitution as guarding individuals. TSH: then "Reference to natural law" is "mandatory" (CJ 101); can he stop at popular morality?
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Read the Constitution only from inside its own pages; don't import foreign values." Fair: Singapore isn't America. But some standards (like basic fairness) are universal even if they look different locally. And a positivist judge can follow the text's own pointers outward, just as commercial law looks to trade practice.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

Remember: universal ≠ foreign; keep it to manifest injustice.

811.6 Art 156

▤ On your sheet: 11.6 Art 156 (word for word)
11.6 Art 156 repeal; marriage; leave it to Parliament; courts are binary
  1. In 2022 [change through Parliament] came: s 377A went, and Art 156, intended as "a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism" (TSH, Marriage), shielded man-woman marriage laws from Part 4.

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

In 2022, Parliament repealed s 377A and, at the same time, added Art 156 to the Constitution, so that courts couldn't use fundamental-rights arguments to change the man–woman definition of marriage. So "leave it to Parliament" happened: but it didn't make the moral question disappear; it just decided where it would be answered.

911.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary?

▤ On your sheet: 11.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary? (word for word)
11.7 The Constitution makes philosophy unnecessary? neither philosophy nor personal morality; always sufficient; I just apply the law; my morals are private; without exception
  1. [The statement] is itself a legal philosophy, too moralised for the positivist and too amoral for the natural lawyer.
  2. Hart, positivism's ablest defender, rejects its conclusion: "Law is not morality; do not let it supplant morality" (PS 618).
  3. So [compliance always gives sufficient moral guidance] fails: law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open terms need theory.
  • Dilemma: Hart's penumbral judge may have to reach beyond the law; Dworkin's finds the answer in community morality that is also law (Harris 122): theory either way.
  • LAWYER Law is a floor: it "is concerned with the minimum and not with the maximum" (Devlin 19); Pepper's own premise implies the same (10.1).
  • Art 5(2): a "special two-thirds majority" amends most provisions (TSH, Marriage), with no express core like Basic Law art 79(3) (Alexy 56–57; implied limits: 11.1); so treating compliance as moral guidance hands judgment to whoever holds two-thirds.
  • STEELMAN Personal morality is subjective, so keep it out; most cases are routine: "to be occupied with the penumbra is one thing, to be preoccupied with it another" (PS 615).
  • AGAINST A natural-law judge refusing manifest injustice "expresses his fidelity to law" and is "not merely acting according to his conscience" (TSH CJ 85); subjectivism defeats itself: 4.7.
  • Without exception: try an as-applied Art 15 challenge, though Art 15(4), read literally, lacks ICCPR art 18(3)'s "necessary" test (TSH CJ 107 n 132): 12.6.
  • CONCEDE TSH's catch (8.5): consensus gauges, not grounds.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

"Judges and lawyers need neither philosophy nor personal morality: the Constitution and laws give all the moral guidance needed." But that sentence is itself a philosophy. Even Hart, the great positivist, said law is not morality and shouldn't replace it. Law is a floor, not a ceiling.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

  2. Even Hart rejects it: "Law is not morality; do not let it supplant morality."
  3. So "compliance always gives enough moral guidance" fails. Law is a floor, not a ceiling, and its open words need theory.

The extras: the dilemma: Hart's judge may have to go beyond the law in unclear cases; Dworkin's finds the answer in morality that is also law. Theory either way. AGAINST (TSH): a judge refusing manifest injustice "expresses his fidelity to law", not just conscience.
