1011.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers

▤ On your sheet: 11.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers (word for word)
11.8 Legitimacy, basic features, separation of powers what makes it legitimate; consent; unamendable; basic features; separation of powers; gatekeeper
  1. [The people's acceptance] cannot found legitimacy: the framers' will "begs the question of why it should continue to bind us", and treating non-revolt "as acquiescence is artificial" (TSH CJ 91).
  2. "Only by understanding our co-equal dignity under natural law is our consent meaningful" (CJ 91); NLT answers from within, while LP must borrow another moral or political theory (Liu, S14).
  3. So [NLT defeats the separation of powers] fails: on the weak thesis morality overrides only at the Radbruch threshold, and TSH agrees "representative legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms" (JO 329).
  • QUALIFY Liu's two further answers: reason converges, so properly applied all three branches reach one result; and NLT v LP asks what law is, separation of powers how power is organised, so a democrat or a dictator could hold either (S14).
  • AGAINST Gatekeeper: an LP judge defers, leaving the legislature as moral gatekeeper; an NLT judge tests law against higher law, so the conflict is real (Radbruch). German courts applied the formula to a fallen regime's laws (Liu, W11); whether Singapore judges hold it is "debatable", and they prefer a constitutional basis; against a sitting legislature it is untested (S14).
  • Basic features: Kesavananda (India) held some unamendable, those suggested including "the separation of powers" and the "secular character" (TSH CJ 91–92); rejected here (11.1). Liu: easier for NLT, as a good constitution has a telos some amendments destroy; TSH: argue from natural law, not by "second-guessing the intention of the constitution-framers" (92).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Why should a Constitution written decades ago bind us today? "Because the people accept it" sounds nice, but not rebelling isn't really consent. TSH says real consent only makes sense if people already have equal dignity: a natural-law idea. And does natural law let judges overrule Parliament? Only at the extreme, so the separation of powers survives.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "The Constitution is legitimate because the people consent to it. Some features must be unamendable. Natural law destroys the separation of powers by making judges moral gatekeepers."

  1. Acceptance alone can't make it legitimate. The framers' will doesn't explain why it binds us, and treating "they didn't revolt" as consent is artificial (TSH).
  2. TSH: consent only means something if we understand our equal dignity under natural law. Natural law answers the legitimacy question from inside; positivism has to borrow another theory.
  3. So "natural law destroys separation of powers" fails. Weak natural law overrides only at the Radbruch threshold, and TSH agrees Parliament should generally prevail on contested moral questions.

The extras: QUALIFY (Liu): natural law v positivism is about what law is; separation of powers is about how power is organised, so either can fit a democracy or a dictatorship. AGAINST (gatekeeper): the conflict is real: a positivist judge defers, a natural-law judge tests laws against higher law. Basic features: India's Kesavananda held some features unamendable; Singapore rejected this.

Remember: consent needs a reason to matter; weak natural law leaves the separation of powers standing.

The statements. "The Constitution is legitimate because the people consent to it." "Some features must be unamendable." "Natural law theory destroys the separation of powers by making judges moral gatekeepers."

The move.

  1. The people's acceptance cannot found legitimacy: the framers' will "begs the question of why it should continue to bind us", and treating non-revolt "as acquiescence is artificial" (TSH CJ 91).
  2. "Only by understanding our co-equal dignity under natural law is our consent meaningful" (CJ 91); NLT answers from within, while LP must borrow another moral or political theory (Liu, S14).
  3. So "NLT defeats the separation of powers" fails: on the weak thesis morality overrides only at the Radbruch threshold, and TSH agrees "representative legislative mandate should generally prevail over judicial opinion on contentious moral norms" (JO 329).

More.

  • QUALIFY (Liu's two further answers, S14): reason converges, so properly applied all three branches reach one result; and NLT v LP asks what law is, separation of powers how power is organised, so a democrat or a dictator could hold either.
  • AGAINST (gatekeeper): an LP judge defers, leaving the legislature as moral gatekeeper; an NLT judge tests law against higher law, so the conflict is real (Radbruch). German courts applied the formula to a fallen regime's laws (Liu, W11); whether Singapore judges hold it is "debatable", and they prefer a constitutional basis; against a sitting legislature it is untested (S14).
  • Basic features: Kesavananda (India) held some features unamendable, those suggested including "the separation of powers" and the "secular character" (TSH CJ 91–92); rejected here (11.1). Liu: easier for NLT, as a good constitution has a telos some amendments destroy; TSH: argue from natural law, not by "second-guessing the intention of the constitution-framers" (92).

11Putting it together: Practice Q104

"The old quarrel over whether a law must be morally sound to count as law is over in Singapore: our written Constitution settled it. Article 4 voids any law inconsistent with the supreme law, and Article 162 requires existing laws to be read so as to conform to it, so judges need no higher law; they need only check the text to know which laws are valid. Even the fundamental liberties are simply rights the text confers, carrying whatever meaning the state gives them. That is why our courts rightly read the Constitution within its own four walls instead of importing universal moral ideals."

Instruction: Hart, Radbruch, TSH; local cases on Arts 9 and 12 required.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "the Constitution settled it" → 11.1 (a master rule can't settle LP v NLT).
  • "only check the text" → 11.1, 11.7.
  • "whatever meaning the state gives them" → 11.1 AGAINST (TSH: the state is not the giver of life), 11.2.
  • "four walls", "universal moral ideals" → 11.4.
  • Arts 9 and 12 cases required → 11.2 (Ong Ah Chuan, Jabar, YVK), 11.3 (LMS).
  • Lead 11; distinction: 1.3(16) mandated v compatible.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Opening

The statement treats Art 4 as the end of jurisprudence. It is the beginning: a supreme Constitution relocates the old quarrel rather than settling it. I make three claims: (1) Art 4 is a master rule only because it is accepted, which the text cannot supply; (2) Part 4's terms, "law" in Art 9 and "equal" in Art 12, force judges to choose a theory, as Ong Ah Chuan, YVK and LMS show; and (3) reading within the four walls need not exclude universal standards if confined, as TSH proposes, to intolerable injustice shown by broad historical consensus.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Body plan
  1. Supremacy and Hart (11.1): master rule by acceptance (CJ 89); trap: "morality in the text, so NLT wins" is LP; Liu's concession that the point "doesn't necessarily lead to much".
  2. Arts 9 and 12 (11.2, 11.3): four readings of "law"; YVK 2015 v TSH on substantive due process; LMS "mini-legislatures"; TSH: equality empty without higher law.
  3. Four walls and Radbruch (11.4, 11.5): Haw Tua Tau charitably read; Liu: TSH's LP too narrow (mandated v compatible); BHC threshold; self-critique: TSH's catch (8.5).
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The statement is therefore overstated. Art 4 and Part 4 relocate, not settle, the debate, so judges choose a theory whenever they read "law" or "equal". The Constitution narrows the practical gap between natural-law and positivist judges and makes Radbruch's formula rarely needed, but leaves open the extreme case and who decides by what standard. Judges should presume validity but void intolerable injustice.

12Recap

Archetype 11 on one card
▤ Sections 11.1–11.8
  1. 1Supremacy rests on acceptance; don't say "morality in the text, so NLT wins" (11.1).
  2. 2Art 9 "law": four readings; each is a theory choice (11.2).
  3. 3Art 12: rational classification; TSH: equality needs higher law (11.3).
  4. 4Four walls need not exclude universal standards; mandated v compatible (11.4).
  5. 5Parliament decides contested rights, until the RF threshold (11.5, 15.13).
  6. 6Art 156 moved the question, not removed it (11.6).
  7. 7"No philosophy needed" is a philosophy; law is a floor (11.7).
  8. 8Legitimacy needs equal dignity; weak NLT keeps the separation of powers (11.8).

LESSON 12 · ARCHETYPE 12 · ABOUT 33 MIN · 33 QUESTIONS

Roles: who decides

⚡ BIG IDEA

Roles have limits, so "stay in your lane" is right as a presumption. But where a role ends is contested, drawing the line is a moral judgment, and refusing your own role's work (abdication) is as much a vice as taking another's (usurpation).

ARCHETYPE 12 IN FULL · WORD FOR WORD FROM YOUR SHEET
12 Roles: who decides
Read it once now, even if much of it is opaque. Every block below teaches one part of it. Hover a dotted abbreviation for its meaning; click a blue number such as 8.3 to jump to that block. How to read a block.
Position [The statement] is right as a presumption: roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too.
Intro [The statement] treats each role's limits as settled. Roles do have limits: a constitutional democracy divides power. But where a role ends is contested, and drawing the line is a moral judgment; refusing one's own work is as much a vice as taking another's; and refusing extreme injustice is fidelity, not usurpation.
Frame (Roles question) The statement is almost verbatim George as TSH reports him: at least in a "basically just regime", natural law requires "that judges and other officials respect the limits of their own authority" (CJ 95). It drops the proviso and adds lawyers.
12.1 Source and frame limits of their own authority; rightfully others'; who decides?; for Parliament, not the courts
  1. [The statement] assumes we know where roles end; for George allocating authority is a determinatio, a prudent choice among morally acceptable options (CJ 95).
  2. TSH's reply is the question George leaves open: "who rightfully decides on whether it is prudentially made?" (CJ 96).
  3. So [what is rightfully others'] assumes its answer: a role's limits come from a theory of the role.
  • STEELMAN Rajeevan (11.5); YVK (2015), citing George: "some have contended" natural law requires judges "to respect the boundaries of authority" (JO 328).
  • CONCEDE TSH's impasse binds my side: natural law condemns vesting authority in "a random group of bandits" (CJ 95) but cannot say who decides; still, the proviso, "impasse notwithstanding, must be right in principle" (CJ 96).
12.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication usurp; leave it to Parliament; non-enforcement; just focus on the law
  1. Every role can fail twice, by doing others' work (usurpation) or by refusing its own (abdication); [the statement] names only the first.
  2. TSH names both for judges: in bad faith they "would either engage in judicial legislation, or rubber-stamp whatever law Parliament passes" (JO 308).
  3. So [respecting the limits of one's role] is half the duty; the other half is doing the role's own moral work.
  • OFFICIAL s 377A (2007), kept but not proactively enforced: arguably Parliament abdicated and the executive quasi-legislated (7.7).
  • JUDGE Bridge's "unwarranted abdication" (McLoughlin 441; 9.2).
  • LAWYER Screening clients usurps (Pepper 617); "just focus on the law" abdicates (Thunder 316).
12.3 Legislator's hat majoritarian will; sole concern; as accurately as possible; poll; referendum; whip
  1. Majority will settles who may make law in a democracy, not what the law is or should say.
  2. Devlin, the statement's natural ally, tells law-makers that majority opinion "is surely not enough": his standard "does not depend on the counting of heads" (Devlin 15).
  3. So the legislator does what [the sole concern] forbids: he judges, as a trustee, not a stenographer.
  • STEELMAN Equal respect amid disagreement; fear of juristocracy (TSH JO 308). Poa (2022) sought a referendum, marriage being "a matter of social norm".
  • LEGISLATOR Masagos to Poa: MPs must "come to a decision even, and perhaps especially, for difficult and polarising social issues" (2022).
  • QUALIFY TSH: non-NLT legislators "may not regard themselves as bound" by higher standards (CJ 85). Liu: need not ≠ will not; one who wants good, not merely valid, laws weighs morality (14.4's minimum content; Hart v Devlin). LP uses morality in one dimension (good law), NLT in two (good law, and law at all).
12.4 Judge's hat if passed, would you enforce it?; strike down; refuse; validly passed; applying the law
  1. The judge asks not whether [the law] is wise, but what it is and what fidelity to it requires.
  2. I climb a ladder: validity, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then discretion within the statute; refusal comes only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So [I would enforce it] is a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role, not an escape from morality.
  • Kennedy's five courses (558–59; 15.10): he endorses or excludes none "a priori". The public's "devil's compact" (defend as plausibly legal, change, or withdraw) presupposes a determinacy "initiates know is false" (556); he finds "unconvincing" that the rule of law means obeying it (559).
  • Candour, my standard, bars his covert last two. Refusal line: genocide, slavery; not Roe (JO 330–31).
  • CONCEDE TSH's own catch (JO 331): concede the risk; her reply: 8.5.
12.5 Official's and junior's hat officials tasked with enforcing; lawful instructions; superiors; junior; deference
  1. Officials owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank: "mere respect for constituted authority must not be confused with fidelity to law" (Fuller, MOL 41).
  2. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches "a judge or another office-holder", "neither a saint nor a hero": if non-positivism prevails, he risks later prosecution (Alexy 50–51).
  3. So [obeying lawful instructions] is not blameless: "to simply point to the role is to give up explaining it" (Thunder 328).
  • CONCEDE Thunder grants that virtue under-determines cases (10.5): dialogue first, refusal only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian, mistreating customers under "official library policies", cannot plead the role (328).
12.6 Two-hats problem frame a bill proposes; would you vote for it?; if passed, would you enforce it?; Ruritania
  1. As an MP I would [vote against the bill and propose narrower measures]; as a judge I would apply it if validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope does the damage: it reaches consumption as well as sale, and [without exception] catches communion and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.
GroundSteelmanTest, then verdict
FaithAddiction subverts practical reasonablenessDenying worship "normally" breaks reciprocity (PRR 138): a voice, not a ground
HarmHart accepts paternalism (LLM 32)It protects buyers: license, not jail
Poll85% at least "somewhat"Not Devlin's "real feeling of reprobation" (17): evidence, not mandate
  • Yaacob Ibrahim (2005): "drinking and other activities that Muslims consider vices are not banned" (Pragmatism 296). Critics' teetotallers (288–89): offence is selected morally.
  • JUDGE Read literally, Art 15(4) has no "necessary" test (TSH CJ 107 n 132): a weak as-applied claim. Harsh, not intolerable (no BHC condemns prohibition): apply it.
Conclusion No role ends moral duty. [The statement] is right that roles have limits, but drawing them is itself a moral judgment, and the vice is not only taking others' work but refusing one's own.

1Start here: archetype 12 in plain English

Archetype 12 asks: who gets to decide what, and how should each person stay within their role? It covers judges, legislators (MPs), officials, junior lawyers, and the classic "two hats" problem: as an MP, would you vote for this bill? As a judge, would you enforce it? The statements usually say each role has clear limits: "officials must respect the limits of their authority", "the legislator should just follow majority will", "judges just apply what's passed". Your answer: right as a starting presumption. Roles do have limits, but where they lie is disputed, drawing the line is a moral judgement, and refusing to do your own job (abdication) is as much a failing as taking over someone else's (usurpation).

📖 WORDS TO KNOW FIRST
WordWhat it means in everyday terms
RoleA position with its own job and limits: judge, MP, official, lawyer.
UsurpationDoing someone else's job: a judge rewriting the law, a lawyer playing judge over clients.
AbdicationRefusing to do your own job: a judge who rubber-stamps everything, an MP who just follows the polls.
DeterminatioA natural-law idea (George): where morality allows several acceptable options, someone must make a sensible choice among them. Deciding which body holds which power is one such choice.
Basically just regimeGeorge's proviso: respecting role limits applies at least where the system as a whole is just.
Trustee v stenographerA trustee MP uses their own judgement for the people; a stenographer just records what the majority wants.
Fidelity to lawBeing faithful to law's purpose and requirements, not just obeying whoever ranks above you.
Risk effectAlexy's point that if non-positivism prevails, an official who follows a monstrous law risks being prosecuted later.
Two-hats problemA question asking you to answer as an MP and as a judge. Different roles, different questions, so different answers can both be right.

Your Position, in everyday words

The Position line says the statement "is right as a presumption: roles have limits, but where they lie is contested, and abdication is a vice too". Put simply: yes, start by respecting role limits. But don't treat the limits as obvious, and remember that hiding behind your role is a failure too.

The Frame tells you where the "roles" statement comes from: it is nearly word for word Robert George, as TSH reports him, but it drops George's condition ("at least in a basically just regime") and adds lawyers. The Intro says: a constitutional democracy does divide power, but where a role ends is contested, refusing your own work is as bad as taking others', and refusing extreme injustice is fidelity, not usurpation. The Conclusion says: no role ends moral duty.

The six blocks at a glance

BlockThe statement says…You reply, in short…
12.1"Respect the limits of your authority; leave others what's theirs."That assumes we know where roles end. Deciding that is itself a judgement, and George leaves open who makes it.
12.2"Refusing instructions usurps; leave it to Parliament."Every role can fail twice: by taking over others' work, or by refusing its own.
12.3"The legislator just expresses majority will."Majority will decides who makes law, not what it should say. Even Devlin says counting heads isn't enough.
12.4"Would you, as a judge, enforce it?"Climb a ladder: validity, interpretation, discretion; refuse only at the Radbruch threshold. "I'd enforce it" is a moral conclusion.
12.5"Officials just follow lawful instructions."Fidelity is owed to law, not to rank. "It's my role" doesn't explain or excuse everything.
12.6The two-hats problem (an alcohol ban).As an MP: vote no, propose narrower measures. As a judge: apply it if validly passed, unless intolerable.
ℹ NOTE
The one sentence to carry into the exam

Respect role limits as a presumption, but drawing them is a moral judgement, and abdication is a vice too.

2The big picture: who decides?

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A football match has a referee, players and a league that writes the rules. The referee shouldn't rewrite the rules mid-game (that's taking over someone else's job). But a referee who never blows the whistle because "it's not my place" is failing too. Every role can fail in two directions. This last archetype asks how judges, MPs, officials and lawyers should each stay in their role without hiding behind it.

This archetype pulls the course together. Its statements usually say something like: "officials must respect the limits of their authority", "majority will is the legislator's sole concern", or "as an MP would you vote for this? as a judge would you enforce it?".

The source of the "roles" statement

The frame
▤ Section 12 Frame; TSH CJ 95–96
  1. 1The statement is almost verbatim Robert George, as TSH reports him: at least in a "basically just regime", natural law requires "that judges and other officials respect the limits of their own authority" (CJ 95).
  2. 2The exam version usually drops the proviso ("basically just regime") and adds lawyers.
  3. 3TSH's reply is the question George leaves open: "who rightfully decides on whether it is prudentially made?" (CJ 96).

Three ideas to carry

  1. Determinatio: for George, allocating authority is a prudent choice among morally acceptable options. Positive law decides who decides.
  2. Twin vices (1.3(11)): usurpation (doing another role's work) and abdication (refusing your own).
  3. Two hats (the format Liu himself uses): the same person answers different moral questions as legislator (what should the law be?) and as judge (what does fidelity to this law require?).
Framework 15.14: who decides?
▤ George, in CJ 95; CJ 96–97
  1. 1Positive law allocates authority (determinatio). In a basically just regime, "judicial usurpations ... even in what judges take to be good causes, are themselves unjust".
  2. 2But "who rightfully decides" whether it was prudent? An impasse (CJ 96).
  3. 3A whipped Parliament may not reflect consensus (6.8); courts may be exhorted to uphold higher law "rather than playing politics".
  4. 4Verdict rule: honour the allocation; depart only at the Radbruch threshold (15.13).

12.1 Source and frame limits of their own authority; rightfully others'; who decides?; for Parliament, not the courts
  1. [The statement] assumes we know where roles end; for George allocating authority is a determinatio, a prudent choice among morally acceptable options (CJ 95).

"Everyone should respect the limits of their authority." Sure, but where are the limits? The statement assumes we already know. George says the limits are set by a sensible choice in the law. TSH asks: who decides whether that choice was sensible? That question has no easy answer.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "Natural law requires judges, lawyers and officials to respect the limits of their own authority, leaving to others what is rightfully theirs."

  1. This assumes we already know where each role ends. For George, deciding who holds which power is a determinatio: a sensible choice among morally acceptable options.
  2. TSH's reply is the question George leaves open: "who rightfully decides" whether that choice was sensibly made?
  3. So "what is rightfully others'" assumes its own answer. The limits of a role come from a theory of that role.

The extras: STEELMAN: Rajeevan and Yong Vui Kong (2015, citing George) both stress respecting the boundaries of authority. CONCEDE: TSH admits the deadlock cuts against natural law too: natural law condemns giving power to "a random group of bandits" but can't say exactly who should decide. Still, she says George's principle "must be right in principle".

Remember: "stay in your lane" assumes someone has already drawn the lanes.

412.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication

▤ On your sheet: 12.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication (word for word)
12.2 Twin vices: usurpation and abdication usurp; leave it to Parliament; non-enforcement; just focus on the law
  1. Every role can fail twice, by doing others' work (usurpation) or by refusing its own (abdication); [the statement] names only the first.
  2. TSH names both for judges: in bad faith they "would either engage in judicial legislation, or rubber-stamp whatever law Parliament passes" (JO 308).
  3. So [respecting the limits of one's role] is half the duty; the other half is doing the role's own moral work.
  • OFFICIAL s 377A (2007), kept but not proactively enforced: arguably Parliament abdicated and the executive quasi-legislated (7.7).

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A judge can go wrong by acting like a legislator (inventing new laws) or by rubber-stamping anything Parliament passes. An MP can go wrong by passing the buck. A lawyer can go wrong by refusing clients he dislikes (usurping the law's job) or by saying "I just do the law" (abdicating his conscience).

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Officials who refuse lawful instructions take over others' authority." "Leave it to Parliament." "Just focus on the law."

  1. Every role can fail in two ways: by doing others' work (usurpation) or by refusing its own (abdication). The statement only mentions the first.
  2. TSH names both for judges: acting in bad faith, they would either make law themselves or "rubber-stamp whatever law Parliament passes".
  3. So respecting your role's limits is only half the duty. The other half is doing your role's own moral work.

Examples for each role: OFFICIAL: keeping s 377A in 2007 but not enforcing it arguably meant Parliament abdicated and the executive half-legislated. JUDGE: Bridge in McLoughlin called stopping at decided cases "an unwarranted abdication". LAWYER: screening clients by your morals usurps (Pepper); "just focus on the law" abdicates (Thunder).

Remember: two vices: taking over and checking out.

12.3 Legislator's hat majoritarian will; sole concern; as accurately as possible; poll; referendum; whip
  1. Majority will settles who may make law in a democracy, not what the law is or should say.
  2. Devlin, the statement's natural ally, tells law-makers that majority opinion "is surely not enough": his standard "does not depend on the counting of heads" (Devlin 15).

  • STEELMAN Equal respect amid disagreement; fear of juristocracy (TSH JO 308). Poa (2022) sought a referendum, marriage being "a matter of social norm".
  • LEGISLATOR Masagos to Poa: MPs must "come to a decision even, and perhaps especially, for difficult and polarising social issues" (2022).

★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An MP isn't a stenographer who just writes down what the majority wants. An MP is more like a trustee: elected to use their own judgement for the people. Even Devlin, the conservative, said majority opinion isn't enough for a law-maker.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statement, in everyday words: "A legislator's only job is to express majority will as accurately as possible: poll the people, and hold a referendum if needed."

  1. Majority will decides who may make law in a democracy, not what the law should say.
  2. Even Devlin, who you'd expect to agree, says majority opinion "is surely not enough" for a law-maker; his test "does not depend on the counting of heads".
  3. So the legislator does what "sole concern" forbids: they use their own judgement, as a trustee, not a stenographer.

The extras: STEELMAN: following the majority shows equal respect when people disagree, and avoids rule by judges. In 2022 Poa asked for a referendum on marriage. LEGISLATOR: Masagos replied that MPs must decide "especially" on difficult, polarising issues. QUALIFY (Liu): positivist MPs needn't consider morality, but one who wants good laws, not just valid ones, will. Positivism uses morality in one way (is it good law?); natural law in two (is it good law, and is it law at all?).

Remember: a mandate tells you who decides, not what's right.

More.

  • STEELMAN: equal respect amid disagreement; fear of juristocracy (TSH JO 308). Poa (2022) sought a referendum, marriage being "a matter of social norm".
  • LEGISLATOR: Masagos to Poa: MPs must "come to a decision even, and perhaps especially, for difficult and polarising social issues" (2022).
  • QUALIFY: TSH: non-NLT legislators "may not regard themselves as bound" by higher standards (CJ 85). Liu: need not ≠ will not: one who wants good, not merely valid, laws weighs morality (Hart's minimum content; Hart v Devlin). LP uses morality in one dimension (good law), NLT in two (good law, and law at all).

612.4 Judge's hat

▤ On your sheet: 12.4 Judge's hat (word for word)
12.4 Judge's hat if passed, would you enforce it?; strike down; refuse; validly passed; applying the law
  1. The judge asks not whether [the law] is wise, but what it is and what fidelity to it requires.
  2. I climb a ladder: validity, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then discretion within the statute; refusal comes only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So [I would enforce it] is a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role, not an escape from morality.
  • Kennedy's five courses (558–59; 15.10): he endorses or excludes none "a priori". The public's "devil's compact" (defend as plausibly legal, change, or withdraw) presupposes a determinacy "initiates know is false" (556); he finds "unconvincing" that the rule of law means obeying it (559).
  • Candour, my standard, bars his covert last two. Refusal line: genocide, slavery; not Roe (JO 330–31).
  • CONCEDE TSH's own catch (JO 331): concede the risk; her reply: 8.5.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A judge doesn't ask "is this law wise?" A judge asks "what is the law, and what does being faithful to it require?" There's a ladder: check it's valid; interpret it by its principles and purpose; use any discretion it gives; and only at the very top (monstrous injustice) refuse.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The question, in everyday words: "If the bill were passed, would you as a judge enforce it?" or "judges must apply whatever is validly passed".

  1. The judge doesn't ask whether the law is wise. The judge asks what the law is and what being faithful to it requires.
  2. Climb a ladder: first, is it valid? Then, interpret it by principle and purpose. Then, use any discretion the statute gives. Refuse only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So "I would enforce it" is a moral conclusion reached through a theory of the judge's role. It isn't a way of escaping morality.

The extras: Kennedy lists five courses a judge might take and rules none out in advance. He says the public's "devil's compact" (a judge may defend a result as plausibly legal, change the law, or withdraw) assumes the law is more settled than insiders know it is. Your standard is candour, which rules out his two hidden options. Refusal line: genocide and slavery, not Roe. CONCEDE: TSH's own "catch" (Lesson 8): consensus could go wrong.

Remember: validity, interpretation, discretion; refusal only at the extreme.

The statement. "If the bill passed, would you as a judge enforce it?" "Judges must apply what is validly passed."

The move.

  1. The judge asks not whether the law is wise, but what it is and what fidelity to it requires.
  2. Climb a ladder: validity, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then discretion within the statute; refusal comes only at the Radbruch threshold.
  3. So "I would enforce it" is a moral conclusion, reached through a theory of the judicial role, not an escape from morality.

Kennedy's five courses (558–59; 15.10): he endorses or excludes none "a priori". The public's "devil's compact" (defend as plausibly legal, change, or withdraw) presupposes a determinacy "initiates know is false" (556); he finds "unconvincing" that the rule of law means obeying it (559).

Framework 15.10: Kennedy's five courses
▤ Kennedy 558–59

Verdict rule (the sheet's): in a basically just system, (1) or (2); (3) only at the Radbruch threshold; (4) and (5) fail candour.

  1. 1Go along, denouncing the law.
  2. 2Withdraw, leaving "the dirty work" to another.
  3. 3Decide openly on what the law should be.
  4. 4Use an implausible legal argument.
  5. 5Find facts known to be false, "obviously an extreme measure".

Candour, the sheet's standard, bars Kennedy's covert last two. Refusal line: genocide, slavery; not Roe (JO 330–31). CONCEDE: TSH's own catch (JO 331): concede the risk; her reply: 8.5.

712.5 Official's and junior's hat

▤ On your sheet: 12.5 Official's and junior's hat (word for word)
12.5 Official's and junior's hat officials tasked with enforcing; lawful instructions; superiors; junior; deference
  1. Officials owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank: "mere respect for constituted authority must not be confused with fidelity to law" (Fuller, MOL 41).
  2. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches "a judge or another office-holder", "neither a saint nor a hero": if non-positivism prevails, he risks later prosecution (Alexy 50–51).
  3. So [obeying lawful instructions] is not blameless: "to simply point to the role is to give up explaining it" (Thunder 328).
  • CONCEDE Thunder grants that virtue under-determines cases (10.5): dialogue first, refusal only at the extreme.
  • Thunder's librarian, mistreating customers under "official library policies", cannot plead the role (328).
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A civil servant or junior lawyer is told to do something lawful but wrong. "I was just following orders" isn't a full answer: loyalty to the law is not the same as obedience to your boss. Under a wicked regime, officials who go along may later be prosecuted, and they don't need to be heroes to see that.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The statements, in everyday words: "Officials tasked with enforcing the law must follow lawful instructions. Juniors should defer to their superiors."

  1. Officials owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank. Fuller: respecting those in authority "must not be confused with fidelity to law".
  2. Alexy's risk effect: in a rogue state, an ordinary official, "neither a saint nor a hero", risks later prosecution if non-positivism wins out after the regime falls.
  3. So obeying lawful instructions isn't automatically blameless. As Thunder says, "to simply point to the role is to give up explaining it".

The extras: CONCEDE: Thunder admits virtue doesn't settle every case, so talk it through first, and refuse only at the extreme. Thunder's librarian, who mistreats customers under "official library policies", can't hide behind the role.

Remember: follow the law, not just the boss.

The statements. "Officials tasked with enforcing the law must follow lawful instructions." "Juniors should defer to superiors." (Q100)

The move.

  1. Officials owe fidelity to law, not deference to rank: "mere respect for constituted authority must not be confused with fidelity to law" (Fuller, MOL 41).
  2. In a rogue state, Alexy's risk effect reaches "a judge or another office-holder", "neither a saint nor a hero": if non-positivism prevails, he risks later prosecution (Alexy 50–51).
  3. So obeying lawful instructions is not blameless: "to simply point to the role is to give up explaining it" (Thunder 328).

CONCEDE: Thunder grants that virtue under-determines cases (10.5): dialogue first, refusal only at the extreme. Thunder's librarian, mistreating customers under "official library policies", cannot plead the role (328).

812.6 Two-hats problem frame

▤ On your sheet: 12.6 Two-hats problem frame (word for word)
12.6 Two-hats problem frame a bill proposes; would you vote for it?; if passed, would you enforce it?; Ruritania
  1. As an MP I would [vote against the bill and propose narrower measures]; as a judge I would apply it if validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope does the damage: it reaches consumption as well as sale, and [without exception] catches communion and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.
GroundSteelmanTest, then verdict
FaithAddiction subverts practical reasonablenessDenying worship "normally" breaks reciprocity (PRR 138): a voice, not a ground
HarmHart accepts paternalism (LLM 32)It protects buyers: license, not jail
Poll85% at least "somewhat"Not Devlin's "real feeling of reprobation" (17): evidence, not mandate
  • Yaacob Ibrahim (2005): "drinking and other activities that Muslims consider vices are not banned" (Pragmatism 296). Critics' teetotallers (288–89): offence is selected morally.
  • JUDGE Read literally, Art 15(4) has no "necessary" test (TSH CJ 107 n 132): a weak as-applied claim. Harsh, not intolerable (no BHC condemns prohibition): apply it.
★ ELI5 · IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Liu's own sample is a two-part problem: a bill bans alcohol. Part A: as an MP, would you vote for it? Part B: if it passes, would you as a judge enforce it? You can answer "no" to A and "yes" to B without contradiction, because the MP asks what the law should be and the judge asks what fidelity to the law requires.

🔍 THE BLOCK, LINE BY LINE · IN EVERYDAY WORDS

The problem, in everyday words: a bill bans the sale and consumption of alcohol, without exception, to protect families and health, and a poll shows 85% at least "somewhat" support it. (a) As an MP, would you vote for it? (b) If it passes, would you, as a judge, enforce it?

  1. Two hats, two answers. As an MP: vote against and propose narrower measures. As a judge: apply it if validly passed, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope is the problem. It bans drinking as well as selling, and "without exception" would catch communion wine and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different questions: the MP asks what the law should be; the judge asks what fidelity to the law requires.

How to read the table: each row tests one reason for the bill. Faith: its best case is that addiction undermines good judgement, but a religious reason is a voice, not a ground on its own. Harm: Hart accepts some paternalism, but it protects buyers, so license sales rather than jail drinkers. Poll: 85% "somewhat" isn't Devlin's "real feeling of reprobation"; it's evidence, not a mandate. JUDGE: an Art 15 (religious freedom) challenge is weak as worded, and the ban is harsh but not intolerable, so apply it.

Remember: MP asks "should it be law?"; judge asks "what does fidelity require?"

The move.

  1. As an MP I would vote against the bill and propose narrower measures; as a judge I would apply it if validly enacted, refusing only at the Radbruch threshold.
  2. The bill's scope does the damage: it reaches consumption as well as sale, and "without exception" catches communion and temple wine.
  3. The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions: what the law should be, and what fidelity to it requires.
The three grounds, tested
▤ 12.6 table
  1. 1Faith: steelman: addiction subverts practical reasonableness. Test: denying worship "normally" breaks reciprocity (PRR 138): a voice, not a ground.
  2. 2Harm: steelman: Hart accepts paternalism (LLM 32). Test: it protects buyers: license, not jail.
  3. 3Poll: steelman: 85% at least "somewhat" support. Test: not Devlin's "real feeling of reprobation" (17): evidence, not mandate.

Singapore texture: Yaacob Ibrahim (2005): "drinking and other activities that Muslims consider vices are not banned" (Pragmatism 296). Critics' teetotallers (288–89): offence is selected morally.

JUDGE: read literally, Art 15(4) has no "necessary" test (TSH CJ 107 n 132): a weak as-applied claim. Harsh, not intolerable (no broad historical consensus condemns prohibition): apply it.

The two-hats word budget
▤ Prep page 0.3, 0.5
  1. 1Part A (MP), about 750 words: bill anatomy 100; three grounds × 180 (steelman, test, verdict); vote and alternatives 100.
  2. 2Part B (judge), about 600 words: validity 100; threshold 120; how to enforce 250; obligation 80.
  3. 3Close, about 80 words: why the answers differ.

9Putting it together: a two-hats problem

The exact wording of Liu's sample (Ruritania) is not in your folder, so here is a problem built on the same pattern the sheet prepares you for:

A bill proposes to ban the sale and consumption of alcohol, without exception, to protect families and public health. A poll finds 85% of citizens at least "somewhat" support it. (a) As a Member of Parliament, would you vote for it? (b) If it is passed, would you, as a judge, enforce it?
✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Scan and route
  • "As an MP … as a judge" → 12.3, 12.4, 12.6 (two hats).
  • "sale and consumption" → split them (7.2).
  • "without exception" → worship; Art 15 as applied (11.7, 12.6).
  • "85% at least somewhat" → 7.11 (polls are not a mandate).
  • Thesis: two hats: "As an MP I would vote against and amend; as a judge I would enforce it; the answers differ because the roles ask different questions."
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Part A opening (MP)

As an MP I would vote against the bill and propose narrower measures. Its aims, protecting families and health, are legitimate, but its scope does the damage: it criminalises consumption as well as sale, and its "without exception" catches communion and temple wine. I test its three grounds in turn: faith, harm and the poll.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Part A body (three grounds × about 180 words)

Vote and alternatives: against; propose licensing, age and hours limits, treatment, and an express exemption for worship.

  1. Faith: steelman (addiction subverts practical reasonableness, Finnis); test: one faith cannot alone justify coercing others; even Devlin requires secular reasons; denying worship normally breaks reciprocity (Rawls). Verdict: a voice, not a ground.
  2. Harm: steelman (Hart accepts paternalism where consent is clouded); test: paternalism protects buyers, so it supports licensing supply, not jailing drinkers; Hart's offence ground does not reach private drinking (teetotallers). Verdict: regulate sale.
  3. Poll: steelman (majority rule treats citizens as equals); test: "somewhat" support is not Devlin's "real feeling of reprobation", and disapproval is not a mandate to criminalise (Hri Kumar). Verdict: evidence, not mandate.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Part B opening (judge)

As a judge I would enforce the Act if validly enacted. My question is no longer whether it is wise but what fidelity to it requires: validity first, then interpretation by principle and purpose, then any discretion the statute leaves, with refusal only at the Radbruch threshold, which a harsh prohibition does not reach.

✎ WORKED EXAMPLE
Part B body
  • Validity (100): passed by Parliament; consistent with Art 4.
  • Threshold (120): no broad historical consensus condemns prohibition; harsh, not intolerable (15.13).
  • How to enforce (250): an as-applied Art 15 claim for sacramental use, though Art 15(4) lacks a "necessary" test; sentencing discretion; read penal provisions strictly; candour bars Kennedy's covert courses.
  • Obligation (80): legal duty to apply; my moral disagreement goes in a judgment that denounces while applying (Kennedy's first course), not in refusal.
✍ EXAM-READY SENTENCES
Close

The answers differ because the roles ask different moral questions. The MP asks what the law should be, and finds the bill's reasons too weak for its coercion; the judge asks what fidelity to a validly enacted law requires, and finds the bill harsh but not intolerable. No role ends moral duty; each assigns a different one.

13 Across topics

13.1 Comparisons
CompareSharedSplit
LP v Rawls: pluralismBoth bracket contested morals: LP finds law in sources, Rawls legitimacy in shared political valuesNeither is neutral: acceptance is LP's test, "reasonable" Rawls's filter; Finnis: some basic rights have one right answer
Autonomy: Mill, Hart, Finnis, PepperValued and bounded by all: Mill by harm to others; Pepper's first-class citizenship serves itHart allows some paternalism; Finnis: practical reasonableness; Pepper: law alone, "not by the lawyer's morality" (626), save "extreme cases" (632)
Kennedy v chain novelBoth put the judge inside inherited materials: fit and value constrain Dworkin's; work and credibility risk, Kennedy's (559)Kennedy starts from "how-I-want-to-come-out" (518), Dworkin from the text (Liu, W11); Kennedy answers "always a right answer" with felt indeterminacy and "free ethical or political choice" (562), disclaiming a verdict (561)
Fuller v RFBoth deny enactment alone settles legality: Fuller tests form, the RF contentFuller grades by degree, an unclear statute "less a law" (MOL 63 n 21); the RF voids only "intolerable" injustice
Religious freedom: Finnis v RawlsBoth protect it, neither neutrally: Finnis as a basic good, Rawls as equal liberty of conscienceRawls takes "the truths of religion off the political agenda" (PL 151); Finnis values inquiry, "whatever the answer" (NLNR 88–89)
Whose morality (obscenity, immoral contracts)Beyond the judge's preference: Devlin's right-minded man; Hart's critical morality (Devlin too invokes a "critical principle"); NLT's objective moralityDevlin: honest belief, "right or wrong"; TSH's second "option", "not favoured in Rajeevan": judges may filter incoherent opinions (CJ 97)
Finnis v liberalismCommon good: "a set of conditions" (NLNR 155); the state's role: "only to maintain peace and justice" (Abortion 77)Not neutral: reason requires us "to favour the basic forms of good" (NLNR V.4); liberal in means, not ends
Finnis v FullerComplementary: Fuller procedure, Finnis substance (Liu, W5)Law "treats them as partners in public reason" by promulgation, clarity, generality, stability (Abortion 77–78); Finnis can condemn punitive retroactivity by its effects
Fuller v Hart on validityCompatibleFuller tests form; Hart takes what officials accept, so Ordinance 11 may pass (Liu, W10)
Hart v DevlinBoth usually spare private acts (7.3)Not fully reconciled: Devlin can punish what meets none of Hart's grounds (cruelty to animals, Devlin 17; Hart: their suffering, LLM 34) (Liu, W9)
Devlin v Rawls, FinnisShared ground; "reasonable" judgementRawls needs only enough overlap, Devlin deep agreement; Devlin's reasonable man feels, Finnis's reasons (Liu, W7)
13.2 Current controversies
  • s 377A repeal and Art 156 (2022)† s 377A went and Art 156 shielded man-woman marriage laws from Part 4, both from 3 Jan 2023. → Theory: the coercion gradient: punishment withdrawn, marriage promoted (15.7, 7.9, 11.6).
  • QUALIFY Hart's lines survive: non-consensual acts, acts with young persons and public indecency stay crimes; only private consensual adult conduct is freed (Shanmugam, 2022). Liu's exercises: 16.5.

14 Theorist bank I

14.1 Fish 'Teaching Law' (NYT 2011) · use: 2.6, 10.5, 10.8
  • PURPOSE Is theory useless to a lawyer, beyond doctrine and tactics?
  • CLAIM Practice marshals doctrine inside a purposive enterprise informed by a vision of how the state may and may not use its monopoly of legalised violence.
  • STRENGTH Searle's football: brute description misses the game; an expert's field is "already configured" by understanding what is at stake.
  • CRITIQUE The complaint Segal reports (NYT): law school, jurisprudence included, never taught the tricks of the trade → reply: the tricks "would not amount to much" without knowing "what the trade is".
  • SAY "surely a practice but it is also a subject".
  • VERDICT Fish is right that practice presupposes a view of the state's force, but he never says which view is true.
14.2 NLT and Aquinas Harris 6–20; TSH CJ 81–100 · use: 2.1, 2.3, 2.8, 8.7, 11.2
  • PURPOSE Must law meet a higher, reason-known standard to bind?
  • CLAIM Human law binds as it derives from natural law, by deduction or determination; law contrary to it is defective as law.
  • TEST Aquinas: unjust law is "a corruption of law", though obedience is owed "perhaps, in certain special cases", to avoid scandal or danger (Harris 9); Finnis: it merely lacks prima facie power "to bind in conscience" (18); TSH: manifestly unjust law "is not law" (CJ 85).
  • CRITIQUE TSH asks who may "pronounce on the content of higher law" (CJ 93) → reply: discernment, unlike fiat, must cohere and stay revisable (CJ 100).
  • VERDICT Natural law explains why some enactments fail as law, but must first settle who decides.
14.3 Austin via Harris 118–20; LE ch 1; TSH CJ 85–88 · use: 2.2, 8.7, 11.1, 12.3
  • PURPOSE What is law, as a fact, without moral premises?
  • CLAIM Law is the command of a sovereign, habitually obeyed and obeying no one, backed by a sanction.
  • STRENGTH Candour: "the existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another" (TSH CJ 85 n 36).
  • CRITIQUE Hart: habits miss the internal "ought"; power-conferring rules enable rather than require (Harris 118–20) → reply: Dworkin grants that Austin's main idea, restated by Hart, "has never wholly lost its grip on jurisprudence" (LE ch 1).
  • SG Against that sovereign is simply Parliament: Art 4 voids statutes to the extent they are inconsistent with the Constitution (TSH CJ 88; 11.1).
  • VERDICT Austin is honest that wicked law gets enforced, but habit or fear cannot explain why officials treat law as binding.
14.4 Hart: concept of law Harris 19–20, 117–23; LE ch 1; TSH CJ 86–89 · use: 2.1, 2.2, 11.1, 11.7, 12.3
  • PURPOSE Why do lawyers say "ought" if law is neither command nor morality?
  • CLAIM Law is the union of primary duty rules and secondary rules of recognition, change and adjudication, which officials accept from an internal point of view.
  • TEST A system exists when primary rules are generally obeyed and officials accept secondary rules, which cure uncertainty, rigidity and diffuse pressure (Harris 122–23); soft positivism lets the rule of recognition contingently adopt moral tests (121).
  • CRITIQUE Dworkin: many Nazi officials obeyed Hitler "only out of fear": if that is acceptance, Hart nears Austin; if not, there was "no law in Nazi Germany" (LE ch 1) → reply: acceptance even from "fear, self-interest or habit" (Harris 119) still treats rules as standards.
  • CRITIQUE TSH: only officials need accept, so Hart "may not be very different from the power view", and LP "is not necessarily democratic" (CJ 87) → reply: describing law is not praising it.
  • SAY "critical reflective attitude" (Harris 118); "the sheep may end in the slaughter-house" (Hart, TSH CJ 87 n 43).
  • TRAP Hart's "minimum content of natural law" is no legality test: men "are not members of suicide clubs", so every society needs rules against violence, theft and deceit (Harris 19), a practical necessity, unlike Radbruch's override (Liu, W10). Harris: a "'sociological' conception", consistent with "institutionalising slavery or racial oppression" (20).
  • VERDICT Hart maps a working legal system most accurately, yet deciding what the map shows is already an evaluation.
14.5 Dworkin LE ch 1; AMP 146–66 · use: 2.4, 2.5, 9.2, 9.5, 9.10
  • PURPOSE Why do judges disagree about the law, and what constrains them in hard cases?
  • CLAIM Law is interpretive: judges read the legal record by fit and political value, so law is political but never personal or partisan.
  • TEST → 15.9. A reading must "both fit that practice and show its point or value" (AMP 160); where several fit, political morality decides (161).
  • STRENGTH Explains theoretical disagreement, which the plain-fact view cannot (LE ch 1), though Liu thinks this unfair to LP (2.5).
  • CRITIQUE Realists and crits: fit leaves readings open, so value is the judge's politics → reply: Dworkin concedes fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation" (AMP 161), not that law is "personal or partisan" (146).
  • CONCEDE A judge's best reading rests on "beliefs other judges need not share" (AMP 162), and integrity gives no exit from a wicked legal history (2.4). Concede both; Radbruch guards the outer limit (14.19).
  • SG LMS (CA) invoked "a central motif" of Dworkin's theory to disregard extra-legal considerations "uniquely within the purview of the Legislature" (TSH JO 319); principle v policy is TSH's surmise (JO 320).
  • SAY "deeply and thoroughly political" (AMP 146).
  • VERDICT Dworkin best explains how principle constrains hard cases, granted that fit often cannot settle them alone.
14.6 Fuller MOL 33–94; PFL 644–57 · use: 3, 8.4, 2.4, 13.1
  • PURPOSE What separates law from naked power, and why do failures of form wrong citizens?
  • CLAIM Law is the enterprise of subjecting human conduct to the governance of rules, with an inner morality of eight desiderata.
  • TEST → 15.1. Total failure in one desideratum yields something "not properly called a legal system at all" (MOL 39); otherwise a legal system's existence is "always a matter of degree" (PFL 646).
  • STRENGTH It binds lawmakers first: the top of the chain of command "intensifies" their duty of legality (MOL 64).
  • CRITIQUE Liu's slides†: "Is it about morality at all? The label seems misapplied"; perhaps it is efficacy (W2 slide 17) → reply: legality respects responsible agents (W2 slide 17†) and grounds the duty by reciprocity (MOL 39–40; 3.3).
  • CONCEDE Legality is thin: a clear, public, prospective law can still be wicked. Concede it; let the Radbruch formula test content (13.1).
  • SAY "no greater legal monstrosity than a secret statute" (PFL 651); "no less an undertaking than being a lawgiver" (MOL 94).
  • TRAP "Not all cases are hard" (MOL 93) concerns legality, not adjudication. Fuller did not adopt the Radbruch formula; he asks "how much of a legal system survived" (PFL 646).
  • VERDICT Fuller shows legality is a genuine but modest morality binding rulers, not that it makes their laws just.
14.7 TSH: moral subjectivism Think 46 (2017) 25–36 · use: 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.5, 4.7
  • PURPOSE Is morality a matter of personal or cultural opinion, and can subjectivists argue with anyone?
  • CLAIM Subjectivists cannot hold others to any standard independent of their belief without ceasing to be subjectivists, so their moral dialogue is gravely limited.
  • TEST Does a sceptic's premise bind someone who rejects it? A relativist who binds outsiders invokes a "meta-cultural standard" (27); if it honours equal moral worth, he "is a moral realist" (28).
  • STRENGTH Genocide hypothetical: "Moral dialogue in fact breaks down" (30). If all may do as they please, "everyone becomes equally worthless" (31); concede limits and the subjectivist is "just another moral realist" (32).
  • CRITIQUE Epistemic sceptics (TSH's second kind, 26): who knows the moral facts? → reply: a legitimate variant, but a dead end for law-making; Finnis's goods offer a way forward (Liu, W3; 14.8); realism "entails a commitment to deliberation", with judgements held "more provisionally" (33).
  • CONCEDE She shows that subjectivists' moral dialogue is "gravely limited" (26), not which realist content is right: the rest is "a squabble within the family of moral realists" (35).
  • VERDICT TSH shows that a subjectivist who argues or demands must turn realist and that subjectivism's case is inconclusive, not that moral facts exist; how we know what is right is left to deliberation.
14.8 Finnis NLNR 85–96, ch V, 154–56; Abortion 75–93 · use: 5, 6.2, 6.5, 2.3, 4.4
  • PURPOSE What makes choices and laws reasonable, without deriving "ought" from nature?
  • CLAIM Seven self-evident basic goods and nine requirements of practical reasonableness yield moral norms and a common good that rules out many laws.
  • TEST → 15.3, 15.4. Requirement plus circumstances: this act ought (not) be done (NLNR V.10; W4 slide 11†).
  • STRENGTH The goods are grasped, not inferred: "there is no inference from fact to value" (NLNR 85).
  • STRENGTH The state's role is "not ... to make people integrally good but only to maintain peace and justice" (Abortion 77), on principles "accessible to all people whatever their religious beliefs" (78).
  • CRITIQUE Liu's slides† doubt self-evidence and the seventh requirement (W4 slide 13); Harris: facts about human nature creep back in (15–16) → reply: "we are not dealing with logical necessities", yet it is still reasoning (Harris 16).
  • CONCEDE Accessible is not accepted: reasonable people dispute the list and its use; concede that this limits the coercion he can justify (5.7).
  • VERDICT Finnis gives lawmakers usable limits and a facilitative state, but his self-evidence rests on contested intuitions, and Liu finds the seventh requirement artificial.
14.9 Seligman and Tierney 'We Aren't Built to Live in the Moment' (NYT 2017; summary only) · use: 5.6, 5.1
  • PURPOSE Does human nature push us by urges or pull us towards ends (Topic 4: follow nature)?
  • CLAIM Minds are built for prospection: memory and emotion serve planning, so we are pulled by ends, not pushed by the past.
  • STRENGTH Fits Finnis's first requirement: living merely "from moment to moment, following immediate cravings" is unreasonable (NLNR V.2).
  • CRITIQUE Hume and Finnis: psychology cannot ground norms (14.8) → reply: the essay shows how goods appear in experience, not that they are goods.
  • TRAP Only a summary is in the folder: paraphrase, never quote.
  • VERDICT Seligman and Tierney make Finnis's planner look true to life: an illustration, never a proof.
14.10 Rawls PL 134–58; PRR 131–48 · use: 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.11, 13.1
  • PURPOSE When is coercion legitimate among citizens who reasonably disagree about the good?
  • CLAIM Power is fully proper only under a constitution whose essentials all citizens, as free and equal, may reasonably be expected to endorse.
  • TEST → 15.5. Scope: constitutional essentials, basic justice and bordering questions, "so far as possible" (PL 137–38), in the public political forum (PRR 134). Reciprocity: offer reasons others "might also reasonably accept", not merely understand, as Servetus understood Calvin (PRR 137–38).
  • STRENGTH Not secularism: public reason is not "secular reason" (PRR 143), and the proviso admits religious argument if public reasons follow "in due course" (144).
  • CRITIQUE Finnis: the principle is "illegitimate, unreasonable, and uncivil" (Abortion 81), leaving the gravest questions to "sheer power of numbers or influence" (84) → reply: Finnis grants the reciprocity ideal "seems broadly reasonable" (85); the dispute is who is reasonable.
  • CRITIQUE TSH: unless Rawls counts heads, "reasonable" needs a standard "external to the citizens" (Religion 516) → reply: his standard is moral though political (PL 140–41), not a head-count.
  • VERDICT Rawls sets the right discipline for public argument, though deciding who counts as reasonable already takes a moral side.
14.11 TSH: religion and public reason J Law & Religion 26 (2010–11) 505–39 · use: 6.4, 6.5, 6.7
  • PURPOSE In a multi-religious democracy, may law-makers rely on religious arguments?
  • CLAIM Judge arguments by their accessibility and merit, not their religious motive; bracketing a metaphysical question already answers it.
  • CRITIQUE Rawls: using state power against reasonable dissenters is "unreasonable or worse" (PL 138) → reply: she asks only for accessible reasons; "the delineation of a political sphere is artificial" (538).
  • CONCEDE Her close: consensus on human worth "does not currently extend" to who counts as human (538); she suggests a "pragmatic strategy" of arguing from consequences (537). Concede that principle alone may not move Parliament.
  • SAY "shatters the illusion of an accommodative solution" (536).
  • VERDICT TSH exposes the unfairness of sorting arguments by motive, but not how a divided Parliament should settle contested questions.
14.12 Mill and Wolfenden via Hart LLM 13–33; Devlin ch 1; TSH Pragmatism 287 · use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.5
  • PURPOSE What may the criminal law prohibit: only harm to others, or private immorality too?
  • CLAIM Coercion is justified only to prevent harm to others; private immorality that neither harms nor offends in public is not the criminal law's concern.
  • TEST Wolfenden: preserve public order and decency, protect from the offensive or injurious, and safeguard the vulnerable against exploitation or corruption (Hart LLM 14).
  • STRENGTH In Hart's words, free choice may be "a value in itself", or valuable because it lets individuals "experiment" in living (LLM 21–22).
  • CRITIQUE Devlin: consent is no defence to murder or assault, so the law already enforces moral principle (Devlin 6–7) → reply: Hart: such rules can be paternalist, not moralist (LLM 32).
  • CRITIQUE TSH: "harm" and "self-regarding" are indeterminate, and if only legal interests count, "there appears to be circularity" (Pragmatism 287) → reply: the harm line needs moral argument, openly made.
  • SG Shanmugam (2022): Singapore's position is "broadly similar" to Wolfenden's (7.5).
  • SAY "not the law's business" (Wolfenden, via LLM 15).
  • VERDICT Mill and Wolfenden rightly make liberty the default, but cannot draw the harm line without moral argument.
14.13 Hart: Law, Liberty and Morality LLM 13–52 · use: 7.1, 7.2, 7.4, 7.9
  • PURPOSE May the criminal law enforce morality as such, beyond preventing harm to others?
  • CLAIM Coercion is prima facie objectionable and needs a countervailing good; paternalism and public decency can supply one, but bare moral condemnation cannot.
  • TEST → 15.7. (1) A question of critical morality about enforcing positive morality (LLM 20). (2) Two costs: punishing offenders and coercing those who never offend (21). (3) Paternalism where consent is defective (33). (4) Decency: punish the public act (41).
  • STRENGTH Bigamy, if punished to protect religious feelings from a public act, is punished "neither as irreligious nor as immoral but as a nuisance" (LLM 41); whether to punish turns on contestable estimates of offence against freedom lost (43).
  • CRITIQUE TSH: "a critique could be made" that paternalism is "in the ultimate analysis, based on morals" (Pragmatism 288) → reply: Hart grants that applying his grounds takes moral judgement (LLM 20); he denies only punishing immorality as such (Liu, W9).
  • VERDICT Hart wins the case against punishing private immorality as such, though moral judgment still decides where his paternalism and decency bite.
14.14 Stephen via Hart LLM 34–37, 48–49 · use: 7.8
  • PURPOSE May criminal law punish vice as such? Stephen's reply to Mill.
  • CLAIM Stephen holds what Hart calls the extreme thesis, that enforcing morality is valuable in itself; Devlin, "for most of his essay", the moderate one, a shared morality as "the cement of society" (LLM 48).
  • CRITIQUE Hart: a "non sequitur"; what to punish and how severely are "distinct and independent questions" (LLM 36) → reply: Hart still lets wickedness be "a partial determinant" of severity (37).
  • SAY "a persecution of the grosser forms of vice" (Stephen, quoted LLM 36).
  • VERDICT Stephen is a useful foil: beside his extreme thesis, Devlin's moderate one and Finnis's "peace and justice" limit look narrow.
14.15 Devlin Enforcement of Morals ch 1 · use: 7.3, 7.4, 15.6
  • PURPOSE May society enforce its shared morality by law, and how is it found?
  • CLAIM Devlin holds that society may use law to protect the shared morality that holds it together, against conduct beyond the limits of tolerance.
  • TEST → 15.6. The reasonable, not rational, man in the jury box: what any twelve people at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on; not majority opinion, not every citizen's assent; it "does not depend on the counting of heads" (15).
  • STRENGTH Consent is no defence to murder, since the offence is "against society" (6–7).
  • CRITIQUE Hart: no evidence; it merits "no more respect than the Emperor Justinian's statement" on earthquakes (LLM 50) → reply: deviation and subversion are only "capable in their nature" of threatening society (13 n); "If morality is changed, the law can be changed" (14 n); but if only "capable", why harsh sanctions now (Liu, W9)?
  • CRITIQUE TSH, for moral realists: treating secular moral judgement as "simply a feeling" (17) "comes close to" non-cognitivism (Pragmatism 289) → reply: her charitable reading, an objective "reasonable" (290), she herself finds "overly generous" (Devlin's relativism).
  • SAY "invisible bonds of common thought" (10).
  • TRAP Devlin argues as a cultural relativist (Liu, W7): monogamy binds as "built into the house in which we live" (9); honest belief, "right or wrong", makes immorality "a question of fact" (22). Privacy is only "to be taken into account" (18–19).
  • VERDICT Devlin rightly denies law's moral neutrality, but wrongly lets common feeling, not reason, fix what it enforces.
14.16 TSH: Pragmatism J Comp L 2008, 285–304 · use: 7.6, 7.7
  • PURPOSE What is criminal law for, and what did the 2007 compromise settle?
  • CLAIM TSH argues that we "simply cannot shun" the moral question (304): by 2007 the camps really clashed over what is right.
  • TEST Six functions (287–90): harm; paternalism; public decency; averting disintegration; morals as intrinsically good; moral ecology.
  • CONCEDE The map ranks no function, and her slope "based upon principle" (304) may read as advocacy; concede both, and rank functions with Hart or Finnis.
  • TRAP "Tangible harm" is TSH's summary of the retention case (298), not retentionists' words.
  • VERDICT TSH's map is the best diagnostic: it shows the moral question unavoidable without answering it.
14.17 TSH: Marriage Law Gazette, March 2023 · use: 7.9, 11.6
  • PURPOSE What did Art 156 add to the 2022 repeal of s 377A?
  • CLAIM TSH argues that repeal answered legal risk, not a finding of unconstitutionality, which would imply parity; so man–woman marriage laws stay coherent.
  • STRENGTH Art 156 shields only the man–woman definition and laws based on it, reaching marriage's "moral, social, and cultural milieu".
  • CONCEDE Shanmugam also called repeal "the right thing to do" (Hansard, 29 Nov 2022), so risk was only part of the rationale; concede that, keeping her point that Art 156 rejects parity.
  • SAY "a pre-emptive strike against judicial activism" (Marriage).
  • VERDICT The 2022 package was a deliberate split: criminal law withdrawn, marriage promoted.
14.18 Hart: separation (1958) PS 615–21 · use: 8.1, 8.2, 8.7
  • PURPOSE Should an iniquitous rule be denied the name of law, or called law and condemned?
  • CLAIM Hart separates law as it is from law as it ought to be: validity never settles whether to obey.
  • TEST If punishment needs retroactivity, choose openly "between two evils" by statute (619).
  • STRENGTH Plain speech: "law but too evil to be obeyed" is among the most powerful moral criticisms because the simplest (620).
  • CRITIQUE Fuller: positivism "never gives any coherent meaning" to fidelity to law (PFL 656); the question then seems to be "who should do the dirty work" (649) → reply: only a statute sacrifices a principle openly; the bridge to obedience is moral (PS 617; 8.7).
  • CRITIQUE Alexy: where the injustice was evident at the time, the court ascertains the law then in force: no covert retroactivity → reply: even Alexy calls candour "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall" (60–61).
  • SAY "not just one among many minor virtues" (620).
  • TRAP Bamberg voided no 1934 statute, as Hart supposed; he later conceded the error (Alexy 59–60).
  • VERDICT Hart wins on labels for observers and historians; a judge deciding today needs more than candour.
14.19 Radbruch and Alexy Alexy 40–62; PFL 656–57; PS 618 · use: 8.3, 8.4, 15.8
  • PURPOSE Does extreme injustice strip a norm of legal character, and for whom?
  • CLAIM Positive law prevails even when unjust, unless its injustice reaches an "intolerable degree" (Alexy 40–41); then, for the participant, it is not law.
  • TEST → 15.8. Participant: e.g. "the court, the lawyer, and the addressee of the law" (Topic 7 seminar); Alexy's example is the judge (41).
  • STRENGTH Every judicial decision "necessarily lays claim to correctness", which extreme injustice fails (58–59).
  • STRENGTH Liu: neither side argues truth, only desirability, and the practical case is "kind of a wash": on what basis, then, decide (W11)? Alexy: the objections were answered "at least well enough to tie the score"; the risk effect, necessity after a regime collapses and fit with nulla poena break the tie (62).
  • CRITIQUE Hart: Radbruch "only half digested the spiritual message of liberalism" (PS 618) → reply: Fuller credits him with seeing the dilemma as order against "good order" (PFL 657).
  • CONCEDE Answering relativism needs "a rational justification for at least some minimum moral requirements" (62). Concede the formula is only as sound as that core; TSH's BHC (14.26) disciplines judges but is evidence, not proof.
  • SAY "both jurist and the people defenceless" (Alexy 44–45).
  • TRAP Radbruch did not oppose denying legal quality; he warned of its "frightful dangers" (PFL 656), and for the informers he too preferred a retroactive statute (655). "Not law" at tier 2 (8.8) is Alexy's reading (40); BHC is TSH's test, not Alexy's.
  • VERDICT The formula earns its place as a narrow backstop, if its minimum core can be defended without counting votes.
14.20 ALR Harris 98–103; W11 slides · use: 9.1, 10.2
  • PURPOSE Do rules decide cases, or officials and the facts they find?
  • CLAIM Realists treat law as a prediction of what officials do: rules leave leeways, and fact-finding steers outcomes.
  • STRENGTH Harris reports Llewellyn: a lawyer steeped in a court's "folkways" could predict most outcomes (9.9).
  • CRITIQUE Thunder: judges are not "predicting" their own behaviour (322) → reply: realism is "a method nothing more" (Llewellyn, Harris 103).
  • SG Cheng San GRC†: does "within a radius of 200 metres" reach a candidate inside the station? The AG said no (9.1).
  • VERDICT Realism is right about leeways and wrong about rules: predictability itself comes from a shared craft.
14.21 CLS and Unger Harris 108–13; Unger 58–75 · use: 9.3, 9.7
  • PURPOSE Is doctrine coherent principle, or a truce between contradictory ideals?
  • CLAIM Crits say doctrine can be argued either way and legitimates hierarchy; Unger finds counterprinciples that may reorganise a whole field.
  • TEST Freedom to contract v community; freedom of contract v fairness (duress, undue influence, frustration†); deviationist doctrine aims "to transform the deviant into the dominant" (Unger 60).
  • CRITIQUE Harris: "there could be no such thing as a crit judge" in today's courts → reply: "So much the worse, a crit might say, for our existing institutions" (113).
  • VERDICT The crits expose real contradictions, but exposure alone cannot tell a judge which side justice favours.
14.22 Kennedy Freedom and Constraint in Adjudication 518–62 · use: 12.4, 15.10, 13.1
  • PURPOSE What is judging like when law and the judge's sense of justice conflict?
  • CLAIM Kennedy's judge is neither simply bound nor free: law is a medium that constrains, but what it rules out depends on the judge's project (526).
  • TEST Strikers' lie-in: the rule first "just applies itself" (520); the judge then works it toward "how-I-want-to-come-out", paying in time and "legitimacy cost" (528).
  • STRENGTH Legality requires building the best case for the other side; what would betray it is "the wrong attitude at the end" (523). Sometimes the rule is "a felt objectivity" he "can't budge" (560–61).
  • CRITIQUE Hart, against rule sceptics: rules have a "core of central meaning" (PS 615) → reply: how much of a field is open, in itself, is "simply unanswerable" (548).
  • SAY "free to deploy work in any direction" (522); "the field is me, resisting myself" (551).
  • TRAP Five courses, never three: 15.10, 12.4. Against "always a right answer" he sets experience of "free ethical or political choice" (562), not a thesis.
  • VERDICT Kennedy describes judging more honestly than he justifies it: he shows the choice is moral, then leaves it "for another time" (559).
14.23 Pepper The Lawyer's Amoral Ethical Role 613–35 · use: 10.1, 10.3, 15.11
  • PURPOSE May a lawyer help a client do lawful things the lawyer thinks immoral?
  • CLAIM Pepper argues that lawful help is morally justified because access to law serves autonomy and equality; the client, not the lawyer, is accountable.
  • TEST → 15.11. Law is "a public good available to all"; autonomy is "a moral good" (616); access needs lawyers, so screening means "rule by an oligarchy of lawyers" (617).
  • STRENGTH Equality: screening would "compound inequality upon inequality" (620); if conduct is bad enough, "it would seem that it ought to be made explicitly unlawful" (618).
  • CRITIQUE Pepper's own problem: realism plus the amoral role leaves "no moral input or constraint" (626) → reply: dialogue, choice of client, and conscientious objection "rarely exercised" (633).
  • CRITIQUE Liu† (W12 slide 5): why is an institutional wrong more acceptable than a personal one, and is the institution justified? → reply: first-class citizenship justifies it (616–20).
  • SAY "Morality comes through the door as part of the client" (627); "not comfortable, but good" (635).
  • VERDICT Pepper justifies access to law, not every service: his own exceptions leave the lawyer a conscience the role cannot silence.
14.24 Thunder Can a Good Person Be a Lawyer? 313–34 · use: 10.4, 10.10, 12.5
  • PURPOSE Can a good person be a lawyer without splitting professional from personal ethics?
  • CLAIM Thunder holds that a lawyer's role is justified only by its contribution to justice and flourishing, so the good lawyer stays a good person.
  • TEST Natural-teleological view: law is "intended ultimately (though not always immediately)" for natural goods such as justice (314 n 4); the lawyer's function is "to further justice, public order, and the rule of law" (323).
  • STRENGTH Diagnosis: the amoral view draws its appeal from "unlikely and unwitting collaborators", neo-Kantian rule-morality and legal realism (318).
  • CRITIQUE Pepper: screening means "rule by an oligarchy of lawyers" (617) → reply: access to law is not access unchecked by others' judgment; projects are properly "hampered" (317).
  • CONCEDE Thunder admits "substantial disagreement on particular cases" (329) and that integrity is "rarely, if ever, fully achieved" (334). Concede he guides character more than cases; settle hard cases by dialogue, with refusal only at the extremes (10).
  • SAY "the slaves of their clients' consciences, however warped" (317).
  • TRAP Thunder's "just focus on the law" (316) voices the amoral view he rejects, as does the practice question's "Just focus on doing your job".
  • VERDICT Thunder says better than Pepper what lawyers are for, but virtue names the goal without deciding the hard case.
14.25 TSH: Constitutional Jurisprudence CJ 79–113 · use: 11.1, 11.7, 12.1
  • PURPOSE Does a written, supreme Constitution make Singapore positivist?
  • CLAIM TSH argues that the natural law–positivism debate "can never be settled" by "any declaration of supremacy" (89): contested terms force a choice of school, and "constitutionalism is an affirmation of a higher law" (102).
  • TEST Two levels (80): a contested term's conception ("law", "life", "personal liberty" in Art 9(1)); the import of Art 4's supremacy clause.
  • CONCEDE Who rightfully decides? George: in a "basically just regime" judges respect their limits (95); TSH admits "no available formula" (113). Concede the impasse: consensus "may be the best gauge" of morality, not its ground (96).
  • VERDICT TSH shows the Constitution relocates the natural law–positivism debate rather than ending it, leaving the authority question open.
14.26 TSH: Judicial Oligarchy SJLS 2016, 307–35 · use: 11.3, 11.5, 15.13
  • PURPOSE How far may courts strike down laws on moral grounds?
  • CLAIM TSH argues that courts should presume legislation constitutional unless Radbruch's threshold of injustice is met, shown by broad historical consensus.
  • TEST → 15.13. Judges show the higher law "by reference to broad historical consensus" (330): racial genocide, slavery; peremptory norms as evidence only.
  • STRENGTH The alternatives are worse: a lower threshold invites judicial "temerity", and positivism leaves "a brute majority" unchecked (333).
  • CRITIQUE TSH's own objection: the RF is not in the Constitution the nation accepted (333) → reply: constitutionalism rests on equal moral worth, so majority vote "must not sanction" its violation, even by amendment (334).
  • CONCEDE Her "catch" (331–32): a lasting worldwide trend could, decades on, override a legislature trying to do right. Concede the risk; her reply: 8.5.
  • SG LMS (CA) rightly avoided a juristocracy but was "overly sanguine" about future Parliaments (334).
  • TRAP Presumed constitutional, not presumed just (JO 329).
  • VERDICT TSH's threshold is the most defensible test for Singapore judges, once her own catch is conceded.
