14.28 Cross-examination lines
  • Hart to Devlin: why preserve a persecuting society whose "disintegration" might be "morally better than its continued existence" (LLM 19)?
  • Fuller to Hart: if positivism gives fidelity no coherent meaning, what does a judge owe a secret or retroactive Nazi statute (PFL 650–51, 656)?
  • TSH to Alexy: if consensus nearly refutes relativism, what may a judge do once it goes "dreadfully wrong" while a legislature "purports to do right locally" (JO 332)?
  • Finnis to Rawls: if public reason brackets moral truth, are the gravest questions not left to "the status quo established by sheer power of numbers" (Abortion 84)?
  • Kennedy to Dworkin: when fit runs out and value is contested, is the chain novelist's best reading more than "free ethical or political choice" (Kennedy 562)?
  • Pepper to Thunder: if each lawyer screens by his own virtue, what prevents "rule by an oligarchy of lawyers" (Pepper 617)?

15 Frameworks

15.1 Fuller: legality checklist key question: can people follow this rule as made and applied? · use: 3.1
  • Desiderata (MOL 39): (1) general? (2) promulgated? (3) prospective? (4) clear? (5) consistent? (6) possible? (7) constant? (8) congruent with official action?
  • Verdict rule: total failure of one yields something "not properly called a legal system at all" (39); short of that, legality is a matter of degree, not substantive justice (15.13).
  • Rex (MOL 33–38): (1) case-by-case rulings; (2) a secret code; (3) rulings with hindsight; (4) an obscure code; (5) contradictions; (6) impossible demands; (7) constant amendment; (8) rulings unrelated to the code: no law at all.
  • TRAP (1) means rules at all, not breadth: palm-tree justice, attainder and unfettered discretion fail it; (2) needs access, not universal knowledge; (3) bars only abuse (Liu, W2).
15.2 Is–ought repair key question: which unstated ought-premise yields this conclusion? · use: 4.4
  • (0) Liu's method: list the premises a neutral listener must accept, mark the moral ones, hidden ones too, and defend each; the dispute shrinks to a bedrock premise (W3). (1) Split facts (is) from conclusion (ought): no ought follows from is alone (Hume, in Harris 12–13). (2) Supply the missing major premise; agreed on it, the parties "can go on to deduce ought-conclusions" (13).
  • (3) Test that premise: self-evident on reflection (Finnis, in Harris 14), or mere preference? Verdict rule: argue about the premise, not the inference.
15.3 Finnis: is this act permissible? key question: does it choose directly against a basic good? · use: 5.3
  • (1) Which basic good is pursued (Harris 15)? (2) Is a basic good damaged as end or means? Then wrong: "Do not choose directly against a basic value" (NLNR V.7).
  • (3) Side effects must pass the golden rule: "would I ... have thought the act reasonable had I been the person harmed?" (V.7). Verdict rule: intended damage, never; side effects, only if fair.
  • Liu's rulings (W5): barred: the hostage (even a volunteer), the footbridge push, self-injury for insurance, the death penalty ("even if it's Hitler"), euthanasia, suicide; permitted or arguable: the trolley switch, triage, a lung-damaging mining job, shooting to disarm with death foreseen. (6) weighs; (7) vetoes.
15.4 Finnis: may the state legislate this? key question: does it serve the common good, intending no harm? · use: 5.5
  • (0) Two uses (Liu, W5; W4 slide 11†): judge laws directly (authorising an act against a good is wrong: for Finnis, the death penalty and abortion) and judge facilitation; coordination counts (one side of the road); requirement (3) bars arbitrary distinctions between citizens. (1) Aim: "peace and justice", not making people "integrally good" (Abortion 77). (2) Means: never intend damage to a good; may prohibit acts that intend it (W4 slide 12†).
  • (3) Reasons "accessible to all people whatever their religious beliefs" (77–78). (4) Prudence: non-enforcement can be reasonable, to avoid "a war that one cannot win" (84). Verdict rule: prohibit intended harm on accessible reasons, where prudent.
15.5 Rawls: is this law legitimate? key question: could every reasonable citizen endorse the reasons? · use: 6.1
  • (1) Constitutional essential or basic justice? (2) Public-forum actor, including citizens voting "as if they were legislators" (PRR 134–35)? (3) Political values, or comprehensive reasons backed by public ones "in due course" (proviso, 144)?
  • (4) Reciprocity: acceptable to others as free and equal, "not as dominated or manipulated" (136–37)? Denying basic liberties "normally" fails (138). Verdict rule: legitimate if (3) and (4) hold.
  • Completeness: no argument "too immediate and fragmentary" from doctrine to policy (PRR 144–46); not political values: moral autonomy, moral desert, monogamy "as such" (146–47).
15.6 Devlin: the interrogatories key question: is it beyond the limits of tolerance? · use: 7.3
  • (1) May society judge morals? (2) May law enforce that judgment? (3) Always, or on what principles (Devlin 7–8)? (4) Not "the counting of heads": ask what twelve at random "might after discussion be expected to be unanimous" on (15).
  • (5) Elastic principles: "maximum individual freedom that is consistent with the integrity of society"; "a real feeling of reprobation" (16–17). Verdict rule: a majority's dislike is "not nearly enough" (17).
  • (6) A vice "so abominable that its mere presence is an offence" may be eradicated; one tolerable if confined calls for a balance (17). Law sets "the minimum and not ... the maximum" (19).
15.7 Hart: may the criminal law prohibit it? (and the coercion gradient) key question: what justifies this coercion, besides immorality as such? · use: 7.9
  • Coercion is "prima facie objectionable" (LLM 20). (1) Harm to others? Distress at "the bare knowledge" of others' conduct does not count (46–47). (2) Paternalism, if consent is defective: punishing drug supply "except under medical prescription" (32–33).
  • (3) Public decency: offence "serious and likely", weighed against the freedom lost (42–43). (4) Moralism alone: never. Verdict rule (mine, on Liu's map: all law rests on force, criminal law most directly, W9): the more coercive the measure (punish, regulate, promote), the stronger the reason needed; Hart's own question is punishment only.
15.8 Alexy: should a judge deny it legal character? key question: is the injustice extreme, to a participant? · use: 8.3
  • (1) Take the participant's view (say, a judge), not the observer's; (2) weak thesis: legal character is lost only at an "intolerable degree" of injustice (Alexy 40–41).
  • Concede: definitions "cannot, as such, change reality" (48–49); candour is "the strongest argument against" non-positivism, "but not its downfall" (60–61). Verdict rule: deny legal character only where the injustice was evident when done: no covert retroactivity.
15.9 Dworkin: fit, then value key question: which principle best fits and justifies the legal history? · use: 9.2
  • (1) List rival principles (AMP). (2) Fit: "interpret the legal history he finds, not to invent a better history".
  • (3) Value: choose what "states a sounder principle of justice" (AMP). Verdict rule: concede that fit "will often fail to produce a unique interpretation"; state the political morality openly.
15.10 Kennedy: the five courses key question: law and how-I-want-to-come-out conflict: what may the judge do? · use: 12.4, 8.7
  • (1) Go along, denouncing the law; (2) withdraw, leaving "the dirty work" to another; (3) decide openly on what the law should be; (4) use an implausible legal argument; (5) find facts known to be false, "obviously an extreme measure" (558–59).
  • Verdict rule: Kennedy endorses or excludes none "a priori" (559). Mine: in a basically just system, (1) or (2); (3) only at the Radbruch threshold; (4) and (5) fail candour (12.4).
15.11 Pepper: the limit and the remedies key question: lawful but wrong: what may the lawyer do? · use: 10.1
  • (1) Law is the limit: conduct bad enough, it would seem, "ought to be made explicitly unlawful" (Pepper 618). (2) Responses to legal realism (628–33): more enforcement ("daunting") or rebuilt moral authority beyond law; for lawyers, not policeman, judge or deceiver, but moral dialogue, costly and needing a receptive client.
  • (3) Conscientious objection, "rarely exercised" (633). Verdict rule: advise on the law, add moral dialogue, object only in extreme cases.
  • Liu (S13): leaving practice is "a pretty weak kind of answer"; choice of client is "more respectable", but assumes someone else will act, which fails if a view is widespread or only the lowest-scruple lawyers remain; Pepper concedes "second-class citizenship" (634).
15.12 Liu's three lawyering scenarios† key question: where is the injustice: system, rule or outcome? · use: 10.11
  • (1) Is the system by and large just? (2) If so, is this rule intolerably unjust? (3) If the rule is just, is only this outcome unjust (a coerced confession excluded: W12 slide 9)?
  • Thunder (W12 slide 8†: the good life over the role; question roles; courage and moderation; personal and professional excellence interdependent): does it serve "justice, public order, and rule of law" (330)? Does it need courage against "pressure to conform", or moderation short of "avoidable injustice" (332–33)?
  • Verdict rule (mine): in (3) defend fully; in (2) refuse, or argue the formula; in (1) the role gives no shelter.
15.13 TSH: should a court strike it down? (RF plus BHC) key question: is it manifestly unjust by broad historical consensus? · use: 11.5, 12.4
  • (1) Presume constitutionality "unless the threshold of injustice in Radbruch's formula is met" (TSH JO 329). (2) Proof: long-lasting consensus across many jurisdictions, on the same reason (317 n 72).
  • (3) Met (genocide, slavery): strike down, even an amendment (330, 333–34); not met (Roe): legislatures decide (330–31).
  • Her "catch": a world trend might carry the formula decades on; consensus can go "dreadfully wrong" (331–32). Verdict rule: courts only; legislators need no such consensus (n 72).
15.14 Who decides? key question: who rightfully decides: is anyone usurping or abdicating? · use: 12.1
  • (1) Positive law allocates authority (determinatio); in a basically just regime, "judicial usurpations ... even in what judges take to be good causes, are themselves unjust" (George, in CJ 95).
  • (2) But "who rightfully decides" whether it was prudent? An impasse (CJ 96).
  • (3) A whipped Parliament may not reflect consensus (6.8); courts may be exhorted to uphold higher law "rather than playing politics" (97). Verdict rule: honour the allocation; depart only at the Radbruch threshold (15.13).

16.3 Hansard: who said what
  • Ho Peng Kee, 22 Oct 2007: feedback "emotional, divided", majority "calling for its retention"; police not "proactively enforcing".
  • de Souza, 22 Oct 2007: "what is in private will not remain private".
  • Siew Kum Hong, 22 Oct 2007: s 377A breaches Art 12(1); citing Hor, harm must be "recognisable and tangible".
  • Indranee Rajah, 22 Oct 2007: in most cases, "we would go with the majority view, unless there is a reason to protect the minority position".
  • Thio Li-ann, 22 Oct 2007: harm "can be both physical and intangible".
  • Hri Kumar Nair, 22 Oct 2007: toothless laws "hurt our credibility".
  • PM Lee, 23 Oct 2007 (paraphrase): keep the status quo; stay a step behind on moral change.
  • Shanmugam, 28 Nov 2022: crime "generally" needs "a public order or public interest issue", "broadly similar" to Wolfenden.
  • Perera, 28 Nov 2022: unenforced law "based on the word of the government of the day, is unsatisfactory and dangerous".
  • Pritam Singh, 28 Nov 2022: "In any secular society, sin and crime are separate categories."
  • Masagos, 29 Nov 2022: Art 156 is meant to prevent a "change in social norms following the repeal"; MPs have a "duty" to "come to a decision".
  • Poa, 29 Nov 2022: a PSP referendum, as marriage "is a matter of social norm".
  • He Ting Ru, 29 Nov 2022: a law "plainly and obviously discriminatory" "sends a signal" that an "identity should be considered criminal, even if it is only on paper".

Termination of Pregnancy Act (as TSH described it, 2010–11)to 24 weeks for any reason, from 16 weeks only by a qualified practitioner; later only to save life or prevent grave permanent injury; counselling, then 48 hours; 1969 Act 32–10 on a free vote; 1974 left the choice to the woman: "one of the most liberal in the world" (Religion 507, 518–21)
  • Professional conduct (Liu, S13): Pepper's limit includes the enforced conduct rules (fairness to unrepresented persons, not misleading the court, disclosing adverse authority), so the more robust they are, the less Pepper v Thunder changes what a lawyer does.
16.5 Applying the theorists: the 2022 package, Liu's prompts
  • Liu's exercise (W6, W9): Mill: not enough, a safeguard kept because the majority wasn't ready. Finnis: likely approves (common good; life, incl. procreation; Art 156 promotes); "arbitrary" depends on your premises.
  • Rawls, on balance, approves: consultation was the background culture; consensus reached "not criminal", not full equality; Art 156 stops courts outrunning it, and sending a divisive question to Parliament, not unelected judges, is a public reason. Against: Rawls's exemplar of public reason is the Supreme Court (Liu, W9).
  • Week 5b prompts†: apply Rawls and Finnis to surrogacy, casino gambling, POFMA and euthanasia (W5b slide 9). → 15.4 (POFMA: 5.5), 15.5, 6.4, 5.7 (casinos); surrogacy: UKM (16.2); euthanasia: Hart's "clouded" consent (LLM 32–33); for Finnis, intending death chooses against life (NLNR V.7).

Glossary: people, terms and abbreviations

1The people

NameWho, in one lineMain lesson
Nicholas LiuYour lecturer (AY2026–27). His views are cited "(Liu, Wn)".All
Tan Seow Hon (TSH)Singapore natural lawyer; four of her articles are set readings (moral subjectivism; religion and public reason; pragmatism and s 377A; the Constitution and judicial oligarchy).4, 6, 7, 11, 12
Thomas AquinasMedieval natural lawyer: an unjust law is "a corruption of law". Four kinds of law: eternal, divine, natural, human.2, 8
John AustinClassical positivist: law is the command of a sovereign, habitually obeyed, backed by a sanction.2
HLA HartLeading 20th-century positivist. Law is a union of primary and secondary rules accepted by officials. Also the liberal side of the Hart–Devlin debate.2, 7, 8
Lon FullerLaw's "inner morality": eight requirements of legality (generality, promulgation, prospectivity, clarity, consistency, possibility, constancy, congruence). Debated Hart in 1958.3, 8
Ronald DworkinLaw as interpretation: judges read the legal record by fit and value. Theoretical v empirical disagreement; the chain novel.2, 9
David HumeSceptic: morality rests on sentiment; no "ought" from an "is".4
John FinnisNew natural lawyer: seven basic goods, nine requirements of practical reasonableness, the common good as a framework.5, 6
John RawlsPolitical liberalism: legitimacy, public reason, overlapping consensus, reciprocity.6
John Stuart MillThe harm principle: power may be used against someone only to prevent harm to others.7
Wolfenden Committee1957 English report: private consensual homosexual acts between adults should not be crimes.7
Patrick DevlinSociety may protect its shared morality by law; the "man in the jury box".7
James Fitzjames StephenVictorian judge: law may punish "the grosser forms of vice" as such.7
Gustav RadbruchGerman jurist: the Radbruch formula (intolerably unjust law is not law).8
Robert AlexyModern defender of the Radbruch formula; the participant's perspective.8
American Legal Realists (ALR)Llewellyn, Frank and others: law is what courts will do; rules leave leeways.9
Critical Legal Studies (CLS)Unger, Kennedy: doctrine is contradictory and legitimates hierarchy.9
Roberto UngerCLS: every principle meets a counterprinciple.9
Duncan KennedyCLS: law is a "medium" that constrains relative to the judge's project; five courses when law and justice conflict.9, 12
Stephen PepperThe lawyer's "amoral ethical role": access to law serves autonomy and equality.10
David ThunderA good lawyer stays a good person: the role serves justice and human flourishing.10
Stanley FishPractice marshals rules inside a purposive enterprise; theory is not a luxury.2
Robert GeorgeNatural lawyer whom TSH reports: in a basically just regime officials respect the limits of their authority.12

2The key terms

TermPlain meaning
Legal positivism (LP)Law is a matter of social fact (what is enacted and recognised). There is no necessary connection between law and morality.
Natural law theory (NLT)Law is answerable to a higher, reason-known standard; a sufficiently unjust "law" is defective as law.
Strong v weak NLTStrong: every rule must embody morality to be law. Weak: legal status is lost only at extreme injustice.
Rule of recognitionHart's master rule that officials accept, telling them what counts as law.
Internal point of viewTreating a rule as a standard you ought to follow, not merely a habit or a threat.
Theoretical v empirical disagreementDworkin: disagreement about what the grounds of law are, as against whether agreed grounds are met.
Inner morality of lawFuller's eight requirements of legality.
Moral realismThere are moral truths independent of what anyone believes.
Subjectivism / relativism / non-cognitivismMorality is personal opinion / varies by culture / is mere feeling, neither true nor false.
Is–ought gapHume: no moral conclusion follows from facts alone.
Basic goodsFinnis's seven: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability, practical reasonableness, "religion".
Practical reasonablenessFinnis's nine requirements for pursuing the goods well.
Double effectIntending harm as a means differs from causing it as a foreseen side effect.
Common goodFinnis: "a set of conditions" letting members pursue their own reasonable objectives.
Public reasonRawls: on basic questions, justify coercion by reasons all reasonable citizens could accept.
Overlapping consensus (OC)Reasonable doctrines each endorsing the same political conception, for their own reasons.
Modus vivendiA truce based on the balance of power, which collapses if power shifts.
Harm principleMill: coercion only to prevent harm to others.
Legal paternalismCoercion to protect people from themselves (Hart: where consent is defective).
Legal moralismCoercion to enforce morality as such.
Positive v critical moralityThe morality a society actually holds v the principles used to criticise it.
Disintegration thesisDevlin: loss of shared morality threatens society, so society may protect it.
Radbruch formula (RF)Positive law prevails even when unjust, unless its injustice is intolerable; then it must yield.
Observer v participantAlexy: an observer reports what is treated as law; a participant (a judge) asks what the right legal answer is.
Broad historical consensus (BHC)TSH's test for when injustice is "intolerable": long-lasting consensus across many jurisdictions.
Fit and valueDworkin: the best reading fits the legal record and shows it in its best moral light.
Principle v policyRights-based arguments (for courts) v collective-goal arguments (for legislatures).
Chain novelDworkin's image: each judge writes the next chapter of a novel others began.
Amoral ethical rolePepper: the lawyer is morally justified in helping with any lawful end.
Conscientious objectionPepper's rare exception: a lawyer may refuse in extreme cases.
DeterminatioA prudent choice among morally acceptable options (George's term for allocating authority).
Usurpation v abdicationDoing another role's work v refusing your own role's work.
Art 4, 9, 12, 156Singapore Constitution: supremacy; life and liberty "in accordance with law"; equality; marriage (added 2022).
s 377APenal Code offence for gross indecency between men; kept but not enforced from 2007; repealed from 3 Jan 2023.
